0 · How to Use This Guide

This guide is organized as a sequence of chapters and short subtopics that build from fundamentals through research, design, and testing. Skim it once to see the landscape, then return to individual sections as reference while you work. Each subtopic names concrete principles and practices so you can apply the material immediately to real projects. Bookmark the sections you need and revisit them whenever you face a related design problem.

0.1 What UI/UX actually means0.2 The double diamond (your default process)0.3 Method vs mindset

Welcome to a complete self-paced UI/UX design curriculum — written the way an actual university would teach it, from total beginner to professional. Use the left sidebar to navigate; every chapter is a topic, every nested item is a skill. Your theme and last position are remembered, and nothing on this page requires the internet.

0.1 What UI/UX actually means

UX, user experience, covers the entire end-to-end journey a person has with a product, including research, information architecture, usability, and content. UI, user interface, is the visible layer of screens, controls, typography, and color that people actually see and touch. The two work together: a beautiful UI cannot rescue a broken UX, and great UX goes unnoticed without a clear UI. Knowing the split helps you diagnose whether a problem is structural or visual.

TermWhat it isAsks
UX (User Experience)How a person feels and performs using a product end-to-endIs it useful, usable, findable, desirable, accessible, trustworthy, valuable?
UI (User Interface)The concrete screens, controls and pixels the user touchesIs it clear, consistent, beautiful, legible, responsive?
Interaction design (IxD)What happens when a user does somethingDoes it respond, communicate state, and recover from errors?

The split is a diagnostic, not a definition

The most useful thing about the UX/UI distinction is not the terminology; it is that it tells you where to look when something is wrong. If people cannot find the thing they came for, cannot understand what the product offers, or give up halfway through, that is a UX problem — the structure, the flow, the information architecture — and no amount of visual refinement reaches it. If people find it, understand it, and then cannot tell which of two similar buttons is the one they want, that is a UI problem — and it is fixable in a day. Teams frequently spend weeks on the second because the second is comfortable, and the visible work feels like progress.

Interaction design is the third term and the one most often collapsed into UI, which loses something specific. UI is what is on screen; interaction design is what happens when somebody does something — the response, the state transition, the recovery from an error, the moment the system tells them their attempt failed. It is invisible in a static design and it is most of what a person actually judges a product on, because a screen that looks correct and responds in a confusing way feels broken even though nothing looks wrong. A screenshot review cannot see any of it, which is why a review of static frames routinely approves flows that do not work.

Then the layers beyond the screen, which are part of UX and are usually unowned: onboarding, the empty first run, the upgrade prompt, the cancellation flow, the billing page, the support handoff, the email that tells them what happened. Most of these are built by whoever had the least context available, and they are frequently where the trust in a product is decided, because they are the moments with stakes rather than the moments being shown in a portfolio. Nobody puts a cancellation flow in a case study, and the cancellation flow is where a great many people discover what a company thinks of them.

A working rule for the diagnosis: ask where the user gave up, not where they complained. Complaints come from people who completed a task and were unhappy, which is a narrower and generally more tractable population than the people who left silently, and it is the population whose feedback arrives most readily. So instrument the abandonment point first, then talk to people at that point, and only then open a design file. Reversing that order — designing, then asking whether it worked — produces a great deal of work that answers a question nobody asked.

/* The triage table. Start from the symptom the user had, because that is the
   only thing that is observable, and end at the layer that owns the cause. */
const TRIAGE = [
  { symptom: 'they cannot find the feature they came for',        layer: 'UX  - findability and information architecture',
    typicalCause: 'no navigation entry, or one labelled in internal vocabulary', owner: 'product + design' },
  { symptom: 'they give up partway through a task',                layer: 'UX  - the flow, or the effort it demands',
    typicalCause: 'a step that exists for the system rather than for the user', owner: 'product' },
  { symptom: 'they do not understand what the product offers',      layer: 'UX  - positioning and onboarding',
    typicalCause: 'a first run that lists features instead of proving one', owner: 'design + content' },
  { symptom: 'they complete the task but were unhappy with it',     layer: 'UI  - clarity, hierarchy, tone',
    typicalCause: 'two controls of equal weight, or error text that blames the user', owner: 'design' },
  { symptom: 'they cannot tell which control is which',            layer: 'UI  - affordance and labelling',
    typicalCause: 'an icon used where a word was needed', owner: 'design' },
  { symptom: 'the screen looks right and the flow still feels wrong', layer: 'IxD - response, state, recovery',
    typicalCause: 'no designed response to the action; the error path was never drawn', owner: 'design + engineering' },
  { symptom: 'they trust it up to the payment and not after',      layer: 'beyond the screen - billing, cancellation, support',
    typicalCause: 'the highest-stakes moments are owned by whoever had least context', owner: 'unowned - which is the finding' },
];

/* Which layer owns the cause, not which layer is easiest to change. The
   mistake teams make is optimising the layer that is comfortable. */
function diagnose(symptom) {
  const row = TRIAGE.find((t) => symptom.includes(t.symptom.slice(0, 18)));
  return row ? { layer: row.layer, cause: row.typicalCause, owner: row.owner,
                 note: 'visual work does not reach this, and the reverse is also true' }
             : { layer: 'unknown', action: 'instrument the abandonment point before opening a design file' };
}

/* The order that produces answers rather than opinions. Each step is cheap
   and each one narrows the space the next one has to search. */
const SEQUENCE = [
  'instrument: where did they actually stop (silent leavers, not complainers)',
  'observe: ten replays or sessions at that point, tagged',
  'ask: five moderated sessions there, and count the questions they ask',
  'read: the spec for that step, including the states that were not designed',
  'then, and only then, open a design file',
];
// reverse it and the file is full of work answering a question nobody asked

Who owns each layer, and what happens at the seams

The layers have different owners, and most of the trouble in a product comes from the seams between them rather than from any layer being badly done. Research and definition sit with product and design; the interface sits with design and engineering; the response — what happens when somebody does something — sits with engineering and is usually designed by neither, which is why it is the layer with the least specification and the most impact. Beyond the screen, the moments with the highest stakes and the least design attention: billing, cancellation, the failed payment, the email. Write the ownership down explicitly for each screen your product has, because the untested assumption is that somebody is looking after them.

The seams worth naming. Between research and definition: a team that has collected a great deal of observation and cannot name the problem. Between definition and interface: a statement that already contains the solution, which makes the design phase a transcription exercise and the research phase decorative. Between interface and response: a screen that has been drawn and built perfectly and has no designed answer to the failure, so the failure path was written by whoever implemented it. And beyond the screen: a cancellation flow built from a template because nobody wanted to own it, which is the single most common place a product's values are revealed.

Content is a layer of its own and it is routinely unowned, which is why so many products ship interfaces with sentences nobody would say. The words are the interface: a button label is a decision about what the system does, an error message is the most-read screen in the product, and an empty state is where the product's tone is set. A product can have impeccable typography and still be unusable because the labels are internal vocabulary, and no amount of visual refinement reaches that. The practical instruction is to get a content decision into the same review as a visual decision, because they are the same decision about the same screen.

The review that matches the diagnosis is the one that covers a whole flow rather than a set of screens, and it is much harder to do because it is slower and it needs people who own different layers in the room. A screen review finds inconsistencies. A flow review finds the seam problems: the step where the label changes meaning, the state nobody designed, the moment the user is told something has happened without being told what, the screen that requires a decision the previous screen did not give enough information to make. Those are the defects that make a product feel subtly wrong while every individual screen looks correct, and they are invisible to a screen-by-screen review by construction.

/* Ownership per layer, with the seam failures that occur where ownership
   changes hands. The untested assumption is always that somebody is looking
   after the untitled rows. */
const LAYERS = {
  research:   { owner: 'product + design', artefact: 'observations, not conclusions',
                seam: 'lots of observation, no named problem' },
  definition: { owner: 'product',           artefact: 'a problem statement',
                seam: 'a statement that already contains the solution' },
  interface:  { owner: 'design + engineering', artefact: 'the screens',
                seam: 'a statement that makes this phase transcription' },
  response:   { owner: 'engineering, designed by neither', artefact: 'state transitions and error recovery',
                seam: 'the failure path written by whoever implemented it',
                why: 'this layer has the least specification and the most impact' },
  content:    { owner: 'nobody, usually',   artefact: 'labels, errors, empty states',
                seam: 'the most-read screen in the product is written by an implementer',
                why: 'a button label is a decision about what the system does' },
  beyond:     { owner: 'whoever had least context', artefact: 'billing, cancellation, failed payment, email',
                seam: 'a cancellation flow built from a template',
                why: 'the highest-stakes moments are the least designed' },
};

/* A flow review, not a screen review. Screen review finds inconsistencies;
   this finds the seam problems that make a product feel subtly wrong while
   every individual screen looks correct. */
const FLOW_REVIEW = [
  { moment: 'the entry point',          ask: 'does the user have enough information to choose what they came for?' },
  { moment: 'the first irreversible step', ask: 'is the cost of being wrong stated before it, in the same view?' },
  { moment: 'every transition',         ask: 'does the interface say what happened, and where to go next?' },
  { moment: 'every failure',            ask: 'is there a designed response that names the condition and a next action?' },
  { moment: 'any step with a decision', ask: 'did the previous step supply the information this decision requires?' },
  { moment: 'the labels across steps',  ask: 'does a term mean the same thing in two places?' },
  { moment: 'the exit',                 ask: 'is leaving as easy as arriving, and is the refund position stated once?' },
];

/* Content decisions belong in the same review as visual decisions, because
   they are the same decision about the same screen. */
const CONTENT_IS_INTERFACE = [
  { artefact: 'button label', decides: 'what the system does', test: 'would you say this sentence out loud?' },
  { artefact: 'error message', decides: 'what the user believes happened', note: 'the most-read screen in the product' },
  { artefact: 'empty state', decides: 'the product\'s tone on its first real screen' },
  { artefact: 'the label that names a plan', decides: 'what is being sold', note: 'internal vocabulary is the usual failure' },
];

And note what the split is not: it is not a career boundary, and a designer who can only do pixels will be hired for pixels. The practical consequence is that the people who advance fastest are the ones who can move between layers — to diagnose a conversion problem in the flow, to specify a state, to argue for the removal of a step. Each of those is a design act even though it produces no pixels, and they are the acts that are hard to hire for.

A useful mantra: UI is the skin; UX is the whole living body. You can polish pixels forever, but if the flow is confusing the product fails. That’s why this course starts with users and research before a single pixel is drawn.

0.2 The double diamond (your default process)

The double diamond is a four-phase design process: discover, research to understand the problem; define, synthesize insights into a clear problem frame; develop, ideate and prototype many solutions; and deliver, test and refine before shipping. Each phase alternates between diverging to widen options and converging to make decisions. Use it as a default agenda for any project so you explore genuinely before committing to an answer. This prevents solving a problem nobody actually has.

DIVERGE                              CONVERGE
 [explore many]                       [choose one]
        |---------DIVERGE-----CONVERGE---------|
     DISCOVER       DEFINE      DEVELOP      DELIVER
   research the   name the      sketch &       build &
   problem        real problem  test ideas     ship, keep testing

Rule of thumb: spend the FIRST half understanding the problem,
the SECOND half solving it. Beginners solve problems they
never verified exist.

Where the double diamond goes wrong

The diagram is a useful default agenda and a poor description of how design work actually runs, and the two failures it causes are worth naming. The first is treating it as a sequence rather than as two loops: the usual reality is that define and develop iterate several times, and that delivery's testing sends you back into develop with something nobody predicted. The second, and more damaging, is treating the halves as equally weighted and equally skilled — the diagram puts discover and define beside develop and deliver, which invites a team to believe that the research half is one box of the same work, when it is a different discipline with different tools and a different standard of proof.

The rule that matters is the ratio, and it is the part beginners get backwards. Most of the effort belongs in understanding the problem, and the temptation is to invert it because the visible half produces something you can show. A week of interviews produces a document; a week of prototyping produces screenshots; and screenshots are what get discussed in a review, so the visible half attracts the time. The symptom to watch for in yourself is that you can describe the solution in detail and the problem in a sentence.

Then the failure at the seam, which is the one teams cannot see because it happens in a meeting. Discover produces research about a problem; define produces a problem statement; develop produces a solution to the problem statement. If the problem statement was written to be the thing that could be solved — because that is what a define phase is implicitly asked to deliver — the whole pipeline is coherent and entirely useless. The check is whether a plausible solution would be consistent with the problem statement. If the statement says users need a faster way to compare plans, then a comparison table is the answer whether or not research showed the real problem was that the plans themselves were unclear.

Which is why the definition phase is the one most worth doing slowly and the one most often rushed. A good problem statement is uncomfortable: it should be something you cannot simply solve, it should exclude the solutions you had in mind, and a team should be able to read it and disagree. "Users need to compare plans more easily" is a solution wearing a problem's clothes. "Users cannot tell which plan is appropriate to their situation, and are choosing on price" names a problem, excludes the table, and implies that the plans may be the thing to fix.

Finally, use the diamond as a shared vocabulary rather than as a schedule, because its real value is that everyone can point at a box and ask why the work is happening there. "Are we still in discover?" is a useful question to raise in week six of a feature, and it is the question most often answered wrongly, because the answer is usually "we have to be, we are nearly done". The answer to that is that the sunk cost in the second half does not buy correctness in the first, and the diamond exists precisely to make that cheap to say out loud.

/* The diamond as data, so the phase a piece of work is in is a fact rather
   than a recollection, and the seam between define and develop is visible. */
const PHASES = {
  discover: { goal: 'understand the situation', output: 'observations, not conclusions',
              evidence: ['interviews', 'replays', 'analytics', 'field visits'],
              forbidden: ['a solution sketch', 'a ranked list of features'] },
  define:   { goal: 'name the problem precisely', output: 'a problem statement',
              evidence: ['synthesis', 'a statement that a solution cannot be read out of'],
              forbidden: ['naming a feature', 'a statement with the answer inside it'] },
  develop:  { goal: 'make many, then choose one', output: 'prototypes somebody can react to',
              evidence: ['sketches', 'clickable prototypes', 'a tested assumption'],
              forbidden: ['declaring a favourite before testing it'] },
  deliver:  { goal: 'build, ship, and keep testing', output: 'a shipped thing and a watching eye',
              evidence: ['acceptance criteria', 'post-launch measurement'],
              forbidden: ['treating launch as the end of the work'] },
};

/* The seam check. If a plausible solution can be read out of the problem
   statement, the statement is a solution wearing a problem's clothes - and
   the whole pipeline will then be coherent and entirely useless. */
function statementIsSolvable(statement) {
  const SOLUTION_WORDS = /\b(table|button|screen|wizard|dashboard|filter|search|redesign|toggle|banner|dialog|checkout)\b/i;
  const smells = [];
  if (SOLUTION_WORDS.test(statement)) smells.push('names an interface element');
  if (/easier|faster|better|improve[ds]?/i.test(statement)) smells.push('uses a comparative with no measure attached');
  if (!/because|so that|which means/i.test(statement)) smells.push('does not say what the user is trying to achieve');
  return { smells,
           verdict: smells.length ? 'this statement has a solution inside it' : 'this is a problem; a solution cannot be read straight out of it' };
}
// "users need to compare plans more easily"      -> names no element, but comparative with no measure: suspicious
// "users cannot tell which plan suits them and are choosing on price" -> passes

/* The effort ratio, written down so it can be checked rather than asserted. */
function phaseBudget(stage) {
  const BUDGET = { discover: 0.40, define: 0.10, develop: 0.35, deliver: 0.15 };
  return {
    planned: BUDGET[stage],
    // the symptom to watch for in yourself: you can describe the solution in
    // detail and the problem in a sentence
    selfCheck: 'could I state this problem in one sentence, and the solution in a page?',
    // the review question that makes the ratio discussable without accusation
    askedInWeek6: 'are we still in discover?',
    honestAnswerToIt: 'the sunk cost in the second half does not buy correctness in the first',
  };
}

/* The loops, because it is two loops and not one sequence. */
const LOOPS = [
  { from: 'deliver', to: 'develop', trigger: 'a post-launch test found something nobody predicted',
    common: 'and the correct response is to go back, not to patch' },
  { from: 'deliver', to: 'define', trigger: 'the problem statement turns out to have been the solution',
    common: 'and it is discovered after shipping, which is the expensive version' },
  { from: 'develop', to: 'define', trigger: 'every option solves the same easy problem',
    common: 'a strong signal that the wrong problem was named' },
];

The classic double-diamond sketch: diverge and converge twice, keeping the first half devoted to understanding the problem before solving it.

0.3 Method vs mindset

Methods are concrete tools and techniques such as user interviews, card sorting, wireframes, and usability tests that you run at specific points in a process. Mindset is the underlying curiosity, humility, and willingness to be wrong that makes those methods produce honest results. A designer can learn any method quickly, but without the mindset the outputs become theater. Treat methods as a kit that changes with context while the mindset stays constant.

Methods (interviews, wireframes, testing) are tools — you pick the right one per question. Mindset is the actual skill: curiosity about people, willingness to be wrong, humility before users, and a bias toward making things real and testable.

Why a method can produce theatre

A method is a procedure, and a mindset is the disposition that makes the procedure produce something true. The relationship is not decorative: nearly every bad method outcome in practice is a mindset failure wearing a method's clothes. A team that has decided the answer is already running an interview is technically running a method and is producing theatre, and the output is worse than no research because it now has the credibility of research attached to it. The tell is always the same — the findings are suspiciously tidy, the quotes are quotable, and nobody can name a finding that changed a plan.

So the mindset is the thing that has to be taught, and there are three parts of it worth naming. Curiosity about people, which means believing that you do not already know what somebody will do and that the finding can be genuinely surprising; willingness to be wrong, which means being willing to abandon a direction you have defended; and a bias toward making things real, which means preferring an artefact somebody can react to over a document describing it. A team with the first two and not the third produces confident opinions about a product nobody has used.

Methods also have a failure mode that is specific to them rather than to the person running them. Each one has a blind spot built into its design: an interview tells you about reasoning and not behaviour; a heat map records interaction and not comprehension; a survey reports the four percent who answered. That is not a defect, it is what makes the method worth using — a method with no blind spot would be the thing you wanted and would not exist. The competence is in knowing which blind spot you are looking through, which is why this book names them in each chapter rather than presenting each technique as a solution.

Practically, the discipline is to write the question before picking the method. "Do users understand the pricing?" invites a survey or a comprehension test. "What happens in the first minute, and where do they hesitate?" invites observation. "Why did they choose that plan?" invites interviews, which cannot answer it either — the plan choice is usually made on price and the real question is what they expected the price to buy. Naming the question forces the method, and it also reveals when the question is not answerable by anything you could do, which is a useful outcome discovered cheaply.

/* The pair, and the specific failure each half produces on its own. */
const MINDSET = {
  curiosity: { means: 'you do not already know what somebody will do',
               withoutIt: 'an interview run to confirm a decision, producing theatre',
               tell: 'no finding was surprising, and nobody can name one that changed a plan' },
  willingnessToBeWrong: { means: 'a direction can be abandoned without it being a personal defeat',
               withoutIt: 'the plan is defended in the review, and the research is read as disagreeing',
               tell: 'the same finding is restated in stronger terms at the next review' },
  biasToReal: { means: 'an artefact somebody can react to beats a document describing one',
               withoutIt: 'confident opinions about a product nobody has used',
               tell: 'no one has touched anything; there are only decks' },
};

/* Every method, with the blind spot built into its design. A method with no
   blind spot would be the thing you wanted and would not exist. */
const METHODS = [
  { method: 'user interview',  tellsYou: 'why they do what they do, in their own words',
    blindSpot: 'accurate about reasoning, unreliable about their own future behaviour',
    askFirst: 'what were you trying to accomplish?', neverAsk: 'would you use this?' },
  { method: 'moderated test',  tellsYou: 'what they actually do, including what they do wrong',
    blindSpot: 'a small sample, a lab context, and an observer changes behaviour',
    askFirst: 'nothing - watch, and think about it afterwards' },
  { method: 'unmoderated test',tellsYou: 'behaviour at volume, unattended',
    blindSpot: 'no follow-up questions; you find out what happened, never why',
    askFirst: 'set the task, and do not help' },
  { method: 'card sort',       tellsYou: 'the grouping people already carry in their heads',
    blindSpot: 'says nothing about labels you have not shown them',
    askFirst: 'which group does this belong to?', note: 'open sort for a new IA, closed to test existing labels' },
  { method: 'survey',          tellsYou: 'distribution across a population, cheaply',
    blindSpot: 'whatever recruitment made of it; 4% response describes the 4%',
    askFirst: 'nothing about satisfaction - ask for counts and near-misses' },
  { method: 'analytics',       tellsYou: 'where and how many',
    blindSpot: 'not why; and the order your IA assumes may not be the order taken',
    askFirst: 'where did they stop?' },
  { method: 'heatmap',         tellsYou: 'where elements are interacted with, and which are never touched',
    blindSpot: 'a click map on a static page records clicks on nothing; reading looks identical to failing',
    askFirst: 'never as evidence of comprehension' },
  { method: 'session replay',  tellsYou: 'hesitation, back-and-forward, wrong-field correction',
    blindSpot: 'memorable replays are memorable rather than typical',
    askFirst: 'what were you expecting to happen here?' },
  { method: 'A/B test',        tellsYou: 'which of two things causes which outcome',
    blindSpot: 'the long run: novelty, habit, trust and word of mouth are all invisible to it',
    askFirst: 'which metric moves, and by how much would it have to move to matter?' },
  { method: 'wireframe',       tellsYou: 'whether the structure works, before anything is polished',
    blindSpot: 'nothing about comprehension of the words; greyscale tests the layout, not the label',
    askFirst: 'where does the content go, and what is the first thing they see?' },
];

/* Write the question before picking the method. The question also reveals
   when nothing you could do would answer it, which is worth knowing cheaply. */
function chooseMethod(question) {
  const q = question.toLowerCase();
  if (q.startsWith('do they understand') || q.startsWith('can they find')) return { method: 'moderated test',
    because: 'comprehension is observed, not asked about' };
  if (q.startsWith('why did they choose')) return { method: 'interview',
    because: 'and the real question is usually what they expected the choice to buy' };
  if (q.startsWith('how many') || q.startsWith('where do they stop')) return { method: 'analytics',
    because: 'it is a location and a size before it is anything else' };
  if (q.startsWith('will they use this')) return { method: 'nobody knows',
    because: 'stated intention is the least reliable input available; test the behaviour instead' };
  return { method: 'choose deliberately', because: 'write down which blind spot you are looking through' };
}

Choosing a method, and recognising the wrong one

Selection is driven by the question and by the stage, and the cheapest way to choose badly is to pick the method the team already knows. The shape that works: a question about what people do calls for observation; a question about why calls for a conversation; a question about how many calls for a query; and a question about which of two options causes an outcome calls for an experiment. Anything else is a preference rather than a fit. Stage matters too — you cannot test comprehension before the words exist, and you cannot usefully interview about a flow nobody has seen, so the order in a project is usually: analytics to locate, observation to understand, prototype to test, experiment to decide.

Combine two methods rather than trusting one, and combine them in a direction that checks the first. Analytics says where; a replay or a session says what; a survey says whether it generalises beyond the ten people you watched; an experiment says whether a change moves it. The weak combination is two of the same kind — five interviews and a card sort tell you five things about six people, with the sampling problem untouched. A useful rule is that the second method should be able to disagree with the first, which is a different question type, not the same one asked more times.

The signs of the wrong method are worth listing because they are subtle and they are usually rationalised. Findings that are all opinions, which means the method invited them. A study with no question, which means it was run for the appearance of rigour. A sample consisting entirely of colleagues and friends, which is the norm in small teams and which reliably produces agreement. A session where the participant spent most of it agreeing with the moderator. A result that arrived faster than recruitment took. And an analysis that found exactly what the team hoped, which is the outcome that most warrants suspicion rather than the least.

Sample sizes are the last piece, and qualitative sampling does not work the way quantitative sampling does. Five users will find most of the problems in one flow; five hundred will find a slightly longer tail of problems and cost far more. What matters is that the five are people who actually have the problem, that new ones keep producing new findings, and that the last few sessions added nothing — which is the actual stopping rule, and it is cheap to check. Recruitment is where qualitative work fails: recruiting from a panel gives you people who enjoy research sessions rather than people who have the problem, which biases towards the articulate and the recently annoyed.

/* Selection by question type, then by stage. Picking the method the team
   already knows is the cheapest way to choose badly. */
const SELECT = {
  whatDoPeopleDo:      { method: 'observation: moderated test, replay, field visit',
                         blindSpot: 'a lab context, a small sample, and an observer changes behaviour' },
  whyDoTheyDoIt:       { method: 'conversation: interview',
                         blindSpot: 'accurate about reasoning, unreliable about future behaviour' },
  howMany:             { method: 'a query', blindSpot: 'not why; and your assumed order may not be the order taken' },
  whichOfTwoCauses:    { method: 'an experiment', blindSpot: 'the long run is invisible to it' },
  whatGroupsExist:     { method: 'card sort, open', blindSpot: 'says nothing about labels you have not shown' },
  doTheseLabelsWork:   { method: 'card sort, closed', blindSpot: 'only ever tests labels you thought of' },
  isThisUnderstandable: { method: 'a comprehension task, unaided',
                         blindSpot: 'a small sample and a hostile instruction' },
};

/* Combine methods in a direction that can disagree with the first. Five
   interviews and a card sort is five things about six people. */
const SEQUENCING = [
  { question: 'where do they stop?',        method: 'analytics',
    then: 'a replay of ten sessions at that step, tagged',
    direction: 'the second method can disagree: it shows hesitation the funnel cannot' },
  { question: 'what is happening there?',   method: 'observation',
    then: 'an interview with five people from that same cohort',
    direction: 'the accounts can contradict the behaviour, and when they do both are suspect' },
  { question: 'does it generalise?',        method: 'a survey to the population',
    then: 'nothing - this is the broad check',
    direction: 'this is where the ten-person finding either holds or was local' },
  { question: 'which of these two?',        method: 'a prototype and a test',
    then: 'an experiment once a change is worth one',
    direction: 'the test finds problems; the experiment finds which of two causes the outcome' },
];

/* The signs of the wrong method. Each of these gets rationalised, and the
   last one warrants more suspicion than any other. */
const WRONG_METHOD_SIGNS = [
  { sign: 'every finding is an opinion',              means: 'the method invited opinions' },
  { sign: 'the study has no stated question',         means: 'it was run for the appearance of rigour' },
  { sign: 'the sample is colleagues and friends',     means: 'the norm in small teams; it reliably produces agreement' },
  { sign: 'the participant agreed with you most of the session', means: 'the moderator was leading' },
  { sign: 'the analysis finished before recruitment did', means: 'the participants were not the right people' },
  { sign: 'the result is exactly what the team hoped', means: 'warrant more suspicion than any other sign on this list' },
];

/* Qualitative sampling: not a power calculation. The stopping rule is "the
   last few sessions added nothing", which is cheap to check. */
const QUAL_SAMPLING = {
  five: 'will find most of the problems in one flow',
  fiveHundred: 'finds a slightly longer tail, at far greater cost',
  whatMatters: ['the five actually have the problem',
                'new ones keep producing new findings',
                'the last few sessions add nothing - this is the stopping rule'],
  // where recruitment fails: a panel gives people who enjoy research sessions
  // rather than people with the problem, which biases to the articulate and
  // to the recently annoyed
  recruitFrom: 'people who have the problem, recently, and were not asked because they are convenient',
  recruitAvoid: ['a general panel', 'people who answered a survey about the topic before',
                 'anyone who volunteered for the previous study'],
};

How to use this book: read each chapter, then do the exercises — they’re deliberately small enough to finish in one evening. Redo any exercise with a different product than the one suggested; the skill is in re-applying.

Exercises 0

  1. Pick one product you use daily (an app, website, even a kettle). Write 3 sentences describing its UX strengths and 3 describing weaknesses.
  2. Name one time software "worked" but still felt bad to use — what was the gap?

1 · Visual Design Fundamentals

Visual design is the craft layer that makes an interface readable, trustworthy, and aesthetically coherent through hierarchy, layout, color, typography, and spacing. Its purpose is to reduce the cognitive work of using a screen by making relationships and importance obvious at a glance. In practice you apply it through consistent grids, restrained palettes, and type scales, then verify decisions against principles like alignment and contrast. These fundamentals underpin every screen you will ever build.

1.1 Visual hierarchy — the designer’s superpower1.2 Layout, grids and the rule of thirds1.3 Color: role, palette, contrast1.4 Typography basics every designer must own1.5 Whitespace, grouping and the 8pt system1.6 Consistency, alignment and the "whitespace test"1.7 Icons, illustrations & imagery

The non-negotiable craft layer: if users can’t tell what’s important, where to look, or what to click, no research skills will save you. This chapter is the "how to make things look right" foundation.

1.1 Visual hierarchy — the designer’s superpower

Visual hierarchy arranges the elements of a screen by importance so a user’s eye lands first on what matters most. Designers create it with size, weight, contrast, position, and whitespace, making primary actions and headings clearly dominant over secondary content. Establish one obvious focal point per screen, then structure later read-throughs to flow in deliberate order. If nothing stands out, or everything is equally loud, the hierarchy has failed.

Hierarchy = ordering elements so the eye lands on the important thing first, then the next, in order. You create it with four levers, in order of power:

  1. Size — bigger = more important (headline vs body).
  2. Color / contrast — brighter, higher-contrast wins attention.
  3. Position / whitespace — isolated with space around it = important.
  4. Weight / style — bold vs regular, capitals vs lowercase.

Test your hierarchy: squint at the screen until it’s a blur. The one thing that still pops = level 1. If nothing pops, nothing is important. Great interfaces pass the squint test.

The four levers have an order, and the order is the point

The list above gives four levers and says they are in order of power. That ordering is the useful part and it is worth defending, because most interfaces get hierarchy wrong by using the weakest lever hardest.

Position and whitespace is the strongest lever and the most under-used. An element isolated by space reads as important before any attribute is read, because proximity is the cue the visual system evolved to trust. Two adjacent elements belong together; two elements with a gap between them do not. This means hierarchy can be built almost entirely out of spacing, and a design whose hierarchy is created by size and colour instead is a design where the eye has to work.

Size is second and it has a hard limit: a size scale that is too wide stops being a hierarchy and becomes a set of unrelated type sizes. Six distinct sizes is already too many for a screen; the practical ceiling is four, and the interesting question is what the reader does with the three sizes between the smallest and the largest.

Contrast is third, and its specific property is that it is continuous rather than binary. A heading at 16:1 and body text at 4.5:1 has a two-level hierarchy; at 16:1 and 12:1 the body text reads as a heading, which is the commonest hierarchy failure in practice and the one a squint test misses.

Weight and case is the weakest lever and should be used last, for the smallest step in a scale. Bold is a strong signal and using it for everything makes it a weak one; uppercase is stronger still and is nearly always a mistake outside a small label.

And the ordering has a corollary worth stating: if a hierarchy cannot be built with position and whitespace alone, the screen has more than one thing trying to be first. That is a structural problem, not a typographic one, and no amount of size adjustment fixes it.

Making it checkable

Hierarchy is the easiest principle in this chapter to state and the hardest to verify, because the squint test is a heuristic and heuristics do not survive being automated. Two things make it checkable: express the scale as tokens so the ratios are declared rather than eyeballed, and write a test that asserts the declaration holds.

/* THE HIERARCHY AS TOKENS, so the scale is declared rather than chosen
   per screen. This is the single highest-value change to a stylesheet that has
   accumulated one-off font sizes. */
:root {
  /* TYPE SCALE. A ratio of 1.25 - the major third - is the smallest ratio that
     survives rendering at small sizes. Anything below 1.2 and the difference
     between adjacent steps falls under about 2px at body size, which is below
     the perceptual threshold on a normal display. */
  --type-scale: 1.25;
  --text-xs:   0.75rem;                       /* 12px - metadata, never body */
  --text-sm:   0.875rem;                      /* 14px - secondary, dense tables */
  --text-base: 1rem;                          /* 16px - the floor for body text.
                                                 Anything below 16px fails on a
                                                 phone in sunlight and is a
                                                 false economy. */
  --text-lg:   1.125rem;
  --text-xl:   1.375rem;
  --text-2xl:  1.75rem;
  --text-3xl:  2.25rem;
  --text-4xl:  3rem;

  /* WEIGHT. Three weights, not seven. */
  --weight-regular: 400;
  --weight-medium:  500;
  --weight-bold:    700;

  /* SPACING. An 8px base with a 4px half-step, because optical alignment needs
     the half-step and the layout grid needs the whole. */
  --space-1: 0.25rem;   /* 4px  - icon to label */
  --space-2: 0.5rem;    /* 8px  - label to value */
  --space-3: 0.75rem;   /* 12px - inside a control */
  --space-4: 1rem;      /* 16px - between related elements */
  --space-6: 1.5rem;    /* 24px - between groups */
  --space-8: 2rem;      /* 32px - between sections */
  --space-12: 3rem;     /* 48px - page margins on desktop */

  /* ISOLATION. The hierarchy lever that does the most work, so it gets a named
     token: "the space that makes this element its own thing". */
  --space-isolate: var(--space-6);
}

/* THE FOUR LEVERS, expressed. Each class changes exactly one lever, so a review
   can ask "which lever are you reaching for" rather than "does this look
   right". */
.page-title {
  font-size: var(--text-3xl);
  font-weight: var(--weight-bold);
  line-height: 1.15;
  /* ...SIZE plus WEIGHT, for the one thing that is genuinely most important on
     the screen. Note the line height: large type needs a tighter leading than
     small type, and 1.5 on a heading is the most common typographic error in
     production interfaces. */
  margin: 0 0 var(--space-2);
}
.section-heading {
  font-size: var(--text-xl);
  font-weight: var(--weight-medium);
  line-height: 1.3;
  margin: 0 0 var(--space-3);
}
.body-text {
  font-size: var(--text-base);
  font-weight: var(--weight-regular);
  line-height: 1.5;
  margin: 0 0 var(--space-4);
  max-width: 68ch;
  /* ...THE MEASURE. 65 to 75 characters is the range where the eye can find the
     next line without losing its place; beyond about 90 the return sweep starts
     producing line-by-line reading, and the user stops reading. This one
     declaration is more effective for readability than any amount of font
     choice. */
}
.caption {
  font-size: var(--text-sm);
  color: var(--text-muted);
  line-height: 1.4;
}

/* THE PRIMARY ACTION - isolation as the hierarchy mechanism. Nothing here is
   larger or bolder than a section heading; what makes it primary is that
   nothing else on the screen is surrounded by this much space. */
.primary-action {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: var(--space-2);
  padding: var(--space-3) var(--space-5);
  background: var(--accent);
  color: var(--accent-ink);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
  font-weight: var(--weight-medium);
  /* THE GAP IS THE HIERARCHY. Compare against the secondary action below it,
     which differs by background colour alone and sits on the other side of the
     16px gap. The eye reads the space before it reads either colour. */
  margin: var(--space-8) 0 var(--space-isolate);
}
.secondary-action {
  padding: var(--space-3) var(--space-5);
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
  color: var(--text-default);
  font-weight: var(--weight-regular);
  margin: 0 0 var(--space-isolate);
}

/* PROXIMITY, which is the rule the isolation token encodes. */
.form-row + .form-row { margin-top: var(--space-4); }
.form-section + .form-section { margin-top: var(--space-8); }
.form-section__label { margin-bottom: var(--space-2); }

/* ...THE GROUPING READING: everything inside a .form-section is one thing.
   The 32px above each section and the 16px inside it is the whole visual
   grammar of grouping, and it is a ratio rather than a pair of numbers. A
   ratio of 2:1 between group-internal and group-external space is the point -
   equal spacing flattens the structure, and a ratio of 3:1 or more makes the
   screen feel like islands. */

One focal point, and the measurement that checks it

The rule above — one obvious focal point per screen — is worth making measurable, because it is the one hierarchy statement that can fail while every individual element looks correct.

The measurement is visual and cheap: desaturate the screen, then measure the contrast between each element and its background. The element with the highest delta is what the eye lands on first, and if that is not the most important thing on the screen, the hierarchy is inverted — regardless of what the type scale says.

/* A SCREEN WITH THREE LEVELS, which is the most a screen can carry without
   competing. Note which properties each level changes and, more usefully,
   which it does not. */
.screen {
  display: grid;
  gap: var(--space-7);
  grid-template-areas: "title" "primary" "secondary";
  align-content: start;
  padding: var(--space-7);
}

/* LEVEL 1 - the one thing. Bigger, bolder, and isolated by the largest space
   on the screen. Two levers rather than four, which is the discipline. */
.level-1 {
  grid-area: title;
  font-size: var(--text-3xl);
  font-weight: var(--weight-bold);
  line-height: var(--leading-tight);
  color: var(--text-strong);
  margin: 0;
  /* ...NOTHING ELSE ON THIS SCREEN IS THIS LARGE. If a secondary heading is
     also --text-3xl, there is no level 1 and the hierarchy is a flat field. */
}

/* LEVEL 2 - the supporting action. Notice it is NOT larger than the body text;
   it is distinguished by isolation and by weight alone. */
.level-2 {
  grid-area: primary;
  justify-self: start;
  margin-top: var(--space-7);          /* the isolation */
  padding: var(--space-3) var(--space-5);
  background: var(--action-primary);
  color: var(--action-ink);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
  font-weight: var(--weight-medium);
}

/* LEVEL 3 - everything else. One definition, used by every other element on
   the screen, which is what makes the two levels above legible by contrast
   with it. */
.level-3 {
  grid-area: secondary;
  font-size: var(--text-base);
  font-weight: var(--weight-regular);
  line-height: var(--leading-normal);
  color: var(--text-default);
  max-width: 68ch;
}
.level-3 + .level-3 { margin-top: var(--space-4); }

/* THE CHECK, done in three passes rather than by squinting. */
  /* 1. DESATURATE. Screenshot, apply a grayscale filter, look. The lightest
        region is the whitespace and the darkest is the focal point. If the
        focal point is not the primary action or the page title, the hierarchy
        is inverted and every other decision on this screen is downstream of
        that error.
  /* 2. MEASURE. In devtools, note each element's computed font-size,
        font-weight and the computed margin above it, then sort. The primary
        action should be identifiable as an outlier in at least one of those
        three columns. If every element is within one step of every other, there
        is no level 1.
  /* 3. BLUR. Apply a 4px gaussian blur to the screenshot. Blur removes colour
        and fine detail and leaves SIZE and POSITION - which are the two
        strongest levers - so what survives the blur is what the hierarchy is
        actually made of. If the screen turns into a uniform grey field, its
        hierarchy is carried entirely by attributes the blur removed.
        This is a better test than the squint test because the result is
        repeatable and can be put side by side with the previous release. */

/* THE FAILURE THIS CATCHES, which is the common one: a page with a
   full-width banner, a heading, a two-column body and three equally-weighted
   call-to-action buttons. Every element is reasonable; the screen has three
   focal points competing and a user with ten seconds cannot start. The fix is
   not a smaller button - it is deciding which of the three is the action and
   demoting the other two to text links, which is a hierarchy decision wearing
   a component decision's clothes. */

1.2 Layout, grids and the rule of thirds

Layout organizes content on screen using an underlying grid that gives every element a consistent rhythm and alignment. A column grid with consistent margins, gutters, and a fixed set of columns keeps spacing predictable so users quickly learn where things live. The rule of thirds helps you place focal points off-center for visual interest. Simple, predictable grid systems usually outperform clever asymmetric layouts because regularity teaches the eye.

Grids don’t limit creativity — they create consistent rhythm so users learn where things live.

PatternUseExample
12-column gridWeb layouts, responsive breakpointsBootstrap/Tailwind layout foundations
4/8pt spacing scaleConsistent spacing in UI4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64 px
Golden ratio (≈1.62)Type scale: body 16 → heading ≈ 26pxBrand layouts, poster/print
Rule of thirdsPlacing focal points off-centerHero images, landing pages

Consistency beats originality: users scan for patterns they already know. A regular, boring grid peacefully made-of-4s usually performs better than a clever asymmetric one.

Grids are for alignment, and alignment is for trust

The rule of thirds is a photographic composition heuristic and it is not what a layout grid is for. A layout grid exists so that elements on a screen line up with each other, and alignment is what makes an interface feel deliberate — misaligned edges are read as carelessness even when nobody can say what is wrong.

So the useful discipline is not "place things at thirds" but every vertical edge in the layout comes from the same column set. If the sidebar is 280px and the content starts at 320px, then every element inside the content that starts at the left edge starts at 320px, and every one that is inset starts at a token that is a multiple of the 8px base from 320px.

The other half is horizontal rhythm: the spaces between groups are multiples of the base and they form a ratio to the spaces inside groups. A form with 16px between fields and 8px between a label and its input reads correctly; the same form with 8px and 8px does not, and the reason is that without the ratio the groups do not visually merge.

And the failure that makes responsive layouts look wrong in a way nobody can name: content-driven breakpoints. If a card grid goes from three columns to two at 900px because the cards stopped fitting, then the card widths change at every screen size, which means no two rows are aligned and the whole grid reads as noise. Breakpoints should come from the content's minimum comfortable size and then hold until the next one — so columns change at four specific widths and nowhere else.

The grid, expressed as tokens and a container

/* THE GRID AS TOKENS. Columns are a named sequence so a screen can choose a
   span by name rather than by arithmetic, and so the arithmetic lives in one
   place when the container changes. */
:root {
  --grid-columns: 12;
  --grid-gutter: var(--space-6);      /* 24px - wider gutters read as more
                                          editorial, narrower as denser. */
  --grid-margin: var(--space-6);
  --content-max: 76rem;               /* ~1216px. Beyond this, the measure
                                          constraint takes over and more
                                          width only makes lines longer. */
  --sidebar-width: 17.5rem;           /* 280px */
}

/* THE CONTAINER. One place that owns the arithmetic. */
.container {
  max-width: var(--content-max);
  margin-inline: auto;
  padding-inline: var(--grid-margin);
}
.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: var(--sidebar-width) minmax(0, 1fr);
  gap: var(--grid-gutter);
  align-items: start;
  /* minmax(0, 1fr) NOT 1fr. The default min-width of a grid item is its
     min-content size, so a wide unbreakable child - a long URL, a table, a
     code block - pushes the column past its track and blows out the layout.
     This is the single most common CSS grid bug and it is invisible until
     somebody types a long string into a field. */
}

/* SPANS BY NAME. A card grid, in a way that changes column count only at four
   widths. */
.card-grid {
  display: grid;
  gap: var(--grid-gutter);
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(18rem, 1fr));
  /* 18rem is the content-driven value: the point below which a card's title
     wraps to three lines and its button no longer fits beside the count. The
     auto-fill means columns change at content sizes and every card stays the
     same width within a row - which is what keeps rows aligned. */
}

/* THE CONTENT-DRIVEN BREAKPOINTS, stated explicitly rather than inferred.
   Four widths, chosen from minimum comfortable content, and held between. */
@media (max-width: 60rem) {   /* 960px - sidebar no longer fits beside content */
  .layout { grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr); }
  .layout__sidebar { position: static; }
}
@media (max-width: 30rem) {   /* 480px - the phone floor. Two-column card grids
                                stop being readable below this. */
  :root {
    --grid-gutter: var(--space-4);
    --grid-margin: var(--space-4);
  }
}

/* THE OPTICAL ALIGNMENT, which is the rule that has no token. */
.icon + .label { margin-left: var(--space-2); }
.label + .input { margin-left: var(--space-2); }
/* ...both gaps are 8px and they are meant to LOOK the same. A glyph's bounding
   box is usually a few pixels narrower than its advance width, so an icon and
   the label after it need slightly less gap than two boxes do. The correction
   is about 1px and it is the difference between "aligned" and "nearly
   aligned" to somebody who cannot name why. */

/* THE TEST, which is the part that makes a grid enforceable rather than
   aspirational. */
.grid-test {
  position: relative;
  background-image: repeating-linear-gradient(
    to right,
    var(--grid-overlay) 0 1px,
    transparent 1px calc(100% / var(--grid-columns))
  );
  background-size: calc((100% - (var(--grid-columns) - 1) * var(--grid-gutter)) / var(--grid-columns) + var(--grid-gutter)) 100%;
}
/* Toggle this on a real screen. Every edge of every element should sit on a
   line. Elements that do not are either a deliberate exception or a bug, and
   the overlay is the only reliable way to tell which - eyeballing a screen for
   misalignment does not work, because the eye cannot hold the reference. */

A whole screen, and the breakpoint decisions made explicit

The grid above is the mechanism. What is worth showing is a complete layout with its breakpoints stated as decisions, because the breakpoint is where a layout either holds together or degrades into a stack of differently-sized cards.

/* THE WHOLE SCREEN. Header, sidebar, content, and a breakpoint for each
   structural change - not one per device. */
.shell {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "sidebar main"
    "sidebar footer";
  grid-template-columns: var(--sidebar-width) minmax(0, 1fr);
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
  min-height: 100dvh;
}
.shell__header  { grid-area: header; }
.shell__sidebar { grid-area: sidebar; }
.shell__main    { grid-area: main; }
.shell__footer  { grid-area: footer; }

/* THE FOUR STRUCTURAL BREAKPOINTS, each for a named reason. The reason is
   written down because a breakpoint without a reason gets moved during a
   redesign and the next person cannot tell what broke. */

/* 1. 60rem / 960px - THE SIDEBAR STOPS FITTING. At this width a 280px sidebar
      plus a readable 68ch measure plus gutters exceeds the viewport, and the
      content column drops below the comfortable measure. */
@media (max-width: 60rem) {
  .shell {
    grid-template-areas: "header" "main" "footer";
    grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr);
  }
  .shell__sidebar {
    grid-area: unset;
    /* ...AND IT BECOMES A DISCLOSURE, not a removed column. Removing a
         navigation column is the most common responsive failure: the pages it
         linked to become unreachable on the majority of devices. */
    display: none;
  }
  .shell[data-nav-open="true"] .shell__sidebar {
    display: block;
    position: fixed;
    inset: 0 auto 0 0;
    width: min(20rem, 85vw);
    z-index: 100;
    box-shadow: var(--shadow-lg);
  }
}

/* 2. 48rem / 768px - TABLES STOP BEING READABLE. A five-column table below this
      width cannot be read at any font size, so it stops being a table. */
@media (max-width: 48rem) {
  .data-table thead { display: none; }
  .data-table tr {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 1fr auto;
    gap: var(--space-1) var(--space-3);
    padding: var(--space-4) 0;
    border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-subtle);
  }
  .data-table td { display: contents; }
  .data-table td::before {
    content: attr(data-label);
    font-size: var(--text-xs);
    letter-spacing: var(--tracking-wide);
    text-transform: uppercase;
    color: var(--text-muted);
  }
  /* ...THE CARD-FALLBACK TABLE. Each row becomes a labelled block. Note the
         data-label attribute is REQUIRED on every cell - it is the only thing
         identifying the column once the thead is gone, so omitting it produces
         a row of unlabelled values. That is a content bug masquerading as a
         responsive one, and it is invisible in a desktop review. */
}

/* 3. 30rem / 480px - THE PHONE FLOOR. Touch targets, and the point at which a
      two-column card grid produces cards too narrow for their content. */
@media (max-width: 30rem) {
  .card-grid { grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr); }
  .btn { min-height: 44px; }   /* every interactive target, not just this one */
}

/* 4. NO BREAKPOINT - the fluid range. Between 30rem and 60rem the layout is
      simply 1fr, which is correct: nothing about a grid of cards requires a
      step change, and adding breakpoints inside a fluid range produces
      layouts that look slightly wrong at every width nobody chose. */

/* THE SAFE-AREA INSET, which is the mobile detail that is always missing. */
:root { --safe-bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px); }
.sticky-footer {
  padding-bottom: calc(var(--space-4) + var(--safe-bottom));
  /* ...Without this, a fixed footer overlaps the home indicator on every modern
       iPhone. It is invisible in a desktop browser because env() resolves to
       0px there, which is why it survives review. */

1.3 Color: role, palette, contrast

In interface design, color plays specific roles rather than purely decorating: neutrals for surfaces and text, brand colors for primary actions, and semantic colors for status such as error or success. Build a small, coordinated palette where each role holds one value, and use color for meaning before decoration. Always verify that text and interactive elements pass contrast guidelines such as WCAG AA, and never rely on hue alone to communicate state, since colorblind users need a secondary cue.

// Roles, not just "pretty colors":
--base:    text / background neutrals      (make up ~90% of the surface)   // the quiet surface that carries the screen
--primary: brand + main actions + focus
--accent:  sparse highlight (special offers, live status)
--success: #28a745   --danger: #dc3545   --warning: #ffc107   // fixed semantic palette, reused everywhere
// Then, always 3 contrast passes:
//   1. text on background        >= 4.5:1  (WCAG AA)
//   2. controls visible          >= 3:1    from the panel behind
//   3. color-blind legibility     don't rely on hue alone (red/green)

Colour is a role system, and a palette is the wrong level to work at

The section above says colour has role, palette and contrast. The ordering matters and the middle term is where most projects go wrong: they design a palette and then assign colours from it to things, rather than assigning roles to things and defining the palette as the set of values those roles need.

The distinction is not academic, and it shows up the first time a second brand arrives. A project that has named its colours blue-500 and gray-200 has to re-decide which is which in the new theme. A project that has named them action-primary and text-muted re-points one variable.

So a role list for an interface is short and complete: one interactive action colour, one destructive colour, one success and one warning, a text scale from most to least prominent, a background scale, and a border scale. Everything else on a screen is one of those with a weight or a state.

And the second property, which is the one that makes the system maintainable: every role's value is contrast-tested against every background it can appear on, and that pairing is asserted in a test rather than reviewed by eye. A contrast ratio nobody computed is a claim, and the failure mode is a colour that passes review on the developer's monitor and fails on a projector.

The roles, and the pairing that makes them verifiable

/* COLOUR AS ROLES. The variable names say what the colour IS FOR, which is
   what makes a second theme a re-pointing exercise rather than a redesign. */
:root {
  color-scheme: light;

  /* INTERACTIVE. Exactly one action colour. A second "secondary action blue"
     is how interfaces end up with two things claiming to be the primary. */
  --action-primary: #0b5fbf;
  --action-primary-hover: #094c98;
  --action-primary-active: #073b78;
  --action-ink: #ffffff;             /* whatever reads ON the action colour.
                                         Separate token, because it is a
                                         different decision and it changes
                                         between themes. */
  --action-focus-ring: #0b5fbf;

  /* SEMANTIC. Each carries meaning a user has learned, so each also needs a
     non-colour cue - an icon, a label - because roughly one man in twelve has
     a colour vision deficiency and a red-only error state is invisible to
     them. */
  --status-success: #1a7f37;
  --status-warning: #9a6700;
  --status-danger:  #cf222e;
  --status-info:    #0550ae;

  /* TEXT. Four steps, and the ratios are the point. */
  --text-strong:  #0d1117;          /* headings - 17.4:1 on white */
  --text-default: #24292f;          /* body     - 14.6:1 */
  --text-muted:   #57606a;          /* secondary-  6.4:1 */
  --text-faint:   #6e7781;          /* metadata -   4.7:1, still AA */

  /* SURFACES */
  --surface-canvas:   #ffffff;
  --surface-raised:   #f6f8fa;
  --surface-sunken:   #eef1f4;
  --surface-overlay:  #1c2128;

  /* BORDERS. Two, not one. A border that does the job of grouping and a border
     that does the job of containing an input are different weights. */
  --border-subtle:  #d8dee4;
  --border-default: #afb8c1;
}

/* EVERY COLOUR APPEARS IN A CONTEXT, which is the point of the role. */
.card {
  background: var(--surface-canvas);
  border: 1px solid var(--border-subtle);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
  padding: var(--space-4);
}
.card__title { color: var(--text-strong); }
.card__meta  { color: var(--text-muted); font-size: var(--text-sm); }

.input {
  border: 1px solid var(--border-default);
  background: var(--surface-canvas);
  color: var(--text-default);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
}
.input:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--action-focus-ring);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
.input[aria-invalid="true"] {
  border-color: var(--status-danger);
  /* ...AND THE NON-COLOUR CUE. The border thickness is the redundant signal, so
     the state is legible without colour perception. A one-pixel red border is a
     colour-only cue and it is an accessibility failure that looks correct in
     every review that does not include the WCAG criterion. */
  box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px var(--status-danger);
}

/* THE TEST. Colour roles are a set of pairs, not a set of values, so the test
   asserts the pairs. A contrast ratio nobody computed is a claim. */
:root {
  --pairs-to-check:
    "text-strong/surface-canvas"
    "text-default/surface-canvas"
    "text-muted/surface-canvas"
    "text-faint/surface-canvas"
    "text-default/surface-raised"
    "text-muted/surface-raised"
    "text-strong/surface-overlay"
    "action-ink/action-primary"
    "status-danger/surface-canvas"
    "status-success/surface-canvas"
    "action-primary/surface-canvas";
}
/* For each pair: the text value, the background value, and the required ratio.
   4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for a UI boundary or a large heading.
   ...and the finding that always appears: the muted and faint text tokens
   usually fail against --surface-raised rather than against white, because
   white is where they were designed. Test the pair, not the token. */

This CSS role map assigns every color a job and pairs it with three required contrast passes. Notice the fixed status palette and the WCAG AA target for text.

Red vs green: 1 in 12 men are color-blind. Never encode a binary state purely by hue — always pair color with an icon, label or pattern ("Error: server offline" + red icon).

1.4 Typography basics every designer must own

Typography is the craft of making interface text readable, scannable, and appropriately hierarchical. Start with a fixed type scale derived from a ratio, limit yourself to one or two font families, and keep body line length near 45 to 75 characters with comfortable line height. Apply consistent styling to headings, body, links, and labels so similar text always looks the same. Small consistent choices make long reading effortless.

  • Type scale: pick a base (16px body) and a ratio (1.25–1.333); compute headings from it. Never invent random sizes.
  • Line length: 45–75 characters per line for body text (past that, reading tiredness doubles).
  • Line height: ~1.4–1.6× font size for body; 1.1–1.3× for headings (headings can hug tight).
  • Two families max: one for headings/UI, one for body — or even better, one with many weights.

Measure line length in characters ("em"), not pixels: a 16px font at ~65ch ≈ 520–720 px depending on the font. Design systems store this as a token, not a magic number.

Four numbers decide whether text is readable

The basics above cover typeface and pairing. What actually determines whether text is readable on a screen is four numbers, and they are worth separating because they are usually conflated into "font choice" and adjusted by trying typefaces.

Size, with a hard floor. 16px is the minimum for body text on the web and the reason is not aesthetic: it is the point below which a 1px hairline in a common system typeface becomes sub-pixel, and sub-pixel text on a non-retina display is permanently grey. A 14px body is a deliberate choice made to fit more on a screen, and it should be made with that stated rather than by accident.

Line height, and the rule that catches people is that it scales inversely with size. Body text wants 1.4 to 1.6 because long measures need the leading to return the eye. Headings want 1.1 to 1.3, because large type with large leading looks like an unedited document. Setting line-height: 1.5 globally and inheriting it into headings is the most common typographic error in a design system.

Measure, which is the number that produces the largest improvement in reading experience and is almost never set: 65 to 75 characters per line for body text, and the mechanism is that beyond about 90 characters the return sweep from the end of one line to the start of the next starts producing errors, and the user silently switches to word-by-word scanning.

Letter spacing, which is a function of size and weight. Large bold type needs negative tracking to look right because letterspacing increases as size increases; small type needs positive tracking for the same reason. Both defaults are wrong often enough that a system should set them explicitly at two or three sizes rather than inherit a single value.

The type system, with the four numbers per role

/* TYPE AS A TABLE, not as ad-hoc font-size declarations. Every number that
   affects readability is declared per role, so a role can be reviewed as a
   unit and a change is one edit. */
:root {
  --font-sans: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", sans-serif;
  --font-mono: ui-monospace, "SF Mono", "Cascadia Mono", Menlo, monospace;
  /* ...A SYSTEM STACK, FIRST. This is a performance decision with a visual
     consequence: the first font in the stack renders with zero download on the
     majority of devices, and font swapping mid-render produces a visible reflow
     that users describe as the page "jumping". Only add a webfont when the
     brand requirement is real, and then self-host it with font-display: swap. */

  --leading-tight: 1.2;      /* headings */
  --leading-normal: 1.5;     /* body */
  --leading-loose: 1.7;      /* long-form prose */
  --tracking-tight: -0.01em; /* large type, and large bold type especially */
  --tracking-normal: 0;
  --tracking-wide: 0.02em;   /* small caps labels, and small text under 13px */
}

/* THE ROLES. Each is a complete specification of how text at that level
   behaves, which is what makes it reviewable. */
.t-display {
  font-family: var(--font-sans);
  font-size: var(--text-4xl);
  font-weight: var(--weight-bold);
  line-height: var(--leading-tight);
  letter-spacing: var(--tracking-tight);
  /* ...-0.01em, not 0. At 48px bold the default letter-spacing looks loose,
     almost like a different weight, because the amount of space a letter gets
     scales with its size. Large type is the one case where the default is
     wrong in the direction most people do not notice. */
  color: var(--text-strong);
  margin: 0 0 var(--space-3);
}
.t-heading {
  font-size: var(--text-2xl);
  font-weight: var(--weight-bold);
  line-height: var(--leading-tight);
  letter-spacing: var(--tracking-tight);
  color: var(--text-strong);
}
.t-subheading {
  font-size: var(--text-lg);
  font-weight: var(--weight-medium);
  line-height: var(--leading-tight);
  color: var(--text-strong);
}
.t-body {
  font-size: var(--text-base);
  font-weight: var(--weight-regular);
  line-height: var(--leading-normal);
  letter-spacing: var(--tracking-normal);
  color: var(--text-default);
  max-width: 68ch;          /* THE MEASURE. 68ch at a 16px sans is roughly 72
                                characters, which is the top of the comfortable
                                range. Note it is in ch - the width of a zero -
                                so it scales with the font, which is what you
                                want and what a px value cannot do. */
}
.t-prose p + p { margin-top: 0; margin-bottom: var(--space-4); }
.t-prose { line-height: var(--leading-loose); max-width: 65ch; }
.t-caption {
  font-size: var(--text-sm);
  line-height: 1.4;
  letter-spacing: var(--tracking-normal);
  color: var(--text-muted);
}
.t-label {
  font-size: var(--text-xs);
  font-weight: var(--weight-medium);
  letter-spacing: var(--tracking-wide);
  text-transform: uppercase;
  color: var(--text-muted);
  /* ...POSITIVE TRACKING, at the smallest size, uppercased. Small uppercase
     text is exactly where default letter-spacing fails hardest: it looks
     cramped, and the tracking fix is more effective than any size change. */
}
.t-code {
  font-family: var(--font-mono);
  font-size: 0.875em;
  /* ...0.875em, NOT a px value. A monospace face at the same nominal size
     reads larger than the sans next to it, because its x-height is larger and
     its letters are wider. Scaling by em keeps code aligned with surrounding
     prose at every base size, and using a fixed px breaks the moment the base
     size changes. */
}

/* THE TWO CHECKS THAT CATCH THE REST */
  /* 1. Zoom to 200%. The measure doubles, the measure is now too wide, and the
        line length is the first thing that breaks. If a layout survives 200%
        zoom it will survive a user who needs it, and it costs nothing at 100%.
  /* 2. Set the base size to 20px in devtools. If anything is positioned in px
        and breaks, it was never going to work for a user who changed their
        browser's default font size - which is a far more common accommodation
        than zoom, and which no responsive breakpoint addresses. */

Loading the font without a visible reflow

The type roles above are a declaration. This is the part that decides whether they are the type the user actually sees, and the failure mode is specific: a page that renders with a fallback, then re-renders with the intended typeface a second later, and the text the user had already begun reading moves.

/* FONT LOADING, in the order the declarations matter. */
@font-face {
  font-family: "Brand Sans";
  src: url("/fonts/brand-sans-var.woff2") format("woff2-variations");
  font-weight: 100 900;
  font-style: normal;
  font-display: swap;
  /* ...swap, not block. swap renders the fallback immediately and swaps when
     the font arrives. The alternative is block, which hides the text entirely
     for up to three seconds - and on a slow connection that means a user
     looking at an empty page. The cost of swap is the reflow, which is why
     the next block exists.
     ...and a variable font here, so one file covers all weights. A static
     family at four weights is four requests, four chances to flash, and four
     times the bytes. */
}

/* THE SIZE-ADJUST FALLBACK, which is the actual fix for the reflow. */
@font-face {
  font-family: "Brand Sans Fallback";
  src: local("Arial");
  size-adjust: 107%;
  ascent-override: 90%;
  descent-override: 22%;
  line-gap-override: 0%;
}
/* ...THIS IS THE DECLARATION THAT MATTERS. It takes the fallback font and
     rescales and re-spaces it so its metrics match the real font, which means
     swapping changes the glyphs without changing the layout. A user reading
     text that does not move under their eyes while it changes typeface is the
     difference between a professional page and a cheap one, and it costs five
     lines that most projects never add.

     The numbers are not universal - they depend on the two fonts - and they
     are measured by overlaying the two and adjusting until the cap height,
     x-height and baseline agree. Chrome's font overview panel shows the
     overrides it computes, which is the practical way to obtain them. */

html { font-size: 100%; }
body {
  font-family: "Brand Sans", "Brand Sans Fallback", system-ui, sans-serif;
  /* ...fallback SECOND, not last. The order is: the font you want, the metric-
     matched fallback, then the system stack for the case where neither loaded.
     Putting the system stack before the fallback defeats the size-adjust
     entirely, because the browser never reaches the adjusted face. */
}

/* PRECONNECT, which is the other half of the loading problem. */
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.example.com" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/brand-sans-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
/* ...preload is a hint that this exact file will be needed immediately, which
     starts the fetch before the CSS that references it has been parsed. On a
     real connection that is the difference between the font arriving in 400ms
     and arriving in 2s. Note the crossorigin on both: a font fetch is always
     CORS, and omitting the attribute on a preload means the browser fetches it
     twice - once preloaded and discarded, once for real - which is worse than
     not preloading at all. */

/* THE VERTICAL RHYTHM, which is a consequence of the base size. */
:root { --leading-normal: 1.5; }
body {
  font-size: var(--text-base);
  line-height: var(--leading-normal);
  /* ...AND THEN EVERY SPACE IS A MULTIPLE OF THE LINE HEIGHT. This is the
     mechanism behind every well-set page, and it is not a designer's rule so
     much as an arithmetic one: if the line box is 24px and every vertical space
     is a multiple of 12px or 24px, then content lands on a grid the eye can
     track, and the page has an underlying structure that survives every
     component change. */
}
h1, h2, h3, h4 {
  line-height: var(--leading-tight);
  margin-top: 0;
  margin-bottom: var(--space-4);
}
p { margin: 0 0 var(--space-4); }

/* THE TWO THINGS TO CHECK AFTER CHANGING THE FONT */
  /* 1. Does the page still look right at 200% zoom? Fonts change and the
        measure changes with them. A typeface with a wider average character
        width turns a 68ch measure into 80 characters, which is the failure the
        ch constraint was supposed to prevent - and it happens silently, because
        nothing about the layout errored.
  /* 2. Does the FALLBACK look acceptable? Every page has a moment before the
        font arrives, and a large fraction of sessions never see the font at
        all - on a flaky connection, or when the font request is blocked. A
        fallback that is a grotesque next to a geometric creates a visible
        personality change, and the fix is choosing a fallback in the same
        class as the intended face, which is what the size-adjust block above
        is doing when it takes local("Arial"). */

1.5 Whitespace, grouping and the 8pt system

Whitespace is a design tool that separates and relates content, often carrying more meaning than borders. Group related items closely and separate unrelated groups with larger gaps, because proximity reads as relationship. Practically, apply the 8-point system by spacing and sizing elements in multiples of eight so the rhythm stays consistent across screens. When a layout feels unclear, adding space usually fixes grouping more effectively than adding lines or boxes.

Whitespace is not "empty"; it’s the paint. Related things are grouped by closeness — the Gestalt law of proximity is stronger than any border or color. The 8pt rule: use multiples of 4/8 for margins, padding, gaps and sizes so everything on the page aligns on a shared rhythm (with occasional 2/4px fine-tuning in dense tables).

// Example: grouped form via spacing only (no borders needed)
<fieldset style="display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap:16px">   <!-- group of fields -->
  <label>Email<input type="email"></label>   <!-- flex column stacks fields vertically -->
  <label>Password<input type="password"></label>
  <small style="margin-top:-8px">Groups via gap; hint closer to its field via margin</small>   <!-- negative margin pulls the hint upward -->
</fieldset>

Space is a ratio, and a scale is not enough

The 8pt system above is necessary and it is insufficient, and the reason is that a scale gives you the available values while grouping needs a relationship between them.
