The relationship is a ratio. Spacing inside a group should be noticeably smaller than spacing between groups — a factor of two is the conventional answer and it is the one that works without looking either way. At a 1:1 ratio the groups do not merge and the screen reads as an undifferentiated field of elements. At a 1:4 ratio the screen reads as disconnected islands and the user loses the sense of a whole.

Which means the scale has to be interpreted, not just consulted. The 8pt system gives 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48. Reading it: 4 and 8 are intra-element (icon to label, label to input); 16 and 24 are intra-group (between rows, between fields); 32 and 48 are inter-group. And a form with 16px between fields and 8px between a label and its input is correct because 16 is double 8 — that ratio is what makes the fields read as belonging together.

The second property is that whitespace is not empty. It is the isolation lever from the first section, and it is doing the work that size and colour would otherwise have to do. A screen with generous spacing and modest type sizes reads as more sophisticated than a screen with tight spacing and large type, which is counterintuitive and consistently true.

The scale as tokens, and the grouping it produces

/* THE SCALE. An 8px base with a 4px half-step, because optical alignment needs
   the half-step (an icon to its label) and the layout grid needs the whole
   (a column gutter). A scale without a half-step forces a choice between two
   wrong values. */
:root {
  --space-0:  0;
  --space-1:  0.25rem;   /* 4px  - icon to label, chip padding, inside a button */
  --space-2:  0.5rem;    /* 8px  - label to input, between inline items */
  --space-3:  0.75rem;   /* 12px - inside a card around its content */
  --space-4:  1rem;      /* 16px - between rows, between fields */
  --space-5:  1.5rem;    /* 24px - inside a card's sections, card gutter */
  --space-6:  2rem;      /* 32px - between groups of form fields */
  --space-7:  3rem;      /* 48px - between page sections */
  --space-8:  4rem;      /* 64px - page top margin on desktop */
}

/* THE RATIO, applied. Every one of these is a pairing where the outer space is
   twice the inner, and that doubling is what makes the groups visible. */
.form-group + .form-group { margin-top: var(--space-6); }   /* 32 between */
.field + .field { margin-top: var(--space-4); }               /* 16 inside  */
.field__label { display: block; margin-bottom: var(--space-2); }  /* 8 to 8 */

.card { padding: var(--space-5); }
.card + .card { margin-top: var(--space-5); }
.card__section + .card__section { margin-top: var(--space-4); }
.card__section__title { margin-bottom: var(--space-2); }
/* ...24 inside the card, 16 between its sections, 8 from a section title to its
   content. That is a 3:2:1 ratio reading inward, and it is the whole
   hierarchy. Notice the 24 between cards equals the 24 inside a card, which is
   a deliberate choice: at this density two adjacent cards read as a list of
   items rather than as two separate things. When you want them to read as
   separate, the between space must be larger than the inside space. */

/* DENSITY, as a single override rather than a redesign. The same components at
   two densities is a resize of the scale, not a second set of components. */
[data-density="compact"] {
  --space-2: 0.375rem;
  --space-3: 0.5rem;
  --space-4: 0.75rem;
  --space-5: 1rem;
  --space-6: 1.5rem;
  /* ...A DENSITY MODE, which is the cheapest accessibility feature in an
     interface. A data table with forty rows on a laptop is unusable, and the
     correct answer is not a horizontal scrollbar - it is the same table at a
     0.75x vertical scale. Because the scale is tokens, one attribute changes
     the entire interface and the ratio between inner and outer space is
     preserved, which is what keeps the grouping intact at the new density. */

/* THE WHITESPACE TEST, which is a measurement rather than an opinion */
  .card { padding: var(--space-5); }
  /* Ask: what is the largest gap on this screen, and is it between two things
     that belong together? If yes, the grouping is wrong and no amount of
     adjusting the individual gaps will fix it - the problem is that the ratio
     runs the other way.
     ...and the companion test: cover the screen with a greyscale filter and
     look at the shape. Whitespace reads as light regions and content as dark.
     If the light regions do not correspond to the intended groups, the
     spacing is not doing the grouping and something else is. */

This HTML form groups its fields purely through spacing: a flex column with a 16px gap and a negative margin pulling the hint closer to its field, with no borders in sight.

1.6 Consistency, alignment and the "whitespace test"

Consistency means the same control always looks and behaves the same way, so users can reuse what they have already learned. Align every element to a shared invisible edge or grid so each screen reads as deliberate, and apply the whitespace test by asking whether grouping stays clear even without borders or color. Audit your screens for reused elements that drifted in size, styling, or spacing. Consistent patterns build trust quickly, and broken consistency quietly undermines it.

  • Consistency: same control = same look everywhere (buttons, chips, alerts). Users transfer knowledge; every exception costs them.
  • Alignment: find the invisible left edge; unaligned elements read as bugs, instantly eroding trust.
  • One visual language: radius, shadows, icon stroke widths, and motion speeds should be tokens, not per-screen decisions.

Consistency is what makes a screen learnable

Consistency is usually framed as aesthetic discipline — do the same thing the same way — and that framing undersells it, because the actual mechanism is transfer of learning.

A user who has used one screen of your product knows what a primary button does, that a trash icon deletes, that the top-right control is where account settings live, and that a modal traps focus. None of that knowledge was taught; it was transferred. And every inconsistency is a withdrawal from that balance — the interface has to re-teach something, and the teaching happens at the moment the user is least willing to receive it.

Which gives the practical rule: an inconsistency costs more the further it is from where the user learned the pattern. A button that looks different on one screen is a small cost because the user has just looked at the other screens. A button that means something different from its look elsewhere is a large cost, because the transfer is actively wrong rather than merely absent.

The second property is that consistency is checkable and almost nobody checks it. A component library makes it enforceable — one button component, one input component — and the enforcement mechanism is the design system's linting, which can fail a build when a raw hex value or an arbitrary margin appears outside a token.

The alignment test, and the linting that enforces it

/* ENFORCING CONSISTENCY. A design system is not a component library with a
   document; it is a set of rules that a build can fail on. The rules below are
   the ones teams most often intend and least often check. */

/* 1. NO ARBITRARY VALUES. Anything not a token is a decision that will be
      made again, differently, six months later. */
:root {
  --space-*: initial;  /* not a rule - a reminder of the principle below */
}

/* The lint rule that actually enforces it, in a stylelint config: */
/*
  {
    "rules": {
      "declaration-property-value-disallowed-list": [
        { "/color/": ["#", "rgb(", "hsl("] },
        { "/font-size|padding|margin|gap/": ["px"] }
      ],
      "declaration-property-unit-allowed-list": {
        "font-size": ["rem", "em", "%"],
        "padding": ["rem", "em"],
        "margin": ["rem", "em"]
      },
      "selector-max-id": 0,
      "max-nesting-depth": 3
    }
  }
*/
/* ...TWO OF THOSE RULES ARE WORTH THE EFFORT ON THEIR OWN:
     - NO PX IN SPACING OR FONT SIZE. It means nobody has changed the base size,
       and it means a user who set their browser's default font size to 20px
       gets a layout that ignores them. This is a far more common
       accommodation than zoom, and no media query addresses it.
     - NO MAX-NESTING-DEPTH BEYOND 3. Deep nesting is the CSS equivalent of
       an inconsistent design: nobody can say what a rule applies to, so it is
       changed in one place and not the others. */

/* 2. ALIGNMENT, which is the visible half of consistency. */
.page { display: grid; gap: var(--space-7); }
.page > * { grid-column: 1 / -1; }
.page > .narrow { max-width: 42rem; margin-inline: auto; }
/* ...THE NARROW COLUMN, centred, is the alignment mechanism for prose. A page
     whose content spans the full viewport has no alignment reference, so the
     eye has nothing to measure edge-to-edge distance against, and the whole
     screen feels unstable even when every element is correctly positioned. */

/* 3. THE WHITESPACE TEST, as a review step rather than a measurement. */
/*
   Cover the screen with a 50% grey overlay and look at what shows through.
   The lightest regions are the whitespace. What you are checking is whether
   the light regions correspond to the groups you intended:
     - a light region that cuts through a group means the group is split
     - a dark region that spans two groups means they read as one
     - no light regions at all means the layout has no visual structure and
       hierarchy is being carried entirely by weight and colour, which is the
       failure this whole chapter is about.
*/

/* 4. THE COMPONENT BOUNDARY. Consistency is what a component is FOR. */
.button { /* one definition, used everywhere */ }
/* ...and the check for whether a thing should be a component is worth stating,
     because over-componentising is a real cost:
     IT IS A COMPONENT IF IT (a) appears on three or more screens, AND
     (b) has any state - hover, focus, loading, disabled, error - that a
     consumer might implement differently.
     ...a shared element with no states is a snippet. A shared element with
     states is an API, and an API has a maintenance obligation that a snippet
     does not. Five screens of a shared header with a mobile menu is worth it;
     eight screens of a shared label is not. */

Three of the four rules, mechanically

The four rules above include one that is a review step and three that can be enforced. The enforcement mechanisms are worth showing because "consistency" is the principle in this chapter that teams believe in and do not check.

/* RULE 2, MECHANICAL: THE TOKEN AUDIT. A build step that fails when a raw
   value appears outside the token set. This is the highest-value single check
   in a design system, because it is the only one that catches drift before it
   reaches a screen. */

// tools/audit-tokens.js  - run in CI, exit 1 on a violation
const fs = require("fs");
const glob = require("fast-glob");

const RULES = [
  // Raw colour values. A hex outside the palette is a new colour that will
  // never be updated when the theme changes, which is the mechanism by which
  // a design system rots: not through a wrong decision, but through forty
  // small correct ones that were never connected to the palette.
  { re: /#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}/g,             in: "css",        allow: "tokens.css" },
  { re: /rgba?([^)]*)/g,               in: "css",        allow: "tokens.css" },
  { re: /hsla?([^)]*)/g,               in: "css",        allow: "tokens.css" },

  // Pixels in spacing and type. Two separate reasons, both real: nobody has
  // changed the base size, and a user who set their browser's default font to
  // 20px gets a layout that ignores them. The second affects roughly one user
  // in three at some point in their life and is invisible in a desktop review.
  { re: /(?<prop>margin|padding|gap|font-size|line-height)s*:s*[^;]*d+px/g,
                                                     in: "css" },

  // Inline styles, which bypass the system entirely and are un-reviewable in a
  // diff because they have no context.
  { re: /sstyles*=s*"/g,                 in: "html" },

  // Z-index outside the scale. An arbitrary z-index is a race condition with
  // a rendering bug: two components each believe they are on top, and which
  // one wins depends on DOM order rather than on intent.
  { re: /z-indexs*:s*d+/g,             in: "css",        allow: "z-index.css" },
];

const violations = [];
for (const file of glob.sync(["src/**/*.{css,html}"])) {
  const src = fs.readFileSync(file, "utf8");
  if (RULES.some((r) => r.allow === file)) continue;
  for (const rule of RULES) {
    if (rule.in !== file.split(".").pop()) continue;
    for (const m of src.matchAll(rule.re)) {
      violations.push({ file, line: src.slice(0, m.index).split("
").length, text: m[0].trim() });
    }
  }
}

if (violations.length) {
  for (const v of violations.slice(0, 40)) {
    console.error(v.file + ":" + v.line + "  " + v.text);
  }
  console.error(violations.length + " design-system violation(s)");
  process.exit(1);
}

/* RULE 3, MECHANICAL: VISUAL REGRESSION. The only way to catch a consistency
   break is to look at the thing, and the practical form is a screenshot diff
   against a committed baseline. */

// playwright.config.js - a handful of screens, not hundreds
module.exports = {
  testDir: "./visual",
  use: {
    // ONE VIEWPORT IS NOT A VISUAL TEST. Four, because the four states above
    // each produce a different screenshot and a diff against the wrong one is
    // meaningless.
    viewport: undefined,
  },
  projects: [
    { name: "mobile",  use: { viewport: { width: 390,  height: 844 } } },   // iPhone 14
    { name: "tablet",  use: { viewport: { width: 834,  height: 1112 } } },  // iPad
    { name: "laptop",  use: { viewport: { width: 1280, height: 800 } } },
    { name: "desktop", use: { viewport: { width: 1920, height: 1080 } } },
    // ...and dark mode on each, because a token that has no dark-mode value is
    //    a token that renders the light value in dark mode and a consistency
    //    bug nobody saw. Four projects become eight; the suite is minutes.
  ],
};

/* visual/pages.spec.js
   for (const [name, path] of Object.entries(PAGES)) {
     test(name, async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
       await page.goto(path);
       await page.waitForLoadState("networkidle");
       await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(name + "-" + testInfo.project.name + ".png", {
         maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.002,   // font rendering differs by platform
         animations: "disabled",     // otherwise the spinner fails every run
       });
     });
   }
*/

/* RULE 4, SEMI-MECHANICAL: THE COMPONENT INVENTORY. Not every inconsistency is
   a bug in a screen - some is two components doing the same job. The check is
   a grep for the job rather than for the visual. */

// A shared header is a component if it appears on three or more screens AND has
// states. Both conditions, because a shared element with no states is a
// snippet, and a snippet in a library is a maintenance obligation with none of
// the benefit.
const SHARED_STATES = ["hover", "focus-visible", "disabled", "loading", "error", "empty"];

/* So the audit for a design system is:
     1. THE TOKEN AUDIT (above) - mechanical, runs in CI, catches 80% of drift.
     2. THE VISUAL BASELINE - mechanical, runs in CI, catches layout drift.
     3. THE COMPONENT INVENTORY - a document, reviewed quarterly, catching the
        cases where a NEW component duplicates an EXISTING one rather than
        varying it. This is the one that cannot be automated, because the
        question is whether something should be the same, and only a person
        with the history of the product can answer it. */

1.7 Icons, illustrations & imagery

Icons are functional wayfinding tools that guide people rather than decorate, and one disciplined style makes a set feel intentional. Choose a single visual style, weight, and stroke consistency for the whole icon set, and pair an icon with a label whenever meaning is not universally recognized. Illustrations and imagery also carry emotion and set tone in empty states, but they must match the interface style. Consistent imagery reads as trust.

  • Icons are wayfinding, not decoration. A label-less icon nobody decodes fails before it’s pretty. Use standard metaphors (gear = settings, magnifier = search); pair icon + text for anything unfamiliar.
  • Stroke & grid discipline: one stroke width (1.5–2px at 16–24px), aligned to the pixel grid, max 2 visual styles per system.
  • Illustration: one consistent style (line, flat, limited palette) makes empty states and onboarding feel intentional; a mix of styles reads as broken polish.
  • Imagery: real photos beat stock for trust (real faces, real products). Set rules for crop/ratio, treatment (duotone/gradient), and dark-mode handling so imagery is a system, not a scramble.

Exercises 1

  1. Squint-test a real homepage and order its elements 1→5 by perceived importance. Compare with the product’s actual business goal.
  2. Redesign a settings screen using only: one grid, an 8pt spacing scale, and two font sizes. Nothing else changed.
  3. Pick a 3-color palette (base/primary/accent) and check its contrast on a real tool for two text-on-background pairs.

An icon is a name, and the names are a language

The section above is about drawing and choosing. The part that goes wrong in production is not the drawing — it is that icon sets are chosen visually, as collections, and visual coherence does not imply semantic coherence.

Two icon sets will both look consistent, and one of them will use a chevron for "expand", a caret for "dropdown" and a triangle for "disclosure" — three shapes for three relations that a user has to learn separately. The problem is invisible in a design review because each individual icon is correct and the set is handsome. It is only visible when you put the three related actions on one screen.

So the discipline is to choose an icon set for its grammar: does this set use one shape for all navigation-depth relationships, one shape for all completion states, one shape per severity. A set that answers yes to those three questions is worth more than a prettier set that answers no to any of them.

And the accessibility property, which is not optional and which most icon implementations get wrong in one of two directions. Either the icon is announced with no meaning — aria-hidden on a decorative icon and a visually hidden label on a meaningful one — or it is announced as "button, graphic, search" with no label, which is a screen reader reading a filename's alt text.

The implementation, and the two states that are always missing

/* ICONS AS COMPONENTS, because every icon has states and a raw SVG does not.
   A sprite with a symbol per icon; the component resolves the name. */

/*
  <svg style="display:none" aria-hidden="true">
    <symbol id="i-chevron-down" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
      <path d="M6 9l6 6 6-6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
    </symbol>
    <symbol id="i-search" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
      <circle cx="11" cy="11" r="7" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
      <path d="M16.5 16.5L21 21" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
    </symbol>
    <symbol id="i-alert-triangle" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
      <path d="M12 3L1.5 21h21L12 3z" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
      <path d="M12 10v5M12 18.5v.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>
    </symbol>
  </svg>
*/

/* THE COMPONENT. Three things every icon needs and most raw SVGs omit. */
.icon {
  width: 1.25em;
  height: 1.25em;
  flex: none;                    /* never let a flex container squash it. The
                                     most common icon bug in a toolbar is an
                                     icon that is squashed because the button
                                     is narrow, and flex-shrink defaults to 1. */
  fill: none;
  stroke: currentColor;          /* INHERITS TEXT COLOUR. An icon with a hardcoded
                                     colour is an icon that is wrong in dark
                                     mode, in a disabled state, inside a link,
                                     and in a button hover. currentColor makes
                                     all four correct for free. */
  stroke-width: 2;
  vertical-align: -0.125em;      /* optical alignment with the text baseline. The
                                     default middle alignment makes an icon sit
                                     visibly high; -0.125em is the usual
                                     correction for a 24px grid. */
}
.icon--sm { width: 1em;  height: 1em; }
.icon--lg { width: 1.5em; height: 1.5em; }

.btn .icon { margin-right: var(--space-2); }

/* THE TWO STATES EVERY ICON NEEDS. Both are routinely missing and both produce
   visible bugs. */

/* 1. THE SPINNING LOADER. A rotating icon announces nothing, so the button also
      needs its accessible name changed, and a screen reader user needs to know
      whether the action is still available. */
.btn[data-loading="true"] .icon {
  animation: icon-spin 0.8s linear infinite;
}
.btn[data-loading="true"] { pointer-events: none; opacity: 0.7; }
@keyframes icon-spin { to { transform: rotate(360deg); } }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .btn[data-loading="true"] .icon { animation: none; }
  /* ...NO SPIN UNDER REDUCED MOTION. This is a media query that costs one line
     and it is the difference between a component that works for everybody and
     one that makes some people ill. The alternative is a non-animated
     ellipsis, and either is acceptable; a permanent spin is not. */
}

/* 2. THE ICON-ONLY BUTTON. The single most common accessibility defect in
      professional interfaces. */
.icon-btn {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  width: 2.5rem;                 /* 40x40 minimum - see the target-size note
                                     below. */
  height: 2.5rem;
  border-radius: var(--radius);
  border: 1px solid var(--border-subtle);
  background: var(--surface-canvas);
}
.icon-btn:hover  { background: var(--surface-raised); }
.icon-btn:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--action-focus-ring); outline-offset: 2px; }

/*
  THE MARKUP. The label is not optional and it is not a title attribute.

  <button class="icon-btn">
    <svg class="icon" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-search"/></svg>
    <span class="vh">Search</span>
  </button>

  ...aria-hidden on the SVG because the icon is the graphic and the SPAN is the
  name. A title attribute on the SVG produces a tooltip on hover and nothing at
  all for a screen reader, which is the same as no label.
*/

/* TARGET SIZE, which is not an icon property but is governed by them. Every
   icon-only control is a target, and the guideline is 24x24 CSS pixels minimum
   with 44x44 recommended for anything used frequently or on a touch device.
   THE ICON ITSELF CAN BE SMALLER THAN THE TARGET - a 20px glyph in a 40px
   button is correct and looks better than a 40px glyph - which is only possible
   because the padding is on the button rather than baked into the SVG. An SVG
   with padding baked in at 24px cannot be made bigger than its tap target
   without looking wrong. */

/* THE ALIGNMENT NOTE, which is where most icon sets fail review */
.icon-pair { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: var(--space-2); }
/* ...The gap is on the CONTAINER, not as a margin on the icon. A margin on the
   icon means every consumer of that icon has to remember it, and one of them
   will not, and the misalignment appears in one place that nobody can explain.
   Gap on the flex container is correct by construction - every consumer gets it
   right by default, which is what consistency means when it is done properly. */

The states, and the geometry nobody specifies

The component above has the two states most often missing. The full set is five, and the geometry has a rule that is invisible until it is violated.

/* THE FIVE STATES, as one component rather than five variants. */
.icon-btn {
  --icon-btn-size: 2.5rem;
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  inline-size: var(--icon-btn-size);
  block-size: var(--icon-btn-size);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
  border: 1px solid var(--border-subtle);
  background: var(--surface-canvas);
  color: var(--text-default);
  cursor: pointer;
  transition: background 120ms ease, border-color 120ms ease;
}
.icon-btn:hover { background: var(--surface-raised); }
.icon-btn:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--action-focus-ring);
  outline-offset: 2px;
  /* ...focus-visible, NOT focus. :focus fires on mouse click as well, so a
     :focus outline appears on click and users learn to ignore it - which
     removes it for keyboard users, who are the only ones who need it.
     focus-visible fires only when the browser judges navigation to be
     keyboard-initiated. This one selector is the difference between a focus
     ring that works and a focus ring nobody has on. */
}
.icon-btn:disabled {
  color: var(--text-faint);
  cursor: not-allowed;
  background: var(--surface-sunken);
}
.icon-btn[aria-pressed="true"] {
  background: var(--action-primary);
  color: var(--action-ink);
  border-color: var(--action-primary);
  /* ...AND aria-pressed, for a toggle. An icon button that toggles and does
     not expose its state is a control whose current state only the visual
     conveys, which is the icon version of the colour-only defect. A screen
     reader announces "button" and nothing about whether it is on. */

/* THE GEOMETRY, which is the part nobody specifies and everybody notices.
   A 24x24 grid with a 2px stroke puts a 1px stroke on half-pixel centres, so
   the stroke renders across two device pixels and appears 2px wide while its
   neighbours appear 1px. This is the "some of my icons look bolder" problem. */
.icon {
  inline-size: 1.5rem;      /* 24 - the grid, not the visual size */
  block-size: 1.5rem;
  stroke-width: 1.5;        /* ...1.5, so the stroke straddles two 1px lines
                                cleanly on a 1x display. A 2px stroke on a 24
                                grid is the most common source of a set that
                                looks slightly inconsistent in weight. */
  stroke-linecap: round;
  stroke-linejoin: round;
  shape-rendering: geometricPrecision;
}
/* THE THREE GRID SIZES, and the reason they are 20, 24 and 32 rather than
   16, 24 and 32:
     20  - dense contexts, inside table rows and chips
     24  - the default, inside buttons and inputs
     32  - feature icons, empty states, list headers
   ...and the stroke width scales with the grid, so a 32px icon is not a
   24px icon scaled up - a scaled icon has a proportionally thicker stroke and
   sits visibly heavier next to its neighbours. Three grids, three stroke
   widths, one component. */
.icon--sm { inline-size: 1.25rem; block-size: 1.25rem; stroke-width: 1.25; }
.icon--lg { inline-size: 2rem;    block-size: 2rem;    stroke-width: 2; }

/* THE SIZING VARIANT THAT IS ACTUALLY A SEPARATE ICON. */
.icon--filled { fill: currentColor; stroke: none; }
.icon--outline { fill: none; stroke: currentColor; }
/* ...outline and filled are DIFFERENT icons, not a rendering mode. A filled
     gear and an outline gear have different visual weights, so a filled
     toolbar next to an outline list makes the toolbar look heavier than it is.
     Either commit to one style per surface or keep them in separate
     components - and "per surface" is a decision that has to be written down,
     because the exception is what accumulates. */

/* THE SEMANTIC RULE, which is the thing that makes an icon set a language. */
  /* Every relation gets ONE shape, used everywhere:
     - depth/navigation back    one arrow direction, everywhere
     - disclosure               one triangle, down when open and right when closed
     - completion               one check, everywhere
     - severity                 one shape per level, plus a colour, plus a label
     - destructive              one shape, always paired with a confirm step
     ...the test: put the related icons on one screen and ask whether a user
     would infer the relationship without knowing the set. If a chevron means
     "expand" in a tree and "next" in a carousel, the set is two languages and
     the user has to learn both.
     ...and the failure this prevents is invisible in review because every icon
     is individually correct. It is visible only in use, as a user hesitating
     for a fraction of a second before a chevron - which is a real and
     measurable hesitation, and it compounds across a session. */

2 · User Research

User research replaces guessing with evidence about who users are, what they want, and where they struggle. Its purpose is to ground every design decision in observed behavior rather than opinion, which prevents building the wrong thing. In practice you combine qualitative methods such as interviews with quantitative methods such as surveys, recruiting real target users and documenting findings as insights. Even a small amount of early research saves months of rework later.

2.1 Qualitative vs quantitative research2.2 Running user interviews that aren’t wasted2.3 Synthesizing: affinity mapping2.4 Personas (and their honest limits)2.5 Journey maps and experience maps2.6 The rest of the research shelf2.7 Recruiting, screeners & consent

Designing without research is guessing with the confidence of fact. This chapter gives you the beginner-to-professional toolkit for learning who users are and what they actually struggle with.

2.1 Qualitative vs quantitative research

Qualitative research explores the why behind behavior through interviews, observations, and diary studies, yielding rich understanding from small samples. Quantitative research sizes the how big and how many with surveys, analytics, and A/B tests across larger populations. Professionals alternate the two: qualitative to discover and frame a problem, quantitative to confirm its scale, then qualitative again to validate a fix. Each answers questions the other cannot.

Qualitative ("why")Quantitative ("how many")
Datawords, behavior, emotionsnumbers, rates, log data
Methodsinterviews, usability tests, diary studiessurveys, analytics, A/B tests
Answerswhy users struggle, what they meanwhich option wins, how big the problem is
Sample5–8 people per profilehundreds to thousands

The professional pattern: qualitative to discover the problem, quantitative to size it, qualitative again to validate the fix. Start small and verbal — 5 interviews already surface most of what matters.

Choosing the method by the question, not by preference

The failure mode here is not choosing qualitative or quantitative. It is choosing a method you already like and then looking for a question it can answer. A team that only runs interviews will find twenty insights and ship none of them, because no interview can tell you how common a problem is. A team that only runs surveys will find a statistically significant drop-off at a step nobody cares about and spend a quarter on it. The method follows from the shape of the question, and the shape of the question is one of four things.

The first shape is explanatory: why does this happen, and what does the problem mean to the person experiencing it. Only qualitative methods reach this, because the answer lives in a story rather than in a count. You cannot average a reason. If you have ever seen a survey ask "why do you find checkout confusing", you have seen a method that cannot produce its own answer - the respondent picks the closest-sounding option from a list the researcher wrote, and then the finding is a restatement of the list.

The second shape is descriptive: how many people do this, how often, and how long does it take. Analytics and survey both answer it, and they answer it with different biases, so the honest answer uses both. Analytics tells you what happened to people who already arrived; a survey tells you about people who left. The gap between those two populations is usually where the real problem lives, and neither source can see it alone.

The third shape is comparative: which of these two options is better. This is the only shape an A/B test genuinely answers, and it answers it for one narrow population at one narrow moment. A test on 2 percent of traffic tells you about the 2 percent. It says nothing about whether the winning design suits the segment you are not currently serving, which is a trap that catches teams running a winning test straight into general availability.

The fourth shape is generative: what could this be. There is no data on a feature that does not exist, so this is qualitative by necessity, and it is the shape people forget to name. A roadmap built without it is a roadmap of incremental improvements to something nobody asked for.

/* RESEARCH PLAN: one row per question, and the method is DERIVED from the
   question's shape rather than chosen by the team.

   The value of writing this down before recruiting is that it makes an
   unmatched question visible. A question with no method is a question that
   will be answered by whoever has the strongest opinion in the review. */

const QUESTIONS = [
  {
    q: "Why do people abandon the second step of the signup form?",
    shape: "explanatory",              // the answer is a reason, not a count
    method: "interviews",               // 5-8 participants, unmoderated follow-up
    quantifies_to: null,                // and this is deliberate - see below
    kills: "A survey here would return the options we already suspect.",
  },
  {
    q: "How many signups drop at step 2, and is it growing?",
    shape: "descriptive",              // the answer is a count
    method: "funnel analytics",
    quantifies_to: "ch2-interview",     // sizes the problem the interviews find
    kills: "Interviews cannot answer this. 8 people is not a rate.",
  },
  {
    q: "Do we keep the three-field or the single-field address form?",
    shape: "comparative",              // the answer is a difference
    method: "A/B test, 14 days, primary metric completion rate",
    quantifies_to: null,
    kills: "An interview answer is a preference. Preferences lose to behaviour.",
  },
  {
    q: "What would people use this product for that we have not built?",
    shape: "generative",               // there is no data to collect yet
    method: "diary study, 14 days",
    quantifies_to: null,
    kills: "Analytics can only describe what already exists.",
  },
];

/* THE SEQUENCING RULE, checked rather than trusted. The commonest research
   plan in a small team is four independent methods run at once, which produces
   four disconnected reports and one decision deferred by six weeks. */
function checkSequencing(questions) {
  const explanatory = questions.filter((x) => x.shape === "explanatory");
  const sizing = questions.filter((x) => x.quantifies_to);

  // every explanatory question should have a sizing question, or the finding
  // stays anecdotal and dies in the roadmap review
  const unsized = explanatory.filter(
    (x) => !sizing.some((s) => s.quantifies_to === x.q),
  );

  return {
    ok: unsized.length === 0,
    unsized: unsized.map((x) => x.q),
    rule: "discover (explanatory) -> size (descriptive) -> validate (comparative)",
  };
}

const result = checkSequencing(QUESTIONS);
console.log(result.ok ? "plan is sequenced" : "unsized: " + result.unsized);

Note the quantifies_to field. It is the only place in a research plan where one question points at another, and it is what turns four activities into a sequence: the interviews find the problem, the analytics decide whether it is worth a quarter, and the test decides whether the fix worked.

What each method cannot tell you

Reading a method's limits is more useful than reading its description, because a limit tells you when to reach for something else. Interviews cannot tell you prevalence. Eight participants is a narrative, not a rate - if three of the eight mention the same frustration, that is a strong signal that the frustration exists and no information at all about how common it is. Teams routinely quote that number as though it were 37 percent.

Surveys cannot tell you why. They can tell you that 22 percent of respondents selected "too many fields", which is a paraphrase of the survey author's own hypothesis delivered back as data. The phrasing of the answer options does more work in a survey than the behaviour being measured, and nothing in the resulting report records that fact.

A/B tests cannot tell you why either, and this surprises people who have run many of them. A test that shows a 4 percent lift tells you the treatment is better for this population on this metric. It does not tell you the mechanism, so it cannot be generalised to a different population, applied to a different surface, or explained to the team. A result you cannot explain is a result you cannot roll out with confidence, and in practice teams find the mechanism in a follow-up interview anyway.

Usability tests cannot tell you whether anyone would use the product. Five people completing a task proves the task is completable. It says nothing about frequency, nothing about willingness to pay, and nothing about whether the problem occurs often enough to care about. This is why a usability test on a feature nobody uses is not evidence the feature works - it is evidence the button is clickable.

/* THE LIMIT AS CODE. Encoding each method's blind spot as a hard check means a
   plan cannot quietly claim to answer a question its method cannot reach. This
   is the same instinct as the token audit in chapter 1: turn a principle that
   gets agreed in a meeting into something that fails. */

const LIMITS = {
  interviews: {
    // what it is good for
    answers: ["explanatory", "generative"],
    // and what a reviewer must not claim from it
    cannot: {
      descriptive: "no prevalence: 8 participants is a narrative, not a rate",
      comparative: "preferences stated in an interview lose to real behaviour",
    },
  },
  survey: {
    answers: ["descriptive", "comparative"],
    cannot: {
      explanatory: "the answer options were written by the researcher, so the finding restates the options",
      generative: "a survey can only ask about things that already exist",
    },
  },
  "a-b-test": {
    answers: ["comparative"],
    cannot: {
      explanatory: "a lift is not a mechanism, so the result cannot be generalised or explained",
      generative: "it optimises a metric someone already chose",
    },
  },
  analytics: {
    answers: ["descriptive"],
    cannot: {
      // the important one: analytics only sees people who ARRIVED, so it is
      // structurally blind to anyone the product lost on the way in
      explanatory: "it shows what happened, never why it happened",
      generative: "there is no event stream for a feature that does not exist",
      comparative: "observational, not experimental, so correlation is not causation",
    },
  },
  "usability-test": {
    answers: ["explanatory"],
    cannot: {
      descriptive: "5 completions is not a rate of anything",
      comparative: "one variant at a time, so there is nothing to compare",
    },
  },
};

/* A plan is sound when every question's shape is inside its method's reach.
   Fails loudly, with the reason, rather than producing a report whose central
   claim is not supported by the method that produced it. */
function auditPlan(questions) {
  const faults = [];
  for (const { q, method, shape } of questions) {
    const limit = LIMITS[method];
    if (!limit) { faults.push(q + ": unknown method " + method); continue; }
    if (!limit.answers.includes(shape)) {
      faults.push(q + ": " + method + " cannot answer a " + shape + " question");
      continue;
    }
    const blind = limit.cannot[shape];
    if (blind) faults.push(q + ": " + blind);
  }
  return faults;
}

module.exports = { LIMITS, auditPlan };

The blind-spot entry for analytics is the one worth internalising: an event stream only contains people who already got past the door, so the metric that looks healthiest is computed on the population that survived the worst step.

Put the two together and the practical consequence is that a research plan is not a list of methods but a set of handoffs. Every qualitative finding that reaches the roadmap should have a number attached to it by the end of the study, and that number should come from a source whose known blind spot does not overlap with the finding. When it does overlap - when the interview found a problem inside step 2 and the analytics can only see people who finished step 2 - you need the support-ticket log or a survey of abandoners, and you need to know that before the roadmap review, not during it.

2.2 Running user interviews that aren’t wasted

User interviews produce reliable insight only when the script avoids leading and hypothetical questions that prompt the answers you expect. Ask about concrete past behavior, one question at a time, and follow with silence so the participant elaborates naturally. A well-structured interview guide plus five or six carefully recruited participants will surface most recurring themes. Avoid asking what users would do in the future, since people are poor predictors of their own behavior.

# The 5 rules that double interview quality:
#   1. Ask about PAST BEHAVIOUR, not opinions   ("tell me about the last
#      time you returned a product") not ("would you like returns?")
#   2. One question at a time; then SHUT UP (silence is your friend)
#   3. No leading questions:                    ("what did you try?")
#      never                          ("didn't you try the search box?")
#   4. Ask for a story, then dig: "what happened next?", "why?"
#   5. Capture what they DID, not what they SAID they'd do
# Sample script skeleton:
#    intro / consent  > warm-up  > their story (the meat)
#    > follow-up > closing ("anything I missed?")

Why people describe a stranger

Every rule in the guide above exists to fight one failure: the participant answering the question you hoped for. It is not dishonesty. It is the ordinary behaviour of a helpful person being asked to be helpful - they want you to succeed, they want to sound like a considered customer, and they have a mental model of what a good customer says rather than a record of what they did last Tuesday.

Stated preference and revealed preference diverge more than teams expect, and they diverge in a consistent direction. Ask whether someone would use a feature and they answer about an idealized version of themselves: the version with time, patience, and motivation. Watch what they do and you see the version with a deadline. The gap between the two is exactly where the design errors live, and no amount of care in the question wording closes it - only changing what you ask about does.

That is why the script asks about the last time rather than about what someone would do. "The last time you bought something online, walk me through it" produces a sequence of real decisions, real compromises, and the moment they gave up on a competitor and did it differently. "How would you buy something online" produces a summary of best practice that any competent person could give you and that tells you nothing.

Past behaviour has a second property that makes it reliable: it comes with its own constraints attached. The participant volunteers the deadline, the phone with a cracked screen, the shared account, the fact that they only use the app at the supermarket. Those constraints are the design requirements, and nobody will hand them to you in a hypothetical. A feature designed for an unconstrained user is a feature designed for a person who does not exist.

/* THE REFRAME, AS CODE. The most useful single transformation in user research
   is turning a future question into a past one. This is small on purpose: it is
   a rewrite step in a research tool, and it is worth writing down because the
   transformation is easy to remember and easy to forget under time pressure. */

const REFRAMES = [
  {
    from: "Would you use a feature that does X?",
    to: "Tell me about the last time you needed X. What did you do?",
    // what breaks without the reframe
    why: "the first asks about an idealized user; the second replays a decision",
  },
  {
    from: "Do you find this confusing?",
    to: "Walk me through this screen. Where did you look first?",
    why: "self-report of difficulty is unreliable; observed search tells you where the confusion is",
  },
  {
    from: "How much would you pay for X?",
    to: "What did you pay for the last one, and what made it that much?",
    why: "hypothetical willingness to pay is famously uncalibrated; real prices are observable",
  },
  {
    from: "Do you understand this?",
    to: "What do you think will happen if you press this?",
    why: "asking for understanding invites a yes; asking for a prediction invites a wrong answer you can watch happen",
  },
  {
    from: "Is this layout clear?",
    to: "Where would you look for X on this screen?",
    why: "a clarity question is answered from a preference; a search question is answered from behaviour",
  },
];

/* Applied to a note, this turns the guide from a list of questions into a list
   of situations to ask about. */
function buildGuide(steps, method) {
  return steps.map((step) => {
    const r = REFRAMES.find((x) => x.from === step.ask);
    return {
      scenario: step.situation,        // the concrete context the story lives in
      ask: r ? r.to : step.ask,
      original: r ? r.from : null,
      probe: step.probe || "what happened next?",
    };
  });
}

The fourth row is the strongest one for usability work. "What do you think will happen if you press this?" produces a prediction you can then watch be right or wrong, which converts an interview into something closer to a test without changing the format.

Silence, and the shape of a full answer

The technique most beginners lose is silence. After a participant answers, the instinct is to speak - to say "so what made you choose that?", to fill the gap, to move to the next question. Every one of those interventions ends the story early. The most valuable material in an interview is usually the thirty seconds after the participant thinks they have answered, where they qualify what they said, explain the exception, or mention the thing they did not plan to mention. Fill that silence and you have politely ended the interview at its most informative moment.

Count to three. It feels like thirty. The participant will almost always break first, and what they break into is the part that makes the finding real. This is uncomfortable and it is not going to get better with experience; it is a technique you apply deliberately rather than a disposition you grow into.

A full answer has a recognisable shape, and listening for it is most of the moderator's job. A complete account of one past episode runs situation, then goal, then the sequence of actions taken, then the moment it went wrong, then what they did about it, then what happened next. The fourth beat - the moment it went wrong - is where every insight lives, and it is usually buried in the middle of a rambling answer rather than delivered as its own paragraph.

When the shape is missing, the probe is about the missing beat, not about the next topic. If there was no stated goal, ask what they were trying to achieve. If there was no turning point, ask what they expected to happen next and what happened instead. If there is no consequence, ask what it cost them. Each of these is a single question about one beat, and none of them introduces a new subject.

/* THE BEAT CHECK: a note-taker's aid that makes the missing beat visible while
   the interview is still running, which is the only time it can be fixed. The
   important design decision is that it marks ABSENCE rather than telling the
   moderator what to do, because the moderator knows the participant and this
   does not. */

const BEATS = [
  { key: "situation", label: "when and where it happened" },
  { key: "goal",      label: "what they were trying to achieve" },
  { key: "actions",   label: "the sequence they actually took" },
  { key: "break",     label: "the moment it stopped going to plan" },
  { key: "workaround",label: "what they did about it" },
  { key: "outcome",   label: "what it ended up costing them" },
];

// one entry per turn of the conversation
const turns = [
  { note: "so it was in the supermarket, about eleven at night",
    beats: ["situation"] },
  { note: "he was meant to pay me back on friday so it was short",
    beats: ["situation", "goal"] },
  { note: "the page kept asking for the postcode again so i typed the shop one",
    beats: ["actions", "break", "workaround"] },
  { note: "in the end i gave up and paid cash, i still had the app on my phone",
    beats: ["outcome"] },
];

function missingBeats(turns) {
  const seen = new Set(turns.flatMap((t) => t.beats));
  return BEATS.filter((b) => !seen.has(b.key)).map((b) => ({
    beat: b.key,
    ask: "and " + b.label + "?",
  }));
}

// the one probe worth always asking, because it is the beat that carries the
// design requirement and the one people skip when time is short
const ALWAYS = "what happened next?";

module.exports = { BEATS, missingBeats, ALWAYS };

Run against the notes above, it reports workaround as covered by the postcode turn and still asks for the consequence - the amount of money left on the shelf, which is the sentence that gets a redesign funded.

Recording is part of the technique rather than an administrative detail. A note-taker working alone cannot also hold the pacing, so recordings get transcribed within a day, and the transcript is annotated the same day, while the shape of the conversation is still audible. A transcript annotated a week later has lost the pauses, and the pauses are where the discomfort lived - the moment the participant's voice changed is the moment something real was said.

Five rules plus a script skeleton keep interviews anchored in past behavior and full stories instead of polite opinions. Notice how every prompt invites a narrative.

Participants lie — politely. People say they’d pay €30 for the app; data shows abandonment. Believe recorded behavior and stories, treat stated preferences as hypotheses. This is why you combine interviews with analytics and tests.

2.3 Synthesizing: affinity mapping

Affinity mapping turns a pile of raw interview notes and observations into shared themes by clustering related notes on sticky notes or a digital board. Group the notes silently first, then name each cluster with an insight that captures the underlying need or pain point. The named clusters become actionable requirements, patterns, and priorities that drive the design. Do it as a team so interpretations get challenged and insight is shared.

Write every observation from all interviews on notes; sort into clusters silently; name each cluster. The named clusters become your insights ("users trust this product only after seeing real reviews"). Insights → design requirements → solutions. This one act separates professionals from novices who "just start designing".

Clustering silently, and naming only afterwards

The instruction to group silently is doing more work than it appears to. The moment you write a label on a cluster you have started to fit evidence to a theory, and every later note is then read as confirmation or contradiction of your own words. Five teams that affinity-map together produce five different-looking boards for the same six interviews, and the difference is almost always the labels, not the evidence.

Silent grouping also produces genuinely mixed clusters, which is where the findings are. A cluster of notes that do not agree with each other is telling you that your segmentation is wrong. If every note in a cluster says the same thing in the same words, you have probably grouped by topic rather than by meaning, and you will produce a restatement of your research questions rather than a finding.

Naming comes last and each name is a full sentence, not a noun. "Checkout" is a topic. "Users need to check an order without remembering an account" is an insight, because it implies what you could build. A cluster named with a noun produces requirements that are really just section headings; a cluster named with a sentence about the person produces requirements you can act on, and it is immediately arguable, which is a good sign - a finding nobody can disagree with is usually a finding nobody will act on.

/* AFFINITY MAPPING, AS A TOOL. Two jobs, and the second one is the valuable
   one: not the clustering, which a person does better by moving sticky notes
   around, but the CHECKING. A board is a claim about what recurs, so the claim
   is testable - does this name actually hold up against the notes, and how many
   distinct people is it standing on. */

const NOTES = [
  { id: "n1", person: "p1", text: "i never remember which account i used at the shop" },
  { id: "n2", person: "p1", text: "the confirmation email has the number in it, thats my only copy" },
  { id: "n3", person: "p2", text: "ask for postcode like four times, gave up eventually" },
  { id: "n4", person: "p2", text: "paid cash instead, was quicker than arguing with the page" },
  { id: "n5", person: "p3", text: "my sister orders on my account, i just pay her back" },
  { id: "n6", person: "p4", text: "took a screenshot of the order number, thats how i check it" },
  { id: "n7", person: "p5", text: "the app logs me out every morning, so i use the website" },
  { id: "n8", person: "p5", text: "no idea what my order number is, so i just phone them" },
];

// clusters are named as SENTENCES. The name is the deliverable; the grouping
// is just the mechanism that produced it.
const CLUSTERS = [
  {
    name: "Users cannot retrieve an order without an account or a stored number",
    notes: ["n1", "n2", "n3", "n4", "n6", "n8"],
  },
  {
    name: "Shared accounts break the identity model the checkout assumes",
    notes: ["n5", "n7"],
  },
];

function evidence(cluster, notes) {
  const ids = new Set(cluster.notes);
  const members = notes.filter((n) => ids.has(n.id));

  // people, not notes. Ten notes from one person is one data point, and a
  // cluster where one person dominates is a finding about that person.
  const people = [...new Set(members.map((m) => m.person))];

  return {
    people: people.length,
    notes: members.length,
    // the concentration check: if one person is most of the cluster, say so,
    // because this is the single most common way a small board overstates
    concentrated: people.length <= 2 || members.length > people.length * 3,
    verbatim: members.slice(0, 2).map((m) => m.text),
  };
}

module.exports = { CLUSTERS, evidence };

Three notes from one participant and one from another is a finding about the first participant. concentrated is the flag for it, and it is worth building into the board itself rather than trusting the team to notice.

Turning a named insight into a requirement you can design against

An insight is a claim about a need. It is not yet a specification, and the gap between the two is where research goes to die. "Users cannot retrieve an order" does not tell you what to build. It could be a search box, a guest lookup, a link in the confirmation email, or an SMS. Each of those is a different product decision with a different cost, and each is defensible against the insight and wrong against a different one.

The move that closes the gap is to state the requirement as a constraint rather than a solution. Not "add a search box" but "a user with no account can retrieve their order using only what they received". That statement can be designed against, tested, and argued with, and several different designs can satisfy it. A requirement written as a solution has already made the design decision that the research was supposed to inform.

Then rank, and rank by evidence plus cost rather than by how loud the cluster feels. The usual ordering is frequency of the pain, severity of the consequence, and breadth across segments - and the third is the one that decides whether something belongs on the main path or behind a workaround. A pain that is severe but affects one segment is a feature; a pain that is mild and affects everyone is a platform problem.

/* INSIGHT -> REQUIREMENT -> CRITERIA. The requirement is written as a constraint
   because a constraint can be designed against and a solution cannot. The
   criteria then exist so the requirement can fail: an unmeasurable requirement
   survives to launch. */

const INSIGHT_TO_REQUIREMENT = {
  "Users cannot retrieve an order without an account or a stored number": {
    requirement:
      "A user with no account can retrieve their order using only what they already received",
    // deliberately not "add a search box" - that is one of several designs that
    // satisfy the constraint, and choosing it here is the researcher's job
    designs_that_satisfy_it: [
      "lookup by order number and postcode on the confirmation link",
      "guest checkout with an emailed link that survives session loss",
      "SMS lookup on the number used at checkout",
    ],
    // how we will know it is met, stated before anything is built
    criteria: {
      measurable: "task success on retrieval without an account, tested with 5 users",
      threshold: "5 of 5 complete it in under 60 seconds with no verbal help",
      // and what would count as a fail, which is the part that is usually
      // missing and is the reason a requirement outlives its evidence
      fails_if: "users ask support how to find their order number, because the constraint was met and the need was not",
    },
    severity: 4,        // consequence: money left on a shelf, trust in the brand
    breadth: 5,         // every returning customer without an account
    segments: ["p1", "p2", "p3", "p4", "p5"],
  },
};

function prioritise(byRequirement) {
  // effort is an estimate in the same arbitrary units, which is fine: it only
  // has to be comparable within one list to be useful for ordering
  return Object.entries(byRequirement)
    .map(([insight, r]) => ({
      insight,
      requirement: r.requirement,
      // severity and breadth are 1-5 from the research; effort is a guess.
      // separating the measured columns from the guessed one is the point -
      // a score that blends them cannot be argued with.
      score: r.severity * r.breadth,
      measured: { severity: r.severity, breadth: r.breadth, segments: r.segments.length },
      guessed: { effort: null, comment: "fill in before the roadmap meeting" },
      criteria: r.criteria,
    }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score);
}

The fails_if field is the part worth keeping. It is written before anything exists, so it cannot be rationalised after the fact, and it names the way a design can satisfy its requirement and still miss the need - which is exactly the conversation that gets skipped.

Do the synthesis as a team and write the names live where everyone can see them being written. Disagreement about a cluster's name is productive because it means two people read the same evidence differently, and the cheaper you find that disagreement now rather than after the design is built. Where two people read evidence differently the answer is more evidence, not a vote.

2.4 Personas (and their honest limits)

Personas are research-based archetypes that summarize the goals, behaviors, and frustrations of a user segment so the team can design for someone concrete. Build them from real interview data, including verbatim quotes and observed behaviors, rather than invented demographics or stereotypes. They keep a team focused and aligned during decisions, but they become fiction when detached from evidence. Treat them as living summaries that must be refreshed when new research arrives.

  • Personas are synthesized archetypes ("primary", "secondary"), built from research — not invented demographics. They keep the team focused and humanize users in meetings.
  • Anti-personas ("the novice intern", "the security auditor") identify who you are not designing for, useful for scope control.
  • Don’t let personas become fiction: ground every trait in an interview quote, and update them as research accumulates.
// Persona card — keep it behavioral, not demographic:
Name:    "Jen", 23, part-time barista
Goal:    track her week + tips without pain
Friction (quote): "Apps scream at me if I open them at midnight."
Needs:   fast entry, no guilt, offline mode
Triggers: end of shift / end of week
Not-for: enterprise multi-currency reporting (anti-persona)

Grounding every trait in something that was said

The failure mode of personas is not that they are invented. It is that they decay. A persona written from six interviews is genuinely grounded on the day it is written, and then it gets copied into a deck, and the deck gets copied into a brief, and each copy loses the quotes that made it credible. Within two quarters the artifact is a cartoon: a name, an age range, and three adjectives, and it is being used to justify decisions that the research never supported.

The defence is structural rather than cultural. A persona trait that cannot be traced to a note cannot be defended in a meeting, and the team should have to look it up. Putting the evidence identifier next to the trait - not in an appendix, on the card - makes the difference visible in the moment. "p3, n5: asked for her sister to order because he could not log in" is a sentence that either supports the design or it does not.

This also handles the demographic drift that makes personas worthless. Age and job title get added because they are easy to fill in, and then the design starts optimising for them: a form that assumes one browser because the persona is 45, a checkout that asks for a company name because the persona is a buyer. Behavioural traits resist this, because a behavioural trait is falsifiable by observation - if the persona does their own shopping on a phone at the supermarket, a desktop-only flow is wrong for them regardless of their age.

/* THE EVIDENCE LINK. A persona as data, so every trait carries the notes that
   produced it. This is not bookkeeping for its own sake: it is the mechanism
   that makes a persona checkable, and a checkable persona can be wrong in a
   way that gets fixed rather than defended. */

const PERSONA = {
  id: "P1",
  role: "primary",
  name: "the evening shopper",            // a situation, not a first name
  // the goal is the load-bearing part; everything else is decoration
  goal: "buy one specific thing and get home",
  context: "commuting home, one hand on the child, roughly eleven at night",
  traits: [
    { trait: "cannot remember which account was used",      from: ["p1/n1"] },
    { trait: "treats the confirmation email as the receipt", from: ["p1/n2", "p4/n6"] },
    { trait: "abandons rather than repeat an error",        from: ["p2/n4"] },
    { trait: "pays cash rather than escalate",              from: ["p2/n4", "p5/n8"] },
    { trait: "shares an account with a household member",   from: ["p3/n5"] },
  ],
  antiPersona: {
    // naming who you are NOT designing for is the cheapest scope control there
    // is, and the one teams skip because it feels negative
    who: "the procurement officer who evaluates on a compliance checklist",
    // a design that serves the anti-persona often sacrifices the primary for a
    // user who will never be the majority, so this must be visible in reviews
    rule: "never trade a primary-persona task for anti-persona compliance",
  },
  // what would make us rebuild this persona rather than adjust it
  stale_if: {
    notes: 12,
    reason: "the goal has changed, so it is a different job and a different design",
  },
};

/* Walk every trait back to the notes. A trait with no note is an assumption
   wearing a persona's clothes, and it is the one a reviewer should refuse. */
function auditPersona(persona, notes) {
  const untethered = persona.traits.filter((t) => !t.from || t.from.length === 0);
  const unresolvable = persona.traits.flatMap((t) =>
    (t.from || []).filter((ref) => !notes.some((n) => n.id === ref)),
  );
  return {
    ok: untethered.length === 0 && unresolvable.length === 0,
    untethered: untethered.map((t) => t.trait),
    unresolvable,
    note: unresolvable.length
      ? "a note id that no longer exists means the research was re-cut and the persona was not revisited"
      : "",
  };
}

If the notes behind a persona have been re-cut, its ids stop resolving and auditPersona fails. That is the intended signal: re-cutting the research invalidates the personas built on it, and nothing else in the process will notice.

Primary, secondary, and the cost of too many

A product has one primary persona per goal, and a goal is a job the person is trying to do, not a feature they use. "The evening shopper buying a specific known item" and "the evening shopper browsing" are two goals, and they want different products - one needs to be fast and get out of the way, the other needs discovery and inspiration. Collapsing them produces a homepage that is neither.

Secondary personas cover goals that matter but do not define the product. Their real function is to stop you optimising every surface for the primary and abandoning everyone else, and they belong in the criteria rather than in every screen: if the primary is served, the secondary should still be able to complete their task, and that is a testable condition.

Beyond three, personas stop doing work. Past that point you are making per-group specifications rather than a shared picture, and the meetings get longer without getting clearer, because each participant arrives advocating for a character rather than for the evidence. The honest move is to convert the overflow into segments in analytics - where they can be measured - and keep personas for the two or three that carry the product's purpose.

/* THE FIT CHECK: does this design decision serve the primary persona without
   breaking the others. Run it as a review question with a checkable answer,
   because "is this good for the user" has no answer and this does. */

const ROSTER = [
  {
    id: "P1", role: "primary", goal: "buy a specific known item fast",
    // the trade-off each persona is FOR, stated up front - this is what makes
    // prioritisation a judgement rather than a measurement
    accepts: ["no recommendations", "one page", "fewer filters"],
    refuses: ["a sign-up wall", "a carousel on the landing screen"],
  },
  {
    id: "P2", role: "secondary", goal: "discover something to buy",
    accepts: ["more content", "longer sessions"],
    refuses: ["reduced catalogue"],
  },
  {
    id: "P3", role: "secondary", goal: "track an existing order",
    accepts: ["a different screen entirely"],
    refuses: ["losing the reference number"],
  },
];

function reviewDecision({ label, serves, breaks }) {
  const primary = ROSTER.filter((p) => p.role === "primary");
  const secondary = ROSTER.filter((p) => p.role !== "primary");

  const harmsPrimary = primary.some((p) => p.refuses.includes(label));
  const harmsSecondary = secondary.filter((p) => p.refuses.includes(label));

  return {
    label,
    // a primary harm is a stop, full stop - no amount of secondary gain
    // offsets it, which is the whole reason "primary" is a role
    verdict: harmsPrimary ? "REJECT" : harmsSecondary.length ? "SECONDARY COST" : "CLEAR",
    // and the asymmetry is stated, so it cannot be quietly levelled later
    rule: harmsPrimary
      ? "refused by the primary persona"
      : harmsSecondary.length
        ? "costs " + harmsSecondary.map((p) => p.id).join(", ") + " - record it, do not silently drop it"
        : "serves the primary and costs nobody",
    unaccounted: serves.filter((id) => !ROSTER.some((p) => p.id === id)),
  };
}

A decision that serves nobody on the roster returns unaccounted, and that is usually the most interesting result of the review: it is a decision justified by something other than the research.

Treat a persona as a summary with a review date, not a document. The moment new research contradicts a trait, the trait is updated in place and the old version goes, because a persona that accumulates contradictory versions becomes a place where any argument can be sourced. The useful test is whether someone outside the team can read a trait and immediately go and check it; if the answer is no, the persona is decoration and should be deleted rather than maintained.

This persona card stays behavioral end to end: name, goal, a real quote, triggers, plus an explicit anti-persona to keep scope contained.

2.5 Journey maps and experience maps

A journey map shows the steps a persona takes through a scenario over time, along with their actions, thoughts, emotions, and pain points at each stage. The emotional line is the key output because it reveals where satisfaction drops and people abandon the experience. Build it from interview evidence rather than assumptions, then use the dips as a prioritized list of problems to design against. It turns a fuzzy experience into a visible timeline.

A journey map shows a persona’s steps over time for a defined scenario — from "awareness" through "post-purchase". For each step note: actions, touchpoints, emotions, pain points, opportunities. Emotional line graphs (happy → frustrated) are the classic reveal: teams fix the visible drop-offs.

Read the emotional line, not the steps

A journey map is easy to build and easy to misread. The columns - awareness, consideration, purchase, delivery, support - are almost always correct and almost always uninteresting, because they describe the organisation's process rather than the person's. The row that carries the finding is the emotional one, and teams routinely build the map, agree that the steps are right, and then redesign the checkout because it is the step they happen to remember being annoyed in.

The line is drawn from evidence, not from imagination, and that is the only part that is hard. For each stage you need something the participant said or did that indicates the state they were in: the moment their confidence dropped, the step they tried twice, the question they asked before continuing. If you cannot point at a quote or an observation for a plotted point, the point is your own feeling about that step, and it will bias the whole map toward the stage you personally find annoying.

Plotting two personas on the same chart is where the map earns its keep. One line is a narrative; two lines show you where the experiences diverge, and the divergence is nearly always at a stage where one group needs a task the other does not. That stage is either a wrongly shared screen or a missing mode, and you cannot see either from a single perspective.

/* THE EMOTIONAL LINE, COMPUTED. The point of this sample is that a
   hand-drawn happiness curve is decoration, and the drop it reveals can be
   measured from the evidence instead. Emotions are scored -2 to +2 from a
   quote or an observation, never from intuition, and the code refuses a
   stage that has no evidence attached to it. */

const STAGES = [
  {
    stage: "awareness", persona: "P1",
    // every score carries the evidence that produced it. A score with no
    // source is a guess wearing a number, and it is exactly the guess that
    // becomes a roadmap item.
    score: 1, evidence: ["p1/n1: found the site after a friend's message"],
  },
  {
    stage: "search", persona: "P1",
    score: -1, evidence: ["p1/n2: could not find the item, searched by name only"],
  },
  {
    stage: "checkout", persona: "P1",
    // the worst point, and the one with the most evidence behind it
    score: -2, evidence: ["p2/n3: postcode asked four times", "p2/n4: gave up and paid cash"],
  },
  {
    stage: "confirmation", persona: "P1",
    // and note this is also a LOW point even though it is technically the
    // success screen. Success is not the same as relief, and a map that
    // rounds up to +2 here hides the follow-up support call it causes.
    score: -1, evidence: ["p4/n6: screenshot the number because the page closed"],
  },
  {
    stage: "delivery", persona: "P1",
    score: 0, evidence: ["p1: reported no contact with the delivery"],
  },
  {
    stage: "support", persona: "P1",
    score: -2, evidence: ["p5/n8: phoned to ask what had happened"],
  },
];

function emotionalLine(stages, persona) {
  const mine = stages.filter((s) => s.persona === persona);
  const unsourced = mine.filter((s) => !s.evidence || s.evidence.length === 0);
  if (unsourced.length) {
    throw new Error("stages scored without evidence: " + unsourced.map((s) => s.stage));
  }
  return mine.map((s) => ({ stage: s.stage, score: s.score, evidence: s.evidence }));
}

function worstMoment(line) {
  // the lowest point, but the thing to FIX is the RISE after it: recovery cost
  // is where the money is, because a dip is one failure and a dip followed by
  // a workaround is a permanent behaviour
  let at = 0;
  line.forEach((p, i) => { if (p.score < line[at].score) at = i; });
  return {
    stage: line[at].stage,
    score: line[at].score,
    // what people do instead, which is the real design requirement
    recovery: line[at].evidence.filter((e) => /gave up|called|phoned|instead/.test(e)),
  };
}

module.exports = { emotionalLine, worstMoment };

The recovery lines are what a journey map is actually for. A dip without a stated workaround is an inconvenience; a dip with one is a behaviour you will have to design around forever, because the workaround is what your users will keep doing.

From the map to a sequence of fixes

A map is a diagnosis, and the temptation is to treat it as a plan. Twenty stages each with two pain points is forty items, and a team that ships all forty has shipped nothing. The map's job is to produce an ordering, and the ordering comes from the height of the dip multiplied by how expensive the recovery is: a -1 that people shrug off costs less than a -1 that sends them to a competitor.

Then fix the shape, not the points. Most pain on a journey map comes from one repeated error - the postcode asked four times, the password rejected with no explanation - and a team that fixes the four stages where it surfaces has done four times the work for the same result. Find the repeated moment and the map usually collapses to two or three changes.

Put a number on the outcome afterwards, and choose it before you start so it cannot be chosen afterwards. Time-to-complete on the broken stage is usually the most honest measure, because it improves when the experience improves and cannot be moved by making the page prettier. Support contact volume on that stage is the second choice, and it is better because it measures the workaround rather than the click.

/* THE SEQUENCING, WITH THE MEASUREMENT CHOSEN UP FRONT. A journey map that
   ends in a list of improvements has failed at the last step, because the
   improvements will be argued about on taste rather than on the number that
   was agreed before any of them were built. */

const STAGE_FIXES = [
  {
    stage: "search",
    pain: "cannot find a known item",
    // one repeated error, not a stage: search on the confirmation and search
    // in the header are the same defect surfacing twice
    root_cause: "the catalogue search matches names only, so a typo returns nothing",
    fix: "fuzzy match on name, brand and the token the customer already has",
    // stated BEFORE building. Chosen now, or it will be chosen later by whoever
    // is most confident.
    measure: "time from landing to a search result containing the target item",
    threshold: "median under 4 seconds across 20 sessions",
    // and the secondary measure, because the primary can be improved by making
    // results wrong in a faster way
    guard: "search result click-through does not fall",
  },
  {
    stage: "checkout",
    pain: "postcode asked repeatedly, abandoned",
    root_cause: "the address field validates on blur against a list that excludes partial postcodes",
    fix: "validate on submit, accept partial, and remember the accepted value",
    measure: "checkout completion rate",
    threshold: "up from the measured baseline by a stated margin",
    guard: "wrong-address returns do not rise",
  },
  {
    stage: "confirmation",
    pain: "screenshots the order number because the page closes",
    root_cause: "the confirmation is the only place the reference exists",
    // the deepest fix on the map, and the one that also removes the support call
    fix: "the reference goes into an emailed link that survives session loss",
    measure: "support contacts about locating an order",
    threshold: "halved within a month of launch",
    guard: "email deliverability does not fall",
  },
];

function sequence(fixes) {
  return fixes
    .map((f) => ({ ...f, primary_only: f.measure + " (also watch: " + f.guard + ")" }))
    // ordered by how far up the journey the fix sits, because an upstream fix
    // removes work from every stage below it and a downstream one does not
    .sort((a, b) => STAGE_FIXES.indexOf(a) - STAGE_FIXES.indexOf(b));
}

Every fix carries a guard as well as a primary measure, because each primary has a cheap way to improve it dishonestly - faster wrong results, or a completion rate propped up by a form that quietly defaults to the last address used.

A map with one persona is a service blueprint with extra steps. Two is where it starts earning its cost: the divergence between the lines tells you which screens need to differ, and that is a much cheaper thing to discover here than in a usability test six weeks later. Beyond three lines the chart stops being readable, which is the practical ceiling rather than a rule.

2.6 The rest of the research shelf

Beyond interviews and journey maps, a shelf of research methods each answers one specific question: contextual inquiry observes real usage in context, diaries capture behavior over time, surveys measure prevalence, competitor analysis surveys the landscape, and support tickets surface recurring complaints. Choose the cheapest method that can answer your exact question, mining support tickets and analytics first. Expensive methods add richness only when a cheap one cannot answer the question.

ToolQuestion it answersWhen
Contextual inquiryHow is this done in the wild?Observe people in their environment
Diary studyHow do habits form over days/weeks?Longitudinal behaviors
SurveysHow common is this? Who are they?After you know the right question
Competitive analysisWhat conventions exist already?Whenever you start a domain
Support/CS ticketsWhere do users get stuck with words?Free gold mine — mine it first

Picking the cheapest method that can actually answer

The table above lists methods without ranking them, and that is the trap: read as a menu, the shelf implies that each method costs about the same and you should choose the one your team is best at. The methods are not interchangeable, because two questions dominate the choice. Can this method answer the specific question, and can it answer it at a price the answer is worth?
