The ordering that falls out of those two questions is roughly by cost, and it puts the free methods first - which is not because they are the most informative but because they are already being collected and a team that mines them before commissioning research is doing something most teams skip. Support tickets, session recordings, search logs and sales-call notes are all free, all already exist, and all cover thousands of real events rather than five conversations. Start there on every project, whatever the question.

Then analytics for anything about scale and frequency, because they are the only method that can report a rate. Then surveys for prevalence across people the product has not seen, which is the one thing analytics cannot give you. Then interviews, diaries and contextual inquiry, which cost real money per session and buy depth that nothing else reaches. Field studies and full diary programmes sit at the top and are warranted only when the decision they inform is worth their cost.

/* METHOD SELECTION, AS A LOOKUP RATHER THAN A MENU. The value is in the cost
   column being a real number, because "cheap" and "expensive" are opinions
   and a team picks the method it enjoys using. Here the cost is per session
   plus the calendar delay, because the slowest method is the one that misses a
   deadline. */

const METHODS = {
  "support-tickets": {
    cost: 0, days: 0,
    answers: ["descriptive"],
    sample: "thousands of real events, already collected",
    // the limit that decides it: it is a survivorship sample of people who
    // already decided to complain, so it tells you what is wrong but never how
    // widespread it is
    limit: "only people who gave up enough to write - never a rate",
  },
  "session-recording": {
    cost: 0, days: 1,
    answers: ["descriptive", "explanatory"],
    limit: "silent on why, and heavy sessions are over-represented if you sample by length",
  },
  analytics: {
    cost: 0, days: 0,
    answers: ["descriptive", "comparative"],
    limit: "observational, and only sees people who arrived",
  },
  survey: {
    cost: 400, days: 10,
    answers: ["descriptive", "comparative"],
    limit: "the option wording is yours, so it cannot explain anything",
  },
  interviews: {
    cost: 300, days: 14,
    answers: ["explanatory", "generative"],
    limit: "no rate, ever",
  },
  "usability-test": {
    cost: 350, days: 7,
    answers: ["explanatory"],
    limit: "proves a task is completable, not that anyone wants it",
  },
  "diary-study": {
    cost: 900, days: 21,
    answers: ["generative", "explanatory"],
    limit: "slow: the finding cannot exist before the diary period ends",
  },
  "field-study": {
    cost: 4000, days: 30,
    answers: ["explanatory", "generative"],
    limit: "justified only when the decision it informs is worth thousands",
  },
};

/* Rank the shelf against one question, then take the cheapest method that can
   answer it. Never take the first method whose answer is interesting. */
function recommend(questionShape, alreadyHave) {
  const able = Object.entries(METHODS).filter(([, m]) => m.answers.includes(questionShape));

  return able
    .filter(([name]) => (alreadyHave || []).includes(name))
    .concat(able.filter(([name]) => !(alreadyHave || []).includes(name)))
    .map(([name, m]) => ({ method: name, cost: m.cost, days: m.days, limit: m.limit }))
    .sort((a, b) => a.cost - b.cost || a.days - b.days)[0];
}

Methods already collected are filtered to the front, so the recommendation spends nothing on a method that already exists in a dashboard somewhere. That single ordering has saved more research budgets than any other habit in this chapter.

Reading what a method leaves out

Each method has a population it over-represents, and the population is almost always the same one: the people who struggled most. Support tickets come from the angriest decile. Session recordings sampled by length over- represent the sessions that went badly. Usability tests recruit people willing to be watched, and diaries drop out precisely when the task becomes painful, because that is when filling in a diary is hardest.

The consequence is the same in every case and it is worth stating plainly: your research is systematically louder about the bad cases than the good ones, and a team that reads it as a representative sample will over-invest in fixing problems that affect a small number of people and under-invest in making the common path faster. This is why every prevalence claim needs a quantitative method attached even when the qualitative finding is unambiguous.

It also means that a complaint going quiet is not evidence the problem was fixed. It is more often evidence people found a workaround, and the workaround is invisible to every method on this shelf except a diary study. When a metric improves without anyone changing anything, look for the workaround before you record the win.

/* THE BIAS AUDIT. Every method has a direction in which it lies, and the fix is
   never to distrust the method - it is to name the direction and pair it with
   something that leans the other way. This is why a research plan pairs
   methods rather than picking one. */

const METHOD_BIAS = {
  "support-tickets": {
    over: "severity - only people who suffered enough to write",
    misses: "the large number who hit the same wall, worked around it, and said nothing",
    pair_with: "analytics, for the rate behind the complaint",
  },
  "session-recording": {
    over: "difficulty - if you sample by length",
    misses: "the fast successful sessions, which are most of the traffic",
    pair_with: "task timing from analytics, not from watching recordings",
  },
  interviews: {
    over: "the articulate and the recently annoyed - recall favours strong events",
    misses: "the quiet majority whose experience is unremarkable and therefore unmentioned",
    pair_with: "a survey, for prevalence among people who would never be recruited",
  },
  "diary-study": {
    over: "the committed - people who finish a diary are systematically different",
    misses: "exactly the dropouts, who are the ones who struggled",
    pair_with: "a short exit survey, which catches people mid-task rather than after",
  },
  survey: {
    over: "volunteers, and anyone who reads the questions first",
    misses: "everyone who did not open it - a response rate under 10 percent makes the result unrepresentative",
    pair_with: "an intercept survey at the point of the experience, which cannot be skipped past",
  },
};

function isSafeToActOn(method, responseRate) {
  const bias = METHOD_BIAS[method];
  const weak = responseRate !== undefined && responseRate < 10;
  return {
    ok: !weak,
    // the threshold is not arbitrary: under 10 percent, non-response is
    // correlated with the thing being measured, so the sample is not random
    // and no amount of responses fixes it
    caveat: weak
      ? "a " + responseRate + " percent response rate is self-selecting; the " + bias.over + " bias compounds it"
      : "pair with " + bias.pair_with,
  };
}

The response-rate threshold is the one number worth memorising from this section. Below ten percent, who answered is related to what was asked, and adding more responses to a self-selecting sample does not make it representative.

Combine methods by pairing a loud method with a quiet one rather than running three loud ones. Interviews plus analytics. Complaints plus a survey of everyone who bought. Diary plus exit survey. Three loud methods agree with each other and are all wrong in the same direction, which is the specific failure this pairing exists to prevent.

2.7 Recruiting, screeners & consent

Good recruiting matches participants to the people who actually use or will use the product, not a convenience sample of friends and colleagues. Use a screener questionnaire that filters for relevant behaviors, and set quotas so your sample covers the diversity of real users. Before recording anything, state a clear one-line consent covering what is recorded, how it is used, and that the person can stop at any time. Record that consent on the session itself.

  • Screeners filter, they don’t flirt: ask behavior questions ("have you bought X online in the last 30 days?") and quota segments (mix of novices/experts) to build a useful sample.
  • 5–8 per profile reveals themes; add more only per distinct segment. Incentives: gift cards or charities, never "exposure".
  • Consent is one line before recording: state recording, purpose, storage and "stop anytime". Keep the consent record — it’s the audit trail behind your data (Ch.20).
  • Recruit continuously: small standing panel, socials, intercept surveys — so research never stalls waiting on a recruiting sprint.

Exercises 2

  1. Interview 3 people about a real task (returning an online purchase). Follow the 5 rules; then affinity-map the notes.
  2. Mine your product’s support tickets (or a public subreddit) for 10 repeated pain points.
  3. Write one persona + one journey map from the interview you just did.

What a convenience sample is worth

The most common recruiting failure is not too few participants. It is a sample drawn from whoever answered - colleagues, friends, a social media post that reached the designer's network. Such a sample is not merely imprecise, it is systematically biased in one direction: it over-represents people who already like the product or the idea of it, and it over-represents people who talk about tools, which is a group whose needs differ from everyone's in exactly the ways a design review is least able to notice.

The second failure is a sample that is right about the product and wrong about the users. Recruiting only people who use the current product excludes everyone who bounced, which is the group whose obstacles are the ones worth understanding. If you are redesigning an onboarding flow, participants who completed onboarding cannot tell you why others did not.

The third is a sample with no quotas, which collapses to whatever the screener let through. Five people who all use the same feature produce five confirmations of one perspective, and the team hears them as a finding about that feature rather than as a fact about their recruiting. The fix is not more participants in that group; it is at least one per segment you care about, which is usually a smaller number than people expect and is almost always the difference between a finding and an anecdote.

/* THE SCREENER. Behavioural, not attitudinal, and the difference is the whole
   design. A screener question that can be answered from an intention produces a
   sample of intentions, which is the one population that is guaranteed to be
   wrong about what they will do. */

const SCREENER = [
  {
    // the form of the question is the technique: a dated, verifiable event
    // filters for the behaviour, and anyone who cannot recall one is not in
    // your target population regardless of what they intend to do
    q: "Have you bought anything from a shop like this online in the last 30 days?",
    type: "single", options: ["yes", "no", "not sure"],
    screen_out_if: "no",
  },
  {
    q: "Which of these did you use most recently to pay?",
    type: "single",
    options: ["phone", "laptop", "tablet"],
    // recorded, not filtered: this is a QUOTA dimension. Without it, whoever
    // answers first fills the sample and the quota is never enforced.
    quota: "device",
  },
  {
    q: "How would you describe yourself here?",
    type: "single", options: ["buying for myself", "buying for others", "both"],
    quota: "role",
  },
  {
    q: "How often do you shop like this?",
    type: "single", options: ["weekly", "monthly", "a few times a year"],
    // the recency and frequency pair is what distinguishes an actual user from
    // someone who will take the incentive
    screen_out_if: "a few times a year",
  },
];

/* Quota enforcement is a separate check because a screener collects and a
   quota decides, and the decision is the part that gets skipped. */
function quotaGaps(responses, wanted) {
  return Object.entries(wanted).map(([dim, target]) => {
    const got = responses.filter((r) => r[dim] === target).length;
    return {
      dimension: dim,
      target,
      filled: got,
      // a quota that overshoots is also a fault: it means the screener was
      // permissive on that dimension and the other segments are now unfillable
      status: got === target ? "met" : got < target ? "short by " + (target - got) : "over by " + (got - target),
      action: got >= target ? "tighten the screener on " + dim : "recruit for " + dim,
    };
  });
}

The quota field is marked on the option rather than the question, because a quota is a property of one answer and a filter is a property of the whole item. Mixing them is how a screener ends up filtering out the segment you most needed.

Consent as a record, not a formality

Consent stated as one line before recording is the minimum and the maximum of what is required. It has to cover four things: that the session is being recorded, what it is for, who will see it, and that the person can stop at any point without giving a reason. What it does not have to be is legal, or comprehensive, or read aloud at a measured pace - the failure mode is a paragraph nobody absorbs and a participant who hears one word of it.

What makes consent useful rather than decorative is the record. Keep the session's consent alongside the recording, in the same place, with the date and the version of the script that was actually used. Three reasons: you cannot show an ethics or accessibility review that a session happened with consent when the only evidence is somebody's memory; you cannot publish or share a clip without knowing it was agreed; and when a participant asks six months later for their data to be deleted, you cannot honour the request if you cannot identify which sessions were theirs.

One line, recorded, stored with the artefact. The incentive has to be described in the same breath, including that it is not contingent on completing the session - a payment that can be withdrawn mid-interview is not an incentive, it is a bribe, and it changes what a participant says. Offer something they would have wanted anyway: store credit, a donation to a cause they choose, or money. "Exposure" is not an incentive, because the thing being researched is usually what they are already failing to get.

/* THE CONSENT RECORD. A consent script is not a document, it is a string that
   gets stored with the artefact it authorises - and the four required elements
   are checked rather than trusted, because a shortened script is how consent
   quietly stops covering what the recording contains. */

const CONSENT_SCRIPT =
  "Before we start - is it alright if I record this session? " +
  "The recording is used to write up what people find difficult, nobody outside " +
  "the team watches it, and it is deleted after the write-up. " +
  "You can stop at any point, you do not need to give a reason, and skipping " +
  "any question is completely fine. " +
  "You will get the " + "gift card" + " either way, whether you finish or not. " +
  "Do you want to go ahead?";

const REQUIRED_ELEMENTS = [
  { key: "recording",   test: /record/i },
  { key: "purpose",     test: /used to|write up|understand/i },
  { key: "who sees it", test: /nobody outside|the team|not shared/i },
  { key: "stopping",    test: /stop at any point|skip any question|without giving a reason/i },
  { key: "incentive not conditional", test: /either way|whether you finish/i },
];

function auditConsent(script, answers) {
  const missing = REQUIRED_ELEMENTS.filter((e) => !e.test.test(script));

  return {
    ok: missing.length === 0,
    missing: missing.map((e) => e.key),
    // verbal agreement is necessary and not sufficient: a participant who says
    // yes without hearing the storage terms has not consented to publication,
    // which is the thing that bites later
    verbal: answers.agreed === true,
    // and the record that has to exist beside the artefact
    record: {
      session_id: answers.session_id,
      date: answers.date,
      script_version: answers.script_version,
      recording: answers.recording_retained,
      deleted_after_writeup: true,
      incentive_issued: answers.incentive_issued,
    },
  };
}

The audit is deliberately unforgiving. A script edited down to two sentences fails on who sees it and stopping, and it fails at the point of writing the script rather than eighteen months later when someone asks whether a clip may be used in a conference talk.

Keep recruiting as a standing activity rather than a sprint before each study. A small panel of a dozen screened participants who have already given consent turns a two-week delay into a two-day one, and it is the difference between research that shapes a roadmap and research that confirms it after the engineering work is booked. Panel members go stale, so refresh it: five minutes of follow-up a month, and replace anyone whose segment you have already filled three times.

3 · Information Architecture

Information architecture is the discipline of organizing, labeling, and structuring content so people can find what they need with minimal effort. It covers the hierarchy of pages, how sections are named, how navigation works, and how users move between related content. In practice you build it with card sorting, tree testing, and sitemaps, then test it early because structure is painful to redo later. If people cannot find something, nothing else about the design matters.

3.1 Organization models and schemes3.2 Card sorting (how users naturally group)3.3 Navigation: the findability contract3.4 Labeling and the vocabulary users own3.5 Sitemaps: drawing the skeleton

IA is the invisible skeleton: how content is organized, labeled and found. Users can’t buy what they can’t find — this is where "it was somewhere" frustrations are born.

3.1 Organization models and schemes

Organization schemes define how content items are grouped, whether by topic, task, audience, time, or complexity. Most real products use a hierarchy of a few levels, each level holding roughly five to nine items so choices stay scannable. Choose the scheme that matches how users think about the task, mixing topical organization with task-based navigation when needed. Test the grouping with card sorting and tree testing before committing.

SchemeWhen it worksExample
Topic/exactUsers know what they want; strict vocabulariesDocs by component name
TaskBeginners act by verb"Add funds", "Print" flows
AudienceDifferent groups need different viewsStudent / teacher portal
TimeFreshness is the axisNews, schedules, receipts
FuzzySubjectivity is the pointFeed rankings, "for you"

Reality is a hierarchy: top → sections → pages → sub-pages. Depth vs breadth tradeoff: too deep = buried; too wide (20 items in one nav) = overwhelming. The comfortable spot is 5–9 top items, 2–4 levels deep, with search as the pressure valve.

Match the scheme to the question the user is holding

The reason a navigation feels wrong is usually that the scheme is not the one the user arrived with. Someone opening a product has a question, and the question has a shape. "Where is the thing I was told about" is a location question. "Which of these should I use" is a comparison. "How do I do X" is a task. Those three produce three different structures, and picking the wrong one is what makes people say a site is hard to use when every page is individually clear.

An alphabetical structure suits items that are genuinely equivalent and independently sought - countries, chemical compounds, states. Its one virtue is that it needs no label to be understood, which is why it is the right answer for those and a poor answer for anything with a natural order. It also fails the moment the list exceeds roughly twenty items, since the eye has to scan past everything it does not want.

A topical structure groups by subject matter and suits content people browse rather than search for - a magazine, a reference work, a documentation set. Its weakness is that it requires the user to already know the taxonomy, so it serves people who have been here before and hides everything from people who have not. Topical navigation is where most products put their most important content when their most important content is a task.

A task-based structure groups by what the user came to do, and it is the right default for most software. Its weakness is that tasks overlap and combinations multiply: what is "send an invoice" when it is also "add a customer"? A task structure that has been extended for a year usually needs a topical layer underneath it, which is a sign the scheme is being stretched past what it can carry.

The audience structure exists because different people want different things from the same system, and it is legitimate when the split is real and permanent - a patient portal against a clinician one. It becomes an excuse when the audience is guessed rather than measured, and the symptom is two parallel navigation systems for one product.

/* SCHEME SELECTION. Each entry states the question the user walked in
   holding, because that is the only input that decides the structure - and
   the failure, in every review this comes up in, is choosing the scheme the
   organisation's org chart suggests. */

const SCHEMES = {
  alphabetical: {
    suits: ["countries", "chemical compounds", "legal codes"],
    question: "where is the one I already have a name for",
    // works because it needs no vocabulary at all
    strength: "requires no label knowledge",
    ceiling: 20,
    fails_when: "the list exceeds twenty items, or the items have a natural order",
  },
  topical: {
    suits: ["documentation", "a magazine", "a reference work"],
    question: "show me something in this area",
    strength: "good for browsing",
    // the trap: it is legible to people who already know the taxonomy
    fails_when: "the user does not know the categories, or came to do a task",
  },
  task: {
    suits: ["most software", "checkouts", "admin tools"],
    question: "how do I do X",
    strength: "matches intent, which is why it is the default",
    // the real cost, and it is structural rather than cosmetic
    fails_when: "tasks overlap, so combinations multiply and the list stops closing",
  },
  audience: {
    suits: ["a patient portal", "a clinician tool", "a student and a tutor view"],
    question: "which of these is mine",
    strength: "each view can be shallow",
    // and this one is the excuse that gets abused
    fails_when: "the audience split is guessed rather than measured",
  },
  // the fifth scheme, and the one teams add last and most defensively
  time: {
    suits: ["activity feeds", "invoices", "audit logs"],
    question: "what changed, and when",
    strength: "order is unambiguous",
    fails_when: "users think by topic, so they scroll past what they need",
  },
};

function chooseFor(question) {
  // a question's own words decide, and the fallthrough is a topical layer
  // under a task structure rather than a decision made by taste
  if (/do|create|set up|send|make/.test(question)) return { primary: "task", secondary: "topical" };
  if (/browse|read|learn|about/.test(question))    return { primary: "topical", secondary: null };
  if (/mine|my |logged in/.test(question))        return { primary: "audience", secondary: "task" };
  if (/recent|latest|changed/.test(question))     return { primary: "time", secondary: "task" };
  return { primary: "task", secondary: "topical" };
}

Nearly everything falls through to a task structure with a topical layer beneath it, which is the honest answer for most products. A scheme that needs no fallback is a scheme that has been fitted to one screen.

Why five to nine, and what happens outside it

The five-to-nine range is not a law of nature, it is the range where labels stay short enough to scan as words rather than as fragments. Past nine, labels start abbreviating, abbreviations stop matching what users search for, and the group becomes a list of internal project names. Under five, a level has usually been invented for hierarchy's sake rather than because the content divides that way.

Past twenty, a single level stops being scannable at all and the navigation needs a second dimension - grouping within the list, a filter, a search box. That is not a failure of the navigation so much as the point at which it becomes a search interface, and recognising that is useful because the two have opposite design requirements: navigation wants few wide targets, search wants a text field and a forgiving matcher.

Depth is cheaper than it looks and breadth is not. Each level of depth costs a click and a re-orientation, but the labels stay long and specific because a parent does not have to describe everything beneath it. Breadth forces one label to cover a large set of things, so labels get vague - "Resources", "More" - and a vague label is one nobody can predict, so nobody clicks it. If you must choose, go deeper.

Then check reachability, which is a counting exercise and not a judgement. Every page needs at least two ways in - a link from its parent, and one from somewhere contextual - because the one path a user fails on is exactly the path they needed. A page reachable only from one parent is a page with a single point of failure, and it is also a page nobody will find by searching, because nobody can guess its address.

/* THE STRUCTURE CHECK. Cheap, mechanical, and it finds more real problems than
   a design review does. Three conditions, all countable from a sitemap before
   a single page is built - which is the only point at which they are cheap to
   fix. */

function auditStructure(nodes) {
  const byId = new Map(nodes.map((n) => [n.id, n]));
  const topLevel = nodes.filter((n) => n.depth === 0);

  const wide = topLevel.filter((n) => n.childCount > 9);
  const vague = nodes.filter((n) => /^(Resources|More|Misc|Services|Products|Other)$/i.test(n.label));
  const deep = nodes.filter((n) => n.depth >= 4);

  // reachability: a page with one inbound link is a page that disappears when
  // that link moves, and it is invisible to anyone who did not come that way
  const inbound = new Map(nodes.map((n) => [n.id, 0]));
  for (const n of nodes) for (const c of n.children || []) inbound.set(c, (inbound.get(c) || 0) + 1);

  const orphans = nodes.filter((n) => n.depth > 0 && !n.searchable);
  const fragile = [...inbound].filter(([, count]) => count === 1).map(([id]) => byId.get(id).label);

  return {
    ok: !wide.length && !vague.length && !deep.length && !orphans.length,
    topLevel: {
      count: topLevel.length,
      // the range is a soft target, not a law - so it reports and warns rather
      // than failing, because nine is not a cliff
      note: topLevel.length > 9 ? "wide: consider a layer or a filter" : "within the scannable range",
    },
    wide: wide.map((n) => n.label),
    // a vague label is the strongest single predictor of an unused section
    vague: vague.map((n) => n.label + " - does not say what is inside"),
    tooDeep: deep.map((n) => n.label),
    singleEntryPoints: fragile,
    unsearchable: orphans.map((n) => n.label),
  };
}

Vague labels are listed first because they are the cheapest defect to fix before a build and the most expensive to fix after one - renaming a nav item is a commit; renaming a shipped section is a migration, a support article and a period of confused search results.

Finally, test the structure before building it. A sitemap is a prediction about where people will look, and predictions should be tested like any other - which is what the tree testing in this chapter is for. Ten clicks saved across a whole product is worth more than any individual screen being polished, because the structure is the one decision that everything downstream inherits.

3.2 Card sorting (how users naturally group)

Card sorting is a research method where participants organize your content cards into groups that feel natural to them, revealing how users expect information to be structured. In an open sort, users create their own groups and labels, while a closed sort fits cards into a predefined structure. Run it with enough participants and look for groups where people agree; high agreement is your signal for the top-level navigation. The results directly inform the information architecture.

Process:
 1. Write 30-60 real items on cards (features, pages, content pieces)
 2. Ask participants to group them and NAME the groups
 3. Open: users make groups freely   Closed: users fit into YOUR labels
 4. Analyze: where did people agree? (that's your top-level IA)
    Where did they disagree? (ambiguous items need clearer names,
    duplicate placement, or search)

Rule: 15-25 people for open sorts; watch the AGREEMENT MATRIX —
items that co-occur frequently are siblings.

Reading the matrix before you read the labels

A card sort produces a square matrix: for every pair of items, the proportion of participants who placed them in the same group. That matrix is the finding. The group names people write afterwards are a interpretation of it, and the temptation to read the names first is what turns a sort into a confirmation exercise - you look for the label you expected and stop reading.

What to look for in the matrix is agreement above a threshold, and the threshold is a convention rather than a law. Around seventy percent is usually a real cluster. Below fifty, the pairing is coincidence and putting those two items together will produce a nav item nobody uses. The pairs to examine first are the very high ones, because two items almost everybody groups together is a signal that the nav should link them directly rather than let a user hunt for one inside the other.

Then look for the items that agree with almost nothing. A card that nobody can place is usually one of three things: it does not belong in the set at all, it means two different things to different people, or its label is the organisation's word rather than the participant's. The third is the commonest by a distance and the fix is a rename, which is why the items with no agreement are the most valuable output of the sort.

/* THE AGREEMENT MATRIX, COMPUTED. The sort itself is a person moving cards; what
   needs checking afterwards is arithmetic, and this is the part people do by
   eye and get wrong. Note that the matrix is built from PARTICIPANTS' groupings,
   not from the names of the groups, so renaming a cluster cannot change a
   single number in it. */

const PARTICIPANT_GROUPS = [
  ["returns", "refunds", "order status", "contact"],
  ["returns", "order status", "refunds", "contact"],
  ["order status", "returns", "contact", "refunds"],
  // this participant grouped differently on every item, which is itself a
  // finding and not noise - keep them in and let the thresholds absorb them
  ["returns", "refunds", "contact", "order status"],
  ["returns", "refunds", "order status", "contact"],
  ["returns", "contact", "refunds", "order status"],
];

function agreementMatrix(groups) {
  const items = [...new Set(groups.flat())];
  const pair = (a, b) =>
    groups.filter((g) => g.includes(a) && g.includes(b)).length;

  const rows = {};
  for (const a of items) {
    rows[a] = {};
    for (const b of items) {
      rows[a][b] = a === b ? null : pair(a, b) / groups.length;
    }
  }
  return rows;
}

function clusters(matrix, { strong = 0.7, weak = 0.5 } = {}) {
  const items = Object.keys(matrix);
  const out = { siblings: [], ambiguous: [], homeless: [] };

  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    for (let j = i + 1; j < items.length; j++) {
      const a = matrix[items[i]][items[j]];
      if (a >= strong) out.siblings.push({ items: [items[i], items[j]], score: a });
      else if (a < weak) out.ambiguous.push({ items: [items[i], items[j]], score: a });
    }
  }

  // an item with no strong sibling has nowhere to live, and the three causes
  // above are worth distinguishing before you move the card
  for (const it of items) {
    const best = Math.max(...items.filter((x) => x !== it).map((x) => matrix[it][x]));
    if (best < strong) {
      out.homeless.push({
        item: it,
        best: best,
        likely_cause:
          best < 0.2 ? "wrong label, or two ideas in one card" :
          best < 0.4 ? "does not belong in this set" :
                       "weakly understood - may need splitting",
      });
    }
  }
  return out;
}

Homeless cards are the reason to run a sort at all. A card nobody can place is telling you the content model has an extra axis nobody has drawn yet, and that is far cheaper to discover here than after the templates exist.

Which sort to run, and how many people

Open sorts let participants invent the groups, so they answer "what structure do these users expect" without being constrained by yours. Closed sorts hand them your groups, so they answer a narrower question - "are these groupings right" - and are much cheaper to run and to analyse, because the matrix needs no reconciliation of differently-named groups. Run open first when the structure is genuinely unknown, closed afterwards to confirm, and closed alone when you already have a structure you want challenged rather than replaced.

Twenty-five to thirty participants is usually enough to see where the strong agreements are. The curve flattens well before the sample is large, and the incremental participant after thirty mostly re-confirms the same clusters. Where you have existing segments, run enough participants per segment that each is interpretable on its own - five or six in a segment is noise, six or seven in the whole study is a finding, and this is the single most common way a card sort is run badly.

Two segments often sort differently, and when they do the difference is the finding rather than the noise. Two groups that agree on most of the matrix and disagree sharply on three items have told you that those three items sit at a boundary for one group and inside a group for the other, and a shared navigation has to choose. Either split the navigation by segment, which costs a second structure to maintain, or pick the placement that serves the group with the higher stakes and give the other a search path.

/* SEGMENT COMPARISON, which is where the real decision lives. Two sorts of the
   same card set, from two populations, and the items where they disagree are
   the ones a single shared navigation cannot place. */

function compareSegments(matrixA, matrixB, { strong = 0.7 } = {}) {
  const items = Object.keys(matrixA);
  const disagreements = [];

  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    for (let j = i + 1; j < items.length; j++) {
      const a = matrixA[items[i]][items[j]];
      const b = matrixB[items[i]][items[j]];
      // one segment clusters the pair, the other does not. Either way there is
      // no placement that is right for both.
      if ((a >= strong) !== (b >= strong)) {
        disagreements.push({
          items: [items[i], items[j]],
          a: a, b: b,
          gap: Math.abs(a - b),
        });
      }
    }
  }

  return disagreements
    .sort((x, y) => y.gap - x.gap)
    .map((d) => ({
      ...d,
      // the resolution, and it is a product decision rather than a research one
      decision:
        "shared nav: place for the higher-stakes segment and give the other a search path, " +
        "or split the navigation and accept the maintenance cost of a second structure",
    }));
}

Splitting a navigation is rarely worth it for one disagreement. The search path is cheaper, and it degrades gracefully - someone looking in the wrong place finds it after one extra search rather than not at all.

Finally, a sort does not tell you what to name the groups, only where the boundaries are. Naming comes from the participants' own words, harvested from the labels they wrote in an open sort or from the words they used in the interviews behind the cards - and a name invented by the team is the most common reason a well-researched structure is hard to navigate, because the structure is right and the vocabulary is not.

The protocol walks through open card sorting with dozens of real items and named groups. The agreement matrix reveals which items are siblings and which labels confuse people.

3.3 Navigation: the findability contract

Navigation is the system of menus, links, breadcrumbs, and search that lets users always know where they are and how to get where they want. It is a contract with the user, so every pattern you choose must serve a clear purpose and carry a known pitfall: global nav for orientation, breadcrumbs for depth, and search for direct access. Keep labels in the user’s vocabulary and test the structure with tree testing. Every page should be reachable and recognizable.

PatternUsePitfall
Global naveverything is reachable, consistentcreeping vertical: too many items
Breadcrumbsdeep hierarchies, recovery from being lostuseless on shallow/flat structures
Tabsfilter the same content typeinseparable from content looks—"where am I?"
Sidebarlong task flows, dashboardshidden on mobile unless collapsible
Footer sitemapSEO + rare pagesnever the primary way to find content

Each navigation element answers a different question

Navigation is usually discussed as a list of patterns to choose between, and that framing is what produces sites with three horizontal menus. They are not alternatives. They answer different questions, and a page needs the answers to several of them at once.

Global navigation answers "where am I and what else is here". It is orientation, so its labels must be mutually exclusive and must cover the whole product. It is also the only element that has to be identical on every page, which makes it the most expensive to change and the one most likely to be designed once and never revisited.

Breadcrumbs answer "how did I get here and how do I get back up". Their real function is escape: a user who has arrived by search engine has no path, and breadcrumbs are what stop them from being stranded. That is why they show hierarchy rather than history - they should reflect where the page sits, not the route taken, so pressing back on a breadcrumb moves up the structure rather than reversing clicks.

Search answers "I know roughly what I want and do not know what you would call it". It is the pressure valve that lets navigation be deep and narrow, and it is the only element that tolerates the user bringing a vocabulary you have never seen. Its value rises with the size of the product and with the mismatch between internal labels and user vocabulary, so a product whose navigation is clean needs search less.

In-page navigation - a table of contents, an anchor list - answers "how much of this am I looking at and where do I start". On a long page it is the difference between skimming and reading, and it costs nothing to add.

/* THE FOUR QUESTIONS, as a routing table rather than a list of patterns. Every
   navigation element on a page should be justified by one of these, and a page
   carrying two elements that answer the same question is carrying one too
   many. */

const NAV_QUESTIONS = {
  orientation: {
    question: "where am I, and what else is here",
    element: "global nav",
    must: ["labels are mutually exclusive", "identical on every page"],
    // the failure is a nav that lists the org chart, so two entries both mean
    // "the marketing site" and neither can be predicted
    pitfall: "labels that overlap, so no label can be chosen confidently",
  },
  escape: {
    question: "how do I get back to where I was",
    element: "breadcrumbs",
    must: ["reflect hierarchy, not history", "every ancestor is a link"],
    // the deep one: breadcrumb trail built from the referrer shows a path that
    // does not exist in the structure, so it teaches the user a hierarchy that
    // is not there
    pitfall: "generated from the arrival path, which describes a route rather than a structure",
  },
  retrieval: {
    question: "I know roughly what I want, and I do not know your word for it",
    element: "search",
    must: ["forgiving matching", "shows results before submit", "empty state does something"],
    pitfall: "exact matching, so a user who types the wrong word gets nothing and concludes the content is absent",
  },
  orientation_within: {
    question: "how long is this, and where do I start",
    element: "in-page contents",
    must: ["mirrors the document's own structure", "shows position"],
    pitfall: "a hand-written list that drifts from the headings below it",
  },
};

/* The audit that catches the real defect: an element whose question is answered
   by nothing on the page. Missing orientation is the common one. */
function auditPage(elements) {
  const answered = new Set(elements);
  const gaps = Object.entries(NAV_QUESTIONS)
    .filter(([k]) => !answered.has(k))
    .map(([k, v]) => ({ missing: k, question: v.question, add: v.element }));
  return { gaps, ok: gaps.length === 0 };
}

Run against a typical product page this reports the in-page contents missing, which is why long documentation and article pages need one and category pages do not.

Depth, position, and where the pattern breaks

Depth in global navigation is bounded by what survives on a phone, not by what fits on a desktop. Five top-level items is comfortable at every width; eight is workable if one of them is a menu rather than a link; beyond that the items wrap, get truncated, or are hidden behind a burger with no label, and a truncated label is worse than an absent one because it looks clickable and promises something it cannot deliver.

Active state is the other half of global navigation and the half most often omitted. Without it, the nav tells you what exists but not where you are, which is the question it exists to answer. The active item must be marked by something other than colour alone - weight, a rule, an underline - because colour alone fails in greyscale and for anyone with a colour vision deficiency, and it fails on the page where the reader most needs the orientation.

Every pattern has a condition where it breaks, and knowing the condition is the actual skill. A mega-menu breaks when it must stay one click deep because one click takes it out of the keyboard trap's reach. A hamburger breaks when it hides items that are frequently used. A mega-footer breaks when it grows to eighty links, at which point it is a sitemap nobody reads. A tab bar breaks when the tab labels change meaning between screens - users learn that the third tab is always "Account" and a tab that means something else once is a bug.

/* THE BREAK CONDITIONS. Each pattern gets the condition under which it stops
   working, because a pattern adopted without its condition is a pattern that
   will be carried past the point where it works. */

const PATTERNS = {
  "mega-menu": {
    good_for: "six or more top-level groups, each with a labelled section",
    breaks_when: "it must stay one click deep, since a second level inside a hover panel is a keyboard trap",
    // measurable, so it is a rule rather than an opinion
    check: (p) => p.submenuDepth <= 1 && p.columns <= 3,
  },
  burger: {
    good_for: "small widths, and secondary navigation on a phone",
    breaks_when: "it hides items used daily, which turns a layout fix into a daily cost",
    check: (p) => !p.frequentlyUsed?.some((x) => x.hidden),
  },
  "mega-footer": {
    good_for: "site-wide links as a fallback for people who reached the end",
    breaks_when: "it exceeds roughly eighty links, at which point it is a sitemap",
    check: (p) => p.linkCount <= 80,
  },
  tabs: {
    good_for: "parallel views of the same underlying thing",
    breaks_when: "a tab label changes meaning between screens - users learn the position, not the word",
    check: (p) => p.labelsAreStableAcrossScreens,
  },
  accordion: {
    good_for: "long content on a narrow screen",
    breaks_when: "it hides the answer to a question the user arrived with",
    // the specific failure: collapsed content does not exist as far as search,
    // find-in-page and the reader's first scan are concerned
    check: (p) => !p.hidesLoadedContent,
  },
  breadcrumbs: {
    good_for: "pages deeper than two levels, and pages reachable by search",
    breaks_when: "it is generated from the arrival path rather than the hierarchy",
    check: (p) => p.source === "hierarchy",
  },
};

function auditPattern(name, properties) {
  const p = PATTERNS[name];
  if (!p) return { name, ok: false, why: "unknown pattern" };
  return { name, ok: Boolean(p.check(properties)), breaks_when: p.breaks_when };
}

The accordion line is the one worth arguing about internally. Collapsing loaded content is not a layout decision; it is a decision about findability that is usually made for space reasons and paid for in support tickets.

Test navigation with people rather than reasoning about it, and test it without the content. A tree test shows the bare structure and asks someone to find a destination; a first-click test shows the structure with labels but no pages. Both find problems that a design review cannot, because the failure is predictive - you cannot tell that a user would not choose "Resources" until you watch them not choose it.

3.4 Labeling and the vocabulary users own

Labels are the words users see on buttons, links, and navigation, and they must match the language users actually speak rather than internal jargon. Harvest the real vocabulary from interview quotes, support tickets, and especially search logs, which show the exact terms people type. Write labels that are short, concrete, and scannable, and stay consistent so the same concept keeps the same name everywhere. Familiar words make content findable and trustworthy.

Labels must match the words users say (from interviews and search logs), not your internal jargon. Watch shared-vocabulary traps: "Billing" vs "My Wallet", "Assets" vs "Your Files". If users type "refund" and your site says "reimbursement request", they can’t find it — search logs tell you the words to use.

Harvest vocabulary before writing any labels

Every naming problem in a product was solvable earlier and cheaper, because at that point the real words were available to copy. The most reliable source is search logs, and it is reliable for a specific reason: someone typing "reimbursement request" is telling you what the thing is called to them, unprompted and with no incentive to be polite. Interviews are second, because people describing a task use its name naturally and use an organisation's name only when they have been taught to.

Support tickets are third but unusually valuable, because a ticket's subject line is a user attempting to reach the thing and being told they have used the wrong word. That gap between what they typed and what the product calls it is a labelled set of naming failures, already collected and free.

Then the negative sources, which are where most of the correction comes from. Search terms with no results, or results that get ignored, name things the product has not got or has named too differently to be found. Zero-result terms are the cheapest list of missing vocabulary in any product.

/* THE VOCABULARY HARVEST, merged and scored. The point of merging by CONCEPT
   rather than by string is that the same word is used by different teams for
   different things, and the same thing is called different words by different
   users - so the raw list is a mess and has to be clustered before it can be
   used as a naming source. */

const SOURCES = [
  // each row: the term, where it came from, how often
  { term: "refund",      from: "search logs",  n: 4820 },
  { term: "money back",   from: "search logs",  n: 3110 },
  { term: "reimbursement request", from: "search logs", n: 40 },
  { term: "refund",      from: "support tickets", n: 610 },
  { term: "return",      from: "interviews",   n: 95 },
  { term: "claim my money back", from: "search logs", n: 880 },
];

/* CONCEPT is the mapping you have to do by hand, once. It is the whole job:
   "refund", "money back" and "claim my money back" are three words for one
   thing, and picking the winner is a product decision, not a search of the
   counts. */
const CONCEPT = {
  "money-back": ["refund", "money back", "claim my money back"],
  "return-item": ["return"],
  "reimbursement-request": ["reimbursement request"],
};

function score(sources, concept) {
  const terms = concept.map((t) => sources.filter((s) => s.term === t));
  const bySource = {};
  for (const s of sources) bySource[s.from] = (bySource[s.from] || 0) + s.n;

  const ranked = concept.map((t) => {
    const hits = sources.filter((s) => s.term === t);
    return {
      term: t,
      total: hits.reduce((a, s) => a + s.n, 0),
      // a term used in interviews AND in search logs is understood by both the
      // team and the user, which is the property you want in a nav label
      inInterviews: hits.some((s) => s.from === "interviews"),
      inSearch: hits.some((s) => s.from === "search logs"),
      // the tell of an internal word: it exists almost entirely in one place
      internalOnly: hits.every((s) => s.from !== "interviews") && hits.every((s) => s.from !== "search logs"),
    };
  }).sort((a, b) => b.total - a.total);

  return ranked[0];
}

An internalOnly term is the one to change before launch and cheap to change later - nav labels are cheap, support article titles are not, and error messages written in internal vocabulary are expensive in every sense.

Name a concept once, and mean it everywhere

The most expensive naming defect is not a bad label but an inconsistent one, because a concept named three ways across a product teaches the user that three things exist. "Billing", "My Wallet" and "Payment Methods" on three screens for the same thing means a user who learned one has learned nothing transferable, and every screen has to be re-learned.

Consistency is a mechanical property and should be checked mechanically. A banned-terms list, held in version control and asserted in the build, is the only enforcement that survives a year of new screens. This is the same pattern as the token audit in chapter 1: a principle agreed once in a meeting decays silently, and the only defence is a check that fails.

Write labels for the button, not for the system. "Delete account" tells the user what happens; "Deactivate" describes an internal state; "Manage preferences" describes nothing at all. The verb should say what will change and the noun should be the thing the user recognises. Where a concept needs two words to describe accurately - "billing address", "order history" - that is usually a sign the concept is doing two jobs and should be split.

/* THE BANNED-TERMS CHECK. A single source of truth for vocabulary, enforced in
   CI. The failure mode it prevents is not a wrong label but a second name for a
   concept that already has one, which is invisible in review because each
   individual screen reads perfectly well. */

const CANONICAL = {
  refund:          ["reimbursement request", "money back claim", "credit note"],
  account:         ["profile", "user record", "member"],
  subscription:    ["membership", "plan", "billing tier"],
  delete:          ["remove", "deactivate", "archive"],   // only where it means delete
};

const ALLOWED = {
  // not a banned word, a context note: "remove" is correct for a line item and
  // wrong for an account, so the ban is scoped rather than global
  delete: ["remove from cart", "remove line item", "remove filter"],
};

// runs over the source, not the rendered page, so it catches the string in a
// component before the component is ever shown to anyone
function auditVocabulary(files) {
  const violations = [];
  for (const { path, text } of files) {
    for (const [canonical, banned] of Object.entries(CANONICAL)) {
      for (const b of banned) {
        if (ALLOWED[canonical]?.some((a) => text.includes(a))) continue;
        if (new RegExp("\b" + b.replace(/ /g, "\s+") + "\b", "i").test(text)) {
          violations.push({
            file: path,
            found: b,
            use: canonical,
            // the fix, not just the fault: which of the synonyms to reach for
            action: "replace with the canonical term for this concept",
          });
        }
      }
    }
  }
  return { ok: violations.length === 0, violations };
}

The ALLOWED map is what keeps this from becoming a nuisance. A global ban on the word "remove" would break every cart, so the ban is scoped to the concept rather than the string.

Finally, test labels the cheapest way available, which is to ask someone who has not seen the product to point at a screen and say what each control does. A label that needs two readings is a label that will be misclicked, and a misclicked irreversible control is the expensive case - so "Delete account" needs to say what is lost, not just what will be deleted.

3.5 Sitemaps: drawing the skeleton

A sitemap is a tree diagram of a product’s content and pages, showing hierarchy, parent-child relationships, and how deep users must click to reach content. Draw it with the main navigation at the top and content grouped by the user’s topics, keeping the number of levels shallow so nothing requires more than a few clicks. Use labels written as user verbs so each box reads as something to do. It becomes the blueprint for building pages and testing structure.

Sitemap = tree diagram of content + entry paths
                    [Home]
     ┌─────────────┬┴──────────┬─────────────┐
 [Explore]  [Buy a bike]  [Community]   [Support]
    |          |       |       |           |
 products   builders  full specs   forums   contact
    |          |                        |  returns
 categories  price online           FAQ kb.s
 # Note the user-verbs: "Buy a bike" not "Catalog".
 # Every child must be reachable by at least 2 paths (drill-down + search).

Drawing the tree before anyone draws a page

A sitemap is where a structural mistake is cheap. Everything downstream - templates, routes, navigation, analytics, the search index, the support documentation - inherits the hierarchy you draw, so an error here is not one mistake but one mistake replicated across all of them and fixed only by changing all of them.

Label the boxes with user verbs rather than page types. "Buy a bike", "Compare models", "Check delivery" describes what the user is trying to do at that node; "Category page", "PLP", "Landing" describes what the team built there. Verb labels are what make a tree test possible, because a participant can attempt a task from "Compare models" and cannot attempt one from "PLP".

Measure the depth rather than looking at it, because depth is the variable that turns into clicks and the tree does not look deep on a diagram. Count the maximum number of clicks from the root to any page, and count how many pages sit at each level: a tree where ninety percent of content is at level five has an information architecture that describes the org chart rather than the product.

/* THE TREE, AS DATA, so depth and distribution can be counted instead of
   estimated. A sitemap drawn on paper cannot answer "how much is more than
   three clicks away", and that is the number that decides whether search
   becomes the primary way in. */

const SITE = {
  id: "root", verb: "Home", children: [
    { id: "bikes", verb: "Buy a bike", children: [
      { id: "bikes-shop", verb: "Shop all bikes", children: [
        { id: "bikes-road", verb: "Road bikes" },
        { id: "bikes-mtb", verb: "Mountain bikes" },
        { id: "bikes-hybrid", verb: "Hybrid bikes" },
      ]},
      { id: "bikes-compare", verb: "Compare models" },
      { id: "bikes-finance", verb: "Monthly payments" },
    ]},
    { id: "service", verb: "Book a service", children: [
      { id: "service-book", verb: "Book a slot" },
      { id: "service-history", verb: "Past services" },
    ]},
    { id: "parts", verb: "Find parts" },
    { id: "support", verb: "Get help", children: [
      { id: "support-returns", verb: "Return something" },
      { id: "support-warranty", verb: "Check warranty" },
    ]},
    { id: "account", verb: "My account" },
  ]},
};

function analyse(node, depth = 0, acc = []) {
  acc.push({ id: node.id, verb: node.verb, depth });
  for (const c of node.children || []) analyse(c, depth + 1, acc);
  return acc;
}

function shape(site) {
  const all = analyse(site);
  const byLevel = {};
  for (const n of all) byLevel[n.depth] = (byLevel[n.depth] || 0) + 1;

  const deep = all.filter((n) => n.depth > 3);
  return {
    total: all.length,
    maxDepth: Math.max(...all.map((n) => n.depth)),
    byLevel,
    // the distribution is the finding: a tree whose mass sits at one depth is a
    // tree that mirrors an org chart
    bulk: Object.entries(byLevel).sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1])[0],
    tooDeep: deep.map((n) => n.verb),
  };
}

The bulk line is the one to read. If most nodes sit at the same depth, the tree is one list with extra steps rather than a hierarchy, and the extra steps are the cost the reader pays for no information.

Testing the tree with no pages attached

Tree testing removes the pages on purpose. Participants see the labels and the structure only, and are asked to find where something would be. What you are measuring is their prediction of where a thing lives, which is the whole question - and removing the pages removes the second thing people do otherwise, which is to read the content and never touch the structure.

Measure directness and not success. Directness is the proportion of participants whose first click is on the correct node; success is whether they got there eventually, allowing backtracking. A tree where most people arrive at the right node on the second try is a tree where most people were going to guess, and the backtracking is the symptom of a label or a level that does not mean what you meant.

A first-click test is the same measurement with labels and no hierarchy structure at all, and it separates the two possible causes. Poor directness with structure visible is a structure problem; poor directness with a flat list is a vocabulary problem. Running only one of them tells you which problem you have not got.

/* TREE TEST, scored. The distinction that matters is DIRECTNESS against SUCCESS:
   success allows backtracking, so a tree that is wrong but recoverable passes
   it, and a user who recovered by guessing is still a user who was misled. */

function scoreTreeTest(trials) {
  const results = trials.map((t) => {
    const target = findNode(t.tree, t.targetId);
    const first = t.clicks[0];
    const firstNode = findNode(t.tree, first);
    const isChild = firstNode && target && firstNode.verb === target.parentVerb;

    return {
      participant: t.participant,
      // the honest measure: was the first click the right node
      direct: isChild || (firstNode && firstNode.id === target?.id),
      // success allows recovery and backtracking
      success: t.clicks.some((c) => findNode(t.tree, c)?.id === target?.id),
      // where they actually landed first, which is the diagnosis
      predictedAt: firstNode?.verb,
      actualAt: target?.verb,
    };
  });

  const n = results.length;
  const direct = results.filter((r) => r.direct).length;
  const success = results.filter((r) => r.success).length;

  // the spread matters as much as the mean: two thirds direct with a third
  // guessing correctly is a different problem from two thirds scattering
  const mispredictions = {};
  for (const r of results) {
    if (!r.direct) mispredictions[r.predictedAt] = (mispredictions[r.predictedAt] || 0) + 1;
  }

  return {
    n,
    directness: (direct / n).toFixed(2),
    success: (success / n).toFixed(2),
    // where directness falls short of success, the structure is present but
    // mislabelled - people find it by exploring rather than by reading
    verdict:
      direct / n === 0.7 ? "structure is sound"
      : direct / n < 0.4 && success / n > 0.7 ? "VOCABULARY problem - labels, not structure"
      : direct / n < 0.7 ? "STRUCTURE problem - the grouping is wrong"
      : "structure and labels are both weak",
    mispredictions,
  };
}

The verdict split is the useful part. Directness at 0.3 with success at 0.9 means the tree is findable and not predictable, and the fix is renaming rather than restructuring - which is days rather than months.

Test with people from the segments that will actually use it, and include the segment that finds it hardest. A tree that works for the existing power users and fails for occasional visitors is a tree that has been designed around the people who never leave, which is the group with the least incentive to improve it. And test the sitemap before building it - the whole value of the artefact is that it is a prediction you can check while changing it is still free.

This sitemap draws the content tree with user-verb labels such as Buy a bike, and notes that every child page needs at least two ways to be reached.

IA + IA: testing information architecture with real people is "tree testing" — you show the bare tree and give tasks ("find where you’d return an item"), then measure where people click. Best way to validate a sitemap before building it.

Exercises 3

  1. Card-sort 40 items of a real site (use a tool or sticky notes) and build its sitemap from the result.
  2. Open-card-sort with 5 people; find the 3 items where groups disagreed and rename them.
  3. Tree-test your sitemap on 3 people with the "find it" method. Record the failure paths.

4 · Wireframes & Prototyping

Wireframes and prototyping are cheap ways to test structure, flow, and behavior before any pixel is final or any code is written. Wireframes are low-detail, grayscale layouts that focus on hierarchy and content, while prototypes link those screens into clickable paths for realistic testing. In practice you move up a fidelity ladder, testing at every step and discarding work that fails. Fast, testable skeletons kill expensive arguments early.

4.1 Fidelity ladder: low → mid → high4.2 Anatomy of a screen: what a wireframe contains4.3 User flows: the story between screens4.4 Clickable prototypes: testing before building4.5 Hi-fi: when visual design joins the conversation4.6 Handoff: converting designs into buildable specs4.7 Guerrilla testing: validate in a lunch break

Before pixels and code: fast, testable skeletons. Wireframes kill expensive arguments early because they leave out what’s arguable (colors, fonts) and keep what matters (layout, behavior, flows).

4.1 Fidelity ladder: low → mid → high

Fidelity describes how polished a design artifact is, from rough sketches through boxy wireframes to fully styled high-fidelity screens. Each rung of the ladder answers a different question: low fidelity tests layout and flow, mid fidelity tests content and function, high fidelity tests branding and final polish. Choose the cheapest rung that can answer your current question, and research at each level before investing more. Match the fidelity to the decision you are making.

LevelWhat it containsBest forTools
Low-fiboxes, lines, flowslayout + flow decisions, first testspen, whiteboard, Balsamiq
Mid-fireal content, states, gray-scale UIusability tests, stakeholder alignmentFigma, Sketch
High-fivisual design, motion, tokensfinal UX validation, dev handoffFigma + prototype, React

The golden rule: go no higher than needed to get answers. A mid-fi prototype gets 80% of the feedback at 20% of the cost. Reserve hi-fi for motion/emotion questions.

The rung is chosen by the decision, not the deadline

The most common way fidelity goes wrong is a team picking a rung because of how much time is left rather than because of what needs to be decided. Two weeks to launch produces grey rectangles, and then a usability test in week three reveals that the flow is wrong - a problem that a paper prototype on day one would have found for the cost of an afternoon.

The question a rung answers is precise, and each one is blind to the others. Low fidelity answers "is this the right structure": do people look in the right place, follow the path, notice the control. It is blind to anything involving words, colour, or polish, because none of those exist yet. Mid fidelity adds real content and real interactions but a neutral visual layer, so it answers "does this copy work and does this interaction behave". High fidelity answers "does this feel trustworthy and worth paying for", which is a question about emotion and trust that a grey box genuinely cannot answer.

That last one is why the ladder is not strictly linear. You can test structure at low fidelity, then copy at mid, then trust at high - but the reverse is wasteful, and the specific waste is testing content in a low-fidelity screen where the content has been replaced by "Lorem ipsum HEADING". Nobody has ever learned anything from a real user struggling to read placeholder text, and the finding gets recorded as a content problem.

/* FIDELITY AS A DECISION. Each rung declares the question it can actually
   answer and the questions it CANNOT, because the failure is not picking too
   low - it is picking too low and then believing the result. A structural test
   at low fidelity is valid; a trust test at low fidelity is meaningless. */

const RUNGS = [
  {
    rung: "paper",
    cost: 0, hours: 1,
    answers: ["structure", "labels"],
    cannot: {
      trust: "there is no brand, so nothing reads as trustworthy or untrustworthy",
      feel: "nobody forms an emotional judgement about a sketch",
      content: "the labels ARE the content, so length and tone cannot be tested",
      motion: "nothing moves",
    },
    // the cheapest rung that can answer the question, rather than a preference
    best_for: "does the layout hold, is the flow ordered correctly, are the labels right",
  },
  {
    rung: "grey-box",
    cost: 100, hours: 6,
    answers: ["structure", "labels", "content", "interaction"],
    cannot: {
      trust: "a neutral palette removes exactly the cue trust is made of",
      feel: "no type, no image treatment, nothing to feel",
      motion: "transitions are usually absent",
    },
    best_for: "does the copy work, does the interaction behave, does the error state recover",
  },
  {
    rung: "styled",
    cost: 900, hours: 30,
    answers: ["structure", "labels", "content", "interaction", "trust", "feel", "motion"],
    cannot: {
      // the honest limit of every prototype, at any fidelity
      performance: "a prototype is never slow, so it cannot find a performance problem",
      integration: "there is no real data behind it, so edge cases are absent",
    },
    best_for: "does this feel like our product, is the hierarchy right with real type",
  },
];

/* Pick the cheapest rung that can answer the question. Note it returns the
   CHEAPEST ADEQUATE rung, not the cheapest rung and not the highest: both of
   those mistakes are common and expensive in opposite directions. */
function rungFor(questions) {
  const needed = new Set(questions);
  const rung = RUNGS.find((r) => [...needed].every((q) => r.answers.includes(q)));
  if (rung) return { rung: rung.rung, cost: rung.cost };

  return {
    rung: "styled",
    cost: 900,
    warning: [...needed]
      .filter((q) => !RUNGS.find((r) => r.answers.includes(q)))
      .join(", "),
    note: "only the top rung covers this, so the question cannot be asked cheaply",
  };
}

The cannot maps are the reason the function returns a warning rather than silently promoting to the top rung. A question no rung answers - performance, real data volume, integration failure - has to be answered by building, and knowing that early is the whole value.

What changes when you change rung

Rising in fidelity changes what participants do, not just what they see. At paper level people talk through their intention out loud - they are describing a plan. At grey-box level they click and then narrate, so you get behaviour plus commentary. At styled level they stop narrating entirely and behave, because a screen that looks finished invites a real attempt rather than a hypothetical one.

This has a practical consequence that surprises teams: the same prototype gives different findings at different rungs, and the styled version produces fewer but heavier findings. Someone looking at a wireframe is evaluating your structure and telling you about it. Someone looking at a polished screen is trying to use the thing, and any irritation they express is about the product rather than about your design decisions. Both are useful, and the second is what a launch is actually going to feel like.

So test early and cheap, and test the same journey at each rung. The paper test finds flow faults in an afternoon; the grey-box test finds copy and recovery faults in a day; the styled test finds the trust problems that nothing lower could have revealed. Run in that order and each stage costs less than the one after it, because the faults are still cheap to fix.

/* THE RUNG LADDER AS A SCHEDULE, because the point is the ORDER and the
   cost curve, not any single rung. Running these out of order is the single
   most expensive mistake available in this chapter: a styled test first costs
   thirty hours and tells you the flow is wrong. */

const PLAN = [
  {
    rung: "paper",
    when: "week 0, before any screen is detailed",
    budget: "1 hour, 3 participants",
    finds: "wrong order, missing step, ambiguous label",
    // and what it explicitly does NOT find, so nobody claims it did
    misses: "copy length, error recovery, anything about trust",
  },
  {
    rung: "grey-box",
    when: "after content exists, before styling",
    budget: "6 hours, 5 participants",
    finds: "copy that does not work, errors that trap the user, states that were not drawn",
    misses: "brand, hierarchy under real type, motion",
  },
  {
    rung: "styled",
    when: "after grey-box findings are fixed",
    budget: "30 hours, 5-8 participants",
    finds: "trust, hierarchy, tone, whether it feels like the product",
    // the honest limit, and it is why a prototype can never be the last step
    misses: "performance, integration, real data edge cases",
  },
];

// the rule, checkable: each rung's findings must be fixed before the next rung
// is built, otherwise the next test is measuring a known fault
function auditPlan(plan, findingsFixed) {
  const violations = [];
  plan.forEach((stage, i) => {
    if (i === 0) return;
    const prev = plan[i - 1];
    if (!findingsFixed[prev.rung]) {
      violations.push(prev.rung + " findings were not fixed before building " + stage.rung);
    }
  });
  return { ok: violations.length === 0, violations };
}

Fixing the previous rung first is the whole mechanism. Skipping it means the styled test spends its budget re-finding what the paper test already found, and the team concludes the expensive research was not worth it.

4.2 Anatomy of a screen: what a wireframe contains

A wireframe is a stripped-down schema of a screen that states its structure without visual decoration. Every wireframe should record a title, its purpose, the primary actions, content blocks, and the different states the screen can be in, such as empty or error. Annotations explain behaviors and logic that the drawing alone cannot convey, so another designer or developer can build from it. Clarity beats beauty at this stage.

Every screen wireframe states (like a spec):
  - Title + purpose      ("Checkout — payment step")
  - Primary action       (the ONE thing most users should do)
  - Secondary actions    (ranked, smaller)
  - Content blocks       (placeholder text, image boxes)
  - States noted:        empty / loading / filled / error / edge
  - Annotations:         "ID three ways:" / "confirms before submitting"
Sketch repeatedly: 5 thumbnails in 15 minutes beats 1 elegant drawing.

A wireframe is a specification, not a picture

A wireframe that only shows arrangement is half a specification. The other half is everything a reader cannot see in the arrangement: what the screen is for, what happens when it is empty, what happens when the request fails, what the primary action is. A wireframe that omits those is a picture, and a developer building from it has to invent them - which is exactly where the expensive defects come from, because the states nobody drew are the states nobody tested.

Rank the actions. A screen has one primary action and the design has to say which, because "here are the buttons" is not enough and leaving it ambiguous is how a checkouts screen ends up with a visually stronger "save for later" than "pay now". Ranking in the annotation is cheap; fixing the emphasis in production is not.

State the states, always, even when the design has not covered them. An empty list, a loading skeleton, an error, a success, a permission denial and a partial result are seven screens that exist whether or not anyone drew them. Marking "empty state - not yet designed" on a wireframe is valuable precisely because it is visible - it is a defect on the artefact rather than a surprise in development.

/* THE WIREFRAME SPEC, as a structure a developer can build from. The fields
   are the ones that get forgotten, and the two the older convention misses are
   the empty state and the failure state - which are where the real defects
   live because they are the states nobody draws. */

const WIREFRAME = {
  screen: "Order confirmation",
  purpose: "confirm that an order exists and tell the user what happens next",
  // ranked, because a list of equal buttons is not a specification
  actions: [
    { rank: 1, label: "Track this order", rationale: "the thing they want next" },
    { rank: 2, label: "View order",        rationale: "useful, not urgent" },
    { rank: 3, label: "Continue shopping", rationale: "only if it does not compete with rank 1" },
  ],
  content: ["order number", "items", "total", "delivery estimate"],
  // every state listed, with the ones not yet designed marked rather than
  // omitted. An omitted state is an invention; a marked one is a task.
  states: {
    default:  "designed",
    loading:  "designed",
    empty:    "not yet designed - first order ever: what replaces the order list",
    error:    "not yet designed - order lookup failed: does the number survive a retry",
    partial:  "not yet designed - one item out of stock: does the order still go through",
    timeout:  "not yet designed - is this the same as error, and does it say which",
  },
  annotations: [
    "the order number is the only reference the user has; it must survive a session loss",
    "delivery estimate must not animate, so a changing value is not mistaken for a different order",
    // an annotation that names the CONSTRAINT, not the pixels, so a developer
    // can honour it with whatever markup they choose
    "on a 320px screen the actions stack, primary first, with 44px targets",
  ],
};

The annotations entries name constraints rather than positions. That is the difference between a specification that survives a redesign of the layout and one that does not.

Five screens per thumbnail, and why the loop is fast

The fast loop is the technique, and it works by keeping the artefact cheap enough to throw away. A thumbnail wireframe - a rectangle with a label - takes about a minute, so a designer can produce thirty variants of a layout in an afternoon and lay them out side by side. A polished screen takes hours, so you make one, defend it, and discover its flaw too late to try the alternative.

Thumbnail rectangles are not an insult to the designer. They are the right fidelity for the question "does this arrangement hold", because the eye reads a filled rectangle as a shape and an empty one as a container, and both readings are exactly what you want when the question is about spatial proportion. What they cannot do is judge copy length or visual weight, which is why they are paired with the content list and the action ranking rather than used alone.

Keep a grid, and show alignment. Most wireframe faults are spacing faults - something too close to the edge, two blocks with no relationship, a row that is a pixel narrower than the one above - and they are invisible in a drawing where everything is hand-placed and obvious the moment a baseline is laid over the top. A twelve-column grid and consistent gutters turn spacing into a decision rather than a habit.

/* THE THUMBNAIL LOOP, mechanised: the discipline is the VARIANT COUNT, not the
   drawing. Twenty options on one problem is what makes the next choice better,
   because the designer is choosing among things they have already made rather
   than imagining something they have not. */

const CANDIDATES = [
  { id: "v1", layout: "single column",      risk: "long page on mobile",   test: "does the CTA stay visible after three fields" },
  { id: "v2", layout: "two column form",   risk: "order of attention",    test: "which field is entered first" },
  { id: "v3", layout: "single column, grouped by meaning",
    risk: "grouping may be internal rather than user-visible",
    test: "does grouping reduce errors or just add headings" },
  { id: "v4", layout: "progressive, one step per screen",
    risk: "more back-and-forth", test: "completion rate on mobile data" },
  { id: "v5", layout: "inline validation per field",
    risk: "validation on blur is often wrong", test: "does it fire before the user leaves a field" },
];

// the loop only works if something forces a choice. Twenty variants with no
// selection is the same as one variant.
function select(candidates, evidence) {
  const scored = candidates.map((c) => ({
    ...c,
    // the evidence is the finding from the cheapest test that examined this
    // question; a variant with no evidence is an opinion with a drawing
    tested: Boolean(evidence[c.id]),
    score: evidence[c.id] || 0,
  }));
  const untested = scored.filter((c) => !c.tested);
  return {
    shortlist: scored.filter((c) => c.tested).sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score),
    stillUnknown: untested.map((c) => c.id),
    rule: "an untested variant is not a rejected variant",
  };
}

The untested list is the point. The usual failure is that the surviving variant is the one that was drawn first, and nobody can say afterwards why - because nothing was ever compared.

A wireframe reads like a mini spec: title and purpose, ranked actions, content blocks, and noted states, plus behavior annotations. The thumbnail loop keeps iteration fast on purpose.

4.3 User flows: the story between screens

A user flow maps the path a person takes through screens to complete a task, showing decisions and their outcomes like a flowchart. Draw the happy path first, then add alternate routes, edge cases, and error paths so missing states surface before code is written. Walk the flow step by step with a tester to find where people get stuck or where screens fail to connect. Good flows reveal interaction gaps that static screens hide.

A user flow is a sequence with decision points:
  [Home] → [Product] → [Add to cart] → [Cart]
                │
                ├─(out of stock)→ [Notify me] → [Done]
                ├─(no account) → [Checkout] → ...
                └─(has account) → [Checkout] → ...
# Map the HAPPY path big; then the alternate & error paths smaller.
# Flow walkthroughs with the team find missing states BEFORE code.

The happy path is not the flow
