A user flow that shows only the successful path is a screenshot list, and it hides the states that consume most of the support you get. People pay attention to a diagram that goes straight through; the branches are where the design work is, and they are exactly what gets deferred.

Draw the happy path first because it exposes the skeleton, then add every branch as a checklist rather than as inspiration. The standard set is: validation failure, network failure, timeout, permission denied, empty result, partial result, and the back-out path from each of them. Then account for the ones specific to your domain - a payment that is authorised but not captured, an upload that fails halfway, an item that sells out between the basket and the checkout.

The most common missing state is also the most damaging: what happens after the action succeeds. A flow that ends at "submit" has specified the system side of the transaction and left the human side to whoever builds it, which is how a user submits a form and receives no confirmation, then submits again.

/* THE FLOW, AS GRAPH EDGES. Modelling it as data rather than as a picture is
   what makes the missing states countable - a diagram hides a missing arrow,
   a graph reports it. The audit at the bottom is the reason to model it this
   way. */

const FLOW = {
  start: "choose-item",
  nodes: {
    "choose-item": { kind: "screen", next: "add-to-basket" },
    "add-to-basket": { kind: "screen", next: "basket" },
    "basket": { kind: "screen", next: "checkout" },
    "checkout": {
      kind: "screen",
      next: "payment",
      // the exits from a screen, which a happy-path diagram never draws
      exits: {
        "validation error": "checkout",
        "address unknown": "checkout",
        "item out of stock": "basket",
        "user abandons": "exit",
      },
    },
    payment: {
      kind: "screen",
      next: "confirmation",
      exits: {
        "card declined": "payment",
        // the branch that costs real money if it is not drawn: authorised but
        // not captured, and the user's money is in an odd state
        "authorised, capture failed": "payment-pending",
        "network timeout": "payment-pending",
      },
    },
    "payment-pending": { kind: "screen", next: "payment" },
    confirmation: {
      kind: "screen",
      // and the state that is missing from most flows entirely: what the user
      // is told while it resolves, and what they can do
      next: "order-tracking",
      exits: { "email not delivered": "order-tracking" },
    },
    "order-tracking": { kind: "screen", next: null },
    exit: { kind: "terminal" },
  },
};

const REQUIRED_EXITS = ["validation error", "network failure", "permission denied"];

function auditFlow(flow) {
  const screens = Object.entries(flow.nodes).filter(([, n]) => n.kind === "screen");
  const noExit = screens.filter(([, n]) => !n.exits || Object.keys(n.exits).length === 0);
  const reachesTerminal = walk(flow, flow.start);
  return {
    ok: noExit.length === 0 && reachesTerminal,
    // a screen with no exits on a diagram is usually a screen with no error
    // handling in the code either
    screensWithoutBranches: noExit.map(([id]) => id),
    // and the specific state the standard checklist names that this flow lacks
    missingStandard: REQUIRED_EXITS.filter(
      (e) => !screens.some(([, n]) => n.exits && n.exits[e]),
    ),
    unreachable: unreachable(flow),
  };
}

payment-pending is the node worth the effort. Authorised-but-not-captured is a real state in every payment integration and it is where a missing flow diagram turns into a support queue.

Walk the flow before testing it

Before anyone sees it, walk the flow yourself out loud, step by step, with a colleague who did not draw it. This catches the majority of gaps in an hour: you say "and then they see the order confirmation" and your colleague asks what happens if the email does not arrive, and you have just found a missing state by accident.

Then walk it with someone who knows the codebase. The designer draws a flow that is optimistic about what exists, and the developer's knowledge of what is actually implemented is the check on that optimism. This is also the moment to discover that a branch is technically impossible - that the API never returns that error - which is worth knowing now rather than discovering that the state is unreachable and the design for it is dead weight.

Keep the flow and the wireframes in sync, and treat a changed flow as a changed artefact requiring its own review. Flows rot faster than screens, because a small interface change - a new field, a renamed action - shifts which branch applies and nobody redraws the diagram. A flow that is six months stale is worse than none, because it is believed.

/* DRIFT DETECTION. A flow that disagrees with the screens is a flow that will
   be trusted and wrong, which is the worst combination available. This compares
   the two artefacts rather than trusting either. */

function detectDrift(flow, screens) {
  const drift = [];

  for (const [id, node] of Object.entries(flow.nodes)) {
    if (node.kind !== "screen") continue;
    const built = screens.find((s) => s.id === id);

    // a node on the flow that no screen exists for: the flow describes a step
    // nobody has designed, so it will be designed from scratch and to spec
    if (!built) { drift.push({ node: id, type: "flow-only", action: "design it or remove it" }); continue; }

    // a screen that exists but is not on the flow: the commonest drift, and it
    // means the flow has stopped describing the product
    if (!flowReachable(flow, id)) {
      drift.push({ node: id, type: "screen-only", action: "add it to the flow or it is unreachable" });
    }

    // the branch names are compared too, because renaming an error is a change
    // that never reaches the diagram
    if (built.exits && node.exits) {
      for (const e of built.exits) {
        if (!node.exits[e]) {
          drift.push({ node: id, type: "new branch", action: "add " + e + " to the flow" });
        }
      }
    }
  }
  return drift;
}

The screen-only drift case is the one that catches most real rot. A screen exists in the product and appears nowhere on the diagram, so the diagram is describing a product that no longer exists.

The flow diagram draws the happy path big and keeps the alternate and error branches smaller. Walking it with the team surfaces missing states before any code.

4.4 Clickable prototypes: testing before building

A clickable prototype links wireframes or screens into a working path that lets someone perform one real task end to end. It captures behavior and flow without the cost of implementation, making it ideal for usability testing before development. During a test, watch what users actually click and where they hesitate, rather than asking for opinions. Fixing a flow at prototype stage costs minutes; fixing it in code costs weeks.

  1. Build mid-fi screens (Figma or HTML/JS).
  2. Link them into a working path for ONE task ("checkout with a promo code").
  3. Give users the task and observe clicks and hesitation, not opinions.
  4. Iterate: fix the 3 worst findings, re-test. Two rounds usually catch the biggest issues.
// A real clickable prototype in pure HTML — no tool needed:
<a href="#step2">Continue</a>   // anchor navigates to the next step
<button onclick="document.getElementById('form1').reportValidity()">Next</button>   // gate on native form validation
<div id="step2" hidden>…payment fields that only appear after step1 valid…</div>
// anchor-based navigation + the browser's native validation = a
// legit prototype for usability testing of form flows.

Build one task, not the product

A prototype answers one question, and the question is a journey rather than a screen. "Test the checkout" is not testable; "test whether someone with an existing basket can pay with a promo code they already hold" is. The second version tells you which screens to build, what has to be linked, and what success looks like.

So build one path and make the rest of the product obviously out of scope. A grey area, a wall, or a link that goes nowhere is more useful than a dead end, because a participant who hits a wall stops and tells you the wall was there - whereas a participant who cannot tell it is unfinished keeps trying and wastes your session. Prototype edges should look obviously prototype.

Fidelity here should be grey-box rather than paper, because the interaction has to behave: a radio that does not select, or a field that does not validate, makes the test a study of the prototype's bugs. This is what browser-native validation gives you for free, and it is why an HTML prototype is often better than a design-tool one for a flow test - the gating is real rather than drawn.

/* ONE-TASK PROTOTYPE, in plain HTML. The technique here is the <fieldset>
   plus native validation: the Next button is not disabled and not wired to any
   state, because a disabled button with no explanation is the single most
   common finding in a flow test and it is always an artefact of the prototype
   rather than of the design. */

<form id="flow" novalidate>
  <fieldset data-step="1">
    <legend>Where should this go?</legend>
    <label>
      <input type="radio" name="ship" value="standard" required>
      Standard, three to five days
    </label>
    <label>
      <input type="radio" name="ship" value="next-day" required>
      Next day
    </label>
  </fieldset>

  <fieldset data-step="2" hidden>
    <legend>Pay with the card ending 4242</legend>
    <label>Card number
      <input name="card" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9 ]{15,19}" required>
    </label>
  </fieldset>

  <!-- the error region exists as MARKUP, before it has content. A validation
       message inserted by script into a container that does not yet exist is
       why so many designs fail their first error test. -->
  <p class="error" role="alert" hidden></p>

  <button type="button" id="next">Pay now</button>
</form>

The error paragraph is present with hidden from the start. That is the detail that separates a prototype which can be tested for error recovery from one that cannot.

Watch the clicks, not the opinions

The measure that makes a prototype session productive is where people click and where they pause. A hesitation is data: the three seconds before a click is the reading time for the label, and a misclick is data about the affordance rather than about the person. Neither appears in a satisfaction survey and neither appears in what people say afterwards.

So keep a log during the session rather than reconstructing it. Three columns: what they clicked, how long before, and what they said. That log is the finding, and writing it live costs nothing while reconstructing it from memory afterwards costs the observation entirely.

Then iterate in rounds rather than continuously. Two rounds of five participants catches the large majority of flow faults, because the faults that survive one round are the ones nobody noticed, and showing the same journey to five fresh people after fixing the first five findings surfaces the next layer. Continuous iteration never converges - you end up fixing what the last participant did, which is not a method.

/* SESSION LOG AND ROUNDING. Two mechanisms. The log captures the evidence a
   satisfaction question throws away - hesitation and misclick. The rounding
   rule stops the endless-iteration failure, where the team fixes what the last
   participant did and calls it a result. */

function logSession(participant, events) {
  const rows = events.map((e, i) => {
    const prev = events[i - 1];
    return {
      click: e.target,
      // hesitation: the gap since the previous action. A long gap before a
      // PRIMARY action is a label problem; a long gap before a secondary one is
      // usually the participant reading your copy, not the interface.
      hesitateMs: prev ? e.at - prev.at : 0,
      said: e.said || "",
    };
  });

  const longPauses = rows.filter((r) => r.hesitateMs > 3000);
  return {
    participant,
    completed: events.at(-1)?.target === "confirmation",
    // a misclick is a measurement of the affordance, never a finding about the
    // participant - this distinction is what keeps the data usable
    misclicks: rows.filter((r) => r.said.match(/no|not that|where/i)),
    longPauses: longPauses.map((r) => ({ at: r.click, ms: r.hesitateMs })),
  };
}

// round-based, and the stop condition is explicit rather than a feeling
function planRound(fixedFromRoundOne, participantsRoundTwo) {
  const outstanding = fixedFromRoundOne.filter((f) => !f.fixed);
  return {
    // re-test the SAME journey with FRESH people, not the ones who failed it -
    // someone who struggled last time now knows the answer and is no evidence
    participants: participantsRoundTwo,
    // the stop rule, so the loop terminates
    stopWhen: outstanding.length <= 2,
    reason: "two rounds of five surface the large majority of flow faults; beyond that, cost per finding rises faster than finding size",
  };
}

Long pauses and misclicks are collected as separate lists on purpose. A pause is a reading problem and a misclick is an affordance problem, and merging them produces a single finding that fits neither.

A complete clickable prototype in pure HTML: anchors move between steps and the browser’s native form validation gates the next button, so no design tool is required.

4.5 Hi-fi: when visual design joins the conversation

High-fidelity design adds the brand layer, real typography, color, spacing, and motion to a validated structure, making the product look and feel like its final form. It is the artifact developers copy from, so it functions as the visual specification and must stay in sync with the actual build. Keep it updated as decisions change, or it turns into a misleading artifact. Hi-fi answers questions low fidelity cannot: trust, polish, and emotional response.

Hi-fi adds the brand layer (color, type, image treatment) and motion. It answers: does it feel like our product? It also becomes the spec developers copy — so keep it in sync or it turns into a lie. Version it like code.

What the brand layer actually does

Type, colour, spacing and motion are not decoration applied after the design works. Each one carries a specific piece of information, and removing it removes that information rather than making the screen plainer. Type hierarchy says what matters. Colour says what is interactive and what is disabled, what is destructive and what is safe. Spacing says what belongs together. Motion says what changed as a result of what you just did.

This is why a validated structure can still fail at high fidelity. A screen that worked in grey can become unreadable in real type, because placeholder text has no line-length behaviour - a heading at the length of "HEADING" is one line, and the real heading is three, and the layout that tolerated one no longer holds. The same applies to a button: a label that was three characters on the wireframe is a sentence in the interface, and every button width in the design was computed for the short one.

Trust is the finding unique to this rung, and it is worth treating seriously because it is measurable. People form a trust judgement in roughly the first fifty milliseconds, from signals that have little to do with whether the product works: alignment, consistent spacing, whether the primary button looks the same as every other primary button, whether anything moves when it should not. A screen that functions perfectly and looks assembled destroys confidence in a way a broken-looking one does not.

/* THE STYLED LAYER, with each declaration tied to the information it carries.
   The column on the right is the reason to make the decision at all: a style
   that carries no information is decoration, and decoration is a legitimate
   use of a design system only after everything else is settled. */

const TYPE_SCALE = [
  { step: "display", px: 40, weight: 700, says: "the one thing on this screen", limit: 1 },
  { step: "title",  px: 24, weight: 600, says: "the section's subject",      limit: 2 },
  { step: "body",   px: 16, weight: 400, says: "the content itself",          limit: "most" },
  { step: "meta",   px: 14, weight: 400, says: "supporting detail",           limit: "any" },
  { step: "micro",  px: 12, weight: 500, says: "a count or a badge",          limit: "short only" },
];

const COLOUR_ROLES = {
  "text-strong":  { says: "the heading of a section" },
  "text-default": { says: "body copy" },
  "text-muted":   { says: "de-emphasised, but still readable" },
  "accent":       { says: "an interactive element, and nothing else" },
  "brand":        { says: "a filled surface: the primary action" },
  "danger":       { says: "an action that destroys something" },
  "disabled":     { says: "unavailable - and it must not be the only cue" },
};

// the check that catches the most common hi-fi regression: an accent applied to
// something that is not interactive. Once a heading is accent-coloured, nothing
// else on the screen reads as a link.
function auditAccentUsage(elements) {
  const misuse = elements.filter(
    (e) => e.colour === "accent" && !e.interactive,
  );
  return {
    ok: misuse.length === 0,
    misuse: misuse.map((e) => e.label),
    rule: "accent means interactive; a non-interactive accent element removes the only link signal on the screen",
  };
}

The limit column on the type scale is the constraint that keeps a hierarchy real: two things on a screen may be display-sized, and if five are, none of them is.

Keeping the specification honest

The styled artefact is what developers copy, so it is a specification whether or not it was intended as one, and an out-of-date one is a specification for something you no longer intend to build. The rule that works is treating the design file the way you treat source: a change in behaviour is a versioned change with a note, and the build is regenerated rather than hand-corrected.

Components are where this either holds or fails. A design system whose components are drawn per-screen drifts within a month, because every screen reinterprets the same card. If a component exists, screens must compose it rather than redraw it, and a design file where the same component appears fourteen times with four variations is a design file that needs a system behind it before it needs more polish.

Decide the responsive behaviour at the same time as the design, per component rather than per page. A card that works at one width and is cropped at another is a component defect, and it will be found once per screen where it appears. Specify the container query rather than a breakpoint: a card in a sidebar and a card in a grid have the same content and different widths, and a single breakpoint cannot serve both.

/* RESPONSIVE BY COMPONENT, and the state matrix. Two specifications that a
   screen-level design usually leaves out and a developer always needs: what the
   component does at each container width, and what it looks like in each
   state. */

const CARD = {
  name: "order-card",
  // container-driven, not viewport-driven: the same card appears in a 320px
  // sidebar and a 900px grid, and a viewport breakpoint cannot serve both
  containers: {
    "narrow":  "stack: reference and total on one row, actions below, full width",
    "medium":  "two columns: reference left, total and actions right",
    "wide":    "single row: reference, meta, total, actions",
  },
  states: {
    default:   { shows: "reference, items, total, actions" },
    loading:   { shows: "three skeleton rows", note: "same height as the loaded card, so nothing jumps" },
    empty:     { shows: "no cards, an illustration, and one action", note: "never an empty list with no explanation" },
    error:     { shows: "one line and a retry", note: "retry must not clear the basket" },
    // the state that gets drawn last and costs most in testing
    paid:      { shows: "reference and total only", note: "actions removed, status shown as text not colour" },
  },
  // every interactive target, because 44px is the number most often lost when a
  // design is rebuilt responsively and padding is trimmed to fit
  targets: { min: 44, note: "the whole row is the target, not the label inside it" },
};

function auditComponent(spec) {
  const noLoading = !spec.states.loading;
  const noEmpty = !spec.states.empty;
  const noError = !spec.states.error;
  return {
    ok: !(noLoading && noEmpty && noError),
    missing: [
      noLoading && "loading - the layout will jump when data arrives",
      noEmpty && "empty - the user sees a blank region with no explanation",
      noError && "error - failure has no design, so it gets improvised in code",
    ].filter(Boolean),
    // and the check that a screen-level design never performs: every state at
    // every container width, which is 3 x 4 combinations rather than 4 screens
    combinations: Object.keys(spec.containers).length * Object.keys(spec.states).length,
  };
}

Three containers times four states is twelve renderings of one component. Drawn per screen rather than per component, that is a number nobody counts and every developer reinvents.

4.6 Handoff: converting designs into buildable specs

Handoff is the step where finished designs are converted into a specification developers can build from without guessing. Package your work as design tokens, spacing and typography specs, component states, and behavior notes, plus exported assets, in a tool the engineers actually use. Write the intent behind the design, not just the pixels, so developers can make sensible adaptations. A good handoff reduces questions and prevents breakdowns between design and code.

  • Exports: Figma dev-mode / Zeplin give CSS-ish properties, assets, and specs automatically.
  • Hand off design tokens (names, not pixel values): "surface/1" not "var(--panel)".
  • Hand off behavior: states, empty/loading/error, animation timings, breakpoints.
  • Leave room: developers are partners who know what’s cheap in CSS and what’s expensive.

Hand over intent, not screenshots

A handoff that consists of exported images has already lost the argument, because an image cannot say why a value is what it is, and a developer without the reason reinterprets it. Ask why the spacing is 24 rather than 20 and the honest answer is usually that a 4px step exists, which is a constraint worth transferring. Ask why the error text says what it says and the answer is usually that it was tested, which is the reason it survived review and the reason it must not be "improved" later.

So the artefact is three layers. Tokens - the names, with the values living in one file that both sides import. Components, with every state enumerated rather than implied. And annotations: the intent behind each decision, stated so that a developer facing an unanticipated situation can make a choice consistent with it rather than a safe-looking choice that ignores it.

Being explicit about what you are not handing over matters just as much. Developers are partners with their own knowledge of what is cheap and what is expensive in CSS, and a designer who has specified everything down to the pixel has removed the judgement they needed to contribute. The handover sets the constraints and the intent, and leaves the mechanism open.

/* THE HANDOFF PACKAGE, as a manifest. Naming the layers is the useful part:
   tokens, components, annotations. A handoff that carries the first two and
   omits the third is the common case, and it is the one that produces a build
   that disagrees with the design for reasons nobody can reconstruct. */

const HANDOFF = {
  tokens: {
    // names, never values: the value lives in one file both sides import, so a
    // change to it is a change everywhere rather than an edit per screen
    surface: ["surface-1", "surface-2", "surface-inset"],
    text:    ["text-strong", "text-default", "text-muted"],
    action:  ["action-primary", "action-secondary", "action-danger"],
    space:   ["space-1 through space-8", "4px steps"],
    radius:  ["radius-xs 3px", "radius 4px", "radius-lg 5px"],
  },
  components: [
    {
      name: "OrderCard",
      states: ["default", "loading", "empty", "error", "paid"],
      containers: ["narrow", "medium", "wide"],
      // measured targets, so the 44px minimum is not trimmed away to fit a
      // narrower layout without anyone deciding to
      targets: { minHeight: 44, note: "the whole row, not the label" },
    },
    {
      name: "PromoField",
      states: ["default", "invalid", "applied", "expired"],
      // an interaction spec, not a picture: this is the part that cannot be
      // inferred from a static frame
      behaviour: "invalid on blur but never while typing; applied state replaces the field in place",
    },
  ],
  annotations: [
    {
      decision: "the order number is 16px mono",
      intent: "it is transcribed from an email, so it must be unambiguous character by character",
      // and the consequence, so a later well-meaning change to the body font
      // does not quietly destroy the reason
      breaks_if: "changed to the body font, where l and 1 and I are indistinguishable",
    },
    {
      decision: "destructive actions use a confirmation dialog",
      intent: "measured twice, both times in error",
      breaks_if: "removed as friction, when the action is unrecoverable",
    },
  ],
  // what is deliberately NOT in the package, stated so nobody fills the gap
  // with a guess and calls it adherence
  notSpecified: [
    "DOM structure - use whatever is correct for the framework",
    "state management - the design does not constrain it",
    "focus order, except where it is stated above",
  ],
};

The breaks_if field is what survives contact with a well-meaning engineer six months later. It is the reason the decision was made, which is the one thing an annotation can carry that a screenshot cannot.

Design and code, or one file

The strongest handoff is the one where there is no handoff, because the tokens are the tokens and the components are the same components. Where that is not available, the next best arrangement is for the design system to export the values the designers use, so a designer selecting "surface-2" in a tool and a developer writing var(--surface-2) are provably referencing the same thing.

What still needs transferring by hand is behaviour, and behaviour is where handoffs quietly fail. The things that get lost are the ones nobody animated: the keyboard order, what happens on an empty result, what a disabled control looks like, whether a destructive action is reversible afterwards, what happens at 320px, and what the focus ring looks like. All six are cheap to specify and expensive to discover during accessibility testing.

/* BEHAVIOUR THAT DOES NOT SURVIVE A SCREENSHOT HANDOFF. Every item here has
   been discovered late in at least one project, and every one of them is a few
   words to specify and a week to fix after the fact. This is the checklist
   that goes with the design, and it is deliberately specific: "make it
   accessible" transfers nothing. */

const BEHAVIOUR_HANDOFF = [
  {
    item: "keyboard order and focus ring",
    specify: "order follows the visual order; ring is 2px solid accent, inset 2px, never removed",
    // why it transfers badly: a screenshot shows a ring in its default state and
    // says nothing about which element comes next
    late_discovery_cost: "keyboard-only testing finds it after the component is in 30 places",
  },
  {
    item: "empty state",
    specify: "what appears, what it says, and what the user can do next",
    late_discovery_cost: "shipped as a blank region, read as a bug",
  },
  {
    item: "loading",
    specify: "skeleton matching final height, or a progress indicator with a stated duration",
    // the specific failure: a skeleton at a different height than the content
    // causes a layout shift that looks like the page broke
    late_discovery_cost: "layout shift on every load, blamed on the framework",
  },
  {
    item: "error",
    specify: "the message text, whether it is recoverable, and whether input is preserved",
    late_discovery_cost: "the most common source of lost form data",
  },
  {
    item: "destructive actions",
    specify: "whether it is reversible, and for how long",
    late_discovery_cost: "an unrecoverable action with no undo",
  },
  {
    item: "the 320px case",
    specify: "what reflows, what is hidden, and what scrolls horizontally if anything",
    late_discovery_cost: "discovered on the oldest supported phone, in production",
  },
  {
    item: "reduced motion",
    specify: "which transitions collapse to none under prefers-reduced-motion",
    late_discovery_cost: "vestibular-triggering animation shipped to everyone",
  },
];

// and the one-line answer to "is this handoff complete" that a screen cannot give
function isHandoffComplete(spec) {
  const missing = BEHAVIOUR_HANDOFF.filter((b) => !spec[b.item]);
  return { ok: missing.length === 0, missing: missing.map((b) => b.item) };
}

Each entry pairs the specification with the reason it is missed. The screenshot cannot carry any of these, which is why they are the recurring late findings rather than occasional ones.

4.7 Guerrilla testing: validate in a lunch break

Guerrilla testing takes your prototype or product out to a public place and asks five or so strangers to attempt one task on the spot, with no recruiter and no lab. It is a fast, cheap way to find the most obvious usability problems before you invest in formal research. Screen the worst candidates quickly and debrief afterwards to catalog findings. Iterating rapidly through several small sessions beats one polished lab study.

  • Take paper or low-fi screens somewhere public, ask strangers for 5 minutes, and watch them attempt ONE task ("buy this, paying by card").
  • Think-aloud optional; you’re tracking hesitation and wrong turns, not taking orders. One note per person: "got it", "paused at step 2", "misread the button".
  • Five strangers reveal most flow-level problems — cheaply and fast. It’s the repetition habit that beats any single fancy lab; do it before hi-fi so feedback lands on structure, not aesthetics.

Exercises 4

  1. Sketch (paper ok) the payment flow of your chosen product from Ch.0: 5 thumbnail wireframes + a user flow with 3 decision points.
  2. Build a clickable mid-fi prototype of it in Figma or HTML and test it on one person.
  3. Note the 3 states your first draft forgot (loading? empty? server error?) and add them.

Why five strangers is a real method

Guerrilla testing is usually dismissed as the cheap version, and it is worth being clear that it is not a weaker version of a lab study. It is a different estimator. A lab session gives depth on a small, recruited, possibly not-representative sample. A street session gives breadth on a convenience sample with no depth at all. For the question "is anything here obviously broken", breadth is the right instrument.

Five strangers are enough because flow-level faults repeat. They are properties of the artefact, not of the person: if a control is ambiguous, most people will find it ambiguous, and the fourth and fifth participants are confirming rather than discovering. That is the reason for the number, and it is also the reason it stops being useful - by participant eight you are getting the same finding for the cost of four more.

So screen, and screen fast. The thirty-second script is: what it is, what you would like to do, five minutes, may I watch, here is the task. Anything longer turns a participant into an audience. And do not coach - the first hint you give destroys the finding, and the participant will politely complete a task they could not complete alone.

/* THE SCRIPT, and the triage that makes it a method rather than an
   afternoon. Twenty notes from five people is noise; the value is in ranking
   them and noticing which faults RECUR, because recurrence is the evidence that
   a fault is in the artefact rather than in the participant. */

const BRIEF = {
  // the whole recruitment conversation, in four sentences
  ask: "I am testing a flow, not you. It takes five minutes. I cannot help you at all - " +
       "if something is confusing that is exactly what I need to see. Here is the task: " +
       "book this appointment paying by card. I will stay quiet and take notes.",
  // what to say, and what NOT to say. Saying the button name is the most common
  // way a session is ruined, and it happens because you can see the answer.
  neverSay: [
    "the button is on the right",
    "try clicking there",
    "most people find this step fine",
    "is this making sense?"     // invites agreement, produces agreement
  ],
};

const NOTES = [
  { who: "p1", seconds: 210, gotIt: false, pause: ["delivery options", "pay"], note: "looked for a total before choosing delivery" },
  { who: "p2", seconds: 95,  gotIt: true,  pause: ["pay"],                 note: "smooth" },
  { who: "p3", seconds: 240, gotIt: false, pause: ["delivery options"],     note: "did not see the next button, tried scrolling" },
  { who: "p4", seconds: 180, gotIt: false, pause: ["delivery options", "card number"], note: "asked whether the price shown was the total" },
  { who: "p5", seconds: 110, gotIt: true,  pause: ["card number"],         note: "slow but finished" },
];

function triage(notes) {
  // recurrence is the signal. A fault one participant hit is a hypothesis; the
  // same place four participants hit is a defect.
  const tally = {};
  for (const n of notes) for (const p of n.pause) {
    tally[p] = (tally[p] || 0) + 1;
  }
  const recurring = Object.entries(tally)
    .filter(([, c]) => c >= 3)
    .sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]);

  const completions = notes.filter((n) => n.gotIt).length;
  return {
    n: notes.length,
    // below 80 percent on a two-minute task, the flow is not shippable, and
    // the number matters more than any individual note
    completion: (completions / notes.length).toFixed(2),
    // median rather than mean: one confused participant must not move the
    // headline number, and with five samples the mean is very fragile
    medianSeconds: median(notes.map((n) => n.seconds)),
    recurring,
    // and the individual notes are kept, because a rare fault on an
    // irreversible action still matters
    rareButSerious: notes.filter((n) => !n.gotIt && /lost|paid|confirm/.test(n.note)),
  };
}

Median seconds rather than mean: one participant who flails for six minutes moves the mean substantially and means nothing. The recurring-pause list is the actionable output, and three out of five is the working threshold.

Running it repeatedly, and reading what it cannot tell you

The unit of value is the repetition, not the session. One guerrilla round finds faults; a weekly round finds the ones that keep coming back, which are the ones somebody is re-adding because they have not been told they are faults. A cheap weekly loop that produces one written line - "four of five paused at the same place, fixed" - is worth more than a thorough study conducted once before a launch.

What it cannot tell you is equally important. There is no recruiting screener, so the sample is whoever was passing, which skews towards confident people in a hurry - and a confident person in a hurry is the person most likely to complete a flow that others abandon. The completion rate is therefore optimistic, and it should be read as a ceiling rather than as a measurement.

And there is no depth. You will not learn why someone paused, only that they did. So a recurring pause is a place to send a proper interview, not a finding in itself - which is the right way to use this method. Cheap and frequent for breadth, then expensive and rare for depth, pointed at whatever the cheap loop keeps surfacing.

/* THE WEEKLY LOOP, with the two limits enforced in code. The point of a small
   frequent method is that it never gets skipped, so the reporting has to be one
   line and the escalation has to be automatic rather than remembered. */

function weeklyRound(session) {
  const t = triage(session.notes);
  return {
    // one line, written the same day, filed in the same place. A method that
    // needs a report nobody writes will be run three times and abandoned.
    headline: t.completion + " completed, median " + t.medianSeconds + "s, worst pause: " +
              (t.recurring[0]?.[0] || "none recurring"),
    fixed: session.fixed,
    // escalation: a fault that recurs across THREE separate rounds has stopped
    // being a hypothesis. Three rounds of five strangers is fifteen people,
    // which outranks most single lab sessions.
    escalate: t.recurring.filter(([, c]) => c >= 4).length >= 2 ||
              session.roundsSinceReported >= 3,
    escalation_target: "a moderated interview, one task, same point",
  };
}

function median(xs) {
  const s = [...xs].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const m = Math.floor(s.length / 2);
  return s.length % 2 ? s[m] : Math.round((s[m - 1] + s[m]) / 2);
}

The escalation rule is what keeps the loop honest. A fault recurring across three weekly rounds means fifteen strangers hit the same wall, which is more evidence than a single polished lab session produces - and it still only tells you where, not why.

5 · Interaction Design

Interaction design defines how an interface responds to every action a user takes, covering feedback, screen states, gestures, and motion. Its purpose is to make the product feel predictable and effortless so people always understand the result of their actions. In practice you map the state of every control, specify immediate feedback for every trigger, and choreograph transitions that explain change. Get the forces of feedback, state, and timing right and the product feels alive rather than broken.

5.1 Feedback: every action needs a response5.2 The state machine of any UI5.3 Motion: the how-much debate5.4 Microinteractions: the soul of a product5.5 Gestures for touch5.6 Timing: response budgets & perceived speed

Interaction design (IxD) is what the interface does when the user acts — the physics of the digital world. Good interaction is invisible and obvious; bad interaction makes users feel clumsy.

5.1 Feedback: every action needs a response

Feedback is the interface’s immediate acknowledgment that an action was registered, whether through a state change, animation, message, or sound. Every click, tap, or press needs a response within a fraction of a second, because silence reads as the product being broken. Plan the feedback for each action before writing code, choosing the form that matches the action’s importance. Predictable responses build trust in the system.

Respond toFeedbackTiming
Click / tappress state, ripple, slight scale< 100 ms
Form submitprogress + success/errorprogress during, result after
Saveconfirmation ("Saved 12:34"), noticeable but quietimmediately
Long taskprogress bar or %, cancel optionimmediately + updates
Failureclear message + next stepimmediately

Silence is the worst error. "I clicked and nothing happened" is how users conclude the site is broken or they broke it. If the system is busy for > 400ms, the user must know work is happening (spinner, skeleton, progress).

Choose the feedback by how much the action cost

The form of feedback is not a matter of taste. It should be proportional to what the action did, and the proportionality is what a user reads subconsciously as quality. An action that saved nothing confirms with a transient colour change on the control. An action that spent money deserves a persistent, unambiguous confirmation that survives scrolling the page. An action that cannot be undone needs its outcome stated in words, not implied by an animation.

The thing every action needs is an acknowledgement inside about a hundred milliseconds, and that threshold is not arbitrary. Below roughly 100ms the response feels like a consequence of the press itself, and the user does not perceive it as feedback at all. Between 100ms and a second it reads as the system working. Beyond a second, silence stops being neutral and becomes an error report - the user assumes the press was missed, and the most common response is to press again.

That double-press is the real cost of slow acknowledgement, and it is why the rule is to disable a control the instant it is pressed rather than after the response arrives. A button that stays enabled for 800ms will be pressed twice by a meaningful fraction of users, which on a payment means two charges and on a form means a duplicated record. Disable synchronously; re-enable on failure rather than on success.

/* FEEDBACK BY COST. Each row pairs the action with the feedback form AND the
   threshold, because "show a spinner" is not a specification - a spinner for a
   200ms request is a flash of nonsense that reads as an error, and the fix is
   simply to not have one at that speed. */

const RESPONSES = [
  {
    cost: "reversible, local",        examples: "toggle, like, expand",
    ack: "the control's own state changes",
    within: 100,
    // no message at all: a toast for a like is noise the user has to dismiss
    message: false,
  },
  {
    cost: "reversible, distant",      examples: "saved, added to basket, sent",
    ack: "persistent confirmation, then a transient message",
    within: 1000,
    message: true,
  },
  {
    cost: "irreversible, small",      examples: "delete a filter, archive an item",
    // the irreversible case is where undo is not optional - it is the feedback
    ack: "undo affordance held for at least 8 seconds",
    within: 1000,
    message: true,
  },
  {
    cost: "irreversible, large",      examples: "delete an account, cancel a subscription",
    ack: "explicit confirmation naming exactly what is lost",
    within: 0,          // no async wait at all: this must be immediate
    message: true,
  },
  {
    cost: "long-running",             examples: "import, export, upload, search",
    // beyond a second, silence is an error report - so the rule changes shape
    ack: "progress with a count, or partial content",
    within: 1000,
    message: true,
  },
];

// the threshold that decides whether a spinner appears at all. Below this the
// spinner itself is the artefact: it flashes for 150ms and reads as a glitch.
const SPINNER_THRESHOLD_MS = 400;
const SKELETON_THRESHOLD_MS = 1000;

function plan(action, measuredMs) {
  const row = RESPONSES.find((r) => action.cost === r.cost);
  const feedback =
    measuredMs < SPINNER_THRESHOLD_MS ? "none beyond the control's own state" :
    measuredMs < SKELETON_THRESHOLD_MS ? "inline progress on the control" :
    "skeleton matching the final layout, or partial content";
  return {
    ack: row.ack,
    // and the double-press guard, which is not optional and is applied
    // synchronously rather than after the response
    disableImmediately: action.irreversible || action.cost === "long-running",
    reenable: "on failure only",
    feedback,
  };
}

The spinner threshold is the number most often missed. A loading indicator for a request that takes 200ms is a flash of clutter, and users read a flash as an error rather than as progress.

Where confirmation goes, and why toast is not it

A transient message is a poor home for anything a user might need to refer back to, and it fails in ways that are invisible in a design review: it disappears, it covers content, it stacks when three arrive at once, it is announced to a screen reader and then removed before the announcement finishes, and on a phone it sits directly over the control the user needs next. It is a good home for "copied" and a bad one for anything that matters.

So the outcome goes where the thing happened. Saving an item changes the item's row. Sending a message shows it in the thread. A destructive action leaves the item visible with an undo affordance, which is better than a message because the evidence persists in place and the correction is next to the mistake.

Then consider silence. For an action with an unambiguous visible result - the row moved, the item appeared - a message is redundant, and users read redundant confirmations as anxiety from the product. The test is whether the user can tell what happened without a message; if they can, the message is noise, and noise costs trust because it teaches people to ignore everything the interface says.

/* FEEDBACK LOCATION, and the announcement that goes with it. The a11y half
   matters here: a toast that is removed before a screen reader finishes
   announcing it produces silence, which is worse than never announcing it,
   because the user learns the interface does not report things. */

const FEEDBACK_PLACEMENT = {
  "toggle, like, expand":        { where: "the control itself", announce: null },
  "saved":                      { where: "the row or field that changed", announce: null },
  "added to basket":            { where: "a persistent count on the basket control", announce: "polite" },
  "sent":                       { where: "the item, in the thread", announce: "polite" },
  "deleted with undo":          { where: "a bar under the header, 8s, with the item named", announce: "assertive" },
  // the one where a toast is right: nothing on the page changed and the user
  // needs to know the system noticed
  "copied to clipboard":        { where: "a transient message, 2s", announce: "polite" },
  "import finished":            { where: "a persistent row in the list of imports", announce: "polite" },
};

/* aria-live regions announce on CHANGE, so a live region created at the moment
   the message appears is usually not announced at all - it has to exist in the
   DOM beforehand, empty. That is why the region below is mounted once. */
const LIVE_REGION = "<div aria-live=\"polite\" class=\"sr-status\"></div>";

function announce(message, { assertive = false } = {}) {
  // assertive INTERRUPTS whatever is being read. Correct for an error or an
  // undo bar; wrong for a count that updates on every keystroke.
  const region = assertive ? "error" : "status";
  return {
    region,
    message,
    // and it must persist long enough to be read: clearing it as soon as the
    // toast disappears produces the silence described above
    keepForMs: 5000,
  };
}

The live region is mounted once, empty, and its contents change. A live region inserted together with its own text is frequently not announced, because the accessibility API only reports changes within an existing region.

5.2 The state machine of any UI

Every component and screen exists in several states, including normal, hover, active, disabled, loading, error, and empty. Map all the reachable states for each element up front, define what triggers each transition, and design them deliberately. When you specify states before building, you design away most bugs and dead ends before they can happen. An unmapped state is where confusion and errors live.

Every component/screen owns states; missing states = bugs users will hit:
  NORMAL  →  HOVER  →  FOCUS  →  ACTIVE  →  DISABLED
  plus   →  LOADING / EMPTY / ERROR / SUCCESS (post-submit)
  plus   →  EDGE (overflow: long names, huge numbers, tiny screens)
Checklist question: "what do I see while waiting? after failure?
  with no data? with 1000 items? with a 200-char name?"

Map the states before the component exists

The reason states get missed is that they are not visible on the happy path. Nobody designs the empty state because there is nothing on screen to react to, and nobody designs the error state because errors happen to someone else. Then the component ships with four of its seven states undefined, and the undefined ones are discovered in production by the users who hit them.

So enumerate them per component rather than per screen, and treat the list as exhaustive until proven otherwise. The standard set is seven: default, hover, focus-visible, active, disabled, loading, error. A component with data adds empty and partial. A component with an asynchronous operation adds pending, which is not the same as loading - pending is the state where the operation has been requested and no response has arrived, and it needs its own design because that is the state where double-submission happens.

Then name the trigger for each transition, because an unmapped transition is a state change nobody designed. Every transition needs a cause: hover from a pointer, focus-visible from a keyboard, loading from a request starting, error from a request failing, empty from a result set returning zero rows. If you cannot name the trigger, the state may not be reachable - which is worth knowing before anyone builds it.

/* THE STATE MATRIX, as data, so it can be checked rather than trusted.
   The check at the bottom is the useful part: a component with no trigger for
   a state it declares is a state that will never appear, and one with a state
   and no trigger is a defect nobody will find until production. */

const COMPONENT_STATES = {
  "submit-button": {
    states: {
      idle:      { visual: "label, enabled",   trigger: "initial" },
      pressed:   { visual: "pressed, darker",   trigger: "pointerdown" },
      pending:   { visual: "spinner, label kept, DISABLED", trigger: "request started" },
      // the failure state, and the reason pending exists as a separate state:
      // it is the only window in which a second press can happen
      succeeded: { visual: "checkmark, 2s, then idle", trigger: "response 2xx" },
      failed:    { visual: "label returns, message beside the button", trigger: "response non-2xx or timeout" },
    },
    // states that are reachable but whose visual is undefined are the defect
    // this whole exercise exists to catch
    invariants: [
      "pending is the only state in which the control is disabled",
      "a failed request restores idle AND keeps the entered data",
      "pressed and pending never coexist - pending replaces pressed synchronously",
    ],
  },

  "results-list": {
    states: {
      loading:   { visual: "skeleton rows at final height", trigger: "request started" },
      populated: { visual: "rows", trigger: "result set non-empty" },
      // the state nobody draws, and the one users describe as a broken site
      empty:     { visual: "explanation, one action, no filter UI", trigger: "result set empty" },
      // also nobody draws it, and it is the one that produces support tickets
      partial:   { visual: "the rows that loaded, plus an explicit partial notice", trigger: "some results failed" },
      error:     { visual: "one line and a retry, filters preserved", trigger: "request failed" },
    },
    invariants: [
      "the skeleton height equals the populated height, or the page jumps on load",
      "empty is not an illustration alone - it always states what would appear here",
      "retry preserves scroll position and every applied filter",
    ],
  },
};

function auditStates(spec) {
  const states = Object.entries(spec.states);
  const noTrigger = states.filter(([, s]) => !s.trigger).map(([k]) => k);
  const noVisual = states.filter(([, s]) => !s.visual).map(([k]) => k);
  // the cross-check that catches the worst omission: a declared state nothing
  // can ever enter, which usually means the trigger is missing rather than the
  // state being unnecessary
  const unreachable = states.filter(([, s]) => s.trigger === "initial").map(([k]) => k);
  return { ok: !noVisual.length && unreachable.length <= 1, noVisual, unreachable, invariants: spec.invariants };
}

The partial state is the one that justifies the whole exercise. A results list that has a loading state, a populated state and an error state but no partial state will silently show ten of two hundred results as though that were all of them.

Transitions, and what changes between them

Two states can both be well designed and still produce a bad component, because the transition between them is a third thing to get right. The most common defect is a state that appears with no animation where everything else animates, which reads as a glitch rather than as a change - so if a component transitions, all of its transitions use the same duration and easing.

Then think about which transitions must not animate at all. A state change that carries a message the user needs should be instantaneous, because animation delays the reading of the message. Error states should not fade in - a slow red box feels like a warning about something that might not be a problem, whereas an immediate one is unambiguous.

Finally, decide which states are mutually exclusive and which can co-occur. A button can be pending and disabled, but not pressed and pending. A row can be populated and selected but not populated and empty. Writing the exclusive pairs down as invariants is what stops an implementation from reaching an impossible combination during an edge case at three in the morning, which is the only time these combinations are discovered.

/* EXCLUSIVITY, checked. Two independently designed states can be combined into
   something nobody designed, and the combinations are where the real bugs are -
   a row that is simultaneously empty and populated renders as nothing at all. */

function combine(component, pairs) {
  const impossible = [];
  for (const [a, b] of pairs) {
    // a state whose trigger is a terminal result cannot coexist with a state
    // whose trigger is the opposite result
    if (isTerminal(component, a) && isTerminal(component, b)) impossible.push([a, b]);
  }
  return { ok: impossible.length === 0, impossible };
}

// each component declares which of its states mean "a result came back"
const TERMINAL = {
  "results-list": ["populated", "empty", "partial", "error"],
  "submit-button": ["succeeded", "failed"],
  "search-input":  ["results", "empty", "error"],
};

// and the rule that falls out of it, which is cheap to enforce at the reducer
// level rather than in the view
const SETTLE_RULES = {
  // a new request cancels the old one rather than racing it, so a slow first
  // response cannot overwrite a fast second one - the single most common state
  // bug in any searchable interface
  onNewRequest: "cancel in-flight, reset to loading, ignore any response from the cancelled request",
  // a failure restores the previous content rather than clearing it, so the user
  // does not lose what they were looking at
  onError: "keep existing content, add the error notice, preserve filters and scroll",
  // and a partial response is a populated state with a flag, not a separate
  // branch, which stops the two from diverging
  onPartial: "render as populated with partialNoticed set",
};

The cancellation rule is worth reading twice. A search box that fires on every keystroke will display results for the fourth request when the second one returns late, and the user sees results that do not match what they typed.

A waiting-room audit: list every state a component shows — normal, hover, empty, error, overloaded — so none get forgotten.

5.3 Motion: the how-much debate

Motion in interfaces exists to explain change, showing where an element came from, what moved, and what the user’s action did. Use it sparingly and consistently, with durations and easing tied to a small shared scale so the whole product has one coherent physics. Fast, functional motion that clarifies state beats decorative animation that distracts. When every element animates, users stop reading motion as meaning.

  • Purpose first: motion should explain (origin of the element, state change, spatial relationship), not decorate.
  • Speed: 150–250 ms UI transitions; longer for full-context changes. Respect users who disable motion (prefers-reduced-motion).
  • Easing: ease-out = fast then settle (standard). Avoid linear bounces except for "drop" moments.
  • Motion as system: same duration/curve for the same type of change → users learn your product’s physics.
/* Consistent motion via tokens */
:root{ --dur-fast:120ms; --dur-base:200ms; --dur-slow:350ms;
       --ease-out:cubic-bezier(.2,.7,.3,1); }
button{ transition:transform var(--dur-fast) var(--ease-out); }
dialog{ animation:pop var(--dur-base) var(--ease-out); }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce){ *{transition-duration:.01ms !important; animation-duration:.01ms !important;} }

Motion is an explanation, or it is noise

Interface motion earns its place by answering one of three questions: where did this come from, what changed, and what did my action do. A panel that slides from the edge answers where it came from. A card that grows answers what changed. A button that depresses answers what the press did. A background gradient that slowly shifts answers nothing, and it costs attention that was available for reading.

The corollary is that animation is only meaningful in relation to something. A fade-in without a fade-out for a corresponding element tells the reader nothing, because there is no pairing to perceive. What makes it legible is continuity: the element's position and size persist through the change, so the eye can follow it. This is why a screen that rebuilds everything on navigation feels slow even when it is not - nothing persists, so nothing can be tracked, and the reader has to re-establish the whole layout.

So the rule is that at most one thing moves at a time in any transition, and it moves for a duration short enough not to be waited on. Between 150 and 250 milliseconds covers almost every interface transition; the range's lower bound is where motion stops being perceivable as motion and the upper bound is where the user is waiting for it to finish.

/* THE MOTION SCALE. Four durations and two curves, and nothing outside them.
   The point of a closed scale is that motion becomes learnable: a user who has
   seen one 120ms fade knows what a 120ms fade means everywhere else in the
   product. An ad-hoc duration per screen teaches nothing. */

const DURATION = {
  micro:  120,   // a colour or opacity change on one control
  ui:     180,   // a control appearing, a menu opening
  panel:  240,   // a panel or drawer moving
  context: 320,  // a whole-screen change, such as a route transition
};

const EASING = {
  // the default for anything entering: fast to start, so the action feels
  // acknowledged immediately, then settling
  out:  "cubic-bezier(.2, .8, .2, 1)",
  // for anything leaving: slow to start, fast to leave, because the element
  // should not appear to hesitate on its way out
  in:   "cubic-bezier(.4, 0, 1, 1)",
  // for anything moving within the screen - a card changing position rather than
  // appearing or disappearing. Symmetric, because there is no start or end to
  // the event, only a change of place
  move: "cubic-bezier(.4, 0, .2, 1)",
};

/* Duration and easing are chosen by the ROLE of the transition, never by the
   element. Two panels moving for different reasons should not move differently,
   or the motion stops describing anything. */
function motionFor(change) {
  const entering = /enter|appear|open|expand|reveal/.test(change);
  const leaving  = /exit|close|collapse|dismiss|hide/.test(change);
  const moving   = /reorder|resize|reposition/.test(change);

  if (moving)   return { ms: DURATION.panel, ease: EASING.move,  label: "move" };
  if (leaving)  return { ms: DURATION.ui,    ease: EASING.in,   label: "exit" };
  if (entering) return { ms: DURATION.ui,    ease: EASING.out,  label: "enter" };
  return { ms: DURATION.micro, ease: EASING.out, label: "state" };
}

Choosing by role rather than by element is what makes the scale a system. If the drawer moves at 240ms because it is a drawer, a different drawer at 200ms teaches the user that the durations mean nothing.

Reduced motion, and what replaces it

Motion is a genuine accessibility problem, not a preference. For people with vestibular disorders a large translating element can cause genuine nausea, and the preference exists because the harm is real and reported. So honour it - but the mistake is to read it as "no animation", which produces an interface that is worse rather than merely plainer.

The correct reading is that the information the motion carried must still be delivered another way. What reduced motion should remove is movement across the viewport: a panel that slides from the edge should instead appear in place. What it should keep is a change with no spatial component: a colour change, an opacity fade of a few hundred milliseconds, a background tint. Those convey state without moving anything through space, which is what causes the problem.

So the reduced-motion block is a re-specification of the same motion in place, not a blanket override. That is why the transitions are declared as tokens with roles: a motion spec that says "animate the drawer" can be re-specified, while one that says "transform: translateX(100%) to 0 over 240ms" cannot, because the meaning is inside the declaration rather than beside it.

/* REDUCED MOTION AS A RE-SPECIFICATION. Note that this is a transform
   OVERRIDE, not a duration override. Setting duration to 0 removes the
   information as well as the movement, and the result is a panel that simply
   appears with no indication of where it came from - which is the whole thing
   the motion was communicating. */

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .drawer {
    transform: translateX(100%);
    transition: transform 240ms cubic-bezier(.4, 0, .2, 1);
  }
  .drawer[open] { transform: translateX(0); }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  /* the element still moves, because that is the information; what is removed is
     the DURATION. 1ms rather than 0 so the transition event still fires, which
     matters if anything waits on transitionend to move focus or remove a node */
  .drawer {
    transform: translateX(100%);
    transition: transform 1ms linear;
  }
  .drawer[open] { transform: translateX(0); }

  /* large travelling elements: no spatial movement at all, because this is the
     specific pattern that triggers symptoms */
  .full-screen-panel { animation: none; }

  /* opacity is retained everywhere. It carries state without displacing
     anything through the field of view, so it is not the thing that harms. */
  .fade { transition: opacity 120ms linear; }
}

/* And the case that argues for the whole feature: an auto-playing animation
   with no user input behind it. It should not run at all, regardless of the
   preference, because it competes with reading for a user who did not start it. */
.banner { animation: none; }

The one-millisecond duration is not a typo. A zero duration does not fire a transition event, and code waiting on transitionend to move focus or clean up a node then never runs.

Durations, easing, and reduced-motion preferences are defined once as tokens, then reused everywhere so motion feels like one system.

5.4 Microinteractions: the soul of a product

Microinteractions are small, focused moments of interaction, such as liking a post, undoing an action, or pull-to-refresh, that loop through trigger, rules, feedback, and state. They carry much of a product’s personality and perceived polish. Design them deliberately: define the trigger, the loop’s rules, the feedback, and all the states, especially the success and failure branches. Get the states right first, then layer charm on top.

A microinteraction is one atomic loop: trigger → rule → feedback → loop/modes. The "like" button that pops, the pull-to-refresh that snaps, the password strength bar — these little loops define how a product feels. Design them deliberately, and prototype motion only after the interaction logic (states!) is right.

The four parts, and which one goes wrong

A microinteraction is a closed loop with four parts: the trigger, the rules that govern what happens, the feedback the user sees, and the modes the loop can rest in. Most of them are designed well and fail in the fourth. The rules and the feedback get attention because they are visible; the modes are invisible until something goes wrong, and they are where the loop actually breaks.

Take a like button. Trigger: the press. Rules: one like per user, no like on your own post, rate limited. Feedback: the icon fills and the count goes up. Modes: liked, not liked, and - the one nobody specifies - the pending state between the press and the response, and what happens if the request fails. A like button with no failure mode will leave the icon filled and the count wrong, and it will do so silently.

The rules are where the design decisions actually live, and they are usually implied rather than written. What happens on a second press within a second? Is the toggle optimistic or does it wait? Does the count update before the server confirms? Each of these is a decision about what the user sees during a latency window, and each has a defensible answer, and none of them is answered by the component's appearance.

/* THE FOUR PARTS, declared. The modes field is the one to insist on: it is the
   difference between a loop that recovers and one that is stuck permanently in
   a state the user cannot leave. Every mode needs an exit, and "reload the
   page" is not one. */

const LIKE = {
  trigger: {
    on: "press, pointer or keyboard",
    // both, deliberately - a like button reachable only by pointer is
    // unreachable by keyboard, and this loop is the smallest possible version
    // of that bug
    accessible: "it is a button, so Enter and Space both activate it",
  },
  rules: [
    "one like per user per item, enforced server-side",
    "no like on your own post",
    "optimistic: the count and the fill change immediately, before the response",
    // and the reason for optimism: the perceived cost of waiting on a like is
    // far higher than the perceived cost of being briefly wrong
    onFailure: "revert the fill and the count, and say so quietly - the count returning is the message",
  ],
  feedback: {
    visual: "icon fills, count increments by one",
    // and the non-visual half, which is the one that gets omitted and the one
    // that makes the loop usable without sight of it
    announced: "polite - the count with its new value",
    // NOT assertive: it interrupts, and a rapid series of likes would make the
    // interface unusable
  },
  modes: {
    unliked:   { on: "press", to: "liking" },
    liking:    { after: "response", to: "liked or unliked", timeout: "5000ms -> unliked with a retry" },
    liked:     { on: "press", to: "unliking" },
    unliking:  { after: "response", to: "unliked or liked", timeout: "5000ms -> liked with a retry" },
    // and the two that never appear in a design file
    offline:   { entry: "network unavailable", to: "unliked, retry queued or discarded visibly" },
    rateLimited: { entry: "server rejected", to: "unliked, with a message that is not an apology" },
  },
};

/* Every mode must be able to leave. A mode with no exit is the defect this
   check exists for, and it is invisible until a user reaches it. */
function findStuckModes(spec) {
  return Object.entries(spec.modes)
    .filter(([, m]) => !m.on && !m.after && !m.entry)
    .map(([k]) => k);
}

Every mode has an exit and a timeout. A like that is still liking after five seconds has failed on a slow connection, and without the timeout the user is left with a button that does nothing.

Charm last, and only where the states are right

The order matters and it is routinely inverted. Delight added on top of a loop with a broken failure mode produces a charming interaction that fails badly - a bouncy animation that plays and then reverses, which is worse to watch than an interface that simply failed quietly. Get the states right and the interaction will already feel good, because responsiveness and consistency are what users experience as polish.

Then charm, sparingly, and only on loops that repeat. A celebration that fires on the first interaction is a reward for discovering the product. A celebration that fires on the hundredth is a texture the user lives with, and it is the hundredth that decides whether they find it delightful or tiresome. So reserve the largest motion for the first occurrence and taper it.

And keep it fast. The most common defect in a charming microinteraction is that the charm happens before the feedback, so the user waits for the animation to find out whether the action worked. Feedback first, always; charm immediately after it, never instead of it.

/* TAPPED DELIGHT. The rule is the taper: the first occurrence gets the full
   expression, and repeat occurrences get progressively less, down to nothing.
   This is a design decision about the hundredth use that is invisible when you
   build the component and is the reason it does not get built. */

function delightFor(occurrence, kind) {
  // kinds differ in how much expression they can afford: a destructive action
  // is not a place for confetti at any count, and an undo confirmation is not
  // either - those are trust moments, not reward moments
  const EXPRESSION = {
    "like":            { full: "icon scale 1 -> 1.25 -> 1, 320ms", reduced: "colour only, 120ms" },
    "milestone":       { full: "a brief banner",                     reduced: "a line of text" },
    "completed-task":  { full: "a check draw, 400ms",                 reduced: "a check, no draw" },
    // these two are deliberately uncharmable, and saying so here is what stops
    // someone adding it later
    "destructive":     { full: "none - confirm clearly instead",      reduced: "none" },
    "undo-offered":    { full: "none - a calm, visible undo bar",     reduced: "none" },
  };

  const e = EXPRESSION[kind];
  if (!e) return { animate: false, why: "unknown interaction kind" };

  // the taper: first use, second use, then reduced to nothing. Nothing here is
  // ever removed from the state model - only the expression is reduced.
  if (occurrence === 1) return { animate: e.full, level: "full" };
  if (occurrence === 2) return { animate: e.reduced, level: "reduced" };
  return { animate: false, level: "none", still: "the state change, the feedback and the announcement all remain" };
}

The still field is the important one. The taper removes the expression and never the feedback, so a user on their hundredth like still sees the count change and still hears it announced.

5.5 Gestures for touch

Gestures such as swipe, pinch, and long press make touch interactions fast and direct, but they are invisible to new users. Every hidden gesture needs a discoverable path to the same action, whether through an on-screen button, an onboarding hint, or an obvious default state. Respect platform conventions so users' instincts transfer, and support undo for destructive gestures. Gestures buy speed; discoverability is the tax.

GestureStrengthRisky use
Tapuniversal, discoverable— (no)
Swipefast, spatial (carousels)uncovering hidden actions (undo) — invisible
Long-presspower actionshidden, can conflict with text selection; desktop mouse users can’t do it
Pinchzoom, naturalneeds a hint; accessibility tools steal it

Every hidden gesture needs a visible path to the same action (an ellipsis menu, a button). Long-press-only features are a common professional blind spot.

The cost of an invisible gesture

A gesture has no affordance. A button shows that it exists by existing; a swipe does not exist until someone knows to try it, and nobody discovers a gesture by looking at a static screen. So every gesture has a discovery cost paid once per user, and the cost is paid by the people who never pay it again - the ones who never find the gesture and never know it existed.

Which means the question is not "should we use a gesture" but "what fraction of users need it, and what happens to the rest". A swipe-to-delete that also appears in a visible overflow menu serves everyone, and the swipe exists for the people who have discovered it. A swipe-only delete serves nobody until they have been told, and the people who need it most - the ones deleting a lot, the ones on a phone with a large target area - are a minority.

There is also a discoverability asymmetry that favours visible controls in almost every case: a visible control can additionally be documented - mentioned in an onboarding hint, a first-run tooltip, an empty state. A gesture can only be hinted at, and a hint is a piece of UI that exists for four seconds and is then gone. So the visible path usually wins on discoverability and the gesture wins only on speed.

/* EVERY GESTURE PAYS FOR ITS DISCOVERY. This maps each gesture to the visible
   path that must exist alongside it, so a gesture cannot be shipped alone. The
   pairing is the rule; the gesture is an optimisation on top. */

const GESTURES = [
  {
    gesture: "swipe to delete",
    // platform convention matters here: on both iOS and Android a horizontal
    // swipe on a list row reveals actions, so the instinct transfers
    convention: "horizontal swipe on a row",
    visible_path: "an overflow menu on every row, containing Delete",
    // and the one that is mandatory rather than merely advisable, because
    // deletion is irreversible and a gesture that is hard to notice produces
    // accidental deletions as well as undiscovered ones
    requires_undo: true,
  },
  {
    gesture: "pull to refresh",
    convention: "vertical pull downward at the top of a scrollable region",
    visible_path: "a refresh control in the toolbar",
    requires_undo: false,
  },
  {
    gesture: "long press",
    convention: "press and hold for about 500ms",
    // the professional blind spot: long-press-only features are common in
    // internal tools and invisible in the ones users see
    visible_path: "an explicit action in a context menu, or a labelled button",
    requires_undo: false,
  },
  {
    gesture: "pinch to zoom",
    convention: "two-finger pinch",
    visible_path: "pinch and a plus/minus control",
    requires_undo: false,
  },
  {
    gesture: "swipe between tabs",
    convention: "horizontal swipe at the screen edge",
    // this one is genuinely optional: it is a shortcut for navigation that is
    // already one tap away, so there is nothing to pair it with
    visible_path: "tab bar, always present",
    requires_undo: false,
  },
];

const violations = (specs) => specs.filter((g) => !g.visible_path).map((g) => g.gesture);

Five gestures, five visible paths. The pairing is not redundancy to be removed in a later cleanup - it is the only way the feature is reachable by a user who has not been told it exists.

Undo, and what a gesture is for

Destructive gestures need undo rather than a confirmation dialog, and the reason is that the gesture is the confirmation. Someone who swipes a row away meant to; asking "are you sure?" immediately afterwards trains people to dismiss dialogs reflexively, which makes the dialog useless for the cases where it was genuinely needed. So: act immediately, then offer undo for long enough to be usable - eight seconds is the floor, and longer is better for anything destructive.

That reframing tells you what gestures are actually for. They are not a way to remove a button; they are a way to make the common case fast while the rare case stays safe. A swipe-to-archive that is instantly undoable beats a three-tap equivalent, and a swipe-to-delete without undo is worse than a labelled button with a dialog.

Respect the platform conventions listed in the table, because they are the accumulated result of every platform having learned the same lesson. A custom gesture with its own threshold and its own direction does not transfer, and a user who tries it and fails concludes the feature is broken rather than that it is unconventional. And where the platform has a system equivalent - a share sheet, a context menu, a picker - use it: it is already installed, already localised, and already accessible.

/* UNDO WINDOWS, with the reason each number is what it is. The window is not a
   UX preference - it is a human-reaction measurement, and shortening it below
   the number a person needs produces a confirmation dialog nobody reads. */

const UNDO = [
  {
    action: "delete a message",
    windowMs: 10000,
    // the work must be genuinely reversible, not just announced. If the delete
    // has already cascaded, undo is a lie the interface tells.
    reversible: "yes - soft delete, restored on undo",
    // and what makes it feel instant: the optimistic removal, so the undo is
    // offered against a state the user can already see is wrong
    note: "removed immediately, undo offered in place",
  },
  {
    action: "delete an account",
    windowMs: 0,
    reversible: "no",
    // the threshold: below this, undo is never enough, because there is no
    // partial recovery. A user who deletes the wrong account and restores it
    // still lost everything in between.
    requires_confirmation: true,
    note: "state exactly what is lost, name it, and do not offer undo",
  },
  {
    action: "archive 40 emails",
    windowMs: 30000,
    reversible: "yes - a move to an archive folder",
    // the number rises with the number of items, because a user who archived
    // forty things needs more time to notice it was wrong than one who
    // archived one
    note: "and the window scales with the size of the action",
  },
];

/* the mechanical check: a destructive action with no undo and no confirmation is
   the defect this whole pattern exists to catch, and it is a one-line audit */
function auditDestructive(actions) {
  const unsafe = actions.filter((a) => a.destructive && !a.undoWindowMs && !a.requires_confirmation);
  return { ok: unsafe.length === 0, unsafe: unsafe.map((a) => a.action) };
}

The account-deletion row is deliberately not an undo. Some actions have no partial recovery, and for those a confirmation that states exactly what is lost is the honest mechanism.

5.6 Timing: response budgets & perceived speed

Users perceive speed rather than measure it, so timing design is about managing the perceived wait. Render something instantly within about a tenth of a second, acknowledge actions that take up to a second, and for longer operations show progress and partial content to anchor attention. Set an explicit performance target, measure against it, and consider optimistic responses. A wait that explains itself is far more forgivable than a silent freeze.

BudgetUX job
< 100 msinstant: press states, immediate nav, optimistic actions
100–300 msthe sweet spot for UI transitions (150–250 ms)
~1 sperceivable wait: show progress the instant work starts
> 10 slost attention: summarize, queue, "we’ll email you the result"

Perceived speed ≠ actual speed: skeletons and optimistic UI make a 400 ms round-trip feel instant; a spinner left for 3 seconds feels broken. Always render something visible immediately, then keep the attention anchored (progress, partial content, % counts).

Exercises 5

  1. List every state your Ch.4 payment flow needs (happy, error, empty, loading) and make a state table.
  2. Prototype 3 microinteractions (like, delete-with-undo, pull-to-refresh) in HTML/CSS/JS.
  3. Identify one product moment where motion helped or hurt comprehension — explain using this chapter’s rules.

Render something before the answer exists

The single most effective timing technique is to render the structure before the data arrives. A screen with its layout, its heading, its navigation and its skeleton rows appears in the first paint, and the user starts reading, deciding and preparing while the request is still in flight.
