The same screen waiting on the request shows nothing at all until the response is complete, and the user has spent that time with nothing to do.

The skeleton must match the loaded layout in height, or the arrival of the content shifts everything below it and the page appears to jump. That jump is worse than the delay it replaced, because the user has to re-find what they were reading. This is why skeletons are specified per component against its populated state rather than added as a generic grey block.

Then optimistic updates, for actions where being slightly wrong for a moment is cheaper than waiting. A like, a reorder, a settings toggle: apply it immediately, send the request, and revert on failure with a quiet message. The exception is anything involving money or anything irreversible - a payment should not display a success it has not been given, and the cost of a false confirmation there is not recoverable.

/* THE TIMING BUDGETS. Thresholds, not aspirations, and each one says what to do
   when it is crossed. The common failure is setting a target nobody measures,
   which is why this is a table with consequences rather than a performance
   goal in a document. */

const BUDGET = {
  renderStructure: {
    ms: 100,
    // below this the response is perceived as a consequence of the input rather
    // than as feedback, so it does not need a spinner
    beyond: "still fine - nothing visible is expected yet",
  },
  acknowledge: {
    ms: 100,
    beyond: "show inline progress on the control; anything slower than 400ms needs a visible indicator",
  },
  showProgress: {
    ms: 1000,
    beyond: "skeleton at the final height, or partial content - never a bare spinner at this point",
  },
  dataOnScreen: {
    ms: 2000,
    // the number that matters for whether anyone reads the page, and it is far
    // below what a good page load should be
    beyond: "partial content with an explicit note that more is coming",
  },
  interactionReady: {
    ms: 2000,
    beyond: "the control is bound but the action is queued; tell the user it is queued",
  },
};

// The optimistic decision, which is not a timing technique but a risk choice.
function canBeOptimistic(action) {
  const UNSAFE = [
    // money: a false confirmation here is not recoverable and the user has
    // already acted on it
    "payment", "transfer", "subscription", "refund",
    // irreversible: there is no state to roll back to
    "delete", "archive-all", "revoke", "transfer-ownership",
    // and anything where the user would act differently if they knew it had not
    // happened yet
    "send-message", "publish", "invite", "share-public",
  ];
  return !UNSAFE.includes(action) && !action.irreversible;
}

Optimistic updates are only for actions where being briefly wrong costs nothing. Anything involving money, anything irreversible, and anything the user would act differently on is excluded outright.

Anchoring attention during a long wait

A wait that is explained is far more forgivable than an unexplained one, and the explanation has to carry information rather than apologise. "This may take a minute, we're processing 40,000 rows" is tolerable because it tells the user the system is working on something specific. "Please wait" is not, because it is what the same interface would have shown if it had crashed.

So for anything over a second, give a count or a stage rather than an indefinite spinner. A file count, a percentage, a named stage - "importing", "matching", "indexing" - all tell the user that time is passing and that something specific is happening. Where the work really is that long, show what exists so far and let the user start using it, because most long operations do not need to complete before their results are useful.

Never show a determinate progress bar when the progress is not actually known. A bar that sits at 90 percent for four minutes is read as a hang, and is worse than the spinner it replaced, because it makes a promise about duration. Use a determinate bar only when the total is known; otherwise an indeterminate indicator plus a count is the honest option.

/* HONEST WAITING. The distinction that matters: a determinate bar is a PROMISE
   about remaining time, so it may only be used when the total is actually known.
   Everything else uses an indeterminate indicator plus a count, because a count
   is true at any moment and a percentage that stalls is a lie. */

function waitingIndicator(job) {
  if (job.totalKnown && job.totalKnown > 0) {
    // honest only when the work is genuinely countable
    return { kind: "determinate", pct: Math.floor((job.done / job.totalKnown) * 100),
             text: job.done + " of " + job.totalKnown + " " + job.unit };
  }

  if (job.totalKnown === 0) {
    // genuinely zero work: say so rather than flashing an indicator for a
    // request that was already resolved
    return { kind: "none", text: "nothing to do" };
  }

  // unknown total. A count is still true if the count is a real quantity, such
  // as records read, files done, or pages processed.
  return {
    kind: "indeterminate",
    // the stage, so the user knows WHAT is happening rather than that something is
    stages: ["reading", "matching", "writing"],
    text: job.countable ? job.done + " " + job.unit + " processed" : job.stage,
    // and an honest ceiling. "This usually takes about a minute" sets an
    // expectation; without it the user has no way to decide whether to wait or
    // to leave the page.
    expected: job.expectedMs ? "usually about " + Math.round(job.expectedMs / 1000) + " seconds" : null,
  };
}

The expected line is what converts a wait from anxiety into a wait. Once the user knows it should take about a minute, four seconds is fine and forty is a problem worth reporting.

6 · Usability & Heuristics

Usability heuristics are a short list of general principles for evaluating whether an interface is easy to use, providing the cheapest quality gate in UX. A trained reviewer can walk a design against the heuristics and find serious problems in an afternoon, before any user is recruited. Use them during design reviews, then combine heuristic findings with real usability testing. Heuristic evaluation is fast, but it still needs real users to catch what reviewers miss.

6.1 Nielsen’s 10 heuristics (the classic checklist)6.2 Affordances, signifiers and discoverability6.3 Mental models and convention physics6.4 Common UX conventions to honor6.5 Writing errors humans can act on

Set-based usability checklists (heuristics) are the cheapest quality gate in UX: one trained reviewer can find a surprising number of real problems in an afternoon, before any users are involved.

6.1 Nielsen’s 10 heuristics (the classic checklist)

Nielsen’s ten heuristics are a classic checklist that includes visibility of system status, match between system and the real world, user control and freedom, consistency and standards, error prevention, and help for users to recover from errors. Use them as prompts for systematic heuristic evaluation, walking each screen and grading each principle from zero to three by severity. Order findings by impact and frequency, then fix the worst first. They remain a reliable, fast screen for common usability problems.

HeuristicIn one line
1. Visibility of system statusAlways show what’s happening
2. Match system & real worldSpeak the user’s language ("cart", not "line_item")
3. User control & freedomEasy undo and exit everywhere ("back", cancel, escape)
4. Consistency & standardsSame meaning = same look; follow platform conventions
5. Error preventionPrevent slips: disable invalid, confirm destructive, constrain inputs
6. Recognition rather than recallShow options; don’t make users remember (save state, lists)
7. Flexibility & efficiencyShortcuts, recent items, defaults, power-user patterns
8. Aesthetic & minimalist designEvery extra element competes; cut noise
9. Help users recognize & recoverErrors state the problem + the action, not blame
10. Help & documentationContextual help exists when users need it

Practice makes these reflex: run a heuristic eval on any screen and grade it 0–3 per heuristic (0 = not a problem, 3 = catastrophe). Then fix the 3s first, then 2s, etc.

Why a rating scale beats an opinion

The ten heuristics are worth using precisely because they are a shared vocabulary rather than a set of opinions. A review where three people say "this feels awkward" produces nothing actionable; a review where three people say "visibility of system status, severity 2" produces a defect with a name, a location and a place in a queue.

The severity rating is the part that makes it usable, and it is four numbers rather than one. How bad is it, how often does it happen, and how hard is it to recover from. A cosmetic problem on a screen everybody sees once is not worth the same as a data-loss problem on a screen five percent of users reach. Rating only the severity and ignoring frequency is how teams end up polishing a settings page and leaving a checkout bug.

Run it with more than one person. A single evaluator's rating is a preference with a number attached, and the heuristics' value is that different evaluators converge on the same defects. Where two people disagree by two or more points, the disagreement is informative - it usually means the finding is real but the severity depends on a context one of them knows and the other does not.

/* HEURISTIC EVALUATION, as a scored record. The rating is four numbers, not
   one, because "severity" alone collapses a cosmetic defect on a high-traffic
   screen into the same queue as a data-loss defect on a rare one - and that
   collapse is the reason these reviews produce the wrong priorities. */

const HEURISTICS = [
  { id: "visibility",      name: "Visibility of system status" },
  { id: "reality",        name: "Match between system and the real world" },
  { id: "control",        name: "User control and freedom" },
  { id: "consistency",    name: "Consistency and standards" },
  { id: "prevention",     name: "Error prevention" },
  { id: "recognition",    name: "Recognition rather than recall" },
  { id: "flexibility",    name: "Flexibility and efficiency of use" },
  { id: "minimal",        name: "Aesthetic and minimalist design" },
  { id: "recover",        name: "Help users recover from errors" },
  { id: "docs",           name: "Help and documentation" },
];

// four axes, each 0-4. The product is what the queue is sorted by.
function rate(severity, frequency, recoverability, prevalence) {
  return {
    // 0 = no problem, 1 = cosmetic, 2 = minor, 3 = major, 4 = catastrophe
    severity,
    // how often the path is taken, which is not the same as how many users
    // exist: a rare screen can still be the only route to a common task
    frequency,
    // 4 means the user cannot get back - the one that outranks everything
    recoverability,
    prevalence,
    // recoverability is weighted highest because an unrecoverable defect is not
    // a worse experience, it is a different kind of thing: it costs the user
    // something rather than wasting their time
    score: severity * frequency + recoverability * 2,
    band:
      recoverability === 4 ? "stop the line" :
      severity * frequency >= 12 ? "fix before launch" :
      severity * frequency >= 6 ? "fix this cycle" : "backlog",
  };
}

function evaluate(findings) {
  return findings
    .map((f) => ({ ...f, ...rate(f.severity, f.frequency, f.recoverability, f.prevalence) }))
    .sort((a, b) => {
      // an unrecoverable finding outranks everything, regardless of score
      if ((a.recoverability === 4) !== (b.recoverability === 4)) return a.recoverability === 4 ? -1 : 1;
      return b.score - a.score;
    });
}

The stop the line band is non-negotiable regardless of frequency: a defect the user cannot get back from is not a worse experience, it is a different kind of one.

Where the heuristics disagree with each other

The ten are not independent and several of them pull in opposite directions, which is where a naive application goes wrong. Aesthetic and minimalist design says remove things that are not essential; recognition rather than recall says keep things visible so they are not forgotten. Both are right, and the resolution is that the removed item must be reconstructible from memory, not invisible.

Help and documentation says provide guidance; minimalist design says do not clutter the screen with it. The resolution is placement rather than compromise: put the guidance where the confusion happens, in the empty state and the error message, rather than on a help page nobody reaches from the moment of need.

Error prevention and user control also conflict - preventing an action removes the user's choice, and giving the user the choice permits the mistake. The resolution is reversibility, which is the more useful goal anyway: let the user do it and make it undoable, rather than blocking it and making the block the decision. This is why the errors section of this chapter pushes undo rather than confirmation dialogs.

/* THE CONFLICTS, declared so a review can name the trade rather than
   oscillate. Each pair is a genuine disagreement between two heuristics that are
   both correct, and resolving one badly is a common source of a review that goes
   in circles. */

const CONFLICTS = [
  {
    between: ["minimal", "recognition"],
    tension: "remove what is not essential versus keep it visible so it is not forgotten",
    // the resolution that satisfies both: the item is not on screen, and it is
    // still reachable without being recalled
    resolution: "hide it behind an affordance, do not delete it",
    test: "can a user who has forgotten the item still find it in one action?",
  },
  {
    between: ["docs", "minimal"],
    tension: "help the user versus do not clutter the screen",
    resolution: "put guidance in the state where the confusion occurs, not on a separate page",
    test: "is the answer visible to someone who has not gone looking for it?",
  },
  {
    between: ["prevention", "control"],
    tension: "stop the mistake versus leave the user free",
    // and this is the one with a clear winner: reversibility dominates, because
    // a block is a decision made on the user's behalf and it is often wrong
    resolution: "prefer reversibility to blocking",
    test: "is there an undo for every action the prevention heuristic wanted to block?",
  },
  {
    between: ["flexibility", "minimal"],
    tension: "shortcuts for experts versus nothing unnecessary for beginners",
    resolution: "accelerators that are invisible until used, with one discoverable default",
    test: "does an expert get the shortcut without a beginner seeing clutter?",
  },
];

// the failure this check catches: a review that raised the same conflict on two
// consecutive passes and produced a different answer each time
function isOscillating(ratings) {
  const a = ratings[0], b = ratings[1];
  if (!a || !b) return { oscillating: false };
  const flipped = a.score > 12 !== b.score > 12;
  return { oscillating: flipped, note: flipped ? "the severity rating changed band between passes - re-measure" : "" };
}

The oscillation check is worth more than it looks. A review that produces a different severity band on two passes over the same screen was measuring the reviewers' mood, not the screen.

6.2 Affordances, signifiers and discoverability

An affordance is an action a design makes possible, such as pressing or dragging, while a signifier is the visual clue that reveals that possibility to the user. Discoverability fails when an action is available but invisible, so most problems are actually missing signifiers. Make obvious buttons look pressable, links look like links, and interactive elements look interactive. Signage through familiar shapes, shadows, and labels makes affordances visible.

  • Affordance = possible action (a button affords clicking).
  • Signifier = the visual clue that reveals it (shadow, border, label, cursor).
  • The design crime is signifier absence: "why did nobody know they could swipe?" Make every interactive element look clickable before interaction, and show state change during it.

The gap between what is possible and what is visible

An affordance is an action the design makes physically possible. A button affords pressing because of what it is made of and how it is mounted. A signifier is the visible clue that tells the user this is possible. The two are separate, and separating them is the whole idea - most usability failures are not missing affordances, they are missing signifiers, which is why "make it more usable" on such a screen produces a bigger button rather than a clearer one.

Where an affordance is real and the signifier is absent, the user does not conclude the action is unavailable. They conclude the screen is not responding, and they try something else. This is why a product with hidden gestures accumulates a support category of "it does not work" rather than "I could not find it", and why the fix is a visible control rather than a tutorial.

Some signifiers are near-universal and cost nothing: a raised surface reads as pressable, an underlined coloured word reads as a link, a caret reads as expandable, a cursor change reads as a target. Use them unconditionally. A custom-drawn control that fails to look like anything is a signifier deficit, and it is the designer's choice rather than a constraint.

/* AFFORDANCE VERSUS SIGNIFIER, as two separate checks. The distinction has
   teeth: an element can pass the affordance check and fail the signifier check,
   and that combination - a perfectly working control that looks like text - is
   the failure that "make it more usable" does not fix. */

const ELEMENTS = [
  { id: "save",        affordance: "button",      signifier: "raised surface, border, label", ok: true },
  { id: "delete",      affordance: "button",      signifier: "raised surface, destructive colour", ok: true },
  { id: "card",        affordance: "clickable",   signifier: "none - no border, no elevation, no cursor", ok: false },
  { id: "nav-link",    affordance: "link",        signifier: "colour and underline", ok: true },
  { id: "icon-action", affordance: "button",      signifier: "icon only, no label", ok: false },
  { id: "avatar",      affordance: "link",        signifier: "image only, no indication it is navigable", ok: false },
  { id: "row",         affordance: "not clickable", signifier: "hover highlight implies it is clickable", ok: false },
];

function auditSignifiers(elements) {
  const missing = elements.filter((e) => !e.sigifier || /none/.test(e.sigifier));
  // and the inverse defect, which is just as damaging and less often noticed: a
  // signifier promising an action the element does not perform. Users learn from
  // this within one session and stop trusting the whole interface.
  const falsePromise = elements.filter((e) => e.sigifier === "raised surface" && e.affordance !== "button");

  return {
    ok: missing.length === 0 && falsePromise.length === 0,
    signifierAbsence: missing.map((e) => e.id),
    falsePromise: falsePromise.map((e) => e.id),
    // the fix for each is different: the first needs a signifier added, the
    // second needs the hover effect removed. Conflating them produces a card
    // with a border that still does nothing.
    fixes: {
      signifierAbsence: "add the missing signifier - do not enlarge it",
      falsePromise: "remove the signifier, or make the element perform the action",
    },
  };
}

The falsePromise check is the one most often missing. A hover effect on a non-clickable row teaches every user once, in one session, that your visual signals are not to be believed.

Depth of sign, and flat design's real cost

A flat interface - no shadows, no borders, distinguished by colour and spacing alone - is not wrong. It is a coherent position with a real cost, and the cost is concentrated on touch devices and for users with low vision. A flat card on a flat background has an edge contrast near zero, and edge contrast is what tells a user where one element ends and the next begins.

The resolution is not to abandon flatness but to replace elevation with other separation: a background tint difference, a wider gap, a hairline in a colour chosen for contrast rather than for decoration. A tint step is invisible as a stylistic choice and legible as a boundary, and it costs nothing in visual weight.

On touch, the signifier problem is sharper still because the user's hand covers the target and there is no cursor to follow. Hit targets should be at least 44 by 44 pixels, which sounds large until it is compared to a 16-pixel icon - and it is the icon that usually needs to be padded rather than the spacing that needs reducing.

/* SEPARATION WITHOUT ELEVATION. The flat-design case, solved by tint rather than
   shadow. The contrast figure is the part that matters: a card against its
   background has to clear 3:1 to be perceivable as a boundary at all, and a
   subtle shadow gives nowhere near that once it is composited. */

const SEPARATION = [
  {
    method: "shadow",
    // works visually, fails the 3:1 requirement, and costs a render layer per
    // elevated element
    edgeContrast: 1.2,
    onTouch: "poor - no edge under a finger",
    verdict: "decorative only, never the sole boundary",
  },
  {
    method: "hairline border",
    edgeContrast: 3.4,
    onTouch: "good - a continuous edge is easy to follow",
    verdict: "reliable, and cheap",
  },
  {
    method: "background tint step",
    edgeContrast: 1.6,
    onTouch: "adequate - the boundary is visible, though the step is subtle",
    verdict: "good for grouping, needs a border for a hard boundary",
  },
  {
    method: "space alone",
    // the strongest of them, and the one flat design gets right: an empty gap is
    // unambiguous in a way that a low-contrast edge never is
    edgeContrast: null,
    onTouch: "excellent",
    verdict: "prefer it - separation needs no contrast calculation",
  },
];

/* The check that catches the flat-design failure: two adjacent surfaces with no
   separator and less than 3:1 between them, which is a boundary the user
   cannot see until they touch it. */
function findInvisibleBoundaries(surfaces) {
  return surfaces
    .filter((s) => !s.border && !s.shadow && s.tintStep === 0 && s.gapPx === 0)
    .map((s) => ({ id: s.id, contrast: s.contrast, why: "no border, no shadow, no gap - the boundary does not exist visually" }));
}

Space is the strongest separator in the table and the only one with no contrast requirement at all, which is why it is the one flat design gets right and the one it is most often talked out of.

6.3 Mental models and convention physics

Mental models are the internal expectations users bring from real life and from every other app they have used, and they drive how people predict behavior. Design against these models by matching familiar metaphors and conventions, because a checkbox that looks like a button misleads even careful users. You may break a convention, but only with a strategy, such as a different marker that signals the deviation. Consistency with expected models makes interfaces feel intuitive.

Users arrive with models from the physical world and every other app (a cart, a save icon, tabs). Leverage the models users already hold; violate them only with a strategy (and then signpost it like crazy). Novel doesn’t equal better — "innovative" is often just "confusing".

What users arrive already knowing

A mental model is a set of expectations a user brings to an interface, and it is not formed by your product - it is formed by everything they have used before. Someone's expectation that a shopping cart holds things is a model learned from every store and every app that has a cart icon. Your product does not create that model and cannot remove it.

This is why a correct design can feel wrong. If you make a cart mean "saved for later" because that is what your data model calls it, you are asking users to override a model that has been reinforced thousands of times. Some will adapt; most will read your interface through their existing model and find it subtly non-functional, which is a far worse outcome than not understanding.

So leverage the models. Where the user's model and the business need differ, the resolution is usually a name change rather than a behaviour change, because the business need is rarely about the interaction and almost always about the vocabulary.

/* MODEL CONFLICTS, with the two resolutions and the test for each. The
   resolution column is the useful part: "violate the model" is not a plan, it
   is the beginning of an argument. Every violation needs a named mechanism that
   teaches the difference, and a mechanism that is missing means the model wins. */

const MODEL_CONFLICTS = [
  {
    model: "a trash icon deletes",
    yourBehaviour: "a trash icon archives",
    // the cheap resolution: the word is doing the work the icon cannot
    resolution: "rename - use an archive icon, or add the word Delete",
    violation_mechanism: null,
    test: "would someone who has never seen this app expect a trash icon to be permanent?",
  },
  {
    model: "an X closes",
    yourBehaviour: "an X cancels the order",
    resolution: "rename and separate the two controls",
    violation_mechanism: "the X still closes, and the destructive action is a labelled button",
    test: "is there any screen where the same glyph means two different things?",
  },
  {
    model: "checkboxes are small squares you tick",
    // the genuinely interesting one, because toggles are now the platform
    // convention AND checkboxes remain the correct choice for form submission.
    // The confusion comes from using a switch where a multi-select is meant.
    model2: "a toggle switch means a setting applies immediately",
    yourBehaviour: "a switch changes a value in a form you then submit",
    resolution: "use checkboxes in forms; use switches only for settings that save themselves",
    violation_mechanism: "the setting shows its saved state and the time it was saved",
    test: "after toggling, does anything else need to be pressed?",
  },
  {
    model: "undo means the last thing",
    yourBehaviour: "undo reverts the last five actions at once",
    resolution: "one step of undo, always",
    // the reason: multi-step undo requires the user to know how many steps they
    // have done, which is precisely what they are relying on undo not to
    // require
    violation_mechanism: null,
    test: "can the user undo once and be sure they are back where they were?",
  },
];

The switch-versus-checkbox row is the one that catches people out. The problem is not that toggles are new - it is that a switch in a form implies the change is already saved, and it is not.

Violating a model, and what it costs

Violating a model is sometimes right, and the bar for doing it is higher than it looks. The bar is: the convention is genuinely worse, the cost of the violation is understood, and there is a mechanism that teaches the difference. Miss any one of the three and the violation is just a bug that users work around.

The teaching mechanism is the part almost always skipped. A novel interaction is not self-documenting, and the user who guesses it correctly on the first try is not representative - everyone else concludes they have missed something and stops. The mechanisms are: a one-time hint at the point of use, a visible affordance that differs from the convention on purpose, and a preference that reverts to the convention for users who ask for familiarity.

Finally, test whether the violation is even noticed. A control that violates a model but is never used is not a violation, it is dead weight - and the effort spent on its teaching mechanism would have been better spent on the controls people actually use.

/* VIOLATION AUDIT. Three conditions, all required. The third - a discoverable
   path to the conventional behaviour - is the safety net that is almost always
   missing, and its absence is what turns an innovation into a support ticket. */

function auditViolation(v) {
  const gates = {
    conventionalIsWorse: {
      ok: v.evidenceThatConventionFails,
      // vague evidence is not evidence: "users complained" without a count and a
      // behaviour is a preference
      needs: "a count and a behaviour, not a report",
    },
    taught: {
      ok: v.teachingMechanism,
      // the mechanism has to be AT the point of use. A help article is not a
      // mechanism, because nobody reads it before their first attempt.
      needs: "at the point of use, once, dismissible",
    },
    escapeHatch: {
      ok: v.conventionalPathAvailable,
      needs: "the conventional interaction still reachable, permanently",
    },
  };
  const failed = Object.entries(gates).filter(([, g]) => !g.ok).map(([k]) => k);
  return {
    ok: failed.length === 0,
    failed,
    // and the check nobody runs: if the feature is rarely used, none of this
    // matters, and the design effort was better spent elsewhere
    worthIt: v.usageShare > 0.2,
  };
}

/* A worked violation that passes all three gates, for contrast with the common
   one that fails the second. */
const DRAWER = auditViolation({
  evidenceThatConventionFails: "navigation was collapsed behind a burger on 320px screens, so the primary destinations were unreachable without two taps",
  teachingMechanism: "the drawer opens on first navigation with a labelled edge, once per device, dismissible",
  conventionalPathAvailable: "the same destinations remain in the page as a visible list on wide screens, and the burger still works",
  usageShare: 0.65,
});

The usageShare gate is the one teams skip because it requires analytics they may not have. But a control nobody uses is not an innovation - it is a control, and its teaching mechanism was effort spent on nothing.

6.4 Common UX conventions to honor

UX conventions are hard-won habits users have learned across the entire web, such as a logo that links to the homepage, underlined blue links, shopping-cart icons, and a prominently placed search box. These patterns carry learned expectations, so honoring them means users operate your product immediately without instruction. Break a convention only when you can demonstrate that the replacement works better. Conventions that look stale to insiders still feel native to your users.

ConventionWhy users expect it
Logo → homebrand memory, escape hatch
Cart in the top cornertask continuity
Underlined blue = linkbrowser muscle memory
Primary action to the right (forms)reading order, Fitts
Search box with magnifier iconrecognition
Trash/undo patternssafety net

Where conventions come from, and why they outlast your reasoning

A convention is a solution that enough products agreed on that it became an expectation. Underlined blue links, a magnifying glass, a shopping cart, a hamburger at three lines, a padlock in the address bar - each was a reasonable local decision that became a default, and each is now free because nobody has to learn it.

That is the economic argument, and it is the strongest one: a convention is a solved problem you do not have to solve. A link that is blue and underlined needs no label, no tooltip, no onboarding, and no test to confirm people recognise it. Replacing one with a "better" card-based navigation means paying for discovery on every page, for every user, in exchange for whatever the improvement was.

Conventions also look wrong from inside. A team building in 2026 sees the underlined link as dated, the footer sitemap as clutter, the hamburger as a compromise - and none of that is how it is experienced from outside, where it is simply known. The asymmetry is structural: you see your exceptions daily and your users see the aggregate.

/* THE CONVENTIONS, and what each one is actually communicating. The right
   column matters more than the left: a convention is not a style, it is a
   compressed instruction, and replacing it means writing the instruction out. */

const CONVENTIONS = [
  {
    convention: "logo links to the home page",
    says: "you can always get back to the start from here",
    // and the corollary, which is the one people get wrong: it means the logo
    // must NOT be the current page, because a link to where you already are is
    // a dead link
    implies: "not the current page; on the home page it is a non-link",
  },
  {
    convention: "underlined coloured text",
    says: "this goes somewhere else",
    implies: "no underline on buttons - underline means navigation, not action",
  },
  {
    convention: "cart icon with a count",
    says: "you have items, and here is how many",
    // the badge is the part that gets omitted, and its absence is read as zero
    implies: "the badge shows the count even when it is zero, or it is absent entirely",
  },
  {
    convention: "magnifying glass in the header",
    says: "you can search instead of navigating",
    implies: "the magnifier is a button, not a decorative icon",
  },
  {
    convention: "hamburger at three lines",
    says: "there is more navigation, off this screen",
    implies: "only when navigation is genuinely hidden - on desktop it means nothing",
  },
  {
    convention: "padlock in the address bar",
    says: "this connection is encrypted and this is who it is",
    // the composition: the padlock alone means encrypted, which is why a lone
    // padlock has become meaningless
    implies: "the domain must also be shown - the lock alone certifies nothing",
  },
];

function auditConventions(elements) {
  // a logo that links to the current page is the most common convention defect
  // in the list, and it is invisible to anyone who does not click it
  const logoOnHome = elements.find((e) => e.isLogo && e.linksToSelf);
  return {
    ok: !logoOnHome,
    faults: logoOnHome ? ["the logo links to the page you are already on"] : [],
  };
}

The padlock row is the best illustration of a convention being a compressed instruction. The lock used to carry meaning on its own; now it carries none, because a lock with no domain beside it certifies nothing.

Judging a break, before making it

The bar for breaking a convention is evidence plus a named improvement, and the evidence has to be behavioural. "Our users find this confusing" is not evidence if the users are employees; if a task-completion test shows the conventional pattern outperforming the alternative by a margin you can defend, you have something.

Then work out what the convention was compressed instruction for, because the usual reason to break one is that it was solving a problem your product does not have. Underlined links exist because links went to new pages with no other signal; if your navigation is unmistakable another way, the underline is solving a problem you do not have, which is the strongest argument for removing it.

Finally, decide whether you can give the signal back more cheaply. Most convention breaks are attempts to fix a specific defect - too many underlines, too little distinction - and those are usually better fixed by adjusting the signal than by removing the whole system.

/* THE CASE FOR A BREAK, made in the only form that survives a review. The
   convention is stated, the compressed instruction behind it is named, and the
   improvement has to be a measurable behaviour - not a preference. */

const BREAK_PROPOSAL = {
  convention: "underline every link",
  // the question that decides most of these: what problem was the underline
  // solving, and does this product have that problem?
  compressed_instruction_solves:
    "links went to a new document with no other cue; the underline was the only signal",
  does_this_product_have_that_problem: false,
  because: "every navigable element here is inside a region with a heading and a border, and the action is always within the same document",

  alternative: "accent colour plus a 2px underline on hover only",
  // the falsification, which is the part that makes this reviewable. If this
  // is false, the proposal is wrong and everyone can tell from the write-up.
  falsified_if:
    "in a task test, users who search for underlined links fail to identify links outside nav regions at a rate above 5 percent",
  test_protocol: {
    design: "within-subject, two versions of the same three screens",
    task: "find the link to billing history and follow it",
    n: 15,
    primary_metric: "correct identification of link elements before clicking",
  },
  // and the escape hatch, which costs little and makes the change defensible
  fallback: "keep underlines on every link inside dense prose, where identification is hardest",
};

function judge(p) {
  return {
    defensible: p.does_this_product_have_that_problem === false && Boolean(p.falsified_if),
    // a break with no way to be wrong is not a break, it is a preference
    testable: Boolean(p.falsified_if && p.test_protocol?.n),
  };
}

The falsified_if field is what makes a proposal reviewable. A change whose author cannot say what result would prove them wrong is not an argument, and it usually will not survive contact with users.

6.5 Writing errors humans can act on

An effective error message tells the user what happened, why it happened, and the concrete next step to fix it, written in plain human language. Place it close to the action that failed, keep the wording specific rather than generic, and never blame the user or expose raw technical logs. In forms, validate inline as the user goes so errors are discovered early. A good error is a helpful conversation, not a verdict.

// Weak                     // Strong
"Invalid input"             "Please enter an email like name@site.com"
"Error 500"                 "We couldn't save (server hiccup). Try again —
                              your draft is safe."
"Access denied"             "You need Viewer permission. Request access here."
// Formula: WHAT happened (plain) + WHY (brief) + NEXT STEP (action).

What, why, and what to do next

An error message has three jobs and they are all required. Say what happened, in terms the user can recognise. Say why it happened, if the reason is something they could act on. And say what to do next, specifically enough to be followed without guessing. A message that does all three is short and reads as competent; a message that does only the first reads as a system reporting on itself.

The failure mode is nearly always the third. "Invalid input" and "something went wrong" state the first and nothing else, and they leave the user to work out what a valid value looks like - which means re-reading the label, guessing, and probably retrying the same thing. The message is the one place where you know the answer, so leaving it there is the waste of a perfectly good explanation.

The second is where tone goes wrong. A message that blames the user - "you entered an invalid address" rather than "we could not find that address" - costs the user the willingness to continue. Prefer a phrasing where the system is the subject and the user is the one with the next move. It is a small grammatical choice with a measurable effect on completion.

/* THE THREE-PART CHECK, applied to real messages. The output is the part that
   matters: a linter that reports which part is missing can be run over the
   codebase, whereas "improve our error copy" can only be acted on by reading
   every string. */

function checkMessage(message) {
  const parts = {
    what: /(could not|couldn't|failed|wasn't|not|unable|invalid|no)/i.test(message),
    // "why" has to be something the user can act on, so it excludes technical
    // causes the user has no access to - "a timeout occurred" is a why that
    // helps nobody
    why: /(because|since|due to|only|already|expired|not been|temporarily|out of)/i.test(message),
    // "next" has to be an instruction, and an instruction with a verb at the
    // start. "Try again" alone is barely better than nothing unless paired.
    next: /(try|check|enter|choose|select|use|contact|wait|open|go to|refresh|sign in)/i.test(message),
  };
  const missing = Object.entries(parts).filter(([, v]) => !v).map(([k]) => k);
  return { ok: missing.length === 0, parts, missing };
}

/* the rewrites, each one changing exactly one part of the pattern, because a
   message that improves everything at once teaches nothing */
const BEFORE_AFTER = [
  {
    before: "Invalid input",
    after: "Enter a postcode like SW1A 1AA",
    fixed: ["what", "next"],
  },
  {
    before: "Error 400: Bad Request",
    after: "We could not find that postcode. Check it and try again",
    fixed: ["what", "why", "next"],
    // a status code is for the developer log, not the user. It is information
    // with zero actionable content, which is worse than no information because
    // it looks technical and therefore authoritative.
    note: "the code belongs in the log; the user gets the reason",
  },
  {
    before: "You entered an incorrect password",
    after: "That password is not right. Try again, or reset it if you have forgotten it",
    fixed: ["why", "next"],
    // and the subjunctive: "that password is not right" is a statement about the
    // world; "you entered an incorrect password" is an accusation about the user
    tone: "system is the subject, user has the next move",
  },
  {
    // the one with no third part available, and it still needs one
    before: "Payment failed",
    after: "Your bank declined the payment. Try another card, or contact your bank",
    fixed: ["why", "next"],
  },
];

The bank example is the hard case, where the message has to give an honest cause the user can act on without knowing anything about payments. "Declined" plus two concrete next steps is the whole solution.

Where the message goes, and when it appears

Place the message next to the thing that failed. A form-level banner at the top of a long form tells the user something is wrong and then makes them find which field, which undoes the point of writing the message carefully. The one exception is a page-level failure where no single field is at fault - a network failure or a server error - where the message belongs where the action was.

Then decide when validation fires, and this is a real design decision rather than a default. Validating while the user is still typing is wrong: they get an error for a half-finished email address, and they learn to ignore errors. Validating only on submit is also wrong, because they find out about the third error after filling everything in. The workable default is on blur for fields they have left, and on submit for the whole form, with the first invalid field focused.

Two things to preserve when an error appears: the input, and the position. Clearing a form because one field was wrong is the most expensive error handling there is, because the user has to reconstruct work the system threw away. And a validation message appearing at the top of the viewport when the field is below the fold is invisible, which is why the first invalid field gets focus rather than the first message.

/* VALIDATION POLICY, and the preservation rule. The rule is stated as an
   invariant because it is the one that gets broken by well-meaning refactors:
   someone changes the error handler, rebuilds the form from state, and every
   keystroke the user typed is gone. */

const VALIDATE_ON = {
  // while typing: never. A half-typed address is not an invalid address, and
  // telling the user so teaches them to ignore the field's error state.
  typing: null,
  blur: "validate - the user has finished with this field, so the value is knowable",
  submit: "validate the whole form and focus the first invalid field",
  // and the case that is easy to miss: a field the user did not visit must
  // still be validated on submit, which is where the first-touch errors come from
  untouched: "no inline error until submit, then the same treatment as any other",
};

const PRESERVE_ON_ERROR = [
  "every field value the user entered",
  "the current scroll position",
  "which fields had already been validated, so untouched fields are not re-flagged",
  // and the one that is easy to lose in a refactor, because it is a rendering
  // decision rather than a data decision
  "focus on the first invalid field, not on the first message",
];

/* The check: an error path that does not preserve input is the defect, and it is
   invisible in every manual pass because the tester retypes the data. */
function auditErrorPath(handler, form) {
  return {
    preservesValues: handler.keepsFormState,
    preservesFocus: handler.focusesFirstInvalid === "field",
    // a message rendered above the fold describing a field below it is the
    // second most common error-handling defect
    focusesVisible: handler.scrollsToFocusedField !== false,
    lostFields: form.fields.filter((f) => !f.inStateOnError).map((f) => f.name),
  };
}

The untouched row is the case teams miss. A field the user never visited has no inline error, so on submit it looks fine until the form refuses - and the user cannot tell which field it is.

Weak messages become strong ones by naming what to do next in plain language; the what, why, next formula works in any tone.

Errors inherit tone from the product: a banking app says "We couldn’t process this transfer" plainly; a game can play. But the three-part formula (what/why/next) survives any tone.

Exercises 6

  1. Run Nielsen’s 10 on one screen of your Ch.0 product; score each heuristic and prioritize fixes.
  2. Find one screen where a convention was broken, and argue whether the break earned its confusion.
  3. Rewrite 3 real error messages you’ve seen using the what/why/next formula.

7 · Accessibility & Inclusive Design

Accessibility is the practice of making products usable by people with a wide range of vision, hearing, motor, and cognitive abilities, and it is a judgment about real users rather than a checklist bolted on at the end. Design it from the start through semantic structure, keyboard support, adequate contrast, and readable typography. Verify the work with automated checks and by testing with disabled users. Inclusive design tends to improve the product for everyone, not only those it was aimed at.

7.1 WCAG 2.2 in 3 minutes7.2 Keyboard & focus: the "keyboard-only power user"7.3 Screen readers: the DOM is the interface7.4 Designing for vision, motor and cognition diversity7.5 Inclusive language and human centeredness7.6 Accessibility shift-left: audits, budgets, culture

Accessibility (a11y) is not a checklist at the end — it’s judgment about who your users are. Roughly 15–20% of people have a disability, and good a11y makes products better for literally everyone (captions help noisy trains, contrast helps sunny parks).

7.1 WCAG 2.2 in 3 minutes

WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, is the international standard for web accessibility built on four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Each principle contains testable success criteria graded from level A through AAA, with level AA set as the professional target for most products. Check conformance with a mix of automated tools and manual testing, including the 2.2 criteria on focus appearance and target size. Meeting WCAG AA is a baseline, not the end of accessibility.

PrincipleMeansSample requirement
Perceivablecan senses receive italt text, captions, contrast ≥ 4.5:1, not color-only
Operablecan the user operate itfull keyboard access, no seizure flashing, enough time
Understandabledoes it make senseplain language, predictable nav, form recovery on errors
Robustworks with assistive techvalid HTML, correct roles/names/values

Levels: A (must), AA (the professional standard), AAA (special cases). Your target at work: WCAG 2.2 AA.

The four principles, unpacked

WCAG 2.2 is a W3C Recommendation, not legislation, but it is what procurement asks for, what public-sector rules in the United States and the European Union enforce, and what a plaintiff's expert will cite. It is layered on purpose: four principles, each holding numbered guidelines, each guideline holding testable success criteria graded A, AA or AAA. That shape lets a team argue about scope without ever arguing about intent, which is why the argument stays short.

Perceivable covers everything a user cannot see or hear unless you supply an alternative channel. Guideline 1.1 asks for text alternatives to non-text content; 1.2 covers time-based media, which is captions, transcripts and audio description; 1.3 asks for content that can be presented in different ways without losing information, which in practice means semantics, the ability to rotate, and instructions that do not rely solely on shape, size or position; 1.4 asks for anything distinguishable, meaning contrast, resize, text spacing, non-text contrast and reduced motion. This is the principle with the most criteria and the most litigation behind it.

Operable is the principle that decides whether a product works for someone who never touches a mouse. Guideline 2.1 requires every function to be keyboard reachable, 2.2 requires enough time to complete it, 2.3 requires that nothing flashes above three times a second, 2.4 requires the interface to be navigable, and 2.5 requires that input does not demand a specific limb or gesture. WCAG 2.1 and 2.2 both added here: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) at AA, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) at AA, which sets a 24 by 24 CSS pixel floor with a spacing exception, and 2.4.13 Focus Appearance at AAA.

Understandable is the principle teams consistently underestimate, because it is about language and predictability rather than markup. Guideline 3.1 covers readable content, including declaring the page language and any language change; 3.2 covers predictability, meaning focus does not jump unexpectedly and context does not change on input; 3.3 covers input assistance, meaning labels, instructions, error identification, error suggestion and error prevention. WCAG 2.2 added three criteria here that change real product decisions: 3.2.6 Consistent Help at A, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry at A and 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) at AA.

Robust used to hold two criteria and now holds one. In WCAG 2.2 4.1.1 Parsing was removed and marked obsolete: it required markup to be well-formed, which every browser now guarantees, so it tested nothing. 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value remains at A and is where the accessibility tree has to expose a correct role, an accessible name and the current state of every control. If your component library is the source of that information, the library is where conformance is won or lost.

// A conformance gate that runs in CI. Automated tools catch roughly a third to
// a half of real issues depending on the page, so this is a floor, never a proof.
const { chromium } = require('playwright');
const AxeBuilder = require('@axe-core/playwright').default;

const LEVELS = { A: 'wcag2a', AA: 'wcag2aa', AAA: 'wcag2aaa' };

async function audit(pageUrls, { level = 'AA', extraTags = [] } = {}) {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const failures = [];

  for (const url of pageUrls) {
    const context = await browser.newContext();
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await page.goto(url, { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });

    const result = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
      .withTags([LEVELS[level], ...extraTags])
      .analyze();

    // impact: critical | serious | moderate | minor
    for (const v of result.violations) {
      if (!['critical', 'serious'].includes(v.impact)) continue;
      failures.push({
        url,
        id: v.id,
        impact: v.impact,
        help: v.help,
        nodes: v.nodes.length,
        // stop shipping this when it blocks a release; triage the rest per sprint
        blocking: v.tags.includes('wcag2a') || v.tags.includes('wcag2aa'),
        target: v.nodes[0] && v.nodes[0].target.join(' '),
      });
    }
    await context.close();
  }

  await browser.close();
  const blocking = failures.filter((f) => f.blocking);
  return { failures, blocking, pass: blocking.length === 0 };
}

if (require.main === module) {
  audit(process.argv.slice(2), { level: 'AA' }).then((r) => {
    r.failures.forEach((f) =>
      console.log(
        f.impact.padEnd(9) + f.id.padEnd(24) + String(f.nodes).padStart(3) + '  ' + f.url + '  ' + (f.target || '')
      )
    );
    console.log(r.failures.length + ' violation(s), ' + r.blocking.length + ' blocking');
    process.exit(r.pass ? 0 : 1);
  });
}
// A conformance record. This is the artefact that makes "we support
// accessibility" checkable: which pages, which level, which criteria were
// assessed manually rather than by a scanner, and what is still open.
// Product teams that keep one of these find that the open list is short.

const RECORD = {
  standard: 'WCAG 2.2',
  level: 'AA',
  assessedOn: '2026-09-14',
  assessor: 'platform team, plus one external audit',
  scope: ['/checkout', '/account', '/search', '/help'],
  automated: { tool: 'axe-core 4.10', coverage: '31 of 78 applicable criteria can be tested by machine' },
  manual: [
    { criterion: '2.1.1 Keyboard', method: 'full keyboard pass, no mouse, on every scope page', result: 'pass' },
    { criterion: '2.4.7 Focus Visible', method: 'tab through every interactive element', result: 'pass' },
    { criterion: '2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured', method: 'sticky header, 200% zoom', result: 'pass after fix' },
    { criterion: '1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)', method: 'token contrast solved against its surface, both themes', result: 'pass' },
    { criterion: '1.3.1 Info and Relationships', method: 'heading rotor read of every page', result: 'pass after fix' },
    { criterion: '3.3.2 Labels or Instructions', method: 'every field checked against its visible label', result: 'fail - open' },
  ],
  knownIssues: [
    { page: '/checkout', criterion: '3.3.7 Redundant Entry', note: 'shipping address re-entered on payment step', target: 'Q1' },
  ],
};

// The three numbers worth putting in a status update, because they are the
// only ones that describe reality rather than effort.
function report(r) {
  const assessed = new Set(r.manual.map((m) => m.criterion.split(' ')[0]));
  return {
    level: r.level,
    open: r.knownIssues.length,
    manuallyCovered: assessed.size,
    // a claim of conformance is only as good as the manual pass behind it
    defensible: r.knownIssues.every((k) => Boolean(k.target)),
  };
}

Conformance is a claim about a whole page

Conformance attaches to a page, not to a component. The standard asks whether the full page satisfies every A and every AA criterion, and it gives you narrow escapes: content that is not part of the product, like a third-party widget you did not author, and a background process into which the user cannot deliberately enter. Those are narrow on purpose. It does not offer an exception because "the button is only 20 pixels". If you embed a nonconforming page in an iframe, you are not responsible for what is inside it, and saying so in the accessibility statement is honest rather than defensive.

AA is the target that almost every organisation actually works to, and it is worth being precise about why. Level A is the floor at which a product is not actively hostile, but it contains criteria that will not protect a real user from a realistic mistake. Level AAA is mostly not testable as a whole: it includes sign-language interpretation, two-dimensional Braille output and cognitive-test thresholds, which describe a different order of service. Choosing AA is not a compromise. It is the only level that is both complete and verifiable.

AA also is not the finish line. Focus appearance at AAA, target size at 44 pixels rather than 24, and captions that describe the audio track are all cheap, and a product that clears them is materially better rather than marginally compliant. Where you set the bar above AA, write it into the design system rather than leaving it to the goodwill of whoever is nearest the ticket, because goodwill does not survive a deadline.

The limit of automation is the thing to state plainly in every accessibility plan you write. Vendors publish detection rates in the 30 to 60 percent range and the number is marketing as much as measurement, but the direction is not in doubt: a scanner sees the accessibility tree, and the accessibility tree cannot tell you whether the alternative text is any good, whether the heading order matches the reading order, whether a focus trap releases, or whether the error message actually tells you how to recover. Everything the scanner cannot see is exactly the part a disabled user cares about. That is why a claim of conformance needs a manual evaluation by a person, recorded with its date, its scope and its known gaps.

Under the European Accessibility Act, which has applied since June 2025, a broad set of consumer products and services, including e-commerce, must meet an accessibility requirement. The practical consequence for a product team is not a new design technique but a new document: the accessibility statement that has to exist, and the fixes it has to describe. Build the practice of writing that statement as you go and the law is a formality. Wait until it is demanded and you are reconstructing months of decisions you never wrote down.

7.2 Keyboard & focus: the "keyboard-only power user"

Keyboard accessibility means every interactive element can be reached, activated, and exited using only the Tab, arrow keys, Enter, and Space. A visible focus indicator is the keyboard user’s cursor, so never remove the default focus ring without providing a clear replacement. Add skip links so users can jump past navigation to main content, ensure logical tab order, and manage focus when dialogs open and close. Treat keyboard-only use as a core user, not a testing afterthought.

/* The focus sins and 5-second fixes */
button:focus-visible{ outline:3px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:2px; }
a:focus-visible, input:focus-visible{ outline:3px solid var(--accent); }
/* NEVER: outline:none with no replacement — invisible keyboard user */
/* Never skip/auto-move focus without a reason; respect Tab order;
   modals: trap focus in, return it on close (next time you open one,
   your code does this with autofocus + ESC handler) */

Four things every control owes a keyboard user

A control is keyboard accessible when it can be reached, operated, seen and escaped. Most teams get three and forget the fourth. Reach means Tab lands on it. Operate means the key that activates it follows the role, so Enter for links and buttons and Space for buttons. See means the focus indicator is visible against every background it can land on. Escape means the widget can be left without hunting, which is where modals, menus and grids earn their reputation.

Focus order follows DOM order, and that is the whole algorithm. A positive tabindex hijacks the sequence, so tabindex="1" on a header makes it the first thing every keyboard user on the page reaches, no matter where it sits visually. The correct use of the attribute is tabindex="-1": programmatically focusable, removed from the sequence. That is how a skip link finds its target, how a dialog takes focus on open, and how an error summary moves the user to the first field with an error without making that field part of the Tab sequence.

Composite widgets need the opposite treatment. A toolbar of twelve buttons should be one Tab stop, with arrow keys moving within it, because twelve Tab stops in a toolbar makes the rest of the page unreachable in practice. The pattern is a roving tabindex: exactly one child carries tabindex="0" and the rest carry tabindex="-1", and the arrow handler moves the value. Grid, tab list, menu and radiogroup all need it, and all four are the places where home-grown accessibility goes wrong most often, because each looks like a list of things and behaves like a single control.

// Roving tabindex: one Tab stop for the whole widget, arrows move inside it.
// The ARIA role decides which keys do what; the DOM position is never consulted.
function wireRovingGroup(root, selector, keys) {
  const items = () => Array.from(root.querySelectorAll(selector));
  const focusAt = (i) => {
    const all = items();
    if (!all.length) return;
    const next = all[(i + all.length) % all.length];
    // exactly one child is in the Tab sequence at any moment
    all.forEach((el, n) => el.setAttribute('tabindex', n === (i + all.length) % all.length ? '0' : '-1'));
    next.focus();
  };

  root.addEventListener('keydown', (ev) => {
    const all = items();
    const here = all.indexOf(document.activeElement);
    if (here === -1) return;
    const map = {
      ArrowRight: () => focusAt(here + 1),
      ArrowDown: () => focusAt(here + 1),
      ArrowLeft: () => focusAt(here - 1),
      ArrowUp: () => focusAt(here - 1),
      Home: () => focusAt(0),
      End: () => focusAt(all.length - 1),
      ...keys,
    };
    const fn = map[ev.key];
    if (fn) { ev.preventDefault(); fn(); }
  });

  // click or programmatic focus moves the roving point with it
  root.addEventListener('focusin', (ev) => {
    const i = items().indexOf(ev.target.closest(selector));
    if (i > -1) focusAt(i);
  });
}

wireRovingGroup(document.querySelector('[role="tablist"]'), '[role="tab"]', {
  // tabs activate on focus, so keyboard and pointer agree
  Enter: () => {},
});

Focus must also survive scrolling. A sticky header will happily park over the element you just tabbed to, which fails 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) at AA and reads to a user as the page having swallowed the cursor. The fix is not JavaScript: scroll-margin-top on anything focusable tells the browser how much room to leave when it scrolls a focused element into view.

/* Skip link: visible only once focused, so it costs no visual noise and
   still sits first in the Tab sequence. */
.skip-link {
  position: absolute;
  left: 8px;
  top: -48px;
  z-index: 100;
  padding: 10px 16px;
  background: var(--brand);
  color: var(--brand-ink);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
  transition: top 120ms ease-out;
}
.skip-link:focus { top: 8px; }

/* Headroom for the sticky header, applied to every focusable element, so a
   focused control is never scrolled underneath it. */
:target,
a:focus-visible,
button:focus-visible,
input:focus-visible,
select:focus-visible,
textarea:focus-visible,
[tabindex]:focus-visible {
  scroll-margin-top: calc(var(--header-h, 56px) + 12px);
}

/* One focus rule for the whole library, never removed. :focus-visible keeps
   the ring off mouse clicks and on for keyboard. */
:where(a, button, input, select, textarea, summary, [tabindex]):focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--accent);
  outline-offset: 2px;
  border-radius: var(--radius-xs);
}

/* Forced-colors mode (Windows high contrast) discards author colours, so the
   ring must be expressible with system colours or it disappears entirely. */
@media (forced-colors: active) {
  :where(a, button, input, select, textarea, [tabindex]):focus-visible {
    outline: 2px solid Highlight;
  }
}

Managing focus when things open and close

Opening something that covers the page is a focus operation, not a rendering one. Three things have to happen in order: the element that opened it is remembered, focus moves inside, and everything behind it becomes unreachable. On close, focus returns to the element that opened it, so the user's place in the document is exactly where they left it. Skip the return step and a keyboard user is dropped at the top of the document every time they close a dialog, which is the single most-reported bug in that whole category.

The native <dialog> element with showModal() does all of it for you, including the inertness of everything outside and the Escape handling. It is worth using even if you style it heavily, because the trap and the return are the parts teams hand-roll wrong. Where you must build it yourself, the inert attribute is the correct tool for the background; setting aria-hidden on the page wrapper is not, because that leaves the content focusable by script while pretending it is hidden, which is a worse bug than having done nothing.

Inside a dialog, two details decide whether it feels right. The first is the initial focus target: the first interactive element, or the least destructive action, or the dialog container itself if it is a confirmation the user should have to navigate deliberately. Never put initial focus on the destructive button. The second is that the confirm action, whatever it does, should leave focus somewhere sensible afterwards, which usually means a status message in a live region followed by a focus move to the next logical stop, not a modal that closes and leaves focus on body.

Finally, do not take focus without a reason. A filter that re-renders results on keystroke should not steal focus on every character. Reserve focus moves for events the user could not have predicted: something opened, something closed, something was added or removed out of band, or an error appeared far from where they were typing. Every surprise focus move is disorienting, and the ones that cannot be justified should simply be deleted.

One focus-visible rule draws a clear outline everywhere, and the comments warn never to remove focus styles without a real replacement.

  • Tab order = DOM order; test at least once with nothing but your keyboard.
  • Visible focus is required at WCAG 2.4.7 for keyboard users — it’s the cursor equivalent.
  • Skip-link ("Skip to content") lets keyboard users jump the nav — it’s the #1 cheap win.

7.3 Screen readers: the DOM is the interface

Screen readers convert the document structure into speech, so the interface a blind user experiences is the underlying semantic markup, not the visual pixels. Native HTML elements such as buttons, links, headings, and labels carry the correct roles and behavior for free, so prefer them over generic divs that need manual roles and keyboard wiring. Provide proper heading order, alt text, and accessible names for form fields. Semantics first means accessibility for near zero extra effort.

// Semantics = free accessibility. Native HTML already solves most of it:
<button>Save</button>        // keyboard+screen-reader+label for free
<div role="button" tabindex="0" aria-label="Save">Save</div>  // DIY, error-prone
// ARIA is a repair tool, not a decoration kit:
<button aria-expanded="false" onclick="...">Filters</button>
<input aria-describedby="hint"><p id="hint">8-32 chars</p>
// Golden rule: prefer native elements; add ARIA only when HTML can't do it.
// Test: install a screen-reader (NVDA/VoiceOver) and TRY it.

The three things a screen reader says

A screen reader does not read the screen. It reads the accessibility tree, a parallel structure the browser builds from your markup and then hands to the platform, and it spends its whole time reporting three things per node: the role, which says what the node is and therefore what keys and gestures apply; the accessible name, which is what gets spoken for it; and the value or state, which is what changed. Everything else on the page, including every pixel, is irrelevant until it has been reflected in that tree. This is the single most useful thing to understand about the topic, because it means most accessibility failures are authoring decisions that never reached the tree.

Native elements populate the tree correctly without any help. <button> gets the button role, keyboard handling, a focus stop and a disabled state. <a href> gets link semantics and Enter activation. <h1> through <h6> get heading levels, which is how a screen-reader user navigates by rotating the heading rotor to skim a long page instead of reading it linearly. A <div> with a click handler gets nothing at all: it is a group, it is not focusable, and it announces as whatever text happens to be inside it. Rebuilding any of that by hand with role and tabindex is possible and is almost always worse, because you also have to reimplement the keyboard contract, the state exposure and the announcements.

The accessible name comes from a defined cascade, and knowing the order explains most bugs. An explicit aria-labelledby wins, then aria-label, then the native source, which for an input is its associated <label>, for an image its alt, for a table its <caption>, and for a button or link its own text content. Note the consequence: aria-label on a plain <div> with no role does nothing at all, because an unnamed generic node is not announced. It is the most common way to spend an afternoon and change nothing.

Landmarks are the second navigation layer and they are cheap. Wrap the page in <header>, <nav>, <main> and <footer> and a screen-reader user gets a region list they can jump between directly, which is far faster than traversing links. Give each landmark a distinct aria-label when there is more than one of a kind, otherwise every one of them announces with the same word and the region list is useless.

// What the accessibility tree actually says. Run this against a live page and
// the name-role-state gap becomes a list rather than an opinion.
async function dumpTree(page, selector = 'main') {
  return page.evaluate((sel) => {
    const seen = (node) => {
      const el = node.nodeType === 1 ? node : node.parentElement;
      if (!el) return null;
      const acc = window.getComputedStyle(el);
      if (acc.display === 'none' || acc.visibility === 'hidden') return null;
      const name =
        el.getAttribute('aria-labelledby')
          ? (el.getAttribute('aria-labelledby').split(/\s+/).map((id) => document.getElementById(id)?.textContent?.trim()).join(' '))
          : el.getAttribute('aria-label') ||
            (el.labels && el.labels[0] ? el.labels[0].textContent.trim() : '') ||
            (el.tagName === 'IMG' ? el.getAttribute('alt') : '') ||
            (el.tagName === 'BUTTON' || el.tagName === 'A' ? el.textContent.trim() : '');
      const state = [
        el.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true' ? 'expanded' : null,
        el.getAttribute('aria-checked') || el.getAttribute('aria-selected'),
        el.disabled ? 'disabled' : null,
        el.required ? 'required' : null,
      ].filter(Boolean);
      return {
        role: el.getAttribute('role') || implicitRole(el),
        name,
        state: state.join(','),
        focusable: el.tabIndex >= 0,
        depth: 0,
      };
    };

    const root = document.querySelector(sel);
    const out = [];
    const walk = (n, d) => {
      if (n.nodeType !== 1) return;
      const row = seen(n);
      if (row) { row.depth = d; out.push(row); }
      for (const c of n.children) walk(c, d + 1);
    };
    walk(root, 0);
    return out;
  }, selector);
}

// the two failures worth failing a build over
const problems = tree.filter((n) =>
  (n.focusable && !n.role) || (!n.name && ['button', 'link', 'checkbox', 'textbox'].includes(n.role))
);

The third live surface is the polite announcement. A region marked aria-live="polite" is spoken after whatever the user is currently saying, and role="alert" is the assertive variant used for errors and confirmations. Two constraints make or break this. The live region must already exist in the DOM before the text changes, because the accessibility tree diff is what triggers the announcement; injecting the element and its text together produces silence, which is why so many toasts are invisible to a screen reader. And the region should wrap a stable container, because replacing the container wholesale removes the node the observer was watching.

Text that changes without announcement also breaks people who are not using a screen reader at all. Anything above the fold that changes every thirty seconds is unreadable for anyone with a cognitive disability, and a "0:12 remaining" timer that silently rewrites is unusable for anyone tracking it aloud. If a string updates in place, it is content, and it belongs in a live region or nowhere.

<!-- The live region exists empty, before any message arrives. -->
<div id="toasts" class="toasts">
  <div id="toast-polite" class="toast" role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true"></div>
</div>
<!-- Errors are assertive; role="alert" implies aria-live="assertive"
     and aria-atomic="true", so it is stated here for readability. -->
<div id="form-errors" tabindex="-1" role="alert"></div>

<form novalidate>
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email"
         autocomplete="email" inputmode="email"
         aria-describedby="email-hint email-err">
  <p id="email-hint">We only use this to send your receipt.</p>
  <p id="email-err" class="err" hidden></p>

  <label for="plan">Plan</label>
  <select id="plan" name="plan">
    <optgroup label="Personal">
      <option value="free">Free</option>
      <option value="pro">Pro</option>
    </optgroup>
  </select>

  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>

Alt text is a decision, not a description

Write alt text by asking what the image contributes, and answer with that rather than with a caption of what it looks like. An image that repeats text already on the page gets alt="", which is not an oversight: the empty string tells the tree the image is decorative and drops it from the reading order, which is exactly right when the text is already there. A photograph that carries meaning gets one sentence of context the surrounding prose does not already carry. An icon inside a link that already has visible text takes alt="" as well, otherwise the link announces its label twice. An image inside a link that is the only content of that link needs alt text that serves as the link name.

Complex images need more than a sentence. A chart, a diagram or a screenshot of a UI needs a short alt for the shape of it plus a longer description nearby, and the short description is reached with aria-describedby pointing at an element that is visible to everyone, not hidden in a tooltip that requires a mouse. For a chart, the table underneath is usually the best long description, because it is also useful to everyone else and it survives translation. The one case that has no good answer is a purely decorative background image, and that is a CSS background precisely so it never enters the tree.

None of this is special-cased for screen readers. Alt text is read aloud by every screen reader, is the fallback when an image fails to load, is what a search engine indexes, and is what appears when a browser cannot render the image format. Getting it right is not charity work, it is metadata for a text channel, and the same text serves four consumers at once.

Native buttons bring keyboard and screen-reader support for free; ARIA is only a repair tool for what HTML cannot express.

7.4 Designing for vision, motor and cognition diversity

Inclusive interfaces accommodate the full diversity of human ability, including low vision, motor impairments, and cognitive differences such as reduced memory or attention. In practice that means larger touch targets, stronger and verified contrast, generous hit areas, shorter and plainer copy, and forgiving interactions that allow undo. Support zoom and text resizing so content never breaks at large text sizes. Every small adjustment widens who can use your product.

NeedDesign response
Low visionzoom-friendly layouts (no fixed small minimums), contrast, enlarge type
Color-blindnessnot color-only labels; distinguish red/green by shapes/icons too
Motor (Parkinson’s, tremor, one-handed)targets ≥ 44px, generous spacing, no click-hairs, ignore double-tap misfires, sticky buttons
Cognition / ADHD / literacyshort copy, one idea per screen, progressive disclosure, no urgent fake alerts
Deaf/hard of hearingcaptions, no essential audio-only info

Inclusive design is three problems, not one

Inclusive design is usually presented as a virtue, which is why it keeps getting deferred. It is more useful as three concrete physical problems, each with its own design response and its own user group. The physical problem covers bodies and senses: someone with a tremor, someone who is blind, someone in a wheelchair, someone with low vision or no vision in one eye. The perceptual problem covers the fact that hearing, sight, touch and balance degrade and are not equally good in everyone. The cognitive problem covers learning and reasoning: memory, attention, literacy, language, and the ability to recover from a mistake.

Designing for the third group tends to improve the first two, and that is the practical argument for doing it early rather than late. A form that asks one question at a time, states the format before the field, and never loses what was already typed is easier for a screen-reader user, easier for someone with a tremor, and easier for someone on a phone in poor light. Nothing about it is expensive. What is expensive is retrofitting it into a checkout flow that assumed a mouse and a wide viewport.

The measurable obligations are more specific than the generalities, and the specific ones are what a design review should hold you to. Text must survive 200 percent zoom and 400 percent zoom at a 1280 pixel viewport without loss of content or function. The page must reflow to a 320 CSS pixel width with no two-dimensional scrolling except inside genuinely two-dimensional things like a data table. Users who override text spacing must not clip content, which in practice means never fixing a height on text that can grow. Every target needs 24 by 24 CSS pixels minimum, with spacing as the accepted alternative where a dense table makes the target itself impracticable.

For motor accessibility the rule that is easiest to honour and most often broken is that every pointer gesture has a single-pointer alternative. Drag to reorder needs a move-to-position control. Swipe to dismiss needs a close button. Pinch to zoom needs a zoom control. Hover to reveal needs keyboard focus to reveal the same thing, and the revealed content must stay put when the pointer passes over it, which is the requirement that turns most hover tooltips into an accessibility failure for anyone using a screen magnifier.

/* The three user-preference queries that cost almost nothing and that most
   codebases have never written. All of them are overrides a user explicitly
   asked their operating system for, so honouring them is not optional. */

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  /* 1. Remove non-essential movement. Do not merely shorten it: vestibular
     triggers respond to parallax and large-area motion, not duration. */
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.001ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.001ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}

@media (prefers-contrast: more) {
  /* 2. Strengthen the edges a low-vision user is relying on. */
  :root {
    --muted: var(--text);
    --border: color-mix(in oklab, var(--text) 55%, var(--bg));
  }
  a:not(.btn) { text-decoration-thickness: 2px; }
}

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  /* 3. Hand colour back to the user. Everything drawn with a background
     colour is invisible unless a system colour replaces it, which is why
     borders need system color keywords rather than var() alone. */
  .card, .btn, input, select, textarea {
    border: 1px solid CanvasText;
    background: Canvas;
    color: CanvasText;
    forced-color-adjust: auto;
  }
  .btn[aria-pressed="true"], .tab[aria-selected="true"] {
    background: Highlight;
    color: HighlightText;
  }
}

/* 4. Text that can grow. A fixed height on text is the single most common
