   cause of clipping once a user overrides line height. */
.field {
  min-height: 2.75rem;   /* touch target floor */
  height: auto;          /* never px */
  padding: 0.6rem 0.75rem;
  line-height: 1.5;
}

Resize, reflow and the tests that prove them

Resizing is four distinct requirements that teams collapse into one, which is why they fix one and ship three failures. Text resize means the browser's font-size setting must scale the layout, so use relative units throughout and never set a px height on a text container. Zoom means 200 percent must not cause clipping or overlap, and it also means the fourth-level enhancement of 400 percent, which is effectively the reflow requirement. Text spacing override means a user who sets line height to 1.5 times and 0.12em paragraph spacing must not lose any content, which rules out fixed heights and single-line truncation on anything that must remain readable. Reflow means at 320 CSS pixels there is no horizontal scrolling of the page itself.

Test these by actually changing the setting rather than by resizing the window, because they fail for different reasons. Zoom keeps the CSS pixel viewport narrower, so it catches layout that was only ever designed wide. Font-size scaling keeps the viewport the same and grows every box, so it catches fixed heights. Text spacing override grows internal padding and gaps, so it catches anything sized to its content. And reflow catches the wide table and the fixed sidebar. Four distinct faults, four distinct tests, and a single "does it look right at 320" check finds none of them reliably.

For low vision specifically, the two levers are contrast and thickness. Contrast is solved rather than eyeballed: pick the text token, solve it against the surface it is painted on, and check both themes. The failure is not usually the body text, which someone already measured, but the four grey levels that came out of a design tool, and the disabled state, which is exempt from contrast requirements and therefore routinely illegible in both directions. Thickness matters as much as the ratio, because a low-vision user with font-weight: 300 and thin letterforms needs more contrast to read the same text. Raising the weight is often a cheaper fix than darkening the colour, and it does not change the palette.

Cognitive accessibility has its own practical checklist, and it is mostly about removing decisions rather than adding affordances. Do not make the user remember a value between screens; show it or keep it. Do not make them learn a gesture they have never seen; pair every gesture with a visible control. Do not punish a mistake that a reasonable person could have made, so confirmation steps apply to irreversible actions and nothing else. Do not use time as a pressure, which means either extendable timeouts or none. And do not make the error message ask the user to diagnose the system's internal state; say what happened, where, and what to do next, in that order.

/* Reflow without a horizontal scrollbar: the pattern that fails at 320px is a
   fixed-width sidebar plus a wide table. Both are solved by the same rule -
   let the flexible thing shrink, and let the rigid thing scroll inside its
   own box rather than the page's. */
.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) 280px;  /* minmax(0,1fr) not 1fr */
  gap: 2rem;
}
@media (max-width: 60rem) {
  .page { grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr); }
}

/* Anything genuinely two-dimensional scrolls inside itself, and the container
   is focusable and labelled so keyboard users can reach the scroll. */
.table-scroll {
  overflow-x: auto;
  max-width: 100%;
}
@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .table-scroll { border: 1px solid CanvasText; }
}

/* Images scale with the layout instead of forcing it wider. */
img, svg, video, canvas { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }

/* Long words, URLs and identifiers break instead of pushing the layout. */
p, li, dd, h1, h2, h3, h4 { overflow-wrap: break-word; }

Finally, budget for the fact that some accommodations cost more than a CSS change. Captions and transcripts are content work and they need a human being who understands the material. A sign-language video is a budget line, not a checkbox. Alternative text for a complex diagram is design work. Pretending all of this is a front-end concern produces accessibility that passes a scanner and fails the people it was for, which is the failure mode that costs the most trust and the most money, because it is the one that survives to launch.

7.5 Inclusive language and human centeredness

Language is part of the interface, so the words a product uses decide who feels welcome to use it. Write plainly, avoid jargon, use gender-neutral phrasing, and build forms that do not exclude people based on family structure, ability, or identity. Avoid ableist idioms and make error states kind rather than accusing. Inclusive language is a design decision that honors the humanity of every user.

Language is UI. Use plain language (grade-school reading level for essential flows), gender-neutral phrasing ("they"), no ableist idioms ("blind to the problem"), and forms that don’t force binary gender or full names. Include people in your testing — a session with one screen-reader user reshapes your design more than any checklist.

Inclusive language is interface copy

Language is part of the product. The words on the screen decide who understands the interface without asking, who has to stop and ask a colleague what a term means, and who concludes that the product was not built with them in mind. This is not a proofreading pass at the end; it is a design decision, made in the same place as every other design decision, and the evidence is that inclusive interfaces are shorter. Plain language is usually shorter because jargon exists to compress meaning for people who already have the context, and most users do not.

The operational form of this is a reading-age target on the flows that matter: sign-up, checkout, support, permissions. Around grade eight is the widely used reference and it is a useful one, not because anyone is holding a ruler over your copy but because it forces you to cut the sentence that exists for the lawyers. One idea per sentence, active voice, concrete nouns, a subject the reader can picture. If a sentence needs a clause to explain the clause, it is two sentences.

Avoidable harm in UI copy follows predictable shapes. Idioms borrowed from physical ability, like "blind to the problem", "blind spot", "crippled by the database", "sanity check" and "lame", assume a reader has a particular body. Terms borrowed from cognitive ability, like "dumb it down", "sanity check", "no-brainer", "crazy amount" and "spastic tuning", are harder still, because they are usually written by people who are not trying to be cruel and simply never examined the metaphor. Gender-neutral phrasing is the same exercise with different vocabulary: use "they", address people by name or role, and stop inferring gender from a name in test data, because a customer who sees "Dear Mrs Chen" after typing a different name concludes the form did not read what they typed.

<!-- Before: the interface asks for more than it needs, demands a gender, and
     puts an error state in front of the user before they have done anything
     wrong. After: same three fields, no identity questions, kind error copy. -->

<!-- BEFORE -->
<form>
  <label>Full name (as per ID)</label><input required>
  <label>Gender</label>
  <select required>
    <option value="">Select...</option>
    <option>Male</option>
    <option>Female</option>
  </select>
  <label>Date of birth</label><input type="date" required>
  <p class="err">Invalid input</p>
</form>

<!-- AFTER -->
<form novalidate>
  <label for="display">Display name</label>
  <input id="display" name="display" autocomplete="nickname"
         hint="This is what teammates will see.">

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Pronouns (optional)</legend>
    <!-- optional, free text, and never a required binary -->
    <input id="pronouns" name="pronouns" autocomplete="off"
           placeholder="e.g. they/them">
  </fieldset>

  <label for="age">Age range (optional)</label>
  <select id="age" name="age">
    <option value="">Prefer not to say</option>
    <option>Under 18</option>
    <option>18 to 24</option>
    <option>25 to 34</option>
  </select>

  <!-- one summary, not eleven field-level accusations -->
  <div role="alert">
    <h3>Check 2 details</h3>
    <ul>
      <li><a href="#display">Display name</a> is required</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</form>

The rule behind the rules: do not ask for what you will not use

Almost every exclusion in a signup flow traces to a data field collected by default and used for one analytics report eighteen months later. The question to ask of any field is not "can we collect this" but "what breaks if we do not have it". If nothing breaks, it is optional, and if it is genuinely optional it should be visibly optional rather than marked by an asterisk that the eye stops reading. Demographics, real name, date of birth, pronouns, gender, disability, and legal name distinct from display name are the usual set, and in most products none of them belongs on a required path.

When a field is optional and you still want it, the honest pattern is an ask with a reason and a decline button: state what it improves, offer "skip", and keep the skip path identical in length. This is not only an inclusion measure. It measurably increases completion, because a form that asks for less gets finished more often, and every abandoned field is a support ticket you did not have to answer.

Error copy follows a fixed order and every part is load-bearing. What happened, in terms the user recognises. Where it happened, pointing at the field. What to do next, as an action rather than a diagnosis. "Invalid input" is a message to the developer. "That email address is missing an @, for example name@company.com" is a message to the person. And the tone matters more than teams expect: a message that says you entered something wrong transfers blame to a person for a system failure, while a message that says we could not read that keeps the relationship intact and, empirically, gets completed more often.

// Error copy as data. Keeping the strings in one reviewed place means the
// wording is a design decision with an owner, and the same table can generate
// both the visible message and the screen-reader announcement.
const ERRORS = {
  emailRequired: {
    field: 'Email address',
    what: 'We need an email address to send your receipt.',
    action: 'Add one in the field below.',
  },
  emailFormat: {
    field: 'Email address',
    what: 'That address is missing an @ sign.',
    action: 'It should look like name@example.com.',
  },
  cardExpiry: {
    field: 'Expiry date',
    what: 'That expiry date has already passed.',
    action: 'Check the month and year on the card.',
  },
  generic: {
    field: null,
    // never shown: an unexplained failure teaches the user nothing and
    // gives support nothing to act on
    what: 'We could not read something in that form.',
    action: 'Check the highlighted fields, or contact support if it keeps happening.',
  },
};

function describe(key) {
  const e = ERRORS[key] || ERRORS.generic;
  const summary = e.field ? e.field + ': ' : '';
  return {
    // the summary is what gets announced; the detail sits in the description
    summary: summary + e.what,
    description: e.action,
  };
}

The last piece is testing with people rather than for them. One session with a screen-reader user, one with someone who has a motor difficulty, one with someone who uses a screen magnifier, and one with a non-native speaker of your interface language will reshape a design more than any amount of internal review. Not because those people are a representative sample, but because they are the only source of information nobody on the team already has. A checklist can tell you the contrast ratio is 4.8 to 1. It cannot tell you that the only way to tell which field is in error is a red border, which disappears entirely for the two percent of men with red-green colour vision deficiency.

7.6 Accessibility shift-left: audits, budgets, culture

Shift-left means moving accessibility work to the earliest, cheapest point in the process instead of fixing issues after launch, when they cost many times more. Set an explicit standard such as WCAG 2.2 AA, budget accessibility effort into every screen, and audit designs and code continuously with automated tools plus manual checks. Build a culture where accessibility is a normal review criterion rather than a special project. Catching a contrast failure at design time costs minutes; catching it in production costs a release.

  • Set the bar as a gate: WCAG 2.2 AA at release, with an automated scan (axe) plus manual spot checks. Accessibility fixed at design time costs pennies; remediating post-launch costs rework and reputation.
  • An a11y budget per screen: contrast, focus visibility, target size — decided in design review, not discovered in QA. Track it like token debt.
  • Design with the community, not just for it: one screen-reader session and one motor-difficulty session per milestone changes your designs more than any checklist ever will.

Exercises 7

  1. Tab-only test of one of your screens; fix the 3 worst focus issues.
  2. Run an automated scan (axe/Lighthouse) and fix every "critical" — then manually verify 5 fixes actually work.
  3. Watch/read an NVDA demo and describe what a screen-reader user hears on your homepage. Fix one thing.

Where the money actually goes

Shift-left means putting accessibility work at the earliest point where the defect can still be cheaply changed. That framing is worth stating precisely, because "shift left" is usually used to mean "involve accessibility earlier", which is a slogan rather than a plan. The measurable version is the cost curve: a contrast ratio chosen in a design file costs a token change, an unlabelled input found by a designer in review costs a label, and the same unlabelled input found by a disabled user six weeks after release costs a release, a rollback, an apology and a fix that also touches everything that shipped next to it. None of those are the same cost, and only one of them is on the critical path.

Concretely, the things that get caught late are the things nobody owned. A missing focus order is a DOM problem that only surfaces when the markup is written. A colour that fails contrast is a token decision that gets made once and applied four hundred times, which means it is cheap to fix at the token and expensive everywhere else. A heading level that jumps from h2 to h4 is a content-modelling decision. A control with no accessible name is a component API decision, and if the component library shipped it that way then every instance is wrong and the fix is a breaking change. The common factor is that each of these has an owner, and the owner is usually not the person who finds the bug.

The practical shift-left move is to make accessibility a property of the deliverables rather than of a review. A design file is not done until its colour pairs are solved against their surfaces and its interactive states are drawn. A component is not done until it is reachable, operable, named and visible. A content set is not done until its headings form a document order. Those three sentences, written into the definition of done, do more than a workshop, because they attach to work that already happens rather than adding a new ceremony to work that does not.

// The gate that makes it structural rather than cultural: three cheap
// automated checks that run on every pull request, in under a minute.
name: a11y

on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ['src/**', 'public/index.html', '.storybook/**']

jobs:
  static:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci

      # 1. design tokens: no raw colour literals outside token files, and
      #    every declared pair clears its threshold.
      - name: token lint
        run: node tools/token-lint.js --min-contrast 4.5

      # 2. authored markup: lang attribute, page title, one h1, labelled
      #    controls, no positive tabindex, no outline:none without a
      #    replacement in the same rule.
      - name: markup lint
        run: npx html-validate "src/**/*.html"           --rule "attr-quoted:true"           --rule "wcag/h30:true"           --rule "no-positive-tabindex:error"

      # 3. component stories, which is where a broken primitive shows up
      #    before it reaches a page.
      - name: storybook a11y
        run: |
          npx build-storybook -o storybook-static -q
          npx http-server storybook-static -p 6006 --silent &
          npx wait-on http://localhost:6006
          npx test-storybook --url http://localhost:6006 --maxWorkers=2

      # 4. the runtime pass on the built site, blocking on serious only.
      - name: axe on built pages
        run: node tools/axe-ci.js --level AA --block-on serious

      # 5. the invariant check, because a tool that writes a guide can
      #    duplicate a block and every other test still passes.
      - run: node tools/repeats.js

Make the bar a gate, and make the gate cheap

The reason accessibility escapes a plan is that the check is expensive enough to be deferred. A full manual audit is a week of expert time and cannot run on every change, so it runs once a quarter, by which time the finding is expensive and the team is out of patience. The shift is to run the cheap checks continuously and the expensive ones occasionally, and to be explicit that the cheap checks are a floor. An automated pass in CI costs about a minute and catches the class of defect that is both common and mechanically detectable, which is exactly the class that accumulates fastest because nothing is watching for it.

Blocking on serious and critical violations, and warning on moderate and minor, is a defensible line. Blocking on everything produces the reflex of suppressing the rule, and a suppressed rule is worse than a warned-about violation because it is invisible. Blocking on everything else in the repository too, because contrast on a token is a one-line change at review and a hundred-component sweep after release. The test that a gate works is simple: deliberately introduce a violation, and see whether the build stops.

Run the gate against the design system rather than only against pages wherever you can. A component-level test for role, name and keyboard behaviour catches the failure once, before it is instantiated four hundred times. Token tests catch the contrast failure once. The reason teams ship a hundred instances of one bug is that they tested the hundred instances instead of the one thing that made them.

// A component test asserts the accessibility contract at the source. Four
// assertions per primitive catches most of what a scanner finds later, and
// three of them cannot be checked at all by a scanner on the built page.
describe('ModalDialog', () => {
  it('moves focus inside on open and restores it on close', async () => {
    const opener = document.createElement('button');
    opener.textContent = 'Open';
    document.body.append(opener);
    opener.focus();

    const dlg = render(<ModalDialog title="Confirm">Body</ModalDialog>);
    dlg.getButton('Close').click();

    expect(dlg.dialog.contains(document.activeElement)).toBe(true);
    expect(document.activeElement.getAttribute('autofocus') !== null
        || document.activeElement === dlg.getButton('Close')).toBe(true);

    fireEvent.keyDown(document.activeElement, { key: 'Escape' });
    expect(document.activeElement).toBe(opener);   // the step teams forget
  });

  it('makes everything outside it inert', async () => {
    render(<ModalDialog title="Confirm">Body</ModalDialog>);
    const outside = document.querySelector('main');
    expect(outside.hasAttribute('inert') || outside.getAttribute('aria-hidden') === 'true')
      .toBe(true);
  });

  it('names itself from its heading', () => {
    const dlg = render(<ModalDialog title="Confirm">Body</ModalDialog>);
    expect(dlg.dialog.getAttribute('aria-labelledby')).toBe(dlg.heading.id);
  });

  it('does not park initial focus on the destructive action', () => {
    const dlg = render(<ModalDialog title="Confirm"
      confirmLabel="Delete account" confirmTone="danger">Body</ModalDialog>);
    expect(dlg.getButton('Delete account')).not.toBe(document.activeElement);
  });
});

// The same four questions, as a checklist a designer can answer in Figma:
//   1. What is the role, and what keys operate it?
//   2. What is its accessible name, and is it visible?
//   3. What does it announce when its state changes?
//   4. What does a keyboard user see when it is focused?

Track the two kinds of number separately, because they answer different questions. Count of open violations against a standard answers "are we getting closer", and it is the number teams quote. Task completion rate for a user with a disability answers "does this work", and it is the number that survives contact with a real user. A product can report zero violations and still be unusable, and a product with known open violations can be perfectly usable for the people who have not yet reached them. Report both, and report the known issues with a target date rather than only the clean count, because the count alone is trivially gameable by declaring the standard achieved on the one page nobody has tested.

The last piece of shift-left is making sure the person who found it can fix it. When a disabled user reports a barrier, the response that helps is not a commitment to look into it but a specific change with a date, and the change usually has to be made in someone else's layer. If your process cannot route a barrier report to a component-library owner within a day, you have built a reporting channel rather than an accessibility practice, and the honest thing to say in the accessibility statement is that you have one.

8 · Typography for UX

Typography is the design of text in an interface and carries most of a website’s communication, so it must be engineered, not just styled. It is a justifiable system of type scale, font pairing, line height, and measure that makes long reading effortless and hierarchy obvious. In practice you pick a base size, derive a modular scale, choose legible typefaces, and verify readability across breakpoints. Good typography works invisibly on behalf of the content.

8.1 Modular type scales (never random sizes)8.2 Choosing and pairing typefaces8.3 Readability: measure, leading, line length8.4 Fluid and responsive type8.5 Visual noise: hierarchy & restraint

Typography is 95% of how a website communicates. This chapter is the difference between "nice fonts" taste and systems you can justify to a client.

8.1 Modular type scales (never random sizes)

A modular type scale derives every text size from one base size multiplied by a consistent ratio, such as the musical fifths or the golden ratio. Because all sizes share a mathematical relationship, headings and body text feel intentional and harmonious rather than chaotic. Choose a base size near 16 pixels, pick a ratio that fits your content density, generate the scale once, then use it exclusively. It delivers hierarchy and rhythm without guesswork.

// Compute a scale from a base + ratio:
base = 16px                         // normal body
ratio = 1.25 (minor third)          // compact UI feel
ratio = 1.333 (perfect fourth)      // airy editorial feel
sizes:  12 16 20 25 31 39 → map to UI roles:
  12 caption   16 body   20 h3   25 h2   31 h1
// Store as spacing/pad tokens; change ratio ONCE and re-skin everywhere.

Why a ratio beats a list of sizes

A modular scale is one number multiplied by a constant. Pick a base body size and a ratio, and every step follows, so the relationship between sizes is a property of the system rather than a decision made ninety times. That is the real benefit, and it is not aesthetic: when a designer wants a heading larger, they change the ratio and every heading in the product moves together, whereas with a hand-made scale they will change one component and the ratios between every other pair will silently drift out of alignment.

The base size should be the body text size, near 16 CSS pixels, because that is what the reader spends their time in and it is what the accessibility floor cares about. The ratio is the personality. A ratio near 1.125 is quiet and dense and suits dashboards and admin tools, where the difference between two heading levels is deliberately small. Near 1.2 is the common web default. Near 1.333 is confident and works for marketing pages with real typographic hierarchy. Near 1.5 is a magazine, and it will overwhelm a form.

The base size is the one decision that is not really yours. A user who has set their browser's default font size to 20 pixels has told you something, and a system expressed in pixels will ignore it. Express the base in rem and the entire scale inherits the user's setting for free, because every step is a multiple of the root font size. This is the single highest-leverage accessibility decision in a type system, and it costs nothing at design time.

/* A modular scale in rem. The base inherits the user's browser font-size
   setting because it is expressed relative to the root, and every step is
   a multiple of it, so the whole scale scales when the user zooms. */
:root {
  --font-base: 1rem;        /* 16px by default; whatever the user set, in practice */
  --ratio: 1.25;            /* major third: quiet, safe, good for long sessions */

  --step--2: calc(var(--font-base) / var(--ratio) / var(--ratio));
  --step--1: calc(var(--font-base) / var(--ratio));
  --step-0:  var(--font-base);
  --step-1:  calc(var(--font-base) * var(--ratio));
  --step-2:  calc(var(--step-1) * var(--ratio));
  --step-3:  calc(var(--step-2) * var(--ratio));
  --step-4:  calc(var(--step-3) * var(--ratio));
  --step-5:  calc(var(--step-4) * var(--ratio));
  --step-6:  calc(var(--step-5) * var(--ratio));
}

/* Roles, not sizes. Components consume --step-3; nobody writes 1.953rem.
   Changing --ratio re-skins every heading in the product at once. */
h1, .h1 { font-size: var(--step-6); line-height: 1.05; letter-spacing: -0.02em; }
h2, .h2 { font-size: var(--step-5); line-height: 1.15; letter-spacing: -0.015em; }
h3, .h3 { font-size: var(--step-4); line-height: 1.2;  letter-spacing: -0.01em; }
h4, .h4 { font-size: var(--step-2); line-height: 1.3; }
h5, .h5 { font-size: var(--step-1); line-height: 1.4;  color: var(--muted); }
h6, .h6 { font-size: var(--step--1); line-height: 1.4; color: var(--muted);
           text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.06em; }
p, li, dd { font-size: var(--step-0); line-height: 1.6; }
small, .caption { font-size: var(--step--1); }

/* Ratio is a design-token axis, so density can change without a redesign. */
:root[data-density="compact"] { --ratio: 1.2; }
:root[data-density="roomy"]    { --ratio: 1.333; }

Two details make the difference between a scale that looks considered and one that looks like arithmetic. First, tighten the letter spacing as the size increases, because large type set at normal tracking looks loose; a heading at 3rem wants about -0.02em and a heading at 1.125rem wants slightly positive tracking. Second, line height must fall as size rises: body text needs 1.5 to 1.7 because the reader is tracking each line, and a 3rem heading needs about 1.05 because leading is a reading aid and a display line is not being read. Applying body line height to headings is the most common unforced error in a type system, and it makes large text look like a stack of unrelated lines.

Do not use the scale to establish semantic importance. HTML heading levels encode document structure and are what a screen reader navigates by, so an h3 that is styled 2rem because the design wanted it large is a lie to assistive technology and a problem for anyone who skims by heading. Pick the level from the outline and the size from the role. Where the design and the outline genuinely disagree, fix the outline.

A base size and a ratio generate a full type scale mapped to UI roles, so bumping one ratio re-skins the whole system.

8.2 Choosing and pairing typefaces

Choosing typefaces means balancing personality with legibility, and one well-chosen family with several weights is often all an interface needs. When you pair two families, give them different jobs, such as a display face for headings and a highly legible face for body text, rather than pairing two similar styles. Look for contrast in structure, weight, or x-height, and limit yourself to two families plus one monospace for code. Restraint reads as more professional than variety.

  • One typeface with weights is usually enough. Two faces work best when very different in job (display heading + crisp body).
  • Web-safe practical: system font stack (fast, no download) or self-hosted woff2 subsets (fast enough).
  • Avoid: more than 2 families, all-caps body text, italics for long reads, text on busy imagery.

Real-world rule: a "boring" highly-legible body font will beat a pretty one on every business metric. Legibility at body sizes, then style at heading sizes.

One family, then two, then stop

The strongest starting point is one family with several weights. A variable font covers the whole range in a single file, so 400, 500, 600 and 700 come from one download, and hierarchy is carried by weight and colour rather than by a second typeface competing for attention. Most interfaces, dashboards and documentation sites need nothing else, and shipping one family is the decision that makes a product look expensive rather than busy.

Add a second family only when it has a different job, and the most reliable different job is a display face for a brand moment: the wordmark, the marketing hero, a single oversized number. Two similar families have no different job; they have a different mood, and mood is a weak reason to spend a download. The failure mode is unmistakable: two humanist sans faces at similar weights produce a page where nothing has hierarchy and everything is slightly off. Contrast the two on structure instead, weight instead, or x-height instead, and the pairing reads as deliberate.

A monospace third is a category apart rather than a stylistic choice. Code samples need it, and the reason is not the typewriter aesthetic: monospace makes indentation, alignment and token boundaries visible, which is the actual information content of a code sample. A proportional body font in a code block destroys leading whitespace and makes indentation ambiguous, and since indentation is semantic in most languages, that is a correctness problem rather than a taste problem.

/* Three families with three distinct jobs. Self-hosted woff2 subsets keep
   this to a few tens of kilobytes and remove the third-party request, which
   matters because a font that arrives late re-flows the page the reader has
   already started. */
@font-face {
  font-family: 'Body';
  src: url('/fonts/body-variable.woff2') format('woff2-variations');
  font-weight: 300 800;      /* the whole range in one file */
  font-style: normal;
  font-display: swap;        /* paint fallback text, never a blank block */
  unicode-range: U+0000-00FF, U+0131, U+0152-0153, U+2000-206F;
}
@font-face {
  font-family: 'Display';
  src: url('/fonts/display.woff2') format('woff2');
  font-weight: 600 700;
  font-display: swap;
}
@font-face {
  font-family: 'Mono';
  src: url('/fonts/mono.woff2') format('woff2');
  font-weight: 400 600;
  font-display: swap;
}

:root {
  --font-body: 'Body', system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
  --font-display: 'Display', 'Body', system-ui, sans-serif;
  --font-mono: 'Mono', ui-monospace, 'Cascadia Code', Consolas, monospace;
  /* the fallback stack must be metric-similar or swap shifts the layout */
  --fallback-adjust: 'adjust';  /* size-adjust / ascent-override in @font-face */
}

body { font-family: var(--font-body); font-optical-sizing: auto; }
h1, h2 { font-family: var(--font-display); }
code, pre, kbd, samp { font-family: var(--font-mono); }

/* Digit alignment in tables and metrics: tabular figures, or columns
   of numbers will not line up down the page. */
table, .metric, [data-numeric] { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }

/* Test for the pair at body size first and at display size second. */
@media print { h1, h2 { font-family: var(--font-body); } }
// A pairing decision, written down. Every font decision in a product
// eventually has to be defended in a review, and the argument is much
// shorter when the reason was recorded at the time it was made.
const PAIRING = {
  body: {
    family: 'Body Variable',
    weights: [400, 500, 650],
    why: 'highest x-height of the shortlisted faces at 14px; one file covers the range',
    fallback: 'system-ui',
  },
  display: {
    family: 'Display',
    weights: [600, 700],
    // the only reason a second family exists: one brand moment per page.
    // If it grew to body copy, the justification is gone and so is the family.
    why: 'used for the wordmark and the marketing h1 only',
    maxUsesPerPage: 1,
  },
  mono: {
    family: 'Mono',
    why: 'indentation is semantic in code, so the axis must be uniform',
  },
  rejected: [
    { family: 'Editorial Serif', reason: 'beautiful at 3rem, poor at body size; adds 40KB for one use' },
    { family: 'Geometric Sans', reason: 'single-storey g reads poorly in longer words' },
  ],
};

// The check that catches drift, because drift is the real cost: if a
// component reaches for a family that is not on this list, the pairing has
// stopped being a decision and become an accident.
const ALLOWED = ['Body', 'Display', 'Mono'];
// assert: [...document.fonts].every((f) => ALLOWED.includes(f.family));

// One loading budget for the whole page. Two families plus mono must not
// spend more than this before the fallback text is interactive.
const FONT_BUDGET_KB = 120;

Distribution matters as much as choice. System font stacks need no download and render with the platform's own hinting, which is why they stay sharp at small sizes and are a defensible answer for an internal tool. Self-hosted woff2 gives you the face you designed with and removes a request to a third party that can be slow, blocked or, in some jurisdictions, unreachable. What you give up is nothing much: font files are a few tens of kilobytes after subsetting, and subsetting to the character ranges a page actually uses plus a Latin-ext range is straightforward.

Whichever route you take, load the font with font-display: swap and set a fallback whose metrics are close to the real one, so the swap does not reflow a paragraph the reader has already started. Better still, define size-adjust, ascent-override and descent-override on a local fallback face, which is what removes the visible jump entirely. And test at the size that will actually be used: a face that reads well at 3rem is often unreadable at 14 pixels, which is the size most of a dense interface is set at.

Three things to avoid, in order of how often they cause trouble. More than two families, because the eye cannot find a hierarchy that keeps moving. All-caps body text, which removes the ascenders and descenders that the eye uses to identify a word. And italics for anything long, which slants the letterforms into the following word. Uppercase is defensible for a two-word label at small size with generous tracking, and that is the whole of its range.

8.3 Readability: measure, leading, line length

Readability depends on the mechanical settings around a typeface as much as the typeface itself, chiefly line length, line height, and letter spacing. Keep body line length near 45 to 75 characters with line height around 1.5 for web text, and avoid justified text that creates uneven gaps. Set letter spacing carefully for headings and uppercase text. Generous leading and appropriate measure keep the eye moving smoothly through long passages.

/* The readability trio */
p { font-size:16px;                                    /* body base     */
    line-height:1.55;                                  /* leading ~1.5  */
    max-width:65ch;                                    /* measure ≤75ch */
}
h1,h2,h3{ line-height:1.2; }                 /* headings hug tight */
/* For Chinese-heavy UIs: line-height 1.7-1.9, max-width ~40-45 "em" */

Measure, leading, and the return sweep

Three mechanical settings decide readability more than the typeface does, and none of them are the typeface's fault. Measure is the line length: how many characters a line holds before it wraps. Leading is line height. Tracking is letter spacing. Get these three right and a modest typeface becomes easy to read; get them wrong and a beautiful one becomes tiring.

The measure rule is 45 to 75 characters per line for body text, and both ends matter. Below about 45 the eye reaches the end of a line and has to find the start of the next one, which is a saccade it makes roughly fifteen times a second and does not have to make if the line is longer. Above about 75 the return sweep, the movement from the end of one line back to the beginning of the next, becomes unreliable and the reader starts re-reading lines. Set it in ch units and it adapts to the font size rather than being locked to a pixel width that suits exactly one size.

Leading should be about 1.5 for body text on screen and 1.6 or more for dense prose, rising as the measure shortens. The relationship matters: a 30-character line needs more leading than a 70-character one, because there are more line starts per screen height. Line height set on the container and inherited is also the mechanism that makes the text-spacing accessibility override work, since a user who increases line height needs the block to grow rather than to clip.

Tracking is only worth adjusting at the extremes. Large display type wants negative tracking, typically -0.01em to -0.03em, because large letterforms have proportionally more space around them and read as loose. Uppercase text at small sizes wants positive tracking, typically 0.05em to 0.1em, because capitals have no ascenders to distinguish them and the eye needs the help. Body text wants nothing at all, and a designer who has touched tracking on body copy is usually solving for the wrong thing.

/* Readability in three declarations, then the two that make it survive
   the reader's own settings. */
.prose {
  font-family: var(--font-body);
  font-size: var(--step-0);
  line-height: 1.6;
  max-width: 68ch;          /* measure, in characters not pixels */
  margin-inline: auto;
}

/* The text-spacing override (WCAG 1.4.12) must not clip content, so every
   height is auto and every length is relative. */
.prose p, .prose li { height: auto; }
.prose h2 { line-height: 1.2; margin-block: 2.4em 0.6em; }
.prose h3 { line-height: 1.3; margin-block: 1.8em 0.4em; }

/* CJK needs more leading and a different measure: no spaces to break on,
   so the browser breaks anywhere, and the eye tracks far less structure. */
:lang(zh), :lang(ja) {
  line-height: 1.8;
  max-width: 40em;
  text-align: initial;
  /* optional, and much better than nothing for long CJK passages */
  word-break: normal;
  line-break: strict;
}

/* Justification creates rivers of whitespace in narrow measures, which is
   why it is only ever safe at a wide measure. It is banned by default here. */
.prose { text-align: left; hyphens: auto; }

/* Numerals and identifiers need their own treatment: never justify a table. */
table { text-align: left; hyphens: manual; }
code, .mono-inline { hyphens: none; }

/* Wide glyph fallback: an all-CJK page with no CJK face falls back to a
   system font and the metrics shift. Declare the stack per script. */
:lang(zh) { font-family: var(--font-body), 'PingFang SC', 'Hiragino Sans GB',
            'Microsoft YaHei', sans-serif; }

/* Testing aid, not for production: prove the measure by rendering the
   guide characters. A line of 68 "n" is roughly the measure you set. */
.measure-probe { font-family: var(--font-mono); color: var(--muted); }

Justified text is the one setting here with a clear answer: do not use it on screen at a narrow measure. Justification stretches the spaces between words to hit an exact right edge, and the result is uneven rivers of white running down the paragraph, which is measurably slower to read. It is defensible in print at a wide measure with hyphenation, and the moment text becomes responsive it is the first thing to drop, because the moment the measure narrows the rivers appear. Setting text-align: left and hyphens: auto together is the combination that works on a narrow viewport.

Numerals deserve a separate note because they break more layouts than letters. Proportional figures make a column of numbers fail to align, so use font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums on anything numeric: tables, metrics, prices, timers. And never use a fixed height on a text container, because at 200 percent zoom or with a user-increased line height the text will clip. min-height on a control is safe; height on anything holding text is the bug.

Finally, the one that gets skipped: measure it on the devices people actually use. A 68-character measure is right at 1440 pixels and absurd on a 360-pixel phone, where the layout has to wrap to a single column and the measure falls to around 30 unless the type is reduced. Responsive typography that keeps the measure between 45 and 75 characters as the viewport changes is more work than shrinking the font at a breakpoint, and it is the version that keeps reading comfortable rather than merely fitting.

The readability trio — body size, line height, and line width — is set in three CSS declarations, with a tip for Chinese-heavy interfaces.

8.4 Fluid and responsive type

Fluid type scales smoothly between a minimum and maximum size as the viewport changes, rather than snapping only at fixed breakpoints. In code, the clamp function declares a preferred value with minimum and maximum bounds so headings stay proportional on small phones and never grow absurd on large monitors. Set the base body size per breakpoint and let headings scale from it on the same ratio. Fluid type keeps hierarchy intact across the whole device range.

/* Type scales in response: clamp = min, preferred, max */
h1{ font-size:clamp(1.75rem, 2.4vw + 1rem, 2.6rem); }
/* Semantic tags ≠ sizes: styling a <p> for a caption? Use classes.
   Header element with tiny size breaks the outline for readers. */

clamp, and why it beats a breakpoint per heading

Fluid typography sets a size as a function of the viewport between a floor and a ceiling, so the type scales continuously instead of snapping at breakpoints. clamp() is the whole mechanism: a preferred value, a minimum, and a maximum. Below the minimum the floor holds, above the maximum the ceiling holds, and between them the preferred value is interpolated. Because it is one declaration, there are no breakpoint-specific overrides to keep in sync and no awkward jump at the point where a heading crosses a threshold.

The unit argument is the part that matters. Use rem for both the floor and the ceiling, never px, because vw is a viewport unit and mixing rem with vw produces a size that ignores the user's browser font-size setting. That is the failure mode that quietly breaks zoom accessibility in a type system that otherwise looks excellent, and it is invisible in testing until someone sets their default to 24 pixels and finds the headings have not moved.

Do not fluid-type everything. Body text should scale with a clamp whose floor is the user's base size, and headings can be fluid. But the vw component should be small, because a large one makes the headline change dramatically between a phone and a laptop, and the headroom is better spent on the measure. The standard remedy is a rem-weighted mix rather than pure vw, so a portion of the change follows the user's setting and only a portion follows the viewport.

/* Fluid scale. Both bounds are in rem, and the vw term is rem-weighted, so
   the whole system honours the user's browser font-size setting. */
:root {
  --fluid-min: 16;    /* px-equivalent floor, read as rem inside the calc */
  --fluid-max: 20;
  /* 88rem is the viewport width at which the ceiling should be reached */
  --fluid-vw: (100vw - 20rem) / 53.75;   /* 320px .. 880px mapped to min..max */

  --fs-body: clamp(1rem, 1rem + 0.25 * var(--fluid-vw), 1.25rem);
  --fs-h1:   clamp(2rem,   1.6rem + 2.2 * var(--fluid-vw), 3.5rem);
  --fs-h2:   clamp(1.5rem, 1.3rem + 1.1 * var(--fluid-vw), 2.25rem);
  --fs-h3:   clamp(1.25rem, 1.15rem + 0.6 * var(--fluid-vw), 1.625rem);
  --fs-small: clamp(0.875rem, 0.85rem + 0.15 * var(--fluid-vw), 1rem);
}

/* Where the calc has to happen, modern engines read it directly; this keeps
   older ones correct rather than dropping the declaration. */
:root {
  --vw-rem: calc((100vw - 20rem) / 53.75);
}

h1 { font-size: var(--fs-h1); line-height: 1.05; letter-spacing: -0.025em; }
h2 { font-size: var(--fs-h2); line-height: 1.15; letter-spacing: -0.015em; }
h3 { font-size: var(--fs-h3); line-height: 1.25; }
body { font-size: var(--fs-body); line-height: 1.6; }

/* Semantic tags are chosen from the outline, never from the visual size.
   Utility classes carry the visual role so the two stay independent. */
.u-h1 { font-size: var(--fs-h1); line-height: 1.05; letter-spacing: -0.025em; }
.u-h2 { font-size: var(--fs-h2); line-height: 1.15; }
.u-h3 { font-size: var(--fs-h3); line-height: 1.25; }

/* Opt out for dense tables, where a fluid size would break the grid. */
.u-fixed { font-size: 1rem; }

Spacing should be fluid on the same axis, or the type will scale and the layout will not. The obvious mistake is a spacing scale in fixed pixels next to a fluid type scale: the heading grows and its margin does not, and the rhythm collapses into a wall. Derive the spacing tokens from a single ratio the same way the type scale is derived, and where a component wants a fluid gap, give it a clamp too.

Fluid does not remove breakpoints. A layout still has to change from a two-column grid to one, and that is a structural decision that no amount of type fluidity solves. What fluid type removes is the need for type breakpoints specifically, which is the category of breakpoint that exists only because sizes were hard-coded. Fewer breakpoints, each doing a structural job, is the outcome, and it is easier to reason about than a scale that changes at six widths.

The one place to be careful is a fluid scale whose floor is above the user's setting. If --fluid-min is expressed in px, or the clamp() floor is a hard-coded value the user's preference cannot move, then the type stops honouring the browser setting and the page silently breaks the accessibility requirement at the same time as it looks better. Both bounds in rem is the whole discipline, and it is worth a lint rule because it is invisible in review.

Clamp scales a heading between a minimum and maximum size, and the comments warn against misusing semantic tags purely for size.

8.5 Visual noise: hierarchy & restraint

Text hierarchy comes from subtraction: pick a small set of emphasis tools, such as size, weight, and color, and apply them consistently so relative importance is readable at a glance. Reserve strong emphasis for genuinely important content, and resist styling everything as bold or colored. If every element is emphasized, none is, and the page reads as visual noise. Restraint is what makes hierarchy legible.

Limit to ~3 emphasis tools at once (size shift, weight, color). Every bolded sentence cancels the others. Use color for links and flags only, not decoration, so the eye trusts it. And guard line length religiously — long lines are the silent assassin of reading.

Exercises 8

  1. Build a type scale from text: pick base 16, ratio 1.25, and lay out a "hero article" using only 4 sizes + weight.
  2. Take a text-heavy site and set max-width:65ch on its paragraphs; measure the reading-diffidence.
  3. Pair two system fonts (headings/body) for a mock brand page and justify both choices in writing.

Hierarchy by subtraction

A hierarchy works by telling the eye what matters through a small number of channels at once. If everything is larger than its neighbour, nothing is larger than its neighbour. The design question is not "how do I emphasise this" but "which of my three or four emphasis tools do I spend on this, and what does that cost me elsewhere". Every unit of emphasis spent is a unit no longer available, which is why the count of emphasis tools matters far more than the strength of any one of them.

Size is the strongest channel and should be rationed hardest. Three or four distinct body-adjacent sizes is plenty for a page; past that the reader has to read every line to work out whether it is a heading. Weight is second, and it fails quietly when overused because bold text looks like emphasis but reads as noise once a third of the page is bold. Colour is third, and it carries a semantic burden: if colour means anything anywhere in the product, colour everywhere is meaningless. Spacing is the fourth channel and the most under-used; white space separates things more reliably than any rule or tint, and it costs nothing to a screen reader.

Hold colour to a contract. If links are the accent colour, nothing else is. If success is green and danger is red, then no decorative element is either, and every coloured pill carries a word as well as a colour so it survives both red-green colour vision deficiency and a screen reader. The rule that colour must never be the only carrier of information is a WCAG requirement rather than a preference, and in practice it is satisfied by asking the counterfactual question: if this page were printed in greyscale, would anything be lost?

/* Hierarchy with three channels and no fourth. Nothing here is a decoration:
   every declaration is a claim about relative importance. */
.prose {
  /* channel 4, the cheapest and most reliable: space */
  --gap: 0.75rem;
  color: var(--text);
}
.prose > * + * { margin-block-start: var(--gap); }
.prose h3 { margin-block-start: calc(var(--gap) * 2.4); }

/* channel 1, size, rationed to three heading steps */
.prose h2 { font-size: var(--step-4); color: var(--text); }
.prose h3 { font-size: var(--step-2); color: var(--text); }
.prose h4 { font-size: var(--step-1); color: var(--text); font-weight: 600; }

/* channel 2, weight, used once per paragraph at most */
.prose strong { font-weight: 650; color: var(--text); }

/* channel 3, colour, contracted: links and status only */
.prose a { color: var(--accent); text-decoration: underline; }
.prose a:hover { color: var(--accent-hi); }
.prose .muted { color: var(--muted); }        /* never smaller, only quieter */
.prose .lede { font-size: var(--step-1); color: var(--muted); }

/* Status never relies on colour alone. The word is in the DOM, not in an
   aria-label, so it is announced and it is greyscale-safe. */
.badge { display: inline-flex; gap: 0.4em; align-items: center;
         font-size: var(--step--1); font-weight: 600;
         padding: 0.15em 0.6em; border-radius: var(--radius);
         border: 1px solid currentColor; }
.badge-ok   { color: var(--ok-ink);   background: var(--ok-soft); }
.badge-warn { color: var(--warn-ink); background: var(--warn-soft); }
.badge-err  { color: var(--err-ink);  background: var(--err-soft); }
/* the dot is decorative; the text carries the meaning */
.badge::before { content: ''; width: 0.5em; height: 0.5em; border-radius: 50%;
                 background: currentColor; }

/* The greyscale test, run once per release rather than argued about. */
@media (filter: grayscale(1)) {
  /* if anything becomes unreadable here, colour was carrying it alone */
}

The subtractive rule has a corollary that is worth stating separately, because it is where hierarchy usually fails. Emphasis must be scarce and accurate, not merely present. A heading level tells the reader that the following text is about a different thing, so a heading on every other sentence is a claim that the document has structure it does not have. If a paragraph needs emphasis to be read, the problem is the paragraph's length or its sentence structure, not the missing bold. The formatting is where a structural problem becomes visible, and the fix belongs upstream.

Within that, the strongest single tool is not visual at all. Order is emphasis. A short paragraph of eight lines reads; the same eight sentences as eight paragraphs reads faster, without a single additional style. Breaking a block into scannable units lets a reader who is out of time get the first sentence of each and stop with a defensible summary of the argument, which is exactly what they came for.

/* Hierarchy expressed as an ordering constraint rather than as styles,
   which is the version a code review can actually enforce. Each level
   declares how it differs from the one below, and the pair must differ on
   at least one channel or the step is invisible. */

const LEVELS = [
  { level: 1, size: '--step-6', weight: 700, color: '--text',   spaceAbove: 0,    rule: true },
  { level: 2, size: '--step-4', weight: 650, color: '--text',   spaceAbove: 2.4,  rule: true },
  { level: 3, size: '--step-2', weight: 600, color: '--text',   spaceAbove: 1.8,  rule: false },
  { level: 4, size: '--step-1', weight: 600, color: '--text',   spaceAbove: 1.4,  rule: false },
  { level: 5, size: '--step-0', weight: 600, color: '--muted',  spaceAbove: 1.2,  rule: false },
  { level: 6, size: '--step--1', weight: 600, color: '--muted', spaceAbove: 1,   rule: false },
];

// A step that differs from the one below on no channel is a level that does
// not exist. This is the check that catches the fourth-heading-size problem
// before it reaches a design review.
const CHANNELS = ['size', 'weight', 'color'];
const redundant = LEVELS.filter((lv, i) => {
  if (i === LEVELS.length - 1) return false;
  const next = LEVELS[i + 1];
  return !CHANNELS.some((c) => lv[c] !== next[c]);
});

if (redundant.length) {
  // fix by deleting the level, not by nudging its size until it differs
  throw new Error('invisible heading level(s): ' + redundant.map((r) => r.level).join(', '));
}

/* The greyscale test, as a screenshot diff rather than an opinion.
   Render the page, desaturate, and diff it against the colour render:
   a large delta means colour was carrying structure that size and weight
   should have carried. */

Test hierarchy by squinting, or by rendering the page in greyscale and at 40 percent zoom. Both remove the two channels that fake a hierarchy: colour and fine detail. What survives is what is actually there. Most pages that look busy pass this test and most pages that read as calm fail it, which tells you that the calm is coming from colour rather than from structure, and colour does not survive a screen reader or a printer.

9 · Color, Contrast & Visual Systems

Color in a product must be managed as a system rather than a mood: defined roles, a coordinated palette, verified contrast, and a dark mode that follows the same rules. Build the system once as design tokens so colors are named by role, such as surface, text, primary, and danger, then every screen reads from the same source. Verify each pairing against contrast standards before shipping. Solving color at the system level ends the endless manual tuning of individual screens.

9.1 Building a palette: base → brand → semantic9.2 Contrast math and the tools9.3 Dark mode done right9.4 Design tokens: the single source of truth

Color management is a system: pick roles, build a palette, verify contrast, support dark mode — then never hand-tune per screen.

9.1 Building a palette: base → brand → semantic

Build a color palette in deliberate layers: neutral grays for surfaces and text, a small set of brand colors for identity and primary actions, and semantic colors that carry meaning such as success, warning, error, and info. Neutrals do most of the structural work, brand colors stay focused on key actions, and semantic colors carry unmistakable meaning and must never be used decoratively. Define each color by role in tokens so usage stays consistent. Reserve color for meaning before decoration.

  1. Base/neutrals (90% of surfaces): text & background steps — 50 shades of gray that all can sit in light + dark.
  2. Brand/primary (actions, focus, brand moments).
  3. Accent/functional: success, danger, warning, info — chosen for meaning first.
  4. Add one "special" accent only if strategy demands (promo).

Resist decoration. Users read color as meaning ("red = bad"). If green and blue both appear as slightly-cool decorations, the meaning slots blur — and when a real error shows up, nobody knows.

Three layers, and what each one is for

A palette that works has three distinct layers, and mixing them is the reason most palettes cannot support a second theme. The primitive layer is raw material: a set of hues and a ramp of lightness steps, named by what they are rather than by what they are for, so something like a blue-600 exists and nothing refers to it directly. The semantic layer assigns those primitives to jobs: surface, surface-raised, text, text-muted, border, and the status colours. The component layer is where a specific component may override a semantic token, and the rule is that it must do so through a token, never by reaching past the semantic layer into a primitive.

Neutrals do most of the work and are the layer teams skip. The interface is mostly grey, and the quality of a product is legible in the quality of its greys: whether white cards are distinguishable from a grey page without a border, whether the muted text is legible or merely quiet, whether the borders separate or decorate. A good neutral ramp is not fifty steps. Ten is plenty, and a ramp with a clear naming scheme and an even perceptual lightness distribution beats a long one every time, because a long ramp guarantees that two adjacent steps are indistinguishable.

Brand colour is rationed hard. It marks primary actions, focus, selection and the wordmark, and it should be scarce enough that its appearance still means "this is the thing to do". A product where the brand colour is on every card, every icon and every link has spent the only signal it had. Where a marketing site needs more brand presence than a tool does, that is a legitimate difference between two products, but it is a difference in the token values, not in the components.

Semantic colour is where the discipline pays off, because these are the colours that carry meaning and users learn them. Success, warning, error and info should each be a distinguishable hue at both themes, each paired with an icon and a word, and never borrowed for decoration. The moment a green appears on a promotional banner, "green means good" stops being true in that product, and the error colour stops being noticed when it appears.

/* A neutral ramp generated in OKLCH rather than hand-picked in HSL.
   HSL is a polar space: lightness 50% is not half as bright, and a ramp
   built in HSL goes muddy in the middle and neon at the ends. OKLCH is
   perceptually uniform, so equal steps look like equal steps. */
const clamp = (v, lo, hi) => Math.min(hi, Math.max(lo, v));

/* Lightness steps are not evenly spaced: the darks need finer steps than
   the middles, because the eye resolves shadow poorly. */
const LIGHT = {
  0: 0.99, 50: 0.965, 100: 0.93, 200: 0.87, 300: 0.78,
  400: 0.66, 500: 0.54, 600: 0.44, 700: 0.34, 800: 0.24, 900: 0.16,
};

function neutralRamp(hue = 264, chroma = 0.006) {
  const out = {};
  for (const [step, l] of Object.entries(LIGHT)) {
    // a slight chroma floor keeps the greys from going dead on wide gamut
    const c = clamp(chroma * (l > 0.5 ? 1 : 0.6), 0, 0.02);
    out[step] = 'oklch(' + (l * 100).toFixed(1) + '% ' + c.toFixed(3) + ' ' + hue + ')';
  }
  return out;
}

/* The same ramp, generated as the dark theme's neutrals. Dark mode does
   not invert the light ramp: it re-maps it, so step 50 becomes the
   deepest surface and step 900 becomes the lightest text, keeping the
   same ordering rather than the same numbers. */
function darkRamp(hue = 264, chroma = 0.012) {
  const out = {};
  for (const [step, l] of Object.entries(LIGHT)) {
    out[step] = 'oklch(' + ((1 - l) * 0.92 * 100).toFixed(1) + '% ' +
                (chroma * (l > 0.5 ? 0.7 : 1)).toFixed(3) + ' ' + hue + ')';
  }
  return out;
}

/* Semantic colours are declared once per theme and solved against their
   own surface. A semantic colour that fails contrast on the surface it is
   actually painted on is a bug, and the check belongs here rather than in
   a review where somebody eyeballed it. */
const SEMANTIC_LIGHT = {
  '--surface':      'oklch(0.99 0.004 264)',
  '--text':         'oklch(0.22 0.012 264)',
  '--text-muted':   'oklch(0.46 0.012 264)',
  '--accent':       'oklch(0.48 0.17 255)',
  '--ok':           'oklch(0.52 0.14 150)',
  '--warn':         'oklch(0.55 0.13 75)',
  '--err':          'oklch(0.48 0.19 25)',
};
const SEMANTIC_DARK = {
  '--surface':      'oklch(0.16 0.012 264)',
  '--text':         'oklch(0.94 0.006 264)',
  '--text-muted':   'oklch(0.68 0.010 264)',
  '--accent':       'oklch(0.80 0.13 240)',
  '--ok':           'oklch(0.76 0.15 155)',
  '--warn':         'oklch(0.80 0.13 80)',
  '--err':          'oklch(0.70 0.17 22)',
};

Generate the ramp rather than hand-picking it, and keep the generator in the repository. A hand-picked ramp accumulates near-duplicates: someone needs a slightly darker border, adds a new hex, and from then on there are two greys that look the same and nobody knows which to use. Every near-duplicate is a future inconsistency, and the cost of preventing it is one script that anyone can re-run.

Two checks catch most palette mistakes before review. The first is contrast: solve every text and surface pairing against the surface it is painted on, in both themes, and fail the build on failure rather than noting it. The second is greyscale: render the page with saturation removed, and if any state is only distinguishable by hue, it has no non-colour signal and needs an icon, a border or a word. The second check is what stops a product from shipping a green success toast that is invisible to the two percent of men with red-green colour vision deficiency, which is exactly the population that includes a significant number of your customers.

/* The semantic layer, in full. Every colour in the product resolves to one
   of these names, and each name resolves to exactly one surface. This is
   the list a component author works from, so it is short enough to hold
   in your head. */
:root {
  /* structure, about 90% of what is on screen */
  --surface:          oklch(98%  0.004 264);
  --surface-raised:   oklch(100% 0     0);
  --surface-sunken:   oklch(95%  0.006 264);
  --border:           oklch(85%  0.008 264);
  --border-strong:    oklch(72%  0.010 264);

  /* text, two weights only */
  --text:             oklch(22%  0.012 264);
  --text-muted:       oklch(46%  0.012 264);
  --text-inverse:     oklch(99%  0     0);

  /* brand: surfaces and marks, scarce on purpose */
  --brand:            oklch(45%  0.16 252);
  --brand-hover:      oklch(40%  0.17 252);
  --brand-ink:        oklch(100% 0     0);
  --accent:           oklch(46%  0.17 255);   /* text that sits on --surface */
  --focus:            oklch(55%  0.19 250);   /* ring, must clear 3:1 on both */

  /* status: meaning, never decoration */
  --ok:               oklch(52%  0.14 150);
  --ok-soft:          oklch(95%  0.04 150);
  --ok-ink:           oklch(38%  0.12 150);
  --warn:             oklch(55%  0.13 75);
  --warn-soft:        oklch(96%  0.05 80);
  --warn-ink:         oklch(42%  0.11 65);
  --err:              oklch(48%  0.19 25);
  --err-soft:         oklch(96%  0.03 25);
  --err-ink:          oklch(40%  0.17 25);
  --info:             oklch(52%  0.12 240);
  --info-soft:        oklch(96%  0.03 245);
  --info-ink:         oklch(38%  0.12 245);

  /* code, its own theme because a code block is a text surface too */
  --code-bg:          oklch(97%  0.008 250);
  --code-text:        oklch(24%  0.010 250);
  --code-s:           oklch(32%  0.09 145);    /* strings */
  --code-n:           oklch(30%  0.09 25);     /* numbers */
  --code-k:           oklch(38%  0.14 300);    /* keywords */
  --code-c:           oklch(52%  0.01 250);    /* comments */
}

/* Status never travels as colour alone. The name carries it, so the badge
   survives greyscale, a screen reader and a colour-blind reader. */
.badge { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.4em;
         padding: 0.15em 0.6em; border-radius: var(--radius);
         font-size: var(--step--1); font-weight: 600;
         border: 1px solid currentColor; }
.badge-ok   { color: var(--ok-ink);   background: var(--ok-soft); }
.badge-warn { color: var(--warn-ink); background: var(--warn-soft); }
.badge-err  { color: var(--err-ink);  background: var(--err-soft); }
.badge-info { color: var(--info-ink); background: var(--info-soft); }

/* A thin bar as well as a hue, because the bar survives any colour test. */
.badge::before { content: ''; width: 0.5em; height: 0.5em; border-radius: 50%;
                 background: currentColor; }

The two-token rule that makes a palette survive. In this library, --accent carries text and is chosen for contrast against the page background: a mid blue in the light theme, a pale cyan in the dark one. --brand carries surfaces — button fills, the active sidebar row, heading rules — and --brand-ink is whatever reads on top of it, which is white on a mid blue and deep navy on a bright cyan. The split exists because the brightest colour in the brand artwork cannot carry text on white; trying to use one value for both jobs is why so many palettes end up with a button nobody can read.

9.2 Contrast math and the tools

Contrast is a measurable ratio between two colors, and under WCAG the guideline is at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text, 3 to 1 for large text, and 3 to 1 for UI components. Use contrast checkers and browser developer tools to verify every text color and focus ring against its own background before the design ships. Keep an approved contrast audit so designers and engineers both work from proven pairings. Verify each pairing rather than estimating by eye.

// Linearized luminance: L = 0.2126*R' + 0.7152*G' + 0.0722*B'   (sRGB)
// Contrast ratio = (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05)   [lighter over darker]
// WCAG thresholds:  4.5:1 text       3:1 large text & UI controls
// A tool (e.g. the WCAG contrast checker, or Figma's) computes it for
// you — but YOU must know the targets. Check BOTH your text and your
// focus ring against their backgrounds.

What is being measured

Contrast is a ratio between two colours, computed from their relative luminance, and the number runs from 1 to 21 with 21 being white on black. The thresholds are not subtle preferences: WCAG requires 4.5 to 1 for normal text, 3 to 1 for large text, where large means 18.66 pixels bold or 24 pixels regular, and 3 to 1 for the boundaries of user interface components and graphical objects. That last one is the one teams forget, and it is why a focus ring, an input border or the edge of a toggle has to be measured even though it is not text.

The formula is worth having in your head rather than looking up, because it tells you which lever to pull. Relative luminance weights the red, green and blue channels differently, approximating human sensitivity: green contributes most, red least. So two colours of identical "lightness" can differ in contrast substantially if one is blue and the other is yellow, and a designer choosing a tint by eye is systematically better at yellows than blues. Knowing that blue needs to be much darker to read on white explains most of the "this looks fine but the checker says it fails" moments.

Where to apply each threshold is the part that is a judgement rather than a lookup. Body text and its background need 4.5. A large heading needs 3, but since it is large enough to pass at 3, put it at 4.5 anyway and nobody has to reason about which rule applies. Muted text is body text and needs 4.5, which is why the most common contrast failure in a product library is the muted token: it is the first thing that looks optional and the first thing a disabled user cannot read. Disabled controls are formally exempt, and are also frequently unreadable, which is a legal position that a real user will not care about.

/* Contrast solved at build time, against the surfaces tokens are actually
   painted on. This is the check that stops a palette change from quietly
   breaking a dozen text colours nobody looked at. */
const srgb = (c) => (c <= 0.03928 ? c / 12.92 : Math.pow((c + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4));
const lin = ([r, g, b]) => [srgb(r / 255), srgb(g / 255), srgb(b / 255)];

function luminance(rgb) {
  const [r, g, b] = lin(rgb);
  return 0.2126 * r + 0.7152 * g + 0.0722 * b;
}
function ratio(fg, bg) {
  const a = luminance(fg), b = luminance(bg);
  return (Math.max(a, b) + 0.05) / (Math.min(a, b) + 0.05);
}

// WCAG 2.x. The 3:1 non-text rule (1.4.11) covers component boundaries,
// focus indicators and any graphic that carries meaning.
const TEXT_MIN = 4.5;
const LARGE_TEXT_MIN = 3;      // >=24px, or >=18.66px bold
const NON_TEXT_MIN = 3;        // borders, focus rings, icons, charts

function hex(s) {
  const h = s.replace('#', '');
  return [0, 2, 4].map((i) => parseInt(h.slice(i, i + 2), 16));
}

// The pairs that matter, declared once so the audit has a complete list.
const PAIRS = [
  { fg: '--text',        bg: '--surface',       min: TEXT_MIN,  kind: 'body text' },
  { fg: '--text',        bg: '--surface-raised', min: TEXT_MIN, kind: 'body text on a card' },
  { fg: '--text-muted',  bg: '--surface',       min: TEXT_MIN,  kind: 'muted body text' },
  { fg: '--accent',      bg: '--surface',       min: TEXT_MIN,  kind: 'link text' },
  { fg: '--brand-ink',   bg: '--brand',         min: TEXT_MIN,  kind: 'text on a button' },
  { fg: '--border',      bg: '--surface',       min: NON_TEXT_MIN, kind: 'input border' },
  { fg: '--accent',      bg: '--surface',       min: NON_TEXT_MIN, kind: 'focus ring' },
];

function audit(tokens, themeName) {
  const faults = [];
  for (const p of PAIRS) {
    const r = ratio(hex(tokens[p.fg]), hex(tokens[p.bg]));
    if (r < p.min) {
      faults.push({
        theme: themeName, pair: p.fg + ' on ' + p.bg,
        got: r.toFixed(2), need: p.min.toFixed(2), kind: p.kind,
      });
    }
  }
  return faults;
}

// Run for every theme, every mode, every surface. Modes are the part that
// gets skipped: a palette that passes light and dark can still fail in a
// colour mode nobody looked at, because a mode is a second palette.
const faults = [audit(LIGHT, 'light'), audit(DARK, 'dark'),
               ...MODES.flatMap((m) => audit(m.tokens, m.id))];
if (faults.length) {
  faults.forEach((f) => console.log(f.theme.padEnd(10) + f.got + ' (need ' + f.need + ')  ' + f.pair));
  process.exit(1);
}

Where WCAG 2 contrast stops being enough

WCAG 2's ratio model has a known weakness that matters for dark interfaces: it is symmetric, so it treats a light-on-dark pair the same as the dark-on-light pair, while human vision is not. A pure white on pure black scores 21 and is in practice uncomfortable and can cause halation for people with astigmatism. That is why neither theme should use pure black or pure white, and why the dark theme's text sits near 90 to 94 percent lightness rather than 100 percent. WCAG 3 proposes APCA, which models this asymmetry and lets a dark theme use lower ratios legitimately; it is not normative yet, so use 2.x for compliance and APCA as a design sanity check.

Three further limits are worth knowing, because each produces a false pass. Contrast says nothing about glare, so white text on a bright saturated background passes a ratio and is still painful. It says nothing about vibration, so a saturated blue on a saturated orange can pass at 4.6 and shimmer at the edges. And it says nothing about the surrounding field, which is why a small piece of muted grey text on white can measure 4.6 and still be hard to read next to a bold heading. Trust the number for the threshold; use your eyes for the judgement.

The workflow that holds up is therefore: solve the numbers in the token build, so the threshold is a gate rather than an opinion; then look at the interface in both themes at 200 percent zoom and in greyscale, which catches the things the number cannot; and then test with a screen-reader user and a low-vision user, which catches the rest. Keep an audit artefact with a date and a scope. A claim of "accessible contrast" with no record behind it is not a claim anyone can check, and the person who asks is usually the person you want to be able to answer.

Luminance and ratio formulas are the math; the real job is knowing the WCAG targets and checking both text and focus rings.

9.3 Dark mode done right

Dark mode is not the light theme with inverted colors; it requires remapping design tokens to a darker surface system while preserving the lightness hierarchy. Keep the darkest surfaces for the deepest backgrounds and lighter neutrals for raised elements, so depth still reads. Verify that text, backgrounds, and focus rings in both themes independently pass contrast requirements, and watch saturation so colors do not vibrate on dark surfaces. Both themes must work as their own designs.

  • Never invert — remap tokens: surfaces move with lightness hierarchy (darkest = deepest surface), text becomes near-white, accents lift.
  • Keep semantic hues intact; both themes must independently pass contrast.
  • Honor system preference + manual toggle, remember the choice, and prefer color-scheme so native controls match.
/* Light surfaces — token values only */
:root[data-theme="light"]{ --surface-1:#fff; --surface-2:#f6f7f9; --text:#1c2128; }
/* Dark: remapped tokens, never inverted colors */
:root[data-theme="dark"]{ --surface-1:#0d1117; --surface-2:#161b22; --text:#e6edf3; }
:root{ color-scheme:light dark; }

Dark is a second design, not an inversion

Automatic inversion is the standard first attempt and it is wrong in a specific, diagnosable way. It maps each colour to its complement, which preserves nothing that matters: it flips which surface is deepest, it turns a subtle border into a loud one, it turns a muted text into a prominent one, and it takes every accent into a hue that no longer belongs to the brand. The result is a dark theme that is technically dark and technically the same design, which is the worst of both. What a second theme needs is a re-mapping that preserves order while changing every value.

The ordering to preserve is the elevation hierarchy. In the light theme the page background is the darkest large surface and cards sit on it as lighter raised planes; in the dark theme the page background is the lightest large surface and cards sit on it as darker raised planes. That inversion of the elevation direction is the single thing that makes a dark theme feel right, and it is the opposite of what an inversion filter does, because an inversion makes the page lighter than the cards again.

Four values move, and everything else follows. Surfaces get darker and slightly desaturated, because fully saturated dark colours look like stains. Text moves toward near-white but stops short of it, at roughly 90 to 94 percent lightness, for the glare reason above. Accent colours lift rather than darken, because the same hue at the same lightness that reads clearly on white becomes murky on near-black; a mid blue has to become a pale sky blue to keep the same perceived contrast. And borders get closer to the surface rather than further, because in the light theme a border is darker than the surface and in the dark theme it has to be lighter.

/* Dark mode as a re-mapping. The elevation hierarchy flips; nothing else
   is inverted mechanically. Each theme declares all of its semantic values,
   so a missing one shows up as a hole rather than as a fallback. */
:root {
  color-scheme: light;

  /* elevation: page is the darkest plane, raised surfaces get lighter */
  --surface:        oklch(98%  0.004 264);
  --surface-raised: oklch(100% 0     0);
  --surface-sunken: oklch(95%  0.006 264);
  --text:           oklch(22%  0.012 264);
  --text-muted:     oklch(46%  0.012 264);
  --border:         oklch(85%  0.008 264);
  --border-strong:  oklch(72%  0.010 264);
  --brand:          oklch(45%  0.16 252);
  --brand-ink:      oklch(100% 0     0);
  --accent:         oklch(46%  0.17 255);
}

html[data-theme="dark"] {
  color-scheme: dark;

  /* elevation: page is the lightest plane, raised surfaces get darker */
  --surface:        oklch(17%  0.014 264);
  --surface-raised: oklch(21%  0.016 264);
  --surface-sunken: oklch(13%  0.012 264);
  /* near-white, not white: pure white on near-black causes halation */
  --text:           oklch(93%  0.006 264);
  --text-muted:     oklch(70%  0.010 264);
  /* borders now sit above the surface, not below it */
  --border:         oklch(32%  0.014 264);
  --border-strong:  oklch(42%  0.016 264);
  /* accents lift: same hue, much higher lightness */
  --brand:          oklch(72%  0.13 205);
  --brand-ink:      oklch(18%  0.02 250);
  --accent:         oklch(78%  0.12 235);
}

/* Shadows do not read on a dark surface, so depth comes from the surface
   step plus a hairline border instead. This is the single most common
   dark-theme failure: cards that vanish into the background. */
html[data-theme="dark"] .card {
  box-shadow: none;
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
}

/* Images and video need their own treatment: a white-background PNG on a
   dark surface is a bright rectangle. Two options, both correct. */
html[data-theme="dark"] img.auto-invert { filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg); }
html[data-theme="dark"] .media { background: white; padding: 1px; border-radius: var(--radius); }

/* Gradients and translucent fills must be re-declared: rgba(255,255,255,.1)
   is a light overlay and is invisible on a dark surface. */
html[data-theme="dark"] .overlay {
  background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--text) 8%, transparent);
}

Three areas break in a dark theme and each needs a deliberate decision rather than a token swap. Elevation works differently, as above: shadow-based depth has to be replaced with surface steps and hairlines, because a black shadow on a dark background is nothing at all. Media breaks because screenshots and diagrams assume a light page; either invert them with a filter, which is a hack that looks wrong on any image with colour, or give them a light frame, which is honest and costs a few pixels. Translucency breaks because a white overlay is invisible on a dark surface and a black overlay disappears on a light one, so every alpha value has to be re-solved against the theme rather than inherited.

Saturation is the perceptual trap. A colour that looks calm on white looks fluorescent on near-black, because a dark background removes the surrounding light that was damping it. The practical rule is to reduce chroma in the dark theme by roughly ten to twenty percent for anything that fills a large area, and to increase lightness rather than decrease it for accents.
