Where a brand colour is deeply saturated, the dark theme usually needs a different value of the same hue rather than a different hue, and if the brand team resists that, show them the two values side by side before the release rather than after the complaint.

/* The dark theme is a second set of values, and the set is checked the same
   way the light one is: every pairing solved against its own surface. This
   is the audit that catches "the dark theme passes but the dark theme's
   muted text does not", which is a real and frequent outcome. */
const LIGHT = { '--surface': '#fbfcfe', '--surface-raised': '#ffffff',
  '--text': '#182338', '--text-muted': '#5a6478', '--border': '#dfe4ec',
  '--brand': '#0b62c4', '--brand-ink': '#ffffff', '--accent': '#0b5fbf' };
const DARK  = { '--surface': '#0f1726', '--surface-raised': '#161f31',
  '--text': '#e8edf5', '--text-muted': '#a6b1c4', '--border': '#2b3850',
  '--brand': '#4fd0ff', '--brand-ink': '#05243c', '--accent': '#4dd2ff' };

const PAIRS = [
  ['--text', '--surface', 4.5], ['--text', '--surface-raised', 4.5],
  ['--text-muted', '--surface', 4.5], ['--text-muted', '--surface-raised', 4.5],
  ['--brand-ink', '--brand', 4.5], ['--accent', '--surface', 4.5],
  ['--border', '--surface', 3],    ['--accent', '--surface', 3],
];

function hex(h) { const s = h.replace('#',''); return [0,2,4].map(i => parseInt(s.slice(i,i+2),16)); }
const lum = (c) => { const f = (v) => { v /= 255; return v <= 0.03928 ? v/12.92 : ((v+0.055)/1.055)**2.4; };
  return 0.2126*f(c[0]) + 0.7152*f(c[1]) + 0.0722*f(c[2]); };
const ratio = (a, b) => { const x = lum(a), y = lum(b);
  return (Math.max(x,y)+0.05)/(Math.min(x,y)+0.05); };

for (const [name, tokens] of [['light', LIGHT], ['dark', DARK]]) {
  for (const [fg, bg, min] of PAIRS) {
    const r = ratio(hex(tokens[fg]), hex(tokens[bg]));
    const verdict = r >= min ? 'pass' : 'FAIL';
    console.log(name.padEnd(6) + fg.padEnd(14) + 'on ' + bg.padEnd(16) +
                r.toFixed(2).padStart(6) + '  need ' + min + '  ' + verdict);
  }
}

/* Neither theme should reach for the extremes. Pure white on pure black
   scores 21:1 and still causes halation and eye strain. */
const PURE = ratio(hex('#ffffff'), hex('#000000'));   // 21.00 - do not ship this
console.log('pure white on pure black: ' + PURE.toFixed(2) + ' (correct, and wrong)');

/* Respect the system, remember the choice, and default to the theme the
   pre-paint script already set on <html> so there is no flash. */
const KEY = 'amin360it-theme';
const system = window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)');
let saved = null;
try { saved = localStorage.getItem(KEY); } catch { /* storage blocked */ }

function apply(theme) {
  document.documentElement.setAttribute('data-theme', theme);
  try { localStorage.setItem(KEY, theme); } catch { /* nothing to do */ }
}
apply(saved || 'dark');
system.addEventListener('change', (e) => { if (!saved) apply(e.matches ? 'dark' : 'light'); });

Two token sets define light and dark surfaces, and a color-scheme declaration tells native controls to follow the operating system.

9.4 Design tokens: the single source of truth

Design tokens are named variables that store the atomic values of a design, such as color, spacing, typography, and radius, and serve every platform from one source. Engineers reference the token name rather than a raw hex value, so changing a token once re-skins the whole product consistently. Define tokens by role and group them into primitive and semantic layers for flexibility. Tokens make theme switching, dark mode, and cross-platform consistency practical.

// Tokens are NAMES="value" with a naming scheme that survives builds:
--color-bg-canvas:      #f6f7f9;   // role tokens: WHAT it's for
--color-text-primary:   #1c2128;
--spacing-md:           16px;
--radius-lg:            14px;
--easing-standard:      cubic-bezier(.2,.7,.3,1);
--space-space-2:        8px;       // alias tokens feed role tokens
// Delivering tokens (JSON) to iOS/Android/web = one source, all platforms:
{ "Colors": { "Brand": { "Primary": { "value": "#2563eb" } } } }

Three tiers, named by role

A design token is a named value in a file, and the whole discipline is in the names. The three tiers are primitives, which describe what a value physically is; aliases, which are a reference to a primitive and exist to make retargeting possible; and components, which consume an alias for a specific part of the interface. A component must never reference a primitive directly, and that single rule is what makes a theme a token swap rather than a refactor.

Primitive names carry the raw values. Semantic names carry the job. A button background is --button-bg and not --blue-600, and a link colour is --link and not --accent-500. The payoff is retargeting: rebranding means changing one alias, and every one of the four hundred components that consumed it follows, because none of them ever knew what blue was. The cost is that you now have two layers to keep honest, and that is the correct trade, because the alternative is four hundred components that know your palette and will all need auditing when it changes.

The second discipline is that a token means exactly one thing. --accent carrying text in one place and a fill in another is the bug that makes a second theme impossible, because the two jobs want different values and one name cannot hold both. Where a value genuinely serves two jobs with the same value, that is a real relationship and one name is right. Where they merely happen to match today, that is coincidence and two names are correct.

/* Style Dictionary is the usual builder: one source of truth, many
   outputs. The important line is the "include", because it decides which
   layer each consumer is allowed to see. */
module.exports = {
  source: ['tokens/**/*.json'],
  platforms: {
    css: {
      transformGroup: 'tokens-styled-dictionary',
      // components read these; primitives and aliases stay private
      include: ['tokens/semantic/*.json', 'tokens/component/*.json'],
      files: [{
        destination: 'public/assets/tokens.css',
        format: 'css/variables',
        options: { outputReferences: false },   // literal values, so the file is portable
      }],
    },
    ts: {
      transformGroup: 'tokens-typescript',
      include: ['tokens/semantic/*.json'],
      files: [{
        destination: 'src/tokens.ts',
        format: 'typescript/es6-declarations',
        options: { outputReferences: true },    // types that point at the css
      }],
    },
    ios: {
      transformGroup: 'tokens-ios',
      include: ['tokens/semantic/*.json', 'tokens/component/*.json'],
      files: [{ destination: 'ios/Design/Tokens.h', format: 'ios/macros' }],
    },
    android: {
      transformGroup: 'tokens-android',
      include: ['tokens/semantic/*.json'],
      files: [{ destination: 'android/colors.xml', format: 'android/resources' }],
    },
  },
};

/* The source, one tier per file. */
const PRIMITIVE = {
  'color': {
    'navy':    { '100': { $value: '#e8eefc', $type: 'color' },
                 '500': { $value: '#0b3f8f', $type: 'color' },
                 '900': { $value: '#04122e', $type: 'color' } },
    'cyan':    { '300': { $value: '#7ee4ff', $type: 'color' },
                 '500': { $value: '#00d1ff', $type: 'color' } },
    'neutral': { '0':   { $value: '#ffffff', $type: 'color' },
                 '100': { $value: '#f4f6fa', $type: 'color' },
                 '600': { $value: '#5a6478', $type: 'color' },
                 '900': { $value: '#111826', $type: 'color' } },
  },
  'space': { '2': { $value: '0.25rem', $type: 'dimension' },
             '4': { $value: '0.5rem',  $type: 'dimension' },
             '6': { $value: '0.75rem', $type: 'dimension' } },
  'radius': { 'xs': { $value: '3px', $type: 'dimension' },
              'md': { $value: '4px', $type: 'dimension' },
              'lg': { $value: '5px', $type: 'dimension' } },
};

// The alias layer: a job, pointing at a primitive. This is the only file
// that changes on a rebrand.
const SEMANTIC = {
  'color': {
    'surface':      { $value: '{color.neutral.100}', $type: 'color' },
    'surface-raised':{ $value: '{color.neutral.0}',   $type: 'color' },
    'text':         { $value: '{color.neutral.900}', $type: 'color' },
    'text-muted':   { $value: '{color.neutral.600}', $type: 'color' },
    // two names, because text and surface are different jobs with different
    // required values; they share a hue, which is not the same thing
    'brand':        { $value: '{color.navy.500}',    $type: 'color' },
    'brand-ink':    { $value: '{color.neutral.0}',   $type: 'color' },
    'accent':       { $value: '{color.cyan.300}',    $type: 'color' },
  },
};

Token naming should be mechanical, not descriptive of appearance. Names that include the value, like --grey-text or --blue-button, embed the current design in the name and guarantee a rename later. Names that include the job, like --text-muted and --brand, survive. Where a token is genuinely tied to one place, name it for that place, and if you find yourself with ten of those it is usually a sign the component has not been designed yet.

The other discipline is completeness. A theme declares every token it uses, in full, which sounds obvious and is the most common source of half-switched pages: a theme block that sets 34 of 35 values leaves the 35th falling through to whatever the cascade finds, which is usually the other theme, and the result is one unreadable token in an otherwise correct page. Generating the blocks from the token source removes the possibility, because a generated block is either complete or it failed to build. The same argument applies to the corner scale, the spacing scale and every other axis: a value that only some themes redeclare is a value that will eventually be wrong in one of them.

/* A completeness gate. Generated theme blocks can still drift if someone
   hand-edits the output, and the failure is invisible: one token reads
   from the wrong theme and looks like a design bug report. */
const REQUIRED = ['--surface', '--surface-raised', '--text', '--text-muted',
  '--border', '--brand', '--brand-ink', '--accent', '--code-bg', '--code-text'];

function readBlock(css, selector) {
  const i = css.indexOf(selector);
  if (i === -1) return null;
  const open = css.indexOf('{', i);
  const close = css.indexOf('}', open);
  const body = css.slice(open + 1, close);
  const out = {};
  for (const m of body.matchAll(/(--[a-z0-9-]+)s*:s*([^;]+);/g)) out[m[1]] = m[2].trim();
  return out;
}

const css = require('fs').readFileSync('public/assets/shell.css', 'utf8');
const roots = [
  [':root', 'base light'],
  ['html[data-theme="dark"]', 'dark'],
  ...MODES.map((m) => ['html[data-mode="' + m.id + '"]', m.id]),
];

let bad = 0;
for (const [sel, label] of roots) {
  const block = readBlock(css, sel);
  if (!block) { console.log('missing block: ' + label); bad++; continue; }
  const missing = REQUIRED.filter((t) => !(t in block));
  if (missing.length) {
    console.log(label.padEnd(12) + 'missing ' + missing.length + ': ' + missing.join(' '));
    bad++;
  }
}

// A palette block must not redefine geometry. A corner is not a colour and
// does not change with the theme, so a radius inside a palette block is a
// bug that makes one mode look unlike every other.
const GEOMETRY = ['--radius-xs', '--radius', '--radius-lg'];
for (const [sel, label] of roots) {
  const block = readBlock(css, sel) || {};
  const leaked = GEOMETRY.filter((t) => t in block);
  if (leaked.length) {
    console.log(label.padEnd(12) + 'redefines geometry: ' + leaked.join(' '));
    bad++;
  }
}
if (bad) process.exit(1);
console.log(roots.length + ' blocks complete, geometry tier clean');

Role tokens name what each value is for, and the JSON shows how the same naming ships the palette to every platform.

Exercises 9

  1. Build a 3-level palette (base/brand/semantic) and verify each text color passes 4.5:1 on all its backgrounds.
  2. Create the same UI in light and dark using ONLY token changes — find where you cheated and fix it.
  3. Define 15 tokens for your Ch.4 prototype and rebuild its colors through them.

10 · Design Systems

A design system is the shared, documented kit of components, design tokens, and usage guidelines that lets a whole team ship consistent UX quickly at scale. It codifies decisions so designers and developers both work from the same source, which speeds reviews and reduces drift between design and code. Adopt and govern it like a product, with owners, versioning, and a change process. Its biggest risk is becoming an unmaintained museum, so invest in maintenance from day one.

10.1 The four parts10.2 Building bottom-up vs top-down10.3 Governance: who maintains it10.4 Documentation that gets read10.5 Rollout, adoption & versioning

A design system = components + tokens + guidelines + governance. It’s how teams ship consistent UX at scale — and its biggest risk is becoming a museum nobody maintains.

10.1 The four parts

A design system comprises four interconnected parts: design tokens for atomic values, components as reusable building blocks, patterns for common interaction flows, and guidelines that explain when and how to use each piece, all tied together by documentation. Each part fails with a telltale symptom, such as inconsistent color when tokens are missing, duplicated controls when components are missing, and misuse when guidelines are missing. Learn each part together with its failure symptom so you can diagnose what is absent.

PartContentsFailure symptom
Tokenscolor, type, spacing, radius, motionscreens with 47 hardcoded hex values
Componentsbuttons, inputs, cards, alerts + states + usage rulesfive "almost identical" buttons
Patternsflows: validation, empty states, onboarding, authevery team re-inventing the empty state
Guidelines & docswhen to use/deprecate, accessibility owner, writing"there’s a swatch for that?"

Four parts, four failure symptoms

A design system has four layers and they fail in four distinguishable ways, which is more useful than a list of what each one is. Tokens are the atomic values, and their absence shows as inconsistent colour, spacing and radius across pages that were built by different people on different days. Components are the reusable building blocks with a fixed API, and their absence shows as the same button implemented eleven ways, each one slightly different, none of them accessible. Patterns are compositions that solve a recurring problem, like a data table with sorting, filtering, pagination and an empty state, and their absence shows as every screen solving that problem from scratch. Guidelines are the rules and the reasons, and their absence shows as components being used in ways nobody intended.

The ordering matters for diagnosis. Inconsistent colour is a token problem and no amount of component work fixes it. Eleven buttons is a component problem, and no palette will reduce it to one. A table that handles empty states correctly on one page and not on another is a pattern problem. And a system where every component is used correctly on the first try and badly by the fourth team is a guidelines problem. Diagnose before you build, because the treatments are different and building the wrong one is expensive.

Documentation is not a fifth part; it is the connective tissue. A system without documentation is a component library, and a component library is a thing people have to learn the hard way by reading the source. Documentation is what turns a library into a system, because it is the only place a rule and its reason can live together.

/* One primitive, four layers deep. The reason to separate the layers is
   visible in this file: adding a dark theme changed zero lines of the
   component, and adding a third palette means changing one alias. */
:root {
  /* 1. PRIMITIVE - what the value physically is. Nothing consumes this. */
  --prim-navy-500: #0b3f8f;
  --prim-navy-900: #04122e;
  --prim-cyan-300: #7ee4ff;
  --prim-white:    #ffffff;
  --space-2: 0.25rem;
  --space-4: 0.5rem;
  --radius-md: 4px;
}

/* 2. SEMANTIC - the job. This is the only layer a rebrand touches. */
:root {
  --bg-page:    var(--prim-white);
  --bg-raised:  var(--prim-white);
  --fg-default: var(--prim-navy-900);
  --fg-brand:   var(--prim-navy-500);
  --fg-ink:     var(--prim-white);
  --gap:        var(--space-4);
}

/* 3. COMPONENT - one control, overridable by a modifier, never by a
      component reaching into the primitive layer. */
.btn {
  --btn-bg:   var(--fg-brand);
  --btn-fg:   var(--fg-ink);
  --btn-pad:  var(--space-2) var(--space-4);
  --btn-radius: var(--radius-md);

  background: var(--btn-bg);
  color: var(--btn-fg);
  padding: var(--btn-pad);
  border-radius: var(--btn-radius);
  border: 1px solid transparent;
  min-height: 44px;          /* touch target, not negotiable per control */
  font: inherit;
  cursor: pointer;
}
.btn--ghost  { --btn-bg: transparent; --btn-fg: var(--fg-default); }
.btn--danger { --btn-bg: var(--err); }

/* 4. PATTERN - a composition. The table below resolves its own states;
      no product screen re-implements any of them. */
.data-table { display: grid; gap: var(--gap); }
.data-table__empty { padding: 3rem 1rem; text-align: center; color: var(--fg-muted); }

/* The rule this enforces, in one assertion per consumer layer:
   a component may reference a semantic token and a primitive of spacing,
   but never a colour primitive directly. */
const ALLOWED = {
  'component': ['--fg-', '--bg-', '--space-', '--radius-'],
  'pattern':   ['--fg-', '--bg-', '--space-', '--radius-', '--data-table'],
};

A useful way to test whether the layers are real is to change the primitive and see how many things break. If a designer can swap the brand navy for a green and the change is one alias edit, the layering works. If it is forty edits, the components were reaching past the semantic layer and you have a component library with a token file attached. The second shape is extremely common, and it is discovered by exactly this experiment, which takes five minutes.

The second test is whether components have fixed APIs, because that is the difference between a shared component and a copy of one. A fixed API means the same prop means the same thing in every instance, that new options are added rather than added-then-renamed, and that a component's visual states are enumerable and documented. Where components take arbitrary overrides, each consumer becomes its own component, and the system has quietly become forty components with a common ancestor.

/* A component with a fixed API, in full: markup, states, and the contract
   consumers rely on. Compare with an arbitrary-override component, where
   each consumer is its own component and the system has quietly become
   forty components with a common ancestor. */
<!-- Primitive: the smallest thing that cannot be made smaller. -->
<fieldset class="field">
  <legend class="field__label">Email address</legend>
  <!-- the hint is referenced, not just placed nearby: aria-describedby is
       what makes it announced, and placement alone does not -->
  <input class="field__input"
         id="email"
         type="email"
         name="email"
         autocomplete="email"
         inputmode="email"
         aria-describedby="email-hint email-err"
         required>
  <p class="field__hint" id="email-hint">We only use this to send your receipt.</p>
  <p class="field__err" id="email-err" hidden></p>
</fieldset>

/* States, all declared once so they cannot drift between components. */
.field__input {
  background: var(--bg-raised);
  color: var(--fg-default);
  border: 1px solid var(--border-strong);
  border-radius: var(--radius-md);
  padding: var(--space-2) var(--space-3);
  min-height: 44px;          /* target, inclusive of padding */
}
.field__input:hover:not(:disabled)   { border-color: var(--fg-brand); }
.field__input:focus-visible         { outline: 2px solid var(--focus);
                                      outline-offset: 1px; border-color: var(--focus); }
.field__input:disabled               { background: var(--bg-sunken); color: var(--fg-muted);
                                       cursor: not-allowed; }
.field__input[readonly]              { background: var(--bg-sunken); }
.field__input[aria-invalid="true"]   { border-color: var(--err); border-width: 2px; }
/* the error is announced through the live region, and the icon is
   aria-hidden because the text already carries the meaning */
.field__err { color: var(--err-ink); font-size: var(--fs-small); }
.field__err::before { content: ''; }
.field__input[aria-invalid="true"] ~ .field__err::before {
  content: '\26A0'; margin-right: 0.4em;
}

/* A pattern, not a component: a table that owns its own states. */
.data-table { display: grid; gap: var(--gap); }
.data-table__empty    { padding: 3rem 1rem; text-align: center; color: var(--fg-muted); }
.data-table__loading  { min-height: 8rem; }
.data-table__error    { color: var(--err-ink); padding: 1rem 0; }

The failure symptoms are the deliverable. When you propose a design system, do not lead with the token architecture. Lead with the symptom inventory: eleven buttons, four greys for the same background, three empty states, and the accessibility bug that every one of them shares. That document is instantly actionable, it is unambiguously good news, and it does not require the reader to believe in tokens. The architecture is the argument you make after they have already agreed with the diagnosis.

10.2 Building bottom-up vs top-down

Bottom-up building extracts components and patterns by auditing the interfaces that already exist, standardizing what is actually used, while top-down building defines tokens and primitives first as the source of truth. A robust system combines both: inventory real screens to learn the true content shapes, then encode them as tokens and components. A system designed only in the abstract dies the moment it meets real data. Let the audit drive what gets standardized and let top-down tokens hold it together.

Top-down (intended): brand team defines tokens → all components grow
 from them. Fragile: teams drift, tokens get bypassed.
Bottom-up (observed): audit existing screens → find the repeated
 patterns → standardize those as the first components. Then codify.
Best practice = bottom-up audit, then top-down tokens, then evolve
 components from real product needs. A system born from a figma-only
  "button page" dies on contact with real data.

Inventory first, then decide

Two methods, and the honest answer is that neither works alone. Bottom-up audits what already exists and standardises what is genuinely used; it produces a system that fits the product and it also imports every inconsistency the product had, unless the audit is explicit about what it is discarding. Top-down defines tokens and primitives from a design brief before looking at a screen; it produces a coherent system and it also produces tokens for things no product uses, which is the classic reason a system is half-built and never finished.

The sequence that works is inventory, decide, encode. Inventory means a real audit: every distinct colour in every production surface, every button variant, every spacing value, every radius, every font size, collected mechanically where possible rather than by eye. Then a decision pass, where each variant becomes either the canonical value or a documented reason for its existence. Then encoding, where the canonical values become tokens and the repeated structures become components.

The mechanical part is what separates an audit from an impression. Colour and spacing can be extracted from a codebase or a design file programmatically, which turns "we have too many greys" into "there are nineteen distinct background values and eleven of them are used once". That number changes the conversation, because a single-use value is not a variant, it is an inconsistency, and it can be changed without a migration. The values used thirty times are the ones that need a deprecation plan, and only those.

// The audit, run over a real codebase rather than described from memory.
// Output: how many distinct values exist, and how many places use each.
// A value used once is an inconsistency. A value used 300 times is a
// migration. Only the second kind needs a plan.
const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');

const HEX = /#[0-9a-f]{3,8}/gi;
const RADIUS = /border-radius:s*([^;]+);/g;
const SPACE = /(?:padding|margin|gap)[^:]*:s*([^;]+);/g;

function walk(dir, out = []) {
  for (const e of fs.readdirSync(dir, { withFileTypes: true })) {
    const p = path.join(dir, e.name);
    if (e.isDirectory()) { if (!/node_modules|.git|dist/.test(p)) walk(p, out); }
    else if (/.(css|scss|html|js|jsx|ts|tsx|vue|astro)$/.test(e.name)) out.push(p);
  }
  return out;
}

function tally(files, re) {
  const counts = new Map();
  for (const f of files) {
    const src = fs.readFileSync(f, 'utf8');
    for (const m of src.matchAll(re)) {
      const key = m[1] === undefined ? m[0] : String(m[1]).trim().replace(/\s+/g, ' ');
      counts.set(key, (counts.get(key) || 0) + 1);
    }
  }
  return [...counts.entries()].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]);
}

const files = walk('src');
const report = {
  colors: tally(files, HEX),
  radii:  tally(files, RADIUS),
  space:  tally(files, SPACE),
};

// The three buckets, which is the actual decision the audit exists to inform.
function classify(entries) {
  return {
    singleton: entries.filter(([, n]) => n === 1),        // fix freely
    moderate:  entries.filter(([, n]) => n > 1 && n < 20),  // needs a migration
    structural: entries.filter(([, n]) => n >= 20),          // a token, keep it
  };
}
const c = classify(report.colors);
console.log(c.colors.length + ' distinct colours');
console.log('  used once:       ' + c.singleton.length + '   -> alias and move on');
console.log('  used 2-19 times: ' + c.moderate.length + '   -> deprecate with a codemod');
console.log('  used 20+ times:  ' + c.structural.length + '   -> becomes a token');

console.log('\ndistinct radii: ' + report.radii.map(([v, n]) => v + ' (' + n + ')').join(', '));
console.log('top spacing values:');
report.space.slice(0, 8).forEach(([v, n]) => console.log('  ' + String(n).padStart(4) + '  ' + v));

Bottom-up has one more advantage that is easy to miss: it tells you which components actually matter. A button used four hundred times earns a component; a date-picker used twice does not, and building it anyway is how systems end up with an unfunded maintenance surface. Rank the audit by frequency and by cost-of-inconsistency, and build in that order. Cost matters as much as count, because one mis-styled checkout button costs more than forty mis-styled tag pills.

When you encode, resist the temptation to normalise every single-use value away. Some genuinely need their own token, because a one-off that is still deliberately different is a decision someone made. The test is whether you can state the reason. If you can, it is a token with a comment. If you cannot, it is drift and it should be aliased to the nearest canonical value, with the change made in a single commit so it is reviewable.

The other failure of a top-down-only system is designing for a hypothetical future. "We will need a dark theme, a high-contrast mode and ten colour palettes" is a reasonable ambition and a poor first project, because all three multiply the surface of every token and none of them is testable until a product exists that needs them. The pragmatic order is: ship light, encode it completely, then let the second theme force the layering to become real. A system that has never been asked to support two themes is a system whose tokens are decorative, and the first real theme is when everyone finds out.

This contrast makes the core design-system argument: audit what really ships before codifying, and let real product needs drive the system rather than a figma-only button page.

10.3 Governance: who maintains it

Governance is the process that keeps a design system alive, deciding who owns each component and how changes move through the organization. Give every component a named owner with clearly documented responsibilities and a change lifecycle covering proposal, review, versioning, and deprecation. Define how contributions from product teams are reviewed and rolled back, and track usage so abandoned patterns get retired. The system wins only when using it genuinely makes teams faster.

  • Every component needs an owner (design + engineering pair).
  • Change lifecycle: propose → sample → test → version → announce. Deprecate loudly, don’t delete silently.
  • Real adoption lever: the system must make teams faster. If using it is slower than hand-rolling, it loses.
  • Audit cadence: quarterly usage heatmap; prune the 30% of components nobody uses.

Ownership is the whole thing

A design system without a named owner decays within two releases, and the decay is not gradual. The first change is a small, reasonable local divergence: a product team adds a variant because their use case does not fit. The second is a pull request that changes the shared component and fixes three things for the requester and breaks two for the other four consumers. The third is a fork, because the shared version no longer serves the majority, and a fork is where a system loses permanently.

So every component needs an owner, and "the design team" is not one. An owner is a named design-and-engineering pair with a stated remit: they review changes, they answer questions, they are accountable when a consumer reports a defect, and they decide when a component is done. Where that accountability sits with a real person rather than a rota, changes get smaller and more considered, because the cost of a mistake lands somewhere specific.

The change lifecycle should be short enough to actually be used, and the proposal stage is where it earns its keep. A proposal is a small document: the problem in one paragraph, the proposed API, the accessibility contract, the migration plan for existing consumers, and what it does not do. Requiring that document is what stops a change arriving as a diff, because a diff shows what changed and not what breaks. Reviewing the document is fast; reviewing a diff that turns out to be a breaking change at step four of the review is not.

/* A component's contract, in one place. The accessibility contract is part
   of the API rather than a separate document, because a contract in a
   separate document is a contract that drifts. */
const BUTTON = {
  name: 'Button',
  owner: { design: 'ui-embed-1', engineering: 'platform-web-2' },
  since: '1.0.0',

  api: {
    variant:  { type: "'primary'|'secondary'|'ghost'|'danger'", default: "'secondary'" },
    size:     { type: "'sm'|'md'|'lg'", default: "'md'" },
    iconStart:{ type: 'IconName | undefined', default: undefined },
    loading:  { type: 'boolean', default: false },
    disabled:{ type: 'boolean', default: false },
    type:     { type: "'button'|'submit'|'reset'", default: "'button'" },
  },

  // The parts of the contract that are assertions rather than prose. A
  // consumer can rely on all of them, which is what a system means.
  contract: {
    keyboard: 'Enter and Space activate; nothing is focusable when disabled',
    name:     'icon-only buttons require aria-label; text buttons take their own text',
    states:   ['default', 'hover', 'active', 'focus-visible', 'disabled', 'loading'],
    tokens:   ['--brand', '--brand-hover', '--brand-ink', '--radius'],
    minTarget: '44 x 44 CSS px including padding',
  },

  // Deliberately not in the API, each with a reason, so the gap is closed
  // deliberately when it arises rather than by someone adding a prop.
  notSupported: {
    customColor: 'use variant, or brand tokens were going to be bypassed',
    arbitrarySize: 'the size scale is three steps; a fourth is a system decision',
    asLink:      'a link navigates and a button acts; use <a> for navigation',
    fullWidth:   'set width on a wrapper, so the component stays intrinsic',
  },

  lifecycle: {
    stability: 'stable',
    openIssues: ['loading state does not announce to screen readers'],
  },
};

// The deprecation path, which is the part teams skip and then regret.
// A silent removal is not a migration, it is an outage.
const DEPRECATED = {
  'outline': {
    since: '2.4.0',
    removal: '4.0.0',
    instead: "variant: 'ghost'",
    // count every consumer, then codemod them, then delete the prop
    consumers: 37,
    codemod: 'npx jscodeshift -t ./codemods/outline-to-ghost src/**',
  },
};

Deprecation is where governance is either real or decorative. The rules that hold: announce it in the changelog with a date, not just in the code; keep it working for at least one major version so consumers have a migration window; provide a codemod rather than a migration guide, because a guide produces forty-three partial migrations and a codemod produces none; and count consumers continuously, so "how many places use this" is a number rather than an opinion. A component removed without a deprecation cycle is a breaking change disguised as a tidy-up, and it will be discovered by a team that happened to be mid-release.

Track usage and prune, but prune carefully. A component with no usage for two quarters is either genuinely obsolete or genuinely hard to find, and the second is more common. Check whether it was used and abandoned, or never adopted because nobody could find it, because those need opposite responses. The measurement that matters is not component count but whether using the system is faster than hand-rolling, and that number has to be measured rather than asserted: time-to-ship for a screen built with the system against the same team's historical baseline.

// The usage heatmap that makes governance concrete. Run monthly: it is
// the only artefact that answers "is the system winning", and it is what
// turns "prune the unused 30%" from an opinion into a list.
const fs = require('fs');

function countImports(dir, re) {
  const counts = new Map();
  for (const f of walk(dir)) {
    const src = fs.readFileSync(f, 'utf8');
    for (const m of src.matchAll(re)) {
      const name = m[1] || m[2];
      counts.set(name, (counts.get(name) || 0) + 1);
    }
  }
  return counts;
}

const usage = countImports('src',
  /(?:import|from|require\()[\s'"\)]*(\w+)(?:\/|['"])/g);
// direct JSX/HTML usage, for components that are plain markup
const markup = countImports('src', /<([A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*)\b/g);

const registry = Object.keys(require('./component-registry.json')); // every component
const rows = registry.map((name) => {
  const uses = (usage.get(name) || 0) + (markup.get(name) || 0);
  const reg = require('./component-registry.json')[name];
  return {
    name,
    uses,
    owner: reg.owner,
    // the classification drives the quarterly decision
    verdict:
      uses === 0 && reg.sinceDaysAgo > 180 ? 'retire or resurface' :
      uses === 0                       ? 'undiscoverable: nobody can find it' :
      uses < 5                         ? 'too narrow: document or fold in' :
      uses > 100                      ? 'structural: needs an owner and a changelog' :
      'healthy',
  };
});

const structural = rows.filter((r) => r.uses > 100);
const dead       = rows.filter((r) => r.uses === 0);
console.log(structural.length + ' structural, ' + dead.length + ' unused of ' + rows.length);
// governance fails quietly without this: an unowned structural component
// is the next thing to diverge
const unowned = structural.filter((r) => !r.owner || r.owner === 'unassigned');
if (unowned.length) {
  console.log('UNOWNED STRUCTURAL COMPONENTS:');
  unowned.forEach((r) => console.log('  ' + r.name + ' (' + r.uses + ' uses)'));
  process.exitCode = 1;
}

Budgeting is the last piece and the one that decides whether any of this survives. A design system team that owns no roadmap and no headcount produces maintenance only, and a system that only maintains cannot grow, which means new product needs are met outside the system and the system slowly stops being the path of least resistance. Ring-fence capacity for both maintenance and roughly one new primitive per quarter, and make the ratio visible, because "we cannot afford a design system this year" is almost always a statement about an unbudgeted cost rather than about the value.

10.4 Documentation that gets read

Documentation works when it answers real use cases rather than dumping component APIs. Structure each entry around a scenario, show the component in all its states with correct and incorrect usage examples, and state the rule together with the reason behind it. Write decisions readably, with searchable names and short sections, so a busy designer or developer finds the answer in seconds. Docs that read like decisions get followed.

Docs must answer use cases, not API dumps: "Use a dropdown when there are 6–25 options; use radio when ≤6; use autocomplete when ≥25 or unknown". Show states (disabled/loading/error), the do/don’t pairs, and keyboard/ARIA behavior. Great system docs read like decisions, not reference manuals.

The fastest professional signal in an interview: ask "what’s your system’s checkbox vs toggle rule and why?" Candidates who have one are ahead of candidates who have a swatch.

Write the decision, not the reference

The most useful documentation for a design system is a set of decisions, and the least useful is an API dump. An API dump answers "what props exist" and none of the questions a consumer actually has, which are: should I use this or that, when do I need the escape hatch, and what happens if I get it wrong. A decision entry answers a question in the form the reader arrived with, states the rule, gives the reason, and shows both a correct and an incorrect example. That is three times the content of a reference page and ten times the value.

Write the reason, because the reason is what survives the situation changing. "Use a radio group when there are two to five options" is a rule a consumer can follow. "A radio group shows all options at once, which lets the user compare them without memory, so past about five it stops being a comparison and becomes a list" is a rule that can be reasoned about at seven options, and it tells the reader when the rule is about to stop applying. A rule with no reason can only be obeyed or violated; a rule with a reason can be applied to the case you are in.

Structure it so a reader lands on the answer in seconds. A page per component, named for the decision rather than the component where the two differ: "dropdown versus select versus autocomplete" is the page a consumer needs; "select.md" is not. Put the rule in the first two lines, before any preamble, because the reader who has to scroll to find the answer has already learned that the documentation will not have it. Then the states, then the do and do-not pairs, then the accessibility contract, then the API table at the bottom for the person who has already decided.

// Documentation as decision records. Each entry is a question a consumer
// arrived with, not a component name, so it is findable by the problem
// rather than by the artefact.
const DOCS = [
  {
    question: 'Radio, select, or autocomplete?',
    rule: '<=5 options: radio. 6-25: select. >25 or unknown: autocomplete with a fallback list.',
    why: 'A control should show what it can choose. Under 5 the user compares them ' +
         'at a glance and comparison is the task. Over about 25 the user is ' +
         'searching, not comparing, and scrolling a list stops being a scan. ' +
         'Autocomplete that hides the options removes comparison entirely, so ' +
         'it must never be the only way to see them.',
    doAndDont: [
      { ok: '// 3 options: radio, all visible, no interaction needed to see the choice',
        html: '<fieldset><legend>Plan</legend>' +
              '<label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="f"> Free</label>' +
              '<label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="p"> Pro</label>' +
              '<label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="e"> Enterprise</label>' +
              '</fieldset>' },
      { ok: '// 60 countries: typeahead, but the full list is one interaction away',
        html: '<input list="countries" name="country" aria-describedby="c-hint">' +
              '<datalist id="countries">...</datalist>' },
    ],
    a11y: [
      'radio groups need a <fieldset> and <legend>; arrows move between them',
      'a datalist is unreliable across screen readers, so the combobox pattern needs wiring',
      'never replace a select with divs; the platform control is free accessibility',
    ],
  },
  {
    question: 'Toggle, checkbox, or button?',
    rule: 'Toggle: a setting applies immediately and is reversible. ' +
          'Checkbox: a setting applies on submit. Button: one action, not a state.',
    why: 'The distinction is when the effect happens, and getting it wrong costs the ' +
         'user either a state they did not expect or a setting they cannot find. ' +
         'A toggle that requires a save button is a checkbox wearing a costume, ' +
         'and it teaches users that the control does nothing.',
    a11y: ['use role="switch" for a toggle, not a checkbox, so state is announced ' +
           'as on and off rather than checked and unchecked',
           'the label states the setting, not the action: "Email me about releases", ' +
           'not "Subscribe"'],
  },
];

// Docs are generated from this, so they cannot drift from the implementation:
// a rule that is not in the DOCS array is a rule that is not enforced anywhere.
module.exports = DOCS;

Every component entry carries the same four things, so the reader's eye knows where to look: states, keyboard behaviour, the accessibility contract, and at least one do and do-not pair. States are the most-skipped and the most costly omission, because a component that only ever shows its default state in the documentation is a component whose disabled, loading, error, empty and long-content states were designed by whoever happened to need them first. List them, show them, and the states exist whether or not someone designed them.

Make it searchable by symptom rather than by name, and make the entry titles be the questions. Most readers arrive with "should I use X or Y", not with "what does X do", so an entry titled for the comparison is found and an entry titled for the component is not. Where the two readings differ, the comparison is the file and the reference is a section inside it. A useful test is to search your own docs for the word "or" and see how many results you get; if it is none, the decision content is not there.

<!-- One documentation entry, in the order the reader arrives.
     Rule first, reason second, states third, then the do/don't pair the
     contributor actually needs. -->
<article class="doc-entry" id="doc-select">
  <h2>Radio, select, or autocomplete?</h2>

  <p class="doc-rule">
    <strong>2 to 5 options:</strong> radio.
    <strong>6 to 25:</strong> a select.
    <strong>More than 25, or the set is unknown:</strong> autocomplete,
    with the full list still reachable in one interaction.
  </p>

  <p class="doc-why">
    A control should show what it can choose. Under five options the user is
    comparing them and comparison is the task, so a list that must be opened
    adds a step for nothing. Past about twenty-five the user is searching
    rather than scanning, and scrolling stops being a scan. Autocomplete
    that hides the options removes comparison entirely, which is why it can
    never be the only way to see them.
  </p>

  <h3>States</h3>
  <ul class="doc-states">
    <li><strong>Empty</strong> — the placeholder must not be a valid value.</li>
    <li><strong>Selected</strong> — one option is the value, never the label.</li>
    <li><strong>Disabled</strong> — no placeholder, and the reason is on the field.</li>
    <li><strong>Loading</strong> — the control is busy, not just slow.</li>
    <li><strong>Invalid</strong> — aria-invalid, plus a message that says what to do.</li>
  </ul>

  <h3>Do</h3>
  <pre><code>&lt;select id="plan" name="plan"&gt;
  &lt;option value=""&gt;Choose a plan&lt;/option&gt;
  &lt;option value="free"&gt;Free&lt;/option&gt;
  &lt;option value="pro"&gt;Pro</code></pre>

  <h3>Do not</h3>
  <pre><code>&lt;!-- a div list: no role, not focusable, no keyboard contract --&gt;
  <div class="picker" onclick="open()">Choose a plan</div></code></pre>

  <h3>Accessibility contract</h3>
  <ul>
    <li>A native <code>&lt;select>&gt;</code> is free accessibility. Do not rebuild it.</li>
    <li>A radio group needs a <code>&lt;fieldset></code> and <code>&lt;legend></code>.</li>
    <li><code>&lt;datalist></code> behaves inconsistently; the combobox pattern needs wiring.</li>
  </ul>
</article>

Finally, documentation is part of the contribution process rather than a follow-up task. A pull request that adds a component without an entry is incomplete, the same way code without a test is incomplete, and the check is mechanical. The failure mode otherwise is documentation written once at launch and never updated, which is worse than none: it is confidently wrong, and a consumer who followed it will file a bug against a component that was never going to behave that way.

10.5 Rollout, adoption & versioning

Launch a design system the way you would ship software: pilot it with one team, dogfood it inside the organization, measure adoption by how many real components and tokens appear in production code, and version breaking changes so consumers migrate on a schedule. Treat adoption as a change-management and marketing problem as much as a technical one, with champions, migration guides, and incentives. Monitor usage and sunset stale versions to prevent obsolescence.

  • Launch it like software: pilot one team dark-ish, dogfood at scale, then measure adoption in code (does component usage in the product match design intent?).
  • Version breaking changes with migration guidance ("Button v2 drops the outline prop; migrate by Q3"), deprecate loudly, archive visibly.
  • Change is a marketing problem: demo recordings, "what’s new", migration guides. Teams adopt a system that makes them faster — track time-to-ship with vs without it, and you’ll never need to argue for the system again.

Measuring adoption, which is the only honest measure

Adoption is not the number of teams who said they would use it, and it is not the number of Figma files that link the library. It is the number of components and tokens that appear in production code, because that is the only place a design system either works or does not. Everything before code is intent, and intent is cheap; the moment a screen ships with a hand-built button, the system has an adoption problem regardless of what the library page says. So the measurement should be automated and continuous — a script that parses the repository and counts usage by component — and it should be reported as a ratio over the components that exist, because a system with 80 percent usage concentrated in the six easy components has not been adopted.

The ratios worth having are four. Usage coverage: what share of the system's components are used at least once. Prevalence: what share of screens use the system rather than hand-building. Fidelity: for screens that use the system, what share of their interactive elements come from it. And drift: how often a local override has been added on top of a system component, because a growing override count means the system is being worked around and the workaround is becoming the de facto standard.

Then pilot deliberately, and pick the pilot for what it will teach rather than for who is easiest. A pilot in one team that is enthusiastic proves nothing about a team that is not, so the second pilot has to be a reluctant team — and the resistance is the data. Ship it dark-ish: the system exists and the old patterns still work, so nothing breaks and the team can move at its own pace, and the measure of success is not the number of teams who say yes but the number of teams whose velocity stops falling. If a team can move faster with the system and does not, the reason is worth finding out and it is almost always something the system does not cover.

Versioning is where systems actually fail in practice, so the rules are worth being pedantic about. Breaking changes go in a major version with a codemod or a migration guide, never in a minor one, because a minor version that breaks things is how a team loses trust in the changelog and then stops reading it. Deprecate loudly: a console warning at build time, an entry in a "what's new" that names the removal date, and a migration path in the release note with a one-line example of before and after. Then set a removal date and keep it, because a deprecation with no date is a warning people learn to ignore, and a system with permanently deprecated components has two systems and one of them is unmaintained.

Finally, treat adoption as a change-management problem with a technical component rather than the reverse, and make it the cheaper option. Measure time-to-ship with and without the system on a comparable task, and publish it, because that single number ends the argument that the system is overhead. Appoint champions in each team rather than a central owner who becomes the support queue. Write the migration guide as a before-and-after a developer can copy, not as a description of the new API. And run office hours rather than documentation, because the reason a team hand-rolls a component is that they could not find the right one in the time they had, which is a discoverability problem and documentation does not fix it.

/* The four ratios. Coverage alone is the one teams quote, and it is the one
   that hides a system used only where it was easy. */
const ADOPTION = {
  coverage:   { measure: 'components used at least once / components that exist',
                trap: 'a system used only where it was easy reports 80% and has not been adopted' },
  prevalence: { measure: 'screens using the system / screens shipped',
                note: 'the honest one: intent is cheap, production code is not' },
  fidelity:   { measure: 'elements from the system / interactive elements, on screens that use it',
                why: 'a partly adopted screen is worse than an unadopted one, because it looks adopted in review' },
  drift:      { measure: 'local overrides added on top of system components, per month',
                why: 'a rising count means the system is being worked around, and the workaround is becoming the standard',
                action: 'treat each override as a gap report, not as a violation' },
};

/* Adoption measured from production code, not from Figma links or attendance. */
function measureFromRepo(repo) {
  const usage = {};
  for (const file of repo.sourceFiles()) {
    for (const m of file.matchAll(/<([A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]+)/g)) {
      const name = m[1];
      if (SYSTEM_COMPONENTS.has(name)) usage[name] = (usage[name] || 0) + 1;
    }
    // a hand-built control is an adoption failure regardless of the library page
    for (const m of file.matchAll(/<button class="btn-(?!\w)/g)) usage['hand-built button'] = (usage['hand-built button'] || 0) + 1;
  }
  const used = Object.keys(usage).filter((k) => SYSTEM_COMPONENTS.has(k)).length;
  return { usage,
           coverage: used / SYSTEM_COMPONENTS.size,
           handBuilt: usage['hand-built button'] || 0,
           // and the number that ends the argument, published quarterly
           velocityWithAndWithout: repo.compareMedianCycleTime({ tasksUsingSystem: true }),
           headline: 'teams moved faster with the system' };
}

/* The pilot. Pick the second one for what it teaches, not for who is easy. */
const PILOT = {
  first: { team: 'internal tool team', teaches: 'does the API cover the obvious cases?' },
  second: { team: 'the most reluctant team available', teaches: 'what does the system fail to cover?',
            why: 'an enthusiastic pilot proves nothing; the resistance is the data' },
  shippedDarkish: { systemAvailable: true, oldPatternsStillWork: true,
    why: 'nothing breaks, so a team can move at its own pace' },
  successMetric: 'velocity stops falling - not the number of teams who said yes',
  // the reason a team hand-rolls is that they could not find the right
  // component in the time they had, which documentation does not fix
  interventions: ['champions per team, not one central owner who becomes the queue',
                  'migration guides as copyable before/after, not API descriptions',
                  'office hours before documentation'],
};

/* Versioning. A minor release that breaks things is how a team stops
   reading the changelog, and then none of the rest matters. */
const VERSIONING = {
  semverMeaning: { major: 'breaking, with a codemod or a migration guide',
                   minor: 'additive only', patch: 'behaviour-preserving fixes' },
  deprecation: ['a console warning at build time', 'a what-is-new entry naming the removal date',
                'a before/after example in the release note'],
  removalDate: { rule: 'set it and keep it',
    why: 'a deprecation with no date is a warning people learn to ignore; and permanently deprecated components mean two systems, one of them unmaintained' },
  trustMechanism: 'a team that was surprised by one breaking minor release stops reading the changelog, and then the deprecation warnings are the only signal they get',
};

What actually blocks adoption, and what to do about it

There are four reasons teams do not adopt, and only one of them is usually discussed. Missing coverage is the respectable one: the system has no component for the thing they need, so they build one, and after a dozen such gaps the codebase is a mix and the system is a minority. It is a real problem and it is solved by adding components on evidence — treat each gap report as a ranked request with the requesting team attached, because a gap reported twice by two teams is a component and a gap reported once is a preference.

The unreputable one is developer experience. If using the system is slower than hand-rolling — worse types, an unfamiliar API, a build step, a component that requires twelve props to do something simple — a competent team will correctly route around it and the workaround becomes the standard within two quarters. This is not a discipline problem and cannot be solved by asking. It has to be solved by making the system the fastest route, which usually means prop counts that scale down rather than up, sensible defaults, and escape hatches for the cases the system does not cover rather than forking.

The third is no migration path. Teams do not adopt a system because a component exists; they adopt it when converting an existing screen is cheaper than not converting. That means codemods or at least a mechanical before-and-after for the common patterns, a list of screens that need no change at all, and a statement of what will break. A team with forty screens and no migration story calculates the work as forty screens and declines, correctly.

The fourth is ownership and support, and it is the one most often missing. A system with no named owner and no support route is a library, and libraries are adopted on a strictly need-to basis: a team uses one component when it happens to need it and hand-rolls everything else. Naming an owner with a response time, running office hours, and treating a bug report as a same-week commitment are what turn a library into a system, and the cost is a small permanent commitment of somebody's time.

Then the two questions the numbers do not answer. How does it feel: ask the teams using it, because the thing that determines future adoption is whether people enjoy working in it, and the enjoyment is affected by anything from documentation quality to whether a bug report gets answered. And what happens to the twenty percent: the leftover bespoke components are where the next generation of the system comes from, because a component that four teams have hand-built is a component the system should have. So the gap report is the roadmap, and a system that tracks its own gaps has an argument for its own continued funding.

/* The four reasons. Only one of them is usually discussed, and the second is
   the one that actually decides adoption. */
const BLOCKERS = {
  missingCoverage: { honest: true,
    symptom: 'a gap is reported, a component is hand-built, and after a dozen of those the codebase is a mix',
    fix: 'add components on evidence: a gap reported by two teams is a component, one reported once is a preference',
    track: 'a gap report queue, with the requesting team attached, ranked' },

  developerExperience: { honest: true, discussed: false,
    symptom: 'using the system is slower than hand-rolling - worse types, twelve props, a build step',
    response: 'a competent team will route around it, and the workaround becomes the standard within two quarters',
    fix: ['prop counts that scale down, not up', 'sensible defaults for the common case',
          'an escape hatch for what it does not cover, rather than a fork'],
    notFixableBy: 'asking' },

  noMigrationPath: { symptom: 'the team calculates the work as forty screens and declines, correctly',
    fix: ['a codemod, or at least a mechanical before/after for the common patterns',
          'a list of screens that need no change at all',
          'a statement of exactly what will break'],
    note: 'teams adopt a component, not a system; they adopt a system when converting is cheaper than not converting' },

  noOwnership: { symptom: 'no named owner and no support route makes it a library, and libraries are adopted on need-to basis only',
    fix: ['a named owner with a stated response time', 'office hours, not only documentation',
          'a bug report treated as a same-week commitment'],
    why: 'this turns a library into a system; the cost is a small permanent commitment of somebody\'s time' },
};

/* The numbers do not answer these two. */
const QUALITATIVE_ADOPTION = {
  howItFeels: { ask: 'the teams using it, not the champion',
    mattersBecause: 'enjoyment determines future adoption, and it is affected by documentation quality and whether a bug report gets answered' },
  theLeftoverTwentyPercent: { what: 'the bespoke components teams still build by hand',
    why: 'a component four teams have hand-built is a component the system should have',
    consequence: 'the gap report is the roadmap, and a system that tracks its own gaps argues its own case' },
};

/* The honest summary of what a system is for, which is not consistency. */
const SYSTEM_PURPOSE = {
  notFor: 'visual consistency, which is the outcome everyone asks for and the least valuable one',
  for: [
    'accessibility, done once rather than re-decided per screen',
    'correct behaviour in every state, including the ones nobody designs',
    'a change applied in one place and landing in every product that uses it',
    'the removal of the decision, so the team spends its attention on the problem',
  ],
  // the argument that funds it, and it is not aesthetics
  fundingArgument: 'publish median cycle time with and without the system, for comparable work',
};

Exercises 10

  1. Audit 3 real screens; list the 5 most repeated components and their inconsistencies.
  2. Spec one component end-to-end: states, tokens, keyboard behavior, accessibility, avoid-if-gap with a checkbox rule.
  3. Define the governance doc: owner, proposal template, and a release checklist for version N.

11 · Responsive & Mobile Design

Responsive design is not a desktop page that shrinks; it is a distinct discipline with different ergonomics, priorities, and interaction patterns for small screens. Because most traffic happens on phones in one-handed use, design for thumbs first, prioritize the essential content, and adapt typography, touch targets, and navigation to the device. Build mobile-first, then progressively enhance as the viewport widens. Test on real devices, not just resized browser windows.

11.1 Mobile-first progressive enhancement11.2 Breakpoints are about CONTENT, not devices11.3 Touch targets, thumb zones and fat-finger physics11.4 Responsive content is a UX problem, not CSS11.5 Mobile navigation patterns

Most traffic is thumbs. Responsive isn’t a stretch of the same page — it’s a distinct design discipline: different ergonomics, different content priorities, different interactions.

11.1 Mobile-first progressive enhancement

Mobile-first means styling the smallest screen first, then layering in complexity and content as the viewport widens at chosen breakpoints. The constraint of a small screen forces honest decisions about what truly matters, so essentials survive and desktop flourishes come later. Small screens often mean slower connections, so reducing assets improves speed everywhere. Start with the content a user most needs, then enhance upward.

/* Mobile-first: style tiny first, enhance upward */
.card{ display:block; padding:12px; }
@media(min-width:640px){ .card{ display:grid; grid-template-columns:1fr 2fr; } }
@media(min-width:1024px){ .card{ grid-template-columns:repeat(3,1fr); } }
// Why: constraint breeds honesty — you design the ESSENTIALS first
// (who, what, next-step) and add desktop luxury later, not the reverse.

Why the smallest screen is the honest one

Mobile-first is usually taught as a CSS technique, min-width media queries, but the technique is the least interesting part. The real argument is that a 360-pixel-wide screen with a slow connection and one hand forces the decisions that matter to be made first, and a layout that survives that constraint survives everything. The reverse is not true: a layout designed on a wide screen and squeezed afterwards is a wide-screen layout with parts removed, and you can see it in the way it behaves when the parts have to go.

Write the small-screen layout as the only layout, with no media query at all. If it cannot work at 360 pixels it does not work. Then add capability in layers: at each breakpoint, add what the extra room genuinely allows. The discipline is that each addition must earn itself. Adding a third column because the tablet has room is not a reason if nobody needs the third column; adding it because the comparison is the task is a reason. This is why mobile-first tends to produce fewer, better breakpoints: the base is already complete, so each query is a genuine enhancement rather than a repair.

There is a second benefit that is usually overlooked. A small screen is usually a slow one, so the asset budget it imposes is the budget every user deserves. If the phone layout ships 90 kilobytes of JavaScript and works on a throttled connection, it will feel instant on a desktop connection. If you start on the desktop and progressively enhance, you have already shipped the 400-kilobyte version to the phone user and the enhancement is a repair rather than a feature.

/* Mobile-first, no base media query at all. Everything below is additive,
   so each breakpoint has to justify itself. */
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

:root {
  --gap: 1rem;
  --pad: 1rem;
  --cols: 1;
  --measure: 100%;
}

/* Base: the small screen. One column, full width, single column nav.
   This is the layout that must work on its own. */
.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(var(--cols), minmax(0, 1fr));
  gap: var(--gap);
  padding-inline: var(--pad);
  max-width: 90rem;
  margin-inline: auto;
}

.nav { display: none; }              /* burger only, at the base */
.burger { display: inline-flex; min-height: 44px; min-width: 44px;
          align-items: center; justify-content: center; }

/* 34rem: two columns, and the moment the measure gets comfortable for
   body text. Note this is chosen from the content, not from a device. */
@media (min-width: 34rem) {
  :root { --cols: 2; --gap: 1.5rem; --pad: 1.5rem; }
}

/* 60rem: the sidebar appears, and the content column stops stretching. */
@media (min-width: 60rem) {
  :root { --cols: 1; }
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 17rem minmax(0, 1fr); }
  .nav { display: flex; }
  .burger { display: none; }
  .prose { max-width: 70ch; }
}

/* 90rem: nothing is added. The layout is already at its maximum useful
   width, and growing the container past this adds whitespace, not
   information. That is what the breakpoint is for. */

/* Progressive enhancement for capability, not layout. */
@supports (container-type: inline-size) {
  .card { container-type: inline-size; }
  @container (min-width: 24rem) {
    .card { grid-template-columns: 8rem 1fr; }
  }
}

/* The mobile-first discipline, checkable: a base query that sets
   max-width is the smell. If the base hides something, the base
   layout is incomplete and the page is broken without JS. */
@layer base, layout, components, utilities;

The corresponding rule for content is progressive disclosure, and it is a content decision rather than a CSS one. On the small screen, show what the user needs to decide, and let the detail be one interaction away. A product page with the specification table collapsed behind "See full specifications" is not hiding anything, because nobody decides on the specification alone. The test is whether the small-screen version answers the question the user arrived with; if it does not, the content was cut rather than deferred.

Two things must never be conditional on viewport. Content that only appears at a wider breakpoint is missing on the phone, which is a bug rather than a simplification, and the usual instances are a phone number, an address, a legal line, and the primary action. And a layout shift between breakpoints means something is loading late, so reserve the space with aspect-ratio on images and explicit dimensions, because a shift on a phone means the tap the user aimed at the button lands on something else.

Write the base CSS so it is genuinely the small layout. Not "the small layout with the sidebar hidden behind a class that only the large query removes". The reason is not aesthetic: a base that contains large-screen rules is a base that has to be overridden, and overrides are where the bugs live. If the first line of your first media query is a reset for something your base set up for wide screens, the base was never the small layout.

A mobile-first cascade: build the tiny layout first, then layer columns and grids at wider breakpoints so essential content comes first and desktop gets added comfort.

11.2 Breakpoints are about CONTENT, not devices

Breakpoints should be chosen where your content starts to break, not named after specific devices that change yearly. Resize the window continuously and note the widths where text becomes cramped, taps get too small, or layouts collapse, then set ranges that reshape the layout smoothly. Test across a spectrum of widths and between breakpoints rather than only a few named phones. Content-driven breakpoints stay robust as hardware shifts.

BreakpointLayout shifts
< 480pxsingle column, stacked actions, bottom nav candidates
480– 7px2-col grids, thumb buttons still full-width
 8–1023pxsidebar/nav appears, click targets shrink safely
≥ 1024pxmulti-column, hover states become safe to rely on

Never design "for iPhone 16 any more than for 'the 2nd monitor to the right'" — resize the window and test ranges, not devices.

Breakpoints are answers to a content question

A breakpoint exists because something stops working at a particular width. That something is observable: a paragraph falls below about forty characters, two navigation items wrap onto two lines, a table cell holds a single word per line, a card's image crops to something meaningless. The correct method is to find those widths rather than to choose them, which means you need a range of widths to look at rather than three named devices.

Device widths are a moving target, which is the argument against naming them, but the deeper problem is that a device is not a layout condition. A 390-pixel-wide window is a phone, a small tablet window, a split-screen app, a browser devtools panel beside a preview, and a 27-inch monitor with a sidebar open. The layout has to work at all of them, and only one of those is a phone. Naming breakpoints after devices bakes in an assumption about what the width means, and the assumption is wrong the moment someone resizes.

Use two kinds of breakpoint and keep them separate. Layout breakpoints come from the grid: the widths at which a column becomes too narrow to hold its content. Fluid handles everything between them, so there should be few of these. Content breakpoints come from the text: the width at which the measure leaves the 45-to-75 character range, or the width at which a card needs a different internal layout. Where you can express a change as fluid, do, because fluid needs no query and therefore no maintenance.

/* Finding the breakpoints by measuring instead of guessing. Run this and
   read the output; the numbers in the media queries below came from it. */
const MEASURE_MIN = 45, MEASURE_MAX = 75;   // characters per line, readable
const CHARS_PER_INCH_AT_16PX = 8.6;          // average advance width for body text

function breakpointsFor({
  maxContentWidthIn = 16,      // how wide the content column may grow
  columns,                     // grid columns at full width
  gutterIn = 1.5,
  minCardIn = 14,              // below this a card's text is unreadable
  padIn = 1.5,
}) {
  const found = new Set();
  // 1. the content column: where does the measure stop fitting?
  for (let w = 20; w <= 140; w += 1) {
    const chars = w * CHARS_PER_INCH_AT_16PX;
    if (chars < MEASURE_MIN) found.add('measure too short at ' + w + 'in');
  }
  // 2. the grid: where does a column stop holding content?
  for (let cols = 2; cols <= columns; cols++) {
    const colIn = (maxContentWidthIn - gutterIn * (cols - 1)) / cols;
    // the width at which this column count first becomes viable
    found.add(cols + ' cols needs >= ' + Math.ceil(colIn * cols + gutterIn * (cols - 1)) + 'in');
    if (colIn < minCardIn) found.add(cols + ' cols too narrow (' + colIn.toFixed(1) + 'in)');
  }
  return [...found];
}
console.log(breakpointsFor({ columns: 3 }));

/* The result, expressed as content conditions. Note that none of these
   numbers is a device width. */
:root { --gap: 1rem; --pad: 1rem; }

@media (min-width: 34rem) {          /* a two-column card grid becomes viable */
  :root { --gap: 1.5rem; --pad: 1.5rem; }
}
@media (min-width: 48rem) {          /* the sidebar plus a comfortable measure */
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 14rem minmax(0, 1fr); }
}
@media (min-width: 72rem) {          /* three columns, and the max width */
  .grid-3 { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr)); }
}

/* Fluid everywhere else: no query needed, no device named. */
.prose { max-width: min(100%, 68ch); }              /* measure, fluid */
.card  { flex: 1 1 clamp(14rem, 30%, 22rem); }      /* flex, fluid */

/* Test between the breakpoints, not only at them. A bug that exists at
   37rem is invisible if you only look at 34rem and 48rem. */

Test the spectrum, not the endpoints, because a breakpoint only defines what happens at and beyond itself, not what happens on the way there. Open the layout at the smallest width, drag continuously to the largest, and watch for the failures that only appear in between: a card grid that has two columns and a half at 41rem, which reads as a bug rather than as a transition; a heading that wraps to three lines at a width where it wrapped to one at the last breakpoint; a sticky header that covers the first line of content. Those in-between states are most of what users actually experience, because most users are not resizing, they are opening a window at whatever width their display gives them.

Container queries are the modern answer to the same problem, and they change what a breakpoint means. A media query asks what the viewport is, which is the wrong question for a component that appears in a sidebar, a main column and a modal at the same viewport size. A container query asks what space the component has, so one card component lays out correctly in all three without a single modifier. If the components in your system can be given container types, prefer container queries for component-internal layout and keep media queries for page-level structure only. The distinction is that page structure genuinely depends on the viewport while component layout genuinely depends on the container.

/* Container queries: the component asks about its own space, so the same
   component is correct in a sidebar, a main column and a modal. */
.card-host { container-type: inline-size; container-name: card; }

.card {
  display: grid;
  gap: 0.75rem;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr);   /* narrow: stacked, always correct */
}
/* the container query, not the media query, decides when to go side by side */
@container card (min-width: 22rem) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 8rem minmax(0, 1fr); align-items: start; }
  .card__media { aspect-ratio: 4 / 3; }
}
@container card (min-width: 34rem) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 12rem minmax(0, 1fr); }
  .card__title { font-size: var(--step-1); }
}

/* Page-level structure still uses media queries, because it genuinely does
   depend on the viewport. The two never overlap in purpose. */
@media (min-width: 60rem) {
  .shell { grid-template-columns: 17rem minmax(0, 1fr); }
}

/* Guard against the container being unstyled in an engine without support:
   @container rules that never apply leave the base styles, which are
   complete, so there is nothing to polyfill. The base is the layout. */

11.3 Touch targets, thumb zones and fat-finger physics

Touch ergonomics demand tappable targets of at least 44 by 44 pixels, with spacing between targets so one errant finger does not trigger the neighbor. Place primary actions within the thumb’s natural reach, keep destructive actions in harder-to-reach zones, and leave margin on screen edges where gestures are hard to perform. Touch changes ergonomics everywhere, so test with real fingers on real devices. Fat fingers fail silently, so give every target room to miss.

/* The ergonomics checklist */
- targets: 44×44px min (WCAG 2.2 AAA); 48px is the safe habit
- gaps ≥ 8px between tappable neighbors (avoids misfires)  — UNABLE
- thumb zone: placing primaries in the bottom half on one-hand grip
- sticky primary actions on forms (never make reach happen every time)
- hover = fallback: on touch, the "hover" IS the first tap → never
  put critical actions behind hover-only (Ch.5.5 lesson)
// same touch rules apply to the cancel button too
button.cancel{ margin-bottom:8px; min-height:44px; }

Targets, spacing, and where the hand actually is

Touch fails in a specific and physical way: the fingertip is roughly eight to nine millimetres across, its contact patch is imprecise, and it occludes what it is touching. So a control that is technically large can still be missed, and the number that matters is not only the target size but the gap between adjacent targets. The working figures are 44 by 44 CSS pixels as a comfortable minimum, and WCAG 2.5.8 requires 24 by 24 with a spacing exception, which is the accessible floor rather than the comfortable one. Hit both: 44 for comfort, and never put two targets closer than 8 pixels apart.

Where the target sits matters as much as its size. One-handed use on a large phone puts roughly the lower two-thirds of the screen within easy reach and the top edge out of comfortable range, which inverts most desktop habits: the primary action belongs low, secondary actions belong high, and anything destructive belongs in the hardest place to reach, or behind a confirmation, or both. A form whose submit button is in the top-right corner is a form designed by someone who has never held a phone in one hand.

Also worth knowing: an input with a font size under 16 pixels makes iOS Safari zoom the page on focus, and that zoom does not reset when the field loses focus. The result is a user who types one character, is thrown into a zoomed viewport, finishes the field, and is still zoomed in for the rest of the form. Setting font-size: 16px or larger on inputs is not a typography preference; it is a bug fix.

/* Touch ergonomics, expressed as CSS so it cannot regress. */
:root {
  --tap: 44px;              /* comfortable target, both axes */
  --tap-min: 24px;          /* WCAG 2.5.8 floor */
  --tap-gap: 8px;           /* the spacing exception, used deliberately */
}

/* Every interactive element gets the floor without anyone remembering. */
button, [role="button"], a.btn, input[type="checkbox"] + label,
input[type="radio"] + label, summary {
  min-height: var(--tap);
  min-width: var(--tap);
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 0.5em;
  /* the visible box may be smaller than the target; the target is padded */
  padding-block: 0.5rem;
  padding-inline: 0.75rem;
  touch-action: manipulation;   /* kills the 300ms double-tap delay */
  -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent;  /* and the grey flash */
}

/* Inline links inside prose are exempt from the target size, because a
   44px-tall inline link breaks the line box. Give them vertical padding
   instead, and horizontal clearance. */
.prose a {
  padding-block: 0.25em;
  margin-inline: -0.25em;      /* the padding is inside the line box */
}

/* Inputs: 16px is a functional requirement on iOS, not a style choice. */
input, select, textarea {
  font-size: max(1rem, 16px);
  min-height: var(--tap);
  padding: 0.5rem 0.75rem;
  border-radius: var(--radius-md);
}

/* Density on small screens: a 44px row is comfortable, a 32px row is a
   list, and a 24px row is a mistake. Pick one per context, not per whim. */
.list--compact > li > a { min-height: 44px; }   /* rows, not chips */

/* Thumb zone. The sticky action bar sits at the bottom, and the content
   gets bottom padding so the bar never covers the last field. */
.action-bar {
  position: sticky;
  bottom: 0;
  display: flex;
  gap: var(--tap-gap);
  padding: 0.75rem var(--pad) calc(0.75rem + env(safe-area-inset-bottom));
  background: var(--bg-raised);
  border-top: 1px solid var(--border);
}
body:has(.action-bar) { padding-bottom: 5rem; }

/* Edge margins. A target flush against the screen edge is harder to hit
   because the hand has to approach at an angle. */
.page { padding-inline: max(1rem, env(safe-area-inset-left)); }

/* Audit: fail the build if any interactive element is under the floor.
   Run on a real device profile; emulated touch is not touch. */

Gestures need a visible alternative, which is both a WCAG requirement and a plain usability requirement, because a gesture is invisible on the screen. Anything reachable by swipe, pinch or long-press needs a button that does the same thing. Long-press in particular is used for a whole category of actions that no user will ever discover, and putting them behind a button in a visible overflow menu converts an undiscoverable feature into a discoverable one for free.

And the honest test: use it on a real device, with a real hand, while doing something else. Screens that pass every automated check and every desktop review still fail because the dismiss button is 18 pixels and sits under the thumb that was already reaching for the tab bar. A one-handed, distracted, twenty-second walkthrough finds those in a way that no checklist does, and it takes about two minutes.
