A checklist for one-handed use — sized targets, thumb-zone primaries, sticky actions — plus the CSS that keeps a cancel button touch-friendly.

11.4 Responsive content is a UX problem, not CSS

The real challenges of small screens are content problems more than styling problems, because text, tables, and forms do the actual work. On mobile, reveal progressively what matters, flatten tables into stacked cards, and rebuild forms as touch-friendly single-column flows with large inputs. Shorten copy so it does not dominate the screen, and reorder content by importance rather than cramming everything in. These decisions matter more than any CSS technique.

  • Reveal progressively: mobile shows the meaning; details expand or wait.
  • Tables: stack into cards on small screens (never let 7 columns scroll horizontally as UX).
  • Forms: one field per row, primary action fixed to thumb; inputs preserve context on focus (iOS zoom fight).
  • Images and video resize without layout shift (aspect-ratio + width/height attrs).

Tables are the hard part, and they are a content decision

The genuinely difficult small-screen problems are content problems, not layout problems. Text reflows. Images scale. Grids collapse. A table does not, because a table is a two-dimensional structure and the phone viewport is one-dimensional wide. Every technique below is a way of losing information deliberately, which means the design question is always "what do we keep", and that has to be answered per table rather than by a generic card transformation.

Three transformations, in increasing order of loss. Horizontal scroll loses the least and feels the worst: the user cannot see that there are more columns, and they discover it by trying. Add a visible affordance and a sticky first column and it becomes acceptable for genuinely wide tables. Column priority loses the columns you declare unimportant, which is honest if you have decided what matters, and dishonest if the CSS picked. Card stacking loses the comparison across a row, which for a data table is often the entire point, so it works for lists of records rather than for a table people read across.

The content discipline underneath all three: on a small screen, a table should show fewer rows and let the user act on one row rather than comparing many. Comparing is a wide-screen task. On a phone the task is almost always "find my one thing and act on it", so the design that wins is the one that serves one row well and makes the rest reachable, not the one that preserves the grid.

/* Three table strategies, chosen per table rather than globally. */

/* 1. Horizontal scroll with an affordance. Keeps every column, loses the
   overview. Minimum viable for a genuinely wide table. */
.table-scroll {
  overflow-x: auto;
  overscroll-behavior-x: contain;   /* no page-level scroll chaining */
  -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
  position: relative;
}
/* the shadow on the edge is the only signal the user gets that more
   columns exist, so it has to be there */
.table-scroll[data-overflow="right"]::after {
  content: ''; position: absolute; inset-block: 0; right: 0; width: 2rem;
  background: linear-gradient(to left, var(--bg-raised), transparent);
  pointer-events: none;
}

/* 2. Column priority, declared per table rather than by column count. */
@media (max-width: 40rem) {
  .data-table th:nth-child(n+4),
  .data-table td:nth-child(n+4) { display: none; }
  .data-table[data-priority="status-last"] th:nth-child(3),
  .data-table[data-priority="status-last"] td:nth-child(3) { display: none; }
  /* the hidden column's content is still reachable, on the detail view */
}

/* 3. Card stacking, for lists of records rather than comparison tables.
   Every cell becomes a labelled row, which is what makes it readable
   rather than a wall of unlabelled values. */
@media (max-width: 40rem) {
  .cards thead { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px;
                 overflow: hidden; clip-path: inset(50%); }
  .cards tr {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) auto;
    gap: 0.25rem 0.75rem;
    padding: 1rem;
    border: 1px solid var(--border);
    border-radius: var(--radius-lg);
    margin-block-end: 0.75rem;
  }
  .cards td { display: contents; }        /* td becomes a grid child */
  .cards td::before {
    content: attr(data-label);
    font-size: var(--step--1);
    color: var(--fg-muted);
    grid-column: 1;
  }
  .cards td[data-label="Status"] { grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1 / span 2;
                                   justify-self: end; }
}

/* Images and video reserve their space so nothing shifts under a tap. */
.media { display: block; width: 100%; height: auto; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }
img[width][height] { height: auto; }        /* intrinsic ratio, no shift */

Forms on a small screen have their own content rules. One field per row, always: two fields side by side at 360 pixels are about 160 pixels each, which is below what iOS will not zoom at and below what makes a mistap likely. The primary action belongs at the end of the form rather than in a header the user has scrolled past. And the error summary has to be reachable: on a long form, a message next to the third field is invisible to someone who submitted from the bottom, which is exactly where people submit from.

/* The decision behind the technique: which strategy, for which table.
   This is the artefact a designer actually needs, and it is a content
   judgement that no CSS can make on the page's behalf. */
const STRATEGIES = {
  scroll: {
    when: 'every column is genuinely needed to answer a question asked across rows',
    cost: 'no overview; the user discovers more columns by trying',
    affordance: 'sticky first column, edge shadow, and a visible column count',
    example: 'invoice line items, audit log, financial comparison',
  },
  priority: {
    when: 'two or three columns carry the task and the rest are reference',
    cost: 'the hidden columns must be reachable somewhere else',
    affordance: 'a detail view per row showing every field',
    example: 'customer list (name, status, last active)',
  },
  cards: {
    when: 'each row is a record to be read once and acted on',
    // the cost is the important part: comparison across a row is lost
    cost: 'loses side-by-side comparison entirely',
    affordance: 'label every cell; keep the primary action per card',
    example: 'order history, inbox list, notifications',
  },
};

/* Reading the width off the content rather than guessing it, so the
   decision is defensible: count how many characters the widest cell needs
   before the layout starts truncating. */
function needsCardStack(columns) {
  // the narrowest width at which N labelled cells can sit on one line
  const perCell = 7;                 // rem per cell including its label
  const minWidth = columns * perCell;
  return { columns, minWidthRem: minWidth, stacksAtPhone: minWidthRem > 20 };
}
[2, 3, 4, 5, 7].forEach((n) => console.log(needsCardStack(n)));

/* The content rules that make a small-screen form work, as a checklist
   that runs against the DOM rather than in a review. */
const FORM_CHECKS = [
  { id: 'single-column',   test: (form) => !getComputedStyle(form).display.includes('grid') ||
                                     getComputedStyle(form).gridTemplateColumns.split(' ').length === 1 },
  { id: 'font-size-16',    test: () => [...document.querySelectorAll('input, select, textarea')]
                                     .every((el) => parseFloat(getComputedStyle(el).fontSize) >= 16) },
  { id: 'label-per-field', test: (form) => [...form.querySelectorAll('input, select, textarea')]
                                     .every((el) => el.labels && el.labels.length > 0) },
  { id: 'inputmode',       test: (form) => [...form.querySelectorAll('input[type="email"]')]
                                     .every((el) => el.getAttribute('inputmode') === 'email') },
  { id: 'error-summary',   test: (form) => !!form.querySelector('[role="alert"]') },
];

Copy is the highest-leverage mobile work, and it is worth treating a phone layout as a copy problem first. A phone has about a third of the vertical space of a laptop and a fraction of the attention, so the same amount of text does not work. Cutting half the words on the small screen is a better answer than any technique for fitting all of them, and the words to cut are the ones that were never read at the larger size either. Everything else is progressive disclosure, deferred loading, and a layout that has been asked to do one job per screen rather than five.

11.5 Mobile navigation patterns

Mobile navigation patterns each serve different jobs: tab bars for a few essential destinations, hamburger menus to hide secondary navigation, search to bypass structure entirely, and floating action buttons for one repeated primary action. Choose by the content’s shape and the user’s typical task rather than habit, and keep the primary path reachable in one hand. Test with a one-handed twenty-second completion test to expose broken flows. If a flow fails that test, the pattern is wrong.

PatternGood atPitfall
Bottom tab bar (3–5)primary destinations, thumb reachadding a 6th item silently
Top nav + hamburgersecondary navs, desktop parityhiding the most-used items
Search-firstexpert users, big catalogsbeginners don’t start with search
FAB (floating action)one repeated primary actioncompeting with tab bar

A great mobile heuristic: "can I complete this task one-handed in 20 seconds?" If not, the flow is mobile-broken regardless of how it looks.

Exercises 11

  1. Rebuild one of your desktop screens mobile-first and write which content you cut/prioritized.
  2. Set up a touch-target audit on a real app (48px + gap rule) and rate it.
  3. Redesign any real table into mobile "cards" — keep scanning ability.

Match the pattern to the job

Mobile navigation patterns are not interchangeable, and the choice follows from the information architecture rather than from habit. A tab bar works when there are three to five destinations of roughly equal weight that a user returns to often. It fails when the destinations are unequal, because a tab bar makes them look equal, and it fails when there are more than five, because the labels truncate into abbreviations. A hamburger works when the navigation is genuinely secondary to the page. It fails when the primary action is inside it, because it costs a discovery step on every single use, and it fails for anything a user needs more than once per session.

Search is the pattern that scales and the one most often omitted. When the item count exceeds what anyone can scan, search is not an enhancement, it is the primary interface, and a search that works across the whole catalogue beats any amount of navigation hierarchy. Floating action buttons are for exactly one repeated primary action, because the whole affordance is a promise that this thing is what you do here. Two floating buttons and it means nothing, and a floating button placed away from the hand it was meant to serve is worse than no button.

The other patterns worth knowing: bottom sheets for a choice that is a choice rather than a page, because a sheet keeps the context visible behind it; a sticky bottom bar for one action that must be reachable while scrolling; and pull-to-refresh only where refreshing is the expected behaviour, which is a list the user has just changed. Every one of these exists to reduce the number of taps between arriving and acting, and that is the metric to judge them against.

/* The pattern chosen by the shape of the information architecture, not by
   habit. Each block states the condition it is valid under, so a
   reviewer can tell whether it still applies. */

/* TAB BAR: 3-5 destinations, roughly equal weight, high return frequency.
   Invalid if the count drifts above 5 or the destinations are unequal. */
@media (max-width: 40rem) {
  .tabbar {
    position: fixed;
    inset-inline: 0;
    bottom: 0;
    display: grid;
    grid-auto-flow: column;
    grid-auto-columns: 1fr;
    background: var(--bg-raised);
    border-top: 1px solid var(--border);
    padding-bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom);
    padding-top: 0.35rem;
  }
  .tabbar a {
    min-height: 44px;
    display: grid;
    justify-items: center;
    gap: 2px;
    font-size: var(--step--2);
    text-decoration: none;
    color: var(--fg-muted);
  }
  .tabbar a[aria-current="page"] { color: var(--fg-brand); }
  .tabbar a[aria-current="page"]::before {
    content: ''; width: 1.5rem; height: 2px;
    background: currentColor; border-radius: 2px;
  }
  /* the label is required: an icon-only tab is a guess */
  .tabbar a span { line-height: 1.2; }
  /* keep content clear of the fixed bar and the home indicator */
  body:has(.tabbar) { padding-bottom: calc(4rem + env(safe-area-inset-bottom)); }
}

/* BOTTOM SHEET: a choice that is a choice. The scrim is a button, so the
   sheet can be dismissed from the keyboard and by a screen reader. */
.sheet-scrim {
  position: fixed; inset: 0;
  background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--fg-default) 40%, transparent);
  border: 0;
}
.sheet {
  position: fixed;
  inset-inline: 0;
  bottom: 0;
  border-radius: var(--radius-lg) var(--radius-lg) 0 0;
  background: var(--bg-raised);
  padding: 1rem;
  padding-bottom: calc(1rem + env(safe-area-inset-bottom));
  max-height: 85vh;
  overflow-y: auto;
}
.sheet__grip { width: 2.5rem; height: 4px; border-radius: 2px;
               background: var(--border-strong); margin: 0 auto 1rem; }

/* HAMBURGER: secondary navigation only. aria-expanded carries the state,
   and focus is managed on open so the menu is reachable. */
.burger { display: inline-flex; min-height: 44px; min-width: 44px;
          align-items: center; justify-content: center;
          background: none; border: 0; color: inherit;
          cursor: pointer; }
@media (min-width: 60rem) { .burger { display: none; } }

/* FLOATING ACTION: exactly one repeated primary action, placed inside
   the thumb reach rather than floating in the bottom-right by reflex. */
.fab {
  position: fixed;
  inset-block-end: calc(1rem + env(safe-area-inset-bottom));
  inset-inline-end: 1rem;
  min-height: 56px;
  min-width: 56px;
  border-radius: var(--radius-lg);
  display: grid; place-items: center;
  background: var(--fg-brand); color: var(--fg-ink);
  box-shadow: 0 4px 16px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.24);
}
/* a FAB covers content, so reserve for it */
body:has(.fab) { padding-block-end: 5rem; }

Whatever the pattern, one rule is worth stating on its own: the primary path must be reachable in one hand and in one screen. Everything on mobile navigation is a tax on the number of taps between arriving and acting, and a pattern that adds a tap to a task done fifty times a day costs more than the design time it saved. So count the taps on your five most common tasks and compare against the desktop equivalent. If the phone needs three taps where the desktop needs one, that is a decision to make deliberately, with the number written next to it.

/* Counting the tax. The number that decides whether a pattern is right is
   the tap count between arriving and acting, and it is measurable. */
function tapsToComplete(page, task) {
  // walk the recorded interaction trace for the task
  const trace = recordSession(task);          // [{ t: 0, target: 'nav' }, ...]
  let taps = 0;
  for (const step of trace) {
    if (step.type !== 'tap') continue;
    taps++;
    // a tap that opens a container costs more than a tap that acts
    if (step.opensDrawer || step.opensSheet) taps++;   // +1 to dismiss or choose
  }
  return { taps, seconds: trace.at(-1).t - trace[0].t };
}

// The comparison that makes the argument: the same task, phone and desktop.
const rows = TASKS.map((t) => {
  const m = tapsToComplete('mobile', t);
  const d = tapsToComplete('desktop', t);
  return { task: t, mobileTaps: m.taps, desktopTaps: d.taps,
           // the tax, expressed as the thing the team actually argues about
           tax: m.taps - d.taps, mobileSeconds: m.seconds };
});
rows.sort((a, b) => b.tax - a.tax);

/* The twenty-second one-handed test, as a script for whoever runs it.
   Nothing here measures anything; the point is that the roles are fixed so
   the observer does not coach. */
const PROTOCOL = {
  setup: 'hand the phone over; do not explain the product; screen off until asked',
  task: 'your five most common first-session tasks, one per participant',
  constraints: [
    'one hand only, the other holding something',
    'twenty second timer, visible to the participant',
    'the observer says nothing except "keep going"',
    'if they ask for help, the task has failed: record where',
  ],
  record: [
    'the first tap: did they look at the screen, or at their thumb',
    'the wrong tap: did the screen change in a way they did not expect',
    'the hesitation: more than two seconds of stillness',
    'the finish: did they know they were done without being told',
  ],
  // the four failure labels, so notes are comparable across participants
  failModes: ['nav-unclear', 'action-misplaced', 'label-ambiguous', 'flow-too-long'],
};

Test with the twenty-second one-handed rule, because it catches the structural failures that a review misses. Pick a task a new user would attempt in their first session, hand the phone to someone who has not seen the product, and let them do it one-handed while you say nothing. Where they hesitate, the navigation is unclear; where they reach with the wrong hand, the action is in the wrong place; where they cannot finish in twenty seconds, the flow is mobile-broken regardless of how good it looks on a desktop screenshot.

12 · UX Writing & Content Design

Content design treats words as part of the interface, because buttons, messages, and empty states do real UX work. Half of usability problems are word problems, such as vague button labels, jargon-filled errors, or empty states that leave people stranded. In practice, design the content alongside the layout, writing microcopy that is specific, plain, and action-oriented. Test the words with users just as you test the visuals.

12.1 Voice & tone: the brand that words build12.2 Microcopy that does engineering’s job12.3 Form copy that doesn’t scare people12.4 Every error is a dialogue, not a slap12.5 Plain language as inclusivity

Content is the interface. Half of UX problems are word problems: the button said "Submit", the error said "Error", and the empty state said absolutely nothing.

12.1 Voice & tone: the brand that words build

Voice is the stable personality of your product expressed through every word, while tone is how that personality adapts to the situation, such as a friendlier tone in onboarding and a calmer, more careful tone in error states. Pin the voice to a memorable three-word statement, such as clear, warm, direct, and test every string against it during review. Create a tone guide describing how the voice shifts across contexts. Consistency of voice is what makes a product feel like a brand.

DimensionVoice (constant)Tone (situational)
Examplesimple, warm, confidentextra-reassuring during errors / checkout
Anti-patternscorporate garble ("leverage synergies")jokey during a payment failure

Write a 3-word voice (e.g. "clear, human, brave") and test every string against it.

Voice is constant, tone is not

The distinction that makes voice and tone usable rather than decorative is that voice is the personality and does not change, while tone is that personality adapting to the situation. Voice is a three-word statement: clear, warm, direct. It describes who the product is being, and it holds from the marketing site to the fatal error page. Tone is a dial: the same voice is warmer in onboarding, plainer in an error, quieter in a destructive confirmation, and more formal in a legal notice. A product has one voice and many tones, and any string that contradicts the voice is wrong even if it is well written.

Three words is not a slogan, it is a constraint. One word cannot be contradicted, two cannot be prioritised against each other, and four is a paragraph nobody will remember. The value of the three words is that they make a string reviewable: somebody can read "clear, warm, direct" and ask whether a given string is warm enough, whether it is warm about that, and whether it is being direct at the expense of the person. Without the statement the review becomes taste, and taste is not a decision a team can repeat.

Write what the voice means in this product, concretely, with examples and anti-examples. "Warm" does not mean chatty or cute; it means it says "your file is too big" rather than "upload failed", and it means it does not use an exclamation mark in an error. "Direct" does not mean terse to the point of rudeness; it means the button says what it will do rather than "OK". Concrete pairs are worth more than adjectives, because a designer or developer reading the guide can act on a pair and only nod at an adjective.

/* The voice as data, so it can be checked rather than remembered. Every
   string in the product is scored against the three words, and a string
   that contradicts one is a review item rather than a matter of taste. */
const VOICE = ['clear', 'warm', 'direct'];

const DO = {
  clear:  ['Delete this project?', 'Your file is 40MB. The limit is 10MB.',
           'We could not sign you in', 'Your session expired. Sign in again.'],
  warm:   ['Nothing here yet', 'Your changes are saved',
           'Welcome back, Ada', 'Start by adding your first team'],
  direct: ['Send invite', 'Remove access', 'Save draft',
           'Sign in', 'Upload file', 'Turn off notifications'],
};

const DONT = {
  // warm without being cute: the failure mode of every voice guide
  warm:   ['Oops! Something went wrong!', 'Yay! Your file is uploaded!',
           'Uh oh, that did not work'],
  // clear without being blunt: blaming the user
  clear:  ['Invalid input', 'You entered an invalid email address',
           'Wrong password', 'Operation failed'],
  // direct without being abrupt: a label that is an action, not a state
  direct: ['OK', 'Yes', 'Submit', 'Click here', 'More', 'Learn more'],
};

/* Two failure modes worth naming, because each is a voice that has drifted
   in a specific and diagnosable direction. */

// 1. exclamation marks on bad news
function isWarmAndCredible(s) {
  const bangs = (s.match(/!/g) || []).length;
  const isBadNews = /error|failed|could not|unable|cannot|expired/i.test(s);
  // one exclamation anywhere is a style choice; two on a failure is a voice break
  if (isBadNews && bangs > 0) return false;
  // "Oops", "Uh oh", "Yay", "Woohoo" are informality without warmth
  if (/\b(oops|uh oh|yay|woohoo|awesome!)\b/i.test(s)) return false;
  return true;
}

// 2. second person, present tense, active voice - the grammar of directness
function isDirect(s) {
  const passive = /\b(was|were|been|being|is being)\s+\w+ed\b/i.test(s);
  const hedged = /\b(might|perhaps|possibly|we believe|we think)\b/i.test(s);
  return !passive && !hedged;
}

// The whole vocabulary, scored. These are the strings teams argue about,
// and having them in one file with a reason attached ends the argument.
function review(s) {
  const problems = [];
  if (!isWarmAndCredible(s)) problems.push('warm: informality or an exclamation on bad news');
  if (!isDirect(s)) problems.push('direct: passive voice or hedging');
  if (/^(ok|yes|no|submit)$/i.test(s.trim())) problems.push('direct: label is not an action');
  if (s.length > 60) problems.push('clear: over 60 characters, check it fits one line');
  return problems;
}
// review('Oops! Upload failed') -> ['warm: ...']
// review('Your file could not be uploaded because it is 40MB. The limit is 10MB.') -> []
/* The tone guide as a lookup table. Tone is not an opinion, so it has to be
   a table: one row per moment, three columns, worked examples. Without
   this, thirty engineers improvise a personality and the product has
   thirty personalities. */
const TONE = {
  'onboarding': {
    does:  'warm, encouraging, one instruction at a time',
    doesnt: 'celebrate before the user has done anything; use the word "easy"',
    was: 'Welcome! Let us get your account set up in three quick steps.',
    now: 'Welcome. Three steps, about a minute.',
  },
  'success': {
    does:  'confirm what happened, then say what happens next',
    doesnt: 'praise the user for something the system did',
    was: 'Congratulations! You have successfully completed your profile setup!',
    now: 'Profile saved. You can edit it any time.',
  },
  'error': {
    does:  'warm and plain; say what happened and what to do',
    doesnt: 'exclaim, apologise twice, or use the word "invalid"',
    was: 'Oops! An error occurred while processing your request.',
    now: 'We could not save that. Your text is still here — try again.',
  },
  'destructive': {
    does:  'serious and quiet; name exactly what will be lost',
    doesnt: 'soften it into ambiguity; the user needs the number, not the tone',
    was: 'Are you sure? This action cannot be undone.',
    now: 'Delete "Q3 forecast"? It and its 14 comments are removed. This cannot be undone.',
  },
  'empty': {
    does:  'explain why it is empty, then offer the one action that fills it',
    doesnt: 'state the absence and stop',
    was: 'No data available.',
    now: 'No invoices yet. Your first one appears here after your first payment.',
  },
  'loading': {
    does:  'name what is happening; offer a way out if it may take long',
    doesnt: 'invent a duration, or say "loading" four times on one screen',
    was: 'Loading, please wait...',
    now: 'Importing 2,400 rows. You can leave this page.',
  },
  'permission': {
    does:  'state the permission, why, and who can grant it',
    doesnt: 'say "access denied" and stop',
    was: '403 Forbidden',
    now: 'You need edit access to this. Ask Sam (the owner) to add you.',
  },
  'legal': {
    does:  'plain, complete, and consistent with the voice; no jokes',
    doesnt: 'inherit the casual tone from onboarding',
    was: null,   // written once, reviewed by legal, never regenerated
    now: null,
  },
};

// The test: does the string belong in this row? A string that reads like
// an onboarding message inside a destructive confirmation has the wrong
// tone, and it is more visible than any rule that says so.
function toneCheck(moment, s) {
  const row = TONE[moment];
  const problems = [];
  if (/[!]{1,}/.test(s)) problems.push('exclamation in ' + moment);
  if (moment === 'error' && /\b(oops|uh oh|invalid|unfortunately)\b/i.test(s)) {
    problems.push('chatty or blaming in an error');
  }
  if (moment === 'destructive' && /^are you sure/i.test(s)) {
    problems.push('ambiguous: name the object and the count');
  }
  if (moment === 'success' && /\b(amazing|awesome|well done|great job)\b/i.test(s)) {
    problems.push('praising the user for a system action');
  }
  if (s.length > 120) problems.push('too long for ' + moment + ': ' + s.length);
  return problems;
}

Tone shifts are needed at specific moments, and the pattern repeats across every product. Success is warm and forward-looking, because it should feel like momentum. Error is warm and plain, and it is the moment where warmth is hardest to keep, which is exactly why it matters most: the user is already frustrated and the string is the difference between a product that apologises and one that blames them. Waiting is neutral and should say what is happening, not how long it might take, because a made-up estimate is worse than none. Destructive confirmation is serious and quiet, no exclamation marks, no cheerfulness. Empty states are instructive, and they are the best opportunity in the product for warmth because nobody is annoyed yet.

The tone guide needs a table or it does not exist, because tone is a lookup rather than an opinion. Rows for each moment in the product lifecycle, columns for what the voice does and does not mean there, and a worked example for each. Teams then apply the table rather than improvising, which is the only way a personality survives contact with thirty engineers writing strings at different times.

12.2 Microcopy that does engineering’s job

Microcopy is the small text in an interface, such as button labels, placeholders, hints, and empty states, and it guides behavior more than any visual polish. Buttons should state the action they perform, placeholders should demonstrate an example value rather than just label the field, and empty states should console the user while explaining how to fill the space. Well-written microcopy prevents errors and support tickets that otherwise fall to engineering. Give each line a job and measure whether it works.

// Buttons say the ACTION, not the data:
"Submit"          → "Create account" / "Save draft" / "Confirm order"
// Placeholders are DEMOS not labels (a field with placeholder+no label
// loses its name once the user types):
label visible + placeholder = "e.g. john@example.com"
// Checkboxes/radio = full sentence, clickable whole row:
<label><input type="checkbox"> Keep me signed in on this device</label>
// Empty states console + act: "No dreams yet. Create your first plan →"

Every string has a job

Microcopy is the small text that shapes behaviour: button labels, placeholders, hints, empty states, confirmations, and the one-line explanations in between. It is worth more attention per character than any other part of the interface, because it is the part that changes behaviour, and it is almost always the part written last and by the person with the least context.

Three rules cover most of it. A button label states the result, not the mechanism: "Send invite" rather than "Submit", "Delete project" rather than "OK". A placeholder demonstrates a format rather than repeating the label: "name@company.com" rather than "Email address", because a label belongs in a label element and a placeholder that repeats it tells the user nothing they could not already see. And an empty state does two jobs: it explains why the space is empty and it offers the action that fills it. "No projects yet. Create one to invite your team." is two sentences and a whole screen's worth of guidance, where "No data" is a dead end.

Length is the next question, and there is a common wrong answer. Microcopy is not a character limit; it is a fit question, and the constraint is the space it has to live in. A button on a small screen with a label of thirty characters either wraps, overflows, or shrinks, and all three are worse than a shorter label. Where the action genuinely needs explaining, the explanation goes next to the button rather than inside it, because a button that explains itself is a button nobody clicks.

/* Microcopy as a table, because that is what it is: a lookup keyed by
   where the string appears. Every row states the job and gives one
   accepted and one rejected version, so a review is a comparison
   rather than an argument. */
const COPY = {
  'button.primary': {
    job: 'state the result of pressing it',
    good: 'Send invite',
    bad:  'Submit',            // states the mechanism, not the result
    alt:  'Add to calendar',   // fine: still names the result
  },
  'button.danger': {
    job: 'name what is destroyed',
    good: 'Delete project',
    bad:  'Are you sure?',      // asks a question and answers nothing
    note: 'if the label does not fit, shorten the noun, never the verb',
  },
  'input.placeholder': {
    job: 'demonstrate the format',
    good: 'name@company.com',
    bad:  'Email address',      // repeats the label; tells the user nothing
    // a placeholder is not a label: it disappears on focus, and it is
    // often not read aloud, so the field needs a real <label>
  },
  'input.hint': {
    job: 'remove the reason for an error before it happens',
    good: 'We only use this to send your receipt.',
    bad:  'Enter your email',
  },
  'state.empty': {
    job: 'explain why it is empty, then offer the action',
    good: 'No projects yet. Create one to invite your team.',
    bad:  'No data',
  },
  'state.loading': {
    job: 'say what is happening; never invent a duration',
    good: 'Uploading your file',
    bad:  'Loading...',         // which loading? of how many?
    bad2: 'This may take a moment',
  },
  'state.error': {
    job: 'what happened, why, what to do next',
    good: 'That file is 40MB. The limit is 10MB.',
    bad:  'Upload failed',
  },
  'state.success': {
    job: 'confirm and say what happens next',
    good: 'File uploaded. Processing usually takes a minute.',
    bad:  'Success!',
  },
};

/* The three mechanical checks that catch most of it, run over the DOM
   rather than in a review. */
function audit(root = document) {
  const problems = [];

  // 1. every control has an accessible name, and it is not a bare "OK"
  for (const el of root.querySelectorAll('button, a[href], [role="button"]')) {
    const name = (el.getAttribute('aria-label') || el.textContent || '').trim();
    if (!name) problems.push({ level: 'error', el, why: 'no accessible name' });
    else if (/^(ok|yes|submit|click here|more|learn more)$/i.test(name)) {
      problems.push({ level: 'warn', el, why: 'label does not name a result: ' + name });
    }
    // truncation is a length problem, and only the layout knows
    if (el.scrollWidth > el.clientWidth + 1) {
      problems.push({ level: 'warn', el, why: 'label is clipped at this width' });
    }
  }

  // 2. every input has a visible label element, not only a placeholder
  for (const el of root.querySelectorAll('input, select, textarea')) {
    if (el.type === 'hidden') continue;
    const labelled = (el.labels && el.labels.length) || el.getAttribute('aria-label');
    if (!labelled) problems.push({ level: 'error', el, why: 'placeholder-only field' });
    if (el.placeholder && el.placeholder.toLowerCase() === el.name.toLowerCase()) {
      problems.push({ level: 'warn', el, why: 'placeholder repeats the field name' });
    }
  }

  // 3. no loading string that names nothing
  for (const el of root.querySelectorAll('[aria-busy="true"], .loading')) {
    const t = (el.textContent || '').trim();
    if (!t || /^loading/i.test(t)) problems.push({ level: 'warn', el, why: 'loading text names nothing' });
  }
  return problems;
}

Two structural habits keep microcopy consistent without a guide. Put every user-visible string in one file per surface, so a tone change is one edit rather than forty, and so a string can be reviewed as a set rather than piecemeal. And give every string an owner who can answer "what is this supposed to make the user do", because roughly a fifth of the strings in a mature product answer nothing and exist only because a screen needed something there. Those are the ones to delete, and deleting them is a design decision rather than a copy decision.

The measurable part is the last piece, and it should be measured rather than asserted. Four numbers are enough: how many support tickets mention a specific string, how many users reach a validation error on a field, how many abandon a step with a long label versus a short one, and how many times an empty state's action is clicked. A label change is then an experiment rather than a preference, and the fifth of the strings that answer nothing gets deleted because a number said so.

Real strings demonstrate action-first copy: buttons name the result, placeholders demo a format, and the whole checkbox row is clickable.

12.3 Form copy that doesn’t scare people

Form copy shapes how safe and willing a person feels to share their data, so explain why each piece of information is collected and how it will be used. Write instructions in plain language, keep labels and helper text near the fields they describe, and write validation errors as what went wrong, why, and how to fix it in the user’s own words. Label every field clearly and only ask for what the product genuinely needs. Reducing the scare factor of fields raises completion rates.

  • Explain why you ask for data, and when commit matters ("We need a phone for delivery — not for marketing").
  • Reduce friction copy: fewer optional fields; "save my progress" reassures.
  • Error text: what + why + fix in their sentence ("That email looks missing an '@' — emails look like name@site.com").
  • Privacy links inline at the moment of asking — "Your card is processed securely by Stripe."

Why people abandon a form

A form is the highest-anxiety screen in most products, because the user is being asked to hand over something and cannot see what happens to it. The abandonment causes are mostly not layout. They are: not understanding why a field is needed, not knowing what format is expected until they are wrong, not knowing whether it was saved, and not trusting the organisation enough to give a real detail. Copy addresses all four; layout addresses none of them.

So the first rule is that every field has a reason that is visible. Either state it inline where it is asked, in the user's terms and without a marketing tone, or remove the field. "We need a phone number for delivery. We will not text you" is one sentence that removes an entire category of anxiety, and it converts a suspicious field into a trusted one. The alternative, a link to a privacy policy, asks the user to do research to resolve a doubt you could have resolved in a sentence.

The second rule is that format is communicated before the error, not after. An input that accepts a date should say what format it wants and what format it is currently in, which on mobile means the right inputmode so the keyboard is correct, and on desktop means a hint or a placeholder that demonstrates the shape. Getting this right removes roughly half of the validation errors a form would otherwise generate, and half of the validation errors is half of the retries.

/* Form copy attached to the field it describes, in the order a person
   meets it: label (what), optional marker (whether), hint (why and how),
   then the error when there is one. */
function field({ id, label, type = 'text', why, hint, required = false, autocomplete }) {
  const hintId = hint ? id + '-hint' : null;
  const errId = id + '-err';
  // the described-by list is what makes hint and error announced; placing
  // them next to the field visually is not enough
  const describedBy = [hintId, errId].filter(Boolean).join(' ');

  // built by concatenation rather than a template literal, so the markup
  // stays inspectable and a translation pass can see the pieces
  const optional = required ? '' : ' <span class="field__optional">(optional)</span>';
  const mode = (type === 'email' || type === 'tel')
    ? ' inputmode="' + (type === 'email' ? 'email' : 'tel') + '"' : '';

  let html = '<div class="field">
';
  html += '  <label class="field__label" for="' + id + '">' + label + optional + '</label>
';
  html += '  <input class="field__input" id="' + id + '" name="' + id + '" type="' + type + '"';
  html += (required ? ' required' : '');
  html += (autocomplete ? ' autocomplete="' + autocomplete + '"' : '') + mode;
  html += ' aria-describedby="' + describedBy + '">
';
  if (why) html += '  <p class="field__why" id="' + id + '-why">' + why + '</p>
';
  if (hint) html += '  <p class="field__hint" id="' + hintId + '">' + hint + '</p>
';
  html += '  <p class="field__err" id="' + errId + '" role="alert" hidden></p>
';
  html += '</div>';
  return html;
}

// Every field with its reason attached. "optional" is stated in words, not
// by an asterisk, because an asterisk is a symbol the reader has to decode
// and half the users never find the footnote it points at.
const FORM = [
  field({
    id: 'email', label: 'Email address', type: 'email', required: true,
    why: 'We use this to send your receipt.',
    hint: 'name@company.com', autocomplete: 'email',
  }),
  field({
    id: 'phone', label: 'Mobile number', type: 'tel',
    why: 'The courier needs it for delivery. We will not text you.',
    hint: 'Digits only, including the country code.', autocomplete: 'tel',
  }),
  field({
    id: 'company', label: 'Company',
    why: 'We use this to check whether we already have your account.',
  }),
  field({
    id: 'vat', label: 'VAT number (optional)',
    hint: 'If your business is registered for VAT.',
  }),
].join('');

/* The reassurance strings that measurably change completion, and where
   each one goes. They are not decoration: each answers a specific doubt
   the user has at that exact point in the form. */
const REASSURANCE = {
  topOfForm:      'Takes about 40 seconds. We will not share your details.',
  nearCardField:  'Card details go straight to our payment provider; they never touch our servers.',
  nearPassword:   'We store a hash, not the password itself.',
  beforeSubmit:   'You can change any of this later in Settings.',
  afterSubmit:    'Check your inbox to confirm. We will not do anything without it.',
};

Progress and saving are the two under-used pieces of copy. A long form that says nothing about position makes the user assume there is more, and they abandon before the end; "Step 2 of 4" costs nine characters and changes the estimate the user is making. And a form that does not say when something is saved removes the reason to be careful, so people abandon instead of committing. Autosave with a visible "Saved just now" is the cheapest conversion improvement available in most checkout flows.

Length is a design decision with a measurable outcome. Every optional field costs completions, and the fields that are optional are usually optional for the business rather than for the user. The correct move is to ask what breaks without it, and to move it after the commitment: ask for the company name after the account exists rather than before it, so the user has already seen the value. Reordering fields by "can we ask this later" is a purely textual change and it outperforms most interface redesigns.

/* Form copy as data, so it is reviewable as a set and translatable as
   fragments. The interesting column is "why", because that is the column
   teams omit and the one that decides completion. */
const FORM_COPY = [
  { id: 'name',     label: 'Full name',      required: true,  autocomplete: 'name',
    why: 'We put it on invoices you send to clients.',
    hint: 'As it should appear on an invoice.' },
  { id: 'email',    label: 'Email address',  required: true,  autocomplete: 'email',
    why: 'We use this to send your receipt.',
    hint: 'name@company.com' },
  { id: 'company',  label: 'Company',        required: false, autocomplete: 'organization',
    why: 'We use this to check whether you already have an account.',
    // a field that is optional for the business is optional for the user,
    // and saying so in words beats an asterisk nobody decodes
    optionalCopy: 'optional' },
  { id: 'phone',    label: 'Mobile number',  required: true,  autocomplete: 'tel',
    why: 'The courier needs it for delivery. We will not text you.',
    hint: 'Digits only, including the country code.' },
  { id: 'address',  label: 'Billing address', required: true,  autocomplete: 'street-address',
    why: 'Needed for the VAT invoice.',
    hint: 'Street, city, postcode. Country is on the next step.' },
  { id: 'vat',      label: 'VAT number',     required: false, autocomplete: 'off',
    why: 'If your business is registered for VAT, add it so we can invoice you correctly.',
    hint: 'GB123456789', optionalCopy: 'optional — skip if you are not registered' },
];

/* The reorder that outperforms a redesign: anything that can be asked
   after the commitment moves after it, because the user has then seen
   the value and answers differently. */
const FUNNEL = [
  { step: 1, ask: ['email'],          why: 'lowest commitment, highest intent' },
  { step: 2, ask: ['name', 'company'], why: 'needed before anything can be created' },
  { step: 3, ask: ['phone', 'address'], why: 'needed only at payment, not at signup' },
  // name is asked twice in many products; the second time it is remembered
  { step: 4, ask: ['vat'],            why: 'optional, and only relevant if they pay' },
];

/* The DOM audit, run against the rendered form rather than the spec. */
function auditForm(form) {
  const problems = [];
  for (const el of form.querySelectorAll('input, select, textarea')) {
    const labels = el.labels;
    if (!labels || labels.length === 0) {
      problems.push({ field: el.name, why: 'no visible label element' });
    }
    if (el.type === 'email' && el.inputMode !== 'email') {
      problems.push({ field: el.name, why: 'no inputmode: iOS will show the wrong keyboard' });
    }
    if (!el.autocomplete) {
      problems.push({ field: el.name, why: 'no autocomplete attribute' });
    }
    if (el.required && !form.querySelector('#' + el.id + '-why, #' + el.id + '-hint')) {
      problems.push({ field: el.name, why: 'required with no stated reason' });
    }
    // 16px is functional on iOS, not stylistic: below it the viewport zooms
    if (parseFloat(getComputedStyle(el).fontSize) < 16) {
      problems.push({ field: el.name, why: 'font under 16px: iOS zooms on focus' });
    }
  }
  // progress and save state are copy, and they are the two most omitted
  if (!form.closest('[data-progress]')) problems.push({ field: '(form)', why: 'no step indicator' });
  return problems;
}

The test for form copy: read it aloud to someone who has never seen the form. Every question that produces "what does this mean?", "why do they want that?" or "will I be charged?" is a question the form should have answered, and it is nearly always answerable in one sentence placed next to the field. Reading it aloud is what surfaces them, because written copy hides its own omissions behind familiarity.

12.4 Every error is a dialogue, not a slap

An error message should read like a helpful conversation between humans, not a system verdict. When the failure is your product’s fault, apologize plainly, state concretely what happened, and then give the immediate next action the user can take. Keep apologies specific rather than vague, place the message where the user is looking, and avoid technical jargon. A good error respects the user and moves them forward.

// The 3 beats:
//  1 APOLOGIZE when it's OUR fault (not when blaming the user)
//  2 STATE plainly what happened (avoid "opps!" alone)
//  3 GIVE the next action (retry, cancel, what's saved, contact)
"Something went wrong saving — it wasn't you. We'll retry; if it
persists, your draft is safe on this device. [Try again] [Download draft]"
// You CAN'T fix a problem you can't NAME. Vague apologies are noise.

Three beats: what happened, why, what next

An error message has three jobs and the order matters. What happened, in terms the user recognises rather than the system's internal name. Why, so the situation is understood rather than merely reported. And what to do next, as an action the user can take in the next five seconds. A message that does the first and skips the third has told the user they have a problem and left them to solve it, which is the definition of a bad error message.

Tone is decided by whose fault the failure is, and there are two cases. When the system failed, apologise plainly and specifically, and never blame: "We could not save your changes. Your work is still on this page — try again, or copy it somewhere safe while we fix this." The second half is the part teams skip and it is the part that matters, because a user who does not know whether their work survived will not retry, they will leave. When the user's input is wrong, name the field and the correction without accusation: "That email address is missing an @, for example name@company.com", not "You entered an invalid email address". "You" plus a past-tense verb transfers blame; naming the value transfers the information.

Placement follows the user, not the code. A validation error next to the field works when the user is at the field. A summary at the top of the form works when the user submitted from the bottom, which is where people submit from, and it needs to be linked to each field so it is a navigation aid rather than a list. Inline errors should not appear before the user has finished with the field, which means validating on blur rather than on every keystroke; validating while someone is still typing their first character is the single most common way to make a form feel hostile.

/* The error copy, keyed by cause. The cause decides the tone, which is why
   the table is keyed by cause and not by screen. */
const ERRORS = {
  network: {
    tone: 'apologise, reassure about the data, offer a retry',
    title: 'We could not reach the server',
    body: 'Your changes are still on this page. Check your connection and try again.',
    primary: 'Try again',
    secondary: 'Save a copy',
  },
  timeout: {
    tone: 'explain, do not blame the user for the server being slow',
    title: 'That took longer than expected',
    body: 'Nothing was charged. This usually clears within a minute.',
    primary: 'Try again',
    secondary: null,
  },
  permissions: {
    tone: 'explain the permission and how to get it, not who is at fault',
    title: 'You need permission to do this',
    body: 'Ask the owner of this workspace to give you editor access, then try again.',
    primary: 'See who owns it',
    secondary: 'Cancel',
  },
  validation: {
    tone: 'name the value and the correction; never "you entered"',
    title: null,            // inline, no title: it is one field's problem
    body: 'That email address is missing an @, for example name@company.com.',
  },
  conflict: {
    tone: 'state the situation and offer both resolutions',
    title: 'Someone else changed this while you were editing',
    body: 'Your version and theirs are both kept. Pick which one to keep.',
    primary: 'Keep mine',
    secondary: 'Keep theirs',
  },
  notFound: {
    tone: 'do not say "not found": say where it went',
    title: 'That project was deleted',
    body: 'It was deleted by someone in your workspace 20 minutes ago.',
    primary: 'See other projects',
    secondary: null,
  },
  forbidden: {
    tone: 'never a dead end: every error needs a next action',
    title: 'You cannot delete this team',
    body: 'Transfer ownership first, then delete it.',
    primary: 'Transfer ownership',
    secondary: 'Cancel',
  },
};

/* Validation timing, which is where most forms go wrong. Validate on blur,
   not on input, and never before the field has been left once. */
function shouldValidate(field, { blurred, touched }) {
  // not while they are still typing the first characters of a new value
  if (!blurred && !touched) return false;
  // once a field has been blurred, live validation is welcome: it turns a
  // submit-time error into feedback at the moment it is useful
  return blurred;
}

/* Rendering a field-level error: the message is associated, announced,
   and the field is marked invalid - all three, or a screen-reader user is
   told nothing. */
function renderError(fieldEl, message) {
  const errEl = document.getElementById(fieldEl.getAttribute('aria-describedby').split(' ').pop());
  errEl.textContent = message;
  errEl.hidden = false;
  fieldEl.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
  // focus stays where the user put it; do NOT move it, because they may be
  // mid-form. The summary at the top is what gets focus on submit.
}

Never expose internals. Stack traces, SQL fragments, status codes, file paths and third-party gateway names are all ways of helping someone who already knows the answer at the cost of alarming someone who does not, and the internal detail belongs in your logs where it is genuinely useful. The exception is a support reference code, which costs nothing, appears in the log keyed to the request, and cuts a support exchange from four messages to one.

Two rules close the subject. Every error must offer an action, including "cancel" and including the case where the only honest action is to tell the user what to do next; an error with no action is a dead end and the user leaves. And error copy is engineering work with a designer reviewing it, not a design deliverable handed over at the end — because the error path is the part of a feature that is written last, tested least, and read most often by the people having the worst day.

The three-beat error script — apologize, state plainly, give the next action — shown in a humane failure message with clear recovery options.

12.5 Plain language as inclusivity

Plain language is an accessibility feature because short sentences, everyday words, and clear structure make content usable by people with reading, cognitive, or language differences. Write for a reading level near the general population, define unavoidable terms, and never require reading comprehension to complete a critical action. Keep instructions next to what they describe and avoid burying key information. Simpler words widen the audience without dumbing anything down.

Write for a grade-6 reading level in essential flows; short sentences; define jargon the first time; never require reading to act (icons + labels). Content design = structuring information so it can be scanned, skipped, and acted on — headings are decisions, not decorations.

Exercises 12

  1. Rewrite the 5 worst strings in any app you use (buttons, errors, empty states) with action-first language.
  2. Write 10 microcopy variants for ONE error and pick the best by your product’s voice.
  3. Turn one form into a complete over-the-shoulder script ("what does this word mean? why is it asking?").

Plain language is an accessibility feature

Short sentences and common words are not a stylistic preference; they are the difference between an interface that works for a reader with dyslexia, a reader whose first language is not this one, a reader who is tired, and a reader with an intellectual disability. All four are better served by the same writing, which is why plain language is cheap: it is one change that helps everyone, and the accessibility benefit arrives without a separate project.

The measurable target is a reading level, and around grade six to eight is the working reference for essential flows: sign-up, checkout, permissions, support, and anything destructive. The measure that matters is not the score but the underlying behaviours: shorter sentences, fewer clauses per sentence, common words, active voice, and a concrete subject. A grade-six score achieved by replacing long words with short words while keeping a forty-word sentence is a worse text than the one before, so measure the sentence, not the vocabulary.

Structure is as much of the answer as wording. Content that can be scanned, skipped and acted on has headings that carry meaning, lists for anything enumerable, a summary before the detail, and the important thing first. This helps everyone, and it helps three specific groups disproportionately: anyone using a screen reader, who navigates by heading rather than by reading; anyone with a cognitive disability, who is scanning for the action rather than the argument; and anyone who came to the page with a specific question and did not arrive to read.

/* A readability pass that measures sentences rather than counting hard
   words, because the two produce opposite advice. The sentence is the unit
   a reader has to hold, and a short-word forty-clause sentence is harder
   than a long-word twelve-word one. */
const FOGL = {
  sentenceWords: (s) => s.trim().split(/[.!?]+\s/).filter(Boolean),
  syllables: (w) => (w.toLowerCase()
    .replace(/e$/, '')
    .match(/[aeiouy]{1,2}/g) || ['x']).length,
  // words of three syllables or more are the usual suspect
  complex: (w) => FOGL.syllables(w) >= 3 && w.length > 6,
};

function readability(text) {
  const sentences = FOGL.sentenceWords(text);
  const words = text.trim().split(/\s+/);
  const hard = words.filter(FOGL.complex);
  return {
    words: words.length,
    sentences: sentences.length,
    // the sentence is the number to hold: over 20 words and it needs splitting
    avgSentenceWords: +(words.length / Math.max(1, sentences.length)).toFixed(1),
    longestSentence: Math.max(0, ...sentences.map((s) => s.split(/\s+/).length)),
    hardWords: hard,
    hardPercent: +((hard.length / Math.max(1, words.length)) * 100).toFixed(1),
    // a clause count catches "which", "that", "in order to", "the fact that"
    clausesPerSentence: sentences.map((s) =>
      (s.match(/\b(which|that|whose|because|in order to|so that|although)\b/gi) || []).length + 1),
  };
}
readability('Your subscription will be cancelled at the end of the current period.');
// { avgSentenceWords: 12, longestSentence: 12, hardWords: [], hardPercent: 0 }
readability('Your subscription will be cancelled, at the end of the current period, unless you renew.');
// { longestSentence: 15, hardWords: ['subscription'], ... }

/* The rewrite, which is the deliverable. Same meaning, shorter sentences,
   concrete subject, active voice, and the action first. */
const BEFORE_AFTER = [
  {
    before: 'Your subscription will be cancelled at the end of the current billing period unless you choose to renew it before then.',
    after: 'Your plan ends on 14 March. Renew before then to keep it.',
    note: 'the date is more useful than "the end of the current billing period"',
  },
  {
    before: 'In order to complete the verification process, a valid form of photographic identification will need to be provided.',
    after: 'To verify your identity, upload a photo ID. A passport or driving licence works.',
    note: '"in order to" becomes "to"; passive becomes active; "valid" removed',
  },
  {
    before: 'We apologise, however, that at this time we are unable to process this request.',
    after: 'We cannot process this request right now. Try again in an hour.',
    note: 'apology kept, hedging removed, next step given',
  },
];

The instruction that never requires reading is the accessibility requirement hiding inside a design rule. An icon with no label is unreadable to someone who does not know the convention; a control with no text needs an accessible name, and an accessible name is not a replacement for a visible one in every case, because voice control users say what they see. So the rule is: never make reading a prerequisite for acting. Every icon that carries meaning has a visible label somewhere adjacent, every gesture has a button, every status has a word and not only a colour, and every abbreviation is spelled out at first use.

Definitions and jargon belong where they are first needed, not in a glossary at the bottom that nobody reaches. If a term cannot be avoided, define it in line in one clause, and then use it. "Sync" is fine after "Sync copies new photos from your phone (that is, fetches them)", and it is useless before it. And keep the structure honest: headings are decisions about what is a topic, a link text describes its destination rather than saying "click here", and the summary leads because the reader who has read nothing should still have the essential thing.

/* Content structure as a document, because structure is what a screen
   reader navigates and what a scanning reader uses. Headings are
   decisions about what is a topic, not decoration. */
<!-- Wrong: three h2s and a heading that skips a level. A screen-reader
     user navigating by heading gets an outline with a hole in it. -->
<h2>Overview</h2>
<h2>Features</h2>
<h4>Advanced</h4>            <!-- skipped h3 -->

<!-- Right: one h1, levels in order, headings that describe their
     sections rather than naming a visual treatment. -->
<h1>Exporting your data</h1>
<p>Short summary. The reader who stops here has the essentials.</p>

<h2>What you can export</h2>
<ul>
  <li>Projects as CSV</li>
  <li>Projects as JSON</li>
  <li>Attachments as a zip</li>
</ul>

<h3>CSV</h3>
<p>One row per project. Formulas starting with = are prefixed with a quote.</p>
<h3>JSON</h3>
<p>Nested, and stable field names. Use this for scripts.</p>

<h2>Limits</h2>
<table>
  <caption>Export limits by plan</caption>
  <thead><tr><th scope="col">Plan</th><th scope="col">Rows per export</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><th scope="row">Free</th><td>1,000</td></tr>
    <tr><th scope="row">Pro</th><td>Unlimited</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

/* Link text describes the destination. "Click here" is unusable with a
   screen reader reading a list of links out of context, and unusable with
   voice control, which says the visible text. */
<!-- Wrong -->
<a href="/pricing">Click here</a> to see our <a href="/pricing">pricing</a>.

<!-- Right: the destination is in the text, and the sentence still reads -->
<a href="/pricing">See pricing</a>, or <a href="/pricing/plans">compare plans</a>.

/* Abbreviations are expanded at first use, not in a glossary at the end. */
<p>Application programming interface (API) keys are per project.</p>

Finally, content is where translation and localisation break, and it breaks early rather than late. Strings built out of concatenated fragments do not reorder in languages with different word order, plurals need real plural rules rather than an "s", and text that assumes a wide layout breaks in languages that expand by thirty percent. Writing short sentences in separate complete fragments is what makes a string translatable, which is an accessibility argument as well, since the audience with the most difficulty reading your language is frequently the one whose language it is not.

13 · Design Thinking & Process

Design process keeps a team honest by making decisions recorded, ideas tested cheaply, and evidence visible at every step. Routines such as the double diamond, structured ideation, and short build-test loops make the classic skip-research rush visible for what it is. Adopt a lightweight toolkit of problem framing, prototyping, and user testing that fits your team’s cadence. The goal of process is to make the best decisions visible and repeatable.

13.1 The double diamond, sharpened into a routine13.2 Ideation: quantity → quality13.3 Framing: problem statements that guide13.4 Lean UX & dscrum: research inside iteration13.5 Artifacts that scale trust

Process is how teams stay honest: decisions recorded, ideas tested cheaply, and "we must ship faster so we skip research" made visible for what it is.

13.1 The double diamond, sharpened into a routine

The double diamond becomes operational when it is compressed into a repeatable routine, such as a two-week rhythm that moves through discover, define, develop, and deliver with research at both ends. Run the cycle at whatever size fits: big swings for product direction, small loops for features. Force at least ten how-might-we framings before any prototype so the team explores the problem space before locking into a solution. The routine, not the ambition, is what makes the diamond work.

Week 1-2:  DISCOVER   interviews, field, logs, desk research
Week 2-3:  DEFINE     insights, problem statement ("How might we ...?")
Week 3-4:  DEVELOP    brainstorm 100 ideas, cluster, 3 prototypes
Week 4-5:  DELIVER    user-test, iterate, spec, ship, measure
Default mistake: DEVELOP with confidence but DISCOVER with a guess.
Force 10 "how might we" frames before any prototype.

The diamond only works as a rhythm

The double diamond is a diagram of four activities, and a diagram is not a process. Teams that adopt it as a shape and then work straight from brief to solution have changed the vocabulary and not the practice, which is why the shape outlives dozens of methods that were more effective. What makes it work is compressing it into a repeating routine with a fixed cadence, where each swing is small enough to actually be run and each cycle ends with evidence rather than a deliverable.

The rhythm that works has four beats and two kinds of output. Discover produces observations about what people do, gathered by observation and conversation rather than by opinion. Define produces a framed problem, which is the one artefact the whole cycle exists to produce. Develop produces several rough options, never one, because the divergence has to be real or the second diamond is a formality. Deliver produces a tested increment, and its test result is the input to the next cycle's discovery. The two evidence points are at the ends, and that is the part teams move: research bolted onto the front of a sprint is a phase, research fed back from the end of the previous cycle is a habit.

Two failure modes are worth naming because both are common and neither looks like failure at the time. The first is confident development on guessed discovery: the team spends its cycle building a well-executed version of an assumption nobody checked, and the test at the end confirms the assumption rather than the idea. The second is premature convergence: the define step produces one frame, so the develop step produces one option, so the test confirms a decision that was already made. A cheap structural guard against both is to require at least three distinct frames and three distinct concepts before any prototype is built, which is a number rather than a principle and therefore survives a bad week.

/* A cycle, written as a state machine, because the ordering constraint is
   the whole method and it is easier to enforce than to remember. */
const CYCLE = {
  'discover': {
    // evidence in, observations out. opinions are not evidence.
    activities: ['contextual inquiry', 'user interview', 'analytics review',
                 'support ticket mining', 'session replay sampling'],
    outputs: ['observation', 'verbatim'],
    requires: [],
  },
  'define': {
    activities: ['affinity mapping', 'problem framing', 'how-might-we'],
    outputs: ['problem frame'],
    requires: ['observation'],
    // the guard against premature convergence, as a number rather than a
    // principle, because principles do not survive a bad week
    minFrames: 3,
    rejectFrameIf: (f) => !f.who || !f.what || !f.constraint,
  },
  'develop': {
    activities: ['sketching', 'converging', 'prototyping'],
    outputs: ['concept'],
    requires: ['problem frame'],
    // three concepts, not one: with one, the second diamond is a formality
    minConcepts: 3,
    rejectIf: (c) => c.frames !== CYCLE.define.minFrames,
  },
  'deliver': {
    activities: ['usability testing', 'implementation', 'release'],
    outputs: ['test result', 'increment'],
    requires: ['concept'],
    // the result is an input to the next cycle, not a report nobody reads
    feedsBackTo: 'discover',
  },
};

/* Ten how-might-we framings, generated before any concept exists. The
   point is the tenth one: the first three are the ones you expected. */
function howMightWe(problem) {
  const ANGLES = [
    (p) => 'How might we make ' + p + ' visible to the people it affects?',
    (p) => 'How might we let ' + p + ' happen without the user asking for it?',
    (p) => 'How might we shrink the effort in ' + p + ' to one step?',
    (p) => 'How might we recover when ' + p + ' goes wrong?',
    (p) => 'How might we know ' + p + ' is happening, before it is reported?',
    (p) => 'How might we let someone else help with ' + p + '?',
    (p) => 'How might we make ' + p + ' work on a bad connection?',
    (p) => 'How might we make ' + p + ' reversible?',
    (p) => 'How might we teach the behaviour that avoids ' + p + '?',
    (p) => 'How might we make ' + p + ' disappear entirely?',
  ];
  return ANGLES.map((f) => f(problem));
}
console.log(howMightWe('checkout abandonment').join('\n'));

Scale the cycle, do not redesign it for each scale. A product direction question needs one big swing measured in weeks, and the same four beats apply. A feature needs a small two-week loop with the same four beats. A single screen improvement can be a four-day loop with the same four beats, and many teams find that a day-long loop on one interaction is the most productive cadence they have. What never works is a big swing at the top and straight-to-build underneath, because the second half of the method is where the learning happens and it is the half that gets compressed away under deadline.

The honest reason the rhythm is hard to keep is that it competes with delivery. Every cycle spends capacity on learning rather than on shipping, and the immediate, visible cost is real while the benefit is deferred and probabilistic. The way teams hold it is by making the learning cheap enough to defend: one interview a week rather than a study, a small panel rather than a recruited cohort, twenty minutes of testing rather than a lab day. A two-week cycle with five participants and a frame at the end is enough to keep the rhythm alive, and a rhythm that survives is worth more than a comprehensive study that happened once.

A two-week starter rhythm through discover, define, develop, and deliver, with the warning that confident developing on guessed discovery is the classic mistake.

13.2 Ideation: quantity → quality

Ideation works by generating a large quantity of ideas first and deferring judgment until later, because volume breaks fixation and widens the option space. Use exercises such as timeboxed brainstorming, crazy eights where each person sketches eight ideas in eight minutes, and storyboards that turn ideas into narratives. Defer evaluation, then converge by voting, clustering, and prototyping the strongest candidates. The best idea usually hides in the pile of the mediocre.

TechniqueGood for
Brainstorm (warm-up, deferred judgment)large option space, team energy
Crazy 8s (8 sketches × 8 minutes)fast breadth, kills fixation
Storyboard / comicscenario-level concepts, context
SCAMPER (substitute/combine/adapt/…)remixing what exists
"How might we" rewritesdefining the right problem before solving

Quantity first, judgement later

Ideation techniques are all variations on one instruction: generate more than you would have, then filter. The reason is not creativity in the abstract, it is fixation. The first idea is the one nearest to the obvious, and everything generated after it is anchored to it, so a session that converges in three minutes produces three refinements of the same idea and calls it options. Separating generation from evaluation is a workaround for a known cognitive limit rather than a facilitation technique, and that is why the separation has to be structural — a timer, a rule, a different person — rather than a resolution.

Three methods cover most situations. Brainstorming, timeboxed, is the general one: a defined problem, a fixed duration, no evaluation until the end, one idea per sticky note so nobody builds on anyone else's in real time. Crazy eights is for breaking fixation specifically: eight ideas, eight minutes, eight sketches, drawn not written, one per minute, no explaining. The drawing matters because it forces a different representation and because a bad sketch is visibly bad, which lowers the cost of proposing it. Storyboards work when the problem is a flow rather than a feature: eight frames that show a sequence, and the value is that the team has to agree on what happens between the frames.

/* The convergence step, made mechanical. Judgement is subjective and
   anchoring is real, so structure it: cluster on meaning, score against
   criteria declared BEFORE scoring, and record why something was dropped
   so the next cycle does not re-propose it. */

// 1. cluster by meaning, not by vote - voting before clustering rewards
//    articulation rather than value
function cluster(ideas) {
  const clusters = [];
  for (const idea of ideas) {
    const hit = clusters.find((c) =>
      c.members.some((m) => overlap(m.words, idea.words) >= 0.4));
    (hit || (clusters.push({ label: idea.words[0], members: [] }), clusters.at(-1)))
      .members.push(idea);
  }
  return clusters.map((c, i) => ({ id: 'C' + (i + 1), count: c.members.length,
                                   ideas: c.members.map((m) => m.text) }));
}
const overlap = (a, b) => a.filter((w) => b.includes(w)).length / Math.max(a.length, b.length);

// 2. criteria declared before scoring, so they cannot be reverse-engineered
const CRITERIA = [
  { key: 'addressesFrame', weight: 3, note: 'does it solve the framed problem, or a neighbouring one' },
  { key: 'feasibility',     weight: 2, note: 'can we build and test it in one cycle' },
  { key: 'differentiation', weight: 1, note: 'is it different from what we already have' },
  { key: 'riskOfHarm',      weight: -2, note: 'what does it break, and for whom' },
];

// 3. score, and keep the rejections with their reason
function converge(clusters) {
  const scored = clusters.map((c) => ({
    id: c.id,
    score: CRITERIA.reduce((sum, cr) =>
      sum + (c[cr.key] || 0) * cr.weight, 0),
    // the top three get built, not the top one: three concepts is the
    // minimum for the develop half of the diamond to be real
    build: false,
  }));
  scored.sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score);
  scored.slice(0, 3).forEach((s) => { s.build = true; });
  scored.slice(3).forEach((s) => { s.rejectedBecause = 'below the top 3 on the declared criteria'; });
  return scored;
}

/* Crazy eights, as a timer rather than a suggestion. One idea a minute,
   drawn not explained, and the facilitator's job is only to say "pen down". */
const CRAZY_EIGHTS = { count: 8, minutes: 8, artefact: 'sketch', rule: 'no verbal pitch' };

Evaluation needs a structure or it is a personality contest. Cluster by meaning first, because grouping similar ideas reveals how much of the session was the same idea in disguise, and that number is frequently the most useful thing the session produced. Then apply criteria that were written down before anyone scored, with weights, so the result cannot be reverse-engineered after the fact to justify a favourite. And select three rather than one, because the develop stage of a cycle needs real divergence and one winner is a decision made too early.

Two techniques add something the others miss. Worst possible idea inverts the constraint: generate deliberately absurd options, and the reason it works is that it removes the social cost of a bad idea, so the person who was going to have the good unconventional idea is finally able to say it. Analogical thinking borrows a solution from a different domain, and the reason it works is that the borrowed domain has no incumbent solution, so there is nothing to anchor to. Both are worth having in the toolbox for a session that has stalled.

/* The rejection log. This is the artefact nobody keeps and everybody
   wants: without it, the next session re-proposes the same ideas and
   argues about them again. Ten seconds to keep, forty minutes to
   reconstruct six weeks later. */
const REJECTED = [
  {
    idea: 'Coupon at the payment step',
    rejectedBecause: 'no frame it serves; the frame is comprehension, not price',
    // the parts that make a rejection reusable rather than merely recorded
    wouldRevisitIf: 'completion stays flat after the terms change',
    testedOn: '2026-03-04',
    byWhom: 'rk',
  },
  {
    idea: 'Mandatory account creation before cart',
    rejectedBecause: 'adds a step to every purchase and blocks guest checkout,
                      which is the majority of our traffic',
    wouldRevisitIf: 'fraud rate rises above 1%',
    testedOn: '2026-02-18',
    byWhom: 'rk',
  },
  {
    idea: 'A progress bar on a 3-step checkout',
    rejectedBecause: 'three steps is not enough to need one; it adds chrome
                      and implies the process is longer than it is',
    wouldRevisitIf: 'the flow grows past five steps',
    testedOn: '2026-02-18',
    byWhom: 'ad',
  },
];

/* The session record, so a rejected idea can be traced to the frame it
   was rejected against rather than to the mood of the room. */
const SESSION = {
  date: '2026-03-04',
  frame: 'F-007',
  method: 'crazy eights, 8 minutes, 8 sketches per person, 5 people',
  // the number that is usually the most useful output of the session:
  // how much of it was the same idea in disguise
  generated: 40,
  clustered: 11,
  distinct: 4,
  carriedForward: 3,
  rejected: REJECTED.length,
  note: '40 sketches became 4 real ideas; the clustering is the finding',
};

/* Convergence, with the winner deliberately not chosen in this function.
   Selecting one here is how a team skips the develop half of the diamond. */
function propose(clusters) {
  return clusters
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score)
    .slice(0, 3)
    .map((c) => ({ ...c, status: 'prototype' }));
}

Keep the record. The discarded ideas, with the reason they were dropped, are the most valuable output of an ideation session after the winners, because without them the next session re-proposes the same rejected options and argues about them again. A single list of "already considered and not chosen, because" is worth more than any set of slides, and it takes ten seconds to keep during the session and about forty of somebody's time to reconstruct six weeks later.

13.3 Framing: problem statements that guide

A problem frame is a deliberately shaped statement of the challenge that guides the whole project, and good framing names the who, the what, the when or where, and the constraints. Weak frames describe the symptom, such as users abandon checkout, while strong frames expose the underlying need and feel designable. Write the frame as a how-might-we question, validate it against real research, and revisit it as evidence grows. The frame decides what counts as success.

// Weak: "Build an onboarding flow"
// Weak: "Users abandon onboarding at step 3"   (symptom only)
// Frame:  "How might we help new users finish setup in under
//          3 minutes, on a phone, without a manual?"
// A good frame names: WHO (new users), WHAT (finish first-run),
// WHEN/where (mobile first time), CONSTRAINT (no manual).
// Test which frames feel DESIGNABLE (they suggest directions).

Why the frame decides the work

A problem frame is the statement the whole project is measured against, and it is worth understanding how much authority it carries: it decides what counts as evidence, which solutions are admissible, and what "done" means. A frame that says "users abandon checkout" makes every metric about checkout abandonment, which is why the team will improve checkout abandonment and nothing else, and a frame that says "buyers cannot tell what is included" makes a change to the pricing table look like the answer. Both are consequences of the frame and neither is a failure of execution.

The shape of a usable frame names four things: who, specifically enough that you can recruit them; what they are trying to do; when or where it happens, because a problem that happens at plan-selection is a different problem from one that happens at renewal; and the constraint that makes it hard. Constraints are the part teams leave out and they are the part that makes a frame designable, because a constraint is what turns a vague problem into something a team can begin to work on.

Distinguish a symptom from a need, because this is where most frames go wrong. "Users abandon checkout" is a symptom: it describes a number, it cannot be designed against, and acting on it produces coupon experiments forever. "First-time buyers cannot tell whether their card will be charged today or in 30 days" is a need: it names the moment, the population and the specific uncertainty, and it immediately suggests that the design problem is about making a term visible rather than about the price. Reframing from symptom to need is the single most valuable move in a discovery cycle, and it usually takes three or four attempts.

/* A frame, with its four parts and the tests it has to pass. Making the
   frame a structured object rather than a sentence means it can be
