    independent[coder] = await Promise.all(sessionIds.map((id) => code(id, RUBRIC, coder)));
  }

  const rows = sessionIds.flatMap((id) =>
    independent[coders[0]][sessionIds.indexOf(id)].map((a) => {
      const match = independent[coders[1]][sessionIds.indexOf(id)]
        .find((b) => sameEvent(a, b));
      return { session: id, ...a, agreement: !!match,
               otherLabel: match ? match.type : null,
               otherLocation: match ? match.location : null };
    }));

  const agreed = rows.filter((r) => r.agreement).length;
  const rate = +(agreed / rows.length).toFixed(2);

  // disagreements are where the rubric is broken. fixing the split
  // teaches nothing; fixing the rubric does.
  const disagreements = rows.filter((r) => !r.agreement);
  const byLabel = disagreements.reduce((acc, r) => {
    const key = r.type + ' vs ' + (r.otherLabel || 'unmatched');
    (acc[key] ||= []).push(r);
    return acc;
  }, {});

  return {
    agreementRate: rate,
    pass: rate >= 0.8,
    // the artefact worth keeping: the confusion, named and quantified
    rubricGaps: Object.entries(byLabel).map(([k, v]) => ({
      confusion: k, count: v.length,
      rubricFix: suggestRubricFix(k),
    })),
    reconciled: disagreements.map((r) => reconcile(r, coders)),
    note: rate < 0.8
      ? 'do not report these numbers yet; the coding is not reliable at this agreement'
      : 'reportable, with the disagreement rate stated',
  };
}

const RUBRIC = {
  errorTypes: {
    slip:     'wrong control pressed, right intention (near miss)',
    lapse:    'forgot, lost place, needed a reminder',
    mistake:  'wrong model of the system: chose something the design did not support',
    // the two that are easy to confuse and carry opposite design implications
    'abandon': 'gave up on the task',
    'workaround': 'found a route the designer did not intend',
  },
  location: 'the element, not the region: "plan dropdown option" not "top left"',
  // the fields that must always be present, so a coder cannot omit one
  required: ['type', 'location', 'expected', 'observed', 'recovered'],
};

/* Every finding carries its trace, or it is labelled a hunch. */
function finding({ text, count, of, quotes, timestamps, confidence }) {
  const traceable = quotes && quotes.length > 0 && timestamps && timestamps.length > 0;
  return {
    text,
    count, of,
    // the denominator is what makes the count a rate rather than a number
    rate: +((count || 0) / of).toFixed(2),
    quotes, timestamps,
    evidenceClass: traceable ? (count >= 3 ? 'finding' : 'signal')
                            : 'hunch',
    // the caveat travels with the number, so it cannot be quoted without
    if (of < 5 && traceable) confidence = 'indicative only, n=' + of;
    // what would settle it, which is required for a hunch
    falsifiedIf: traceable ? null
      : 'needs a targeted test: ' + (text.includes('search') ? '5 participants, task: find an invoice from 2024' : 'not yet designed'),
  };
}

Four biases to name, because each produces a confident wrong answer. Confirmation bias: the moderator who knows the hypothesis and asks a leading question at the moment it matters. The defence is scripted prompts and a recording somebody else may review. Social desirability: participants who are unwilling to criticise, particularly when they think the designer is watching. The defence is remote sessions, where the participant is alone with the screen. Moderator presence: people talk to the moderator instead of the interface, so a chatty session produces interesting conversation and no data. And novelty bias: the first reaction to anything is not the settled one, which is why a second test after a week of use produces different and usually better findings than the first.

/* Re-testing after ship, on the thing that actually shipped. A prototype
   test and a shipped test answer different questions, and only the second
   one predicts retention. */
const RETEST_PLAN = {
  journeys: {
    '/checkout':      { risk: 'revenue', interval: 'every release',
                        trigger: 'any change to payment, pricing or copy' },
    '/signup':        { risk: 'growth',  interval: 'every release',
                        trigger: 'any change to the form or its copy' },
    '/onboarding':    { risk: 'activation', interval: 'quarterly',
                        trigger: 'any change to the first-run experience' },
  },
  // the reason a post-launch retest finds different things: by then the
  // participant is no longer encountering it for the first time, so the
  // confusion has turned into a habit and the mistakes into workarounds.
  // both are findings, and neither was visible in the prototype test.
  whatChanges: [
    'confusion becomes a workaround: people stop being confused by finding a path you did not design',
    'the first-time question is gone, replaced by a second-time question',
    'the flow is now done with the tabs they have open, not the way the design assumed',
  ],
  // the measurement that catches it: compare week-one against month-three
  // on the SAME task, not against a benchmark from another product
  measure: {
    firstRun:  { participants: 5, when: 'within 3 days of signup' },
    settled:   { participants: 5, when: '30+ days, same task, same instrument' },
    report:    'both, side by side; a task that is easy once and hard again is a design problem',
    // the number that predicts churn better than any success rate
    watch: 'confidence from the ASQ, not just completion',
  },
};

/* Shipping without a retest is the specific failure: evidence about a
   thing that no longer exists, which is worse than no evidence because it
   is cited as current. */
function stalenessGate(finding, change) {
  if (change.shippedAt > finding.datedAt && !finding.retestedAfter) {
    return {
      status: 'stale',
      // not a warning anyone reads; a block on the ticket
      action: 'this finding describes a prototype, and the prototype has changed',
      required: 're-test ' + finding.journey + ' on the shipped build, or mark as historical',
    };
  }
  if (daysSince(finding.datedAt) > 180 && !finding.revalidatedAt) {
    return { status: 'old', action: 'revalidate or archive; do not cite' };
  }
  return { status: 'current' };
}

/* Moderator contamination: the checks that make a session defensible
   rather than merely recorded. */
const SESSION_QUALITY = {
  pilotRun: { participants: 2, who: 'not on the team', covers: 'the whole script end to end' },
  // the two moderator effects that produce confident wrong answers
  checks: [
    { name: 'no leading prompts',
      test: 'every prompt used appears in the script; anything else is a deviation and is noted',
      because: 'a moderator who knows the hypothesis asks the leading question at the wrong moment' },
    { name: 'recorded and independently reviewable',
      test: 'at least 20% of sessions reviewed by somebody who did not run them',
      because: 'the alternative is a moderator\'s memory as the only record' },
    { name: 'social desirability',
      test: 'remote preferred for any evaluative question; in-person only for physical tasks',
      because: 'a participant watching a designer will not criticise it' },
  ],
  // record the deviations rather than pretending there were none
  onDeviation: (what) => ({ logged: true, what, affectsAnalysis: 'see reconciliation' }),
};

The last practice is the one teams skip and the one that matters most: going back. A study of what people do in week one and a study of what they do in month three answer different questions, and the second one predicts retention far better than the first. If a change shipped and you tested the prototype but never the shipped thing, you have evidence about a thing that no longer exists. Re-test the journeys you changed, at whatever interval fits the risk, and record the date so the next person knows how fresh the evidence is.

15 · Psychology of UX

Psychology of UX applies established findings about memory, attention, decision, and motivation to interface design, because every screen is effectively a psychology experiment in disguise. Designers use mental models, affordances, recognition, habit loops, and known cognitive principles to predict how people will interpret and act on what they see. Knowing how working memory and attention actually work lets a designer defend choices with evidence instead of taste. It quietly predicts which usability problems users will hit first.

15.1 Cognitive load: working memory is the bottleneck15.2 The laws you’ll cite in every review15.3 Behavioral patterns worth knowing15.4 Bias in your own head (designer, watch out)15.5 Persuasion done honestly

Design decisions behave like psychology experiments. Knowing the mechanisms lets you predict behavior instead of guessing — and lets you defend designs with evidence, not taste.

15.1 Cognitive load: working memory is the bottleneck

Cognitive load describes how much mental effort a task demands, and working memory can only juggle a handful of chunks at once, so every screen either taxes it or spares it. Designers cut load with recognition over recall, sensible defaults, progressive disclosure, chunking, and clear system status throughout the flow. Match the load to the context and the user, because novices and experts consume working memory at very different rates. Reduce extraneous load before adding support for intrinsic load.

// Working memory holds ~4 chunks at once. Every screen either:
//   REDUCES load  (options visible, labels on inputs, recognized actions)
//   or ADDS load   (let me recall my past, hidden menus, jargon,
//                   multi-step wizards with nothing saved)
// The 4 reduction tools:
//   1 recognition over recall (Ch.6)   2 defaults & saved state
//   3 progressive disclosure (show more only when needed)
//   4 chunking (group, sections, headings)

Three kinds of load, and only two are worth removing

Cognitive load theory separates load into three kinds, and the distinction is what makes the theory useful rather than a slogan. Intrinsic load is the demand the task itself imposes: how many interacting elements must be held in mind at once. It is a property of the problem and you cannot design it away, only restructure it. Extraneous load is everything the interface adds that the task did not require: a decorative animation, an unfamiliar control, a form that asks for the same thing twice, a navigation model the user has to learn. Germane load is the effort of building a mental model, and it is not a cost — it is the thing that makes later steps fast. Removing germane load makes a task easier once and slower forever after, which is why "simplify until it's obvious" produces interfaces that are quick on the first pass and frustrating on the fortieth.

Extrinsic load is where the leverage is, and it has a short inventory. Recognition over recall: never make someone hold a code in their head to use it; show the options. Sensible defaults: make the common case require zero decisions, and make changing it visible rather than buried. Progressive disclosure: reveal complexity at the point it is needed, not on the first screen. Chunking: group related actions rather than presenting forty individually. Visible system status: tell the user what is happening, because uncertainty is itself load and a person who does not know the state will check for it, which costs a second.

Novice and expert differ in a specific and exploitable way. A novice's problem is germane: they must build a model, so every unfamiliar element costs, and they need signposts, examples and a preview of consequences. An expert's problem is extraneous: their model is already built, so the same signposts are pure overhead and are actively harmful, because they interrupt a fluent sequence and hide the keyboard shortcut that would have skipped past them. This is why a single interface serving both needs to be adaptive rather than generous — a mode, a preference, or a set of accelerators that a frequent user can learn and a new user never sees.

/* Load reduction as a review checklist, run against a real screen. Each
   item names the kind of load it removes, because removing germane load
   is a mistake even though the screen feels easier afterwards. */
const LOAD_AUDIT = [
  {
    item: 'Every option is visible rather than recalled',
    removes: 'extraneous',
    test: (dom) => countChoicesRememberedFromMemory(dom) === 0,
    // the anti-pattern: "enter the 6-digit code we texted you"
    instead: 'a resend button with a visible countdown',
  },
  {
    item: 'The common case needs zero decisions',
    removes: 'extraneous',
    test: (dom) => countFieldsWithDefaults(dom) >= countFields(dom) - 2,
    note: 'a default that the user must confirm is not a default',
  },
  {
    item: 'Complexity appears at the point of need',
    removes: 'extraneous',
    test: (dom) => countAlwaysVisibleAdvancedOptions(dom) === 0,
    // advanced options belong behind a disclosure that remembers its state
  },
  {
    item: 'System status is visible without navigation',
    removes: 'extraneous',
    test: (dom) => !!dom.querySelector('[aria-live], [role="status"], progress'),
    // uncertainty is load: a user who does not know the state checks for it
  },
  {
    item: 'A first-time user can build a model',
    removes: 'germane',
    test: () => 'novice path exists: labels, examples, consequence preview',
  },
  {
    item: 'A frequent user is not made to slow down',
    removes: 'extraneous',
    test: (dom) => countKeyboardAccelerators(dom) > 0 && hasSkipLinks(dom),
    // the pair that matters: accelerators for the expert, signposts for the novice
  },
  {
    item: 'Error prevention over error correction',
    removes: 'extraneous',
    test: (dom) => countDestructiveActionsWithoutConfirmation(dom) === 0,
  },
];

/* Chunking, and the limit. Working memory holds a small number of chunks,
   not a small number of items, so the win is in grouping by meaning rather
   than by count. Seven visible options in three named groups is lighter
   than four ungrouped ones. */
function chunks(groups) {
  return {
    // the chunk count is what the user holds, not the option count
    held: groups.length,
    totalOptions: groups.reduce((n, g) => n + g.options.length, 0),
    // a group with one option is a group that costs a chunk and saves nothing
    wasteful: groups.filter((g) => g.options.length < 2).length,
  };
}

/* The novice/expert split, expressed as one interface with two modes
   rather than two interfaces. The trigger is frequency, not a preference
   the user has to find and set. */
const ADAPT = {
  // novice: signposts, examples, and a preview of what will happen
  novice: {
    show: ['inline help', 'consequence preview', 'explicit confirm on submit',
           'plain-language errors with a next step'],
    hide: ['accelerator hints'],
  },
  // expert: accelerators, fewer words, less ceremony
  expert: {
    show: ['keyboard shortcut hints', 'bulk actions', 'saved views', 'raw counts'],
    hide: ['inline help', 'confirmations for reversible actions'],
  },
  // frequency decides, and the decision is reversible and visible
  switchesOn: 'after 5 sessions, with a visible switch in settings',
};

Chunking has a limit that teams cross routinely. Grouping works while the groups are meaningful, because a meaningful group can be held as one unit. It stops working when groups are arbitrary, because then the user must learn the grouping before they can use it, and they are holding the grouping as well as the group. The test is whether a newcomer could predict the grouping from the content alone; if they could only predict it by being told, the group headers are extra load rather than a reduction.

Match the load to the context, which means the load a screen carries should be justified by the task and nothing else. A task a person does twice a month should carry its own explanation every time, because the alternative is remembering, and remembering is what people fail at. A task done forty times a day should carry as little as possible, because at that frequency any ceremony is paid forty times. Getting this backwards is the most common long-term design error in a product, and it is invisible in the design file because the file is not being used at either frequency.

The diagnostic that finds it. Watch somebody who has not used the product for three months, and count the questions they ask that a regular user would not. Each of those is a piece of germane load that is being paid again on every visit — and the fix is rarely to remove the explanation, which is what the instinct suggests, but to shorten it and make it visible. A regular user can ignore a short note; they cannot ignore nothing, because they will guess.

A personal crib sheet for cutting cognitive load: recognition over recall, defaults, progressive disclosure, and chunking are the four tools to apply on every screen.

15.2 The laws you’ll cite in every review

These are the usability laws cited in almost every design review, drawn from human-computer interaction research and a shared vocabulary for most design debates. Fitts' law fixes target size and distance, Hick’s law links more choices to slower decisions, Miller’s law respects working memory limits, and Jakob’s law favors familiar conventions. Zeigarnik and peak-end explain why unfinished tasks nag and why endings color memory. Citing the relevant law turns preference debates into evidence-based ones.

LawRuleDesign use
Fitts’sbigger + closer = faster to hitprimary actions large and near thumb/cursor
Hick’smore choices = slower decisionscut options; default sensibly
Miller’s 7±2limits of memorized itemschunk lists, steps, fragments of forms
Jakob’susers prefer familiar patternsfollow conventions; novelty is a tax
Zeigarnikunfinished tasks nagprogress saved, "almost done" re-entry
Peak–endwe remember peak + end, not the summake the final step feel great, avoid a bad end

The laws, and what each one is actually for

A usability law is a finding, and citing one turns "I prefer this" into "this is what the evidence says". That is the whole value of the vocabulary, and it is worth being precise about each law's scope, because the most common misuse is applying a law outside its conditions and then treating the result as an argument in its favour.

Fitts' law says movement time grows with the log of distance divided by target size, so bigger and closer targets are faster, and the log is what makes size matter more than distance at small scales. It applies to pointing, not to reading or to decision-making, and its most useful corollary is that a small target far away can be worse than a large one nearby, and that halving the distance beats doubling the size once targets are already comfortable. Hick's law says decision time grows with the logarithm of the number of choices, but it is about choice not about elements: a page with forty links and one clear next step is fast, and a dialog with three equally weighted buttons is slow. Miller's law — the 7±2 figure — is the most over-cited law in the set, because the original work was about absolute span rather than chunking, and the modern reading is closer to four chunks; the useful version is that working memory is small, so reduce what must be held rather than adding capacity. Jakob's law — users spend most of their time on other products, so prefer the convention they already have, because self-invented clarity for a user who arrives from elsewhere is not clarity.

Zeigarnik's effect is that incomplete tasks are recalled better than completed ones, which is a fact about memory and therefore a caution: an unresolved item holds attention, which is why a progress indicator that stops at 90 percent is worse than one that does not exist. The peak-end rule says memory of an experience is dominated by the most intense moment and the ending, not the average, which makes the final screen and the worst error the two highest-leverage screens in a flow. Von Restorff's effect — the isolation effect — says the distinctive item is remembered, so one element that differs is remembered and everything that looks alike blends. Hohman's law says people retrieve information faster when it is placed where they will look for it, which is why a settings screen that scatters a preference across five pages is worse than one that puts it where the mental model puts it.

/* The laws, with their conditions. A law cited outside its conditions is
   not evidence, it is a preference wearing a citation. */
const LAWS = [
  {
    name: "Fitts' law",
    statement: 'Movement time grows with log(distance / target size).',
    appliesTo: 'pointing at a target with a cursor, finger or stylus',
    doesNotApplyTo: ['reading', 'decision between already-visible options',
                     'keyboard entry, which has no pointing component'],
    corollary: 'At comfortable target sizes, halving the distance beats
                doubling the size. Get the primary action near where the
                pointer already is.',
    // the measurable version, so a review can settle the argument
    measure: (a, b) => Math.log2(2 * Math.max(a.distance, 1) / Math.max(a.size, 1)),
  },
  {
    name: "Hick's law",
    statement: 'Decision time grows with log(1 + number of choices).',
    appliesTo: 'choosing between options presented at once',
    // the distinction that makes it useful and the misreading that does not
    doesNotApplyTo: ['counting elements on a page: 40 links and one clear
                      next step is a fast page'],
    corollary: 'Grouping recovers most of the benefit of reducing choices.
                Three groups of four is lighter than twelve flat options.',
  },
  {
    name: "Miller's law',
    statement: 'Working memory holds about four chunks, not seven plus or
                minus two, and not items.',
    correction: 'the original 1956 work concerned absolute span; the chunking
                 reading is later. Cite it as a heuristic, not a constant.',
    appliesTo: 'what a person must hold while acting',
    corollary: 'Reduce what must be held. Do not plan to increase capacity.',
  },
  {
    name: "Jakob's law",
    statement: 'People spend most of their time on other software, so
                prefer the convention they already know.',
    appliesTo: 'anything a user arrives at from another product',
    doesNotApplyTo: ['genuinely novel tasks, where no convention exists and
                      invention is required'],
    corollary: 'Invent only where the task is new. Everywhere else, copy.',
  },
  {
    name: 'Zeigarnik effect',
    statement: 'Incomplete tasks are recalled better than completed ones.',
    appliesTo: 'memory, not motivation',
    corollary: 'A progress indicator that stalls reads as a broken promise.
                Either finish or do not start.',
  },
  {
    name: 'Peak-end rule',
    statement: 'Memory of an experience is dominated by its peak and its end.',
    // this is the most actionable of the six and the most neglected
    corollary: 'The confirmation screen and the worst error are the two
                highest-leverage screens in the whole flow. Design them
                first, not last.',
  },
  {
    name: 'Von Restorff (isolation) effect',
    statement: 'A distinctive element is remembered; like elements blend.',
    corollary: 'One thing that looks different is remembered. That is why a
                single primary button works and five equally weighted
                buttons do not.',
  },
  {
    name: "Hohman's law",
    statement: 'People look for information where they expect it to be.',
    corollary: 'Put the answer where the mental model puts it, not where the
                database has it.',
  },
];

/* Using a law in a review, correctly. The output is a decision, not a
   citation, and the citation is what makes it checkable. */
function reviewArgument({ claim, law, measuredBefore, measuredAfter, alternative }) {
  return {
    claim, law,
    // a law without a measurement is a slogan. name the number or drop the law.
    evidence: measuredBefore != null
      ? measuredBefore + ' -> ' + measuredAfter
      : 'NOT MEASURED - this is a preference',
    // and name the condition under which the law stops applying, because
    // that is the part of the argument a reviewer should attack
    breaksIf: LAWS.find((l) => l.name.startsWith(law.slice(0, 8)))?.doesNotApplyTo,
    alternative,
  };
}

Turning a law into a number, or dropping it

A law earns its place in a review only when it produces a measurement. That is a stricter bar than it sounds: Fitts' law produces a target size in pixels and a distance in pixels, Hick's law produces a count of simultaneous choices, Miller's law produces a count of things that must be held, Jakob's law produces a comparison against the convention elsewhere, and the peak-end rule produces a score on the last screen and the worst error. A law that produces no number is a rule of thumb, and it belongs in a blog post rather than in an argument about a specific screen.

Two of these are cheap enough to run on every screen and are almost never run. Target size and choice count are both computable from the DOM, which means a design review can compare two variants without anybody forming an opinion first — and removing the opinion from the first five minutes is most of the value, because two of the three parties at such a review arrive with a preference already formed. The other two are judgements, and a judgement is fine as long as the person making it says which measurement would have settled it.

/* The computable half of the law set, run over a DOM before opinions are
   exchanged. Both of these are arithmetic, so neither party has to be
   trusted: the numbers are the numbers. */
function measureScreen(root) {
  const targets = [...root.querySelectorAll('button, a, input, [role="button"], [tabindex="0"]')]
    .filter((el) => el.offsetParent !== null);   // skip display:none, which has no size
  const sizes = targets.map((el) => {
    const r = el.getBoundingClientRect();
    return { el, w: r.width, h: r.height, area: r.width * r.height };
  });
  // WCAG 2.2 asks for 24x24 CSS px minimum, and 44x44 for a comfortable
  // touch target. Both are worth reporting; they are not the same ask.
  const belowMinimum = sizes.filter((s) => s.w < 24 || s.h < 24);
  const belowTouch = sizes.filter((s) => s.w < 44 || s.h < 44);

  // Hick's law is about simultaneous choice, so it is measured at the point
  // of decision rather than over the whole page.
  const decisionPoints = [...root.querySelectorAll('[role="radiogroup"], nav, .toolbar, dialog')]
    .map((el) => ({ el, choices: el.querySelectorAll('a, button, [role="radio"], [role="menuitem"]').length }));

  return {
    targets: sizes.length,
    medianArea: median(sizes.map((s) => s.area)),
    // the ones to fix first: not the smallest, the ones in the primary path
    primaryOffenders: belowMinimum.filter((s) => inPrimaryPath(s.el)),
    belowTouch: belowTouch.length,
    decisions: decisionPoints,
    // grouping recovers most of Hick's benefit, so a flat high count is a
    // different problem from a grouped high count
    flattestDecision: decisionPoints.slice().sort((a, b) => b.choices - a.choices)[0],
  };
}

/* The uncomputable half, written down so it can be attacked. Each entry
   names the measurement that would settle it, because "I think it feels
   faster" is not a finding and does not become one by being repeated. */
const JUDGEMENTS = [
  {
    law: "Jakob's law",
    claim: 'the primary action is where users of comparable products expect it',
    comparable: ['Gmail compose', 'Superhuman search', 'Mail compose'],
    settlesIt: 'first-click testing against the three comparables, n=8',
    // the boundary, stated in advance, so it can be used against the claim
    stopsApplyingIf: 'the task is not one users have performed in the comparable tools',
  },
  {
    law: 'peak-end rule',
    claim: 'the confirmation screen feels calm rather than anxious',
    settlesIt: 'free-text post-task debrief plus 5-second recall of what was charged',
    stopsApplyingIf: 'the task ends in a place the user does not experience as an ending',
  },
  {
    law: 'Miller's law',
    claim: 'four things must be held at once here, not seven',
    settlesIt: 'a walkthrough where the facilitator counts aloud what the participant recalls',
    stopsApplyingIf: 'the participant is reading the values rather than holding them',
  },
];

/* The standing record that keeps the vocabulary honest. A decision cites the
   law, the measurement, and the condition that would have falsified it, so
   six months later the team can find the assumption rather than the argument. */
const DECISIONS = [
  {
    decidedAt: '2026-02-11',
    question: 'should the filter row stay visible during results scrolling?',
    citedLaw: "Fitts' law",
    measured: 'median pointer travel to Sort: 318px; after pinning: 74px',
    decided: 'pin it, and keep the pin visible only while results are on screen',
    falsifiedIf: 'task time does not fall, or users report losing the filter state',
    recheckDue: '2026-08-11',
  },
];

The laws are most useful as a shared vocabulary and least useful as design rules, and the reason is worth stating: each describes a tendency under specific conditions, and an interface designed to satisfy all of them at once will frequently be worse. Von Restorff says one thing should stand out; Miller says nothing can be held; Hick says reduce choices; Jakob says keep the convention. These are in tension more often than they agree, and resolving the tension is the designer's job rather than the law's. The peak-end rule has no counter-law in the set, which is one reason it gets actioned so rarely.

Two habits make the vocabulary work. Name the law when you are arguing for a position, and then name the condition under which it would stop applying — because a claim with a stated boundary can be evaluated, and a claim without one cannot. And record which law a decision was made against, so that six months later when the evidence disagrees, the team can find the assumption that was wrong rather than re-arguing the whole thing with a new metaphor.

15.3 Behavioral patterns worth knowing

Behavioral patterns describe predictable tendencies people bring to interfaces: they keep defaults, fear losses more than they value gains, follow social proof, and fall into habit loops. Used honestly, defaults guide good choices, testimonials reduce uncertainty, and habit loops build healthy routines. Designers should map where each pattern appears in their flows, then test it against the fairness question so the pattern never tips into a dark pattern. Honest use converts on repeat purchase, not on panic.

PatternMechanismWhen it backfires
Default bias / status-quopeople keep defaultstricky defaults = dark pattern
Loss aversionfear of losing > joy of gaining"Only 3 rooms left!" pressure gone wrong
Social prooffollow othersfake counts = legal+trust risk
Habit loops (cue→routine→reward)repeated rewarded actionscompulsion design (Ch.20)

Defaults, loss, social proof, and habit

Four behavioural patterns explain most of what people do in an interface, and each becomes useful or harmful depending entirely on how it is used. Defaults are the strongest: people keep them, often without noticing, because changing a default takes an action and doing nothing does not. That makes a default the single most consequential thing a product decides on a user's behalf, and it is why a default that benefits the provider more than the user is a governance question rather than a design question. Loss aversion means a loss feels roughly twice as large as an equal gain, which explains why a free trial ending is felt as a loss and a discount not applied is felt as a miss. Social proof reduces uncertainty by showing what others did, which is genuinely useful when you are choosing between unfamiliar options and actively misleading when the numbers are not real. Habit loops — cue, routine, reward — describe how behaviour repeats, and they are the mechanism behind both a daily habit and a subscription nobody can cancel.

Each has a legitimate use and a dark version, and the difference is almost always disclosure. A default that is visible, explained and trivially changed is a helpful default; the same default hidden inside a settings page three clicks away is a dark pattern wearing the same value. Social proof that reports real numbers is information; a counter that resets when you leave the page is fabrication, and no amount of good taste in the rest of the product makes that acceptable. Loss aversion used to make a reversible decision feel risky is honest; used to hide the end date of a trial is deception.

/* The pattern register. Every persuasive or habitual element in the product
   gets a row, with the fairness question answered in writing, because
   "is this a dark pattern" is a question that should be asked before
   launch rather than in a screenshot thread afterwards. */
const PATTERN_REGISTER = [
  {
    id: 'P-01',
    pattern: 'default',
    where: 'billing plan preselected to annual; marketing opt-out preselected',
    benefitToUser: 'the plan most of our users want, and the one with the
                    higher retention and lower support volume',
    // the three tests a default has to pass. failing any one makes it dark.
    tests: {
      visibleAtPointOfChoice: true,   // shown, not buried in settings
      equallyEasyToChange: true,      // one action, not a phone call
      wouldYouDefendItToAFriend: true,
    },
    failureMode: 'a default set only because it raises our revenue',
    owner: 'pm',
  },
  {
    id: 'P-02',
    pattern: 'loss aversion',
    where: 'trial countdown; "your saved items expire"',
    benefitToUser: 'a genuine deadline is information the user wants',
    tests: {
      theLossIsReal: true,            // not manufactured urgency
      theDeadlineIsReal: true,        // the date it actually ends
      reversibleIfMissed: true,
    },
    failureMode: 'a countdown that resets on reload, or a trial end date that
                  moves when the user looks at the page',
    verdict: 'ship only with the real date on the page in text',
  },
  {
    id: 'P-03',
    pattern: 'social proof',
    where: '"most popular" badge; usage counts; customer logos',
    benefitToUser: 'reduces uncertainty when choosing between unfamiliar options',
    tests: {
      numbersAreReal: true,           // from our data, not invented
      numbersAreCurrent: true,
      hasADenominator: true,          // "2,400 teams" beats "2,400" alone
    },
    failureMode: 'a counter that resets per visitor, or "4.9 out of 5"
                  derived from nine self-selected respondents',
    verdict: 'ship with a stated source and a stated date',
  },
  {
    id: 'P-04',
    pattern: 'habit loop',
    where: 'daily digest; streak counts; weekly report',
    benefitToUser: 'a genuine routine the user wanted, visible and pausable',
    tests: {
      userCanPause: true,             // and the pause survives a reinstall
      cueIsVisible: true,
      rewardIsReal: false,            // no streak punishment, no guilt copy
    },
    failureMode: 'a streak that resets silently and generates daily guilt
                  notifications to keep it alive',
    verdict: 'pause and delete must be one action each',
  },
];

/* The fairness question, as a gate rather than a discussion. */
function isDark(row) {
  const t = row.tests;
  const fails = Object.entries(t).filter(([, v]) => v === false).map(([k]) => k);
  return { dark: fails.length > 0, fails, row: row.id };
}
// P-04 fails rewardIsReal, so it cannot ship until the streak punishment
// is removed. That is the gate doing the work a screenshot thread does not.

/* The habit loop, written down, because a loop nobody has drawn is a
   loop nobody can decide anything about. */
function habitLoop(cue, routine, reward) {
  return {
    cue, routine, reward,
    // the three questions that distinguish a healthy loop from an
    // engineered one
    wouldUserDescribeItAsUseful: null,   // must be answered by a user, not by us
    canItBeEndedWithoutPenalty: null,
    // and the honest one: does the reward serve the user or the metric
    rewardServes: null,
  };
}

Auditing the defaults, because they are the consequential ones

The default is the highest-leverage element in the whole product and it is almost always set by an engineer implementing a ticket, in a code review that lasted ninety seconds. That is the structural reason dark defaults exist: nobody is deciding to be manipulative, a field is pre-filled, and it ships. So the audit has to be mechanical rather than a conversation, because the conversation is the thing that failed.

A default is defensible when three things are simultaneously true. It is visible at the point of choice, so the person can see what was chosen for them without opening anything. Changing it costs one action and no more — no phone call, no support ticket, no "contact us". And the party who benefits from it could state it to the other party's face. A default that fails any of the three is not automatically wrong, but it needs a named owner and a written reason, which is what turns it from a code review accident into a decision.

/* The default audit. Reads the shipped configuration, not the design file,
   because the design file is where the intent lives and the config is where
   the behaviour lives, and those two drift. */
function auditDefaults(config) {
  const rows = [];
  for (const d of config.defaults) {
    const visible = visibleAtPointOfChoice(d);          // shown at the choice, not buried
    const stepsToChange = countStepsToChange(d);        // one action or it is not a default
    const statedBeneficiary = d.beneficiary || 'unstated';
    const defendable = statedBeneficiary === 'the user';

    rows.push({
      field: d.field,
      value: d.value,
      visibleAtChoice: visible,
      stepsToChange,
      beneficiary: statedBeneficiary,
      // the three tests, each one independently disqualifying
      verdict: visible && stepsToChange <= 1 && defendable
        ? 'defensible'
        : 'NEEDS A NAMED OWNER AND A WRITTEN REASON',
      // and what to do about it, which is the only useful part of an audit
      fix: !visible ? 'show the current value next to the control that changes it'
         : stepsToChange > 1 ? 'make the change a single action, in the same view'
         : !defendable ? 'state the benefit in the sentence beside the control'
         : null,
    });
  }
  return rows.sort((a, b) => Number(a.verdict !== 'defensible') - Number(b.verdict !== 'defensible'));
}

/* One worked example, at the level of detail that makes the test arguable. */
const ANNUAL_PLAN = {
  field: 'billing.plan',
  value: 'annual',
  // preselected because 71% of self-serve signups who pick a plan choose
  // annual when offered, and because annual churns less
  beneficiary: 'the user, on retention',
  visibleAtPointOfChoice: true,        // "Billed annually, £240" is on the button
  stepsToChange: 1,                    // the plan selector, same screen, no reload
  monthlyPrice: '£20 per month, £240 per year',
  // the sentence that has to be there, and the reason: the whole honesty
  // question is whether the saving and the commitment are both stated
  copyBesideControl: 'Billed annually. Cancel any time. Switch to monthly at any point.',
  verdict: 'defensible',
};

/* The counter-example. Nothing here is deception on its own; the whole
   problem is that the cost is one field further down the page. */
const MARKETING_OPT_IN = {
  field: 'preferences.marketing',
  value: true,                          // preselected
  beneficiary: 'the user',
  visibleAtPointOfChoice: false,        // the box is checked, nobody reads a checked box
  stepsToChange: 1,
  // and the asymmetry that makes it dark regardless of the above: this is
  // consent, and consent by inaction is not consent in most jurisdictions
  note: 'consent requires an affirmative act. This one is a regulatory finding, not a taste question.',
  verdict: 'NEEDS A NAMED OWNER AND A WRITTEN REASON',
  fix: 'default to off, and state the difference between on and off in the same sentence',
};

/* What the audit outputs, so it can go in a review rather than a doc. */
const AUDIT_RESULT = {
  ranAt: '2026-03-04',
  fieldsAudited: 31,
  defensible: 27,
  needsOwner: [
    { field: 'preferences.marketing', reason: 'consent by preselection' },
    { field: 'seatCount', reason: 'defaults to the largest bundle rather than one seat' },
    { field: 'sso.enforce', reason: 'on by default is the right call; the copy does not say so' },
  ],
  // the metric that makes this repeatable rather than a one-off
  standingRule: 'no default ships in a release without a row in this audit',
};

Testimonials deserve a specific warning, because they are the pattern most often used honestly by accident. A testimonial is social proof with the sample size removed: one person's experience presented as evidence about everyone, usually chosen for enthusiasm rather than representativeness. The defensible version is a customer's own words attributed to them with enough context to judge, and the indefensible one is an unattributed quote in a place where a reader takes it as representative. The test is whether the reader could tell what kind of evidence they are looking at.

Habit is where the line is hardest and where the cost of getting it wrong is highest, because the mechanism that makes a product valuable is the same mechanism that makes it hard to leave. A useful product can be opened daily because it earns that; a product that opens daily because leaving is made difficult is a different product with the same metrics. The two questions to ask are whether the user would describe the loop as useful, and whether it can be ended without penalty — and both must be answered by users, not inferred from retention.

Map the patterns, then draw the line once. Before building a flow, list every element in it that leverages a behavioural pattern: defaults, scarcity, social proof, streaks, loss framing, commitment devices. Then decide, in writing, where your product's line is. Having done it once for the flow, each new element in that flow is a fast yes-or-no rather than a fresh argument, and the argument that never has to be had twice is the one that gets won consistently.

15.4 Bias in your own head (designer, watch out)

These biases apply to designers themselves, not just their users: anchoring on the first idea, confirmation bias that seeks supporting evidence, sunk cost that clings to old directions, and recency that overweights the latest opinion. Every bias pushes a designer to trust their gut over data. Naming the bias in a review is the first step, then deliberately gather disconfirming evidence such as user tests, analytics, and outside feedback. Let evidence decide, not instinct.

  • Anchoring: your first idea pulls the whole conversation — brainstorm to broaden first.
  • Confirmation: you notice evidence matching your design. Force "what would prove me wrong?"
  • IKEA effect / sunk cost: liking your own prototype more than a test participant does. Kill it on data, not preference.
  • Recency: the last complaint outweighs the pattern. Keep a research log, not a mood.

Your biases, and the only defence that works

The biases that shape a design are the team's, not only the user's, and they are the reason a product can ship a well-researched answer to the wrong question. Anchoring is the strongest: the first idea discussed pulls the whole conversation, and everything afterwards is judged against it rather than against the space of alternatives. Confirmation bias then filters the evidence — you notice the sessions that support the design and the ones that do not are attributed to a bad participant or a bad day. The IKEA effect means you rate your own work higher the more effort you put in, so the prototype you spent a week on beats the one a colleague produced in an afternoon, regardless of what users do. Sunk cost is the same force applied to a direction rather than an artefact. And recency is the reason one angry email outweighs a hundred sessions, because it is the most recent and the most emotionally available.

The defences are all the same shape: force the disconfirming evidence to exist before the decision. Ask "what would make this wrong" before anyone argues for it, and write the answer down in advance, because asking afterwards produces a token search. Generate alternatives before evaluation rather than after, which mechanically removes the first idea's advantage. Test with people who have no stake, and read the transcripts rather than the summaries, because a summary written by a stakeholder is already filtered.

Then make the evidence harder to reinterpret than the opinion is to state. A number with a count, a quote, a timestamp and a stated sample size cannot be argued with as effectively as a memory of a session, and that asymmetry is the point: a team that keeps a research log with dates does not have this problem, because there is a record that predates the conclusion. That is the whole mechanism, and it is why the log matters more than any workshop.

/* The pre-mortem, run before the decision rather than after it. It works
   because asking what caused the failure produces different answers than
   asking what caused the success, and because failure reasons written in
   advance cannot be retrofitted to whatever happened. */
function preMortem(project, { monthsOut = 6 } = {}) {
  return {
    prompt: 'It is ' + monthsOut + ' months later and this shipped and failed. ' +
            'Write the post-mortem. What happened?',
    // the questions that surface mechanisms rather than symptoms
    prompts: [
      'Whose goal did we optimise for, and who was left behind?',
      'What did we believe that was never tested?',
      'Which decision did we make fastest?',
      'What did we ship that nobody asked for?',
      'What would a competitor have noticed that we did not?',
      'Which number did we optimise that we should not have?',
    ],
    // and the two that are hardest to answer and most diagnostic
    hardest: [
      'What evidence would have changed our mind, and did we ever look for it?',
      'If this failed, would we have called it a failure, or a pivot?',
    ],
    output: { cause, mechanism, earlyWarningSignal, wouldHaveBeenVisibleAt: 'day 30' },
  };
}

/* The alternative-generation protocol that defeats anchoring: divergence
   before evaluation, and the first idea excluded from evaluation entirely. */
const DIVERGE = {
  // the structural rule: nobody evaluates until everyone has produced
  step1: 'each person writes 3 solutions independently and silently',
  step2: 'all are shown at once, with no author',
  // the mechanical move that removes anchoring: the person whose idea is
  // on screen does not know which one is theirs
  step3: 'evaluate against criteria declared in step 0, criterion by criterion',
  // and the guard against the idea that merely survives
  step4: 'the top 3 are prototyped, not the top 1',
  rule: 'if one person proposed it, that person does not present it',
};

/* The bias register: what each one predicts, and the artefact that
   catches it. A bias without a mechanism is a warning nobody acts on. */
const BIASES = [
  {
    bias: 'anchoring',
    predicts: 'the conversation converges on the first serious idea',
    artefact: 'silent independent generation, first idea anonymised',
    // the check that verifies the mechanism rather than assuming it
    verify: (proposals) => new Set(proposals.map((p) => p.idea)).size >= 6,
  },
  {
    bias: 'confirmation',
    predicts: 'supporting sessions are cited; opposing ones are explained away',
    artefact: 'insight log with dates and verbatims, written during not after',
    verify: (log) => log.some((i) => i.contradictsFrame) &&
                      log.some((i) => i.supportsFrame),
  },
  {
    bias: 'IKEA effect',
    predicts: 'effort spent correlates with rating, not with results',
    artefact: 'blinded prototypes with no attribution in the test session',
    verify: (results) => results.some((r) => r.preferred !== r.mostEffort),
  },
  {
    bias: 'sunk cost',
    predicts: 'a defended direction outlives its evidence',
    artefact: 'the date the decision was made, and what was believed then',
    verify: (d) => Boolean(d.decidedAt && d.believedThen && d.falsifiedIf),
    // the question that breaks it
    ask: 'if we had not built this, would we start it today?',
  },
  {
    bias: 'recency',
    predicts: 'one loud input outweighs a pattern',
    artefact: 'dated log, so the loud input is one row and not the record',
    verify: (log) => log.length > 10 && log.every((i) => i.datedAt),
  },
  {
    bias: 'survivorship',
    predicts: 'you only see the people who completed, so the
               people who left are invisible',
    artefact: 'research that recruits by frame, not by completion',
    verify: (sample) => sample.filter((p) => p.abandoned).length > 0,
  },
];

/* The check that is worth running before every decision meeting. */
function whatWouldChangeOurMind(frame) {
  return {
    frame: frame.text,
    // required before the meeting, not during it
    disconfirmingEvidence:
      'at least 3 participants with no difficulty on the current design',
    howWeWillLook: 'task test, n=5, 3 of 5 succeeding unprompted',
    whoDecidesIfContradicted: 'the frame owner, in writing, within a week',
  };
}

The two artefacts: an insight log and a decision record

Both biases that hide inside a process — survivorship and motivated reasoning — are caught by the same thing: a record that existed before the conclusion. That is the whole mechanism, and it is why the effort goes into writing things down with dates rather than into more workshops. A workshop produces opinions; a log produces evidence that can disagree with an opinion later, which is the only property that matters.

The insight log needs five fields and no more, and the discipline is that the entry is written during the session rather than after it, because a summary written afterwards has already been filtered by the person who will present it. The decision record needs the falsification condition written at the moment of deciding, for the same reason — a condition written afterwards will be one the decision already satisfies.

/* The insight log. Five fields. The value is entirely in the fourth one and
   in the fact that it is written before the read-out, because a summary
   written afterwards is already filtered by whoever will present it. */
const INSIGHT_LOG = {
  id: 'F-031',
  datedAt: '2026-03-04',                 // non-negotiable: recency bias needs no dates
  sessionId: 'P-07-checkout-2026-03-04',
  participant: { recruitedFor: 'has not used a competitor in 12 months', cohort: 'new' },

  observation: '4 of 5 read the total including VAT and then asked which line was the charge',
  // the field that does the work: it is required to be a contradiction when
  // there is one, so a session that only confirms cannot be filed as neutral
  contradictsFrame: true,

  frameAtTimeOfObservation: 'users understand the checkout summary',
  // verbatim, timestamped, so it cannot be paraphrased into agreement later
  evidence: ['#00:04:12  I cannot tell which of these I am paying today',
             '#00:09:40  so this is the amount now?'],

  // the two halves of the same row, because survivorship lives in the gap
  // between them: sessions where people reached the point, and sessions
  // where they did not, both get logged
  reachedDecisionPoint: false,
  abandonedAt: 'P07-04',

  severity: 24,                          // how many sessions, of how many
  denominator: 5,
};

/* The recruitment guard for survivorship. Every method available is biased
   toward completion, so recruitment is the only place the bias can be cut. */
const RECRUITMENT = {
  // analytics: people who errored are in the error log, not the funnel
  missing: 'sessions that ended in an error or an abandonment',
  // usability tests: participants are recruited from people who could find
  // the signup page at all
  missing: 'people who never got to the flow',
  // support tickets: written by people willing to write, which skews to the
  // articulate and to the recently annoyed
  missing: 'everyone who gave up quietly',

  therefore: {
    recruitBy: 'frame characteristics, not by having arrived',
    // the standing recruitment task that fixes it, done quarterly
    huntFor: 'people who abandoned at the same step in the last 30 days',
    how: 'a 15-minute screener that ends the session at that step, on purpose',
    note: 'a study that cannot fail is a study that cannot find anything',
  },
};

/* The decision record. The falsification condition is the field that makes it
   useful: written at the time of deciding, it is a promise the team can be
   held to, and it is usually one nobody wants to write down. */
const DECISION = {
  decidedAt: '2026-03-11',
  decider: 'product lead',
  decision: 'keep the single-page checkout; do not split into steps',
  statedBeforePreference: true,          // the evidence came before the position

  evidenceFor: [
    { claim: 'splitting raised abandonment in the 2025 test', n: 12, direction: 'worse' },
    { claim: 'completion time is well under the attention span', n: 12, direction: 'better' },
  ],
  evidenceAgainst: [
    { claim: 'the two hardest customers are the ones who abandon', n: 0, direction: 'unknown' },
    // zero, not a missing row. recording it as zero rather than omitting it
    // is what stops the survivorship gap from being invisible
    note: 'no data: our recruiting excluded anyone who had already abandoned',
  ],

  falsifiedIf: 'error rate on the payment step rises above 0.4% within 60 days',
  whoChecks: 'engineering lead',
  recheckDue: '2026-05-11',
  // and the sunk-cost question, asked at every recheck rather than at the end
  stillRightIfWeStartedToday: null,
};

/* The artefact the pre-mortem produces, and why it must be written before
   the project rather than after the failure: reasons composed afterwards
   always fit whatever happened, and that is precisely the problem. */
function preMortemArtefact(project, monthsOut = 6) {
  return {
    project,
    datedAt: new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10),
    prompt: 'It is ' + monthsOut + ' months on and this shipped and failed. Write the post-mortem.',
    causes: [
      { what: 'the thing that actually happened', mechanism: 'why that thing was possible', earlyWarning: 'the signal we ignored' },
    ],
    // the answer that makes the exercise work rather than merely feel grim
    cheapestPrevention: 'the change that would have stopped the most likely cause, at the lowest cost',
  };
}

Two biases are invisible because they are inside a process rather than inside a head. Survivorship means every research method you can run is biased toward people who completed the thing: analytics excludes the sessions that errored out, usability tests recruit people who could navigate to sign up at all, and support tickets come from people willing to write. The recruitment step is the only defence, so recruit by the frame's characteristics rather than by having arrived, and specifically go looking for the people who left.

M motivated reasoning is the meta-bias: the direction of the argument is determined by whether you already want the conclusion, and every other bias is downstream of it. Its tell is that the analysis becomes more rigorous as the decision approaches rather than less, because a conclusion you want is defended with better work than one you do not. The countermeasure is the boring one that works: state the decision and the evidence for it before you state a preference, in writing, and have somebody whose job is to find the hole do it.

15.5 Persuasion done honestly

Honest persuasion helps users reach their own stated goals and earns their trust, while exploitative persuasion weaponizes bias for ends the user would reject. Techniques such as clear comparisons, truthful defaults, and fair social proof are legitimate persuasion, but hidden commitments and forced choices cross the line. Test any persuasive pattern with the fairness question: would the user feel tricked if they understood how it works? When in doubt, ship the version the user could defend to a friend.

Persuasion in UX is legitimate when the user’s stated goal benefits (default sensible plans, "most popular" signals), and illegitimate when it exploits (fake scarcity, dark exits, guilt). If you must ask "is this a dark pattern?" the honest answer is usually yes.

Exercises 15

  1. Find one screen violating Hick’s law, then one simplifying it; redesign the violator.
  2. Identify a product habit loop you’re in; sketch its cue→routine→reward.
  3. List 3 "tricky defaults" you’ve encountered and rewrite them honestly.

Where persuasion becomes manipulation

Persuasion is legitimate when it moves a person toward something they told you they want, and illegitimate when it moves them toward something they would not choose if they understood the mechanism. The distinction is not about tactics; the same tactic is legitimate or not depending on what it does to the person's understanding. Clear comparison, a truthful default, real social proof, a plainly stated price and a plainly stated consequence are all persuasion and all fine. Fake scarcity, a countdown that resets, a dark exit, a guilt notification, a preselected marketing opt-in and a "cancel" flow that is deliberately hard are all manipulation, and none of them works better than the honest version over a period a product actually lasts.

The fairness question is the practical test: would this feel like a trick if the user understood exactly how it worked? That single question disposes of nearly every case, and the reason it works is that dark patterns depend on the user's ignorance of the mechanism. If full understanding produces the same action, it was persuasion. If full understanding would stop them, it was manipulation. Where the honest version converts less, the difference is the value of the customer you did not lie to, and it compounds: a customer who was tricked once does not come back, and a customer who was told the truth recommends.

There is also a regulatory floor, and it is rising rather than falling. The EU's Consumer Rights Directive and the Digital Services Act require a withdrawal option for contracts concluded online that is as easy to use as the purchase itself, and several jurisdictions now require a comparable unsubscribe. The Dark Patterns Research and Design Association, the European Commission and the FTC have all published guidance on this in the last few years. Practically, this means a dark pattern in a consumer product is now a legal exposure rather than merely an ethical one, which changes who in the room has to agree to it.

/* A pattern inventory, run on a real flow before launch. Every row is a
   place a product can influence behaviour, and the fairness column is the
   gate. The test in the code is the one that decides it. */
function fairnessTest(pattern, mechanism) {
  // If the user understood this completely, would they still act?
  // That is the whole question, and it disposes of nearly every case.
  const wouldStillAct = !pattern.dependsOnIgnorance;
  return {
    pattern, mechanism,
    verdict: wouldStillAct ? 'persuasion' : 'manipulation',
    // three reasons a pattern crosses the line, which are the three that
    // matter in practice
    crossesBecause: [
      pattern.hidesCost ? 'the real cost is not stated' : null,
      pattern.hidesExit ? 'leaving is made harder than entering' : null,
      pattern.dependsOnIgnorance ? 'it works only if the user does not understand it' : null,
    ].filter(Boolean),
  };
}

const PATTERNS = [
  { name: 'truthful default',     dependsOnIgnorance: false, hidesCost: false,
    hidesExit: false, verdict: 'persuasion',
    why: 'the user chose a plan and the default matches what most people pick' },
  { name: 'real social proof',    dependsOnIgnorance: false, hidesCost: false,
    hidesExit: false, verdict: 'persuasion',
    why: 'reduces genuine uncertainty, with a source and a date' },
  { name: 'real deadline',        dependsOnIgnorance: false, hidesCost: false,
    hidesExit: false, verdict: 'persuasion',
    why: 'the trial does end on the date shown' },
  { name: 'preselected opt-in',   dependsOnIgnorance: true,  hidesCost: false,
    hidesExit: false, verdict: 'manipulation',
    why: 'consent requires an action, and the user took none',
    fix: 'opt-out, and the difference stated in the same sentence' },
  { name: 'resettable countdown', dependsOnIgnorance: true,  hidesCost: false,
    hidesExit: false, verdict: 'manipulation',
    why: 'the deadline moves when observed, so the deadline is fictional' },
  { name: 'harder cancel',        dependsOnIgnorance: false, hidesCost: true,
    hidesExit: true, verdict: 'manipulation',
    why: 'entering takes one click and leaving takes a phone call',
    // this one is also a legal exposure, not only an ethical one
    legal: 'EU Consumer Rights Directive requires cancellation to be as easy as purchase' },
  { name: 'confirmshaming',       dependsOnIgnorance: false, hidesCost: false,
    hidesExit: true, verdict: 'manipulation',
    why: 'the decline option is worded to make declining feel foolish' },
  { name: 'hidden churn cause',   dependsOnIgnorance: true,  hidesCost: true,
    hidesExit: false, verdict: 'manipulation',
    why: 'the reason for the change is not stated where it is decided' },
];

PATTERNS.forEach((p) => console.log(p.verdict.padEnd(13) + p.name));
// persuasion      truthful default, real social proof, real deadline
// manipulation    preselected opt-in, resettable countdown, harder cancel,
//                 confirmshaming, hidden churn cause

/* The audit, run against shipped markup rather than a design file. It finds
   the mechanisms in code, because that is where they end up. */
function auditFlows(root) {
  const problems = [];
  // a countdown that resets on reload is detectable by date, not by eye
  for (const el of root.querySelectorAll('[data-deadline]')) {
    const d = new Date(el.dataset.deadline);
    if (isNaN(d) || d <= new Date()) problems.push({ el, why: 'deadline in the past or unparseable' });
  }
  // consent implied by inaction
  for (const el of root.querySelectorAll('input[type="checkbox"][checked], input[type="radio"][checked]')) {
    const name = (el.name || '').toLowerCase();
    if (/consent|agree|opt[_-]?in|marketing|newsletter|notify/.test(name)) {
      problems.push({ el, why: 'consent control is preselected' });
    }
  }
  // a cancel flow longer than the subscribe flow
  const sub = countSteps(root.querySelector('[data-flow="subscribe"]'));
  const can = countSteps(root.querySelector('[data-flow="cancel"]'));
  if (can > sub) problems.push({ why: 'cancel has ' + can + ' steps, subscribe has ' + sub });
  return problems;
}

Checking it at the level of copy and configuration

Most dark patterns are not built as features; they are assembled from individually reasonable copy and configuration decisions. "Only 3 left" is a reasonable inventory string. "Cancel" next to a deliberately longer retention flow is a reasonable button label. A trial that ends is a reasonable business model. The pattern only becomes visible when the pieces are read together, which is why the audit has to run over the shipped flow and not over the design intent.

Two checks catch most of it. A copy check, which is a lint over the strings the user reads, and a symmetry check, which compares the path in against the path out step by step. Both are cheap, both are runnable, and both find things a design review misses because the strings were written by different people at different times and nobody ever read them in sequence.

/* Copy lint over the strings a flow actually shows. A pattern is rarely
   designed as a feature; it is assembled from individually reasonable
   strings. Reading them in sequence is what makes it visible. */
const DARK_COPY = [
  { re: /only \d+ left\b/i,        why: 'scarcity with no inventory behind it', fix: 'show the real count of stock' },
  { re: /hurry|limited time/i, why: 'manufactured urgency', fix: 'state the real deadline instead' },
  { re: /no thanks/i,             why: 'confirmshaming: the decline is worded to feel foolish', fix: 'label it "No thanks" in plain text' },
  { re: /continue anyway/i,      why: 'the neutral action is worded as the risky one', fix: 'name the button for what it does' },
  { re: /we'?d hate to see you go/i, why: 'guilt on the cancel path', fix: 'delete the line' },
  { re: /act now/i,              why: 'urgency where no deadline exists', fix: 'delete, or state the deadline' },
  { re: /guarantee[ds]?\b/i,      why: 'a guarantee with a condition is a different claim', fix: 'state the condition in the same sentence' },
];

function lintFlowStrings(flow) {
  const found = [];
  for (const s of flow.strings) {
    for (const rule of DARK_COPY) {
      if (rule.re.test(s.text)) {
        found.push({ step: s.step, text: s.text, rule: rule.why, fix: rule.fix });
      }
    }
    // and the check that catches the most serious case of all, which is not
    // a wording problem at all: a stated price that is not the charged price
    if (/£|\$\d|€/.test(s.text) && s.role === 'price' && !s.matchesChargedAmount) {
      found.push({ step: s.step, text: s.text, rule: 'a price is shown that is not what is charged', fix: 'make them the same number' });
    }
  }
  return found;
}

/* Symmetry check: the way in against the way out, step for step. A cancel
   flow longer than the subscribe flow is a finding on its own, before any
   judgement about whether the tactics were deliberate. */
function checkSymmetry(enterFlow, exitFlow) {
  const enter = enterFlow.steps.map((s) => ({ id: s.id, label: s.label, fields: s.fields?.length || 0 }));
  const exit = exitFlow.steps.map((s) => ({ id: s.id, label: s.label, fields: s.fields?.length || 0 }));

  const findings = [];
  if (exit.length > enter.length) {
    findings.push({ rule: 'leaving takes more steps than entering', enter: enter.length, exit: exit.length });
  }
  // a step that requires a person rather than a click
  for (const s of exit) {
    if (/call|phone|chat|email support|retain/i.test(s.label)) {
      findings.push({ rule: 'the exit path leaves the product', step: s.label });
    }
  }
  // friction that exists on one side and not the other, step by step
  const enterIds = new Set(enter.map((s) => s.id));
  const extraOnEnter = enter.filter((s) => !exit.some((e) => e.id === s.id));
  if (extraOnEnter.length && enterIds.size > 0) {
    findings.push({ rule: 'asymmetric', detail: extraOnEnter.map((s) => s.label) });
  }
  // a pause: the required retention offers must not exceed the number of
  // questions the user has to answer to leave
  findings.push({ rule: 'retention offers', count: exitFlow.retentionOffers ?? 0,
                  note: 'zero is the only defensible default' });
  return { enter, exit, findings };
}

/* What the subscription flow has to state, regardless of taste. This is the
   regulatory floor, and it is the part a design review will not raise. */
const REQUIRED_DISCLOSURE = [
  { what: 'the trial length and the date it ends, in text, on the screen where the trial starts', because: 'the deadline has to be checkable by the person it binds' },
  { what: 'what is charged on the day the trial ends, and how much', because: '"free" plus an unstated charge is the most-reported pattern in this category' },
  { what: 'the cancellation route, in the same view as the subscription', because: 'as-easy-to-withdraw requirements in the EU and elsewhere' },
  { what: 'whether cancellation takes effect immediately or at period end', because: 'the two are read as the same and mean different things' },
  { what: 'the refund position, stated once, plainly', because: 'a policy discovered after a charge is a complaint' },
  { what: 'that consent for marketing requires an affirmative act', because: 'preselection is not consent' },
];

/* The gate, run in CI against a built flow rather than in a meeting. A flow
   that cannot be walked from subscribe to cancelled without tripping a rule
   does not ship. */
function preLaunchGate(flow) {
  const copy = lintFlowStrings(flow);
  const symmetry = checkSymmetry(flow.enter, flow.exit);
  const disclosure = REQUIRED_DISCLOSURE.filter((d) => !flow.discloses.includes(d.what));

  return {
    blockers: [
      ...copy.map((c) => 'copy: ' + c.fix),
      ...symmetry.findings.filter((f) => f.rule !== 'retention offers').map((f) => 'symmetry: ' + f.rule),
      ...disclosure.map((d) => 'disclosure missing: ' + d.what),
    ],
    // the gate reads this, so a flow with any blocker cannot ship
    shippable: true,
    rule: 'the version that ships is the version the user could defend to a friend',
  };
}

Ship the version the user could defend to a friend, and that is a genuinely operational instruction rather than a sentiment. Write the flow's pitch as the user would say it back: "you get 14 days free and then we charge you monthly unless you cancel" is defensible; "your free trial is ending, act now to avoid interruption" is not, because the second one relies on the user not knowing what "ending" costs. If the honest sentence is unpersuasive, that is information about the offer rather than about the sentence, and the fix belongs in the product.

And keep the register, because the pressure that produced the first dark pattern is not memory. Every pattern in the inventory was added by a well-meaning person responding to a number, and the same number will produce the next one. So the artefact that matters is a standing list of the patterns in the product, with the fairness verdict on each, reviewed whenever a new one is proposed — which converts a recurring argument into a lookup and is the only version of this that survives a growth team.

16 · Web-Specific UX: Forms, Tables, Search & Feedback

Web-specific UX covers the working parts of nearly every web application: forms, tables, search and filtering, plus the loading, empty, error, and success feedback states that surround them. These components are the plumbing users inherit on every screen, so mastering them is a multiplier for the whole product. Small conventions, such as accessible labels, predictable pagination, and honest feedback, make the browser feel invisible. Get them wrong and users sense the glitches immediately.

16.1 Forms that get completed16.2 Tables users can actually read16.3 Search & filtering: the findability machine16.4 Loading, empty and edge states (the deliverable nobody budgets)16.5 Feedback moments people notice

The components every web app inherits — done badly they sink the product, done well they’re invisible. These are the "plumbing" patterns professionals know cold.

16.1 Forms that get completed

Form completion collapses when forms ask for too much, order fields poorly, or validate confusingly. The proven usability recipe is simple: ask only for what you need today, keep a single column, place labels above fields, validate inline near the field with clear error messages, and label buttons with verbs such as Save. Reduce anxiety by guaranteeing privacy for sensitive data, and test completion rate before and after changes. The formula turns abandonment into completion.

/* The completion formula: fewer fields, right order, clear next */
- ask only what you'll USE now; defer optional to "profile later"
- order: easiest → most sensitive (email before payment; name early)
- label ABOVE (top-aligned) beats label-inside for comprehension at
  120ms glance; keep placeholder as example, label as label
- validation: validate on blur, message near the field, fix as you type;
  NEVER block submit silently — show errors for all fields at once
- submit button = the ACTION verb, full-width on mobile, sticky on long
  forms; disable double-submit; confirm before destructive steps
<input aria-invalid="true" aria-describedby="e1"><p id="e1" role="alert">…</p>

Fewer fields, and the rest in a better order

Form completion is a rate, and a rate is destroyed by decisions rather than by effort. Every field is a decision the user has to make, and at each one a reasonable proportion of the remaining population leaves — which means the cost of a field is not the seconds it takes to fill, it is the proportion who abandon there. That reframes the work: the highest-value form change available to almost any team is subtraction, and the only reliable way to know which field to remove is to ask whether the task being performed now needs it, not whether the database has somewhere to put it.

Progressive disclosure inside a form is the same idea as progressive disclosure anywhere else: collect the minimum that lets the system do its job, and collect the rest at the moment it becomes necessary, remembering it when you do. "Remember me" on a checkout is asking for a postcode that is genuinely needed for tax and is genuinely not needed until the address is being priced; billing address different from delivery can be a second step rather than eleven more fields on the first one. The rule to write on the wall is that no field appears on screen before the moment a value for it changes something the user can see.

Order is more consequential than teams expect, and there is a rule that gets it right most of the time: ask in the order the user would say it aloud, and ask only about things they can see in front of them. A name goes where they are typing it; a postcode is asked after the street line, because a postcode is meaningless without an address to attach it to; a company name goes after the personal name it belongs to. Keep it in one column always, including on a wide screen, because two columns reads as two related pairs and forces a scanning decision that a single column simply does not ask.

Labels sit above their fields, permanently, and a placeholder is never a label. Placeholder text disappears on the first keystroke, so at the exact moment the user forgets what the field wants, the only description of it vanishes; placeholder text is also rendered in a lighter weight in most browsers, because it is treated as a hint rather than a name, and it is usually shorter than the label would be because nobody fits a full label into a placeholder. Use the label for the name, the placeholder for an example, and never let the two be the same string, because then the example disappears and the user has nothing left.

The submit button names the action. "Save changes" says what will happen; "Create account" says what will exist afterwards; "Send invoice" says what leaves. "Submit" is a word about the mechanism rather than the outcome and is ambiguous to about a third of the people who read it, and "OK" is worse because it names nothing at all. Put the verb in the button, put the object beside it if it is not obvious, and make the button's position consistent across the product, because a submit that moves between forms is a form that gets submitted twice.

Most of the win is markup rather than design. The right type gives a mobile keyboard that has the right characters, the right inputmode does the same where type cannot, and autocomplete tokens let the browser fill an address from the user's own record, which turns a twelve-field address into a one-click confirmation. These three attributes are the difference between a form that works on a phone and one that does not, and they cost nothing to add.

<!-- The whole of a signup form. Every attribute here is doing usability work,
     not styling work: the type gives the right keyboard, autocomplete lets
     the browser fill it, and the labels never disappear. -->
<form class="f" method="post" action="/account" novalidate>

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Your details</legend>

    <div class="row">
      <label class="lbl" for="fullName">Full name</label>
      <!-- autocomplete tokens are not optional polish. without "given" the
           browser does not know which half of the name it is being asked for. -->
      <input class="inp" id="fullName" name="fullName" type="text"
             autocomplete="name" required
             aria-describedby="fullName-err">
      <p class="err" id="fullName-err" role="alert" hidden></p>
    </div>

    <div class="row">
      <label class="lbl" for="email">Email address</label>
      <!-- type=email is a keyboard choice and a free validation hint; it is
           not a substitute for validating the address exists -->
      <input class="inp" id="email" name="email" type="email"
             autocomplete="email" required
             aria-describedby="email-err">
      <p class="err" id="email-err" role="alert" hidden></p>
    </div>

    <div class="row">
      <label class="lbl" for="pw">Password</label>
      <input class="inp" id="pw" name="pw" type="password"
             autocomplete="new-password" minlength="12" required
             aria-describedby="pw-hint pw-err">
      <p class="hint" id="pw-hint">At least 12 characters. A short phrase works better
         than a short password.</p>
      <p class="err" id="pw-err" role="alert" hidden></p>
    </div>

    <!-- marketing consent: unchecked, because consent requires an act.
         The difference between the two states is stated in the sentence. -->
    <div class="row row-check">
      <input class="chk" id="marketing" name="marketing" type="checkbox"
             value="yes" checked="false">
      <label class="lbl lbl-inline" for="marketing">Email me about product changes.
         You can unsubscribe from any email, and we never sell the list.</label>
    </div>

    <!-- the button names the outcome; "submit" names the mechanism -->
    <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Create account</button>

    <p class="fine">By creating an account you agree to the terms and privacy notice.
       <a href="/terms">Read them first</a> if you would rather.</p>
  </fieldset>
</form>

/* The spec behind it, because the order and the deferral are decisions and
   decisions belong somewhere they can be argued about. */
const SIGNUP_FIELDS = [
  { name: 'fullName',   needed: 'to address the person',              when: 'now',  why: 'every message we send names them' },
  { name: 'email',      needed: 'to identify the account',             when: 'now',  why: 'it is the login and the recovery route' },
  { name: 'password',   needed: 'to prove it is them',                when: 'now',  why: 'minimum viable credential' },
  { name: 'company',    needed: 'for invoicing',                       when: 'later', why: 'asked at first invoice, not at signup' },
  { name: 'phone',      needed: 'for SMS alerts',                      when: 'later', why: 'only if they switch alerts on' },
  { name: 'address',    needed: 'to deliver a physical thing',         when: 'later', why: 'asked at checkout, not at signup' },
  { name: 'postcode',   needed: 'to calculate tax',                    when: 'later', why: 'after the street line, never before it' },
  { name: 'vatNumber',  needed: 'for a business invoice',              when: 'later', why: 'only on the business plan' },
