  { name: 'timezone',   needed: 'to render times correctly',           when: 'never', why: 'detected from the request, never asked' },
];

/* The audit, run against the spec rather than the design file: a field that
   is marked "later" and is still on the first screen is the defect. */
function auditSignup(fields, step1) {
  const premature = fields.filter((f) => f.when === 'later' && step1.includes(f.name));
  const never     = fields.filter((f) => f.when === 'never' && step1.includes(f.name));
  const unordered = fields.filter((f) => f.when === 'now')
    .map((f) => step1.indexOf(f.name))
    .filter((i, a, arr) => arr.indexOf(i) !== i);
  return { premature, never, duplicateOrder: unordered,
           onFirstScreen: step1.length, verdict: premature.length ? 'fields are early' : 'ok' };
}

Validation is the second half of the section, and the rule that matters is that it must be near the field, specific, and about how to fix it. "Invalid input" tells a person nothing they can act on; "Enter an email address like name@example.com" tells them exactly what to type. Validate on blur rather than on every keystroke, so a person is not told they are wrong while they are still typing the thing, and validate the whole field rather than a fragment of it, so the message appears once rather than once per character class.

Sensitive data, and what reassurance has to contain

A form that asks for something sensitive has a job beyond collecting it: it has to make the person comfortable enough to type it, and reassurance only works when it is specific. "We value your privacy" is the phrase people have learned to scroll past, because it is the phrase that appears above the same field in every product and says nothing about what happens to the value. What works is the specific consequence, at the point of the field: what it is used for, who can see it, how long it is kept, and whether it is optional. Four sentences, and one of them has to be the honest one.

Not collecting something is always better than collecting it well. A phone number field that exists only to enable an SMS alert the user may never turn on is a field that must be justified in a data-protection review, and the review is a much slower conversation with the user than simply removing the field and adding a toggle in settings. The specific version of this rule: if the value can be collected later at the moment it becomes necessary, collect it later, and remember it then. Every field removed this way is also one fewer thing to encrypt, breach, export, delete on request, and explain in a privacy notice.

Password fields deserve their own treatment, because the current conventions are a mess and the accessible ones are easy. Tell people the rules before they type rather than after, show a strength measure that reflects the rules the server actually enforces, offer a reveal toggle that is a real button with a label rather than an icon, and let the password manager fill it — which means never disabling paste, never obscuring with a custom widget, and never writing your own password rules in JavaScript when minlength, autocomplete and new-password already do the job. A password field that fights the password manager is a field that gets typed on a phone keyboard, in a public place, with the caps-lock key on.

Length beats composition, and this is one place where the recommendation has genuinely changed: a long passphrase is easier to remember, faster to type and stronger than a short password with a symbol and a digit, so the rule to enforce is length and the rule to say is why. What you must not do is enforce composition rules that push people towards substitutions, because P@ssw0rd1 is in every cracking dictionary while correct horse battery staple is not.

Anonymised and sensitive fields need different affordances, and the difference is mostly about reversibility. A postcode the user types can be validated against a real format; a postcode the user enters to check coverage is fine to be approximate and should say it is; a field that is genuinely anonymous cannot be recovered, supported or refunded, and a product that offers a password reset on an account that has no password is promising something it cannot deliver. Where a field is one-way, the label says so before the field rather than in an error after submission.

Measure the rate, not the opinion. Completion rate before and after any change to a form is the metric that settles it, and it should be measured on the same traffic rather than across a launch boundary, because a launch changes the traffic as well as the form. The secondary metrics matter too — time to complete, error rate per field, and the abandonment point that moved — because a change that raises completion by hiding a required field will usually show up first as a rise in support contacts rather than as a fall in completion.

/* The reassurance copy, written per field. The test is that each line
   contains a consequence rather than an adjective, and that the four
   questions are all answered for anything genuinely sensitive. */
const REASSURANCE = {
  email: {
    usedFor: 'Signing in and, if you ask for it, product news.',
    seenBy: 'Nobody else. We do not sell or share it.',
    keptFor: 'Until you delete your account, then 30 days in backups.',
    optional: false,
    // the sentence that goes beside the field, not in the privacy notice
    beside: 'We email you about your account. Nothing else unless you ask.',
  },
  phone: {
    usedFor: 'SMS alerts about outages, if you turn them on.',
    seenBy: 'Our SMS provider, to deliver the message.',
    keptFor: 'Until you turn alerts off, then deleted.',
    optional: true,
    // the honest one, and the reason the field exists at all
    beside: 'Optional. We only ask because alerts are useful when we break things.',
  },
  address: {
    usedFor: 'Delivering what you bought, and calculating tax.',
    seenBy: 'The courier, and nobody else.',
    keptFor: 'Seven years, because tax law requires it.',
    optional: true,
    beside: 'Needed at checkout, so we are asking then rather than now.',
  },
};

/* The collection rules, because a field that exists without a purpose is a
   field that cannot be justified in a data-protection review. */
const FIELD_JUSTIFICATION = [
  { field: 'phone', rule: 'never collect at signup; collect when alerts are switched on',
    withoutThatRule: 'a field most people fill with a fake number, which then breaks the one feature it was for' },
  { field: 'dateOfBirth', rule: 'never collect; derive the age gate from a verified source or ask at the point of use',
    withoutThatRule: 'a rejection of a real customer over a typo, in the one flow with the fewest retries' },
  { field: 'preciseLocation', rule: 'collect only while the map is on screen, and say so on the permission prompt',
    withoutThatRule: 'a permanent record of where people live, from a feature that needs it for four seconds' },
];

/* The measurement. Same traffic, before and after, with the field-level
   breakdown that shows which change actually did the work. */
function measureFormChange({ before, after, windowDays = 14 }) {
  const rate = (s) => s.submitted / s.started;
  const abandonAt = (s) => {
    const field = Object.entries(s.dropOffByField).sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1])[0];
    return { field: field[0], drops: field[1], ofTotal: s.abandoned };
  };
  return {
    completion: { before: rate(before), after: rate(after),
                  lift: +( (rate(after) - rate(before)) * 100 ).toFixed(1) },
    // the number that catches a field hidden rather than removed
    supportContacts: { before: before.contacts, after: after.contacts,
                       note: 'a rise here with a completion rise means something was deferred, not fixed' },
    biggestAbandonPoint: { before: abandonAt(before), after: abandonAt(after) },
    // guard against the launch boundary: compare like with like
    valid: before.trafficSource === after.trafficSource && before.deviceMix === after.deviceMix
      && before.windowDays === after.windowDays,
  };
}

/* Password rules, expressed the way a browser can enforce them. No custom
   strength meter, no blocked paste, no composition requirement. */
const PASSWORD_POLICY = {
  minLength: 15,
  maxLength: 200,                  // bcrypt silently truncates above 72 bytes, so bound it and say so
  requiredComposition: [],          // none: substitutions produce the passwords in every wordlist
  breachCheck: true,               // check against a k-anonymity range, never send the password anywhere
  rulesShownUpFront: true,         // told before typing, not in an error afterwards
  revealIsAButton: true,           // with a label, focusable, not an unlabelled icon
  allowPaste: true,
  allowPasswordManager: true,      // which means no custom widget and no input masking
};

The other half of a form is what happens after it, and it is the half that decides whether the user believes the submission. Say what is happening in the moment — a real pending state on the button, not a spinner that leaves the button looking available for a second click — and disable the button for the duration, because double submission is the most common and most expensive form defect there is. Then say what happens next, in the same place: an email is on its way to this address, we have sent a verification link, your reference is 4C91. A form that ends on the word "Submit" makes the user construct the rest themselves, and many of them construct it wrongly.

And keep the field values if the submission fails. This costs almost nothing — the browser will repopulate, and a server-rendered form can echo the values back — and it is the difference between a person fixing one field and starting again. Only clear a value if it is sensitive and the reason for clearing it is the reason they need to see the error. Re-typing twelve fields because one was rejected is the moment a lot of people decide the product is hostile, and they decide it silently rather than writing to tell you.

Server-side validation is the authority and client-side validation is a courtesy. The two disagreeing is the classic failure — a rule expressed in two places that has drifted, so the form accepts something the server rejects and the user is told they were wrong after the fact. Derive both from one source of truth: define the rules once, generate the client attributes from them, and run the same functions on the server. A form that rejects valid input is a bug in the same class as one that accepts invalid input, and it is the more common of the two because nobody tests the boundary from the user's side.

A forms completion checklist: fewer fields, top-aligned labels, validation near the field, and an action verb on the submit button. Note the ARIA-invalid error markup at the bottom for accessible validation.

16.2 Tables users can actually read

Tables are scanned and compared more than they are stared at, so reading conventions matter more than decoration. Right-align numeric columns so values line up for comparison, left-align text labels, provide sortable headers and filters, and use zebra stripes sparingly. Give each row an obvious action, keep column headers visible while scrolling, and stack rows or switch to cards on mobile. Alignment is what makes a wide dataset readable at a glance.

RuleWhy
Sort on headers (with direction indicator)users expect it; remember it
Filter up front for big sets; paginate or infinite-lazy-load1000 rows is a database, not a page
Align numbers right, text left; consistent decimal placesscanning + comparison literally work that way
Row actions per row (ellipsis menu) + bulk actions on selectionrecognized patterns, no accidental misses
Mobile stack into cardsCh.11.4; never 7-col horizontal scroll

Alignment, and why it is most of the job

Tables are read by scanning columns and comparing values, not by reading rows left to right, and the only thing that makes that comparison possible is alignment. Numbers align on the decimal point, which is why numeric columns are right-aligned with tabular figures; text aligns on its left edge, because a ragged left edge for text destroys the eye's ability to find the next line; labels that identify a row align with the values they label. Get those three right and a wide dataset becomes readable at a glance. Get them wrong and no amount of striping, hover states or colour will help, because the reader has to reconstruct the alignment their eye expects.

Consistency of units and decimals matters for the same reason. A column where 4 rows say "1,240" and one says "1.24k" cannot be compared without reading each value; a money column mixing two currencies is worse, and a duration column mixing "90s" with "2 minutes" forces a conversion in the reader's head at every row. Pick one unit per column, print it in the header rather than in every cell, and use a tabular-figures font so the digits occupy equal width — the last of these is a font feature, not a design decision, and it is the single cheapest improvement available to a numeric table.

Sorting is a contract, not a feature. Users expect it on any column with more than a handful of values, they expect the current sort to be visibly indicated, and they expect clicking the same header again to reverse the direction rather than to do nothing. State the default sort in the header on first paint, because a table that arrives unsorted makes the user wonder what happened to the order they were given. And keep the sort across pagination and filtering, which is the single most commonly broken behaviour in tables of this kind: a user sorts by date, pages to two, filters by status, and finds the sort silently reset, which reads as data loss rather than as a bug.

Row actions and bulk actions solve different problems and both are needed. The per-row ellipsis menu handles the action that applies to one thing — edit, duplicate, archive — and it hides actions that would be dangerous or rare, which is exactly why it is a menu rather than a row of buttons. Bulk selection handles the case where the task is inherently many-at-once, and it needs a visible count ("4 selected"), a selection that survives sorting and filtering, and a header checkbox that offers select-all-matching rather than select-all-loaded, because a user who filters to 12 of 4,000 and clicks select-all expecting 4,000 will do something they did not intend.

On a narrow screen, do not scroll a seven-column table horizontally. It is the most common responsive failure in a data product and it fails by making every column too narrow to read the values that matter, so the user scrolls back and forth and loses their place on every row. Two workable answers: stack each row into a card with the label-value pairs visible, which suits a handful of columns; or, when the columns are genuinely many and numeric, choose two or three to keep and drop the rest behind a row detail view, which suits comparison. Whichever you pick, the identifier and the one value the user came for must be visible without interaction in both layouts.

Everything above is a reading decision, and it is worth separating from the visual one. Zebra striping is not a reading aid — it is a wayfinding aid, useful on a wide table with many columns and actively harmful on a short one, where it doubles the apparent length of the list and suggests grouping that does not exist. Row hover highlighting is a locating aid and it is the one thing that earns its place on nearly every table, because it tells the reader which line they are reading and where the clickable area is.

/* The table's state, in one object. Sorting, selection and filters are one
   model, and the failures people report come from them being three
   independent pieces of state that disagree with each other. */
const TABLE_STATE = {
  sort: { column: 'updatedAt', dir: 'desc', isDefault: true },
  filter: { status: 'open', assignee: null },
  selection: new Set(),          // ids, not indexes: survives sorting and filtering
  page: { index: 0, size: 50 },

  // the rule that fixes the most-reported bug: sorting is never reset by a
  // filter or a page change, only by the user clicking a header
  reset() { this.page.index = 0; return this; },      // page goes to one
  toggleSort(column) {
    if (this.sort.column === column) this.sort.dir = this.sort.dir === 'asc' ? 'desc' : 'asc';
    else this.sort = { column, dir: 'asc', isDefault: false };
    this.page.index = 0;
    return this;
  },
};

/* select-all means select-all-matching. A header checkbox that selects the
   50 loaded rows out of 4,000 is a footgun with a checkbox on it. */
function toggleSelectAll(rows, totalMatching) {
  const allLoadedSelected = rows.every((r) => TABLE_STATE.selection.has(r.id));
  if (allLoadedSelected) {
    for (const r of rows) TABLE_STATE.selection.delete(r.id);
    return { mode: 'off', selected: TABLE_STATE.selection.size };
  }
  for (const r of rows) TABLE_STATE.selection.add(r.id);
  return {
    mode: 'all-matching',
    // the label has to tell the truth about what was just selected
    label: totalMatching > rows.length
      ? 'All ' + rows.length + ' loaded rows selected. Select all ' +
        totalMatching + ' matching rows'
      : 'All ' + rows.length + ' rows selected',
    selected: TABLE_STATE.selection.size,
  };
}

/* The column spec. Alignment and format are declared once and used by both
   the renderer and the mobile card view, which is why they cannot drift. */
const COLUMNS = [
  { key: 'title',     label: 'Invoice',  align: 'left',  format: 'text',      alwaysShow: true },
  { key: 'client',    label: 'Client',   align: 'left',  format: 'text',      mobile: 'stack' },
  { key: 'amount',    label: 'Amount',   align: 'right', format: 'currency',  unit: 'GBP', alwaysShow: true },
  { key: 'issuedAt',  label: 'Issued',   align: 'left',  format: 'date',      sortable: true, mobile: 'stack' },
  { key: 'updatedAt', label: 'Updated',  align: 'left',  format: 'relative',  sortable: true, mobile: 'stack' },
  { key: 'status',    label: 'Status',   align: 'left',  format: 'enum',      filter: true },
  { key: 'actions',   label: '',         align: 'right', format: 'menu',      alwaysShow: true },
];

// the two rules that make numeric columns readable, expressed as data
const NUMERIC = {
  align: 'right',
  fontFeatureSettings: "'tnum' 1, 'lnum' 1",   // tabular figures: equal digit widths
  decimals: 2,                                  // one convention for the whole column
  unit: 'GBP',                                  // declared once, in the header
  // and never abbreviate inside the column: 1.24k cannot be compared with 1,240
  abbreviate: false,
};

/* Narrow screens: stack, do not scroll. The columns kept without interaction
   are the identifier and the value the user came for. */
function narrowLayout(width, columns) {
  if (width >= 900) return { mode: 'table', columns: columns.map((c) => c.key) };
  const keep = columns.filter((c) => c.alwaysShow).map((c) => c.key);
  return {
    mode: 'cards',
    visibleWithoutInteraction: keep,
    // everything else is one tap away, and the tap target is the whole row
    detailOnTap: columns.filter((c) => !c.alwaysShow).map((c) => ({ key: c.key, label: c.label })),
    // the rule the previous layout broke: no horizontal scroll on a data table
    horizontalScroll: false,
  };
}

None of this is a visual style, and it is worth saying so because tables are usually handed to a designer when what they need is a data model and a decision about alignment. The column spec is the deliverable: it fixes alignment, unit, format and sortability in one place, it feeds both the wide layout and the stacked one, and it makes the awkward conversations — which columns survive on mobile, which are money, which sort — happen once at the start rather than in every screen review for two years. A table built from an explicit column list is also a table that can be exported, and an export that agrees with the screen is a thing customers notice and never mention.

How a table is actually read by a screen reader

A table is one of the few layout decisions that carries semantics automatically, and getting it right gives a non-visual user something genuinely good: the ability to move cell by cell in reading order while the screen reader announces the header for each cell, so "invoice 4C91, amount, £1,240" rather than a stream of bare numbers. That behaviour comes from real table markup with header cells and a scope, and it is destroyed by the single most common shortcut in front-end work, which is building the grid out of divs with CSS grid and leaving it looking exactly right.

So the non-negotiables are: a <table> element, <th> for headers, and scope on each so the association is explicit rather than inferred from position. A <caption> names the table and is read before it, which is the first thing a screen-reader user hears and the first thing a sighted keyboard user misses entirely. And if a grid is being used purely for layout, it must be marked as presentational — because a layout table read as a data table is one of the more confusing things a screen reader can produce, since it announces relationships that do not exist.

Sortable headers need a button inside the header cell. Making the <th> itself clickable works with a mouse and is unreachable by keyboard, and it is the reason so many data grids are unusable without a pointer. The button needs a name that says what it will do — "Sort by amount, currently ascending, activate to sort descending" — because the direction indicator is a visual convention that carries no meaning to anyone who cannot see it, and the change in order needs to be announced, which means a live region or a focus move rather than a silent re-render.

Keyboard behaviour for the grid as a whole is a smaller decision than it looks. Arrow keys move between cells in the non-modal pattern, which is the W3 recommendation for a simple data table: Tab moves out of the grid, arrows move within it, and the grid is not a composite widget unless it has selection or in-cell editing, in which case it becomes one and needs the full pattern with a documented key model. Row actions inside a grid need Escape to close and focus to return to the control that opened the menu, which is the most frequently missed behaviour in tables of this kind.

Mobile stacking has a semantic version too, and it is the awkward one: a card is a div, so every label-value pair that used to come from a <th> now has to be explicit text inside the card. That means the label is rendered in the DOM rather than implied by a header cell, which is a small amount of duplication and a large gain — a screen-reader user on a phone now hears "Amount, £1,240" rather than "£1,240". Where the card view and the table view are both live in the DOM at once, one of them must be hidden with the hidden attribute rather than by CSS alone, or both get read.

Finally, contrast and target size apply inside a table like anywhere else, and the failures are concentrated in one place: the small grey text in the meta column. It is usually below 4.5:1, usually 12px, and usually carrying information that is the only place a date appears. Sorting by clicking a column header is also a target size question, because a header is not a button and does not look like one, which means the whole cell should be the target and the cell is at least 44px tall if the row height allows it.

<!-- An accessible data table. Every one of these attributes is load-bearing:
     the caption is read first, scope makes the header association explicit,
     and the sort buttons are real buttons so the table is reachable by
     keyboard and the direction is announced rather than only drawn. -->
<div class="table-scroll">
  <table class="tbl" aria-describedby="tbl-count">
    <caption class="vh">Invoices, newest first, 214 matching</caption>

    <thead>
      <tr>
        <th scope="col" class="col-check">
          <input type="checkbox" id="sel-all" aria-label="Select all 50 loaded rows">
        </th>
        <th scope="col" aria-sort="descending">
          <button type="button" class="sortbtn" data-sort="title">
            Invoice
            <!-- the direction is a word as well as a glyph: a caret means
                 nothing to a screen reader and nothing to a sighted user who
                 has not learned the convention -->
            <span class="vh">, sorted descending, activate to sort ascending</span>
            <span class="sort-caret" aria-hidden="true">&#9660;</span>
          </button>
        </th>
        <th scope="col">Client</th>
        <th scope="col" class="num">
          <button type="button" class="sortbtn" data-sort="amount">
            Amount
            <span class="vh">, not sorted, activate to sort ascending</span>
            <span class="sort-caret" aria-hidden="true"></span>
          </button>
        </th>
        <th scope="col">Status</th>
        <th scope="col"><span class="vh">Actions</span></th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr>
        <td><input type="checkbox" name="sel" value="4C91" aria-label="Select invoice 4C91"></td>
        <th scope="row"><a href="/i/4C91">4C91</a></th>
        <td>Northwind Ltd</td>
        <!-- class="num" applies tabular figures, so digits line up:
             tnum is a font feature and costs nothing -->
        <td class="num">£1,240.00</td>
        <td><span class="pill pill-open">Open</span></td>
        <td class="cell-actions">
          <button type="button" class="iconbtn" aria-haspopup="menu"
                  aria-label="Actions for invoice 4C91">&#8942;</button>
        </td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
</div>

/* Announcing a sort. The order change is silent to a screen reader
   otherwise, and this is the moment the user needs to know. */
function announceSort(el, columnLabel, dir) {
  let region = document.getElementById('sort-status');
  if (!region) {
    region = document.createElement('div');
    region.id = 'sort-status';
    region.className = 'vh';
    region.setAttribute('role', 'status');
    region.setAttribute('aria-live', 'polite');
    document.body.appendChild(region);
  }
  region.textContent = 'Sorted by ' + columnLabel + ', ' + dir + 'ending';

  // and aria-sort belongs on exactly one header at a time
  for (const th of el.querySelectorAll('th[scope="col"]')) {
    th.removeAttribute('aria-sort');
    const btn = th.querySelector('.sortbtn');
    if (btn && btn.dataset.sort === columnLabel) {
      th.setAttribute('aria-sort', dir === 'asc' ? 'ascending' : 'descending');
      btn.querySelector('.vh').textContent = ', sorted ' + dir + 'ending, activate to reverse';
    } else if (btn) {
      btn.querySelector('.vh').textContent = ', not sorted, activate to sort ascending';
    }
  }
}

/* Non-modal grid keyboard: Tab leaves the grid, arrows move within it.
   Modal (composite) is only correct if the grid has selection or in-cell
   editing, and then it needs a documented key model. */
function gridKeys(e, api) {
  const moves = { ArrowRight: 'col+1', ArrowLeft: 'col-1', ArrowUp: 'row-1', ArrowDown: 'row+1' };
  if (e.key in moves) { e.preventDefault(); return api.move(moves[e.key]); }
  if (e.key === 'Home')     { e.preventDefault(); return api.rowStart(); }
  if (e.key === 'End')      { e.preventDefault(); return api.rowEnd(); }
  if (e.key === 'PageDown') { e.preventDefault(); return api.pageDown(); }
  if (e.key === 'Escape')   { return api.closeMenuAndRestoreFocus(); }
  // Tab is NOT handled: leaving the grid is the point of the non-modal pattern
  return undefined;
}

/* The CSS that makes the alignment claim true. */
const TABLE_CSS_NOTES = {
  '.tbl td.num, .tbl th.num': 'text-align:right; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; font-feature-settings:"tnum" 1',
  '.tbl caption.vh':         'visually hidden but present, so it is the first thing read',
  '.sortbtn':                'the whole header cell is the target; min-height 44px',
  '.tbl tbody tr:hover':     'the one decoration that earns its place: it says which line you are reading',
  '.tbl':                    'border-collapse: collapse, and no zebra striping below 8 visible rows',
};

The last thing a table has to get right is what happens to a row's actions while a bulk selection is active, and the answer is that they get out of the way. Per-row ellipsis menus next to checkboxes are two adjacent targets per row, and on a narrow screen they overlap; the usual resolution is to replace the row's action control with the checkbox while the selection mode is on, so a person who taps in the wrong place is not choosing a row and deleting it in one gesture. The destructive per-row action also belongs inside the menu rather than beside it, for the same reason it does everywhere else in the product.

16.3 Search & filtering: the findability machine

Search and filtering make large collections findable, but they are different machines: search queries the whole collection while filters narrow the view you already have. In practice, place the search box where users expect it, debounce typing to avoid over-searching, label filters clearly, and show live result counts. Design the zero-result state as a real screen that says what happened, suggests relaxed queries or spelling, and offers category fallbacks. Recover gracefully when nothing matches.

// The search agreement:
- debounce input (~300ms) real-time as you type; show result COUNT
- when zero results: offer did-you-mean + your top 3 category links
- spell tolerance ("recieve"→"receive"); synonyms via thesaurus
- filter vs search distinction: filter narrows current view, search
  spans the whole collection — label them distinctly
- sorts/filters should PERSIST through pagination and reloads
  (or state it: "Filters reset: X")

Search and filter are different machines

Search queries the collection; filtering narrows the view you are already looking at, and the distinction is not pedantic because the two have different interaction models, different performance characteristics and different failure modes. A search box is for when the user knows some property of the thing and cannot picture where it is. Filters are for when the user does not know what they want yet and wants to browse a constrained slice. A product that puts a search box where a filter row belongs makes people search for "open" and finds nothing, because open is a property rather than a name; a product that offers only filters for a collection of 40,000 records makes people page for an hour.

Search should be available where the user expects it, which in a list view means at the top, and it should be the widest thing on the screen because it is the widest thing they will type into. Debounce the query — 200 to 300 milliseconds is the range, and the reason is that a request per keystroke both costs more and makes results flicker, which reads as instability even when the data is stable. Search-as-you-type is the expectation now and a submit button is not, but the state has to be visible while it runs, because a list that is briefly unchanged after typing reads as "no results" rather than "still loading".

Show the count, always, and show it honestly. "1 of 214 results" is more useful than a bare "214 results" because it tells the user whether anything was actually filtered out, and "No results" is a statement the user cannot act on whereas "No results for widgt" tells them what was searched. Filters need labels that name the property rather than the values — "Status" rather than three checkboxes labelled Open, Open and Closed — and the active set has to be visible and individually removable, because a filter applied six interactions ago is invisible to the person deciding whether to loosen it.

The zero-result state is the one everybody budgets last and everybody needs. It has four parts: what was searched, what happened, what to try instead, and a route out that does not depend on the search working. The second part is "nothing matched" and it should be followed by a specific relaxation — drop a filter, search a broader term, or look at a category — rather than an apology. The fourth part is the one that converts a failure into a sale: a category landing page, a "browse everything" link, or a search for a related term, because a person who searched for a specific thing and got nothing is at the exact moment of highest intent and is otherwise very likely to leave.

Spell correction should be offered, not applied silently. "Showing results for widget" tells the user their input was wrong and what was understood, and costs one line; silently returning different results teaches people that the search box is unreliable, which is a lesson that generalises to the whole product. Do not correct a proper noun or an identifier — "XY-1182" is not a misspelling — and do not correct when the correction returns a very different number of results, because then the user is looking at somebody else's answer.

Relevance, and what to fix first when results are bad

"Search is bad" is not a diagnosis, because it is at least four different defects with different fixes and different owners. Recall failures are items that should have matched and did not — a typo tolerance setting, a stemming rule, an unindexed field, a filter that is silently ANDed where the user wanted OR. Precision failures are items that matched and should not have — substring matching inside a word, a stopword list missing the term the user meant, an index that is not field-aware. Ranking failures are the right items in the wrong order, which is a product decision about what matters rather than a bug. Latency failures are correct results that arrive after the user has typed the next thing, and which are indistinguishable from no results at all.

Fix recall first, because a missing item is worse than a badly ordered one: a person searching for an invoice number who does not get it will conclude the invoice does not exist, whereas one whose list is oddly ordered will simply scroll. And fix latency before precision, because latency is the failure mode people abandon in rather than complain about. Precision and ranking can then be tuned with the actual queries in front of you.

The thing that makes search good in a product with structured data is treating a query as structure rather than as text. "overdue northwind" is not three tokens to match, it is a client filter with a status filter; "from last tuesday to a ksjdf" is a date range with a typo; "£1,240 invoice" is an amount and a document type. Each of these is a parse of the query against the domain's own schema, and each is worth a great deal more than another synonym list, because it answers the question the user actually typed rather than the one the tokeniser could match.

Typo tolerance is a dial, not a switch. One edit is nearly free and catches the common single-key slip; two edits catch half-typed words and are actively harmful on short queries, where they match everything and make the results feel random. Same for length: tolerance should scale with token length, so a four-character token gets almost none and a twelve-character one gets two. And never correct an identifier, a code or a person's name — the fields where a near-match is worse than no match.

Latency has a budget and the budget is about the user's typing, not about your server. If the median query takes 400 ms and people type at a sustained 150 ms per character, the UI must be doing something during that gap — which is why an in-flight indicator beats a longer server-side wait, and why a result count can be shown from a cheap count query while the full rows are still arriving. Anything over about a second without any response reads as broken regardless of the fact that it is about to succeed.

Instrument it, because search quality decays silently. Log the query, the result count, the zero-result flag, the position of the first click, and the time to first result — and put a dashboard on the zero-result rate, because that is the number that tells you when something has broken: an index that dropped a field, a filter that changed its semantics, an analyser upgrade. A rising zero-result rate is the earliest signal available and it costs nothing to watch.

/* The search contract, with the four defects named. A request that is only
   a string cannot be diagnosed; these fields are what make "search is bad"
   separable into recall, precision, ranking and latency. */
const SEARCH_QUERY = {
  q: 'overdue northwind',
  filters: { status: null },        // may also arrive inside q, parsed below
  sort: 'relevance',
  page: { index: 0, size: 25 },
  // the instrumentation that turns a complaint into a diagnosis
  instrument: { queryId: null, sentAt: null, firstResultAt: null },
};

/* Query understanding: parse structure out of the string before matching.
   This is where most of the relevance win lives in a product with a schema. */
function parseQuery(raw, schema) {
  const tokens = raw.trim().split(/\s+/);
  const out = { terms: [], filters: {}, ranges: {}, unparsed: [] };

  for (const t of tokens) {
    const money = t.match(/^[£$€](\d[\d,]*(\.\d{1,2})?)$/);
    const date  = t.match(/^(last|this|past|next)?\s*(week|month|year|mon|tue|wed|thu|fri|sat|sun)/i);
    const enumV = schema.enums.find((e) => e.aliases.some((a) => a === t.toLowerCase()));
    const entity = schema.entities.find((e) => e.aliases.some((a) => raw.toLowerCase().includes(a)));

    if (money)      out.ranges.amount = Number(money[1].replace(/,/g, ''));
    else if (date)   out.ranges.date = resolveRelativeDate(date[0], raw);
    else if (enumV)  out.filters[enumV.field] = enumV.value;
    else if (entity) { out.filters[entity.field] = entity.value; }
    else             out.terms.push(t);
  }
  // tokens consumed as filters must be removed from the text terms, or the
  // engine will try to match "northwind" and "overdue" as free text too and
  // return nothing
  out.unparsed = tokens.filter((t) => !String(raw).includes(t) === false && t.startsWith('-'));
  return out;
}

/* Typo tolerance as a dial that scales with token length. Two edits on a
   four-character token matches essentially everything. */
function toleranceFor(token) {
  if (token.length <= 4) return 0;         // codes and short words: never correct
  if (/^[A-Z]{2,3}-\d+$/.test(token)) return 0;  // identifiers: never correct
  if (token.length <= 6) return 1;
  if (token.length <= 11) return 1;
  return 2;
}

/* The latency budget, stated against the user's typing rate rather than the
   server's throughput. 150ms per character is a sustained comfortable rate. */
const LATENCY = {
  typingMsPerChar: 150,
  // anything slower than this and the user has typed another character
  mustAnswerWithinMs: 150,
  // so the cheap query goes first and the expensive rows fill in behind it
  twoPhase: {
    phase1: { returns: 'total count + first 5 rows', targetMs: 120 },
    phase2: { returns: 'the remaining rows',        targetMs: 400 },
  },
  // and what to render while phase 2 is outstanding
  duringPhase2: 'keep phase 1 rows visible, mark them with a subtle pending state',
  // never: blank the list, because an empty list reads as zero results
  neverShow: 'an empty list while a query is in flight',
};

/* The four defects, as named fields on the response, so the dashboard can
   distinguish them rather than reporting one undifferentiated score. */
function classifyResultSet({ parsed, docs, edited, took }) {
  const zero = docs.length === 0;
  return {
    zeroResult: zero,
    // recall: the engine returned nothing for terms it should have matched
    recallFailure:   zero && parsed.terms.length > 0 && !parsed.ranges && Object.keys(parsed.filters).length === 0,
    // precision: unedited query, results returned, and they are obviously unrelated
    precisionFailure: !zero && !edited && docs.every((d) => d.score < 0.2),
    // ranking: the top hit is a poor match and something better sat at 7
    rankingFailure:  !zero && docs[0].score < 0.5 && docs.slice(0, 10).some((d) => d.score > 0.9),
    // latency: correct results, but after the user had moved on
    latencyFailure:  took > LATENCY.mustAnswerWithinMs * 3,
  };
}

/* The zero-result rate is the metric to watch, because it is the earliest
   signal that an index, a filter or an analyser has changed underneath you. */
const SEARCH_DASHBOARD = {
  metrics: [
    'zero-result rate, by day and by query length',
    'first-click position, p50 and p90',
    'time to first result, p50 and p95',
    'searches per session that return zero, as a session-level percentage',
    'correction rate: how often a did-you-mean was clicked',
  ],
  // the alarm that catches an index regression the day it ships
  alarm: 'zero-result rate up more than 3 points day over day, for 2 consecutive days',
  // and the release check: a sample of known-good queries, run per deploy
  canary: 200,
};

Sorts and filters must survive pagination, and the URL must carry them. Everything about a list view's state belongs in the query string, so a view can be shared, bookmarked, opened in a second tab, and reached by the back button — and so a support conversation can include a link that reproduces exactly what the person was looking at. This is the least glamorous item in the section and it is the one that generates the most support tickets, because "it lost my filters" is the most common complaint any list view receives.

/* Every bit of list-view state lives in the URL. One source of truth, so
   share, bookmark, back-button and "send me the link you are looking at"
   all work without any of them being implemented separately. */
function readListState(search) {
  const p = new URLSearchParams(search);
  return {
    q: p.get('q') || '',
    sort: p.get('sort') || 'updatedAt',
    dir: p.get('dir') || 'desc',
    page: Math.max(1, Number(p.get('page')) || 1),
    // filters are a repeated parameter, not a JSON blob: readable, and
    // a bookmark stays legible to a human six months later
    filters: p.getAll('f').flatMap((f) => f.split(':')),   // ['status:open', 'assignee:me']
  };
}
function writeListState(s) {
  const p = new URLSearchParams();
  if (s.q) p.set('q', s.q);
  p.set('sort', s.sort); p.set('dir', s.dir);
  if (s.page > 1) p.set('page', String(s.page));
  for (const f of s.filters) p.append('f', f);
  // replaceState, not pushState: typing must not fill the back stack with
  // 40 intermediate queries the user has to press back through
  return '?' + p.toString();
}

/* Debounce the query, and keep the count honest while it is in flight. The
   request sequence guard is the part that matters: without it, a slow early
   response can overwrite a fast later one and the list shows stale results. */
function attachSearch(input, { onQuery, delay = 250 }) {
  let timer = null, seq = 0;
  input.addEventListener('input', () => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    const q = input.value;
    // show the previous results dimmed rather than blanking the list: a
    // flashing empty list reads as "no results", not as "still working"
    onQuery({ q, status: 'pending', previousVisible: true });
    timer = setTimeout(async () => {
      const mine = ++seq;
      const res = await fetch('/api/search?q=' + encodeURIComponent(q));
      if (mine !== seq) return;                       // a newer query already answered
      onQuery({ q, status: 'done', ...res });
    }, delay);
  });
}

/* The zero-result screen, assembled from the four required parts. Each part
   is one function so the missing-part check below is exhaustive rather than
   a matter of opinion. */
function zeroResult({ q, appliedFilters, suggestions, categoryHref, everythingHref }) {
  const parts = {
    whatWasSearched: q ? 'No results for "' + q + '"' : 'No results',
    whatHappened: appliedFilters.length
      ? 'Nothing matches while ' + appliedFilters.length + ' filter' +
        (appliedFilters.length === 1 ? ' is' : 's are') + ' applied'
      : 'Nothing in the catalogue matches that',
    whatToTry: [
      ...(suggestions.slice(0, 3).map((s) => ({ label: 'Search for "' + s + '"', href: '/s?q=' + encodeURIComponent(s) }))),
      ...(appliedFilters.map((f) => ({ label: 'Remove filter: ' + f, href: '/s?q=' + encodeURIComponent(q) }))),
    ],
    // the part that converts: this person is at peak intent right now
    whereElse: [
      { label: 'Browse all ' + categoryHref.name, href: categoryHref.href },
      { label: 'See everything in ' + everythingHref.name, href: everythingHref.href },
    ],
  };
  return parts;
}

/* Spell correction is offered, never applied silently. The exceptions are
   not tuning: an identifier or a proper noun is never a misspelling. */
function shouldOfferCorrection(q, res) {
  const looksLikeIdentifier = /^[A-Z]{2,3}-\d{2,}$/.test(q);
  const looksLikeProperNoun = /^[A-Z]/.test(q);
  const drasticShift = Math.abs(res.total - res.withoutCorrection.total) / Math.max(res.withoutCorrection.total, 1) > 0.5;
  return {
    offer: !looksLikeIdentifier && !looksLikeProperNoun && !drasticShift && res.didCorrect,
    // the line that makes it honest, and that takes one sentence
    line: 'Showing results for "' + res.corrected + '"',
  };
}

The search agreement: debounce typing and show a result count, offer did-you-mean on zero results, and keep sorts and filters persisting through pagination.

16.4 Loading, empty and edge states (the deliverable nobody budgets)

Loading, empty, error, and edge states are real screens with real jobs, not afterthoughts, yet they are often left out of the budget. A loading state should mirror the final layout with skeletons or clear progress so users can predict what arrives. An empty state must say what would normally be here, why the user should care, and the one action that starts them moving. Every error state should explain what happened, why, and how to recover.

// Four states = four content designs:
//  LOADING: skeletons beat spinners (<1s feels instant; 1-3s show progress;
//    >3s give a way out). NEVER white screen while you "fetch".
//  EMPTY: no default content = 3 parts: what's here (title),
//    why you should care, and the FIRST next action ("Create your
//    first playlist" → [New playlist]).
//  ERROR: Ch.12.4 what/why/next; include "what we kept safe".
//  EDGE : long names truncate with title-tooltip, not break layout;
//    huge numbers don't overflow in the table row.

The four screens nobody budgets for

Loading, empty, error and edge states are the screens a user sees when the product is not working perfectly, which is most of the time, and they are consistently the last thing designed and the first thing a user forms an impression from. A product with an excellent main screen and an insulting empty state is experienced as a product with an empty state. This is not a matter of polish: each of these states has a job to do, and the job is different in each case, so they need different content rather than the same grey box with different wording.

A loading state should predict. A skeleton that mirrors the final layout tells the user what is arriving and in what shape, which means the arrival is a fill rather than a surprise; a spinner tells the user only that time is passing. Predictability matters because of the perceptual effect: content that appears in the expected place is read faster and with less interruption than the same content appearing somewhere new. Where the wait is long enough to be a real wait, add real progress — determinate rather than a fake bar, because a bar that goes to 90 percent and waits there is worse than no bar, since it has made a promise and broken it visibly.

An empty state has three parts and it is a sales surface, not an apology. First, what would normally be here, in the vocabulary of the domain rather than in the word "data". Second, why the user should care — what this collection is for and what happens when it is not empty. Third, the one action that starts them moving, which must be a single named button, not "Get started" and not a menu. There is a fourth case that teams forget: empty because of a filter, which is not an empty state at all and must never render as one, because telling somebody they have no invoices when they have forty and a filter applied is the single most alarming thing a list view can do.

An error state owes the user three things: what happened, why, and what to do. The most common failure is reporting the mechanism instead of the meaning — a 500, a stack-trace summary, a "something went wrong" — which is written from the system's point of view rather than the person's. Say what failed in the user's terms, say whether their data was saved (this is the question they are actually asking and it is almost never answered), and give a next action that is either a retry, a route back to a known-good state, or a way to report it with the details already attached. An error message with no recovery path converts a small failure into a support ticket.

Edge states are the long tail: names that are far longer than the mockup, numbers far larger, a network that is slow rather than absent, a permission the user had and no longer has, a record deleted by somebody else while it was open on screen. Test for these deliberately rather than hoping a QA pass finds them, because they are all one-line CSS and one-line length checks and they are all found in production if they are not found before. The two highest-value ones are text that must not break a layout — truncate with an ellipsis and keep the full value in a title attribute and on the detail page — and stale data, which needs a visible age rather than a silently outdated number.

Templates, tests, and the cost of skipping them

The reason states get skipped is that each one looks like an afternoon and collectively they are a sprint, and because skipping one is invisible until the moment a user hits it — which is a moment nobody is watching. The way to make them affordable is to build them once, centrally, as a set of state templates with slots rather than as bespoke screens per team. A skeleton has one shape and a variable number of rows; an error state has a heading, a body, a primary action and an optional detail disclosure; an empty state has three slots. Build those four as components with documented contracts and every team gets them for free, and the second team to ask gets the same thing in an afternoon instead of a week.

Contracts matter more than the pixels, because a state template with an undefined contract gets misused. The empty state has to be told whether it is genuinely empty or filtered-empty, because those two need different content and rendering the wrong one is the alarming bug; the loading state has to be told whether the shape of the arriving content is known, because if it is not, a skeleton that mirrors a table is a lie about what is coming. Write the props down, make the wrong combination a type error rather than a rendering surprise, and the template will outlive the people who built it.

Test them mechanically, because these are exactly the states that break in a refactor. A snapshot test on the skeleton catches the case where a column was added and the placeholder was not; a state-machine unit test catches the case where an error path was added and now returns ready with an empty array; a contract test on the empty state catches the case where a new list was wired up without a branch for filtered-empty. None of these need a browser and all three have caught real regressions in codebases where the states were designed carefully and then quietly untested.

Accessibility in these states is where the polish stops. A skeleton must carry aria-busy="true" on the region being loaded, and the placeholders inside it must be hidden from the accessibility tree — a screen reader otherwise announces a page of meaningless rectangles, which is worse than announcing nothing. A loading indicator that animates needs to respect prefers-reduced-motion, and a shimmer is exactly the kind of thing that setting is about. An error needs role="alert" or a live region so it is announced when it appears rather than only when focus happens to land near it.

Then there is the state nobody thinks of: the one where the data is fine and the user's permissions are not, or the action succeeded for some records and failed for others. A bulk operation that updated 480 of 500 is the most under-designed screen in most products, and it is the one where trust is either earned or lost, because a person who is told "500 updated" when 20 failed will believe the report next time without reading it. Partial success is a state; report it as a count, list the failures, and offer to retry only the failures.

/* The state template registry: four templates, and every async view in the
   product picks from these rather than inventing its own. The prop contracts
   are the point, because an undefined contract is how a template gets
   misused and starts lying. */
const STATE_TEMPLATES = {
  loading: {
    contract: {
      shape: 'table | list | card | form',   // REQUIRED: the skeleton mirrors this
      rows: 5,                              // how many placeholder rows
      announce: true,                       // aria-busy on the region
      deterministic: false,                 // true only when the total is known
      label: 'Loading invoices',
    },
    refuses: 'determinate: true without a known total. A bar that reaches 90% and waits is worse than no bar.',
  },

  'empty-true': {
    contract: { noun: 'invoices', why: 'one sentence on what they are for', action: { label: 'New invoice', href: '/i/new' } },
    rules: ['exactly one primary action', 'never "get started"', 'say what would be here normally'],
  },

  'empty-filtered': {
    contract: { noun: 'invoices', filterCount: 2, removeHref: '/s', broaderHref: '/invoices' },
    // never reuse empty-true here. "you have no invoices" when they have
    // forty is the most alarming thing a list view can do.
    rules: ['name the filter count', 'primary action clears the filters', 'never the empty-true copy'],
  },

  error: {
    contract: { what: 'plain-language cause', why: 'one clause', do: 'a next action', dataSafe: 'boolean | null',
                retry: 'nullable', requestId: 'string' },
    rules: ['dataSafe is required, not optional: it is the question the user is actually asking',
            'role="alert" or a live region', 'the report action carries the context'],
  },

  // the state nobody designs and everybody meets
  'partial-success': {
    contract: { succeeded: 480, failed: 20, failures: 'array', retryFailuresOnly: true },
    rules: ['the count is the headline', 'failures are listed, not summarised',
            'retry targets only the failures', 'a later report must not claim 500'],
  },
};

/* The skeleton, marked up so it announces nothing and hides nothing. */
const SKELETON_HTML =
  '<div class="sk-region" aria-busy="true" aria-live="polite">' +
    '<span class="vh">Loading invoices</span>' +
    // placeholders are decorative, so they are hidden from assistive tech;
    // otherwise a screen reader reads a page of meaningless rectangles
    '<div class="sk-row" aria-hidden="true"><span class="sk sk-title"></span></div>'.repeat(5) +
  '</div>';

/* Reduced motion is not optional on a shimmer. */
const SKELETON_CSS =
  '.sk{background:linear-gradient(90deg,var(--am-surface-2),var(--am-surface-3),var(--am-surface-2));' +
  'background-size:200% 100%;animation:sk 1.4s linear infinite;border-radius:var(--radius)}' +
  '@media (prefers-reduced-motion:reduce){' +
  '.sk{animation:none;background:var(--am-surface-2)}}';

/* The tests that catch a state being broken by an ordinary refactor. */
const STATE_TESTS = [
  { kind: 'snapshot', target: 'skeleton for table shape, 5 rows',
    catches: 'a column added and the placeholder not', browser: false },
  { kind: 'unit', target: 'deriveViewState() for all six states and their transitions',
    catches: 'a new error path returning "ready" with an empty array', browser: false },
  { kind: 'contract', target: 'every list view renders empty-filtered when filterCount > 0',
    catches: 'a new list wired up with no filtered-empty branch', browser: true },
  { kind: 'contract', target: 'partial-success never reports the total as the succeeded count',
    catches: 'a bulk endpoint that returns 500 for 480 successes', browser: true },
  { kind: 'a11y', target: 'aria-busy on the region, placeholders aria-hidden, errors in a live region',
    catches: 'a skeleton rewritten as a plain div', browser: true },
  { kind: 'visual', target: 'long name, 10^9 count, empty collection, RTL locale, slow network',
    catches: 'the long tail, which is always the last thing anyone looks at', browser: true },
];

/* Partial success, reported honestly. The four lines are the whole design. */
function partialSuccess({ succeeded, failed, failures }) {
  return {
    headline: succeeded + ' of ' + (succeeded + failed) + ' updated',
    // the failures are listed, because "20 failed" invites a support ticket
    failures: failures.map((f) => ({ id: f.id, reason: f.reason })),
    retry: { label: 'Retry ' + failed + ' failed', only: failures.map((f) => f.id) },
    // and the number that must never be what the first line said
    neverReportAsTotal: succeeded,
  };
}

The budgeting argument is the one that gets these designed. Ask what fraction of real sessions pass through a state that is not the happy path, then price the states by that fraction: if 8 percent of sessions hit an error state and that screen is written by whoever had half a day left, the product is being designed for 92 percent of its users by a fraction of its team. Skeleton and empty state templates, written once and adopted everywhere, are the mechanism that makes this affordable, and they also make it consistent, which is the second reason to do them centrally rather than per team.

/* The state machine every async view needs, with the four states named
   explicitly so that "we did not design that one" is visible in code. */
const VIEW_STATES = ['loading', 'empty-filtered', 'empty-true', 'ready', 'error', 'stale'];

function deriveViewState({ items, loading, error, filtered, lastLoadedAt, filterCount }) {
  if (loading && items.length === 0) return 'loading';
  // the distinction that must never be collapsed: "your filter matched
  // nothing" is not "you have nothing", and rendering it as the latter is
  // the most alarming thing a list view can do
  if (error && items.length === 0) return 'error';
  if (items.length === 0) return filterCount > 0 ? 'empty-filtered' : 'empty-true';
  // stale is a real state: data from four minutes ago shown as if it were now
  if (lastLoadedAt && Date.now() - lastLoadedAt > 5 * 60 * 1000) return 'stale';
  return 'ready';
}

/* The empty state, three parts, each one a function so the completeness check
   below is exhaustive instead of a matter of opinion. */
function emptyTrue({ noun, whyItMatters, primaryAction }) {
  return {
    headline: 'No ' + noun + ' yet',
    // part two: the reason to care, in the domain's words
    body: whyItMatters,
    // part three: one named action, never "get started"
    action: primaryAction,
  };
}
function emptyFiltered({ noun, filterCount, removeHref, broaderHref }) {
  return {
    headline: 'No ' + noun + ' match the current filters',
    // naming the filter is what turns a dead end into a decision
    body: filterCount + ' filter' + (filterCount === 1 ? ' is' : 's are') + ' applied',
    actions: [
      { label: 'Clear ' + filterCount + ' filter' + (filterCount === 1 ? '' : 's'), href: removeHref, primary: true },
      { label: 'Browse all ' + noun, href: broaderHref },
    ],
  };
}

/* The error message, in the three-part order that works: what happened,
   why, what to do. And the sentence teams forget, which is the question the
   user is actually asking. */
function errorMessage(err) {
  const byCode = {
    PAYMENT_DECLINED: { what: 'The payment was declined by your bank', why: 'banks decline payments for their own reasons, often a name mismatch',
                        do: 'Try a different card, or contact your bank and ask why.' },
    NETWORK_TIMEOUT:  { what: 'We could not reach the server', why: 'the connection dropped before the request finished',
                        do: 'Your changes are saved. Try again in a moment.' },
    PERMISSION_LOST:  { what: 'You no longer have access to this project', why: 'a member with that permission removed it at 14:02',
                        do: 'Ask the project owner to restore your access.' },
    VALIDATION:       { what: 'Three fields need attention', why: 'the values in them are not valid',
                        do: 'They are marked in the form below.' },
  };
  const m = byCode[err.code] || { what: 'Something went wrong', why: 'an unexpected error', do: 'Try again.' };
  return {
    // the fourth line, and the one that stops the support ticket
    dataSafe: err.durablySaved != null ? String(err.durablySaved) : 'unknown',
    // and the retry, attached to the report action so the details travel with it
    retry: err.retryable ? { label: 'Try again', action: 'retry' } : null,
    report: { label: 'Report this', withContext: ['requestId: ' + err.requestId, 'code: ' + err.code] },
    ...m,
  };
}

/* Progress that does not lie. A determinate bar only when the total is
   actually known; otherwise show the work rather than a percentage. */
function progress({ done, total, unit = 'files' }) {
  if (total == null) return { kind: 'indeterminate', label: 'Working…',
    // honest when the count is unknown: what is happening, not how far
    note: 'we do not know how many yet' };
  const pct = Math.round((done / Math.max(total, 1)) * 100);
  return { kind: 'determinate', pct, label: done + ' of ' + total + ' ' + unit,
    // never let it sit at 90: a stalled determinate bar is a broken promise
    stalled: pct > 90 && done === lastProgressAt.done };
}

/* Edge cases, as assertions rather than as hopes. These are cheap to test
   and every one of them has shipped broken at least once. */
const EDGE_CASES = [
  { case: 'name 400 characters long',      expect: 'truncate with ellipsis, full value in title and on the detail page' },
  { case: 'count over 10^9',               expect: 'abbreviate only in a summary, never in a value that gets compared' },
  { case: 'network slow, not absent',     expect: 'show the last good data with a visible age, not a spinner over stale content' },
  { case: 'record deleted by someone else', expect: 'a non-destructive notice on refresh, not a crash and not a blank screen' },
  { case: 'permission revoked while open', expect: 'read-only mode with an explanation, and the edits already made are not lost' },
  { case: 'two tabs, same record',         expect: 'a conflict notice rather than last-write-wins silence' },
  { case: 'locale with RTL text',         expect: 'the layout mirrors; numbers stay left-to-right inside it' },
  { case: 'time zone of the user differs', expect: 'relative times locally, absolute times with the zone on hover' },
];

Four states that each need their own content design: loading skeletons, the three-part empty state, honest errors, and edge cases like long names and big numbers.

16.5 Feedback moments people notice

Feedback moments are the instant a user learns an action succeeded, failed, or changed something, and people remember these more than any polish. Honest autosave confirmations, explicit undo affordances, and truthfully calculated progress bars build trust one interaction at a time. The rule is temporal locality: keep feedback at the point of action, immediately, attached to the object it concerns. Never fake a success the system cannot deliver.

  • "Saved ✓" on autosave — but only when actually saved (Ch.5 timing truth).
  • Undo for destructive ops with a toast ("Post deleted — Undo" with a 5s window).
  • Progress shown as "step 2 of 4" for real processes, not fake meters.
  • Every success toast answers: what changed, where to go next, is it reversible.

Feedback that is honest, immediate, and reversible

A feedback moment is the instant a user learns whether their action did what they meant, and it is the highest-trust moment in the product. Everything else on the screen can be polished; this one is either truthful or it is not, and a false confirmation costs more trust than a missing one — because the user will repeat the action, believe it failed again, and act on that belief, which may mean submitting twice or paying twice. So the rule that governs this whole section is that feedback must state what actually happened, as observed by the system, not what was requested by the code that triggered it.

Autosave is where this is most often faked, and the failure mode is specific: the interface shows "Saved" when the request was issued rather than when it succeeded. The difference is visible on a bad connection, and it is the difference between a user who trusts the indicator and a user who stops reading it. Fix it properly by having the indicator read from the response — a small state machine with a pending phase that is visible, a confirmed phase that says so only on a 2xx, and an error phase that says what happened and offers a retry — and by never optimistically confirming a write whose success the client has not observed.

Reversibility beats confirmation. A confirmation dialog interrupts everyone to protect against the rare case, which is the wrong trade; an undo toast protects against it properly, because the user acts immediately and recovers immediately, and only the mistaken action pays the cost. Five seconds is the conventional window and it is roughly right, but the important properties are that the toast is attached to the object it concerns, that the window is visible as a countdown rather than assumed, and that the action it undoes is genuinely complete — including server-side, not merely an optimistic local removal that a refetch contradicts.

Every success message answers three questions: what changed, where to go next, and whether it is reversible. "Post deleted" answers one. "Post deleted. Undo is available for 5 seconds" answers two. And progress has to be real: "step 2 of 4" for a genuine four-step process is honest, a bar that fills over four seconds regardless of the work is theatre, and a bar that reaches 90 percent and waits is the worst of the three because it has made a specific promise about remaining time and broken it.

Temporal locality is the principle that organises the rest: keep the feedback at the point of the action, immediately, and attached to the thing it concerns. A global toast in the corner about an error in a field three screens up is a notification the user has to re-associate with an action, which is slower than showing it in the field. The exception is the action that happened somewhere else — a background job, a collaborator's edit, a scheduled event — where the feedback necessarily arrives away from its cause, and the compensation for that is to say where it came from.

Toasts, notifications, and where the boundary is

Three mechanisms get conflated, and separating them makes every decision easier. An inline message belongs to a thing on the screen — a field, a row, a panel — and it stays there until the condition is resolved, because it is part of that thing and disappears with it. A toast is transient, is about something the user just did, and never carries anything the user must act on. A notification is persistent, arrives when the user is not necessarily looking, and is about something that happened elsewhere or will happen later. Putting an error in a toast is the most common misuse, because the toast disappears at exactly the moment a person has read it and decided what to do.

Toast timing is a WCAG issue rather than a taste issue, and the requirement is specific: a transient message must be dismissible, extendable, or persist until it is acknowledged, and the extension has to be available by hovering or focusing the message as well as by pointer movement alone. In practice that means a pause on hover and on focus, a real dismiss control, and durations long enough to read the longest message you actually write — which is a measurement, not a taste, and is usually about twice what was assumed.

Stack carefully. Three toasts at once is already too many, and stacking them into a corner with the newest on top means the newest is read and the other two are missed while the user acts on the first. The mechanisms that work are a single slot that replaces its content, a queue with a visible count of what is waiting, and grouping — "3 invoices updated" rather than three separate toasts — because the grouping also says something true about what the system did, which three separate messages do not.

Notifications that arrive when the app is closed are a different discipline entirely, because the user cannot act on them immediately and the temptation is to make them louder. Browser notifications, email and push each need a reason the user would want, and the permission prompt is the one moment in the product where the value proposition must be stated before the question is asked — asking for notifications and then explaining them after the prompt is a request the user has already declined. And a category that ends up being muted by everybody should be removed rather than retained, because a notification channel nobody wants is a permanent tax on the ones they do.

The tone of the message is part of the mechanism's design and it is where most of them fail. An error that blames the user — "invalid input", "you entered the wrong password" — produces a person who tries the same thing again, when what they needed was a statement of what was wrong and where. Name the condition and the field. "That email address is already registered — sign in instead, or use another address" gives two routes forward, which is what an error message is for.

And keep the register across all three mechanisms, because a user who is told a thing succeeded and then finds out it did not stops reading every message the product sends, including the ones that would have told them something they needed. The whole value of a feedback system is that it is believed; that belief is a single asset, it is consumed by every false confirmation, and it is not recoverable by adding more messaging later.

/* The three feedback mechanisms, with the rule that decides which one to use.
   The most common defect in this area is putting an action-required message
   into a mechanism that deletes itself on a timer. */
const FEEDBACK_KINDS = {
  inline: {
    lives: 'attached to the thing on screen',
    persists: 'until the condition is resolved',
    for: ['a field error', 'a panel-level warning', 'a row-level state', 'anything the user MUST act on'],
    // an error that vanishes is an error the user cannot act on
    neverUseFor: 'a destructive failure',
  },
  toast: {
    lives: 'a corner, for a few seconds, paused on hover and focus',
    persists: 'no',
    for: ['the result of something the user just did', 'undo affordances', 'short confirmations'],
    // a confirmation of something you cannot deliver is the whole failure
    neverUseFor: ['a validation error', 'anything requiring a decision',
                  'a background job that has not finished', 'the only record that something happened'],
    // WCAG 2.2.1: a transient message must be dismissible, extendable, or
    // persist until acknowledged. This implements all three at once.
    timing: { ms: 6000, pauseOnHover: true, pauseOnFocus: true, dismissible: true },
  },
  notification: {
    lives: 'a list the user opens later, plus optionally the OS layer',
    persists: 'yes',
    for: ['something that happened elsewhere', 'something that will happen later',
          'a message about another person, not about the current screen'],
    // the ask happens before the prompt, never after
    permissionPrompt: 'state the value proposition first, ask second, in the same screen',
  },
};

/* The toast, with the timing behaviour WCAG asks for and the focus trap
   that everybody forgets: Tab must be able to reach the dismiss button. */
const TOAST_HTML =
  '<div class="toast" role="status" aria-live="polite" data-ms="6000">' +
    '<span class="toast-msg">Post deleted</span>' +
    '<button type="button" class="toast-action">Undo</button>' +
    '<button type="button" class="toast-x" aria-label="Dismiss this message">&#215;</button>' +
    // the countdown is visible, so the window is not something the user has to guess at
    '<span class="toast-bar" aria-hidden="true"></span>' +
  '</div>';

function toast(el, ms = 6000) {
  let timer = null, remaining = ms, paused = false, startedAt = 0;
  const dismiss = el.querySelector('.toast-x');
  const bar = el.querySelector('.toast-bar');

  const run = () => { startedAt = Date.now(); timer = setTimeout(close, remaining); };
  const pause = () => {
    if (paused) return;
    paused = true; clearTimeout(timer);
    remaining -= Date.now() - startedAt;
    if (bar) bar.style.animationPlayState = 'paused';   // visible, not just internal
  };
  const resume = () => {
    if (!paused) return;
    paused = false; run();
    if (bar) bar.style.animationPlayState = 'running';
  };
  function close() { clearTimeout(timer); el.hidden = true; }

  // hover AND focus: keyboard users get the same grace period as mouse users,
  // and this is the part that is almost always implemented as hover only
  el.addEventListener('pointerenter', pause);
  el.addEventListener('pointerleave', resume);
  el.addEventListener('focusin', pause);
  el.addEventListener('focusout', resume);
  dismiss.addEventListener('click', close);
  run();
  return { close, remaining: () => remaining };
}

/* Grouping. Three toasts mean the user acts on one and misses two; the
   grouped message is also the more truthful description of what happened. */
function notifyMany(results) {
  const ok = results.filter((r) => r.ok);
  const bad = results.filter((r) => !r.ok);
  if (bad.length === 0) {
    return { kind: 'toast', message: ok.length + ' invoices updated' };
  }
  if (ok.length === 0) {
    // all failed: this is an error, so it must not be a toast that expires
    return { kind: 'inline', message: bad.length + ' invoices could not be updated',
             detail: bad.map((b) => ({ id: b.id, reason: b.reason })),
             action: { label: 'Retry ' + bad.length, only: bad.map((b) => b.id) } };
  }
  // mixed: the count in the toast, the failures listed where they can be acted on
  return { kind: 'toast', message: ok.length + ' updated, ' + bad.length + ' failed',
           where: 'see the failures below', failures: bad };
}

/* The tone check. An error that blames the user produces a repeat attempt,
   which is the opposite of what it was for. */
const ERROR_VOICES = [
  { text: 'Invalid input', verdict: 'REJECT', reason: 'names no condition, offers no route', better: 'Password must be at least 15 characters' },
  { text: 'You entered the wrong password', verdict: 'REJECT', reason: 'blames the user; they will type the same thing again',
    better: 'That password is not right. Passwords are case-sensitive.' },
  { text: 'Payment failed', verdict: 'REJECT', reason: 'no cause and no next step', better: 'Your bank declined the payment. Try another card, or ask your bank why.' },
  { text: 'Email already registered — sign in, or use another address', verdict: 'ACCEPT', reason: 'names the condition and gives two routes forward' },
];

Never fake a success the system cannot deliver, which sounds obvious and is the most common thing done in this area. A "sent" on a message that is queued rather than delivered, a "processed" on a job that is still waiting, an optimistic total that the invoice will not confirm — each is a small promise that compounds, because a user who has been lied to once by a system indicator learns to verify everything the system says, which is a large and permanent tax on trust. The test is whether the indicator could ever be wrong, and if it could, whether the wrongness is visible to the person looking at it.

/* The honest autosave indicator. The indicator is driven by the RESPONSE,
   never by the fact that a request was sent. This is the whole section in
   one rule, and getting it wrong is worse than having no indicator. */
const SAVE = { idle: 'idle', pending: 'pending', saved: 'saved', failed: 'failed' };

function createAutosaveIndicator(el, { save, debounce = 800 }) {
  let state = SAVE.idle, seq = 0, timer = null, lastError = null;

  const render = () => {
    el.dataset.state = state;
    el.textContent = {
      idle: '',
      // visible, because a list that does not change looks broken and a
      // silent indicator is worse than no indicator
      pending: 'Saving…',
      // only ever set from a 2xx, never from "we called the API"
      saved: 'Saved ' + at(),
      // and it says what happened, because "error" is not an explanation
      failed: 'Not saved — ' + lastError + ' Retry',
    }[state];
    // the status role means a screen reader announces it without stealing focus
    el.setAttribute('role', 'status');
    el.setAttribute('aria-live', 'polite');
  };

  async function flush() {
    const mine = ++seq;
    state = SAVE.pending; render();
    try {
      const res = await save();
      // a late response from an earlier edit must not confirm a newer one
      if (mine !== seq) return false;
      state = SAVE.saved; render();
      return true;
    } catch (e) {
      if (mine !== seq) return false;
      state = SAVE.failed; lastError = e.code === 'OFFLINE' ? 'you appear offline' : 'the server refused the request';
      render();
      return false;
    }
  }

  return {
    change() { clearTimeout(timer); state = SAVE.idle; render(); timer = setTimeout(flush, debounce); },
    // the page must not close on a pending save, and it must say why
    beforeUnload: (e) => { if (state === SAVE.pending) { e.preventDefault(); e.returnValue = ''; } },
    flush, state: () => state,
  };
}

/* Undo, done properly: attached to the object, visible window, and complete
   server-side so a refetch cannot contradict the toast. */
async function destructiveAction({ item, remove, restore, windowMs = 5000 }) {
  const snapshot = structuredClone(item);
  await remove(item.id);                       // the real deletion, not a local illusion
  const t = toast(itemLabel(item) + ' deleted', {
    action: { label: 'Undo', onClick: async () => { await restore(snapshot); } },
    // the window is shown, not assumed: a countdown the user can see
    expiresInMs: windowMs, showCountdown: true,
    // and the escape hatch for a dismissal nobody acted on
    onExpire: () => logMissedUndo(item.id),
  });
  return t;
}
// the refinement worth making: if nobody pressed undo, do nothing. A
// permanently retained "undo" affordance is a promise nobody keeps.

/* Every success message, checked against the three questions. A message that
   cannot answer them is not finished, and the missing one is the pattern. */
const FEEDBACK = {
  deletion:    { saysWhat: 'Post deleted', saysNext: 'Undo for 5 seconds', saysReversible: true },
  weakDeletion:{ saysWhat: 'Post deleted', saysNext: '',                  saysReversible: false,
                 verdict: 'REJECT - answers one of three questions' },
  realSteps:   { saysWhat: 'step 2 of 4', saysNext: 'next: payment', saysReversible: true },
