  fakeSteps:   { saysWhat: 'Processing…', note: 'bar fills over 4s regardless of the work',
                 verdict: 'REJECT - progress that is not progress' },
  stalledBar:  { saysWhat: '90%', note: 'sits there because the remaining 10% is unknown',
                 verdict: 'REJECT - a specific promise about remaining time, broken' },
  remoteChange:{ saysWhat: 'Ana edited this document', saysNext: 'View changes',
                // the exception to temporal locality, and its compensation
                because: 'the cause is on another screen, so the feedback must name its source' },
};

/* The test that catches every fake in one place. */
function indicatorIsHonest(indicator, groundTruth) {
  return indicator.state() === SAVE.saved ? groundTruth.lastWriteSucceeded
       : indicator.state() === SAVE.failed ? !groundTruth.lastWriteSucceeded
       : true;   // idle and pending make no claim, which is the point
}

  2. Build a zero-result screen that still sells (you choose the product); state the 3 parts.
  3. Add sortable headers + row selection to a table mock you own; write its states table.

17 · App (Mobile) UX Deep

Mobile UX deep dives past the surface of apps into the platform physics users feel: gestures, notifications, back stacks, and the constant fight for a home-screen slot. Native feel comes from matching each platform’s conventions, never from copying a web layout. Learn comfortable thumb zones, standard interaction patterns, and when a sheet, dialog, tab, or notification should appear. These small details decide whether an app feels native or transplanted onto the device.

17.1 iOS vs Android: the two dialects17.2 Gestures & navigation signatures17.3 Onboarding & first-run: the 3-minute contract17.4 Notifications: permission is a promise17.5 App perceived performance & offline

Apps add platform physics: gestures, notifications, app-switching, and the endless home screen battle. The difference between a web clone and a "native-feeling" app is these details.

17.1 iOS vs Android: the two dialects

iOS and Android are two dialects of mobile design with different habits for back navigation, content organization, and system controls. iOS leans on swipe-from-left back, bottom navigation, and platform-native components, while Android relies on a system back stack, navigation drawers, and per-field input rules. Match the platform’s conventions for selection, toggles, and text entry so users feel instantly familiar. Design each platform where behavior differs and share only what truly behaves the same.

AspectiOSAndroid
Backtop-left + gesture edgesystem back (universal)
Navtab bars, back-stackdrawer + back-stack blended
Dialogs/buttonssheets, rounded, "Cancel/Save"Material, dialog + snackbar
Icons/labels styleSF symbols, tighterMaterial symbols, bolder

Two dialects, and what actually has to be shared

iOS and Android are two populations rather than two skins, and the evidence is behavioural: the same person uses a back gesture on one and a hardware key on the other, and a product that imposes one model's back behaviour on the other platform is not being inconsistent, it is being wrong about which user it has. The practical cost lands in one place above all others. The Android system back button is among the most-used controls in any Android app, and users press it reflexively from every screen including sheets, dialogs and menus; an app that handles it incorrectly fails several times per session, every session, for as long as it ships.

Share the layer that describes the product's structure and keep the layer that describes the platform's habits separate. Share: layout structure, the spacing and type scales, colour tokens, radii, motion durations and easing, all business logic, all content, and all analytics events. Let differ: the navigation model, gestures, back behaviour, pickers, share and payment sheets, the permission flow, and every platform-idiomatic control — a switch rather than a toggle, a wheel picker rather than a dropdown, a bottom tab bar rather than a top one. The rule for deciding anything in this grey area is to ask whether a user of that platform would be surprised by it, and if they would, let it differ.

Back navigation is the single most consequential difference, so treat it as the primary platform contract. On iOS there is no system back and the edge swipe is the idiom, so navigation needs a visible alternative and a consistent title; on Android the system back must pop exactly one level from anywhere — a dialog consumes it and closes, a bottom sheet consumes it and dismisses, a stack pops one frame, and a root tab either switches to the home tab or exits the app, which has to be the last thing it does and not something surprising. Predictive back, where the OS shows the destination during the gesture, is worth supporting because it is the platform's current expectation and an app that ignores it produces a visibly wrong animation.

Text entry differs per field and per platform in ways that are cheap to honour. Input types drive the keyboard, so email, tel, number, URL and password each have a correct declaration and using type="text" for all of them costs a frustrated user on every screen. iOS offers an autofill bar and QuickType suggestions from the user's own history, which works only if the input carries the right autocomplete token; Android's autofill service is the equivalent and has the same requirement. Date and address entry is where the platforms diverge most visibly and where copying one dialect to the other is most obvious: separate pickers on iOS, an inline or dialog calendar on Android, and a typed field as a fallback on both, because plenty of users prefer typing a date they already know.

Permissions are the clearest case of a shared design with two implementations. On Android the system dialog is what the user sees and it cannot be styled or reworded, so the value explanation has to come before it, in your own screen, and it has to be at the moment of need — and because "don't ask again" turns the permission into a Settings-only route, the ask must be worth one chance and must not be spent on a feature the user might never touch. On iOS the equivalent pre-permission screen is the platform's own recommendation, with a soft outcome in between, so the same value statement is used with different UI around it.

Share tokens, not components. A component whose behaviour differs between platforms should not be one component with a platform flag threaded through it, because the flag becomes a permanent source of untested branches; it should be a shared token and intent layer with two behavioural implementations selected at the platform boundary. That way a change to the spacing scale or the colour palette lands on both platforms at once, while a change to a picker's behaviour stays on one, and neither has to wait for the other.

/* The platform matrix, as data. One table, consulted rather than
   remembered, because every row here is a decision somebody will get
   wrong at least once. "share" means identical; "differ" means two
   implementations behind one intent. */
const PLATFORM_MATRIX = [
  { area: 'back',                 ios: 'edge swipe + a visible title; no system key', android: 'system key/gesture pops exactly one level from anywhere', share: false },
  { area: 'root navigation',      ios: 'bottom tab bar, 3-5 peers', android: 'bottom nav, sometimes a drawer above 5 sections', share: false },
  { area: 'primary action',       ios: 'nav bar right, or a FAB', android: 'FAB bottom right, or a top bar action', share: false },
  { area: 'selection control',   ios: 'switch', android: 'toggle (checkbox for multi)', share: false },
  { area: 'date entry',           ios: 'wheel picker in a sheet', android: 'inline or dialog calendar', share: false },
  { area: 'permission prompt',    ios: 'your pre-permission screen, then the system', android: 'your screen, then the system dialog', share: 'copy only' },
  { area: 'share sheet',          ios: 'system share sheet', android: 'system chooser via intent', share: false },
  { area: 'pull to refresh',      ios: 'supported, not expected', android: 'expected everywhere', share: false },

  { area: 'spacing scale',        ios: 'shared', android: 'shared', share: true },
  { area: 'type scale',           ios: 'shared', android: 'shared', share: true },
  { area: 'colour + radius tokens', ios: 'shared', android: 'shared', share: true },
  { area: 'motion durations',     ios: 'shared', android: 'shared', share: true },
  { area: 'business logic',       ios: 'shared', android: 'shared', share: true },
  { area: 'analytics events',     ios: 'shared, one schema', android: 'shared, one schema', share: true },
];

/* Android back, handled as a stack rather than a boolean, because the
   questions are always "what does back consume here" and "is there
   anything above me". */
function createBackHandler(root) {
  const stack = [];                       // frames pushed on navigate()
  let transient = null;                   // a dialog or a sheet consumes back itself

  function push(frame) { stack.push(frame); root.render(frame); }
  function pop() { const f = stack.pop(); root.render(stack.at(-1) || root.home()); return f; }

  function onBack() {
    // a transient layer consumes back and nothing else happens: a dialog
    // that does not close on back is a dialog users leave by force-quitting
    if (transient) { transient.dismiss(); transient = null; return 'dismissed-transient'; }
    if (stack.length > 1) { pop(); return 'popped-one-frame'; }
    // at the root tab: go home rather than exit, which is what the gesture
    // preview has to show, or the animation is visibly wrong
    root.selectHomeTab();
    return 'went-home';
    // exiting is handled by the OS after a second back, and is deliberately
    // the last thing this handler does
  }
  return { push, pop, onBack, depth: () => stack.length };
}

/* Predictative back: the OS needs the destination up front so it can show
   it during the gesture. Returning it from a resolver rather than
   ignoring the callback is the whole feature. */
const predictiveBack = (handler) => ({
  handler: () => {
    if (handler.depth() > 1) return { destination: 'previous-screen', animate: 'back' };
    return { destination: 'home-tab', animate: 'home' };
  },
  // iOS needs the same information for the edge swipe, without the callback
  iosSwipeEquivalent: handler.depth() > 1 ? 'pop' : 'goHome',
});

/* Text entry, declared per field, because this is the single largest
   source of avoidable friction on a form and it is entirely markup. */
const INPUT_TYPES = {
  email:    { type: 'email',    inputmode: 'email',   autocomplete: 'email',          autocapitalize: 'none' },
  tel:      { type: 'tel',      inputmode: 'tel',     autocomplete: 'tel',            // no national format guessing in UI
             note: 'ask the country separately; a formatted field breaks international numbers' },
  password: { type: 'password', autocomplete: 'current-password', autocapitalize: 'none', spellcheck: 'false' },
  name:     { type: 'text',     autocomplete: 'name',  autocapitalize: 'words' },
  address1: { type: 'text',     autocomplete: 'address-line1', autocapitalize: 'words' },
  postcode: { type: 'text',     autocomplete: 'postal-code', autocapitalize: 'characters' },
  amount:   { type: 'text',     inputmode: 'decimal', autocomplete: 'off', // 'off' because partial input of "1.2" is valid
             note: 'not type=number: it strips the decimal point and scrolls the value' },
  date:     { type: 'text',     inputmode: 'numeric', autocomplete: 'off',
             platformDiffer: true, note: 'picker plus a typed fallback on both platforms' },
};

/* The permission ask, sequenced. Ask once, at the moment of need, with the
   value stated before the system dialog - which cannot be worded. */
async function askForPermission(ctx, { capability, valueStatement, use }) {
  if (ctx.granted.has(capability)) return 'already-granted';
  if (ctx.deniedPermanently.has(capability)) return 'settings-only';
  if (ctx.askedOnce.has(capability)) return 'already-asked-once';

  // the pre-permission screen: one sentence, then the system prompt
  ctx.ask(valueStatement, use);
  const result = await ctx.systemRequest(capability);
  ctx.askedOnce.add(capability);
  if (result === 'denied-permanently') {
    // on Android this means Settings is now the only route, so say so plainly
    // rather than leaving a button that does nothing
    ctx.offerSettingsLink('Camera needs permission. Open Settings to allow it.');
  }
  return result;
}

Testing both, and the places where the two still diverge

Cross-platform work is tested twice, and the second pass is not a formality because the failures are invisible on the other platform by construction. The minimum is one flow exercised on a real device of each kind — not an emulator, because the things that break are the things the emulator does not have: a real keyboard, a real back gesture, a real notch, real low memory, a real half-charged battery. And then the specific list, which is where the divergence that survives review actually lives.

Safe areas are the first of these and the most reliably forgotten, because the notch, the dynamic island, the gesture bar and the three-button nav bar all eat a different part of the screen and none of them is visible on a desktop browser. Content has to sit inside the safe area on every screen and in both orientations, and the controls a user reaches for — the tab bar, a primary action, the composer — are the ones that end up underneath a system bar when this is missed. Fixed elements need the bottom inset and a scroll padding that accounts for it, or the last row of a list is permanently unreachable.

Accessibility follows the same standard on both platforms but is reached through different components, and the differences are worth knowing. VoiceOver's rotor and TalkBack's navigation are not the same model: VoiceOver moves through headings, links and form controls as groups, while TalkBack's granularity and its linear navigation differ, so a hierarchy that is well-formed on iOS can be tedious on Android. Dynamic type scaling goes further on iOS and has its own settings on Android, which means a layout tested at 200 percent on one platform has not been tested at all on the other. Focus indicators, colour contrast and target sizes are identical requirements, and identical failures are the most common findings in both audits.

Motion differs more than most teams expect, and the reason is physical rather than aesthetic: platform motion is tuned to the platform's own animation curve, so an app that uses a different curve on the other platform reads as slightly wrong in a way nobody can name. There is also the behaviour half — a spring on iOS is a spring on Android in name and in feel, and matching the feel means using each platform's own primitive. The design-level consequence is that motion timing is part of the platform matrix rather than part of a shared style, even though the durations can be shared.

Then there is the one that bites in review rather than in testing: dark mode. The convention is not identical — Android's system surfaces and iOS's differ in elevation and in how a card is distinguished from a background — so a card that works on one may disappear on the other. And elevation is a word that means different things: a shadow on iOS, a surface tint on Android. Sharing the elevation intent as tokens and implementing it per platform is the pattern; porting the shadow is the mistake.

Write the platform matrix down as a document with an owner and a review date, because every row in it is a decision that somebody will make differently on a Tuesday without noticing that a rule exists. The document's real purpose is not to record the answers — those are in the code — but to record the reasoning, so that when a new platform arrives, or a convention changes, or two teams disagree, there is something to argue with. Without the reasoning, the convention becomes folklore and gets relitigated every quarter.

/* The abstraction: one intent layer, two implementations, selected at the
   boundary. No platform flag threaded through components - that is what
   turns into permanent untested branches. */
const platform = {
  ios:     require('./platform/ios').default,
  android: require('./platform/android').default,
};

const PLATFORM_API = [
  // each entry is an intent, not a widget: both implementations do the same
  // job by different means, which is what makes sharing the token safe
  { intent: 'back',           ios: 'pop via edge swipe or nav bar', android: 'pop one level from anywhere', owner: 'shell' },
  { intent: 'primaryAction',  ios: 'nav bar trailing item',         android: 'FAB bottom right',             owner: 'shell' },
  { intent: 'pickDate',       ios: 'wheel in a sheet',              android: 'inline calendar',               owner: 'forms' },
  { intent: 'toggle',         ios: 'switch',                        android: 'toggle',                        owner: 'forms' },
  { intent: 'share',          ios: 'UIActivityViewController',      android: 'Intent.createChooser',          owner: 'shell' },
  { intent: 'permissionAsk',  ios: 'pre-permission screen + system', android: 'own screen + system dialog',  owner: 'auth' },
  { intent: 'elevation',      ios: 'shadow',                        android: 'surface tint',                  owner: 'tokens' },
  { intent: 'motionCurve',    ios: 'spring',                        android: 'emphasised deceleration',      owner: 'tokens' },
];

// one component, two behaviours, selected once at the boundary
class DateField {
  constructor(el) {
    this.el = el;
    this.impl = el.dataset.platform === 'ios' ? platform.ios : platform.android;
    // the component never branches on platform; it calls an intent
    this.impl.mountDatePicker(el, { onChange: (iso) => this.commit(iso) });
  }
  commit(iso) {
    // and the date is stored as an ISO string on both, because the storage
    // format must never be a platform opinion
    this.el.value = iso;
  }
}

/* Safe areas. Fixed elements need the inset, and scroll containers need
   padding that accounts for it, or the last row is unreachable. */
const SAFE_AREA_CSS =
  /* bottom navigation that also clears the home indicator and the 3-button bar */
  '.tabbar{padding-bottom:calc(8px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom));}' +
  /* the composer sits above the keyboard AND above the gesture bar */
  '.composer{padding-bottom:calc(10px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom,0px));}' +
  /* scroll padding is what makes the last row reachable rather than hidden */
  '.scroll{padding-bottom:calc(72px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom));}' +
  /* and the top inset matters on the screens with a notch in landscape */
  '.header{padding-top:calc(10px + env(safe-area-inset-top));}';

/* The cross-platform test pass. The columns are the divergences that
   survive code review and are found in QA or not at all. */
const CROSS_PLATFORM_CHECK = [
  { check: 'back from a dialog, a sheet, a menu, and a stack screen', ios: 'edge swipe + nav bar back', android: 'system back consumes each', both: 'same route, different input' },
  { check: 'content inside the safe area, both orientations',       ios: 'notch + home indicator',    android: 'punch hole + gesture bar + 3-button', both: 'usually caught on only one platform at a time' },
  { check: 'dynamic type at 200%',                                   ios: 'largest setting',            android: 'largest font + display size', both: 'a layout that passes one has not passed the other' },
  { check: 'dark mode, including elevation',                         ios: 'shadow',                     android: 'surface tint', both: 'a card that disappears is a platform-specific bug' },
  { check: 'screen reader traversal of the same screen',             ios: 'VoiceOver rotor',            android: 'TalkBack linear', both: 'same standard, different components' },
  { check: 'tap targets at 44pt',                                    ios: '44x44 pt',                   android: '48x48 dp', both: 'the numbers differ; use the larger' },
  { check: 'cold start on a low-memory device',                      ios: 'didReceiveMemoryWarning',     android: 'onTrimMemory', both: 'the crash nobody reproduces on a flagship' },
];

What is shared is a larger proportion than it looks, and it is worth being precise about where the boundary sits: it is not "same pixels, same behaviour". It is one design system with two behaviours. The spacing scale is the same on both because a 4pt grid is not a platform opinion; the picker is different on both because a picker is. Teams that draw this line correctly ship platform-appropriate products from one source, and teams that draw it as "iOS design shipped on Android" ship an app that reads as a port on both platforms.

Follow the freight shorthand: users bring platform expectations from the OS itself. "Cross-platform consistency" is mostly about logic/tokens; controls should still behave like the platform.

17.2 Gestures & navigation signatures

Navigation signatures are the default structures that tell users where they are: tabs for peer-level sections, navigation stacks for drill-in detail, sheets for quick choices, and a floating action button for the primary action. Gestures extend this vocabulary, but only where they are discoverable and fail gracefully. The two cardinal sins are nesting tabs inside tabs and letting the back stack behave unpredictably. When in doubt, choose a visible signature over a hidden gesture.

// Screens the app owns:
- Tabs (top/bottom) for peer destinations     - Stack for drill-in flows
- Sheet (bottom) for quick choices            - Full for focused creation
- Swipe actions visible but secondary          - FAB for THE primary action
// The two navigation sins:
//  1 nesting tabs inside tabs (users never reconstruct the map)
//  2 back-stack misbehavior ("back closes the app instead of going
//    back to home") — verify system back after EVERY flow in build.

Signatures first, and a gesture only as an accelerator

A navigation signature is the shape a user recognises before reading anything: a row of tabs, a stack that pushes, a sheet that slides up, a floating button. People navigate by silhouette, which is why the signature has to be consistent across the app and why introducing a new one mid-flow is expensive even when it is the right answer. The test for a signature is whether a user who has used the app once can predict where a screen will go back to from its shape — and if they cannot, the screen is missing something rather than the shape being wrong.

Match the signature to the relationship. Tabs are for peers — three to five sections that are the same kind of thing, and switching between them does not lose context. A stack is for drill-in: the detail of one thing, where back returns to exactly where you were, with the list's scroll position and filter intact. A sheet is for a quick choice made in service of the screen beneath it, and its defining property is that the context stays visible behind it; a sheet that pushes a screen of its own has stopped being a sheet. A floating action button is for the one action that creates something, on exactly one screen at a time — a second FAB on the same screen means the priority was never decided.

The rule for gestures is short and absolute: every gesture is an accelerator for something reachable without it, and the gesture itself must be safe to get wrong. Swipe to delete without an undo is a gesture whose failure destroys data; swipe to reveal actions with no visible equivalent is a gesture that some users will never find; long-press as the only route to a menu is a gesture that excludes everyone who does not know it exists. Discoverability is not the reason for the rule — even perfectly discoverable gestures are missed — it is that a hidden route is a route that some users will never have.

Swipe-to-delete is where this goes wrong most often, and it goes wrong in three specific ways. It removes on gesture completion with no confirmation and no undo, so a horizontal scroll that overshoots deletes a row. It leaves no visible row action, so the capability exists only for people who know the gesture. And on a horizontally scrollable table or carousel, the same gesture means something else entirely, so the two collide. The mitigation is not to remove the swipe but to give it an undo toast, keep an explicit action in the row, and never put a horizontal swipe target on a surface that scrolls horizontally.

The two navigation sins are worth stating as rules because they are cheap to test and they are the ones that make an app feel broken. Nesting tabs inside tabs is the first: a tab that contains another tab bar means the outer tab's count grows past what fits, the back behaviour becomes ambiguous, and no user has a model that predicts it. Letting the back stack behave unpredictably is the second, and it has three forms — back clearing the whole stack instead of one frame, a sheet that pushes rather than presents, and a dialog that does not consume back on Android.

Test the signature under the conditions that break it: a 200 percent text size, a small phone, a long localised label, and a screen reader where the visual signature is unavailable and the heading hierarchy is the only structure. A tab bar whose labels truncate to "Set" and "Acc" is no longer a recognisable signature, and the layout has to fall back to something — fewer tabs, icons plus labels, or a drawer — before it ships rather than after.

/* The signature registry. Every screen declares which signature it is and
   what its back behaviour is, so the two can be checked against each other
   rather than remembered. */
const SIGNATURES = {
  tabs: {
    peer: true,
    maxCount: 5,                  // 6 and the labels truncate, which breaks the silhouette
    keepsScrollPosition: true,    // switching tabs must not lose the list
    backAtRoot: 'goHome',         // never exit from a tab; exit is the OS's job
    sins: ['a tab containing another tab bar'],
  },
  stack: {
    peer: false,
    keepsScrollPosition: true,
    backAtRoot: 'pop',
    restores: ['scroll offset', 'applied filter', 'expanded rows', 'typed search text'],
    // the forgetting that makes a stack feel broken: returning to a list
    // that has reset itself is read as the app having lost the user's place
  },
  sheet: {
    peer: false,
    maxDepth: 1,                  // a sheet that pushes is a stack wearing a sheet's clothes
    contextVisibleBehind: true,
    dismissBy: ['tap outside', 'swipe down', 'back', 'escape', 'an explicit close'],
    // every dismiss route must be present: the users who cannot swipe need
    // a button, and the users who cannot see need the outside tap
  },
  fab: {
    maxPerScreen: 1,
    action: 'creates something',
    rule: 'a second FAB means the priority was never decided',
    labelOnLongPress: true,       // icon alone is ambiguous; the label must exist
  },
};

/* The gesture rule, as data, so it can be checked in a review. */
const GESTURES = [
  { gesture: 'swipe to delete',        visibleRoute: 'row action menu -> Delete', safeWhenWrong: true,  undo: 'toast, 5s',
    note: 'overshoot on a horizontal scroll container deletes a row, so never put it on one' },
  { gesture: 'swipe to reveal actions',visibleRoute: 'row action menu',                safeWhenWrong: true,  undo: 'n/a',
    note: 'reveal hides actions behind a second gesture, which is why the menu must also exist' },
  { gesture: 'pull to refresh',       visibleRoute: 'a refresh control in the bar',    safeWhenWrong: true,  undo: 'n/a',
    note: 'expected everywhere on Android, tolerated on iOS' },
  { gesture: 'long press',            visibleRoute: 'a visible overflow menu',         safeWhenWrong: true,  undo: 'n/a',
    note: 'the only way this is a route in its own right is if the menu is genuinely richer' },
  { gesture: 'pinch to zoom',         visibleRoute: 'a zoom control for documents',     safeWhenWrong: false, undo: 'n/a',
    note: 'the exception, and only for content that is genuinely pannable' },
];

/* Screen declarations, checked against the signatures above. The three
   failures listed are the ones that make an app feel broken and are the
   cheapest things in this file to test. */
const SCREENS = [
  { id: 'home', signature: 'tabs', tabs: ['Today', 'Projects', 'Alerts', 'You'], back: 'goHome' },
  { id: 'project', signature: 'stack', pushesFrom: 'home', back: 'pop', restores: 'scroll+filter' },
  { id: 'task', signature: 'stack', pushesFrom: 'project', back: 'pop', restores: 'scroll' },
  { id: 'newTask', signature: 'sheet', dismissBy: ['tap outside', 'swipe down', 'back', 'escape'], maxDepth: 1 },
  { id: 'settings', signature: 'stack', pushesFrom: 'You tab', back: 'pop' },
];

function auditNavigation(screens) {
  const faults = [];
  for (const s of screens) {
    // sin 1: nesting
    if (s.signature === 'tabs' && s.tabs.some((t) => /tab|nav/i.test(t))) faults.push({ screen: s.id, sin: 'a tab bar containing another tab bar' });
    // sin 2a: an over-long tab bar, whose labels truncate and destroy the silhouette
    if (s.signature === 'tabs' && s.tabs.length > SIGNATURES.tabs.maxCount) faults.push({ screen: s.id, sin: s.tabs.length + ' tabs' });
    // sin 2b: a sheet that pushes
    if (s.signature === 'sheet' && s.pushesFrom) faults.push({ screen: s.id, sin: 'a sheet that pushes a screen' });
    // sin 2c: a sheet missing a dismiss route
    if (s.signature === 'sheet' && (s.dismissBy || []).length < 4) faults.push({ screen: s.id, sin: 'a sheet with fewer than four dismiss routes' });
    // sin 2d: a stack screen that forgets its position
    if (s.signature === 'stack' && !s.restores) faults.push({ screen: s.id, sin: 'a stack screen that does not restore scroll or filter' });
  }
  return faults;
}
// auditNavigation(SCREENS) must be empty before release, and it is a test,
// not a code review, because it is the same check every time.

And one practical note that is not a gesture but behaves like one: gesture thresholds have to be consistent, and a gesture that fires at a different distance in different places will be misfired constantly. Pick one threshold, apply it in one place in the code, and make sure that a horizontal gesture never competes with a horizontal scroll on the same element without a direction or context check. Nothing about this is visible in a design file, which is why it is worth writing down rather than discovering it in testing.

A map of navigation signatures: tabs, stacks, sheets, and FABs. It also names the two navigation sins every build should verify for.

17.3 Onboarding & first-run: the 3-minute contract

First-run onboarding is a three-minute contract that must prove value before asking for anything in return. Start by demonstrating the core value with guided steps and early wins, then request permissions and login only when they meaningfully improve the experience. Cut every step that is not essential, let users skip or undo, and never block the core task behind setup. Revisit the flow with user research, because churn drops measurably when onboarding matches real goals.

  1. Value first, permission later: show the core action, ask for camera/notifications only when the moment needs them.
  2. Onboarding < 3 minutes on a phone; revisit with goals (churn drops proven).
  3. Enable pulls and momentum: progress saved, "almost done" reminders.

The three-minute contract, and the first sixty seconds

First run has one job: prove the value before asking for anything. Not explain the value, not describe the features, not collect the data — prove it, by letting somebody do the thing the product is for and seeing the result happen. Every permission, account and preference requested before that is a tax levied on a person who has no reason to pay it yet, and the churn evidence is consistent enough that this is not a matter of taste: the largest activation improvements in onboarding come from removing steps, not from adding carousel screens explaining what the app can do.

So the first sixty seconds get designed, precisely, because it is the whole first impression and it is the part everyone builds by accident. One screen, one action, one visible result, and — this is the part that is usually missing — the result must be something the user made. A dashboard they are looking at is not a beginning; a first project they named, a photo they imported, a message they sent to a colleague is. Then one line saying what to do next with it. Three things on screen: what this is, what just happened, what to press. Everything else is later.

Ask for nothing until the moment of need. Camera when they tap "scan a receipt", location when they open the nearby feature, notifications after they have done the thing once and would recognise a nudge about it, and an account at the first moment an account creates value rather than at launch — for a product usable without one, an account wall is a wall. This is not only good manners: a permission requested at launch is a request made before the user has any idea what they would receive, so the accept rate is a fraction of what the same ask achieves at the moment of use.

Budget three minutes on a phone and measure it rather than estimating it: five people, cold, timed, with their questions counted. Every step then has to justify itself against one question — does this have to happen before the first value, or can it wait until the moment it is used? The answers are usually surprising. Choosing an avatar, entering a company name, confirming an email, and picking a notification frequency are all individually small and collectively the reason a two-step flow becomes a five-step one.

Make it skippable and resumable. "Skip for now" must leave the app fully usable, because a user who cannot get past the flow will uninstall rather than fight it, and the skipped step has to be reachable later at the moment it becomes relevant. Persist progress so a person who backgrounds the app mid-flow returns to the step they were on rather than the top. That persistence is also what a genuine "you are almost done" reminder is for — and only for something actually incomplete, never for a feature they declined, which is the moment a reminder becomes harassment.

Testing it with real people, and the metrics that lie

The onboarding test is a protocol rather than a session, and it works the first time you run it. Five people, none of whom have seen the product, recruited from the population that will actually use it rather than from colleagues. Cold: no help, no explanations, and a rule that the moderator does not answer a question until the person has tried to answer it themselves, because the count of attempted answers before help is one of the most informative numbers in the whole exercise. Then time it, count the questions, count the wrong turns, count the back presses, and count how many times somebody says "where do I..." — because every one of those is a step that failed to explain itself.

What you are looking for is not whether they complete it. It is the moment of hesitation and what precedes it. The person who pauses for four seconds before a screen is the person the screen is failing, and the reason is nearly always that the screen is asking them to make a decision with information they have not been given yet. Record the pause rather than the completion, because the pause is the finding and the completion is a symptom of several findings having been resolved.

The funnel metrics are worth reading with care, because several of them are actively misleading. Step-by-step drop-off attributes abandonment to the step where it happened rather than to the decision it caused, so a form that ends in a password field looks like a password problem when the real cause was the email field four steps earlier. Skipping is not completing: a flow where most people skip has a low completion rate and can have a perfectly good activation rate, which is why the two have to be read together and never summed. And the "onboarding complete" event, if it fires when the flow ends rather than when the core action happens, measures nothing.

Then read by cohort rather than in aggregate, because onboarding is a promise about a specific intent and the average of several intents is a number nobody can act on. A product used for two different jobs needs two first-run paths, and the only way to find out which one a new user needs is to ask at the first screen which brought them here — one question, three options, which is also the beginning of the personalisation that makes the rest of the flow correct.

Test the changes properly when you make them, which means a holdout rather than a before-and-after. Ten percent of new users keep the current flow for two weeks, and the comparison is against them rather than against last month's number, because traffic mix, season and acquisition source all move and a before-and-after on onboarding measures mostly the difference between the two periods. And the ethical floor is worth stating explicitly because it is where growth pressure lands: an onboarding flow may not use a pattern that works only because the user does not understand it. That is the same standard as anywhere else in the product, and onboarding is where a team most often argues for an exception.

/* The five-person cold protocol, in the order it has to run. The moderator
   rule is the whole protocol: help is offered only after an attempt, and the
   attempt is what gets counted. */
const ONBOARDING_TEST = {
  recruit: { n: 5, from: 'the population that will actually use it, not colleagues',
             screenOut: 'anyone who has seen the product or works in software' },
  setup: { device: 'a real mid-range phone, not a simulator', network: 'ordinary, not a hotspot',
           permissions: 'denied at first, which is the realistic state' },
  moderatorRule: 'do not answer a question until they have attempted an answer; note the attempt',
  recordPerParticipant: {
    secondsToFirstValue: null,
    pauses: [],              // where they stopped for more than 4 seconds - the finding
    questionsAsked: [],      // exact wording
    wrongTurns: [],          // a navigation that was not what they expected
    backPresses: 0,
    whereDoISays: 0,         // the phrase that most often means the screen did not explain itself
    completed: false,
    performedCoreAction: false,
  },
  // the number that predicts the design fix: pauses, not completions
  primaryFinding: 'every pause over 4 seconds, and what the person was deciding at that moment',
  usualCause: 'a decision with information they were not given yet, one screen earlier',
};

/* The metrics, with the traps named. Three of these four are misleading on
   their own, which is why they have to be read in pairs. */
const FUNNEL_METRICS = [
  { name: 'completionRate', formula: 'finished all steps / started',
    trap: 'counts skipping as failure and conflates the steps',
    readWith: 'activationRate' },
  { name: 'skipRate',       formula: 'skipped a step / saw it',
    trap: 'a high skip rate is not a problem when the step was correctly deferred',
    readWith: 'activationRate' },
  { name: 'activationRate', formula: 'performed the core action in session one / started',
    trap: 'depends entirely on where the event fires: at the end of the flow, or at the action',
    readWith: 'completionRate' },
  { name: 'secondsToFirstValue', formula: 'median time to the first real outcome',
    trap: 'skewed by the one person who needed help; use the median, not the mean',
    readWith: 'pause count from the test, which explains it' },
];

/* Holdout, not before-and-after. Last month answers a different question
   from this month, and mostly reports the change in traffic. */
const EXPERIMENT = {
  holdout: 0.10,
  duration: '14 days, or until the sample reaches significance on activation',
  compare: 'new users on the new flow vs. new users on the holdout',
  whyNotBeforeAndAfter: 'traffic mix, season and acquisition source all move; a before-and-after measures the two periods, not the change',
  primaryMetric: 'activationRate',        // not completion: completion can rise while activation falls
  guardrailMetrics: ['support contacts in week one', 'uninstall rate in day one', 'time to first value'],
  stopRule: 'a guardrail breach ends the experiment regardless of the primary metric',
  // the floor, stated because this is where the pressure lands
  prohibited: 'any pattern whose effect depends on the user not understanding it',
};

/* Read by cohort. The average of several intents is a number nobody can act on. */
const COHORTS = [
  { intent: 'track personal finances', firstScreen: { kind: 'question', options: ['track spending', 'save for something', 'split with a partner'] },
    firstRunPath: 'import a statement, show a category breakdown within 60 seconds' },
  { intent: 'work invoices for clients', firstScreen: { kind: 'question', options: ['solo', 'a small company', 'an agency'] },
    firstRunPath: 'create a client, raise a draft invoice, send it' },
  { intent: 'keep notes', firstScreen: { kind: 'question', options: ['notes', 'tasks', 'both'] },
    firstRunPath: 'one note, then one task drawn from it' },
];

/* The one question at the first screen, and why it is worth the step it costs. */
const FIRST_SCREEN_QUESTION = {
  prompt: 'What brought you here?',
  options: 3,                       // more than 3 and the choice itself becomes the barrier
  why: 'the answer selects the first-run path, the empty state copy, and the default view',
  cost: 'one screen, under five seconds, skippable',
  // and it should never gate anything: skipping it falls back to a default path
  onSkip: 'the most common cohort, which is a guess worth making rather than a question worth blocking on',
};

Finally, measure activation rather than completion. Onboarding completion rate is a vanity number that improves by removing steps that mattered; the number that predicts retention is whether the user performed the core action within their first session, and a flow can have a high completion rate and a low activation rate whenever the last step does not lead anywhere. Onboarding is also not a one-time event: revisiting it by goal — "you have not used X yet, here is the 30-second version" — is worth more than a longer first run, because it is delivered to a person who now has a reason to care.

/* The onboarding contract, as data. "when" is the important column: every
   step is either "before first value" or deferred to its moment of use, and
   the deferred ones are the majority. */
const ONBOARDING_STEPS = [
  { id: 'see-core',      title: 'Do the thing',           when: 'before first value', seconds: 20,
    why: 'the whole point: a person must have made something before we ask for anything' },
  { id: 'see-result',    title: 'See what it produced',    when: 'before first value', seconds: 10,
    why: 'the result has to be attributable to their action, or it is not a proof of anything' },
  { id: 'one-next-thing',title: 'One next action',        when: 'before first value', seconds: 15,
    why: 'a named thing, not a tour; tours convert worse than one clear instruction' },
  { id: 'create-account', title: 'Create an account',      when: 'first time it creates value',
    trigger: 'when they try to sync, share, or come back on another device',
    why: 'a signup wall before value is a wall; the ask converts far better once there is something to keep' },
  { id: 'grant-camera',  title: 'Camera access',          when: 'moment of use', trigger: 'tapping "scan a receipt"',
    why: 'one chance, at the moment it is needed; a second attempt is a Settings deep link' },
  { id: 'grant-notify',  title: 'Notifications',          when: 'after first success',
    trigger: 'after they have completed the core action once',
    why: 'a person recognises a nudge about something they did; before that, the same nudge is noise' },
  { id: 'set-frequency', title: 'Notification frequency', when: 'never ask', trigger: 'settings, defaulted sanely',
    why: 'one more step before value, about a feature they have not used' },
  { id: 'choose-avatar', title: 'Pick an avatar',         when: 'never ask', trigger: 'defaults, editable in settings',
    why: 'the classic removable step: nobody misses it and somebody always abandons over it' },
  { id: 'set-company',   title: 'Company name',           when: 'first invoice', trigger: 'at invoicing time',
    why: 'nobody can supply it accurately before they have one' },
];

/* The first sixty seconds, expressed as the only three things on screen. */
const FIRST_SIXTY = {
  headline: 'Send your first message',      // an instruction, not a description
  action:   { label: 'Write a message', verb: true },
  result:   'the message, in the conversation, attributed to them',
  next:     { label: 'Add someone to the conversation', why: 'one thing, named, and it works offline' },
  // and the rule the review checks: nothing else is on this screen
  mustNotContain: ['feature list', 'carousel of benefits', 'notification opt-in',
                   'avatar picker', 'tour with "next" buttons', 'sign-up form'],
};

/* Skippable and resumable. Both properties, because a flow with only the
   first is a wall and a flow with only the second loses people at the
   app switcher. */
const ONBOARDING_STATE = {
  stepsCompleted: ['see-core', 'see-result'],
  stepIndex: 2,
  deferred: { 'create-account': 'not-yet', 'grant-camera': 'not-yet' },
  // persisted on every transition, because a person who backgrounds the app
  // mid-flow must return to the step they were on, not to the top
  persistOn: ['stepComplete', 'appBackgrounded', 'flowDismissed'],

  canSkip() { return true; },               // skipping must leave the app usable
  skipBehaviour: 'complete what is done; queue the rest against their triggers',
  // and the reminder rule: only for something genuinely incomplete
  reminderFor: 'a step they started and did not finish',
  neverRemindAbout: 'a feature they declined or skipped',   // this is the harassment line
};

/* Measure activation, not completion. Completion improves by removing
   steps that mattered; this is the number that predicts retention. */
function onboardingHealth(steps, sessions) {
  const completed = sessions.filter((s) => s.completedAll).length;
  const core = steps.find((s) => s.when === 'before first value');
  return {
    completionRate: completed / sessions.length,          // a vanity number on its own
    // the metric: did they do the thing, in the first session
    activationRate: sessions.filter((s) => s.performed[core.id]).length / sessions.length,
    timeToFirstValueSeconds: median(sessions.map((s) => s.secondsToCore)),
    // and the pair that catches a flow that helps completion and hurts activation
    verdict: (function () {
      const c = completed / sessions.length, a = sessions.filter((s) => s.performed[core.id]).length / sessions.length;
      return c > 0.7 && a < 0.4 ? 'completing the flow without reaching value' : 'ok';
    })(),
  };
}

/* Revisit by goal rather than by calendar: delivered to a person who now
   has a reason to care, which is the difference between help and nagging. */
const GOAL_REVISITS = [
  { trigger: '3 sessions without using the feature they signed up for', offer: '30-second version of that one feature',
    notThis: 'a tour of features they already declined' },
  { trigger: 'they have 3 items and have not opened the shared view', offer: 'show the shared view with their own items in it',
    notThis: 'an invitation to invite more people' },
];

17.4 Notifications: permission is a promise

Notification permission is a promise to deliver value, not a checkbox to tick, and users remember products that abuse it. Ask contextually, at the moment a notification would genuinely help, and briefly state what they will receive. Each message must then earn the channel by being timely, relevant, and easy to control, with clear frequency and muting options. One irrelevant burst can cost the permission for good, and opt-out analytics will show it.

Notifications are a financing model for attention, not a checkbox. Ask contextually ("want a nudge when your batch uploads?"), then deliver value or lose the channel. Default frequency; a "quiet hours" control; delete = refundable trust.

A channel has to exist before the permission is requested

Notification permission is a loan and every message repays it, so the design question comes before the prompt: write the first three notifications this user would actually receive, with real trigger conditions, and read them as the user will. If the three cannot be written, there is no channel, and asking for a permission you cannot use is worse than not asking — because the first message that arrives when nobody expected it is the reason the second one is never delivered either. It also makes the ask honest, since the pre-permission screen can then state exactly what will arrive rather than gesturing at it.

Then ask contextually, at the moment a specific notification would help, with the reason stated before the system prompt. "Want a nudge when your batch finishes uploading?" is a question somebody can answer, because they know what the batch is. "Allow notifications?" at launch is a question nobody can answer, because they have no idea what they would receive — and the accept rate for the same permission, asked at the moment of use, is several times higher. Never ask twice: a second refusal is usually permanent, and on Android the second refusal often takes it to Settings, so the first ask has to be worth one chance.

Every message has to earn its place on three axes. Timely means now, rather than whenever it was generated — a notification about something that has already been resolved is noise with a push. Relevant means about this user's thing, with enough context to act without opening the app; "Build finished" is not a message, "Your site is live at example.com" is. And controllable means it belongs to a category the user can silence, because the real behaviour is that people mute categories rather than muting everything, which makes the category structure more important than the copy in every message.

Frequency and quiet hours are product decisions, not settings-page afterthoughts, and defaults decide almost all of the outcome. Deliver in the user's local morning rather than at whatever hour the server queued the job; ship a per-category frequency rather than one global setting; and default quiet hours from the device's clock with an override, because the alternative is waking people up at 3 a.m. once and losing the channel. A per-category opt-out that is one tap from the notification itself is not a nicety either — a person who has to open settings to stop something is a person who uninstalls instead.

The failure modes are three and each of them costs the channel permanently. The burst is an incident: a migration, a bug, or a retry storm sends forty messages in a minute, and the user does not distinguish it from you. Rate-limit at the sending layer rather than at the client, and treat a spike as something to page on. The irrelevant message is a category problem — it is one notification that should have been in-app. And the untappable one is a notification whose action is not possible in the app, which teaches the user that tapping is a waste.

Three channels, one system, and the rules for the words

Push, email and SMS are three channels with different reach, different cost and different etiquette, and the useful question is not which to use but what each is for. Push is immediate and interruptive, so it is for something that has changed and that the user is waiting on. Email is durable and skimmable, so it is for a summary, a receipt, or something worth reading later. SMS is expensive per message, reads as intrusive, and in most markets needs prior consent, so it is for a genuinely urgent thing and almost nothing else. A product that treats them as interchangeable sends the same message three times and then wonders why the opt-out rate rose.

Transactional and marketing have to be separable, and that is partly a legal requirement rather than a preference. A receipt, a password reset, a security alert and an offer are different categories with different consent bases; a preference centre that cannot separate them is broken, and mixing them is how a notification permission becomes the mechanism by which somebody is opted into marketing they never asked for. The system should be able to send every one of the four categories with every one of the others switched off, because a user who turns off "tips" must not then find they have also turned off password resets.

Write the content against a locked screen, because that is where it will be read. The whole message has to fit in roughly two lines of the notification preview, which means the first line carries the event and the second carries the consequence or the action — "Your site is live" then "example.com, deployed 14:02". No sentence that would mean nothing out of context, because a notification is read without the app open and it has to survive being read without it. And the action belongs in the notification itself rather than only in the app, because the action is the reason to tap and tapping to find it is a worse experience than not having it.

Deep links have to land where the message says they do, which is a small contract that is broken constantly. "View site" must open that deployment, not the deployments list; "See the 3 failures" must open those three rows, not the import screen. A deep link that lands one level short is not a broken link, it is a wasted tap and a small signal that the product does not listen. The same applies after the app has been reinstalled or after the session has expired, so the link has to survive a cold start and an unauthenticated launch and still land correctly after sign-in.

Then the quiet failure mode, which is a scheduling mistake rather than a content one: everything queued during quiet hours and delivered in one burst at 07:30, which is a firehose that reads as an outage. Coalesce, summarise and cap — "3 new comments overnight" rather than three notifications, and at most one per category per waking period. The cap has to be enforced at the sender, because a client-side cap is a cap the background job does not have, and the background job is what sends the burst.

And keep a preference centre as a first-class screen rather than a buried settings row, because it is where the channel's health is actually managed. It should show each category with its current state, its frequency, and a plain-language description of what it sends; it should remember per device, so turning off collaboration on a phone does not turn it off on a tablet; and it should be reachable from a notification itself. A channel that can only be managed inside the app is a channel that will be uninstalled rather than configured.

/* The channel separation, which is a consent requirement as much as a UX one.
   Every one of these must be independently switchable: a user who turns
   off marketing must not have turned off their password resets. */
const MESSAGE_CATEGORIES = [
  { id: 'security',       consentBasis: 'contract',  userMutable: false, why: 'the user cannot consent to not being told their account was accessed' },
  { id: 'billing',        consentBasis: 'contract',  userMutable: false, why: 'a receipt is part of the transaction, not marketing' },
  { id: 'transactional',  consentBasis: 'contract',  userMutable: true,  why: 'receipts and confirmations; mutable because a muted receipt is not dangerous' },
  { id: 'product',        consentBasis: 'opt-in',    userMutable: true,  why: 'changes to something they rely on' },
  { id: 'tips',           consentBasis: 'opt-in',    userMutable: true,  why: 'marketing; off by default even where permission was granted for product' },
];

/* Copy, written against a lock screen. Two lines, event then consequence,
   and it has to survive being read without the app open. */
const COPY_RULES = {
  line1: 'the event, in four or five words: "Your site is live"',
  line2: 'the consequence or the action: "example.com, deployed at 14:02"',
  totalLines: 2,
  mustWorkOutOfContext: true,      // read with the app closed and no other notifications
  noJargon: true,
  noUrgencyUnlessReal: true,
  // the specific defect that reads as a bug: a first line that is only
  // meaningful in the app, like "Your deployment succeeded"
  reject: [
    { text: 'Your deployment succeeded', why: 'means nothing outside the app' },
    { text: 'Action required', why: 'action about what, and by when' },
    { text: 'Alert!', why: 'shouting, and it says nothing' },
    { text: 'We missed you!', why: 'marketing language in a push the user granted for something else' },
  ],
  accept: [
    { text: 'Your site is live', body: 'example.com, deployed at 14:02', action: 'View site' },
    { text: '1,204 rows imported', body: '3 failed validation', action: 'See the 3 failures' },
  ],
};

/* The deep-link contract. "View site" must open that deployment, not the
   deployments list - landing one level short is a wasted tap and a signal
   that the product does not listen. */
const DEEP_LINK = {
  match: /\/d\/deployments\/(?<id>[a-f0-9]{8})/,

  // and the cold-start case, which is where these usually break: the link
  // has to survive an unauthenticated launch and still land correctly
  async resolve(url, session) {
    const m = url.match(this.match);
    if (!m) return { kind: 'unknown' };
    if (session) return { kind: 'screen', route: '/deployments/' + m.groups.id };
    // unauthenticated: queue the destination, restore after sign-in rather
    // than dropping the user on the home screen and losing their intent
    return { kind: 'deferred', save: url, afterAuth: '/deployments/' + m.groups.id,
             copy: 'Sign in to view this deployment' };
  },

  // and the audit that catches the wrong landing page
  audit(cases) {
    return cases.filter((c) => c.landed !== c.expected)
                .map((c) => ({ message: c.label, landed: c.landed, expected: c.expected }));
  },
};

/* Quiet hours, properly handled: coalesce, summarise, cap - and enforce it
   at the sender, because a background job has no client-side cap. */
const COALESCE = {
  rule: 'at most one message per category per waking period',
  summarise: (n, cat) => n + ' new ' + cat + ' since ' + lastNightLabel,
  cap: { perCategory: 1, perUserPerWakingPeriod: 2, overflow: 'one "N others" line' },
  // the firehose is the failure mode that reads as an outage
  never: 'delivering 12 queued messages in a burst at 07:30',
  // and the other one: a burst at any time is an incident, not a schedule
  alertWhen: 'more than 3 messages queued for one user in 10 minutes',
  enforcedAt: 'the sending layer, not the client',
};

/* The preference centre, as a screen rather than a settings row. Per device,
   because turning collaboration off on a phone should not turn it off on a
   tablet, and reachable from a notification itself. */
const PREFERENCE_CENTRE = {
  perDevice: true,                 // and this surprises people when it is not
  reachableFromNotification: true,
  perCategory: [
    { show: 'plain-language description of what it sends', frequency: 'own control', state: 'on/off', muteUntil: 'one tap' },
  ],
  // and what it exists to prevent: a channel that can only be configured
  // inside the app gets uninstalled rather than configured
  rule: 'if it cannot be reached without opening the app, it will never be used to stop a message',
};

Leaving must be as easy as arriving, and the opt-out rate is the health metric for the channel rather than a conversion figure to be minimised. Every notification needs an unsubscribe that works from the notification itself, category by category; deleting the app is the ultimate version of the same action, and treating it as a support ticket rather than as a refund is a misreading of what just happened. A channel with a rising opt-out rate and a stable delivery rate is a channel that is dying, and the honest response is to send fewer messages, not to send them differently.

/* The channel, written before the prompt. If these three cannot be written
   with real triggers, there is no channel to ask for. */
const NOTIFICATION_CHANNEL = [
  { id: 'build-finished', trigger: 'a build the user started finishes',
    text: 'example.com is live', body: 'Deployed at 14:02. 42 kB in 6.1s.',
    action: { label: 'View site', deepLink: '/deployments/latest' }, category: 'deployments' },
  { id: 'batch-done',     trigger: 'a batch import finishes, and it took more than a minute',
    text: '1,204 rows imported', body: '3 rows failed validation.',
    // the action is the reason this is a push rather than an in-app badge
    action: { label: 'See the 3 failures', deepLink: '/imports/882/failures' }, category: 'imports' },
  { id: 'comment',        trigger: 'somebody comments on a thing the user owns',
    text: 'Ana commented on "Q3 invoice run"', body: 'Does this include the contractor line?',
    action: { label: 'Reply', deepLink: '/c/9912' }, category: 'collaboration' },
];

/* Asking contextually, once, with the value stated first. */
const PERMISSION_ASK = {
  when: 'the moment a specific notification would help, and after first success',
  neverAt: ['launch', 'after sign-up', 'before the core action has ever been completed'],
  statement: 'Get a nudge when a deploy finishes? We will send these three things and nothing else.',
  // the proof in the prompt: the actual messages, so the answer is informed
  showExamples: true,
  onSecondRefusal: 'offer a Settings link, or drop the channel; never ask a third time',
};

/* Categories are the real control surface: people mute categories, not
   everything, so categories must match what somebody would want to silence. */
const CATEGORIES = [
  { id: 'deployments',   default: 'on',  quietHoursRespected: true,  why: 'time-sensitive and infrequent' },
  { id: 'imports',       default: 'on',  quietHoursRespected: true,  why: 'the user is usually waiting for it' },
  { id: 'collaboration', default: 'on',  quietHoursRespected: false, why: 'another person is waiting; may arrive at 2am' },
  { id: 'tips',          default: 'off', quietHoursRespected: true,  why: 'marketing in a permission the user granted for something else' },
  { id: 'system',        default: 'on',  quietHoursRespected: false, why: 'security and billing; not user-mutable' },
];

/* Rate limiting at the sending layer, because a burst is an incident and
   the client cannot be trusted to enforce it. */
const SEND_LIMITS = {
  globalPerUserPerHour: 8,
  perCategoryPerHour: { collaboration: 6, deployments: 10, imports: 4 },
  // the rule that matters: a burst is coalesced, not dropped at random
  burstPolicy: 'coalesce into one message per category per 10 minutes, summarising the rest',
  // and the thing that has to page somebody
  alertWhen: 'more than 20 messages queued for any user in 5 minutes, from any cause',
  suspectCauses: ['a retry storm', 'a migration with per-row notifications', 'a timezone bug in quiet hours'],
};

/* Quiet hours, from the device clock, with an override. The alternative is
   waking somebody up once and losing the channel. */
const QUIET_HOURS = {
  default: { from: '22:00', to: '07:30', source: 'device local time' },
  overrideIn: 'settings, per category',
  duringQuietHours: {
    collaboration: 'deliver at 07:30, with the count: "3 new comments overnight"',
    deployments: 'deliver at 07:30: the user is asleep, not waiting',
    imports: 'deliver at 07:30 with a summary, never silently dropped',
    system: 'always: security and billing are not quiet',
  },
  // the rule: never drop, always delay and summarise
  neverDiscard: true,
};

/* Health of the channel, measured per category rather than as one number. */
function channelHealth(sent, delivered, muted, uninstalls) {
  return sent.map((s) => {
    const d = delivered[s.category] || 0, m = muted[s.category] || 0;
    return {
      category: s.category,
      deliveryRate: d / Math.max(s.count, 1),
      // the honest health metric is opt-out, and it is reported rather than minimised
      muteRate: m / Math.max(d, 1),
      uninstallsAfter: uninstalls[s.category] || 0,
      verdict: m / Math.max(d, 1) > 0.08 ? 'sending too much for this category' : 'ok',
      action: m / Math.max(d, 1) > 0.08 ? 'send fewer, not different messages' : 'none',
    };
  });
}

17.5 App perceived performance & offline

Users judge app speed by feel rather than by raw numbers, so perceived performance and offline behavior are design work. Optimistic UI updates the interface before the server confirms an action, skeleton screens hold layout while content loads, and offline-first caching keeps core screens usable without a connection. Always tell people their true state, such as three edits pending sync. Honest progress and sync indicators make even slow operations feel trustworthy.

  • Instant optimistic UI: act on the tap, sync in background, reconcile on conflict ("saved locally ✓").
  • Offline-first: cache reads; queue writes; tell users their state simply ("you have 3 edits pending").
  • Reduce perceived load: skeleton screens, priority to what’s meaningful, defer the rest.

Perceived performance, and the reconciliation you owe

People judge an app by feel and never by a number, and the mechanisms that produce feel are design decisions rather than engineering ones. The core one is that the interface must respond within a frame of the tap, regardless of what the network is doing — because the perception of an app's speed is dominated by the delay before anything happens, not by the total time to completion. Optimistic UI is the technique: apply the change locally on the tap, send the write in the background, and reconcile when the server answers. The interface is doing the thing the user asked for immediately, which is what makes it feel instant.

The price of optimistic UI is a mandatory honest reconciliation path, and this is where the technique gets faked. An optimistic update that is never reconciled is a promise the system cannot keep, and it surfaces later as a value that silently reverts, which is worse than a spinner because the user has already acted on the wrong information. So the local change carries a pending state, the pending state is visible on the object rather than only in a global banner, and the failure path has to be a real screen: here is what did not save, here is your local version, retry or discard. "Saved locally" is the honest label until the server confirms; "Saved" before the confirmation is the lie that teaches people not to trust the app.

Then reduce what people wait for. Skeletons hold the layout so the arrival is a fill rather than a surprise; prioritisation means rendering the thing they asked for first and the rest behind it, which is better than a single slower request; and deferring below-the-fold content beats blank space. The last of these is under-used and cheap: the fold is a well-defined line and everything below it can arrive after the user has started reading what is above it.

Offline-first is a design decision with a specific shape. Cache the reads the user needs to keep working, queue the writes with their ordering, and on reconnect replay in order and surface what failed rather than dropping it. The states have to be legible: an online or offline indicator that is honest about which it is, a count of pending edits, a per-item sync state, and a way to resolve a failure. "You have 3 edits pending" is a sentence somebody can act on; a spinner that never ends is not, and it is what most offline implementations produce when they treat the network as reliable.

Progress has to be real, and there are three legitimate shapes. Determinate, when the total is known — "3 of 8 files", a genuine percentage. Indeterminate with an explanation, when it is not — "working on the slowest step", which tells the user why the wait is long. And a staged shape, when there are phases: "checking, then uploading", which sets an expectation and then meets it. What is never legitimate is a bar that goes to 90 percent and waits, because a determinate bar is a specific claim about remaining time and this one breaks it visibly.

The four levers a designer actually has

Most of the perceived latency in an app comes from work nobody needed yet, and most of the work a designer can remove is in the interface rather than in the network. Rendering order is the first: everything above the fold first, everything below it deferred, and the fold treated as a design decision rather than as a viewport measurement, because the fold differs by device and the section that matters is the one the user's eye lands on. The second lever is payload, and the part of it that is a design decision is which images are needed for the first screen — a hero image at 3 MB because the source file was 4000 px wide is a layout decision that was never made explicitly.

The third is the list. A collection of any size is a virtualisation decision, and the design inputs into it are the row height, whether rows are uniform, and what happens at the end of the list. Uniform row heights virtualise trivially and cheaply; a variable-height feed needs measurement and will jump as it measures, which is worse than being slightly less efficient. The fourth is scripts that run before anything visible: analytics, chat widgets, tag managers and A/B frameworks, each of which is a blocking cost paid on the critical path for the benefit of somebody who is not looking at the screen yet.

Motion is the lever people get wrong in both directions. A short, functional transition genuinely masks latency, because it covers the moment the data arrives and its completion is what the user perceives as the response; a long decorative animation makes the same wait feel longer, because it draws attention to the absence of the thing being waited for. So: short and purposeful beats long and beautiful, and the test is whether the motion communicates something — a relationship, an origin, a direction — rather than whether it looks smooth on its own.

Then the performance of the motion itself. Animate transform and opacity, which the compositor handles without touching layout, and avoid animating width, height, top, left or box-shadow, each of which forces layout or paint on every frame and drops frames on exactly the low-end devices that need the help. Respect prefers-reduced-motion for anything beyond a fade, and check it because vestibular sensitivity is a real accessibility requirement rather than a preference. A skeleton that shimmers is the standard case, and its reduced-motion version is a static placeholder of the same shape.

Cold start deserves its own number because it is the first-run experience and it is the worst one: process launch, framework boot, first data fetch, and the first frame, all on a device that is also doing a hundred other things. First-run is where a user decides what they think of the app, and it is measured on a mid-range device on a cold process rather than on a development machine with a warm cache. Whatever the framework does, the first frame should be something real — a shell with the brand, not a white rectangle — and everything else should arrive after it.

Finally, give the performance work a budget it can be held to, expressed in the interface's own terms: a payload ceiling for the first screen, a time-to-first-interaction ceiling, a maximum third-party script cost before anything else runs, and a frame budget for animation. A budget nobody checks is an aspiration, and the moment it is in the repository as a threshold in the build, the conversation about a new analytics tag becomes a thirty-second argument instead of a redesign.

/* The budget. Expressed in interface terms rather than in server terms,
   because the complaint is about the interface. Enforced in the build or it
   is an aspiration. */
const BUDGET = {
  firstScreen: {
    payloadKB: 300,                  // compressed, above the fold only
    requests: 25,
    timeToFirstInteractionMs: 1000,  // on a mid-range phone, cold process
    // the one that is a design decision rather than an engineering one
    maxHeroImageWidth: 1200,         // px at the widest breakpoint; 3 MB hero images are a layout choice nobody made
  },
  scripts: {
    thirdPartyBlockingCostMs: 150,   // analytics, chat, tag manager, A/B framework - all of them before content
    rule: 'deferred, or loaded after first interaction',
  },
  animation: {
    // transform and opacity only: the compositor handles them without
    // touching layout. width, height, top, left and box-shadow force layout
    // or paint every frame, which drops frames on low-end devices
    allowedProperties: ['transform', 'opacity'],
    forbidden: ['width', 'height', 'top', 'left', 'box-shadow', 'filter'],
    durationMs: { short: 150, medium: 250, long: 400 },
    longLimitPerInteraction: 1,      // one long transition per interaction; two reads as slow
    reducedMotion: 'fade or instant, never a transform, never a shimmer',
  },
  coldStart: {
    firstFrame: 'a real shell with the brand - never a white rectangle',
    measuredOn: 'mid-range phone, cold process, ordinary network',
    // and this is the number first-run is actually judged on
    timeToUsableMs: 1500,
  },
};

/* List virtualisation: the design inputs decide whether it is cheap. */
const LIST = {
  virtualiseAbove: 200,             // below this the browser is faster than your code
  rowHeight: 'uniform',             // uniform virtualises trivially; variable needs measurement and will jump
  // the design questions, and the answers that make it cheap
  questions: {
    areRowHeightsIdentical: true,
    doesScrollRestoreNeedTheOffset: true,
    isThereACardAtTheEnd: 'yes, always - an unterminated list feels broken',
  },
  overscan: 8,                      // rows rendered above and below the viewport
  // what variable heights cost: measuring changes the content, which changes
  // the scroll position, which is a worse experience than the frames saved
  variableHeightWarning: 'measure once, cache, and accept the jump on first render - or fix the height in the design',
};

/* Image strategy. Three decisions, all made in design, all of which look
   like performance work and are not. */
const IMAGES = {
  sizes: 'srcset at the widths the layout actually uses; a 3x asset for a 1x slot is 9x the bytes for no gain',
  format: 'AVIF with a WebP and JPEG fallback; a legacy format is an acceptable cost, a legacy size is not',
  // the one that is really a layout decision
  hero: { maxWidthPx: 1200, lazy: false, note: 'above the fold, so it is not lazy - but it must be small' },
  belowFold: { lazy: true, note: 'lazy loading is a design decision about priority, not an optimisation' },
  placeholder: 'a dominant-colour block of the same aspect ratio: no layout shift, and it is free',
  never: ['a full-bleed 4000px source image', 'a hero with no width and height attributes', 'an animated GIF where a video frame would do'],
};

/* The cold-start order, and the one mistake that makes it worse. */
const COLD_START = {
  order: ['shell frame', 'brand and navigation', 'above-the-fold content', 'below-the-fold', 'deferred scripts'],
  // the mistake: optimising the framework boot and leaving the first frame
  // blank, which is the only part the user actually perceives
  mistake: 'spending the budget on framework startup while the first frame is a white rectangle',
  // and the consequence nobody models: on a low-memory device the app may
  // never reach the end of this list at all
  budgetForTheBottom: 'the last step must be safe to never run, or the app is judged on a blank screen',
};

Measure it as a design metric, because the numbers that matter are not the ones engineering reports. Time to first interaction, the share of taps that produce visible response within 100 milliseconds, time to a usable screen rather than to a complete one, and the rate at which the core task completes with no network at all. A team that watches those four will find and fix perceived-performance problems that a p95 request time never surfaces, because p95 describes the server and the complaint is about the interface.

/* The optimistic mutation queue. The local change is immediate and carries a
   pending state; the label never says "Saved" until a 2xx says it. */
function createOptimisticStore(send) {
  const state = new Map();      // id -> { local, server, pending, error }

  async function mutate(id, change) {
    const prev = state.get(id) || { local: null, server: null, pending: false, error: null };
    // the optimistic step: the interface has already changed
    state.set(id, { ...prev, local: { ...(prev.local || prev.server), ...change }, pending: true, error: null });
    notify(id);

    try {
      const res = await send(id, change);
      if (!res.ok) throw Object.assign(new Error(res.message), { code: res.code, server: res.server });
      // the reconciliation: what the server actually holds, which is the
      // authority, and may differ from what we guessed
      state.set(id, { local: res.server, server: res.server, pending: false, error: null });
    } catch (e) {
      // a failure keeps the local value visible and says what happened,
      // because silently reverting is how a user loses work they believed saved
      state.set(id, { ...state.get(id), pending: false, error: { code: e.code, message: e.message, canRetry: true } });
    }
    notify(id);
  }

  // the label, which is the entire honesty mechanism
  const labelFor = (s) => s.pending ? 'Saved locally'
                   : s.error ? 'Not saved - ' + s.error.message
                   : 'Saved';

  return { mutate, labelFor, get: (id) => state.get(id), pendingCount: () => [...state.values()].filter((s) => s.pending).length };
}

/* Offline: cache the reads that keep the task possible, queue the writes,
   replay in order, and surface the failures rather than dropping them. */
const SYNC = {
  states: ['online', 'offline', 'syncing', 'conflict', 'failed'],

  reads: {
    cache: 'the screens the user needs to keep working offline, with a last-fetched timestamp each',
    strategy: 'stale-while-revalidate: show the cached copy, fetch behind it, update quietly',
    never: 'a blank screen because the network is gone',
  },

  writes: {
    queue: 'ordered, with a stable id per mutation so a replay is idempotent',
    replayOn: 'connectivity restored, app foregrounded, or the user taps Sync now',
    // the failure surface, which is the part offline-first usually omits
    onPermanentFailure: { keepLocal: true, show: 'a list of what did not save, with retry and discard per item',
                          never: 'dropping the mutation and reporting success' },
  },

  conflicts: {
    // last-write-wins is only acceptable for a value nobody else can see
    policy: 'field-level merge where the fields do not overlap; explicit resolution where they do',
    sharedRecord: 'show both versions with who changed what, and never silently pick one',
  },

  // and the four sentences that make all of it legible to a user
  userFacing: {
    offline: 'Offline - your changes will sync when you reconnect',
