    pending: (n) => n + ' change' + (n === 1 ? '' : 's') + ' pending',
    failed: '2 changes did not save. Review them.',
    never: ['a spinner with no end', '"Saved" for something only stored locally', 'silent reversion of a value the user typed'],
  },
};

/* Progress, in the three legitimate shapes, and the one that is never
   legitimate because it is a broken promise with a number on it. */
function progress({ phase, done, total, slowStep }) {
  if (total != null) return { kind: 'determinate', label: done + ' of ' + total, pct: Math.round(100 * done / total) };
  if (phase)     return { kind: 'staged', label: phase, note: 'the phase names what is happening now' };
  // the honest version of "we do not know": say why it is slow
  return { kind: 'indeterminate', label: 'Working on ' + (slowStep || 'the slowest step') + '…' };
}
const REJECTED_PROGRESS = [
  { shape: 'a bar that fills over 4s regardless of the work', why: 'theatre' },
  { shape: 'a bar that reaches 90% and waits', why: 'a specific claim about remaining time, broken' },
  { shape: 'a bar that goes backwards when a parallel job finishes', why: 'worse than no bar' },
];

/* The four numbers that describe perceived performance, and none of them is
   a p95 request time, because the complaint is about the interface. */
const PERCEIVED_METRICS = [
  { name: 'time to first interaction', target: '< 1s on a mid-range phone', why: 'the first moment anything responds' },
  { name: 'taps with visible response within 100ms', target: '> 0.95', why: 'the tap-response perception, and the cheapest to improve' },
  { name: 'time to usable rather than to complete', target: '< 1.5s', why: 'usable arrives well before complete, and the user does not wait for complete' },
  { name: 'core tasks completable with no network', target: '> 0.8', why: 'the offline promise, measured rather than claimed' },
];

Exercises 17

  1. Map iOS vs Android conventions for your Ch.0 app’s back + tab behavior.
  2. Redesign a first-run to the 3-part contract; define the first 60 seconds.
  3. Write your notification policy: triggers, frequency, quiet hours, unsubscribe — from the user’s seat.

18 · Measuring UX: Analytics & Experimentation

Measuring UX replaces intuition with evidence through analytics, happiness metrics, and controlled experimentation. Funnels show where users drop off, satisfaction instruments such as SUS, NPS, and CSAT capture sentiment, and A/B tests isolate the effect of a change. The discipline is deciding the question first, then choosing the smallest measurement that answers it. A team fluent in these tools keeps decisions honest and funding secure.

18.1 Funnels, drop-off and event design18.2 The happiness metrics (SUS, NPS, CSAT — with caveats)18.3 A/B testing done honestly18.4 Triangulating: qual + quant together18.5 Dashboards teams act on18.6 The honest limits of experiments

Intuition chooses the right hill sometimes; measurement climbs it consistently. This chapter makes you fluent in the numbers desk where UX gets funded.

18.1 Funnels, drop-off and event design

Funnels trace users step by step toward a goal, and drop-off analysis finds exactly where real users leave. Define events by action, such as clicked-checkout, rather than by page view, so the funnel reflects behavior rather than navigation. Fix the largest leak first, but segment new versus returning users, device, and source before deciding, because a single flat number hides different stories in different groups. The biggest honest leak is where the effort belongs.

// Define events by ACTION, not page:  "signup_completed",
// "checkout_abandoned (step:payment)", "search_no_result"
// A funnel shows each step's rate; the professional move is to find
// WHICH step loses the most REAL users (the "leak") — then that step
// gets the redesign + A/B, not the prettiest one.
// Funnel truth: rate = completed / entered. Compare by segment
// (new vs returning, mobile vs desktop) before declaring a global leak.

An event is an action, not a screen

A funnel is only as honest as the events it is built from, and the most common way to build a dishonest one is to use page views as steps. Page views describe navigation, which is a property of your information architecture rather than of user intent: a funnel of screens measures how often people moved between screens, and a person who clicks back three times looks like three steps of engagement. Define events at the moment of intent instead, with names that read as a verb phrase about the person using the product — checkout_started, address_entered, payment_attempted, order_completed. If the name needs a page name to make sense, it is a page view wearing a product name.

Each event needs a schema, and the schema is where an analytics programme quietly dies. That means a name, a version, typed properties with documented meanings, and a named owner of the taxonomy. The failure that matters is silent: a property whose meaning changes between releases — plan going from "the plan id" to "the plan name" to "the price tier" — rewrites the history of every query ever written against it, and nothing errors, because the data is still arriving and still looks plausible. So the version belongs on the event and the owner belongs on the taxonomy, and changing the meaning of a property means a new name rather than a new value.

Steps should be commitments, not renderings. A step that fires when a screen loads measures arrival rather than action, and arrival is not what you are interested in — the question is who completed what. Where a flow auto-advances, instrument the transition rather than the arrival, and where a step can legitimately be skipped, record the skip as its own event rather than pretending the funnel is linear, because a funnel that assumes an order it does not have will report steps in the wrong sequence for a meaningful slice of users.

Fix the largest absolute leak first, not the largest percentage leak. A step that loses 400 of 4,000 is worth more than one that loses 30 of 60, and teams reliably fix the 30 of 60 because 50 percent is more alarming than 10 and reads better in a slide. Rank by real users lost per period, act on the top one, and expect the shape of the rest to change afterwards — fixing a large upstream leak frequently moves a later step's numbers entirely, so re-read the funnel rather than trusting the previous ranking.

Segment before deciding anything, and segment in a particular order. Source first, because a leak concentrated in one campaign is a mismatch between what the marketing promised and what the product delivered, and rebuilding the checkout will not fix a promise the product never intended to make. Then new versus returning, because a leak in the first session is an onboarding problem and a leak in the fifth is a habit or a trust problem, and they have nothing in common. Then device, then geography and platform. A single flat number hides all of these stories behind an average, and the average is the one number that cannot be acted on.

Before rebuilding anything, confirm the leak is the problem you think it is. Check whether the people leaving are the people you wanted — an unqualified campaign audience will abandon at any step and is not a design defect — and check the shape of the drop, because an instant exit at one step is usually a technical failure or an unexpected cost, while a gradual fade across a step is confusion. Then read ten session replays from that step. It is the fastest available method for turning a number into a cause, and it takes about an hour.

/* The event schema. Names read as verb phrases about the user; a name that
   needs a page name to make sense is a page view wearing a product name. */
const EVENT_SCHEMA = {
  version: 3,
  owner: 'product analytics',            // a person, not a team: a team never becomes accountable
  events: {
    checkout_started: {
      props: { cartValueGBP: 'number', itemCount: 'number', source: 'enum[app,web,email]' },
      fires: 'the user clicks the checkout action, not when the page renders',
    },
    address_entered: {
      props: { country: 'ISO-3166 alpha-2', method: 'enum[typed,autofill,apple,google]' },
      // why the method is recorded: a rise in "typed" on mobile is a real
      // finding about autofill breaking, and it is invisible without this
      fires: 'blur on the postcode field, or a debounce after the last keystroke',
    },
    payment_attempted: {
      props: { method: 'enum[card,paypal,sepa]', attemptsSoFar: 'number' },
      fires: 'submit of the payment step, including retries',
    },
    order_completed: {
      props: { orderId: 'string', valueGBP: 'number', deliveryDays: 'number' },
      fires: 'server confirmation, never the client-side redirect',
    },
    // a skip is recorded, not inferred: a funnel that assumes an order it
    // does not have reports steps in the wrong sequence for a real slice
    checkout_step_skipped: { props: { step: 'string', via: 'enum[back,link,keyboard]' } },
  },
  rules: [
    'changing the MEANING of a property means a new name, never a new value',
    'every event carries its schema version, so a year of data stays comparable',
    'server-side where the outcome is real; client events are attempts, not facts',
  ],
};

/* The funnel, and the analysis that ranks leaks by people rather than by
   proportion - which is the fix teams most often need. */
const FUNNEL = [
  { step: 'visited a product page', event: 'product_viewed' },
  { step: 'started checkout',      event: 'checkout_started' },
  { step: 'entered an address',    event: 'address_entered' },
  { step: 'attempted payment',     event: 'payment_attempted' },
  { step: 'completed the order',   event: 'order_completed' },
];

function analyseFunnel(steps, { period = '7d' } = {}) {
  const rows = [];
  for (let i = 1; i < steps.length; i++) {
    const from = steps[i - 1], to = steps[i];
    const dropped = from.count - to.count;
    rows.push({
      step: to.step,
      entered: to.count,
      // the number that decides the priority: real people lost per period
      lost: dropped,
      lostShare: dropped / from.count,
      // and the shape of the drop, because it separates confusion from failure
      shape: dropped > 0 && instantExitRate(to) > 0.6 ? 'instant - technical or unexpected cost' : 'gradual - confusion or doubt',
    });
  }
  // 400 of 4000 beats 30 of 60, whatever the percentages say
  return rows.sort((a, b) => b.lost - a.lost);
}

/* Segment in this order, and stop when the story resolves. Source first,
   because a leak concentrated in one campaign is a promise mismatch, not a
   design defect, and no redesign fixes it. */
const SEGMENT_ORDER = [
  { dimension: 'source',      why: 'a leak in one campaign is marketing promising something the product does not do' },
  { dimension: 'isNewUser',   why: 'session one is onboarding; session five is habit or trust' },
  { dimension: 'deviceClass', why: 'a mobile-only leak is a layout or a keyboard problem' },
  { dimension: 'country',     why: 'payment methods and address formats differ' },
  { dimension: 'intent',      why: 'the reason they arrived changes which steps are even relevant' },
];

/* Before rebuilding: confirm it is the problem you think it is. Two of
   these three checks have killed more proposed redesigns than any design. */
function triageBeforeRedesign({ leak, cohort }) {
  return {
    areTheyPeopleWeWanted: cohort.shareOfTraffic,
    // unqualified campaign traffic abandons at any step and is not a defect
    note: 'if under 40% of traffic is the audience you are building for, fix acquisition first',
    dropShape: leak.instantExitRate > 0.6 ? 'one technical or unexpected-cost failure' : 'confusion, spread across the step',
    nextAction: 'read 10 session replays from this step',
    // because a number is a location, not a cause, and an hour of replays
    // is the cheapest method for converting one into the other
    estimatedCostOfReadingTen: '1 hour',
  };
}

Define events by action rather than page, then hunt the funnel step losing the most real users. Segment new versus returning before declaring a global leak.

18.2 The happiness metrics (SUS, NPS, CSAT — with caveats)

The happiness metrics each capture a different slice of sentiment: NPS measures loyalty and recommendation intent, CSAT measures satisfaction with a recent interaction, and SUS measures perceived usability on a validated scale. Each has known limits, such as NPS being reactive to brand perception and CSAT capturing only short-term mood. Use them as mood signals and rolling benchmarks over time, never as product truth alone, and interpret them alongside behavioral data.

MetricWhat it’s good atDon’t
NPS (would recommend 0-10)mood signal, brand trackingtreat as product truth
CSAT (satisfaction 1-5)service momentscorrelate with actual behavior
SUS (10 statements, 0-100)usability benchmark pre/postskip its 10-question load — it IS the method
HE (heuristic evaluation)expert audit, cheap pre-testsubstitute real users
Behavior (time, clicks, retention)what people dowhat people say

Reading a satisfaction score without over-reading it

Three instruments measure three different things, and the mistake is treating them as interchangeable. NPS asks one question about likelihood to recommend and produces one number that correlates weakly with actual behaviour and strongly with brand perception, price sentiment and whatever happened to the product in the last fortnight. CSAT asks about a specific recent interaction, which makes it a diagnostic of a moment rather than a measure of the product — genuinely useful for finding which interaction is bad, and almost useless as a headline. SUS is ten validated items about perceived usability, with a large benchmark database and a score that is comparable across projects, which makes it the most useful of the three for interface work and close to useless as a measure of value.

Sampling decides what the number means, and it is where most of these surveys go wrong. Ask CSAT about a specific interaction, inside a short window, and only from people who completed one — a CSAT sent to everyone on a schedule measures a random mixture of interactions and is noisier than it needs to be. Send NPS on a cadence to a sample rather than to everyone, because a survey sent to everyone is a survey that trains people to dismiss pop-ups. And never send either immediately after a failure, a support contact or a price change, because the number you get back is a measurement of the incident rather than of the product.

Read them as time series and compare against your own history. A benchmark answers "are we normal", which is not a decision anyone can take; your own history answers "are we getting worse", which is. A rolling window of about 30 days smooths weekly noise without burying a real trend, and the thing to actually watch is the direction and the rate of change rather than the level. A score that is 42 and falling for six weeks is a different and more urgent situation from a score that is 38 and rising.

Know the failure modes before quoting a number. NPS moves on things it has nothing to do with — a competitor announcement, a price rise, an outage three weeks ago — and it moves slowly, so it is a lagging indicator that reports a change after the behavioural data has already shown it. CSAT is volatile, sensitive to who was asked and when, and measures the last interaction rather than the whole thing, so a single bad afternoon moves it. SUS measures perceived usability and is insensitive to value, to trust and to anything emotional, which is exactly what makes it stable and exactly what makes it the wrong instrument for a pricing or brand question.

Keep a behavioural counterpart beside every score, and prefer it. The retention curve, the task success rate, and the proportion of sessions in which somebody did the thing the product exists for are harder to move and much harder to argue with. A satisfaction score that rises while the retention curve flattens is a survey instrument improving rather than a product improving, and the two are confused often enough that the pairing is worth making explicit in every report.

Asking, and the questions that return nothing

The instrument decides the answer more than the product does. A leading question — "how easy was it to find the setting?" after a session where somebody spent four minutes looking for it — produces a politeness answer, because the respondent can infer the answer the questioner wants and there is no social cost to giving it. The neutral form asks about the behaviour rather than the evaluation: "how many of the six items on the list did you find without difficulty?", or "what, if anything, nearly stopped you finishing?" The second of those has a property worth preferring: a respondent who had no trouble says so in one word, so the questions that only apply to people who struggled can be asked only of them, and the survey stops being long for everybody to be short for the people who need it.

Recruitment is where a satisfaction survey quietly loses its validity. A survey sent to a list of long-standing customers measures that population and reports it as the customer base; a survey shown to people who just cancelled measures cancellation, which is the least representative sample available in the building. Ask what you can about the respondent — tenure, plan, and the feature they were last using — so results can be read by segment, and accept an order-of-magnitude smaller sample in exchange for being able to attribute the difference. Twenty responses from three distinct cohorts is worth more than two hundred from one, and it is worth more even when it is not statistically significant.

Then handle non-response, which is a measurement rather than an inconvenience. Compare who answered with who was asked, on whatever you know about both: tenure, plan, and whether they opened the app since the survey was sent. If the respondents skew long-tenured and high-plan, the score is describing your most loyal users, and the fix is not more responses but targeted chase-ups to the segments that did not reply. A survey with a 4 percent response rate is not four percent of your customers — it is the four percent who cared enough to click, and everything reported from it describes that four percent.

Order matters and is usually ignored. Put the most important question first, because respondents abandon and the trailing questions are answered by whoever is still there; do not put a satisfaction question before the diagnostic questions, because a positive opening anchors the rest. And do not ask what features they want. Feature questions are answered from the last thing somebody used, so a product whose users mainly use one feature hears overwhelmingly about that feature, and the request that comes back is almost always "more of the thing I already use" rather than the thing you did not build.

And run the whole thing as a habit with a named owner and a written question set, because a survey whose wording changes between sends is a series of unrelated surveys wearing one name. Keep the question text, the audience, the trigger and the cadence in one file that is versioned; keep every response with the version that produced it; and report the version next to every number. This is the same discipline as the event taxonomy, applied to the other half of the measurement stack, and skipping it is why two years of NPS data sometimes cannot be compared.

/* The question set. Wording is the instrument, so it is versioned with the
   responses rather than retyped each time. */
const SURVEY_V2 = {
  version: 2,
  changedFromV1: 'Q3 reworded from "how easy" (leading) to a count (neutral)',
  triggers: { after: ['a completed task', 'a resolved support contact'], neverAfter: ['a failure', 'a cancellation'] },

  questions: [
    { id: 'Q1', type: 'count', text: 'Of the items on the list, how many did you find without difficulty?',
      max: 6, why: 'neutral, and it quantifies rather than evaluates' },
    { id: 'Q2', type: 'scale', text: 'How likely are you to recommend us to a colleague?', scale: '0-10',
      why: 'NPS wording exactly: the alternative phrasing does not correlate the same way' },
    { id: 'Q3', type: 'open', text: 'What, if anything, nearly stopped you finishing?',
      // a respondent with no trouble answers in one word, so the long
      // diagnostic questions can be skipped for them
      skipIf: 'Q1 == 6', why: 'asks about the near-miss, which is more useful than satisfaction' },
    { id: 'Q4', type: 'scale', text: 'How satisfied were you with that?', scale: '1-5', why: 'CSAT, bound to the interaction' },
    { id: 'Q5', type: 'segment', text: 'How long have you used this?', options: ['< 1 month', '1-6 months', '> 6 months'] },
    { id: 'Q6', type: 'segment', text: 'What are you on?', options: ['free', 'paid monthly', 'paid annual'] },
    { id: 'Q7', type: 'segment', text: 'Which did you use most recently?', options: FEATURES },
    { id: 'Q8', type: 'segment', text: 'Have you opened the app since you were asked?', options: ['yes', 'no'] },
    // deliberately absent: "what features do you want?" - it is answered from
    // the last thing they used and returns "more of what already works"
    absent: ['feature requests', 'any question whose answer the respondent can infer you want'],
  ],
};

/* Non-response analysis. A 4% response rate is not 4% of your customers -
   it is the 4% who cared to click, and everything reported describes them. */
function nonResponseBias({ asked, answered, knownAboutBoth }) {
  const out = { responseRate: answered / asked, segments: [] };
  for (const key of knownAboutBoth) {
    const a = answered.filter((r) => r[key] === 'high').length / Math.max(answered.length, 1);
    const q = asked.filter((r) => r[key] === 'high').length / Math.max(asked.length, 1);
    out.segments.push({ key, respondentShare: a, invitedShare: q, skew: a - q });
  }
  const worst = out.segments.sort((s, t) => Math.abs(t.skew) - Math.abs(s.skew))[0];
  out.verdict = Math.abs(worst.skew) > 0.15
    ? 'respondents skew to ' + worst.key + ': the score describes your most loyal users'
    : 'respondents are broadly representative of those invited';
  // and the fix is not more responses - it is chasing the missing segments
  out.fix = 'targeted chase-up to the segments that did not reply, not a bigger blast';
  return out;
}

/* Recruitment criteria, stated so the population is visible rather than assumed. */
const RECRUITMENT = {
  include: ['tenure under 6 months as well as over', 'free and paid', 'every major cohort',
            'people who used the feature, and people who have not'],
  exclude: ['internal accounts', 'anyone in the company', 'accounts opened after the change under test'],
  sampleSize: { note: 'not the same maths as an experiment: a few dozen per cohort is enough to read a pattern',
                rule: 'spread across cohorts beats a larger single cohort, even when not significant' },
};

Never report one overall number for any of the three, because the overall figure is the average of your onboarding, your pricing change and one outage, and knowing which of those moved it is the only actionable part of the measurement. Segment by cohort, by plan, by tenure and by the feature the person was using, and report the segment with the worst number rather than the average. The number that matters is the one somebody is going to do something about, and an average is nobody's number.

/* The three instruments, with the job each one is actually good at. They are
   not interchangeable and reporting them as one signal is the mistake. */
const INSTRUMENTS = {
  nps: {
    asks: 'How likely are you to recommend us? 0-10',
    goodAt: 'a single comparable trend number over years, for a mature product',
    // it correlates weakly with behaviour and strongly with brand, price
    // sentiment and recency - which is why it moves on things unrelated
    badAt: ['diagnosing a specific interaction', 'comparing two sub-products',
            'reacting quickly', 'meaning anything on its own in a single period'],
    sampling: { cadence: 'quarterly', to: 'a sample of active users', never: 'everyone, on a schedule' },
    lag: 'weeks to months - it reports a change after the behavioural data already has',
  },
  csat: {
    asks: 'How satisfied were you with [the interaction you just finished]?',
    goodAt: 'locating which interaction is bad - it is a diagnostic, not a scoreboard',
    badAt: ['being a headline metric', 'comparing across periods without controlling for who was asked',
            'sent on a schedule rather than after an interaction'],
    sampling: { cadence: 'per interaction', to: 'only people who completed one',
                window: 'immediately after', never: 'after a failure or a support contact' },
    volatility: 'high; a single bad afternoon moves it',
  },
  sus: {
    asks: 'the 10-item System Usability Scale',
    goodAt: 'perceived usability, comparable across projects, with a benchmark database',
    badAt: ['value, trust, price, brand', 'anything emotional', 'a measure of whether the product is worth using'],
    sampling: { cadence: 'after first meaningful use', to: 'a mixed sample, not power users' },
    whyItIsStable: 'it measures usability and nothing else, which is the limitation and the reason it is useful',
  },
};

/* When to send each, and when not to. Every exclusion below exists because
   the measurement it prevents is of an incident rather than of the product. */
const SURVEY_TRIGGERS = {
  csat: {
    sendAfter: ['a completed purchase', 'a resolved support contact', 'a completed multi-step task'],
    neverAfter: ['a payment failure', 'an error screen', 'a cancellation', 'a support contact that is still open'],
    why: 'a survey sent immediately after a failure measures the failure',
  },
  nps: {
    sendTo: 'a random sample of active users on a fixed cadence',
    neverTo: 'everyone on a schedule',
    why: 'a survey sent to everyone is a survey people learn to dismiss, and the bias is permanent',
  },
  sus: {
    sendAfter: 'first meaningful use, which is when the user has a model to report on',
    exclude: 'internal accounts, accounts under 24 hours old',
  },
};

/* Every score, read against the behavioural counterpart. The pairing is the
   whole discipline: one of the two is easy to move without the product moving. */
const PAIRS = [
  { score: 'NPS',      behaviour: 'retention curve at 90 days',     tellsUs: 'whether recommendation intent tracks staying',
    contradiction: 'NPS up 6 points, retention flat: the survey instrument changed, not the product' },
  { score: 'CSAT',     behaviour: 'task success rate on the same flow', tellsUs: 'whether satisfaction tracks succeeding',
    contradiction: 'CSAT up, task success down: the flow works and does not feel good, which is a different problem' },
  { score: 'SUS',      behaviour: 'task completion time and error rate', tellsUs: 'whether perceived usability tracks actual usability',
    contradiction: 'SUS flat while completion time doubles: the interface got prettier and slower' },
  // and the summary that stops the report being read as good news
  headline: 'a score without its behavioural pair is not evidence',
};

/* Reporting rules. The last two are the ones that change what a room does. */
const REPORTING = {
  window: 'rolling 30 days, so weekly noise is smoothed without burying a trend',
  compareAgainst: 'our own history, not a benchmark',
  watch: 'direction and rate of change, not level',
  neverReportOverall: true,
  // the overall figure is the average of onboarding, a price rise and one
  // outage, and knowing which of those moved it is the only actionable part
  insteadReport: 'the worst segment with a named cohort and a named cause',
  alwaysShow: ['n', 'the window', 'the last time this metric changed definition'],
  // and the reason a dashboard without these is a screenshot
  required: ['a date on every chart', 'an owner', 'a target', 'an action if it crosses'],
};

18.3 A/B testing done honestly

An honest A/B test starts from a mechanism, a concrete hypothesis about why one design should win, rather than from a vague desire to try something. It declares one primary metric plus one guardrail metric, pre-computes the sample size and duration with a power calculation, and refuses to peek at results early. Minimum detectable effect is set in advance. Release only if the measured effect beats the cost of the change.

// The honest A/B loop:
// 1 hypothesize mechanism ("bigger CTA shortens think-time AND raises
//   done-rate", not "it looks better")
// 2 pick ONE primary metric + ONE guardrail (no 40-metric cherry-pick)
// 3 a-priori sample size:  n ≈ 16 · variance / effect²  (or power calc)
// 4 run to planned end date; NO peeking; evaluate with p<.05 & CI
// 5 release only if: significant, effect > cost, no guardrail damage
//   (e.g. CTA raised clicks but cut signup-completion → don't ship)
// Segments: new vs returning users almost always behave differently.

An experiment that can actually conclude

Start from a mechanism, not from a variant. "The new button will win" is not a hypothesis because it cannot be wrong in an interesting way and it does not say why. "Because the current label asks the user to translate a system concept into an action, a verb-first label naming the outcome will increase completed signups without reducing clicks on the alternative route" is a hypothesis: it names a belief about the user, predicts a direction, names what would change if the belief is wrong, and it can be argued about before anything is built. Teams that write the variant first always find a mechanism for whatever they built, which is the ordering error this is meant to prevent.

Declare one primary metric and one or two guardrails before the test starts, and derive the minimum effect that would matter from the business rather than from the statistics. That number is the MDE, and it is a decision: a redesign that moves activation by 0.4 percent is not worth shipping if it costs a fortnight of engineering, so an experiment with an MDE below the cost of the change is not worth running. Then the guardrails, which are the metrics that must not get worse — typically retention, error rate, and something like support contacts — because without them a variant that wins on the primary by damaging everything downstream looks like a success.

Compute the sample size before starting, from the baseline rate, the MDE, the observed variance and a power of about 80 percent. Then run for the duration that sample size requires. Running "for a week" because the calendar says so produces a test whose confidence interval nobody knows and whose conclusion is a coin flip dressed as a finding — and it is the single most common way teams arrive at a result they then argue about for a month. The power calculation also tells you when to stop asking, which removes the temptation to peek.

Do not peek, and the reason is arithmetic rather than discipline. Testing a p-value at every interim look inflates the false-positive rate without bound, so a team that checks a daily test every day will "find" a winner in a test that had a 5 percent chance of producing one — and it will usually be a finding that reverses. The options are a pre-committed end date, a sequential test with a valid stopping boundary, or an alpha-spending function; what is not an option is peeking and applying the ordinary threshold, and the reason to know this is that the temptation is structural rather than moral.

Randomisation has edge cases that quietly break the test. Assign on the server and persist it, so it does not change on login, on device change or on a second tab. Watch anything that leaks across the boundary: shared accounts, cached HTML, sticky sessions, and any page served to both variants from a CDN. Count exposures and check them — an experiment on people who never saw the variant tests nothing at all, and "the variant was slower" sometimes means "the variant never loaded". And watch for the sample-ratio mismatch, which is the diagnostic for exactly this problem.

Then decide against the rules you set, which is the part that requires the discipline. A significant primary with healthy guardrails ships. A significant primary with a breached guardrail does not ship, whatever the primary says, and the guardrail is the reason you declared it in advance. A flat result is information — most often that the change did not matter, which is a genuinely useful finding about where the effort is not — and the correct response is to record it so the test is never run again. And an effect smaller than the MDE is not a win, however significant it looks.

/* The hypothesis, written before the variant. A hypothesis that cannot be
   wrong in an interesting way is not a hypothesis. */
const HYPOTHESIS = {
  belief: 'the current label asks the user to translate a system concept ("workspace")
           into an action, and that translation is where they stop',
  prediction: 'a verb-first label naming the outcome raises completed signups',
  direction: 'up',
  primaryMetric: { name: 'signup_completed / landing_viewed', why: 'the thing the change is for' },
  guardrails: [
    { name: 'activation_rate_7d',  why: 'a variant that signs people up and they leave is a loss' },
    { name: 'support_contacts_week_1', why: 'ambiguity shows up as questions' },
    { name: 'demo_request_clicks', why: 'the alternative route must not be cannibalised' },
  ],
  // the MDE is a business decision, not a statistical one, and it is the
  // number that decides whether running the test was worth anything
  mde: { absolute: 0.02, chosenBecause: 'below this the fortnight of engineering is not repaid' },
  falsifiedIf: 'signups rise while activation falls, which means the label attracted the wrong people',
  runtime: '14 days, pre-computed below',
};

/* Power and sample size, computed once, before anything is built. */
function sampleSize({ baseline, mde, power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05, ratio = 1 }) {
  const p1 = baseline, p2 = baseline + mde;
  const z = { alpha: 1.959963985, power: 0.8416212336 };   // two-sided 5%, 80% power
  const pBar = (p1 * 1 + p2 * ratio) / (1 + ratio);
  const se = Math.sqrt(pBar * (1 - pBar) * (1 + 1 / ratio));
  const n = ((z.alpha + z.power) * Math.sqrt(2 * pBar * (1 - pBar)) / mde) ** 2;
  return { perVariant: Math.ceil(n),
           days: Math.ceil((n * 2) / dailyTraffic),
           // the duration is part of the sample size, not a calendar decision
           rule: 'running for a fixed week because the calendar says so produces a coin flip dressed as a finding' };
}

/* The peeking problem, stated as the reason the end date is pre-committed. */
const PEEKING = {
  why: 'testing a p-value at every interim look inflates the false-positive rate without bound',
  consequence: 'a test checked daily reports a "winner" about as often as it should, and it usually reverses',
  options: [
    { option: 'pre-committed end date', cost: 'none', note: 'the default, and it is enough' },
    { option: 'sequential test with a valid stopping boundary', cost: 'some maths, needs a library' },
    { option: 'alpha-spending function', cost: 'as above, for teams already running many tests' },
    { option: 'peek and apply the ordinary threshold', cost: 'the whole problem' },
  ],
  commitBefore: 'the first exposure, recorded in the same system as the data',
};

/* Randomisation, and the ways it leaks. */
const ASSIGNMENT = {
  where: 'server-side, persisted',          // never client-side: a reload would re-roll it
  stableAcross: ['login', 'device change', 'second tab', 'cookie clear', 'app reinstall'],
  // anything that can show both variants to one user invalidates the result
  leakRisks: ['shared accounts', 'CDN-cached HTML', 'sticky sessions', 'server-side caches',
               'email links that skip the assignment step'],
  // the diagnostic for exactly this problem, and it is free
  alertIf: { sampleRatioMismatch: 'expected 50/50 in variant counts; anything outside 0.5 +/- 0.01 means leakage',
             exposuresBelow: 'if exposures are far below expected traffic, some users never saw it' },
};

/* The decision rule. Written before the result, which is the only time it
   can be written honestly. */
function decide(result, hypothesis) {
  const guardrailBreached = result.guardrails.find((g) => g.worseBy > g.tolerance);
  if (result.primary.p < result.primary.alpha) {
    if (guardrailBreached) return { ship: false,
      why: 'the primary wins but ' + guardrailBreached.name + ' is worse; that is what the guardrail was declared for' };
    if (result.primary.effect < hypothesis.mde.absolute) return { ship: false,
      why: 'the effect is below the MDE, so it is not the change we agreed was worth making' };
    return { ship: true, why: 'primary significant, guardrails healthy, effect above the MDE' };
  }
  // a flat result is a finding, most often that the effort was not worth it
  return { ship: false, why: 'no effect. Record it so the test is never run again.',
           record: 'a negative result here saves two teams a fortnight each' };
}

The honest A/B loop: a mechanism hypothesis, one primary metric plus one guardrail, a pre-computed sample size, and no peeking until the planned end date.

18.4 Triangulating: qual + quant together

Triangulation combines quantitative analytics with qualitative research because numbers say where and people say why. Analytics and funnels locate where users struggle, while interviews, heatmaps, session replays, and moderated tests explain what is happening at that exact spot. The habit is to cross-check both directions: let numbers locate the problem, let qual people explain it, then verify those hypotheses with numbers before committing to a redesign.

Triangulation, and running it in both directions

Quantitative data says where and qualitative data says why, and the mistake is treating that as a one-way division of labour. The habit worth having runs both directions: numbers locate a step and sessions or interviews explain it, and then the explanation goes back to the numbers as a prediction that can be checked — if the hypothesis is "they distrust the shipping information", then shipping-information questions should be measurably higher among the people who abandoned at that step than among those who did not, and if they are not, the hypothesis was wrong and no redesign is warranted. That last step is what turns triangulation from a research activity into a decision procedure, and it is the step that is usually skipped, which is how confident-sounding causes get attached to numbers that never implied them.

Each method has a specific blind spot, and choosing between them means choosing a bias. Heat maps show where people click and where they do not, which is excellent at finding dead areas and misleading everywhere else — a click map on a static page records clicks on nothing at all, and a page that people simply read looks identical to a page that defeated them. Scroll depth is the same problem in one dimension: reading to the bottom of a settings page is not evidence of reading it. Treat both as evidence that a specific element was interacted with or not, and never as a proxy for comprehension.

Session replays are the most useful of the three and the easiest to misuse. They show the hesitation, the back-and-forward, the wrong-field correction and the abandoned form in a way no aggregate can, and they are also the method most likely to be over-read, because a memorable replay is a memorable experience rather than a typical one. Watch ten at the leaking step to form the hypothesis, then go back to the numbers to test it — and be careful about what you can legitimately watch, because a replay can contain anything the user typed, and the consent and storage rules for that are not optional.

Interviews and moderated tests answer different questions and are confused more often than any other pair. An interview asks why, and gets a reason, which is a statement about the participant's account of their own behaviour and is accurate about their reasoning and unreliable about their own future behaviour — people are extremely good at narrating an intention they will not execute. A moderated test shows what happens, and produces behaviour rather than account: it finds the four-second stare, the mis-tap, the reading of a label as an instruction. Use the test to find the problem and the interview to understand it, and treat any claim about what somebody would do next as a hypothesis about behaviour rather than a finding.

Never decide a redesign on one source, and be able to say which kind of mistake you would be making. Numbers alone produce a solution to the wrong problem — optimising the step with the largest leak, which is sometimes a symptom of an upstream promise. Qual alone produces a well-understood problem nobody has budget for — a finding about a screen that affects two percent of sessions. The loop is the point: numbers locate, qual explains, numbers verify, and if the verification fails you have learned something worth more than the redesign would have been.

Running a session that produces something

Recruitment first, because it decides what the session can answer. You want people who have the problem and had it recently — for a checkout problem, people who abandoned an order in the last month, not people who have bought from you for six years. Do not recruit a general panel: panel participants are disproportionately people who enjoy research sessions, which is a demographic of people comfortable talking to researchers and disproportionately untroubled by the problem. The screener should take two minutes and its real job is to reject, because a poorly-screened participant costs thirty.

The script is short and mostly not questions. State the aim, state the think-aloud instruction with a worked example, and then stop talking. The reason for the example is that "please think aloud" produces participants who narrate nothing until asked, and the first thirty seconds of silence is where most people either recover and talk or conclude they have done something wrong. Then let them talk. The questions worth having are about the past and about the specific rather than the general — "walk me through the last time you did this", "what did you expect to happen here", "what made you go back to the previous screen" — because the general ones produce the general answers, and "is the checkout easy" produces an opinion rather than a report.

Silence is the technique. The urge to fill a pause is the moderator's problem, not the participant's, and the findings that matter usually arrive three seconds after the point at which you would have spoken. Then the follow-up discipline: ask what they expected before the moment, what they thought was happening, and what they would do next. Each of these is about a specific moment rather than a general impression, and each is checkable against what actually happened on screen. Never ask whether they would use a feature — stated intention is the least reliable input available, and it is worthless even when true.

Role-split the observation. One person moderates and does not write; one person writes and does not speak. The moderator who is also taking notes starts asking confirming questions, which is how the whole session becomes a conversation in which the participant agrees with things. The notes should be quotes with timestamps rather than paraphrases, because a paraphrase written in the room already contains the moderator's interpretation and the raw words are the only version that survives being disagreed with later. And do not correct the participant when they are wrong about how the product works — the wrongness is the finding, and correcting it destroys the evidence.

Debrief immediately, while it is fresh, and separately from the participant. Everyone leaves the room before the team discusses anything, and the discussion starts with what each person noticed before what anyone concluded. That order is not politeness: the first interpretation announced in a debrief becomes the frame for every subsequent observation, and a team that argues about a conclusion before reading the notes converges on the most senior person's reading of a five-minute session. Write the findings up within a day, with the quotes, the count of sessions, and the hypotheses they support or contradict.

/* The script. Mostly not questions; the work is in the silence. */
const SESSION = {
  recruit: { from: 'people who had the problem in the last 30 days',
             avoid: ['a general panel - panel participants disproportionately enjoy research sessions, and are disproportionately untroubled by the problem',
                     'long-tenure customers when the problem is in acquisition',
                     'anyone who volunteered for the previous study'],
             screener: { minutes: 2, realJob: 'to reject; a poorly-screened participant costs thirty minutes' } },

  script: [
    { say: 'I am testing the product, not you. There are no right answers and I cannot help.',
      why: 'removes the two things that make people perform rather than report' },
    { say: 'Please think aloud as you go. I will remind you if you go quiet.',
      // without a worked example, "think aloud" produces silence until prompted,
      // and the first thirty seconds decides whether they talk at all
      example: 'you are trying to buy a mug; you notice the delivery price only at the bottom; say what you are thinking',
      why: 'the example is the mechanism, and it is the part teams forget' },
    { say: 'and then stop talking',
      // the finding usually arrives three seconds after the point at which
      // the moderator would have spoken
      silence: 'the urge to fill a pause is the moderator\'s problem, not the participant\'s' },
  ],

  questionsWorthHaving: [
    'walk me through the last time you did this',
    'what did you expect to happen here?',
    'what did you think was happening at that moment?',
    'what made you go back to the previous screen?',
    'what would you do next?',
  ],
  questionWorthNeverAsking: 'would you use this? - stated intention is the least reliable input available, and worthless even when true',

  // role-split the observation
  roles: { moderator: { does: 'talk', mustNot: ['write', 'correct the participant', 'confirm'] },
           noteTaker:  { does: 'write', mustNot: ['speak'] },
           why: 'a moderator who takes notes asks confirming questions, and the session becomes a conversation in which the participant agrees with things' },

  notes: { format: 'verbatim quotes with timestamps',
           why: 'a paraphrase written in the room already contains the moderator\'s interpretation' },

  // the wrongness is the finding
  neverCorrect: 'do not tell a participant how the product works; the wrongness is the evidence and correcting it destroys it',

  debrief: { when: 'immediately, while fresh', rule: 'everyone leaves the room first',
             order: ['what each person noticed', 'then what anyone concluded'],
             whyOrder: 'the first interpretation announced becomes the frame for every later observation, and a team arguing about a conclusion converges on the most senior reading of a five-minute session' },
  writeUp: { within: 'a day', include: ['the quotes', 'the number of sessions', 'which hypotheses they support and which they contradict'] },
};

And keep a record of the hypothesis separately from the change, because the two are frequently confused afterwards. A dated entry saying "the leaking step is shipping information; predicted: shipping questions appear disproportionately in the abandonment survey for that step" is checkable in a fortnight; a note saying "we fixed the checkout because of the research" is not checkable at all, and it guarantees the next team repeats the same investigation from the same starting position.

/* The loop. Three steps, and the third is the one that is skipped - which is
   how a confident cause gets attached to a number that never implied it. */
const TRIANGULATION = {
  1: { step: 'locate',      method: 'quantitative',
       output: 'a step, a segment and a date range, with the count of people affected',
       rule: 'rank by real users lost, not by proportion, and segment source first' },
  2: { step: 'explain',     method: 'qualitative',
       output: 'a hypothesis about the cause, in the participant's vocabulary',
       rule: 'behaviour from a test, reasoning from an interview - they are not interchangeable' },
  3: { step: 'verify',      method: 'quantitative',
       output: 'the hypothesis restated as a prediction, checked against a segment',
       rule: 'if it does not hold, the hypothesis was wrong and no redesign is warranted' },
  // example, run end to end
  example: {
    located: '58% of the address step's exits, 412 people in 7 days, concentrated in paid search',
    hypothesis: 'they distrust the shipping information',
    prediction: 'the "cost of shipping" question appears more often among abandoners at this step than among completers',
    check: 'survey split by funnel position; if the rate is equal, the hypothesis fails',
    onFailure: 'return to step 1 with a different hypothesis, having spent one survey rather than a quarter',
  },
};

/* Method selection: each has a specific blind spot, so choosing between them
   means choosing a bias. */
const METHODS = [
  { method: 'funnel', tellsYou: 'where people stop, and how many',
    blindSpot: 'not why; and step order it assumes may not be the order users take',
    useWhen: 'you need a size and a location' },
  { method: 'heatmap', tellsYou: 'where elements are interacted with, and which are never touched',
    blindSpot: 'a click map on a static page records clicks on nothing; reading looks identical to failing',
    useWhen: 'hunting dead areas - never as evidence of comprehension' },
  { method: 'scroll depth', tellsYou: 'how far down a page people reach',
    blindSpot: 'reaching the bottom of a settings page is not evidence of reading it',
    useWhen: 'finding content below the fold that nobody reaches' },
  { method: 'session replay', tellsYou: 'hesitation, back-and-forward, wrong-field correction',
    blindSpot: 'memorable replays are memorable rather than typical; and the content may be anything typed',
    useWhen: 'forming a hypothesis at a step - never for sizing the problem' },
  { method: 'moderated test', tellsYou: 'what people actually do, including what they do wrong',
    blindSpot: 'a small sample, a lab context, and an observer changes behaviour',
    useWhen: 'finding the problem' },
  { method: 'interview', tellsYou: 'why, in the participant's own vocabulary',
    blindSpot: 'accurate about reasoning, unreliable about their own future behaviour',
    useWhen: 'understanding a problem that has already been found' },
  { method: 'survey', tellsYou: 'distribution across a population, cheaply',
    blindSpot: 'whatever the recruitment made of it; 4% response describes the 4%',
    useWhen: 'testing whether a cause generalises beyond the ten people you watched' },
];

/* Replay tagging. Ten replays at a step, tagged, because the alternative is
   ten replays watched and remembered. */
const REPLAY_TAGS = [
  { tag: 'four-second-stare',  means: 'reading something they did not understand', confirm: 'the element read is the one they later say confused them' },
  { tag: 'clicked-non-clickable', means: 'an affordance that does not read as one', confirm: 'the click count is above the interaction rate for that element' },
  { tag: 'wrong-field-correction', means: 'the label does not match what they typed', confirm: 'corrections cluster on one field' },
  { tag: 'back-and-forward',   means: 'lost, and trying to recover', confirm: 'the same two URLs alternate' },
  { tag: 'abandon-then-return', means: 'interrupted rather than lost', confirm: 'the session resumes within a day' },
];

/* Recording the hypothesis separately from the change, which is what makes
   it checkable in a fortnight rather than uncrossable forever. */
const HYPOTHESIS_LOG = {
  datedAt: '2026-03-04',
  located: { step: 'address', segment: 'paid search, new users', count: 412, window: '7d' },
  hypothesis: 'they distrust the shipping information',
  prediction: 'shipping questions appear more among abandoners than completers at this step',
  checkBy: '2026-03-18',
  changeShipped: 'not yet - the check has not been run',
  // the reason the two are separate fields: shipping the change before the
  // check destroys the ability to ever know whether the cause was real
  rule: 'never write "we fixed X because of the research"; write the check and its date',
};

Quant says where (step 3 funnel leak), qual says why (they distrust the shipping info). Analytics point you at the invisible: heatmaps show the "clicking the non-clickable" orphans; session replays show the 4-second stare the metrics can’t see. Never decide a redesign on one source alone.

18.5 Dashboards teams act on

A dashboard earns its place only when it drives a decision each week. Keep it to one screen focused on the handful of numbers people can actually act on, date every chart so stale data is never mistaken for news, and give it a named owner responsible for accuracy and interpretation. Annotate anomalies, link each metric to a target and an action, and review it in a regular cadence.

A dashboard is a weekly meeting, not a chart collection

The test of a dashboard is not whether it looks informative; it is whether it drives a decision each week. If nobody opens it and changes something on the strength of it, it is a screenshot with a query behind it — and screenshots accumulate because they are cheap to make and expensive to retire. The design problem is therefore not layout, it is scope: a dashboard earns its place by being small enough that every number on it has an owner, a target, and a defined action, and those two conditions together rule out most of what dashboards contain.

One screen, and the numbers have to be the ones somebody acts on. A working set is roughly four: how many people are using the product at all (activation), where the core flow loses them (the funnel), whether they came back (retention), and what the current experiment is doing. Everything else belongs one level down, and the discipline is that it must be reachable rather than absent — a dashboard that hides detail behind a link still supports an argument, while one that puts forty numbers on a screen supports none.

Every chart needs a date, and every chart needs its definition. A chart without a date is a screenshot by another route, because a stale number looks exactly like a fresh one and a weekly meeting is where that confusion is most expensive. The definition matters just as much: two people reading "conversion" mean different things unless the funnel, the window and the denominator are written on the chart, and the first week somebody spends twenty minutes re-deriving a definition is the week the dashboard loses its authority.

Then the versions and the events. Every chart carries the release it was last calculated from, because a redesign is an event and a number that jumps on the day a button changed colour is very often the change itself rather than a behaviour change — and either way the two must be distinguishable. Annotate the anomalies rather than only charting them: a marked deploy, a pricing change, an outage, a marketing push. A chart with unexplained jumps invites the team to explain them, and they will explain them consistently with what they want to be true.

Give it a named owner, and the owner is responsible for two things: that the numbers are right, and that they are read. Those are different jobs and the second is the one that fails. A weekly review with a fixed time, a fixed agenda, and one question per number is what makes the dashboard live; without the meeting the dashboard decays into a page nobody opens, and the decay is invisible because nothing breaks. So the review is the artefact and the dashboard is a prop in it.

Choosing the metrics, and the definitions behind them

Metrics should be chosen from the decisions the dashboard has to support, not from what happens to be queryable. That sounds obvious and is almost always violated, because a number that already exists is cheaper than a number that has to be defined, and the dashboard fills with whatever the analytics team already produces. The test for each row is a question of the form "if this moved by ten percent, what would we do differently?" — a metric that cannot answer that is context, not a metric, and it belongs in a drill-down rather than in the review.

Then the structure, which is three tiers and it should be visible which is which. One north star that expresses the value being delivered rather than the activity generating it — for a product that exists to help people finish invoices, that is invoices completed rather than time in the app. Two to four input metrics that the team can influence, one per team, which is what makes the review actionable: activation, the core funnel, retention, and the current experiment. And guardrails that must not get worse, which belong on the same dashboard as the north star, because a north star that can be improved by breaking something is not a measure of value.

Definitions belong in version control, beside the code that computes them, with an owner and a date. This is the least glamorous and highest-value item on the list. Two people meaning different things by "conversion" will spend twenty minutes per week re-deriving it, and worse, will occasionally ship a decision based on one of the two meanings. Write the metric as a sentence with the event names, the window, the denominator and any cohort restriction — "orders completed per signups in the same week, excluding internal accounts, 7-day rolling" — and require the definition to change as a deliberate, dated, announced act.

Freshness and failure have to be visible, because a stale number looks exactly like a fresh one and a dashboard is where that confusion is most expensive. Put the last-updated time on every tile and make it red when the pipeline is behind rather than grey when nobody has looked. Alert on staleness separately from alerting on change, because they are different failures with different owners: a broken pipeline is engineering's, a genuine movement is the product's, and a review that discovers yesterday's outage by looking at a flat line wastes the meeting it discovers it in.

Finally, most alerts should not be dashboards. A dashboard is for a human who is looking; an alert is for a number that crossed something while nobody was looking. The design failure is a dashboard with forty metrics and no alerts, which means everything is discovered by a person noticing, and the noticing is unreliable. So alerts should be few, tied to thresholds that correspond to actions, and quiet by default — and a dashboard row should say whether it has an alert, so the review can tell the difference between "nothing happened" and "nobody is watching".

/* The test for a row: if this moved by 10%, what would we do differently? A
   metric that cannot answer that is context, not a metric. */
function isAMetric(m) {
  const reasons = [];
  if (!m.respondsToAnAction) reasons.push('no action follows a change in it');
  if (!m.owner) reasons.push('no named owner');
  if (!m.target) reasons.push('no target, so no threshold and no alarm');
  if (!m.definition) reasons.push('definition not written down');
  if (/time in the app|sessions|page views/.test(m.name || '') && !m.guardrail) reasons.push('activity metric presented as value');
  return { isAMetric: reasons.length === 0, reasons };
}

/* Three tiers, and it should be visible on the dashboard which is which. */
const METRIC_TREE = {
  northStar: { name: 'invoices completed', why: 'the value delivered, not the activity generating it',
               notIt: 'time in the app, which is activity' },
  inputs: [
    { name: 'activation',              owner: 'growth',    influences: 'how many people ever reach the north star' },
    { name: 'core funnel completion',  owner: 'checkout',  influences: 'how many who reach it get to the end' },
    { name: 'week-2 retention',        owner: 'product',   influences: 'whether the north star repeats' },
    { name: 'current experiment',      owner: 'growth',    influences: 'the one thing being decided this fortnight' },
  ],
  guardrails: [
    { name: 'refund rate at 30 days', against: 'checkout conversion',
      why: 'a north star that can be improved by breaking something is not a measure of value' },
    { name: 'support contacts per 100 new users', against: 'activation',
      why: 'confusion that users tolerate and then complain about later' },
  ],
};

/* Definitions in version control. Two people meaning different things by
   "conversion" costs twenty minutes a week and occasionally a decision. */
const DEFINITION = {
  format: ['the event names', 'the window', 'the denominator', 'any cohort restriction'],
  example: 'orders completed per signups in the same week, excluding internal accounts, 7-day rolling',
  located: 'in version control, beside the code that computes it',
  has: ['an owner', 'a date', 'a change history'],
  changeIs: 'a deliberate, dated, announced act - not a diff that lands on a Tuesday',
  why: 'a dashboard where nobody can state the definition will be argued about instead of used',
};

/* Staleness and movement are different failures with different owners. */
const FRESHNESS = {
  visible: 'last-updated time on every tile, red when the pipeline is behind rather than grey when nobody has looked',
  alertSeparately: { pipelineBehind: 'engineering', genuineMovement: 'the product' },
  // a review that discovers yesterday's outage by noticing a flat line has
  // wasted the meeting it discovered it in
  why: 'a stale number looks exactly like a fresh one, and the dashboard is where that confusion is most expensive',
};

/* Most alerts should not be dashboards. */
const ALERTING = {
  dashboard: 'for a human who is looking',
  alert: 'for a number that crossed something while nobody was looking',
  failure: 'forty metrics on a dashboard and no alerts: everything is discovered by a person noticing, and noticing is unreliable',
  alerts: { few: true, tiedToActions: true, quietByDefault: true },
  everyRowSays: 'whether it has an alert, so the review can tell "nothing happened" from "nobody is watching"',
};

Finally, link every metric to a target and to the action that follows when it crosses, because a number without a consequence is trivia. "Activation 31%, target 35%, owner: growth, action: the onboarding funnel leak at the account step" is a useful row. "Signups: 4,102" is a fact with no owner, and facts with no owner are the ones that generate discussion instead of decisions. When a metric crosses its threshold, the row should already say who does what, so the meeting can skip the diagnosis and start with the work.

/* The dashboard spec: four rows, each with an owner, a target and an action.
   Every row here is a decision somebody makes; a row without all three is a
   fact, and facts generate discussion instead of decisions. */
const DASHBOARD = {
  name: 'Weekly product review',
  owner: 'named person, not a team - a team never becomes accountable for accuracy',
  cadence: 'Mondays, 30 minutes, fixed time',
  // and the reason it decays without this: nothing breaks, so nobody notices
  meetingIsTheArtefact: true,

  rows: [
    { metric: 'activation (core action within first session)',
      current: 0.31, target: 0.35, trend: '+4pts over 6 weeks',
      owner: 'growth', actionIfBelow: 'the onboarding funnel leak at the account step - read 10 replays first',
      definition: 'users who performed the core action within 24h of signup / users who signed up' },

    { metric: 'core funnel completion (product page to order)',
      current: 0.58, target: 0.65, trend: 'flat for 3 weeks',
      owner: 'checkout', actionIfBelow: 'rank leaks by users lost, not by proportion; 412 people are lost at the address step',
      definition: 'order_completed / product_viewed, same cohort, 7-day rolling' },

    { metric: 'retention: sessions in week 2',
      current: 0.44, target: 0.50, trend: '-2pts since the March release',
      owner: 'product', actionIfBelow: 'check whether the release changed the first-run path; annotate the chart',
      definition: 'users with a session in days 7-14 / users who signed up in the same week' },

    { metric: 'current experiment: variant B on the CTA',
      current: 'n=4,180 of 12,000', target: 'full sample at day 11',
      trend: 'no interim reading - the end date is pre-committed',
      owner: 'growth', actionIfStopped: 'roll back, and record the negative result so it is not rerun',
      definition: 'signups per landing view, 10% holdout, guardrail: 7-day activation' },
  ],

  rules: [
    'one screen; everything else reachable by a link, not by crowding',
    'a date on every chart, and the definition written on the chart',
    'a release or version marker on every chart, because a redesign is an event',
    'an annotation for every anomaly: a deploy, a price change, an outage, a campaign',
    'never an overall average of a segmented metric',
  ],
};

/* The annotation format, because an unexplained jump invites the team to
   explain it consistently with what they want to be true. */
const ANNOTATIONS = [
  { at: '2026-02-18', type: 'release', what: 'checkout rebuild, 3 steps to 1', effect: 'address-step exits fell 58% to 41%' },
  { at: '2026-03-01', type: 'pricing', what: 'annual plan default changed', effect: 'checkout start rose, completion flat' },
  { at: '2026-03-03', type: 'outage', what: 'payments degraded for 4 hours', effect: 'the week-2 dip is explained; do not act on it' },
];

/* The weekly agenda. The dashboard is a prop in this meeting, which is the
   only reason the meeting happens. */
const REVIEW_AGENDA = {
  duration: '30,
  items: [
    { minutes: 2, topic: 'last week\'s decisions and whether they happened', why: 'an unexecuted decision is the real failure mode' },
    { minutes: 16, topic: 'four rows, one question each', why: 'a fixed slot per row stops one metric eating the meeting' },
    { minutes: 8, topic: 'annotations: what changed that would move these', why: 'prevents the team explaining a jump consistent with what it wants' },
    { minutes: 4, topic: 'actions, owners, dates', why: 'a meeting without assigned actions is a status report' },
  ],
  // and what is explicitly not in it
  never: ['a metric without an owner or a target', 'a number explained from memory',
          'anything on the dashboard that has no row with an action'],
  decaysWhen: 'the review is skipped twice. A dashboard without a meeting is a screenshot within a month.',
};
  • One screen: activation + core-funnel + retention + the current experiment; everything else goes deeper.
  • Show dates + versions on every chart (a redesign is an event).
  • A dashboard without an owner and a weekly review is a screenshot.

18.6 The honest limits of experiments

Experiments have honest limits that responsible teams plan for rather than hide. Short A/B tests miss long-run effects such as trust, habit formation, brand sentiment, and learning, none of which can be measured cheaply in a two-week window. They also miss the impact on the existing user base and word of mouth. Gradual rollouts with guardrail metrics and longitudinal tracking cover what isolated experiments cannot see.

  • Short A/Bs miss long-run effects (novelty spike, habit formation). Keep guardrail retention metrics running after the test before trusting the click-win.
  • Some things can’t be A/B’d cheaply: trust, brand, onboarding curves. Use gradual rollout (release to 10% → 50% → 100%) as the mechanism instead of a fake experiment.
  • Metrics respond to incentives: optimizing signups can starve retention. Every experiment ships with a primary metric AND a guardrail set — the habit beats any single dashboard.

What a two-week experiment cannot see

The honest limits of an A/B test are all long-run, and that is structural rather than a matter of sample size. Novelty makes anything new look good for a while, so a two-week test systematically overestimates a redesign's value and its effect decays in ways the test never observes. Habit formation runs the other way: an interface that is good the first time and annoying the fortieth can win a test and lose a cohort. Trust, learning, brand sentiment and word of mouth are the ones nobody can measure cheaply at all, because they take longer to develop than any experiment can afford to run, and a change that improves conversion while reducing trust is a trade the data cannot see.

Then there is the population. An experiment measures the effect on the people who saw it, and says nothing about the ones who did not hear about it from those people. If the change makes the product easier to use but less shareable, the experiment wins on every metric it measured and the referral rate quietly declines over the following quarter. The mitigation is longitudinal tracking that outlives the test — cohort retention and referral rate at 90 days, tracked for every significant change — rather than a bigger sample in a shorter window.

Some things cannot be A/B tested at all, and pretending otherwise produces a fake experiment that ships on faith. Pricing and packaging change what the product is and who buys it, and a two-week test at one price answers a question nobody asked. Brand, trust and positioning have no primary metric that a two-week test could move honestly. And onboarding curves are the hardest case of all, because the change affects every new user for months, and there is no cohort you can run the control against for that long without stalling the entire roadmap.

For those, use a gradual rollout as the mechanism rather than an experiment as a decoration. Release to 10 percent, watch the guardrails for a set period, go to 50, watch again, then to 100 — with each stage having a written rollback condition and a named person who can trigger it. This is a weaker instrument than an experiment because there is no control group, and it is honest about that: the residual comparison is against the historical trend, which is confounded by everything else that changed in the same period. Its value is that the rollback is cheap and available at every stage rather than being a decision made at the end.

Metrics respond to incentives, and this is the failure mode with the longest tail. Optimising signups starves retention; optimising session count starves task completion; optimising time-on-app optimises the app. The habit that catches it is the guardrail set — a primary metric plus a small number of metrics that must not get worse — declared before the test, and enforced after it, and applied to the roadmap as well as to the experiments. Every metric somebody is being paid to improve has a corresponding metric somebody should be watching, and the pair is what makes the incentive honest.

The other things people call experiments

A before-and-after comparison is the most common method in the building and it is the weakest, and the reason is specific rather than general: everything that happened at the same time is attributed to the change. A pricing test, a marketing push, a seasonal peak, a competitor's release, a tracking bug, a device mix shift — each of these lands in the same period and each of them is indistinguishable from the change in a two-line chart. The method is not useless, it is just much weaker than it feels, and it becomes much better with three additions: annotate every known event on the chart, use a control that was not exposed, and state in advance what would have counted as the change having worked.

A difference-in-differences comparison fixes the largest part of this at low cost. Split the population into two groups on a dimension unrelated to the change — a country not served, a feature-flag cohort, a customer segment — measure the change's effect in the exposed group and the change in time's effect in the unexposed group, and take the difference of the differences. The assumption is that without the change both groups would have moved together, which is a real assumption and a much smaller one than "nothing else changed". Where a randomised holdout is not possible this is the standard substitute and it is worth doing imperfectly rather than skipping.

An interrupted time series is for when there is no control group at all and the series is long enough to establish a baseline. Model the level and trend before the interruption, then compare what actually happened against what the pre-interruption pattern predicted, and inspect the data immediately around the change for a step, a slope change or a transient. The strength is that it uses the whole history rather than one window; the weakness is that every other event in the series still lands somewhere, which is why the annotations matter more here than anywhere else.

Then the two that are most often mislabelled. A survey of perceived change is not an experiment: asking people whether the new version is better produces a strong effect in almost any direction, because the mere novelty of a change registers as improvement and because respondents want to please. Treat it as a comprehension and preference measurement, and never as evidence that behaviour changed. And a holdout at the top of the funnel — permanently withholding a feature from a small group to measure its long-run contribution — is the closest thing to a genuine experiment for anything with cumulative effects, and it is cheap: the cost is one group of users permanently without a thing they mostly do not use.

/* Before-and-after: the weaknesses are specific, not general. Everything that
   happened at the same time is attributed to the change. */
const CONFOUNDS = [
  'a pricing test running concurrently',
  'a marketing push',
  'a seasonal peak',
  'a competitor release',
  'a tracking bug, which moves the metric without any behaviour changing',
  'a device or traffic mix shift',
  'a change in the definition of the metric itself, with no announcement',
];
// the method is not useless - it is much weaker than it feels, and it
// becomes much better with three additions
const BEFORE_AFTER_FIXES = ['annotate every known event on the chart', 'use a control that was not exposed',
                             'state in advance what would count as the change having worked'];

/* Difference-in-differences: split on a dimension unrelated to the change. */
function diffInDiff({ treated: { before, after }, control: { before, after } }) {
  const treatedEffect = after - before;
  const controlEffect  = after - before;              // what would have happened anyway
  return {
    effect: treatedEffect - controlEffect,
    assumption: 'without the change, both groups would have moved together',
    // a real assumption, and a much smaller one than "nothing else changed"
    sizeOfAssumption: 'the gap between "nothing else changed" and "these two groups track each other"',
    whenWorthIt: 'a randomised holdout is not possible and the split is on a dimension the change cannot touch',
    // the failure to check first
    testParallelTrends: 'did the two groups track each other before the change? if not, the method is invalid',
  };
}

/* Interrupted time series: for when there is no control and the series is
   long enough to have a baseline. */
const ITS = {
  use: { requires: 'no control group, and a long enough pre-interruption series',
         advantage: 'uses the whole history rather than one window' },
  method: ['model level and trend before the interruption',
           'compare what happened against what the pattern predicted',
           'inspect immediately around the change for a step, a slope change, or a transient'],
  weakness: 'every other event in the series still lands somewhere, so the annotations matter more here than anywhere else',
  shapes: { step: 'an immediate level change - usually the real effect',
            slope: 'a change in trajectory - usually the honest measure of a durable change',
            transient: 'a spike that decays - usually an announcement effect, not a behaviour change' },
};

/* The two most often mislabelled. */
const MISLABELLED = [
  { called: 'an experiment', is: 'a survey of perceived change',
    whyItOverstates: 'novelty registers as improvement, and respondents want to please',
    effectSize: 'an effect in almost any direction',
    treatAs: 'a comprehension and preference measurement',
    neverAs: 'evidence that behaviour changed' },
  { called: 'an A/B test', is: 'a permanent top-of-funnel holdout',
    what: 'withhold a feature from a small group indefinitely to measure its cumulative contribution',
    why: 'the closest thing to a genuine experiment for anything with cumulative effects',
    cost: 'one group of users permanently without a thing they mostly do not use' },
];

/* Reading the chart properly, which is most of the skill. */
const READING = [
  'the annotation layer: every deploy, price change, campaign and outage on the axis',
  'the definition marker: a metric definition change moves the line without any behaviour changing',
  'the direction of the effect against the direction you predicted, in advance',
  'whether the effect decays, which usually distinguishes a real change from an announcement',
];

Keep the record, because the value of a limitation is in what it prevents being repeated. Write down what the experiment could not see, alongside the result, and review the significant changes again at 90 days against the cohort numbers. Roughly one change in ten will show something at that point that the test could not have seen, and that one is worth more than the nine it was shipped with.

/* What an experiment cannot see, per change type. This is the list that has
   to be written down before the test, because afterwards it is a rationalisation. */
const LIMITS = {
  novelty: { window: 'days 1-14', direction: 'overestimates', note: 'anything new looks good for a while, so a two-week test systematically overvalues a redesign' },
  habit: { window: 'weeks 3-12', direction: 'underestimates', note: 'good once and annoying on the fortieth wins a test and loses a cohort' },
  trust: { window: 'months', direction: 'invisible', note: 'a change that raises conversion while reducing trust is a trade no two-week test can see' },
  learning: { window: 'weeks', direction: 'invisible', note: 'an interface that teaches eventually pays off in a way the test does not measure' },
  brand: { window: 'quarters', direction: 'invisible', note: 'no primary metric moves in two weeks and everything the product is judged on is slower' },
  wordOfMouth: { window: 'quarters', direction: 'invisible', note: 'the experiment measures people who saw it, not those who heard about it' },
};

/* The mitigation: longitudinal tracking that outlives the test. The referral
   rate in particular only moves once the people who saw it have told people. */
const LONGITUDINAL = [
  { metric: 'cohort retention at day 90', why: 'habit formation, which the test cannot see', check: 'for every significant change, at 90 days' },
