  { metric: 'referral rate per active user', why: 'word of mouth moves a quarter after the change, if at all', check: 'quarterly, by cohort' },
  { metric: 'support contacts per hundred new users', why: 'confusion that users tolerate and then complain about later', check: 'week 4' },
  { metric: 'churn in the segment most affected', why: 'the test sample was mostly new users; the base is not', check: 'day 60' },
];

/* Things that cannot be A/B tested honestly. For these, a rollout with a
   rollback is the honest instrument and a two-week test would be theatre. */
const NOT_TESTABLE = [
  { thing: 'pricing and packaging', why: 'changes what the product is and who buys it; one price for two weeks answers nothing',
    instead: 'a staged price test across regions or cohorts, with a modelled revenue guardrail, over a full billing cycle' },
  { thing: 'brand, trust, positioning', why: 'no primary metric moves in two weeks',
    instead: 'qualitative and expert review, plus long-run brand tracking, plus a rollout with a rollback' },
  { thing: 'onboarding curves', why: 'every new user is affected for months; there is no cohort to hold back without stalling the roadmap',
    instead: 'sequential cohort measurement: ship, then compare the next cohort to the previous one over 8 weeks' },
  { thing: 'anything touching trust or safety', why: 'the downside is not symmetric with the upside and a sample cannot price it',
    instead: 'the most conservative rollout available, expert sign-off, and monitoring of the worst outcomes rather than the average' },
];

/* Gradual rollout. Weaker than an experiment because there is no control -
   the comparison is against the historical trend, which is confounded by
   everything else that changed in the same period. Say so. */
const ROLLOUT = {
  stages: [
    { at: 0.10, holdFor: '7 days', gate: 'guardrail metrics inside tolerance, no support spike' },
    { at: 0.50, holdFor: '14 days', gate: 'the same guardrails, plus day-7 retention for the exposed cohort' },
    { at: 1.00, holdFor: 'the 90-day cohort review', gate: 'longitudinal metrics as defined above' },
  ],
  rollback: { condition: 'any guardrail outside tolerance for more than 24 hours',
              authority: 'one named person, without a meeting',
              note: 'a rollback that needs approval is not a rollback' },
  honestAboutIt: 'this is not an experiment: there is no control group and the trend is confounded by everything else shipping in the same period',
  whenToPreferIt: 'when the change is not cleanly separable, when the effect is long-run, or when the downside is not symmetric',
};

/* Guardrails, and the incentive conflict each one closes. Every metric
   somebody is paid to improve needs one somebody is watching against it. */
const GUARDRAILS = [
  { primary: 'signups', conflictsWith: 'retention', guardrail: '7-day retention must not fall',
    failureSeen: 'an acquisition push that fills the top of the funnel with people who never return' },
  { primary: 'session count', conflictsWith: 'task completion', guardrail: 'sessions with the core action completed must not fall',
    failureSeen: 'more sessions of nothing in particular' },
  { primary: 'time on app', conflictsWith: 'time to task done', guardrail: 'median time to complete must not rise',
    failureSeen: 'the classic: an app that is pleasant to use and slow to get things done with' },
  { primary: 'checkout conversion', conflictsWith: 'refunds and chargebacks', guardrail: 'refund rate within 30 days must not rise',
    failureSeen: 'a checkout that converts by letting people buy the wrong thing' },
  { primary: 'feature adoption', conflictsWith: 'task completion', guardrail: 'the core action rate must not fall',
    failureSeen: 'a notification feature that people turn on and then do their work somewhere else' },
];

Exercises 18

  1. Define 6 events for your product and a funnel with a real user story.
  2. Integrate one analytics tool into a demo app; fire 3 events and watch them arrive.
  3. Design a "dashboard for the CEO": 4 numbers + the story each tells.

19 · Design Critique, Presentation & Working with Teams

Design critique, presentation, and collaboration are the delivery vehicle for all the work around them, because great design dies in review meetings at least as often as in code. Critique, run well, improves the work while preserving the designer, and presentation, done right, moves decisions. Mastering how to give and receive feedback and how to work with developers and stakeholders multiplies everything else in the course. These are the skills that make good work actually ship.

19.1 Receiving critique without eating it19.2 Running critique your team keeps attending19.3 Designing WITH developers (not to them)19.4 Presenting to stakeholders who don’t care about pixels

UX dies in review meetings at least as often as it dies in code. Communication skill isn’t the "soft part" of this job — it’s the delivery vehicle for all of it.

19.1 Receiving critique without eating it

Receiving critique well protects both the work and the working relationship. Remember that critique targets the design, never the designer, so treat each comment as data about the artifact rather than about your worth. Clarify the problem being solved, separate verifiable facts from personal preference, and probe for the concern behind the comment. Ask good questions, record what is useful, and thank every good critic.

// The mindset shift: critique is about the DESIGN, not the DESIGNER.
// Script for receiving:
//  1 clarify first: "what problem are you seeing the user face?"
//  2 separate facts from preference: "you're right the empty state
//     has no next step" ≠ "the color should be pink"
//  3 hold a posture: "that's a concern at X — worth testing; here's
//     what I'll measure" — you DO know the evidence trail, use it
//  4 thank. Every good critic is a free user-testing session.

Taking it, which is a skill rather than a temperament

Critique targets the work, and the practical form of that is treating every comment as a data point about an artifact rather than about the person who made it. The behaviour that makes this real is small and specific: write the comment down verbatim before responding to it. Responding while still hearing it produces defensiveness and loses the content, because the response has to be composed before the thought is finished, and a designer who answers the first third of a comment has usually answered a different comment than the one being made.

Then ask what problem it solves, because most actionable critique arrives as a symptom. "This is confusing" is a report of an experience; the useful follow-up is what the person was trying to do at that moment, which turns a mood into a task, and a task can be designed for. Almost every vague comment becomes concrete the moment somebody is asked what they were trying to achieve — not always, sometimes the vague comment was honest and vague, and knowing that is also worth the time.

Separate what is verifiable from what is preference, because conflating them produces arguments that cannot be settled. "The caption is 12 pixels and the contrast is 2.4:1" is checkable and actionable, and if it is true it is a defect regardless of anyone's opinion. "It feels cramped" is a perception, which is real data about an experience and is not a specification. Both are useful; the failure is answering a perception with a specification, or dismissing a specification because the person who raised it had a preference attached to it. Write both down in the same list and treat them as different kinds of claim.

Probe for the concern behind the comment, because the concern is portable and the suggestion usually is not. "Move that button" almost always means "I could not find that button", and the concern — that the primary action is not discoverable — can be solved in several ways, only one of which is the one suggested. Asking the question costs one sentence and converts a solution into a requirement, which is the single highest-value habit in the whole practice.

Look for the pattern rather than reacting to the loudest comment. Three people mentioning hierarchy is one problem, and the count is the measurement. Counting the themes is what stops a designer optimising for the most articulate person in the room, which is a failure mode with no name and a very high frequency; the theme is the signal and the individual suggestion is one possible response to it.

Close every critique with an explicit response: what you are changing, what you are not, and what you need from whom. A comment with no response teaches the room that comments do not matter, and the next session is worse — and it is worse in a way nobody announces, because the polite disengagement looks like professionalism. Thank every good critic by name, because the thank-you and the critique are the same signal: it is the way you tell people which kind of comment you want more of.

And allow for disagreement, which is the case most receiving guides skip. You may be right, and the correct response is not to implement something you believe is worse but to say plainly that you hear it and are going to do it differently, with the reason. What is not acceptable is leaving a comment unanswered, because that is what teaches people that effort does not matter — and the effort being abandoned is always the people who gave the best comments, because they were the ones willing to be specific.

/* The critique log. Comments are recorded verbatim before any response,
   because responding while still hearing produces defensiveness and loses
   the content. Themes are counted; individuals are not optimised for. */
const CRITIQUE_LOG = {
  work: 'checkout single page, v3',
  date: '2026-03-04',
  facilitator: 'AM',

  comments: [
    { verbatim: "I could not tell what the shipping cost was until I got to the bottom",
      kind: 'fact',                 // checkable: the figure is present, or it is not
      check: { claim: 'shipping cost visible before payment', result: 'not until the summary row',
               verified: true },
      concernBehind: 'the total is not knowable before committing',   // the portable part
      suggested: 'show it at the top',                                 // the disposable part
      theme: 'cost transparency' },
    { verbatim: "it feels cramped",
      kind: 'preference',            // a real perception, not a specification
      response: 'asked what they were trying to do; they were comparing plans',
      theme: 'comparison' },
    { verbatim: "the primary button is the same colour as the secondary one",
      kind: 'fact', check: { claim: 'two buttons share a token', result: 'confirmed by token, not by eye', verified: true },
      theme: 'hierarchy' },
  ],

  // the count is the signal. Optimising for the most articulate person in
  // the room is a failure mode with no name and a very high frequency
  themes: { 'cost transparency': 3, hierarchy: 2, comparison: 2 },

  // every comment gets a response, or the next session is worse
  response: [
    { theme: 'cost transparency', change: 'show shipping in the cart summary before the address step', by: 'design', when: 'this sprint' },
    { theme: 'hierarchy',         change: 'primary uses --brand; secondary is outline only', by: 'design', when: 'today' },
    { theme: 'comparison',        change: 'none yet; the plan table is being tested first', by: 'design', need: 'two days from research' },
  ],
  disagree: { allowed: true, must: 'state the reason, never leave the comment unanswered',
              why: 'an unanswered comment is what makes good critics stop' },
};

A script for receiving critique: clarify the problem first, separate facts from preference, keep an evidence posture, and thank the critic.

19.2 Running critique your team keeps attending

A critique your team keeps attending starts with the designer stating their goal and what they want feedback on, then fills the room with observers rather than judges. Feedback follows a format of observation, impact, and suggestion so comments stay concrete and fixable. Timebox the session, keep it to works in progress, record decisions while fresh, and close with the designer’s explicit next steps. If you do not act on it, they stop coming.

Running one that people keep attending

A critique session survives or dies on two rules that are both procedural. The designer states the goal and what they want input on before any feedback is given, and the room is observers rather than judges. The statement is what makes the session specific — "I want a reaction to whether the flow map is the right sequence, not whether these buttons are right yet" tells eight people where to aim, and without it they default to the most visible thing on the screen. And observers is a change of role rather than of temperament: the room's job is to say what they see and what they would expect to happen, not to decide whether the work is good, which is a decision nobody in the room is qualified to make about a market they do not know.

Then the format: observation, impact, suggestion. Each comment has all three, which forces it to be concrete, and the suggestion is optional and frequently wrong — the designer owns the solution, and a session that accepts solutions as answers produces a list of the room's ideas rather than a review of the designer's idea. "Make it pop" fails the format because there is no observation and no impact; "I paused for four seconds at the delivery row and re-read it" passes both and hands over something actionable. The format is best enforced by the facilitator stopping any comment that cannot state its observation, because the rule is much easier to hold on others than on oneself.

Timebox it to thirty minutes for works in progress. Long sessions produce fewer and vaguer comments because social pressure rises with the clock, and the first ten comments are the valuable ones — after that the room starts negotiating rather than observing. Take the notes yourself rather than asking a volunteer or an assistant, because the act of writing is what makes a designer hear the comment, and delegating it converts a session into a transcript. Record the decisions during, not after: the reason a comment was rejected is the part that is lost, and it is the part that prevents the same comment from being raised again in four weeks.

Close with the designer's explicit next steps, out loud: what is changing, what is deliberately not changing, and what is needed from whom and by when. This is the part that determines whether the next session happens, and the rule behind it is simple — if you do not act on the critique, people stop coming, and the loss is silent. Nobody announces that they have stopped attending a critique; the session just becomes smaller and vaguer until it is not worth anyone's time, and the team loses its best quality mechanism without a decision being taken.

Keep the room small and to the people who will do the work. Eight is plenty and twelve takes three times as long while producing eleven different styles of feedback, most of them from people with no stake in the outcome. A critique is not a vote and not a consultation: it is a way of getting a group of people who know things the designer does not to look at the work closely and say what they see. If somebody in the room will never touch the thing, they add latency and noise.

Rotate the role, because everyone presenting is what makes the practice a team skill rather than a designer-only one. It also removes the reason people are quiet in other people's sessions — they have not yet been in the chair and discovered that a badly-framed request draws vague comments and feels like failure. And every presenter should close by asking one specific question about the artifact rather than inviting general feedback, because "does anything look off" is answered by politeness.

The parts that fail in practice, and what to do about them

The room's dynamics break the format more often than the format does. The senior person who speaks first and most often sets the frame for everyone else, and their first comment is heard as consensus — so the facilitator's job includes managing airtime rather than only managing content: round the room in a fixed order, and take the least senior first, because everything said afterwards is conditioned by what came before it. This is uncomfortable for about four minutes and then it is not, and the alternative is a critique in which the same three people do all the talking and the remaining five have learned that attending is a waste of an hour.

Remote critiques break it in a specific way, which is that the room's reactions are invisible. Nobody can see that three people are nodding and two have already switched off, and the person most willing to say the awkward thing online is often the person least willing to say it in a room. Three fixes work: go round in order with names visible so nobody can hide, take comments written first and read aloud by the facilitator so writing quality rather than confidence sets the floor, or make it anonymous with the author revealed afterwards — which reliably produces the observations nobody would have volunteered.

The asynchronous version is worth having, because most useful critique happens when people have actually looked. It needs three things the synchronous version does not: a deadline, because a thread without one is a thread that dies quietly; the format enforced as fields rather than as a convention, so observation, impact and suggestion are separate boxes and the impact box cannot be left blank; and a rule that the author decides, in their own time, what to do with each comment. Without the last one the thread becomes a queue of requests with an implicit obligation attached, and the person who posted it stops posting.

The language is worth policing lightly, because "make it pop" and "this feels dated" are not useful but they are not rudeness either — they are imprecise. The move is to ask what someone expects to happen instead, which converts a verdict into an expectation, and to answer the expectation rather than defending the design. And it is worth separating the critique of the output from the critique of the constraints, because a session that only discusses outputs misses the useful observation that the thing cannot be done in the time available. Say explicitly whether constraints are in scope: sometimes they are, and "this cannot be built in a sprint" is a legitimate finding that belongs in the record.

Then follow up, dated. A session produces decisions, and decisions that are not checked are the reason people stop attending — the same mechanism as an unanswered comment, at group scale. A five-minute follow-up with three questions — what changed, what did not, what was displaced — is enough, and its main function is to make the displacement visible, because the thing that was quietly dropped is usually the reason the next session is weaker than the last.

/* Airtime management. The senior person's first comment is heard as
   consensus, so this is the facilitator's actual job. */
function roundRobin(order /* least senior first, by design not by luck */) {
  return {
    order,
    // everything after is conditioned by what came before it, which is why
    // the order is the intervention
    rule: 'the room is called in a fixed order; nobody speaks twice before everyone has spoken once',
    stop: (comment) => !comment.observation,
    // the four minutes of discomfort are the cost of the fix
    uncomfortableFor: 'about 4 minutes, and then it is not',
  };
}

/* The async version. Three things the synchronous one does not need. */
const ASYNC_CRITIQUE = {
  requires: [
    { thing: 'a deadline', why: 'a thread without one dies quietly, and the author is left unsure whether anyone read it' },
    { thing: 'the format as fields', why: 'observation, impact and suggestion as separate boxes; the impact box cannot be left blank' },
    { thing: 'the author decides, in their own time', why: 'without this the thread is a queue of requests with an implicit obligation attached' },
  ],
  fields: {
    observation: { type: 'text', required: true, example: 'I re-read the delivery row twice' },
    impact: { type: 'text', required: true, why: 'the field that makes it a comment rather than an opinion',
              example: 'I would not be sure which option to pick' },
    suggestion: { type: 'text', required: false, note: 'optional, and often wrong: the author owns the solution' },
    isConstraint: { type: 'boolean', default: false,
                    why: 'whether the comment is about the output or about what the time budget allows' },
  },
  authorOwns: 'which comments to act on, without owing an account for the rest',
};

/* Remote, where the reactions are invisible and confidence substitutes for
   clarity. Three fixes, in order of how much they help. */
const REMOTE = [
  { technique: 'named round-robin with visible order',
    fixes: 'the invisible airtime problem: nobody can see that two people have switched off' },
  { technique: 'write first, facilitator reads aloud',
    fixes: 'writing quality becomes the floor rather than confidence',
    why: 'the person most willing to say the awkward thing online is often the person least willing to say it in a room' },
  { technique: 'anonymous, author revealed afterwards',
    fixes: 'the reluctance entirely',
    why: 'reliably produces the observations nobody would have volunteered' },
];

/* Language, converted rather than defended against. "Make it pop" and "this
   feels dated" are imprecise, not rude. */
function convertVerdict(comment) {
  if (comment.observation) return comment;                 // already usable
  return { ...comment,
    question: 'what did you expect to happen instead?',
    // the expectation is what can be answered; the verdict is what has to be
    example: 'from "make it pop" to "I expected the primary action to be the only filled button on the screen"' };
}

/* Follow-up, dated. This is the group-scale version of an unanswered comment. */
const FOLLOW_UP = {
  minutes: 5,
  questions: ['what changed', 'what did not', 'what was displaced'],
  // the third is the whole point: what was quietly dropped is usually why the
  // next session is weaker than the last
  displaced: 'record it, and name who owns the thing it displaced',
  ifMissedTwice: 'people stop attending, and nothing announces it',
};

Finally, be clear about what a critique cannot do, because it is regularly asked to. It cannot validate a direction you have already shipped, since nobody in the room is a customer and a designer's confidence is not evidence. It cannot tell you whether the market wants it. And it cannot substitute for testing, because the room shares your context and your vocabulary and none of the biases you are trying to correct. What it is good at is finding problems in the artifact — inconsistencies, ambiguities, missing states, an implied flow that contradicts the stated one — and finding them cheaply, before they are built.

/* The session. Two procedural rules carry most of the value: the statement
   before any feedback, and observers rather than judges. */
const CRITIQUE_SESSION = {
  duration: '30 minutes, hard timebox',
  stage: 'works in progress only - a shipped thing gets opinions, not critique',

  agenda: [
    { minutes: 3, who: 'designer', topic: 'the statement',
      // the most important three minutes, because without it the room aims
      // at the most visible thing on the screen instead of the real question
      mustContain: ['the goal in one sentence', 'what feedback is wanted',
                    'what is explicitly not up for discussion today'] },
    { minutes: 20, who: 'room', topic: 'observation, impact, suggestion',
      rule: 'the facilitator stops any comment that cannot state its observation' },
    { minutes: 5, who: 'designer', topic: 'decisions, recorded as they are taken',
      why: 'the reason a comment was rejected is what stops it being raised again in four weeks' },
    { minutes: 2, who: 'designer', topic: 'next steps, out loud',
      mustContain: ['what is changing', 'what is deliberately not changing', 'what is needed, from whom, by when'] },
  ],

  format: {
    observation: 'what I see, concretely - "I re-read the delivery row"',
    impact:      'what I expect to happen as a result - "I think I would pick the wrong one"',
    suggestion:  'optional, and often wrong: the designer owns the solution',
    rejected:    '"make it pop" - no observation, no impact, unusable',
    example:     'I paused four seconds at the delivery row and re-read it [obs]; I would not be sure which to pick [impact]; maybe show the price difference on each row [suggestion]',
  },

  // the rule that determines whether the next one happens
  ifNoActionIsTaken: 'people stop coming, and the loss is silent: nobody announces they have stopped attending, the room just gets smaller and vaguer',

  room: { size: 'about 8', rule: 'people who will do the work, not people with opinions',
          why: 'twelve takes three times as long and produces eleven styles of feedback' },
  roles: { rotate: true, why: 'removes the reason people are quiet in other sessions: they have not yet been in the chair' },
  notes: { takenBy: 'the designer', why: 'writing is what makes a designer hear the comment' },
  question: { ask: 'one specific question about the artifact', never: '"does anything look off"', reason: 'the latter is answered by politeness' },

  cannotDo: ['validate a direction already shipped - nobody in the room is a customer',
             'tell you whether the market wants it',
             'replace testing: the room shares your context and your vocabulary'],
  goodAt: ['inconsistencies', 'ambiguities', 'missing states', 'a flow that contradicts the stated one'],
};
  1. No feedback until the designer states the GOAL and what they want input on ("I want a reaction to the flow map, not the buttons yet").
  2. Feedback = observation + impact + suggestion ("Users paused at this step [obs]; likely unclear [impact]; maybe a caption [sugg]") — no vague "make it pop".
  3. Timebox (30 min), take notes by the designer, decisions recorded.

19.3 Designing WITH developers (not to them)

Designing with developers turns handoff into a collaboration. Hand your work over early and complete, with the states, motion, and edge cases developers actually need, and reuse an agreed design system instead of inventing fresh components each time. Version the design file like code and co-own changes together. When developers treat the design as a live spec rather than a pixel dump, what ships matches what was designed.

Developer realityDesign response
Tokens/behaviors cost dev timespecify states + motion + edge cases explicitly; reuse system
Designs age in sprint limbohand off early, version like code, co-own the change
Accessibility is built, not addedhand keyboard/ARIA requirements with the design (Ch.7)
"That’s a one-liner" is a red flagdig for the actual interaction cost before accepting scope

Handoff as a collaboration rather than a delivery

Hand over early and hand over complete. Early because the first handoff should be something rough that a developer will actually build, and the questions it raises are the work — a rough thing built in week one and a finished thing built in week six cost the same and produce the same list of surprises, and the surprise is cheaper early. Complete because the absence of a specified state is the single most expensive thing in a handoff, and it is expensive in a way nobody notices until the build is blocked or the feature ships with an error screen nobody designed.

So the deliverable is more than the frames. It is every state the feature can be in: loading, empty, filtered-empty, error, partial success, permission denied, offline, and the edge cases the layout will meet in production — a name forty characters long, a number with six digits, a ninth language, right-to-left text, a user whose permission was revoked while the screen was open. Each of those is a decision, and a decision nobody made is a decision a developer makes alone at 5pm on a Friday. Give the states as designed components rather than as notes, because a note about an error state is interpreted and a component is not.

Motion is specified as duration and curve rather than as a feeling. "Feels snappy" is unimplementable and "180 ms, standard ease-out, opacity and transform only" is not, and the difference between the two is where a week's rework comes from. State the permitted properties while you are there — transform and opacity, never width or height or top, because those force layout on every frame and drop frames on exactly the devices that need help.

Reuse the design system rather than inventing a component per screen, and treat a genuinely new component as a request to a team rather than as a file in your own library. Every bespoke control is a component somebody has to maintain, document, test, keep accessible and keep in sync with the rest, and the cost is paid by people who did not choose it. Where the system genuinely cannot cover a need, that is a finding about the system: raise it with the evidence, get it added, and then use it everywhere it applies.

Version the design file like code and co-own the changes. A design system only one person can edit is a bottleneck, and a bottleneck in the system is a bottleneck in every product that uses it. Practically: the file is in version control, changes go through the same review as code, and the components have named owners outside the design team. When the system changes, the consumers are notified — because "the secondary button changed and four products need updating" is a message that must be sent deliberately rather than discovered.

Then talk about cost, early and specifically, because the expensive surprises are predictable. Three tiers are enough: cheap and boring, which is a layout and a colour; moderate, which is a real component with real states; and expensive, which needs real data rather than fixtures — a virtualised list, a chart, an animation that has to coordinate with scrolling, anything with offline behaviour or a permissions model. The category that surprises people is the one that looks cheap and is not: a table of two hundred rows, a dropdown with server-side search, a progress bar that has to be honest about a total it does not know.

Acceptance criteria, which is what a handoff actually is

Most handoff documents describe what the screen looks like and leave out what makes it acceptable, and the second is what determines whether it comes back. Write acceptance criteria that a developer can check and a designer can verify, and that between them settle every argument about a state or an edge case without a meeting. This is not bureaucracy: a handoff without them is a series of interruptions during the build, each of which costs a context switch for two people, and the total is reliably larger than the time it took to write.

Accessibility criteria belong in the spec rather than in a later audit, because a screen built without them cannot be fixed by an audit without rebuilding parts of it. Keyboard order and focus visibility, the accessible name of every control, the contrast targets, the live-region behaviour of anything that updates asynchronously, and the focus management for anything that opens. These are five lines in a spec and the difference between a screen that passes and one that needs a week. Naming the criteria also removes the recurring argument about whether a particular interaction is acceptable, which is a design decision rather than an engineering one and should be made in the document.

Specify responsive behaviour as rules, not as frames. A set of desktop, tablet and phone screenshots tells a developer what you drew and leaves every question open: what happens between those widths, what wraps first, when a table becomes cards, what the minimum supported width is and what happens below it. Write it as constraints — the content order, the first thing to drop, the width below which the layout changes and to what — and the resulting behaviour is consistent because it follows a rule rather than three intentions.

Specify the data contract, including the absence cases. A component should declare what it needs, what it does when a value is missing, when it is null, when it is zero and when it is very large, because zero and null are rendered identically by almost every default implementation and they are not the same thing to a person reading a number. This is the single most common source of late-stage defects that were entirely predictable: an amount that shows "—" when it should show "0", a date that shows "Invalid Date" for a value that was never set.

Content is part of the design, and content rules belong in the spec. Minimum and maximum realistic lengths, what happens at both ends, what happens with a string in a script the layout does not accommodate, and which strings are translated and which are not. Mark the string that must be translated, the one that must not be — a brand name, a code, a currency symbol chosen by locale — and the ones that must not be broken across lines. Each of those is a two-word annotation now and a layout bug later, and "later" is when four other people have built on top of it.

Then treat the built result as a design review rather than as a QA sign-off, because the last ten percent of fidelity is where design intent is most often lost and least often noticed. Compare the built screen against the spec, state by state, at each viewport, with real content. Where they differ, decide which is right rather than which is intended — a spec that the platform cannot deliver is a spec that should change, and the change belongs in the spec rather than in a workaround nobody documented. Then feed the differences back into the system, because the third time a specific screen produces the same discrepancy is a system problem and not a screen problem.

/* Acceptance criteria: checkable by a developer, verifiable by a designer,
   and sufficient to settle an argument without a meeting. */
const ACCEPTANCE = {
  states: [
    { name: 'loading',       check: 'skeleton mirrors the final row count; aria-busy on the region' },
    { name: 'empty-true',    check: 'three-part empty state; never the filtered copy' },
    { name: 'empty-filtered',check: 'names the filter count; primary action clears the filters' },
    { name: 'error',         check: 'what / why / what-to-do; dataSafe present; role="alert"' },
    { name: 'partial-success', check: 'count headline, failures listed, retry targets only the failures' },
    { name: 'permission-denied', check: 'read-only mode with an explanation; already-made edits are not lost' },
  ],

  // in the spec rather than in a later audit, because a screen built without
  // these cannot be fixed by an audit without rebuilding parts of it
  accessibility: [
    'keyboard order matches the visual order; no positive tabindex',
    'a visible focus indicator on every interactive element, inset against overflow:hidden',
    'an accessible name on every control, from the visible label where there is one',
    'text contrast 4.5:1; non-text and UI edges 3:1',
    'asynchronous updates go to a polite live region; errors to role="alert"',
    'focus moves into an opened dialog and returns to the trigger on close',
    'a layout table is marked presentational; a data table has th and scope',
    // the criteria also settle the recurring "is this acceptable" argument,
    // which is a design decision and belongs in the document
    settles: 'any question about whether an interaction is acceptable',
  ],

  // rules, not frames: three screenshots describe what you drew and leave
  // every question between them open
  responsive: {
    minWidth: 320,
    breakpoints: { belowMd: 'table becomes cards; the identifier and one value stay visible without interaction',
                  belowSm: 'the filter row becomes a sheet' },
    firstToDrop: 'the third-lowest-priority column',
    mustNot: 'horizontal scroll on a data table at any width',
    orderingRule: 'content order is the same at every width, so a stacked layout reads in document order',
  },

  // the most predictable source of late-stage defects: zero and null are
  // rendered identically by almost every default implementation
  data: {
    null:   { render: 'an em dash, with an accessible name saying "not available"',
              never: 'a blank cell, which reads as an oversight' },
    zero:   { render: '0', note: 'never the null treatment: zero is a value and null is an absence' },
    missing:{ render: 'the field omitted', note: 'rather than shown empty' },
    large:  { render: 'abbreviated in summaries only, never in a value that gets compared',
              example: '1.24k in a card, 1,240 in a table that is sorted numerically' },
    date:   { render: 'absolute with a timezone on hover; relative in narrative contexts',
              never: '"Invalid Date" for a value that was never set' },
  },

  // content rules: two words now, a layout bug later, when four other people
  // have built on top of it
  content: {
    minLength: 3, maxLength: 48, sampleReal: 'not "Lorem ipsum" and not "John Smith"',
    testWith: ['a hyphen and an apostrophe', 'a 48-character string', 'a value in a script the layout does not accommodate'],
    translate: { mustTranslate: 'anything a user reads',
                 mustNotTranslate: ['brand names', 'codes', 'currency symbols chosen by locale'],
                 mustNotBreak: ['units', 'short codes', 'email addresses'] },
  },

  // the last 10% of fidelity is where intent is most often lost, and it is a
  // design review rather than a QA sign-off
  reviewOfBuilt: {
    compare: 'built screen against the spec, state by state, at each viewport, with real content',
    onDifference: 'decide which is right, not which was intended; a spec the platform cannot deliver is a spec that changes',
    whereChangeGoes: 'into the spec, never into an undocumented workaround',
    // the third time a screen produces the same discrepancy is a system problem
    feedbackRule: 'a repeated discrepancy goes back into the system, not into the next brief',
  },
};

/* One source of truth for tokens, and the pipeline that makes it true. */
const TOKENS = {
  source: 'design tokens, versioned in version control',
  build: ['tokens.json (source of truth)', 'CSS custom properties', 'TS types / Swift / Kotlin accessors',
          'Figma variables, generated rather than hand-maintained'],
  // the failure this prevents: the design file and the code each having
  // their own value, discovered during implementation
  rule: 'a token is defined once and generated everywhere; a value that exists only in a design file is a value that will not match',
  naming: { semantic: ['surface', 'text-primary', 'border-strong'], never: ['blue-500'],
            why: 'semantic names survive a theme change; literal names become a lie the moment a mode exists' },
};

The most useful single question in this relationship is "what has been the most expensive design you have ever received?", and the answer is almost always the same two things: unspecified states, and content that was never designed. Real strings at real lengths, in every language you support, in the states the feature can reach. A design that works with "John Smith" and fails with a name containing a hyphen and an apostrophe has not specified content, and that is the finding a developer will make alone on a Friday.

/* The handoff spec. Everything in "states" is a decision; a decision nobody
   made is a decision a developer makes alone at 5pm on a Friday. */
const HANDOFF = {
  feature: 'checkout, single page',
  version: 'v3, in version control like code',
  designer: 'AM', owners: { design: 'AM', system: 'shared design systems team' },

  delivered: [
    'the flow map, with every branch named',
    'every screen in every state, as components rather than as notes',
    'content: real strings at real lengths, in all nine supported languages',
    'motion: duration and curve, not adjectives',
    'the data contract: what the component needs, and what it does when it is absent',
  ],

  // the two answers to "what was the most expensive design you received"
  states: [
    { name: 'loading',      provided: 'skeleton component, mirrors the layout' },
    { name: 'empty-true',   provided: 'three-part empty state component' },
    { name: 'empty-filtered', provided: 'separate component; never reuse empty-true here' },
    { name: 'error',        provided: 'what / why / what-to-do, plus dataSafe' },
    { name: 'partial-success', provided: 'count headline, failures listed, retry only the failures' },
    { name: 'permission-denied', provided: 'read-only with an explanation' },
    { name: 'offline',      provided: 'pending count per object, honest labels' },
    { name: 'long-content', provided: 'truncation rule, title attribute, detail page fallback' },
    { name: 'rtl',          provided: 'the layout mirrors; numbers stay ltr inside it' },
  ],

  motion: [
    { what: 'row entrance', durationMs: 180, curve: 'ease-out', allowed: ['opacity', 'transform'] },
    { what: 'summary expand', durationMs: 250, curve: 'ease-in-out', allowed: ['opacity', 'transform'] },
    // and the constraint, given at the same time as the values, because it
    // is the thing that decides whether a frame budget is met
    forbidden: ['width', 'height', 'top', 'left', 'box-shadow'],
    why: 'each forces layout or paint every frame, and drops frames on low-end devices',
    reducedMotion: 'fade or instant; never a transform, never a shimmer',
  ],

  // three tiers, and the surprising category named
  cost: {
    cheap: 'layout, colour, spacing',
    moderate: 'a new component with its states, in the system',
    expensive: [
      'anything needing real data rather than fixtures',
      'a list over ~200 rows: virtualisation, and a design decision about row height',
      'a chart: bespoke or a library, both with real-world edge cases',
      'anything with offline behaviour or a permissions model',
      'a dropdown with server-side search: debounce, cancellation, empty and error states',
    ],
    looksCheapButIsNot: ['a table of 200 rows', 'a progress bar with an unknown total',
                         'a dropdown with 5,000 options', 'anything whose width is driven by its content'],
  },

  // the system, and the point about it being co-owned
  designSystem: {
    rule: 'reuse; a bespoke control is a component somebody must maintain forever',
    newComponent: 'a request to a team with evidence, not a file in your own library',
    governance: 'versioned in version control, changes reviewed like code, named owners outside the design team',
    onSystemChange: 'consumers are notified deliberately, because "four products need updating" must be a sent message',
  },
};

19.4 Presenting to stakeholders who don’t care about pixels

Presenting to stakeholders who do not care about pixels means leading with the problem rather than the mockup. State the user need, the business context, and the evidence, then offer two or three choices with their real costs and trade-offs. Frame the review as decisions about outcomes, not taste. Keep a recorded clip of a real user struggling, because a minute of someone trying finishes more arguments than any slide deck.

Getting a decision rather than an approval

Lead with the problem, and let the screens be evidence rather than the subject. The order that works is the user need, the size of it, the business context, and only then what you propose — and the reason is that every slide of interface shown before the problem is established is a slide on which the room is being asked to evaluate a designer's taste, which is the one thing they are least qualified and most opinionated about. "Twelve percent of users abandon checkout at the shipping step" is a fact they can act on; a screenshot of the step is evidence for the fact and should appear in support of it, not before it.

Then bring the clip. A forty-five second recording of a real person stuck at exactly the step being changed is the most efficient artefact available in this situation, because it removes the need to argue about the premise. Almost every disagreement in a design review is really a disagreement about whether the problem is real and whether it matters, and a video ends that argument in a way a chart cannot — it is also the only artefact in the room that a sceptical executive cannot reinterpret, since they can see the person's face at the moment they give up. Edit it: start a few seconds after the pause becomes visible so the room already knows what is happening, and cut everything that is not the hesitation.

Bring choices, not a single proposal, and bring a recommendation. One option is a request for approval, and approval is passive: it can be given, deferred indefinitely, or never mentioned again. Three options with real costs is a request for a decision, and a decision is active — it has to be made, it has an owner, and it has a date. Two is usually enough, three at most, and each must have an honest cost: a sprint count, a date, and the risk you are accepting. An option whose cost is not stated is not really an option, and a room that knows this will pick the one whose cost is vaguest.

Be precise about uncertainty rather than confident about it, because a stakeholder who understands the uncertainty can weigh it while one handed false precision will discount everything else you say later. Give a range, state the assumption that produced it, and say what would make it wrong. "Between four and nine percent, assuming the current mix of traffic holds; if the campaign changes the mix it will be at the low end" is a sentence a finance partner can act on, and it is more persuasive than a single number precisely because it can be checked.

Put the decision at the top of the agenda with the deadline in the invite, and frame the meeting as a decision about outcomes rather than a review of work. "We are asking which of two options to build by 14 April" is a different meeting from "here is the checkout redesign". Reviews that are framed as presentations produce agreement in the room and no decision afterwards, which is the specific failure mode this whole approach exists to prevent.

Then write the one-line decision after each meeting and circulate it immediately, with the rationale attached. In a week the decision will be reopened by somebody who was not in the room or has forgotten it, and the rationale is the only thing that can settle it without a second meeting. Put the date in it, so a decision nobody acted on is visibly nobody's fault and gets noticed — that is the whole mechanism, and it costs one paragraph.

The four arguments that recur, and how each one ends

"It is too expensive" is a budget conversation wearing a design costume, and the way to answer it is to put the cost on the scale next to the cost of not doing it. 412 users a week is a number that can be priced in a way a sprint estimate cannot be argued with, and the framing that works is comparing against an alternative rather than defending your own — the cost of shipping nothing, which is a cost the room already accepts as zero because nothing is happening. Where the money genuinely is not available, the useful move is to propose the smallest version that tests the assumption rather than to defend the full one.

"The evidence is not strong enough" is usually right and should be treated as such, because it is the objection a designer is most tempted to argue with and least equipped to win. The productive version of it names the specific gap: which cohort, which segment, how many sessions. That converts a general doubt into one more measurement with a date, which is a thing to do rather than a thing to argue about. Presenting evidence as complete when it is not is the failure that produces this objection in the first place, and the habit of stating assumptions and what would falsify them is what prevents it.

"We tried this and it failed" is the objection most often raised and most often resolvable, because it is a question about a specific past attempt whose circumstances are usually knowable. What was different — the audience, the traffic source, the state of the product, the price at the time, who ran it — is findable, and finding it either explains the failure or reveals a genuine repeat. The version of this that is difficult is when nobody can find the previous attempt, which usually means there was no previous attempt and the memory is a story about a different change.

"It does not look like the other products" is a consistency argument and it is about risk rather than taste: the room is expressing a fear that an unfamiliar screen will confuse customers or support staff. Answer it with evidence about comprehension rather than with a mockup, and never by designing towards the least novel option, because the argument would then be lost and the next change would face the same one. Say what will be measured after launch, which converts an argument about risk into a commitment to find out.

Then the part most guidance leaves out: saying no and staying alive. The right outcome is not always the proposal being accepted, and a stakeholder who has been overridden once by good evidence will find a way to override you later on worse evidence. When you disagree, say so, put the reasoning in writing, offer to be told what would change your mind, and commit to measuring the outcome afterwards — including your own. That is the only version of pushback that preserves the relationship, and it is also the version that produces honest post-launch learning instead of a quiet relitigation.

Keep a rhythm, because decisions that are never revisited drift and decisions that are revisited weekly never settle. Monthly is enough for most of this: what we decided, what we measured, what has changed, and one decision to close. It also produces the record that makes the next argument shorter, because the reasoning is written down and dated rather than remembered, and a decision reopened after a month is settled by its own record rather than by whoever is most senior in the room.

/* The recurring objections, with the answer that actually ends each one. */
const OBJECTIONS = [
  {
    objection: 'it is too expensive',
    reallyAbout: 'budget, not design',
    answer: { do: 'put both costs on the scale: the work, and the cost of shipping nothing',
              number: '412 users a week, priced', // a sprint estimate cannot be argued with; an abandonment can
              ifNoMoney: 'propose the smallest version that tests the assumption, rather than defending the full one' },
    never: 'arguing about whether the estimate is accurate',
  },
  {
    objection: 'the evidence is not strong enough',
    reallyAbout: 'doubt, and usually the right doubt',
    answer: { do: 'ask which cohort, which segment, how many sessions',
              convertTo: 'one more measurement with a date - a thing to do rather than a thing to argue about' },
    // the habit that prevents this objection: state assumptions and what
    // would falsify them, so the evidence is never presented as complete
    never: 'arguing with the doubt; it is usually correct',
  },
  {
    objection: 'we tried this and it failed',
    reallyAbout: 'a specific past attempt with knowable circumstances',
    answer: { ask: 'what was different: audience, traffic source, product state, price, who ran it',
              outcomes: ['it explains the failure', 'it was a genuine repeat, which is a different conversation'],
              hardCase: 'nobody can find the previous attempt, which usually means there was no previous attempt' },
  },
  {
    objection: 'it does not look like the other products',
    reallyAbout: 'risk: an unfamiliar screen confusing customers or support staff',
    answer: { do: 'evidence about comprehension, not a mockup',
              commitTo: 'what will be measured after launch, which converts a risk argument into a commitment to find out' },
    // the mistake: designing towards the least novel option, which wins the
    // argument and guarantees the same one next change
    never: 'making it look like the other products',
  },
];

/* Saying no, and staying alive. A stakeholder overridden once by good
   evidence will override you later on worse evidence. */
const DISAGREEMENT = {
  steps: [
    { say: 'I disagree, and here is why', inWriting: true },
    { say: 'here is what would change my mind', inWriting: true, why: 'it converts a disagreement into a falsifiable position' },
    { say: 'I will measure the outcome afterwards, including my own prediction', why: 'honest learning rather than quiet relitigation' },
  ],
  goal: 'preserve the relationship, not win the meeting',
  predicts: 'you will be wrong sometimes; the prediction on record is what makes that recoverable',
};

/* The decision record. One paragraph, same day, with the date - an
   unexecuted decision is nobody's fault until the date is visible. */
const DECISION_LOG = {
  date: '2026-03-11',
  decision: 'build option A: shipping in the cart summary before the address step',
  rationale: 'reversible, one sprint, does not trade conversion for margin; B needed a margin analysis we do not have',
  owner: 'checkout team',
  due: '2026-04-14',
  // and what will be measured, committed to in advance
  measureAfter: { primary: 'checkout completion, 7-day rolling, by source',
                  guardrail: 'shipping cost per order, and refund rate at 30 days',
                  reviewAt: '2026-05-14' },
  predicted: '+3 to +6% completion',
  // the sentence that makes an unexecuted decision visible to anybody looking
  notExecutedBy: 'the date above. Nobody is at fault until it passes, and then everybody is.',
};

Watch for the objection that is really about something else, because it is nearly always about budget, risk, or whether the problem is big enough rather than about the design. Name the real concern and answer it, or say plainly that you will come back with the answer by a specific date. Treating a budget objection as a design preference is the most common way a good proposal dies, because the room then argues about the thing nobody was actually asking about while the thing they were asking about goes unanswered.

/* The brief. Order matters: problem, size, context, then the screens as
   evidence. An interface slide shown before the problem is established is a
   request to evaluate a designer's taste. */
const BRIEF = {
  title: 'Checkout: what to do about the shipping step',
  ask: 'a decision between two options, by 14 April',
  // not "here is the redesign" - the framing is what makes it a decision
  notAsk: 'approval of a single proposed design',

  problem: {
    statement: '12% of users abandon at the shipping step',
    size: { abandonedUsers: 412, window: '7d', share: 0.12, trend: 'flat for 3 weeks' },
    concentratedIn: 'paid search, new users - which is a promise mismatch as much as a design problem',
    // and this is what stops the redesign being the answer to a traffic problem
    check: 'is the source mix representative? if not, fix the acquisition message first',
  },

  evidence: [
    { type: 'video', seconds: 45, what: 'a participant re-reading the delivery row twice before giving up',
      why: 'removes the need to argue about whether the problem is real; ends more arguments than any chart',
      edit: 'start after the pause is already visible; cut everything that is not the hesitation' },
    { type: 'analytics', what: 'exit rate by step, by source, by device, 7-day rolling' },
    { type: 'qualitative', what: '7 moderated sessions at that step; the shipping row is read as a price, not a choice' },
  ],

  options: [
    { name: 'A', change: 'show shipping in the cart summary before the address step, and put the price on each delivery row',
      cost: 'about 1 sprint', expected: '+3 to +6% checkout completion', risk: 'low', affectsNothingElse: true },
    { name: 'B', change: 'replace the delivery selector with a precomputed "cheapest" badge and a details table',
      cost: '2 sprints', expected: '+5 to +9%', risk: 'medium: it can raise shipping cost per order', needs: 'a margin analysis' },
    { name: 'do nothing', change: 'leave the flow as it is',
      cost: 'zero', expected: '412 users a week continue to leave', risk: 'compounding, and the funnel keeps its worst step' },
    // and the option whose cost is not stated is not an option
  ],
  recommendation: 'A, because it is reversible, cheaper, and does not trade conversion for margin',
  uncertainty: { range: '3-6%', assumption: 'current traffic mix holds',
                 falsifiedIf: 'the campaign changes the mix; expect the low end' },

  agenda: { topItem: 'the decision', deadline: 'in the invite', not: 'a review of the work' },
  after: { write: 'the one-line decision with its rationale and date, circulated same day',
           why: 'in a week somebody who was not in the room will reopen it, and the rationale is what settles it' },
  // and the objection that is really about something else
  realObjections: {
    budget:   'answer it or commit to a date for the answer; never treat it as a design preference',
    risk:     'name the specific risk and its mitigation, or say you will come back with it',
    notBigEnough: 'size it in users and in money; "how many" ends this argument faster than any chart',
  },
};
  • Lead with the problem, not the mock: "12% of users abandon checkout at shipping." Show screens as evidence, not art.
  • Decision-ready framing: "Option A (cost ~1 sprint, +8% expected) vs B (2 sprints, riskier)" — choices, not presentations.
  • Write the one-line decision after each meeting; hold everyone to its rationale later.

The single most reliable stakeholder trick: bring the video. A 45-second clip of a real user stuck at the exact step being "fixed" ends more arguments than any deck has ever settled.

Exercises 19

  1. Roleplay critique: give feedback on 3 real designs using observation+impact+suggestion only.
  2. Prepare a 3-slide stakeholder brief for a redesign decision with choices + trade-offs.
  3. Ask one developer the question "what’s the most expensive design you’ve ever received?" — write the lesson.

20 · Ethics & Dark Patterns

Ethics in design begins with recognizing dark patterns, manipulation dressed as design that spends durable user trust for short-term conversion. This chapter builds your eye for spotting deceptive patterns so you can name them and draw your own line before a deadline forces the choice. The counter-practice is replacing each manipulation with an honest equivalent that keeps the business goal intact. Deceptive UX is a liability that compounds as word spreads.

20.1 Dark pattern taxonomy (spot them on sight)20.2 The ethical line (draw it before you need it)20.3 Privacy is a UX feature20.4 Persuasion that builds trust, not panic

The same psychology that makes products delightful can make them predatory. This chapter is the accountability course: recognizing manipulation, your professional line, and the honest practices that also — as it happens — build durable products.

20.1 Dark pattern taxonomy (spot them on sight)

A dark pattern taxonomy is your pattern-spotting flashcards: the classic families include deception, forced action, misdirection, obstruction, and social pressure. For every pattern you find, name the exploit it uses on the user, then replace it with an honest equivalent that keeps the business goal intact. Naming converts a vague discomfort into a specific, addressable design problem. Review any new flow against the taxonomy before shipping it.

PatternExploitHonest replacement
Confirmshaming ("No thanks, I’m poor")guilt to force consentplain neutral options
Roach motel (easy in, hard out)subscription gone on autopilotcancel = subscribe flow, any time
Hidden costs revealed latesunk-cost at checkouttotal upfront, breaks explained
Forced action ("sign up to read")data as toll boothvalue+data explained at the moment
Trick wording (opt-out pre-ticked)defaults the wrong wayopt-in, choice framing, easy undo
Bait & switch (premium surprise)feature moved behind paywallclear pricing and plan matrix

The five families behind the list

The table above is a spotting sheet, and it works because each row is really one of five mechanisms wearing different clothes. Coercion applies pressure to act now — the fake countdown, the limited-stock badge, the trial that is about to expire. It exploits the fact that a decision made under time pressure is a decision nobody reviews, and the person who benefits from it is you. Obfuscation hides the term that matters: the price revealed at the last step, the renewal buried in a paragraph, the unsubscribe link in 40-point grey text at the bottom of 4,000 words. It exploits the fact that almost nobody reads to the end when they have already decided to buy, so the hidden term is read by almost nobody. Friction asymmetry makes it easy to enter and hard to leave, and it is the mechanism behind the roach motel, the twelve-tap unsubscribe, the plan that takes one click to downgrade and six to cancel. Presumptive defaults does not need persuasion at all: a pre-ticked box is a decision made on the user's behalf, and defaults are the single most powerful and least examined lever in interface design. And synthetic social proof manufactures the evidence a decision would need if the user were thinking — "1,284 people are viewing this", "only 3 left".

Separating the mechanism from the instance matters for two reasons. It makes the review repeatable: you cannot enumerate every dark pattern because new ones are invented monthly, but you can ask five questions and cover the space. And it makes the fix reusable: an honest replacement for a fake countdown is not "remove the timer" but "tell the user the real deadline, once, in advance", which also fixes the real-deadline case. The taxonomy will grow. The five questions do not need to.

Five questions that cover the whole space

One. Does the design require the user to fail in order for them to benefit? If the product's advantage comes from something the user will not notice, will not understand, or cannot act on, then the advantage is being taken rather than offered. This catches the forced-action toll booth, the trick wording, and the mislabelled button — three patterns that look nothing alike and share one structure.

Two. Does it exploit a bias the user cannot detect? Anchoring, loss aversion, the default, social proof, the sunk cost, the scarcity heuristic: each is a real cognitive shortcut and each is useful, and the ethical question is not whether you used it but whether you used it in a way that would disappear under inspection. A default that is right for the great majority of users is service. A default chosen because it converts is extraction wearing the same clothes, and the difference is visible in one question — would you choose this default if you could not measure the conversion lift?

Three. Would the user feel deceived if they understood exactly how it works? This is the court-room test with the grandmother attached, and it is the most reliable of the five because it does not require you to know the law or the intent. It requires only that you can explain the mechanism accurately and then honestly ask whether the user would have gone along. Fake scarcity passes this for nobody, because "only 3 left" that is always "only 3 left" is a lie told in pixels.

Four. Is the exit as easy as the entry? Reversibility is a structural property and it is measurable without any ethical reasoning at all: count the steps to start and count the steps to stop, and the gap is the pattern. One click to subscribe and six to cancel is a roach motel. A trial that converts in one tap and cancels in one tap is honest even though nobody likes it. The same asymmetry appears in free trials that are hard to leave, in account deletion hidden behind a phone call, and in the "are you sure you want to leave" interstitial with a red button — which is a dark pattern for the specific reason that it is deliberately difficult.

Five. Who bears the cost, who gets the benefit, and how long does the cost last? Dark patterns are almost always asymmetric: a small, immediate, certain benefit to the business against a small, delayed, uncertain cost to the user. That asymmetry is not inherently wrong — every paid product has it — but it becomes a pattern when the delay is engineered so the user will not pay it. A three-year commitment hidden at checkout is the archetype: the benefit is immediate and legible, the cost is far away and hidden, and the user's only route to avoiding it is to notice something the design has made hard to notice.

The five questions are worth keeping as a standing review ritual rather than a one-off exercise, because dark patterns arrive through accumulation rather than through a decision. Nobody decides to build a roach motel. A billing page gets a confirmation interstitial, then a retention offer, then a second interstitial, then a "are you really sure" — and at that point the flow is a pattern that no individual review would have blocked. So the review runs per flow, not per change, and it runs on the flow as it now exists rather than on the diff, which means it belongs to somebody who did not write the flow and who is not being measured on its conversion.

/* The five mechanisms. The taxonomy grows every quarter; these do not. */
const MECHANISM = {
  coercion:      { exploit: 'decisions made under time pressure are not reviewed',
                   instances: ['fake countdown', 'limited-stock badge', 'expiring trial', 'flashy urgency banner'],
                   honestVersion: 'state the real deadline once, in advance, and honour it' },
  obfuscation:   { exploit: 'nobody reads past the point where they have decided to buy',
                   instances: ['price revealed at the last step', 'renewal inside a paragraph',
                               'unsubscribe link in 40-point grey', 'fees in a linked PDF'],
                   honestVersion: 'the total, the term, and the exit on one screen before the commitment' },
  frictionAsymmetry: { exploit: 'entry is optimised and exit is neglected, because exit is not measured',
                   instances: ['easy in, hard out', '12-tap unsubscribe', 'one click to downgrade, six to cancel',
                               'deletion behind a phone call'],
                   honestVersion: 'the exit costs the same number of steps as the entry' },
  presumptiveDefaults: { exploit: 'a default is a decision made on the user behalf',
                   instances: ['pre-ticked consent', 'pre-selected add-on', 'auto-renew on by default',
                               'newsletter on, notifications on, marketing bundled'],
                   honestVersion: 'opt-in, with the default chosen because it is right for most users' },
  syntheticProof: { exploit: 'manufactures the evidence a thinking user would demand',
                   instances: ['only 3 left', '1,284 people viewing', '47 people bought this today',
                               'reviews that are not reviews'],
                   honestVersion: 'real counts, real time window, and a real link to the full list' },
};

/* The five questions. Ask all five; a pattern only needs to fail one. */
const QUESTIONS = [
  { q: 'Does the design require the user to fail in order for them to benefit?',
    catches: ['forced action', 'trick wording', 'mislabelled buttons', 'hidden costs'],
    rationale: 'if the advantage comes from something the user will not notice, it is being taken rather than offered' },
  { q: 'Does it exploit a bias the user cannot detect?',
    test: 'would you choose this default if you could not measure the conversion lift?',
    distinction: 'a default right for most users is service; a default chosen because it converts is extraction' },
  { q: 'Would the user feel deceived if they understood exactly how it works?',
    name: 'the court-room test',
    why: 'it needs no knowledge of the law or of intent - only an accurate explanation and an honest question' },
  { q: 'Is the exit as easy as the entry?',
    measure: 'count the steps to start, count the steps to stop, the gap is the pattern',
    note: 'measurable without any ethical reasoning, which is why it survives a deadline' },
  { q: 'Who bears the cost, who gets the benefit, how long does the cost last?',
    archetype: 'a three-year commitment hidden at checkout: immediate legible benefit, distant hidden cost',
    note: 'asymmetry is not itself wrong; an engineered delay so the cost is never paid is' },
];

/* The review has to be about the flow as it exists, not about the diff,
   because dark patterns arrive by accumulation. */
const REVIEW_RITUAL = {
  scope: 'the whole flow as it now exists, on every platform it exists on',
  frequency: 'per flow, and again whenever it is touched',
  reviewer: 'somebody who did not write it and who is not measured on its conversion',
  failureMode: 'no individual review would have blocked any one of the steps; the pattern is the accumulation',
  exampleSequence: ['a confirmation interstitial', 'then a retention offer',
                     'then a second interstitial', 'then are-you-really-sure',
                     'at which point the flow is a pattern and each step was defensible alone'],
};

The harm ledger, which is the part that belongs in a review

Naming a pattern is necessary and not sufficient, because a name does not tell you how much damage is being done or to whom, and those two numbers are what make a priority argument winnable. So write the ledger: what is the cost, who bears it, how immediate it is, how long it persists, whether it is reversible, and how many people are exposed. A fake countdown costs a user a few seconds of irritation and a business a fraction of a percent of trust. A hidden three-year commitment costs a real amount of money, arrives in year three, and is not reversible at all — and only one of those two would survive a room full of stakeholders who can see the number.

The asymmetry is the thing to make explicit, because it is what lets the pattern keep working. Almost every dark pattern is a transaction in which the business receives a small, immediate, certain, measurable benefit and the user incurs a small, delayed, uncertain, unmeasured cost. That shape is stable over time because the benefit compounds for the business and the cost accumulates for the user, so at any given quarter the pattern still looks correct from inside. The design question that breaks the loop is to ask what the pattern is worth if you assume the cost is eventually paid — usually by churn, by a refund, by a bad review, or by a chargeback — and to compare that against the lift. The honest version of that comparison is uncomfortable only because the delayed costs are rarely attributed to the pattern that caused them; they land in a different metric, in a different quarter, owned by somebody else.

The second column of the ledger is reversibility, and it deserves more weight than it usually gets. A reversible harm is an annoyance. An irreversible one is a claim on the user's future that they did not knowingly grant — the three-year contract, the data collected for a purpose that no longer exists, the habit formed by a streak that the user would not choose to have. Irreversibility is also what regulators have been moving toward: the direction of travel in every major jurisdiction is toward consent that is specific, revocable, and as easy to withdraw as to give, which is precisely the definition of an error you can take back.

/* The ledger. Naming a pattern does not tell you how much damage is done or
   to whom, and those two numbers are what make a priority argument winnable. */
function harmLedger(pattern) {
  return {
    cost: pattern.whatTheUserLoses,
    bearer: pattern.whoBearsIt,
    immediacy: pattern.userNoticesInSeconds ? 'immediate' : 'delayed',
    persistence: pattern.reversible ? 'reversible' : 'an irreversible claim on the users future',
    exposure: pattern.percentOfSessionsAffected,
    asymmetry: {
      business:  'small, immediate, certain, measurable',
      user:      'small, delayed, uncertain, unmeasured',
      whyStable: 'the benefit compounds for the business and the cost accumulates for the user, so each quarter still looks correct from inside',
      breakIt:   'ask what the pattern is worth if you assume the cost is eventually paid - by churn, refund, bad review, chargeback',
      whyHard:   'delayed costs are attributed to a different metric, in a different quarter, owned by somebody else',
    },
    comparison: [
      { pattern: 'fake countdown',            cost: 'a few seconds of irritation', persists: 'reversible',  priority: 'low' },
      { pattern: 'confirmshaming',            cost: 'a decision made out of embarrassment, often correct', persists: 'reversible', priority: 'medium' },
      { pattern: 'hidden three-year term',     cost: 'real money, arriving in year three', persists: 'irreversible', priority: 'high' },
      { pattern: 'data kept for a dead purpose', cost: 'a claim on the users future they did not knowingly grant', persists: 'irreversible', priority: 'high' },
    ],
  };
}

/* The screens nobody reviews, which is where the leverage is. */
const UNREVIEWED = [
  'the billing portal', 'the account deletion page', 'failed-payment recovery',
  'the second cancellation attempt', 'the consent screen', 'the export tool',
  'the empty state after deleting everything', 'the downgrade path',
];
// a review that only covers signup and checkout has reviewed the two flows
// with the most competition and the least harm

/* How a pattern becomes invisible: introduced, normalised, defended. */
const LIFECYCLE = [
  { stage: 'introduced',  by: 'somebody with a number attached, deliberately' },
  { stage: 'normalised',  by: 'a second person who assumes it was already reviewed' },
  { stage: 'defended',    by: 'a third who cites the first as precedent' },
];
// by the time it appears as one of five options it is invisible to the team,
// because it is familiar - and familiarity is how a decision stops being one

When the pattern is the business model

Some patterns are not a designer's decision at all. Subscription churn targets, retention offers, pre-ticked consent on a partner integration, a cancellation flow engineered by a growth team three departments away: these arrive as a requirement rather than as an idea, and the designer's only real options are to execute it, to escalate, or to leave. It is worth being concrete about the middle option, because it is the one that is almost never attempted and it is usually available.

Escalate with a proposal attached. "This would be a dark pattern" is a position and it loses. "Here is the same metric achieved honestly, here is the lift I expect, here is what it costs us, here is the risk if we do not" is a proposal and it can be accepted. In practice the honest replacement is often not worse for the business than people assume, and the pitch that works is the one that names the second-order number: the complaint rate, the refund rate, the chargeback rate, the credibility of every other prompt from this brand. A pattern that teaches users that this product's messages are unreliable has a cost that is legible to nobody in the room and enormous over eighteen months.

Name the pattern in the artefact. Whatever channel, the issue should say what the pattern is, name the taxonomy entry, and link the honest alternative. Not as an accusation — as a heading. This costs nothing, and it does three things: it gives the decision-maker the option of overriding knowingly, it creates a record for the day the complaint arrives, and it makes the pattern discussable by the next person who touches the flow. The people who are not named are the ones who lose the argument later.

Escalate once, then commit or leave. Repeated objection without a proposal is obstruction and it will be characterised as such, correctly. So object once, in writing, with an alternative; if the decision goes against you, then it is somebody else's decision with their name on it — and your remaining job is to make sure the flow is at least legible, which is a much lower bar than ethical and the one thing entirely within your control. Save the analytics, note the date, and revisit it at the point where the delayed cost lands.

And then the case where the answer is genuinely no. Where the business model depends on the pattern — where the revenue model is a hidden commitment or an undeclared renewal or a data sale dressed as a feature — redesigning the flow honestly is not a design task, it is a business-model change, and no amount of design quality gets you there. That is worth saying plainly because the alternative is spending months polishing an honest version of a flow that will be relitigated at the next board meeting. If the business model requires the pattern, the conversation that has to happen is about the business model, and the most useful thing you can do is bring the ledger: the current cost of the pattern in the numbers the business actually reports on, and what the same revenue looks like with the honest version. That is a business conversation with data in it, and it is a very different position from a design objection that nobody can price.

Two more things about spotting them. First, the ones you will not see are the ones in screens nobody looks at, and those are exactly where the leverage is: the billing portal, the account deletion page, the failed-payment recovery, the second cancellation attempt, the consent screen, the export tool. A pattern review that only covers the signup and checkout path has reviewed the two flows with the most competition and the least harm. Second, dark patterns have a lifecycle. They are introduced deliberately by somebody with a number attached, then normalised by a second person who assumes it was reviewed, then defended by a third who cites the first as precedent. By the time it appears in a list of options, the pattern is invisible to the team precisely because it is familiar, and familiarity is the mechanism by which a decision stops being a decision.

20.2 The ethical line (draw it before you need it)

The ethical line is easiest to draw before a deadline turns it into a judgment call under pressure. Adopt a few blunt tests you can run on any sticky decision: would you be comfortable explaining this to the user face to face, and would they feel cheated if they understood how it works? If a pattern depends on the user not knowing how it works, it has drifted from nudge to manipulation. Write the rule down so it survives a tough quarter.

  • Mechanism vs manipulation: "nudge" is honest when the user’s stated goal is served; it’s a trap when it serves only yours.
  • The choke test: if the pattern would embarrass you explaining it to your grandmother — or a court — change it.
  • Diffusion of responsibility is real: a dark pattern shipped by committee is still a dark pattern. Say it once, clearly, in writing.

Why the line has to be written before you need it
