Almost every line-crossing is not a character flaw discovered under pressure; it is a principle that was never made specific, meeting a quarter with a number attached. Values are useless in that moment because they are stated in the vocabulary of the person who wrote them, and the person asking you to cross the line is not going to use that vocabulary — they will use the vocabulary of the quarter. So the line has to exist in advance, in writing, in the vocabulary of the specific decision, and it has to be short enough that it can be read in the meeting where it is needed.

That is the whole design problem here, and it is a design problem because the failure mode is the same one as any interface: a rule that cannot be applied to a concrete case has not been specified. "Be honest" cannot be applied. "The total price, including shipping and any recurring charge, is stated on one screen before the user commits" can be applied, and it can fail or pass, and it can be checked afterwards by somebody who was not in the room. The test of whether a rule is written properly is whether a colleague could use it to veto a design without needing to ask you what you meant.

So write the rules as sentences about interfaces, not as sentences about virtue. Each one names a screen, a moment, and a state. Each one is falsifiable. And each one is short — five rules is a workable number, and twelve is not, because a checklist nobody remembers is a checklist that never runs. The blunt tests from the list above belong in it as the last-resort version: the face-to-face test and the court test, because both are cheap and both work on a case your rules did not anticipate, which is the only situation in which you will actually need them.

/* The line, written in the vocabulary of the decision rather than of virtue.
   Each rule names a screen, a moment and a state, and is falsifiable. */
const LINE = [
  { rule: 'The total price a user will pay, including shipping, tax and any recurring charge, is stated on one screen before the user commits.',
    falsifiableBy: 'checkout screenshot review',
    why: 'the alternative is a price that is technically disclosed and practically discovered' },
  { rule: 'Cancelling takes no more steps than subscribing.',
    falsifiableBy: 'count both, on every platform',
    why: 'measurable with no ethical judgement required, which is why it survives a deadline' },
  { rule: 'Nothing is pre-ticked. Every optional thing starts off.',
    falsifiableBy: 'settings screenshot',
    why: 'a default is a decision made on the users behalf' },
  { rule: 'Any countdown or stock count shown to a user is true, updates, and is visible without scrolling or hovering.',
    falsifiableBy: 'ask the engineering owner for the source of the number',
    why: 'the falsification test is one question to one person' },
  { rule: 'Deletion and export are available from the same screen as the data, without contacting support.',
    falsifiableBy: 'attempt it with a clean account',
    why: 'a feature behind a ticket queue is a feature that does not exist for a churning user' },
];

/* Last resort, for the case your rules did not anticipate. */
const LAST_RESORT = {
  faceToFace: 'would you be comfortable explaining this decision to the user, looking at them, in person?',
  court: 'would you be comfortable describing it in a deposition?',
  whyTheseWork: 'they need no knowledge of the law, no policy document, and no argument about intent',
};

/* Diffusion of responsibility: say it once, clearly, in writing. */
function whoseDecision(design) {
  const asked = design.approvers.filter((a) => a.sawThisSpecificIssue);
  const presentAtApproval = design.approvers.filter((a) => a.approved);
  if (asked.length === 0) return { status: 'nobody was asked',
    consequence: 'nobody owns it, so the default is yes and silence reads as consent' };
  if (asked.length < presentAtApproval.length) {
    return { status: 'some of the approvers never saw the specific issue',
      consequence: 'the absent approver is the shield, which is how committee decisions become irreversible' };
  }
  return { status: 'the people who saw it all approved it',
    consequence: 'at this point the resistance is not that nobody noticed' };
}

Drawing the line under pressure

The line gets tested in a meeting, and the shape of that meeting is predictable. Someone will frame it as a trade — "if we do not do this we will miss the quarter", "the legal team has signed it", "everyone else does it". Three responses, in order. The trade framing deserves the actual question back: what is the size of the lift, and what is the plan if we do not do it? A large lift with no alternative plan is usually an argument for trying something else, and a small lift is usually not worth the cost of being the kind of product that does it. The legal signature deserves a second signature: legal reviews whether something is defensible, and defensible is a lower bar than right, and you are the one who will be asked what the pattern was meant to do.

The "everyone else does it" argument is the one that has actually ended careers, and the reason is worth stating plainly: a pattern you introduce alone is attributable to you, and a pattern the industry has normalised is invisible. So the strategic move is to be visibly the second person rather than the first. Say the pattern's name out loud in the meeting, write it in the issue, attach the screenshot. It is still a decision you are making, but it is now a decision the record shows you made consciously, which is a very different position from the one where the diff shows you made it quietly.

Then the part nobody tells you: you will sometimes be overruled, and there is a way to be overruled that you can live with and a way that you cannot. What you can live with is a decision that is recorded, has a name on it, and is one you raised in writing. What you cannot live with is making it silently, because the day it becomes visible — in a complaint, a screenshot, a regulator, a journalist — it will be visible as yours and the fact that you objected privately helps you not at all. So the practical instruction is to object in writing in the issue, once, clearly, with the pattern named, and then to decide whether the cost of being associated with the thing is one you are willing to pay. That last sentence is the honest one, and it is the only part of this that requires a person's judgment about their own situation rather than a rule.

Running it when it costs you something

The tests are cheap and the situation is not, so it is worth separating the two. The tests are: could you say this out loud to the user, and could you describe it in writing to a regulator. Both are self-administered and both take about ten seconds. The situation is: somebody with authority over your compensation has asked you for this by Friday, and saying no has a cost you can estimate and I cannot. What follows is not advice about whether to say no; it is the shape of the decision, because the shape is at least partly knowable.

Start by separating the four things people conflate in the meeting. The legal question — is this defensible — has an owner, and it is not you, and legal signing off tells you something about regulatory exposure rather than about whether the pattern is right, because the two standards are genuinely different and defensible is lower. The business question — what is the lift, and what is the plan if we do not — is usually unanswerable in the room, and asking for it in writing is the most effective single move available to you, because a request with no answer is itself an answer. The design question — is there an honest version that hits the number — is the one you are uniquely qualified to answer, and answering it converts the meeting from an argument about ethics into an argument about options. The personal question — what does this cost me, and what am I willing to pay — is yours alone and should be made last, with real information.

Then the escalation ladder, in order, because most people skip straight to the top and lose the two rungs that would have helped. One: ask for the honest alternative to be tried, with a defined success measure and a date. Two: ask for the lift to be stated with its second-order costs attached, and put them in writing. Three: name the pattern in the artefact, using the taxonomy, with the replacement attached. Four: escalate above the requester, without drama, with the four lines of record attached — decision, who asked, what you said, what was decided. Five: decline, explicitly, in the same channel. Rung four is the one that is skipped and it is the one that changes outcomes most often, because most requests do not survive being described accurately to somebody who was not in the room.

What not to do is important enough to name. Do not go quiet — a quiet objection is indistinguishable from not caring, and the flow ships anyway with no record. Do not comply and complain privately later — that is the version that makes the outcome bad and leaves you associated with it. Do not refuse without a replacement, because a refusal with no alternative is a demand for someone else to do your work, and it is usually the reason refusals fail. And do not make it personal in the channel; the disagreement is with a decision, not with a person, and staying on the first is what makes it survivable.

/* Four questions that arrive tangled in one meeting. Untangle them first;
   each has a different owner and a different standard. */
const FOUR_QUESTIONS = {
  legal:   { asks: 'is this defensible?', owner: 'legal',
             tellsYou: 'regulatory exposure',
             doesNotTellYou: 'whether the pattern is right - defensible is a lower bar than right',
             note: 'legal signing off is not design sign-off' },
  business:{ asks: 'what is the lift, and what is the plan if we do not?',
             usuallyUnanswerableInTheRoom: true,
             bestMove: 'ask for it in writing',
             why: 'a request with no answer is itself an answer' },
  design:  { asks: 'is there an honest version that hits the number?',
             owner: 'you, uniquely',
             effect: 'converts the meeting from an argument about ethics into an argument about options' },
  personal:{ asks: 'what does this cost me, and what am I willing to pay?',
             owner: 'you alone', when: 'last, and with real information' },
};

/* The ladder. Most people skip to the top and lose the rungs that help. */
const LADDER = [
  { rung: 1, do: 'ask for the honest alternative to be tried, with a success measure and a date' },
  { rung: 2, do: 'ask for the lift to be stated with its second-order costs attached, in writing',
                 secondOrder: ['complaint rate', 'refund rate', 'chargeback rate',
                               'the credibility of every other prompt from this brand'] },
  { rung: 3, do: 'name the pattern in the artefact, using the taxonomy, with the replacement attached',
                 creates: ['the option of overriding knowingly', 'a record for the day it surfaces', 'a precedent that is discussable'] },
  { rung: 4, do: 'escalate above the requester, with the four-line record attached, without drama',
                 whyItMatters: 'most requests do not survive being described accurately to somebody who was not in the room' },
  { rung: 5, do: 'decline explicitly, in the same channel' },
];

/* What not to do. Each of these is the reason refusals usually fail. */
const DONT = [
  { dont: 'go quiet',            because: 'a quiet objection is indistinguishable from not caring; the flow ships with no record' },
  { dont: 'comply and complain privately later', because: 'the outcome is bad and you are associated with it' },
  { dont: 'refuse without a replacement', because: 'it reads as a demand that someone else do your work' },
  { dont: 'make it personal in the channel', because: 'the disagreement is with a decision, not a person, and staying on the first is what makes it survivable' },
];

/* The four-line record. Four lines per decision. */
function recordLine(entry) {
  return [entry.date, entry.decision, entry.whoAsked, entry.youSaid, entry.outcome].join(' | ');
}
// it is the difference between having a position and having a recollection of one

Two things that make the position easier in practice, and neither is about courage. The first is having done the work in advance: a written line, a taxonomy, a ledger, and a named honest alternative for the specific pattern in the room. Every one of those converts a difficult conversation into a review of a document, and a review of a document is a conversation almost anybody can have. The second is having allies, and the honest version of that is not a coalition against management — it is one other person who has read your line and agrees with it. One is enough for the first time; a single named second reader changes the meeting from an individual objection into a documented position that somebody else has verified.

And then the case for accepting that you will sometimes lose, which is worth stating because the expectation of never losing is what makes people lose badly. People who treat every decision as a referendum on their integrity take every outcome personally, and a person who has decided that they will be overruled on this one thing and overruled on that one thing is defending an undefendable position. The version that works is narrower: the version where you insist only on being able to see, name and record, and you accept that visibility is not going to be granted in every case. That is an achievable standard, it is one you can keep for years without burning out, and — because the pattern you named keeps operating and its costs keep accruing — it is also the standard that leaves you in a position when the complaint arrives.

Finally, keep the record. A short log — decision, who asked, what you said, what was decided, when — is the difference between having a position and having a recollection of one. It costs four lines per decision. It is what makes an issue about the pattern three months later answerable, and it is the reason people who keep one can talk about their judgment with confidence while people who do not have to describe it in the present tense.

20.3 Privacy is a UX feature

Privacy becomes a product feature rather than a legal chore when it is visible and controllable. Show users plainly what data is collected and why, make settings easy to find and change, and turn consent into clear, default-respecting choices the user can actually understand. Handle people’s data the way you would want your own handled, and consent becomes clarity. Transparency is a trust and retention feature competitors cannot copy.

// Privacy as product value:
- collect MINIMUM: purpose-labeled, retention-limited (Ch.32 GDPR habits stay)
- consent = informed (plain language), individual (per purpose), revocable
  (delete + download = supported forever, not a ticket queue)
- transparent UI: "we store your location for X — here, on-device, delete
  anytime" beats burying the legal doc
- if you wouldn't show it to a court, don't show it in a consent screen

Designing consent somebody can actually give

The consent problem is usually described as a legal problem and it is really an interface problem, because consent has three properties that are all interface properties. It must be informed, which means the person understands what they are agreeing to — and the test is whether they could describe it back to you afterwards, which almost nobody can after reading a paragraph of dense legal text. It must be granular, which means consent is collected per purpose rather than bundled, because a single "I agree to the terms and the privacy policy and the cookie policy" is not three consents, it is one signature over three documents, and treating it as consent is what regulators have spent the last decade correcting. And it must be revocable, which means withdrawing it is as easy as giving it — one screen, not a ticket, not an email, not a phone call, and as close to instant as deleting data allows.

The legal direction has now travelled in all the major jurisdictions and it always arrives at the same three design requirements, which is worth knowing because it means the ethical version and the compliant version are the same design here. Consent must be freely given, which in practice means no pre-ticked boxes and no bundling. It must be specific and informed, which means per-purpose, in plain language, at the moment the purpose is relevant rather than at signup. And withdrawal must be as easy as giving it, which means the same number of steps and the same place. A product that treats those as three good ideas rather than three legal obligations has a compliance advantage as a side effect, and a product that waits for the regulator gets the compliance at three times the cost and none of the trust.

The plain-language rewrite is the highest-leverage work in this chapter and it is unglamorous. Take every purpose and write it as a sentence a person would say to a friend: not "we may share your data with selected third-party partners for cross-context behavioural advertising" but "we use your activity to show you ads on other websites". Then say why, in one clause. Then say what the user gets, because a purpose with no benefit to the person is a purpose nobody consents to and nobody should. Then, on the same screen, the control. The test for the finished screen is that a person can answer four questions from it without scrolling: what are you collecting, why, who else sees it, and how do I stop.

/* Consent has three properties, and all three are interface properties. */
const CONSENT = {
  informed:   { test: 'could the person describe it back to you an hour later?',
                failure: 'a dense paragraph, which is understood by nobody and signed by everybody' },
  granular:   { requirement: 'one decision per purpose, not one signature over three documents',
                failure: 'a single agree-to-terms-and-privacy-and-cookies checkbox',
                note: 'bundling is the most common form of unobtainable consent and it is the one that gets enforced' },
  revocable:  { requirement: 'as easy to withdraw as to give it - same number of steps, same place',
                reality: 'one screen, not a ticket, not an email, not a phone call' },
};

/* The plain-language rewrite. Four questions answerable without scrolling. */
function consentCopy(purpose) {
  return {
    what: 'a sentence a person would say to a friend - no legal nouns, no "we may",
    why: 'one clause, in the same sentence',
    benefit: 'because a purpose with no benefit to the person is a purpose nobody consents to',
    control: 'on the same screen, not three clicks away',
    before: 'we may share your data with selected third-party partners for cross-context behavioural advertising',
    after:  'we use your activity to show you ads on other websites, so they fit what you are looking for',
    test: 'four answerable without scrolling: what are you collecting, why, who else sees it, and how do I stop',
  };
}

/* Data minimisation as a design constraint, decided at design time rather
   than audited afterwards. */
const MINIMISATION = {
  questionsAtDesignTime: ['does this feature need this field, or this resolution, or this timestamp?',
                          'what is the coarsest value that answers the question?',
                          'if we deleted it tomorrow, which feature breaks and would anyone notice?',
                          'on whose device could this live instead of ours?'],
  outcomes: ['fewer fields means fewer validation errors and shorter forms',
             'less collection means a smaller breach surface and a smaller legal surface',
             'on-device by default means no transfer, no processor list, no disclosure at all'],
  default: 'on-device or computed-at-the-edge wherever the feature allows, because a thing never sent cannot be leaked',
  reviewTrigger: 'any new field, any new vendor, any new purpose - each one reopens the question',
};

Making privacy visible is what converts it into a feature

Nobody is persuaded by a privacy policy. People are persuaded by seeing a thing work. So the privacy work that changes behaviour is the work that makes the data visible to its owner: an export that produces a file in seconds, a deletion that removes everything including backups within a stated window, a settings screen that shows what is stored and where, and a history of what changed. Each of these is a small amount of engineering and a large amount of trust, and the reason competitors cannot copy them easily is that they are all things a company that does not want to delete cannot easily build.

The three that matter most, in order. First, deletion that actually deletes, with a stated window that includes backups — a delete button that leaves the data in backups forever is a delete button that is a lie, and one that is technically defensible in a document and obvious to anybody who asks. Second, export in a usable format, because data portability is the exit that makes a lock honest; a product people cannot leave is a product people do not trust, whatever the terms say. Third, a settings surface reachable in two clicks from anywhere, because consent is only real if it is reversible at the moment it matters and nobody visits a settings page in a good mood.

Then the design of the consent moment itself, which is where most products still get it wrong for a reason that is not malice: consent is asked at the moment of least attention. Signup is the worst possible moment to ask for five permissions, because the user has a goal that is not yours and every question is a cost on the path. Ask for what the current action needs — the camera for the camera feature, the location for the thing that is genuinely local — and ask for the rest later, in context, at the moment its value is visible. Permission requests get a much higher acceptance rate when they arrive with an explanation of what the person is about to get, and a much lower abandonment rate on the screen that asked for them, because the question no longer sits between the user and their goal.

Finally, the part that is a design metric rather than a compliance one: measure it. Consent acceptance by purpose tells you which purposes are unclear, because a purpose nobody accepts is one nobody understood. Settings visits after a privacy email tell you whether the disclosure was alarming in the right way. Deletion-request volume tells you something about trust that no survey will. And the number worth putting in front of a business audience is the one that is hardest to argue with: the rate at which people who exercised a control — exported, deleted, opted out — stay. Controls that work are usually followed by retention rather than churn, because the alternative to exercising a control is leaving, and leaving is what a person was considering.

A privacy checklist recast as product value: collect the minimum, keep consent plain and revocable, and show honest UI. Notice the court-room test that decides what belongs in a consent screen.

20.4 Persuasion that builds trust, not panic

Honest persuasion converts more slowly but it repeats, and retention is where products win. Replace scarcity timers and shame with truthful framing, genuine social proof, and gentle reminders that respect the user’s pace. A customer who buys because they trust the pattern stays and returns, while one who is panicked into a purchase leaves and tells others. Measure repurchase and referral, not just conversion spikes.

The durable alternative: honest social proof (real counts), genuinely useful defaults, auto-renewals you auto-remind about ("your trial converts Tuesday — cancel in one tap"). Products built without dark patterns convert slower but repeat — and (measurably) earn retention nobody can switch away from.

A persuasion inventory, with the honest version of each lever

Every honest persuasion technique has a dark twin, and the twin is not a different technique — it is the same technique with the truth removed. That is worth stating plainly because it means the choice is not between persuasion and honesty; it is between which of your levers you are willing to have inspected. Scarcity is persuasive and honest when the thing is genuinely scarce. Social proof is persuasive and honest when the numbers are real, the time window is stated, and the people are actually people. Urgency is honest when the deadline is real and told once in advance. Loss aversion is honest when the loss is real and the framing does not invent it. Defaults are honest when they are the right choice for most users rather than the profitable one for you. Streaks and variable rewards are honest when the reward is real rather than a random number that happens to pay out.

So the inventory is the work: write down every persuasive device currently in the product, and for each one mark whether a user who fully understood it would still be content. That last column is the whole test and it takes a sentence per device. A device that fails it is not necessarily removed — some are legitimately matters of legal disclosure or platform constraint — but each one that fails should be a decision somebody made deliberately, with the reason written down, rather than a default that arrived with a component.

/* Every lever, with its honest and its dark twin. Not two techniques - the
   same technique with the truth removed. */
const LEVERS = [
  { lever: 'scarcity',            honest: 'the thing is genuinely scarce, and it says so',
    dark: 'a countdown that resets, or a stock count that is a constant',
    test: 'would a user who understood this still be content?' },
  { lever: 'urgency',             honest: 'the deadline is real and told once, in advance',
    dark: 'pressure manufactured so the decision is not reviewed',
    test: 'is there a real date behind this, and did we tell them when it was?' },
  { lever: 'social proof',        honest: 'real counts, real window, real people, link to the rest',
    dark: 'unfalsifiable counts with no time window; reviews that are not reviews',
    test: 'can the user check it, and would it survive checking?' },
  { lever: 'loss aversion',       honest: 'the loss is real and does not outweigh the alternative',
    dark: 'inventing a loss - "your cart expires" for a cart that did not exist',
    test: 'if the user does nothing, do they actually lose something?' },
  { lever: 'defaults',            honest: 'the right choice for most users',
    dark: 'the profitable choice, pre-ticked, for everyone',
    test: 'would this default be the same if we could not measure the lift?' },
  { lever: 'streaks',             honest: 'a real habit the user wanted to build',
    dark: 'a streak that breaks for reasons outside the users control, then is sold to recover it',
    test: 'does the streak serve the user goal or the retention goal?' },
  { lever: 'variable rewards',    honest: 'the reward is real, and the bad outcome is disclosed',
    dark: 'a random number tuned to be near-miss occasionally close',
    test: 'is the distribution disclosed in the interface?' },
  { lever: 'free trial',          honest: 'a real trial, the conversion date stated in advance, one-tap cancel',
    dark: 'a trial that converts silently, is hard to leave, and warns you after the charge',
    note: 'the honest version is: your trial converts Tuesday - cancel in one tap' },
];

/* The inventory as a working artefact. One row per device currently shipped. */
function inventoryAudit(product) {
  return product.persuasiveDevices.map((d) => {
    const understood = d.userWouldUnderstand ? 'somewhat' : 'no';
    return { device: d.where, mechanism: d.lever || 'unclassified',
             verifiableByUser: !!(d.source || d.trueCount),
             understood,
             honest: understood === 'yes' && d.trueCount !== false,
             action: 'remove, or write down why it stays' };
  });
}
// a device that fails is not necessarily removed, but it should be a decision
// somebody made deliberately rather than a default that arrived with a component

What urgency is actually for

Urgency exists because a considered decision and an impulsive decision are worth different amounts of money, and because most products are competing for a decision the user was not planning to make on that day. That is not an argument for manufacturing pressure — it is an argument for finding the real deadline and stating it. Almost every honest product has one: a price that genuinely changes, a cohort that genuinely closes, an inventory that genuinely runs out, a release that genuinely happens on Tuesday, an offer that genuinely expires. The honest version of urgency is the real date, given in advance, once, in plain language, with no repetition. Users act on a real deadline at a perfectly good rate, and they respond better to it than to a fake one because the fake one has to be disbelieved and disbelieving costs effort.

The false economy here is worth spelling out because it is usually argued at board level. A fake urgency device produces a measurable lift this week. Within a quarter, some fraction of the users it worked on either learned to disbelieve the product's claims, waited for the next countdown, or told somebody. Each of those has a cost that appears somewhere other than the experiment's metric: a lower baseline conversion on the honest prompts, a higher refund rate, a worse review section, more support contacts about the "sale that was not real". The product is now running a promotion that permanently reduces the value of its own promotions. You can measure this, and the measurement is worth putting next to the lift, because the argument that survives scrutiny is always the one with both numbers on the same line.

The mechanics of a good reminder cadence are unglamorous and they are the whole job. Tell people at signup exactly when their trial converts and what it will cost. Remind once, a few days before, with the amount and the date and a one-tap cancel. Remind again on the day, only if they have not acted. Then never again without a real change. No countdown on a page that is merely open. No "we miss you" escalation with invented scarcity. No surprise charge followed by an apology email — that is the pattern that generates a complaint and a chargeback rather than a renewal, and a chargeback is materially worse for a merchant than a lost customer.

Measuring the honest version

The conversation above always ends at the same place: the honest version has a slower, smaller, less legible lift. So the work is to find a metric that captures the difference, and there are four, in increasing order of how long they take to become real and decreasing order of how easy they are to measure.

Refund and chargeback rate is the fastest and the most damning, because it is a direct financial cost that is already counted somewhere else in the business. A flow that uses a hidden term produces refunds; a flow that produces surprise charges produces chargebacks, and a chargeback is materially worse for a merchant than a lost customer because it carries a fixed fee, it is counted against the merchant, and it can affect the account. Nobody has to accept an argument about trust here — the number is already being tracked and it moves.

Repeat purchase and second-year revenue share is the one that decides the argument. A cohort acquired with manufactured urgency converts well in week one and repeats at a fraction of the rate of a cohort acquired with a true deadline, because a person who was rushed into something they did not choose has a relationship with the product that begins as a debt. Revenue from the second year is the number that prices this honestly, and it is also the number that is hardest to present, because it is far from the decision. Presenting it as a projection with the assumptions written out is acceptable and normal; presenting it as a certainty is not.

Referral rate is the one that surprises people most, because referral is the metric least affected by the tactics that produce the shortest-term lift. A product that surprises its users does not get recommended by them, and the recommendation is the mechanism by which a product's acquisition cost falls over time. Where the team can see referrals at all, the honest version usually shows up there first.

Control exercisers who stayed is the most specific and the most persuasive, because it uses the data privacy work already produced. People who exported their data, deleted their account, changed a privacy setting, or cancelled a subscription: what fraction of them were still active a month later? The intuition is that exercising a control is the alternative to leaving, and a person who successfully exercised a control has had the objection resolved rather than suppressed. If that cohort retains at the same rate as everyone else, then the honest version costs nothing in retention — and the honest version was never actually the risky option, only the slower one.

/* Four metrics, in increasing time-to-real and decreasing ease to measure. */
const HONEST_METRICS = [
  { metric: 'refund and chargeback rate', horizon: 'weeks', alreadyTrackedSomewhereElse: true,
    why: 'a flow that uses a hidden term produces refunds; surprise charges produce chargebacks',
    force: 'a chargeback carries a fixed fee, counts against the merchant, and can affect the account',
    close: 'nobody has to accept an argument about trust - the number is already being tracked and it moves' },

  { metric: 'repeat purchase and second-year revenue share', horizon: 'quarters', decidesTheArgument: true,
    mechanism: 'a cohort acquired with manufactured urgency converts well in week one and repeats far worse, because the relationship began as a debt',
    presentAs: 'a projection with the assumptions written out - normal, and defensible',
    neverPresentAs: 'a certainty' },

  { metric: 'referral rate', horizon: 'quarters', surpriseFactor: 'high',
    why: 'referral is the metric least affected by the tactics that produce the shortest-term lift',
    mechanism: 'a product that surprises its users does not get recommended by them, and referral is what lowers acquisition cost over time' },

  { metric: 'control exercisers who stayed', horizon: 'weeks to a quarter', mostPersuasive: true,
    cohort: ['exported their data', 'deleted their account', 'changed a privacy setting', 'cancelled and stayed'],
    hypothesis: 'exercising a control is the alternative to leaving - resolve the objection rather than suppress it',
    ifTrue: 'the honest version costs nothing in retention',
    therefore: 'the honest version was never the risky option, only the slower one' },
];

/* The thirty-day test. What a fair trial of the honest version looks like,
   stated before it runs, so the result cannot be reinterpreted after. */
const THIRTY_DAYS = {
  before: ['one metric with a stated direction and magnitude',
           'one guardrail that must not get worse - refund rate',
           'the date the decision is made, whatever the numbers say'],
  during: ['weekly, on the same day, without re-deciding the test'],
  ifLiftMeetsTarget: 'ship it, and put the second-order numbers in the release note too',
  ifLiftMisses: 'the honest version has a price; state it and stop arguing about ethics and start arguing about size',
};

/* The test that gets forgotten: does the honest version lose revenue that
   the dishonest version was only borrowing from the future? */
function borrowedVersusEarned({ dishonest, honest, horizonMonths }) {
  const immediateLift = dishonest.monthOne - honest.monthOne;
  const atHorizon = honest.horizonRevenue - dishonest.horizonRevenue;
  return { immediateLift, atHorizon,
    readsAsAMistake: horizonMonths < 12 && atHorizon <= 0,
    correctReading: atHorizon > 0
      ? 'the dishonest version borrowed this month\'s revenue from a later month it will never see'
      : 'the honest version is genuinely worse here, and that is a finding worth publishing' };
}

The trust flywheel, and what breaks it

Honesty compounds through a specific mechanism rather than as a general good feeling, and it is worth being able to describe it in one sentence for internal audiences: a user who has been told the truth once has a much lower cost to trusting you the next time, so every honest message is more effective than it was, and every dishonest one spends a balance that took a long time to build. That is why the dishonest version has a decreasing marginal return — the same countdown works on a new user and works less well on the fifth, and the product has to keep inventing new pressure to maintain the same output. The honest version has an increasing one, because credibility is exactly the asset that makes communication cheaper.

The mechanism is visible in three specific places. Promotional email: a list that you sent a real deadline to and were right about is a list that opens. Pricing changes: a company that once published a price rise with a real explanation can do it again, and a company that once hid a term can never do it without a fight. And support: the cost of a support contact is a number the business tracks, and the honest version of a product generates measurably fewer of them, because there is nothing to ask about. None of this is a moral argument, and that is the point — the flywheel exists whether or not anybody is persuaded by ethics.

What breaks it is almost always one specific thing rather than a general decay, and the four candidates are worth naming because they are each fixable. A single incident, which is why the response matters more than the fault: an honest acknowledgement of a mistake and a clear statement of what changed recovers most of the trust, and a defensive one loses the rest of it permanently, because the defensive response teaches every other user that the next admission will also be denied. A change in ownership, where the new owners inherit credibility they did not earn and then spend it on something the old owners would not have done. A shift in the metric, where the team starts being measured on something the flywheel does not affect — and the honest answer here is that the flywheel has to be defended in the metric review, in advance, or it will be optimised out within two quarters. And finally, a genuine strategic change of direction, which is legitimate and still needs to be disclosed honestly, because a change announced as something else is a lie whatever the intent behind it.

Finally, the last practical thing, and it is the thing to do on Monday. Pick the single flow with the highest stakes — usually cancellation, billing, or the account deletion page — and rewrite it honestly, keeping the same business goal, and measure it. Do not start with the loudest device in the product. Start with the one a person would be angriest about, because that flow has the most complaints, the most support contacts, and the clearest internal sponsor: the person who is currently answering those tickets. That person has a reason to want the fix that no one has for a countdown timer, and the rewrite is small enough to finish in a week. One honest flow, measured, with the second-order numbers reported — and that is a repeatable precedent rather than a position.

And the thing that makes honesty commercially defensible rather than merely virtuous: the metrics that reward honesty are slower to move and much larger in aggregate. Repeat purchase, referral rate, refund rate, support contacts per user, the share of revenue from users in their second year, and — the one that settles most arguments — the rate at which people who exercised a control stayed. A product that stops surprising its users stops generating complaints, stops generating refunds, and starts generating recommendations, and the compounding is not subtle at a two-year horizon. It is invisible at a six-week horizon, which is the horizon most decisions are made on, and that mismatch is the actual reason honest design loses internal arguments rather than any defect in it.

Exercises 20

  1. Identify and photograph/archive one real dark pattern; rewrite it honestly with the same business goal.
  2. Draft your "ethical line" in 5 sentences and post it in your workspace.
  3. Review YOUR last shipped flow against the taxonomy table. Grade it. Fix anything scored.

21 · Career, Portfolio & Hiring

Career, portfolio, and hiring are where design talent turns into a job and a trajectory, and your career lands on evidence, not intentions. The portfolio demonstrates decision-making rather than decoration, and interviews test increasingly deeper judgment as you climb in seniority. Prepare process stories backed by research, shipped work, and measurable results. Keep learning in motion and make your work visible enough that hiring managers can find it.

21.1 A portfolio that demonstrates process (not screens)21.2 Choosing and building your 3 cases21.3 The interview circuit by seniority21.4 Staying in motion (read, ship, test, teach)21.5 Visibility: notes, talks & decision logs

The final chapter is about the actual job market: what a competitive portfolio proves, how interviews work at different career stages, and how to keep learning after the course ends.

21.1 A portfolio that demonstrates process (not screens)

A portfolio that demonstrates process treats screens as decoration and process as the signal reviewers actually read. For each project, show the question, the research, the iterations, the decision reasoning, and the measurable result, because hiring managers are looking for judgment rather than images. Include failures and pivots to prove honesty. The goal is a reviewer finishing with a clear picture of how you think.

// The case study skeleton that gets calls back:
// 1 Problem & user evidence (the research, with quotes + data)
// 2 Your role & constraints (team, timeline, tools — honest)
// 3 The process cliff: frames → insights → options → chosen
// 4 The solution (mockups/screens) + states + motion
// 5 Result: what was tested/mesured & what you'd change NEXT
// Screens without 1&5 are decoration. 2-4 strong cases > a gallery
// of 30. Show judgment about what didn't work — that's the signal.

What a reviewer actually reads, and in what order

A hiring manager spends about ninety seconds on a case before deciding to read more, and the ninety seconds are not distributed the way designers assume. They are roughly: is this about a real problem (10 s), do they seem to have worked on it rather than been handed it (15 s), is there any evidence in here (10 s), is there a decision with a reason attached (20 s), and is there an outcome (10 s) — with the remaining time spent on the first image. Which means the screens are read late and briefly, and the order that works is the reverse of the order people build in: the problem and the result first, the screens as proof, the process in between as the argument that connects them.

So the case opens with the problem, in the user's words, with a number attached, and with a stake: what it cost the business and who was hurting. Then the constraint that made the problem hard — team size, timeline, the platform, the regulation, the thing that was already shipped and could not be changed. That paragraph is doing more work than it appears to, because it is the evidence that you worked on it rather than were handed it; a designer who cannot name a real constraint either had none or did not notice, and both readings are bad. Then the decision, stated as a decision: here were the options, here is what we chose, here is what ruled the others out. Then the evidence that the choice was right, or that it was not. Then the outcome, with a number, and then what you would do differently, which is the section that most people leave out and which is the section that most reliably distinguishes a senior candidate from a junior one.

Format, length, and the two delivery problems

Length: a case is 900–1,400 words plus six to twelve images, and a case study longer than that is not being read at length — it is being skimmed, which means the first screen and the last screen carry all of the weight and everything in the middle is decoration. Three cases, so a portfolio someone will actually finish is about twelve pages of reading. The corollary is that every screenshot must earn its place: if an image does not support a sentence in the argument, cut it, because the visual density that feels like evidence to you reads as volume to a reviewer and volume is read as padding.

Format: the PDF is still the expected default and it is a genuinely bad one — it cannot be skimmed, it does not reflow, it does not load on a phone in a waiting room, and it will not be read by anyone who prefers reading on screen. A site is better and has its own failure: it renders beautifully at full width, so a reviewer scrolling fast sees the images at enormous size and no words at all, because the text is the part they skip. The fix for the site is to constrain the reading column, put the argument above the fold of each section, and never let an image be the first thing on a section. The best answer is both, plus a two-page PDF for the meeting: because the meeting is often the only place a portfolio gets looked at, and a link somebody has to load is a link that sometimes does not get loaded.

Two accessibility points that are worth more than they cost. If you produce a PDF, it needs real text, not images of text — a recruiter on a phone with a screen reader will abandon a scanned portfolio in under a minute, and there is no recovering from that. And captions: video is increasingly expected in process-heavy work, and a muted autoplaying clip with no captions is a portfolio that says something about how you think about access. Both are five minutes of work and both are read as evidence of professional maturity by exactly the reviewers who would otherwise be left wondering.

Building the wall of evidence

The difference between a case that reads as rigorous and one that reads as a narrative is usually one artefact: a wall of evidence assembled before the writing started. Four things in it, and they are cheap to gather while the project is live and impossible to recreate a year later. The raw quotes with timestamps. The sessions conducted, with dates, so the count is verifiable and the coverage is visible. The numbers, at whatever resolution exists, including the ones that went the wrong way. And the decision points — the moments where something could have gone another way, with what was known at the time and not after.

That last item is the one nobody keeps and the one that carries a case. A decision log in its simplest form — a list of the five or six moments where the project turned, with the options that were live at that moment and the reason — is what a reviewer cannot reconstruct from the artefact and what a candidate almost never has. It also protects you against the reading where the outcome looks inevitable in retrospect, which is the single most common criticism of a portfolio: the reviewer cannot tell whether the work was difficult or whether the case was simply arranged so that the answer was obvious afterwards.

Gather it continuously and it costs nothing. The failure mode is doing it at portfolio time, at which point you have a finished project, no raw quotes, no session count, and only the numbers somebody remembered. So the practice is a weekly five-minute addition to a single file per project, and the discipline is that it must be added in the week it happens, because the version you could reconstruct in six months is a summary and a summary of your own work is marketing.

/* The wall of evidence. The difference between rigorous and narrative is
   usually one artefact, and it is impossible to recreate a year later. */
const WALL = {
  cheapWhileLive: true,
  impossibleLater: true,
  contents: [
    { what: 'raw quotes with timestamps', note: 'not paraphrases - a paraphrase already contains your interpretation' },
    { what: 'sessions conducted, with dates', why: 'the count becomes verifiable and the coverage becomes visible' },
    { what: 'numbers, at whatever resolution exists', mustInclude: 'the ones that went the wrong way' },
    { what: 'the decision points', mustInclude: 'what was known at the time, not after' },
  ],
  practice: { frequency: 'five minutes a week, one file per project',
              rule: 'added in the week it happens',
              failure: 'doing it at portfolio time, with no raw quotes and no session count - only the numbers somebody remembered' },
};

/* The item nobody keeps and the one that carries the case. */
const TURNING_POINTS = {
  what: 'the five or six moments where the project could have gone another way',
  each: { optionsLiveAtTheTime: [], knownThen: [], chosen: '', reason: '' },
  why: 'a reviewer cannot reconstruct this from the artefact, and almost no candidate has it',
  protectsAgainst: 'the reading where the outcome looks inevitable in retrospect - the most common criticism of a portfolio',
  diagnosis: 'if the reviewer cannot tell whether the work was difficult or the case was arranged so the answer was obvious afterwards',
  warning: 'a summary of your own work written six months later is marketing',
};

/* What each section is doing, and what it is not doing. The most common
   portfolio mistake is claiming a second role for every section. */
const CLAIM_DISCIPLINE = [
  { claim: 'user research', do: 'show the sessions, the counts and a quote that changed something',
       doNot: 'present a wall of insights with no decision downstream - that is research performed, not used' },
  { claim: 'systems thinking', do: 'show the constraint, the rule, and the thing you gave up to get it',
         doNot: 'show a component in isolation - the skill is the trade-off, not the artefact' },
  { claim: 'leadership', do: 'show a disagreement you resolved without authority, and what it cost you',
          doNot: 'show a consensus - nobody learns anything from a story where everyone agreed' },
  { claim: 'craft', do: 'show one decision about a detail and the rule behind it',
            doNot: 'show a screenshot gallery - craft is invisible in a gallery and visible in one explained detail' },
];

Then the failure modes, because they are specific and each is easy to check. The gallery: thirty screens with no argument, which reads as decoration because that is what it is. The agency showreel, where the work is the client's product and the thinking is not visible. The process theatre, where the research page shows a wall of quotes and no decision, which is worse than no research because it demonstrates that research was performed rather than used. The vanishing constraint, where every project was ideal except the one where the team and timeline were impossible. And the outcome gap: no number anywhere, which leaves the reviewer to assume there was no result and to be right.

/* The ninety seconds, and how they are actually spent. Not distributed the
   way designers assume - the screens are read late and briefly. */
const NINETY_SECONDS = [
  { seconds: 10, reading: 'is this about a real problem' },
  { seconds: 15, reading: 'do they seem to have worked on it rather than been handed it' },
  { seconds: 10, reading: 'is there any evidence in here' },
  { seconds: 20, reading: 'is there a decision with a reason attached' },
  { seconds: 10, reading: 'is there an outcome' },
  { remainder: 25, reading: 'the first image' },
];
// so the case opens with the problem and the result, and the screens are
// proof rather than the headline

/* The skeleton, in the order it should be read. */
const CASE_ORDER = [
  { part: 1, what: 'the problem, in the users words, with a number and a stake',
    mustContain: ['a quote', 'a cost', 'who was hurting'],
    why: 'first, because it is the only thing that earns the next ninety seconds' },
  { part: 2, what: 'the real constraint - team, timeline, platform, regulation, the thing already shipped',
    doesTheMostWork: true,
    why: 'it is the evidence you worked on it; no constraint named reads as either none or not noticed' },
  { part: 3, what: 'the decision, stated as a decision: the options, the choice, what ruled the others out',
    why: 'the whole reason the reviewer is still reading' },
  { part: 4, what: 'the evidence the choice was right, or that it was not' },
  { part: 5, what: 'the outcome with a number, then what you would do differently',
    why: 'the last section most people omit, and the one that most distinguishes senior from junior' },
];

/* Length and the corollary that follows from it. */
const FORMAT = {
  perCase: { words: '900 - 1400', images: '6 - 12' },
  portfolio: 'three cases, so about twelve pages of reading',
  corollary: 'every screenshot must earn its place - an image that supports no sentence is padding, and padding reads as volume',
  pdf:  { problem: 'cannot be skimmed, does not reflow, will not load on a phone in a waiting room',
          accessibility: 'real text, not images of text - a screen reader abandons it in under a minute',
          still: 'the expected default in the meeting itself' },
  site: { problem: 'renders at full width, so a fast scroller sees images and no words',
          fix: ['constrain the reading column', 'argument above the fold of every section', 'never let an image open a section'] },
  video: { problem: 'a muted autoplaying clip with no captions reads as indifference to access',
           fix: 'captions - five minutes of work, read as professional maturity' },
  both: 'plus a two-page PDF for the meeting, because a link somebody has to load is sometimes not loaded',
};

/* The specific failure modes, each with the check that catches it. */
const FAILURE_MODES = [
  { mode: 'the gallery',              looksLike: 'thirty screens with no argument', reveal: 'it is decoration, and it reads as decoration' },
  { mode: 'the agency showreel',      looksLike: 'beautiful screens, the thinking invisible', reveal: 'the work is the clients and the evidence is missing' },
  { mode: 'process theatre',          looksLike: 'a wall of quotes and no decision', reveal: 'worse than no research: it shows research performed, not used' },
  { mode: 'the vanishing constraint',  looksLike: 'every project was ideal', reveal: 'except the one where the team and timeline were impossible' },
  { mode: 'the outcome gap',          looksLike: 'no number anywhere', reveal: 'the reviewer concludes there was no result, and is right' },
];

The five-part case study skeleton that earns callbacks, front-loading research and honest constraints. Notice the rule that screens without problem and result are only decoration.

21.2 Choosing and building your 3 cases

Choosing three contrasting cases proves more than a large gallery, because each case type showcases a different skill. Pick one case that shows deep end-to-end product thinking, one that shows research changing direction with evidence, and one that shows execution quality and craft. For each, tell the story with context, decisions, and outcomes. Interviewers read for decision quality: why you did what you did.

Case typeProvesPick one you did…
Redesign of existing productresearch + reasoninga public app you used & analyzed
New feature from 0the full double diamonda problem you had compelling evidence for
Design-system/component workstructure + tokens + governancea pattern library you actually shipped to

Why three, and why they must contrast

Three is a practical number rather than a magic one, and it is derived from a constraint reviewers apply without stating: they are trying to build a model of how you think, and they need to see it applied under more than one set of circumstances. Two cases gives one shape and no evidence that the shape generalises; five gets skimmed, which is worse than three read properly. So pick three, and then make the pick do work by having them contrast — because contrast is what lets a reviewer infer a characteristic rather than observe a coincidence.

The contrast that matters is not aesthetic, it is about the axis each case proves on. One case should be depth: a single flow, end to end, where you owned the outcome and the decisions were consequential. One should be breadth or influence: research that changed the direction of something, a problem you found rather than one you were handed, a case where the visible output is a decision rather than a screen. And one should be systemic: tokens, a component library, a system that other people then used — which proves that you can build for other designers rather than only for yourself, and that is the single most common differentiator between a mid-level candidate and a senior one, because it is a different unit of work.

There is a fourth kind of case that people leave out and should not: the failure. A project where you were wrong, with what you believed, what the evidence said, and what you changed as a result. This is disproportionately persuasive for two reasons that are both about the reviewer's risk rather than about your honesty. First, most portfolios contain a claim they cannot verify, and a documented failure is a claim about your judgment that they can check against your own account of it — it is more credible than an unverified success because it costs you something to report. Second, a reviewer who is about to hire you is modelling how you will behave when you are wrong about something, and no success story answers that question.

Choosing what to show, and what to hide

The selection rule is evidence, not glamour: rank your candidate projects by the quality of the evidence you can put around the decision, not by how good the screenshots look or how big the company was. A small internal project with five sessions and a clean decision beats a flagship redesign with three slides, every time, and the reason is specific — the reviewer is trying to assess judgment, and judgment is only visible where there was a real choice with real alternatives. Projects with no choice in them — a spec handed to you, a pixel push on an existing design, a marketing page with a conversion target set by finance — are structurally incapable of demonstrating judgment, no matter how large they were.

The contrast matrix, and the gaps it exposes

Lay the three cases out as a matrix — cases across, competencies down — and mark each cell with the strength of the evidence you actually have. The output is immediately useful in two directions. The empty row tells you the competency you cannot currently claim, which is the more valuable half of the exercise because a portfolio that quietly leaves a row blank is one nobody asks about, and a portfolio that claims the row with thin evidence is one somebody asks about and you fail. And the three-full-cells column tells you which case is doing too much work, which is worth fixing by going deeper on a case that already has two competencies rather than by adding a fourth case.

The competencies worth using as rows are the ones interviewers actually ask about, and they are stable: comprehension of the user and the business, research judgement including knowing when to stop, framing and prioritisation, the ability to make and defend a decision under real constraint, systems thinking, execution and craft, and collaboration and influence without authority. Note that four of those seven are invisible in a screenshot, which is the structural reason portfolios from people with strong execution skills so often read as weak — the evidence they have is concentrated in the one row that shows up least.

For each cell, use a three-level mark and be honest about the middle. Strong means there is an artefact and a number. Partial means there is an artefact and a story. Absent means there is nothing, and the honest treatment of absent is to fix it before the interview rather than to hope nobody asks — and the fastest fix is usually not a new project but a section that was in the project you already have and was not written up, because most people under-report their own collaboration and craft.

/* The matrix. The empty row is the more valuable half of the exercise. */
function contrastMatrix(cases) {
  const COMPETENCIES = [
    'comprehension of the user and the business',
    'research judgement, including knowing when to stop',
    'framing and prioritisation',
    'making and defending a decision under real constraint',
    'systems thinking',
    'execution and craft',
    'collaboration and influence without authority',
  ];
  const rows = COMPETENCIES.map((c) => ({ competency: c,
    cells: cases.map((k) => ({ case: k, mark: strongestEvidenceYouActuallyHave(k, c) })) }));
  return { rows,
    emptyRows: rows.filter((r) => r.cells.every((c) => c.mark === 'absent')).map((r) => r.competency),
    overloadedColumns: cases.filter((k) => rows.filter((r) => r.cells.find((c) => c.case === k).mark === 'strong').length >= 2),
    note: 'overloaded columns mean the case is doing too much - go deeper on a case that already has two competencies rather than adding a fourth case' };
}

const MARK = {
  strong: 'there is an artefact and a number',
  partial: 'there is an artefact and a story',
  absent:  'nothing - fix it before the interview, do not hope nobody asks',
  honestTreatmentOfAbsent: 'the fastest fix is usually a section that was in the project you already have and was not written up',
  usuallyUnderReported: ['collaboration and influence without authority', 'execution and craft'],
  whyThisHappens: 'most people under-report their own collaboration and craft, because the work felt like coordination rather than design',
};

/* Four of seven competencies are invisible in a screenshot - which is the
   structural reason portfolios from strong executors read as weak. */
const INVISIBLE_IN_A_SCREENSHOT = ['the business', 'knowing when to stop', 'the constraint',
                                   'the trade-off', 'influence without authority'];

/* The quarter-hour red team. */
const RED_TEAM = [
  { minute: 0,  action: 'time the read', target: '90 seconds to the decision point' },
  { minute: 2,  action: 'cover the result and the constraint', then: 'can you still explain the case?' },
  { minute: 5,  action: 'ask the skeptic questions and write them down',
    skeptic: ['what did the user actually say?', 'what was the alternative?', 'who decided, and did they listen?',
              'would this work for a different user?', 'what is not shown here?'],
    note: 'the last question is the one that matters - a reviewer always asks it and the answer is rarely in the case' },
  { minute: 10, action: 'check it against the three cases: does the set prove a range, or one thing three times?' },
  { minute: 15, action: 'decide the three fixes, and fix them before the interview rather than during' },
];

Be more careful about what you leave in. The confidential constraint: if you worked under NDA, do not show the screen at all if it identifies the product — rebuild the case around the decision, the evidence and the outcome in words, with a generic or abstracted visual, and say plainly that the artefacts are obscured. A portfolio that shows an NDA-protected screen tells the reviewer you did not think about it; a portfolio that explains the constraint tells them you did. The unmeasurable outcome is the other one: if there was no result, say so and give the strongest available proxy with its limits stated — a task success rate, a support ticket count, a count of teams who adopted it, a first version of it that you then removed. An honest "there was no number, here is what I could observe instead" reads as competence; an invented number reads as a reason not to hire you.

/* Three cases, each proving a different axis. Contrast is what lets a
   reviewer infer a characteristic rather than observe a coincidence. */
const THREE = [
  { case: 'depth', proves: 'one flow, end to end, decisions were consequential',
    mustContain: ['the constraint', 'the option you rejected and why', 'a result'],
    ifYouHave: 'the flagship work, defended in depth' },
  { case: 'breadth', proves: 'research that changed direction; the visible output is a decision, not a screen',
    mustContain: ['the finding', 'what it overturned', 'who acted on it and what they did'],
    note: 'a problem you found rather than one you were handed - the rarest and the most persuasive' },
  { case: 'systemic', proves: 'you can build for other designers, not only for yourself',
    mustContain: ['adoption by name', 'a governance decision', 'what it cost other people'],
    differentiator: 'the most common separator between mid and senior, because it is a different unit of work' },
  { case: 'bonus - the failure', proves: 'how you behave when you are wrong',
    mustContain: ['what you believed', 'what the evidence said', 'what you changed'],
    whyItWorks: [
      'a documented failure is a claim they can check, and it costs you something to report',
      'a reviewer is modelling how you will behave when you are wrong; no success story answers that',
    ] },
];

/* Projects that cannot demonstrate judgment, however large they were. */
const CANNOT_DEMONSTRATE_JUDGMENT = [
  'a spec handed to you',
  'a pixel push on an existing design',
  'a marketing page with the conversion target set by finance',
];
// no choice means no visible decision means nothing to assess, no matter the scale

/* Selection by evidence quality, never by how the screenshots look. */
function rankCandidates(projects) {
  return projects
    .map((p) => ({ p,
      score: (p.realChoices ? 2 : 0) + (p.evidenceBehindDecision ? 2 : 0) +
             (p.outcomeObservable ? 1 : 0) + (p.constraintWasReal ? 1 : 0) }))   // glamour scores 0
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score);
}

/* The two things that quietly disqualify a case. */
const SELECTION_HAZARDS = {
  nda: { bad: 'showing the screen at all if it identifies the product',
         good: ['rebuild the case around the decision, evidence and outcome in words',
                'a generic or abstracted visual', 'say plainly that the artefacts are obscured'],
         readsAs: 'a portfolio that shows it says you did not think about it; one that explains it says you did' },
  unmeasurable: { bad: 'an invented number',
                  good: ['say plainly there was no number',
                         'give the strongest observable proxy with its limits stated - task success rate, support ticket count, teams that adopted it, a version you then removed'],
                  readsAs: 'an honest no-number reads as competence' },
};

Contrast matters: different cases prove different skills. Interviewers read for decision quality — the "here’s what I chose and why, here’s what I measured" loop.

21.3 The interview circuit by seniority

Interviews probe differently at every seniority level, so prepare stories that match the stage. Junior loops check craft, process, and communication, mid-level loops add product judgment and measurable impact, and senior loops examine strategy, systems thinking, and leadership. Research each company’s products and read their design decisions as material. Back every claim with evidence from shipped work, measurements, and decisions you can defend.

StageAsksPrep
Juniorportfolio walk, tools, basics of processdefend 2 case decisions in depth
Midportfolio + a whiteboard "design a X" taska 20-min constraint task framework
Seniorportfolio, system thinking, team friction storiesSTAR stories (Situation/Task/Action/Result) with metrics
Lead/Stafforg change, strategy, trade-offs at scalea story about changing process, not screens

What each round is actually measuring

A loop has four or five rounds and they are measuring different things, and treating them as five interviews is how people prepare badly. The recruiter screen is not an assessment; it is a filter on three things — comp expectations, notice period and location, and whether you can describe your work in one sentence without a preamble. It can be failed by rambling, which is a strange outcome for a conversation that was never supposed to evaluate you. Prepare the one sentence anyway, because it is the sentence the recruiter will repeat to the hiring manager, and if it is vague the loop ends before the portfolio is ever opened.

The portfolio review is a live conversation about work you have shown, and it is the round most people over-prepare for screens and under-prepare for discussion. The reviewer is testing whether you can defend a decision, extend it to a hypothetical, and identify what you would change — which is three different skills, and only the first is demonstrated by the artefact itself. Have a "what I got wrong" answer ready for every case, because that question is always coming and an answer that is not prepared sounds like either an inability to evaluate your own work or a case with no problems in it.

The whiteboard or constraint task is not a design exercise and treating it as one is the standard mistake. You are not being assessed on the artefact; there is no artefact. You are assessed on how you decompose an unfamiliar problem, how you decide what to ask, how you talk while you think, and whether you can hold a constraint. The task is a diagnostic of process, and a strong process with a mediocre sketch beats a beautiful sketch with no visible thinking, every time.

The critique or team round is where your relationship with other designers is assessed — can you critique a design without insulting the person, can you take a critique without defending, do you ask before you suggest. It is also the round where senior candidates are caught, because they review rather than participate, and a lead who cannot build in the room is a lead who will be measured on it. And the values or leadership round is a conversation about how you have handled disagreement, failure and influence without authority, and the only reliable preparation is a small number of real stories with specifics — because this round has no artefacts and it is decided entirely on how concretely you can talk about your own behaviour.

/* Each round, what it is really for, and the standard way to lose it. */
const ROUNDS = [
  { round: 'recruiter screen', isNot: 'an assessment - it is a filter',
    filters: ['comp expectations', 'notice period and location', 'can you describe your work in one sentence without a preamble'],
    loseBy: 'rambling, which is a strange outcome for a conversation never meant to evaluate you',
    prepare: 'the one sentence, because the recruiter repeats it to the hiring manager verbatim',
    consequence: 'if it is vague, the loop ends before the portfolio is opened' },

  { round: 'portfolio review', is: 'a live conversation about work you have shown',
    measures: ['can you defend a decision', 'can you extend it to a hypothetical', 'can you identify what you would change'],
    note: 'only the first is demonstrated by the artefact itself',
    prep: 'a what-I-got-wrong answer for every case',
    whyPrepMatters: 'an unprepared answer reads as either inability to evaluate your own work or a case with no problems in it' },

  { round: 'whiteboard / constraint task', isNot: 'a design exercise',
    hasArtefact: false,
    actuallyMeasures: ['how you decompose an unfamiliar problem', 'what you decide to ask',
                       'how you talk while you think', 'whether you can hold a constraint'],
    loseBy: 'treating it as a design task and making something beautiful',
    verdict: 'a strong process with a mediocre sketch beats a beautiful sketch with no visible thinking' },

  { round: 'critique / team round', is: 'an assessment of how you relate to other designers',
    measures: ['critique without insulting', 'receive critique without defending', 'ask before you suggest'],
    seniorTrap: 'reviewing rather than participating - a lead who cannot build in the room is measured on it' },

  { round: 'values / leadership round', hasArtefacts: false,
    decidedOn: 'how concretely you can talk about your own behaviour',
    preparation: 'a small number of real stories with specifics - disagreement, failure, influence without authority' },
];

Constraint tasks, whiteboard problems, and how to run them

The twenty minutes of a whiteboard task are spent on a sequence, and the sequence is the thing to practise rather than the drawing. Two to three minutes restating the problem in your own words, because the restatement is what reveals whether the brief is actually clear and it is the only moment where asking a question is obviously appropriate. Three to five minutes asking and prioritising questions, out loud, with the user answer prioritised over the nice-to-haves — and the discipline here is to ask about the user, the success measure and the constraint, not about the brand. Five minutes framing: the user, the job to be done, the one thing this must achieve, and the constraint that makes it hard. Ten minutes exploring, on paper, out loud, with at least three genuinely different options and a note on what each trades away. The last three minutes summarising: what you would do next, what you would need to learn, and which assumption is riskiest.

What matters is that all of it is said out loud, continuously, in a form another person could follow and disagree with. That is the actual assessment, and it is why a silent ten minutes of drawing loses to five minutes of talking and five of drawing. It also matters that you explore three options rather than one. A single early direction that you then refine reads as decision-hitting; three options with a stated trade-off reads as a designer, and the reviewer is frequently checking whether you would notice if the first option were wrong.

The two failure modes worth naming. Producing: treating the first thing you draw as a solution to a problem you have not confirmed, and treating the sketch as the deliverable. And optimising the wrong constraint: spending the whole time on visual refinement when the brief's constraint was time, or on the happy path when the brief said the hard case is the interesting one. Before you start, restate the constraint explicitly — "the constraint is that this ships in two weeks, so I am going to prioritise the common path and hand off the rest" — because saying it out loud is worth more than demonstrating it silently.

/* Twenty minutes, in order. The sequence is what to practise, not the drawing. */
const TWENTY_MINUTES = [
  { minutes: '2-3',  phase: 'restate the problem in your own words',
    why: 'it reveals whether the brief is clear, and it is the only moment where a question is obviously appropriate' },
  { minutes: '3-5',  phase: 'ask and prioritise questions, out loud',
    prioritise: 'the user, the success measure, the constraint',
    avoid: 'brand questions - they are not the constraint and they waste the time' },
  { minutes: 5,      phase: 'frame: the user, the job to be done, the one thing this must achieve, the constraint that makes it hard' },
  { minutes: 10,     phase: 'explore, out loud, on paper',
    mustProduce: ['at least three genuinely different options', 'a stated trade-off per option'],
    why: 'one refined direction reads as decision-hitting; three options read as a designer' },
  { minutes: 3,      phase: 'summarise: what next, what to learn, which assumption is riskiest' },
];
// all of it said out loud, continuously - a silent ten minutes of drawing
// loses to five of talking and five of drawing

/* Two failure modes. */
const TASK_FAILURES = {
  producing: { is: 'treating the first thing you draw as the solution to an unconfirmed problem',
               and: 'treating the sketch as the deliverable' },
  wrongConstraint: { symptom: 'visual refinement when the constraint was time; the happy path when the brief said the hard case is interesting',
                     counter: 'restate the constraint before starting, out loud',
                     why: 'saying it out loud is worth more than demonstrating it silently' },
};

What to ask them is a separate discipline and it is where the mutual assessment happens. Useful: how long is the loop and what is the bar; who would I be working with and what is the hardest thing about them; what did the last hire inherit and what went wrong with it; how do you decide what not to build; what is the current state of the design system here, honestly; how do designers and engineers disagree on this team and what happens when they do. Not useful, and worth recognising when you get them: questions about the exercise, questions about the comp that were not taken, and any question whose answer will not change whether you want the job. The last one is the filter — if the answer would not change your decision to take the job, you are asking out of nerves rather than out of interest, and both of those read the same way to the other side.

21.4 Staying in motion (read, ship, test, teach)

Staying in motion means learning that compounds: read primary sources and original research rather than recycled lists, and ship real work monthly to convert knowledge into evidence. Test designs weekly on real people to keep the feedback loop tight, then teach once a year, because explaining your practice sharpens it. The cadence matters more than the volume. This loop is what keeps a designer’s judgment current.

  • Read primary sources: Nielsen Norman Group, design systems' docs, measurement books (think "Measuring the User Experience").
  • Ship monthly: a component, a case, a test — your portfolio compounds on evidence, not intention.
  • Test weekly on real people; each session teaches more than a course.

What to read, and how to evaluate a source

The reading problem is not volume, it is that most design content is commentary on primary sources, so reading it twice gets you nothing and reading the primary source once gets you everything. The reliable producers are few: the original usability studies rather than the summaries, the original specification rather than the interpretation, the design-system documentation of systems actually in production at scale, the accessibility guidelines themselves rather than blog posts about them, and the papers — which are readable and are almost nobody's habit. Everything described as a framework is usually a diagram of something simpler that you could have derived yourself, and there is nothing wrong with deriving it.

So the evaluation rule is short: ask whether this would have been written before or after the thing it describes existed, and whether the author has shipped anything. Content written before a practice existed is either prediction or criticism, and neither is instruction. Content written after it can be reporting, which is the only kind worth your time — and the corollary is that any source with a publication date, an author with a portfolio, and no shipped work is a source to skip. This filters about ninety percent of what a search returns, and it is the whole reason a two-hour curated session beats a week of following feeds.

Keep the notes in a form that makes them usable: one paragraph per idea in your own words, with the source, and with the one situation in which you would apply it. The last clause is what turns a note into knowledge — an idea with no application condition is trivia, and trivia is what makes reading feel useless and stops the habit.
