22.5 Measuring the design org (without vanity metrics)

Measuring a design org exists to prove value and find friction, and it must measure outcomes rather than activity. Track speed such as cycle time from kickoff to ship, adoption such as design system usage, quality such as rework and defect rates, and health such as engagement and satisfaction. Review these alongside business results with product leads. Vanity dashboards that count output without impact only feed self-congratulation.

// Bad metrics: "designs delivered", "story points of design"
// Good metrics: 4 Sides
//   Speed : discovery→validated prototype time; handoff lag
//   Adoption: system component coverage, token usage in code
//   Quality: usability defects per release; NPS moves after redesigns
//   Health: researcher hours per product; % releases that shipped tested
// Pick 4-6, review quarterly WITH the product leads, and tie them
// to product outcomes — DesignOps earns trust by pointing at outcomes.

A metrics shortlist that points DesignOps at outcomes by dismissing vanity numbers. Notice the four sides — speed, adoption, quality, health — each tied to something measurable.

One definition per metric, and where each of the four sides breaks

The failure mode of a design-org dashboard is not that the metrics are wrong; it is that four different people mean four different things by each one, so the quarterly review becomes an argument about definitions before it becomes a review of results. So the first piece of work is not choosing metrics, it is writing each one as a sentence with the population, the window, the denominator and the exclusions — and requiring a change to a definition to be a dated, announced act rather than a diff that lands before a review. Under that discipline, two of the four sides turn out to be much harder than they look, and it is worth knowing which.

Speed is the easiest to define badly. Cycle time from kickoff to ship is easy to compute and almost useless on its own, because it goes down when people skip discovery, which is the exact behaviour the measurement was supposed to encourage. So split it: discovery-to-validated-prototype, which is the part design controls, and design-to-production, which is the part design does not. And report the distribution, not the mean — the mean hides the case that took nine weeks, and the mean is what lets a team claim improvement after removing its hardest project. Handoff lag is genuinely useful and almost nobody measures it: the time between the ticket being marked ready and the first code change. It is directly actionable, it names a queue rather than a person, and it is the number that falls when the handoff contract gets good.

Adoption is the side where the definitions are contested and where the honest answer is that most teams measure the wrong thing. Component coverage — the share of components used at least once — is the number teams quote and it is nearly meaningless on its own, because a system used only where it was easy reports high coverage while a third of the codebase hand-builds the rest. So pair it with prevalence: the share of shipped screens that use the system, and within those, the share of interactive elements that come from it. And add drift, which is the number nobody publishes: how often a local override is added on top of a system component per month. A rising drift count means the system is being worked around and the workaround is becoming the standard, and it is the earliest warning available that the system is failing — earlier than coverage, earlier than satisfaction.

Quality and health have the opposite problem: they are genuinely easy to state and genuinely hard to attribute. Usability defects per release falls when you ship less, so pair it with something that measures volume. Rework rate — work redone after being called done — is a better signal than defect count because it catches the class of defect where the design was ambiguous rather than wrong, which is the class DesignOps can actually prevent. And for health, the two measures that predict attrition are not satisfaction scores: it is the ratio of a person's time spent on work they chose against work they were asked for, and whether the ritual commitments are being honoured. A team that is in a quarterly crunch knows it is on every measure that matters, six months before anybody resigns.

/* First the definition, then the metric. Without this the quarterly review is
   an argument about definitions before it is a review of results. */
const DEFINITION_RULE = {
  shape: ['the population', 'the window', 'the denominator', 'the exclusions'],
  changeProcess: 'a dated, announced act - not a diff that lands the day before the review',
  why: 'four people meaning four things by "adoption" is the actual reason design metrics are distrusted',
};

const FOUR_SIDES = {
  speed: {
    splitInto: ['discovery-to-validated-prototype (design controls it)', 'design-to-production (design does not)'],
    trap: 'cycle time falls when people skip discovery - the exact behaviour the metric was meant to encourage',
    report: 'the distribution, not the mean',
    whyDistribution: 'the mean hides the nine-week case, and the mean is what lets a team claim improvement after removing its hardest project',
    theUsefulOne: { name: 'handoff lag', definedAs: 'time between the ticket being marked ready and the first code change',
      whyUseful: 'directly actionable, names a queue rather than a person, and falls when the handoff contract gets good' },
  },
  adoption: {
    componentsQuote: 'coverage - share of components used at least once',
    whyItMisleads: 'a system used only where it was easy reports high coverage while a third of the codebase hand-builds the rest',
    pairWith: ['prevalence: share of shipped screens that use the system',
                'fidelity: within those, share of interactive elements that come from it',
                'drift: local overrides added on top of system components, per month'],
    theOneNobodyPublishes: 'drift',
    whyDriftMatters: 'a rising count means the system is being worked around and the workaround is becoming the standard - the earliest available warning that the system is failing, earlier than coverage and earlier than satisfaction',
  },
  quality: {
    easyToStateHardToAttribute: true,
    defectPerRelease: { problem: 'falls when you ship less', pairWith: 'anything that measures volume' },
    better: { name: 'rework rate', definedAs: 'work redone after being called done',
              why: 'catches the class where the design was ambiguous rather than wrong - the class DesignOps can actually prevent' },
  },
  health: {
    doNotLeadWith: 'satisfaction scores',
    whatPredictsAttrition: [
      { measure: 'ratio of time spent on work you chose to work you were asked for' },
      { measure: 'whether the ritual commitments are being honoured' },
    ],
    why: 'a team in a quarterly crunch knows it on every measure that matters, six months before anybody resigns',
  },
};

/* Vanity metrics, and what to say when somebody reports one. */
const VANITY = {
  list: ['designs delivered', 'story points of design', 'screens per designer', 'components created'],
  sharedProperty: 'they count output, and output is a function of how you decompose work, not of value',
  answer: 'ask what decision this number would change; if none, it is a report of activity and belongs in a standup, not a review',
  replacementQuestion: 'what would we do differently if this moved by ten percent?',
};

And the review itself, because a good dashboard reviewed badly is worse than no dashboard. Quarterly, with the product leads rather than with the design team alone, because a set of metrics reviewed by the people who produced them is a report rather than a review. Three things on the agenda in this order: what moved and what we believe caused it, including the things that got worse; one decision, with a date and an owner; and the adoption review, where the components nobody used are explicitly considered for removal. That last one is the item people skip and it is the one that keeps a design system from becoming a museum — a system with three hundred components of which thirty percent have had no use in two years has a maintenance cost that appears nowhere in any of the four sides, and the only time it can be addressed is a review with a removal item on the agenda.

Exercises 22

  1. Audit a design folder’s file-naming chaos and write a 4-line naming convention doc.
  2. Write the 10-point handoff checklist (states, tokens, a11y, edges) for ONE component.
  3. Choose your 4 DesignOps metrics and draft the quarterly review format.

23 · UX Strategy & Product Thinking

UX strategy is where design meets money, converting research into product decisions that survive the roadmap table. It frames problems with tools such as jobs-to-be-done, defines what success looks like with a north star metric and guardrails, and sequences work with prioritization frameworks. Strategy work is evidence-based arguing: each tool turns design judgment into an understandable, defensible product decision. The artifacts let teams argue about value, not taste.

23.1 Jobs-to-be-Done: hiring your product23.2 North Star metric & guardrails23.3 Prioritization frameworks designers can actually use23.4 The discovery/delivery split (dual-track agile)23.5 The business case for UX

Strategy is where UX meets money. This chapter turns design judgment into product decisions: which problems to solve, what "good" means, and how to argue with evidence at the roadmap table.

23.1 Jobs-to-be-Done: hiring your product

Jobs-to-be-Done reframes features into the underlying jobs people hire a product to do, such as the progress a customer is trying to make in a particular situation. It kills vague feature wish lists by asking what outcome the user actually wants to achieve. The framework also exposes your real competitors: any substitute someone could use to make that progress. Interview users about context, struggles, and the moment your product is hired.

// JTBD lens: people "hire" products to get a job done in a situation.
//   "When I'm commuting [situation], I want to brief my team on a doc
//    [job], so I look prepared for the 10am call [outcome]."
// Why it beats feature lists:
//   - a feature is a guess about the job; the job is the requirement
//   - it kills the "well, some users might want X" argument
//   - it exposes the REAL competitor (the sticky note, the email)
// Opportunity framing: jobs with high importance AND low satisfaction
// = your roadmap. Build from job statements, not from a wall of ideas.

How to actually run the interview

The job statement is the easy part; the interview that produces a true one is the whole technique, and it has a specific shape that differs from a normal user interview. You are not asking what features they want — you are reconstructing a past episode. The frame is a "story about the last time", and the discipline is to stay in the past: what were you doing, what had happened just before, what were you worried about, what did you try first, what made you try something else, what did you end up doing, and how did you decide it was finished. Every question is anchored to a moment, and the moment that matters most is the one just before they looked for a solution, because that is where the situation reveals itself — the deadline, the person they were reporting to, the thing that had gone wrong last time, the constraint they were operating under.

Two things kill this interview. Asking about the future, in any form — "would you use this", "would you pay for that", "how would you like this to work" — and the reason is not just that stated intention is unreliable; it is that it is unreliable in a specific direction, because a person asked to imagine a product will describe the version of it that would be pleasant rather than the version that would be used. And letting them generalise: "how do you usually manage your invoices" produces a summary of a practice, while "tell me about the last time an invoice was late" produces an episode with a date, a person and an emotion. Push on the specific until you get one, and treat "usually" as a signal to go back.

Then the competitor question, which is the part people skip and which is the most valuable output of the whole framework. Ask what they did the last time they made this progress and before they encountered your product, or the last time it was too expensive. The answer is almost never a named product: it is a spreadsheet, a shared folder, a person who knew the answer, a phone call, a workaround, or nothing at all. Those are your real competitors, they are what your positioning is measured against, and the fact that one of them is a person changes the design problem completely — because you are not competing with a feature list, you are competing with a colleague who is available right now.

/* The JTBD interview is a past-episode reconstruction, not a question about
   intentions. Every question is anchored to a moment. */
const JTBD_QUESTIONS = [
  { moment: 'the situation', ask: 'what were you doing, and what had happened just before?' },
  { moment: 'the trigger',  ask: 'what made this come up this time rather than last week?' },
  { moment: 'the stakes',   ask: 'who were you reporting to, what was the deadline, what had gone wrong last time?' },
  { moment: 'first attempt', ask: 'what did you try first, before you thought of using anything?' },
  { moment: 'the pivot',   ask: 'what made you try something else?' },
  { moment: 'the resolution', ask: 'what did you end up doing, and how did you decide it was finished?' },
  // the moment that matters most is just before they looked for a solution,
  // because that is where the situation is visible: the deadline, the
  // person, the constraint they were operating under
];

const JTBD_FAILURES = [
  { failure: 'asking about the future in any form', why: 'stated intention is not merely unreliable, it is unreliable in a direction - asked to imagine a product, a person describes the pleasant version rather than the used version' },
  { failure: 'letting them generalise',
    bad: 'how do you usually manage your invoices - a summary of a practice',
    good: 'tell me about the last time an invoice was late - an episode with a date, a person and an emotion',
    rule: 'treat "usually" as a signal to go back' },
];

/* The competitor question, which produces the most valuable output. */
const COMPETITORS = {
  ask: 'what did you do the last time you made this progress, before you encountered us - or the last time it was too expensive?',
  usuallyAnsweredWith: ['a spreadsheet', 'a shared folder', 'a person who knew the answer', 'a phone call',
                        'a workaround', 'nothing at all'],
  implication: 'those are the real competitors and your positioning is measured against them',
  theHardOne: 'when the competitor is a person',
  whatItChanges: 'you are not competing with a feature list, you are competing with a colleague who is available right now',
};

/* Turning statements into opportunities, and the two mistakes in the scoring. */
const OPPORTUNITY = {
  formula: 'importance x (importance - satisfaction)',
  inputs: { importance: 'what happens if they fail at this job', satisfaction: 'how well the alternatives do it' },
  becomes: 'the ranked opportunity list that the roadmap is drawn from',
  mistakes: [
    { mistake: 'satisfaction measured against your product only',
      why: 'satisfaction is a property of the whole competitive set - a job your product does badly may be one the alternatives do perfectly, which is why it is not an opportunity' },
    { mistake: 'importance treated as constant within a job',
      why: 'importance rises with stakes: the same job is important and unimportant in different situations, and the situation is half the statement' },
  ],
  sanityCheck: 'if a job scores high, you should be able to name a person in the last month for whom failing at it mattered a lot',
};

/* Turning an opportunity into a roadmap item. */
function opportunityToRoadmap(opportunity) {
  return {
    job: opportunity.statement,
    forWhom: opportunity.situation,          // keep the situation attached
    competingWith: opportunity.alternatives, // what it is measured against
    candidateSolution: 'the smallest thing that could plausibly move the job',
    riskiestAssumption: opportunity.keyUncertainty,
    cheapestTest: opportunity.nextTest,
    decidedBy: 'the test result, not the strength of the argument',
  };
}

A JTBD job-statement template built from situation, job, and outcome, with reasons it beats feature lists. Notice the opportunity framing that turns importance and satisfaction into a roadmap.

23.2 North Star metric & guardrails

The north star metric is the one number a product rallies behind, the best leading indicator of sustained value delivered to customers. Guardrails are the things a product refuses to trade for that number, such as retention, trust, or integrity, so both are tracked together. Value-centric metrics beat vanity counts such as raw signups. Define the north star around activated, ongoing value and report guardrails alongside it.

  • North Star: one business + user value metric the whole product rallies behind ("weekly active learners completing a lesson" beats "sessions" — it captures value, not vanity).
  • Guardrails: quality metrics you refuse to trade away (retention, CSAT, a11y) — growth loops that eat quality are time bombs.

    • Choosing a metric that is a leading indicator

    The test for a north star is not that it is a good number; it is that it is a leading one and that it is hard to move without delivering value. Every team that picks a vanity metric makes the same mistake in the same direction — choosing something easy to move and easy to report. Signups, sessions, page views, time in app, feature adoption: all four are easy, all four are reportable, and all four can be improved by making the product worse in a way that takes months to become visible. The reason is structural: they measure activity, and activity is a proxy for value that decays as the product grows — a metric that stops being useful tends not to become useless but to become gameable, and then the team optimises it and the product degrades on a lag nobody can trace back to the decision.

    So the construction is value-shaped: a user, doing the thing they came for, repeatedly. "Weekly active learners completing a lesson" rather than sessions, because the first names the user, the activity and the object, and the second names a unit of time. "Invoices completed" rather than time in the app. "Weekly teams that invite a second member" rather than invitations sent. In every case the test is whether the number can only go up while the product gets better for users, and if a plausible improvement in the product would not move it, it is a proxy for something else and the something else will drift away from value over time.

    Then the harder part, which is that one metric for a product with several distinct kinds of user is always a compromise, and the compromise should be deliberate. A product with a free tier and a paying tier has one metric that measures value delivered, not two that measure two things — a north star that is a weighted blend of two numbers is not a metric, it is a policy, and the moment it becomes a policy it gets argued about and then gamed. The workable answers are to have one north star for the whole product that expresses the shared job, plus per-surface metrics underneath it that nobody is measured on. And for a genuinely two-sided product, the honest north star is the completed exchange, not the action on either side — matching a rider to a driver, not rides requested, which can be raised by making the app annoying to drivers.

    /* The test: hard to move without delivering value. */
function isNorthStar(candidate) {
  const problems = [];
  if (/signups|sessions|page views|time in app|dau|mau/i.test(candidate.name)) {
    problems.push('measures activity, which decays as the product grows');
  }
  if (!candidate.namesAUser) problems.push('no user named - a unit of time is not a measure of value');
  if (!candidate.namesTheActivity) problems.push('the activity is unnamed');
  if (!candidate.namesTheObject) problems.push('the object of the activity is unnamed');
  if (candidate.measurableWithoutImprovement) {
    problems.push('a plausible improvement in the product would not move it, so it is a proxy for something else');
  }
  return { ok: problems.length === 0, problems,
    consequenceIfWrong: 'a metric that does not become useless becomes gameable, and then the team optimises it and the product degrades on a lag nobody can trace back to the decision' };
}

const CANDIDATES = [
  { vanity: 'sessions', better: 'weekly active learners completing a lesson',
    why: 'the first names the user, the activity and the object; the second names a unit of time' },
  { vanity: 'time in the app', better: 'invoices completed' },
  { vanity: 'invitations sent', better: 'weekly teams that invite a second member' },
  { vanity: 'rides requested', better: 'completed exchanges (rider matched to driver)',
    why: 'rides requested can be raised by making the app annoying to drivers' },
];

/* One metric for a product with several kinds of user. */
const MULTI_USER_PRODUCT = {
  multiTierRule: 'one metric that measures value delivered - not a blend',
  because: 'a weighted blend of two numbers is a policy, and a policy gets argued about and then gamed',
  structure: ['one north star expressing the shared job', 'per-surface metrics underneath that nobody is measured on'],
  twoSided: 'the completed exchange, not the action on either side',
};

    Guardrails, and the failure they exist to prevent

    A guardrail is a quality metric a team agrees not to trade, and the agreement matters more than the number because the number is what makes the agreement checkable. The set is small on purpose — three to five — and each has a threshold, an owner and a defined response when it is breached. Without a defined response it is not a guardrail, it is a metric with good intentions, and the breach will be discussed and then absorbed. With one, the guardrail does its job: the team stops the thing that is moving the north star until the guardrail recovers. That is expensive and it is the point; a guardrail that never costs anything has never been tested.

    The classic set: retention or churn, because almost every growth tactic eventually trades it. Latency, because almost every visual optimisation eventually trades it, and the trade is invisible to the user until it is not. Accessibility conformance, because the growth tactics that degrade it — a modal that traps focus, a countdown that excludes, a low-contrast variant to increase the clickable area — all produce short-term lifts. Support contact rate, because it is the metric that catches design debt earliest and it is attributed to nobody so it moves freely. And trust, measured the ways in chapter 20: complaints, refund and chargeback rates, opt-outs from anything.

    Leading versus lagging, and the trap of a beautiful lagging metric

    The distinction that matters for a north star is whether it moves before the outcome or after it. A leading metric is one where a change in it is followed by a change in revenue or retention within a timeframe short enough to act on. A lagging metric is one where revenue is the metric itself. Most organisations pick a lagging metric because it is the most defensible number in the building, and a north star that is a lagging metric has a serious practical consequence: it cannot be improved by design work, because design work takes weeks and the metric responds in quarters. A team whose north star is revenue is not being asked to design; they are being asked to wait, and the predictable result is that the number nobody can move in a sprint is quietly replaced by one they can.

    So the construction is a proxy that is early and honestly chained. "Weekly active learners completing a lesson" is leading because a change in it plausibly precedes a change in renewal, and the chain is arguable — you can state why completing lessons leads to staying. The honest version includes the chain explicitly, because a proxy without a stated reason to believe in it is a correlation somebody noticed, and correlations found in a dashboard are usually coincidental. Write the chain in one sentence: this number leads to that one because of this reason. If the sentence cannot be written, the metric is a vanity metric with a good name and it should be replaced with something whose chain you can state.

    And then the honest admission worth making in a metrics review, because it defuses the most common objection: a north star is a choice, and other choices would also be defensible. What the choice buys is alignment — one number that a product manager, an engineer and a designer can all be shown improving, which is a genuinely scarce thing. What it costs is that the product will be optimised for that number and therefore distorted in the direction of that number, and the guardrails exist to bound the distortion. Choosing well is not about finding the perfect metric; it is about finding one whose distortion you can live with and can see. This framing also settles the recurring argument about whether the metric should be growth or value or engagement: ask instead which distortion you can afford, and the question becomes answerable.

    /* Leading versus lagging, and the practical consequence of getting it wrong. */
const LEADING = {
  definition: { leading: 'a change here is followed by a change in revenue or retention within an actionable timeframe',
                lagging: 'revenue is the metric itself' },
  whyTeamsPickLagging: 'it is the most defensible number in the building',
  consequence: 'a lagging north star cannot be improved by design work - design takes weeks, the metric responds in quarters',
  predictableResult: 'the number nobody can move in a sprint is quietly replaced by one they can',
};

/* The chain must be writable. */
function chainIsWrittable(candidate) {
  const chain = candidate.leadingToWhy;   // "this number leads to that one because of this reason"
  const problems = [];
  if (!chain) problems.push('no stated reason to believe in it');
  if (/because people like it|it went up when/.test(chain || '')) problems.push('the chain is a correlation found in a dashboard, and those are usually coincidental');
  if (!candidate.movesBeforeRevenue) problems.push('it moves at the same time as revenue, so it is not a leading indicator');
  return { ok: problems.length === 0, problems,
    verdict: problems.length ? 'a vanity metric with a good name - replace it' : 'honestly chained: a proxy that is early and arguable' };
}

/* The admission that defuses the most common objection. */
const NORTH_STAR_IS_A_CHOICE = {
  is: 'a choice, and other choices would also be defensible',
  buys: 'alignment - one number a product manager, an engineer and a designer can all be shown improving, which is genuinely scarce',
  costs: 'the product will be optimised for that number and therefore distorted in its direction',
  boundedBy: 'guardrails',
  soChoosingWellMeans: 'not finding the perfect metric, but finding one whose distortion you can live with and can see',
  reframes: 'ask which distortion you can afford, rather than whether the metric should be growth or value or engagement',
};

    And the operating rule, which is the part that makes the pair work: the north star is never reviewed without the guardrails on the same screen, and any change in the guardrail is reported at the same moment and at the same prominence as the change in the north star. The failure this prevents is specific and common — a team reports a large positive movement in the north star in the quarterly review, the guardrail numbers are in the appendix, nobody connects them, and three months later the metric that was paying all the bills is down. Design's particular role here is defensive rather than offensive: a design team is usually the only group in the company positioned to notice that a lift in conversion was bought with something invisible, and the contribution that matters is naming it before the lag closes.

  • Design contributes to the North Star through flows that move that number — and defends it when others optimize trash metrics.

23.3 Prioritization frameworks designers can actually use

Prioritization frameworks turn opinion into ranked, arguable choices by scoring candidate work against the same criteria. RICE weighs reach, impact, confidence, and effort, value-versus-effort plots quick wins against big bets, Kano sorts features into basic, performance, and delight categories, and cost of delay prices the loss of waiting. Choose the framework that matches the decision and show the scoring so the ranking can be challenged.

FrameworkFormula / ideaDesign uses it for
RICE(Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effortcomparing feature bets across teams
Value vs effort 2×2plot, then sequenceroadmap conversations; quick wins vs strategic
Kano modelmust-haves → performance → delighterswhat to ship vs what to fix first
Opportunity scorecardimportance × (dissatisfaction gap)from JTBD research to ranked priorities
Cost of delayvalue lost per week of waitingarguing for sequencing, not popularity

Every framework scores something, so ask what

The reason prioritization frameworks fail is not that they are bad arithmetic; it is that every one of them scores a different thing and teams pick them by familiarity. RICE scores estimated value per unit of effort and requires you to produce three numbers you cannot know — reach, impact and confidence — from a document written by the person proposing the work. A value-versus-effort plot scores judgement, and is the one most honest about the fact that the estimates are estimates. Kano scores the shape of demand, and is the only one that changes what you build rather than only what order you build it in. An opportunity scorecard scores the gap between importance and satisfaction, which is a research output rather than a product opinion. And cost of delay scores the rate at which value is being lost, which is the only one that addresses the question people actually argue about, which is not "what should we do" but "why this now".

So pick by the decision in front of you. If the decision is which of these twenty things, use a scored list with the criteria written down, because the value is in the shared criteria and the scoring is only the arithmetic. If it is whether a category of work is worth doing at all, use Kano, because the categories answer a question a ranked list cannot: doing a delighter before a basic is not merely lower priority, it is wasted. If it is sequencing within a fixed team, use cost of delay, because it makes the argument about time rather than about popularity. And if it is a single bet with real uncertainty, none of these help, and what is needed is a test.

What a real prioritisation session looks like

The arithmetic is trivial and the session is the work, so it is worth describing what a good one does. It starts with the constraints, not the list: how many people, for how long, and what is already committed. That ordering matters, because a ranking produced without a capacity constraint is a wish list, and a wish list ranked in a room full of senior people produces a ranking that reflects seniority rather than value. Then the list is split by the kind of decision each item implies. A bet — an uncertain idea that could change the product's direction — is separated from an improvement — a known thing that is known to be incomplete — and from a commitment — something already promised to a customer. Mixing the three in one ranking is the most common structural error in prioritisation, because a bet scored against a commitment will always lose, and a bet that always loses is never funded.

Then the argument, which is not about the scores. Each item gets one question from whoever is most affected: what happens if we do not do this? If the answer is genuinely "nothing happens for a year", the item is a bet with a low opportunity cost and it should be scheduled late, and the cost-of-delay number falls out of the answer rather than needing to be estimated. If the answer is "something we will have to pay for later", then the item has a real cost of delay and the sequencing argument is about magnitude, which is measurable. The question is more productive than the score because it forces the proposer to state the counterfactual, and the counterfactual is where the real disagreement usually lives.

Then the decisions, recorded with the inputs and the dissent. Three outcomes: schedule it with an owner, schedule it conditional on a test, or reject it with the reason. Rejecting with a reason is worth the effort, because the reason is what stops the same idea returning every quarter with a slightly different name — and the reason is only recorded if somebody writes it, and it is only useful if it is a reason about the world rather than about this quarter's capacity. And record the dissent: an item that lost by a small margin against an item whose premise was never tested is a candidate for next quarter, and losing it by a small margin is the signal. The alternative, which is what usually happens, is that the item disappears and its proposer re-enters it in six months having learned nothing from the loss.

/* The arithmetic is trivial; the session is the work. */
const SESSION_ORDER = [
  { step: 1, do: 'state the constraints first', how: 'how many people, for how long, what is already committed',
    why: 'a ranking produced without a capacity constraint is a wish list, and a wish list ranked in a room full of senior people reflects seniority rather than value' },
  { step: 2, do: 'split the list by the kind of decision each item implies',
    kinds: [{ kind: 'bet', meaning: 'uncertain, could change the direction' },
            { kind: 'improvement', meaning: 'known and known to be incomplete' },
            { kind: 'commitment', meaning: 'already promised to a customer' }],
    why: 'mixing them is the most common structural error - a bet scored against a commitment always loses, and a bet that always loses is never funded' },
  { step: 3, do: 'ask the counterfactual instead of debating the scores',
    question: 'what happens if we do not do this?',
    extracts: 'the cost of delay falls out of the answer rather than needing to be estimated',
    whyItWorks: 'it forces the proposer to state the counterfactual, which is where the real disagreement usually lives' },
];

/* The three outcomes, and what must be written down. */
const DECISIONS = [
  { outcome: 'schedule it with an owner' },
  { outcome: 'schedule it conditional on a test', note: 'the test is named and dated' },
  { outcome: 'reject it with the reason',
    why: 'the reason is what stops the same idea returning every quarter under a different name',
    whatCountsAsAReason: 'a fact about the world',
    whatDoesNot: 'this quarter\'s capacity' },
];
const RECORD_DISSENT = {
  rule: 'an item that lost by a small margin, against an item whose premise was never tested, is a candidate for next quarter',
  signal: 'losing by a small margin',
  withoutIt: 'the item disappears and its proposer re-enters it in six months having learned nothing from the loss',
};

/* The question that beats a score, for each kind of item. */
function askTheProposer(item) {
  const q = 'what happens if we do not do this?';
  if (/nothing (much )?for a year|nobody notices/i.test(item.answer)) {
    return { reading: 'low opportunity cost', action: 'schedule late', note: 'the cost-of-delay number falls out of the answer - do not estimate it' };
  }
  if (/we will pay for it later|it will cost more to fix/i.test(item.answer)) {
    return { reading: 'real cost of delay', action: 'argue magnitude, which is measurable' };
  }
  return { reading: 'the counterfactual is unclear', action: 'the item is not ready to be scored - go and find out what happens' };
}

The common misuse, and it is worth naming because it is the way these frameworks acquire a bad reputation: treating the score as the answer. Every score is a set of assumptions written by the person who benefits from the work, and a scoring meeting is therefore a meeting about who wrote the assumptions. The fix is not a better formula; it is showing the working. A ranking whose inputs are visible can be challenged on the input, which is a productive argument, and a ranking whose inputs are hidden can only be challenged on the conclusion, which is a political argument. So the rule is: publish the table with the columns, let the person who proposed each item fill in their own reach and confidence estimates, and require the confidence column to state why it is low when it is low. That last column is the one that does the most work — a proposal with low confidence is not a bad proposal, it is a proposal that needs a test before it needs a slot.

/* What each framework actually scores. Picking by familiarity is why they
   get a bad reputation. */
const SCORES = [
  { framework: 'RICE', scores: 'estimated value per unit of effort',
    requires: ['reach', 'impact', 'confidence'],
    problem: 'three numbers you cannot know, written by the person proposing the work',
    decisionItServes: 'which of these twenty things' },
  { framework: 'value vs effort plot', scores: 'judgement, honestly labelled',
    decisionItServes: 'sequencing when the estimates are estimates' },
  { framework: 'Kano', scores: 'the shape of demand',
    unique: 'the only one that changes WHAT you build, not only the order',
    decisionItServes: 'whether a category of work is worth doing at all',
    whyItAnswersAQuestionAListCannot: 'a delighter before a basic is not lower priority, it is wasted' },
  { framework: 'opportunity scorecard', scores: 'importance minus satisfaction',
    note: 'a research output rather than a product opinion',
    decisionItServes: 'where the dissatisfaction is real' },
  { framework: 'cost of delay', scores: 'the rate at which value is being lost',
    unique: 'the only one that addresses why NOW',
    decisionItServes: 'sequencing within a fixed team' },
  { framework: 'none', scores: '-',
    decisionItServes: 'a single bet with real uncertainty - what is needed is a test, not a score' },
];

/* The common misuse: treating the score as the answer. A scoring meeting is
   a meeting about who wrote the assumptions. */
const SCORING_MEETING = {
  reality: 'every score is a set of assumptions written by the person who benefits from the work',
  therefore: 'a scoring meeting is a meeting about who wrote the assumptions',
  fixIsNotAFormula: true,
  fix: ['publish the table with the columns',
        'the person who proposed each item fills in their own reach and confidence',
        'the confidence column must state WHY it is low when it is low'],
  whyVisibleInputsWork: 'a ranking with visible inputs can be challenged on the input, which is productive; a ranking with hidden inputs can only be challenged on the conclusion, which is political',
  theColumnThatDoesTheWork: 'confidence',
  interpretation: 'low confidence is not a bad proposal - it is a proposal that needs a test before it needs a slot',
};

/* Kano, in enough detail to be usable rather than as a diagram. */
const KANO = {
  categories: {
    basic:     { what: 'absence is unacceptable, presence is unremarkable',
                 example: 'an invoice can be downloaded',
                 errorWhenMissed: 'angry users - they will not pay for it, they will only complain',
                 order: 'must exist before anything else is judged' },
    performance:{ what: 'linear value as it improves',
                 example: 'search that finds the right invoice quickly',
                 errorWhenMissed: 'neutral, and expensive, because everybody assumes a competitor has done it',
                 order: 'where differentiation happens, but never before basics' },
    delighter: { what: 'unexpected above the line; absence is tolerated',
                 example: 'the system explains why a payment failed and what to do',
                 errorWhenMissed: 'nobody asks for it and nobody complains when it is gone',
                 order: 'last, or not at all - never as a substitute for a missing basic' },
  },
  method: 'ask users about a feature that does not exist: how would you feel if it were there (positive), how would you feel if it were not (negative).',
  caution: 'the answers are about the category, not your feature, and people are poor at predicting delighter response - which is why delighter claims need a test rather than a survey',
};

/* Cost of delay, computed rather than asserted. */
function costOfDelay({ value, weeksWaiting, confidenceInEstimate }) {
  const perWeek = value / 12;            // a year of value, spread
  const discounted = perWeek * weeksWaiting * confidenceInEstimate;
  return { perWeek, totalBurned: discounted,
    compareTo: 'the cost of building it, which is fixed',
    decision: 'if the burn exceeds the build cost before it is scheduled, waiting has already cost more than the work',
    // this is the number that ends "it is too early to start"
    note: 'people compare against the build cost and forget the counterfactual is the burn' };
}

23.4 The discovery/delivery split (dual-track agile)

Dual-track agile splits work into a discovery track that continuously tests problems and solutions and a delivery track that builds and ships what has been validated. Research runs as a steady drip of real user tests, interviews, and prototypes that feed a constantly validated backlog. Delivery rarely blocks on research, and discovery never waits for one giant phase. A steady loop beats one massive study followed by one massive build.

Discovery (every sprint, small):    Delivery (the agreed build track):
  frame a hypothesis                  take groomed, discovered stories
  run 2-3 interviews / prototype     build + test + ship in-sprint
  test 3 options cheaply             learn, feed findings back
  ✓ validated → hand to delivery     ✓ shipped → measure → discover next
// Anti-pattern: a 3-month research phase followed by a 3-month build.
// The steady drip — a little discovery ALWAYS running — is the enterprise
// version of "test weekly" (Ch.21.2) and it works for the whole team.

What "small" means, and the size of the unit

Every explanation of dual-track agile omits the part that decides whether it works, which is the size of the discovery unit. Too big and it is the three-month research phase wearing a new name: a broad area is examined, findings are presented, and by the time anything is tested the context has moved. Too small and discovery becomes a formality — a team "does discovery" by writing three hypotheses nobody intends to test, which is worse than not doing it because it produces artefacts that look like evidence. The workable unit is one question that, if answered "no", would stop the work. If answering the question yes would not change what gets built, it is not a discovery question; it is a justification exercise, and it should be deleted.

So the shape is: one hypothesis, stated as a belief about somebody's behaviour, with a prediction that would falsify it. The standard of evidence is also worth being strict about, because this is where dual-track programmes rot. Three options tested with five people each is not the same as one option tested with fifteen, and the difference is not statistical — it is that testing alternatives compares them to each other, while testing one option against a task tells you whether it works at all. The second is what a discovery track is for. Comparing your own options is a delivery-track activity, and mixing them up is why teams run three-week option bake-offs and learn nothing about whether the problem was real.

The handoff between the tracks is where the method is most often lost, and the standard should be a testable artefact rather than a document. A validated item carries: the problem stated as somebody's behaviour, the user and the situation attached, the evidence with counts, the riskiest assumption, and the specific thing that was tested. What it should not carry is a design — because a discovery track that hands over a design has quietly become a delivery track, and the next thing that happens is that the finding is treated as an instruction to build what was already decided.

/* The size of the unit decides whether this is dual-track or a rebranded
   three-month research phase. */
const DISCOVERY_UNIT = {
  test: 'if the answer is no, does the work stop?',
  ifNo: 'it is not a discovery question - it is a justification exercise, and should be deleted',
  tooBig: { symptom: 'a broad area examined, findings presented, and by the time anything is tested the context has moved',
            reallyItIs: 'the three-month research phase wearing a new name' },
  tooSmall: { symptom: 'three hypotheses nobody intends to test',
              worseThanNothing: 'because it produces artefacts that look like evidence' },
  rightSize: { hypothesis: 'a belief about somebodys behaviour',
               shape: 'plus a prediction that would falsify it',
               evidenceStandard: 'one option tested against a task, with fifteen people, is not the same as three options tested with five each' },
  whyThatDifference: 'testing alternatives compares them to each other; testing one option against a task tells you whether it works at all',
  misattribution: 'comparing your own options is a delivery-track activity, and mixing them is why teams run three-week bake-offs and learn nothing about whether the problem was real',
};

/* What a validated item carries, and what it must not carry. */
const HANDOFF_CONTRACT = {
  carries: ['the problem stated as somebodys behaviour',
            'the user and the situation attached',
            'the evidence with counts',
            'the riskiest assumption',
            'the specific thing that was tested'],
  mustNotCarry: 'a design',
  why: 'a discovery track that hands over a design has quietly become a delivery track, and the next thing that happens is that the finding is treated as an instruction to build what was already decided',
};

/* What each track is allowed to do to the other. */
const TRACK_RELATIONS = {
  discoveryToDelivery: { handoff: 'a testable artefact', cadence: 'weekly, small',
    whatIsForbidden: 'handing over the solution' },
  deliveryToDiscovery: { obligation: 'ship and measure',
    whyThisDirectionMatters: 'the loop closes only when a shipped thing is looked at, so a delivery track that does not measure has broken the method rather than shortened it',
    whatGetsFedBack: ['the number after launch', 'the support contacts', 'what users did that nobody predicted'] },
  bothBlockedBy: 'the three-month phase - the same failure in both directions',
};

/* The artefacts a dual-track programme must produce, and their only purpose. */
const ARTEFACTS = [
  { artefact: 'the hypothesis board', purpose: 'makes visible what is currently believed, including the beliefs nobody has tested',
    failureIfAbsent: 'three beliefs in the room, one of them tested, nobody knowing which' },
  { artefact: 'the test log', purpose: 'records what was tested, with what, and what happened - and it is what stops the same test being run twice',
    failureIfAbsent: 'the team re-tests the assumption it refuted in month one, because the finding was verbal' },
  { artefact: 'the decision record', purpose: 'what was decided and on what evidence',
    failureIfAbsent: 'the same question returns in two quarters because nobody can find the answer' },
];

A side-by-side view of dual-track agile: small discovery always running while delivery builds. Notice the anti-pattern warning against a giant research phase before a giant build.

23.5 The business case for UX

The business case for UX is money talk: estimating what usability problems cost and what improvements return. Convert findings into dollars where possible, such as support tickets, refunds, churn, or abandoned conversions, then present choices rather than complaints. Fixing a high-cost failure usually pays for itself, and the numbers make the request defendable. A phrase such as users are confused becomes a costed, prioritized claim the budget can evaluate.

  • Poor UX has measurable price tags: abandoned checkouts, support tickets, failed onboarding, churn.
  • Presenting: "fix onboarding checkout = +4% conversion" (from research) beats "users are confused". Estimate in money, present in choices (Ch.19).
  • Know where design ROI is highest at your company: acquisition, activation, support deflection, retention — go where the biggest leak is (Ch.18.1 funnel instinct).

Building the number, and being honest about it

The cost of a usability problem is countable in three ways and they should be used in a fixed order, because they get less speculative as you go and the more expensive one is the one that sounds best in a business meeting. Direct cost: support contacts, chargebacks, refunds, returns, failed payments, manual workarounds. These are in the finance system, they are attributable, and they are the easiest number to defend — so start here, because a number the CFO already recognises needs no argument about method. Lost value: the conversion rate, the churn, the users who never activate, the seats that were never sold. These are the biggest and the most frequently overstated, because they multiply an assumed counterfactual — the lift you would have got from the fix. Opportunity cost: the roadmap capacity spent on the workaround instead of the thing. This is the largest and the least credible, and it should be the last thing you say rather than the first, because a number that large and that soft undermines everything else in the argument.

The estimation method matters more than the arithmetic, and the method is what protects you. For a direct cost, count it: pull the ticket volume for the failing flow and multiply by the handling cost. For a lost conversion, do not multiply the whole funnel — find the step where people leave, take the traffic that reaches it, and multiply by the observed abandonment rate and the value of the thing they abandoned. The distinction is not pedantic: multiplying a whole funnel by a rate is how a design team ends up claiming a number two orders of magnitude too large, and being caught doing it destroys the credibility of the next three requests. For opportunity cost, do not quantify it at all — name it, and put a name and a headcount next to it.

Then how to present it, which is the actual skill. Present as a choice with two options and two numbers, not as a request with one number: here is what this problem costs per month in support volume, here is what the fix costs in engineering time, and here is the month it breaks even. That framing survives a budget meeting because it is not asking for anything — it is presenting a fact about which of two things is cheaper, and the room chooses. It also survives the objection, because there is nothing to object to beyond the inputs, and you can show the inputs. Add the confidence explicitly: state whether the number is measured, derived from a benchmark, or estimated, and never present the three with equal weight. A stated estimate is defensible; an estimate presented as a measurement is not, and the difference between those two is the whole reputation of design in a finance-led organisation.

The objections, answered before they are made

Every business case for design work meets the same four objections, and each has a specific answer that works better than a defence. "We do not know the counterfactual." True, and it cuts both ways: nobody knows what would have happened without the work either, which is why the honest presentation is a range rather than a point. Give the low case, the central case and the high case, say which inputs they rest on, and let the room pick the case it believes. A range survives a sceptical finance partner; a point estimate does not, and the point estimate is the one that gets picked apart. "Users are used to this." Also true, and it is a statement about tolerance rather than about experience — being used to an interface is not evidence that it works, and the honest test is behavioural: does this flow have a support cost, an abandonment rate, and an error rate, and are those numbers good? A habit that costs a hundred support contacts a month is a habit the company is paying for.

"We can fix it in engineering for less." Sometimes true, and the productive version of the conversation is about which fix. The design work is not the whole fix; it is the part that decides what the fix should be, and a cheap engineering fix to an ambiguously specified problem produces a screen that is technically faster and still confusing. If they want to do it in engineering, the useful contribution is a decision record: what the problem is, what has been ruled out, what the state should be, and what would tell us it worked. That document is worth more than the fix, and it is a way of being useful in a room where your work is not being bought. "We need to hit the date." Then scope down rather than compromise on quality: which of these three parts of the flow is the date actually waiting for? Frequently a small part of a large redesign is on the critical path and the rest was added because the redesign was already happening — and removing the rest is a design decision, and it is the cheapest one available.

What design ROI actually looks like over time

The four places it is highest were named above, and the pattern across all of them is that the return is not in the flow itself but in everything downstream of it. A first-run experience that works produces an activated user base, and an activated base changes every downstream number — retention, support cost, referral, expansion — rather than one of them. That is why the first-run experience is usually the highest-return design work in a product and why it is chronically under-invested, because the work is invisible in any single month's numbers. The same logic applies to self-service and to the surfaces that remove a need to contact a company, where the return shows up in a cost centre rather than in a product metric and is therefore invisible to the people who own the product metric.

Two honest caveats to state before somebody else states them. Design work has a long tail, and the value of a design system or of an accessibility programme does not appear in the quarter it was built; anyone who claims a three-week return on a system has described a tactical fix and called it a system. And attribution is genuinely hard, because the strongest design work changes what a team believes, and belief changes take eighteen months to appear in a number — so a design organisation that only measures directly attributable flow improvements will systematically under-invest in exactly the work that compounds. The way out is not a better attribution method; it is to keep a small number of the direct measurements, so the organisation has numbers it trusts, and to be honest about the rest.

/* The four objections and the answer that works better than a defence. */
const OBJECTIONS = [
  { objection: 'we do not know the counterfactual',
    truth: 'true, and it cuts both ways - nobody knows what would have happened without the work either',
    answer: 'give a range: low, central, high; name the inputs each rests on; let the room pick the case it believes',
    why: 'a range survives a sceptical finance partner; a point estimate gets picked apart, and the point estimate is what gets attacked' },

  { objection: 'users are used to this',
    truth: 'true, and it is a statement about tolerance rather than experience',
    counter: 'behavioural: does this flow have a support cost, an abandonment rate and an error rate, and are they good?',
    line: 'a habit that costs a hundred support contacts a month is a habit the company is paying for' },

  { objection: 'we can fix it in engineering for less',
    sometimesTrue: true,
    productiveFraming: 'the question is which fix, not whether',
    insight: 'design work is not the whole fix; it decides what the fix should be, and a cheap engineering fix to an ambiguously specified problem produces a faster screen that is still confusing',
    ifTheyProceed: ['a decision record: the problem, what has been ruled out, what the state should be, what would tell us it worked',
                    'worth more than the fix, and a way of being useful in a room where your work is not being bought'] },

  { objection: 'we need to hit the date',
    answer: 'scope down rather than compromise on quality',
    question: 'which of these three parts of the flow is the date waiting for?',
    insight: 'frequently one small part of a large redesign is on the critical path and the rest was added because the redesign was happening - removing it is a design decision, and the cheapest one available' },
];

/* Where the return actually is: everything downstream of the flow. */
const ROI_SHAPE = {
  mechanism: 'the return is not in the flow, it is in everything downstream of it',
  example: 'a working first-run experience produces an activated base, and an activated base changes retention, support cost, referral and expansion - not one of them',
  whyUnderInvested: 'the work is invisible in any single months numbers',
  second: 'self-service and surfaces that remove a need to contact a company',
  whyAlsoInvisible: 'the return lands in a cost centre rather than a product metric, so it is invisible to the people who own the product metric',
};

const HONEST_CAVEATS = [
  { caveat: 'design work has a long tail',
    consequence: 'the value of a design system or an accessibility programme does not appear in the quarter it was built',
    trap: 'anyone claiming a three-week return on a system has described a tactical fix and called it a system' },
  { caveat: 'attribution is genuinely hard',
    why: 'the strongest design work changes what a team believes, and belief changes take eighteen months to appear in a number',
    resultingBias: 'an organisation measuring only directly attributable flow improvements under-invests in exactly the work that compounds',
    wayOut: 'not a better attribution method - keep a small number of direct measurements so the organisation has numbers it trusts, and be honest about the rest',
];

Where to spend the effort is a funnel question, not a preference. Acquisition problems are usually marketing's, and design's contribution is usually the form, the trust signals and the friction — worth working on if the traffic is qualified, because improving a conversion rate on unqualified traffic mostly produces more unqualified traffic. Activation is almost always design's, because activation is a first-run experience and first-run experiences are pure interface. Support deflection is design's and is measured in the cost centre. Retention is design's only when the churn is caused by something a person does rather than something they were promised — a product that churns because the plan did not fit is a pricing problem wearing a design costume. So: go where the biggest leak is, and go where the leak is caused by something you can actually change.

/* Three ways to count it, in order of decreasing defensibility. Present in
   this order - the biggest and softest is the last thing you say. */
const COST_METHODS = [
  { method: 'direct cost', largest: false, defensible: 'highest',
    examples: ['support contacts', 'chargebacks', 'refunds', 'returns', 'failed payments', 'manual workarounds'],
    where: 'the finance system', whyStartHere: 'a number the CFO already recognises needs no argument about method',
    how: 'pull the ticket volume for the failing flow and multiply by the handling cost' },

  { method: 'lost value', largest: true, mostOverstated: true,
    examples: ['the conversion rate', 'churn', 'users who never activate', 'unsold seats'],
    whyOverstated: 'it multiplies an assumed counterfactual - the lift you would have got from the fix',
    how: { doNot: 'multiply the whole funnel by a rate - this produces a number two orders of magnitude too large',
           do: 'find the step where people leave, take the traffic that reaches it, multiply by the observed abandonment rate and the value of the thing abandoned' },
    consequenceOfGettingItWrong: 'being caught destroys the credibility of the next three requests' },

  { method: 'opportunity cost', largest: 'largest', credible: 'lowest',
    how: 'do not quantify it - name it, and put a name and a headcount next to it' },
];

/* How to present, so the room chooses rather than grants. */
const PRESENTATION = {
  notThis: 'a request with one number',
  this: 'a choice with two options and two numbers',
  script: ['this problem costs this much per month in support volume',
           'the fix costs this much in engineering time',
           'it breaks even in this many months'],
  whyItSurvives: 'it is not asking for anything - it is presenting a fact about which of two things is cheaper, and the room chooses',
  survivesObjection: 'because there is nothing to object to beyond the inputs, and you can show the inputs',
  confidenceMustBeStated: ['measured', 'derived from a benchmark', 'estimated'],
  neverPresentEqually: true,
  why: 'a stated estimate is defensible; an estimate presented as a measurement is not, and that difference is designs reputation in a finance-led organisation',
};

/* Where the effort goes. A funnel question, not a preference. */
const WHERE_TO_SPEND = [
  { leak: 'acquisition', usuallyOwnedBy: 'marketing',
    designContributes: ['the form', 'trust signals', 'friction'],
    worthItIf: 'the traffic is qualified',
    warning: 'improving conversion on unqualified traffic mostly produces more unqualified traffic' },
  { leak: 'activation', usuallyOwnedBy: 'design',
    why: 'activation is a first-run experience and first-run experiences are pure interface' },
  { leak: 'support deflection', usuallyOwnedBy: 'design', measuredIn: 'the cost centre' },
  { leak: 'retention', designOnlyWhen: 'the churn is caused by something a person does rather than something they were promised',
    warning: 'a product that churns because the plan did not fit is a pricing problem wearing a design costume' },
];
// go where the biggest leak is, and where the leak is caused by something you can change
