24 · Service Design & Blueprints

Service design extends UX off the screen to entire journeys across apps, channels, people, and departments. Its core tools include journey maps and service blueprints that expose both frontstage touchpoints and the backstage operations beneath them. The goal is a service that behaves well end to end through every handoff and system, not just a polished touchpoint. It coordinates product designers, operations, and support behind one shared picture.

24.1 Service vs product: the whole journey24.2 Reading & building a service blueprint24.3 Omnichannel: one memory across channels24.4 Back-stage UX: your employees are users too24.5 Prototyping services (before you build the whole thing)24.6 Measuring a service (not just its app)

Products live inside services. A refund touches the app, the warehouse, the courier and support. Service design is UX taken off the screen: designing entire experiences across channels, people and departments.

24.1 Service vs product: the whole journey

A product is a moment in a journey, while a service is the whole journey from need to outcome across channels and over time. Screen-level UX optimizes each touchpoint, but service design manages the complete experience including arrivals, handoffs, and endings. The distinction changes what you measure and where you look for breakdowns. Design the end-to-end experience and let screen-level UX serve the whole rather than the reverse.

Screen-level UXService design
Unit of designa flow or screenthe end-to-end customer journey
Crossesone channelapp + web + phone + physical + back-office
Involvesusersusers + staff + operations + partners
Key outputprototypeservice blueprint + prototypes of parts

Where services break, and why screens hide it

A service breaks at its seams, and the reason screen-level UX cannot see them is structural rather than a matter of attention: the seam is between two actors, and each actor's screen is designed by a different person with a different success definition. The customer has finished; the colleague has begun. Nobody owns the interval. So the classic failures are not interface defects at all — they are the customer repeating information the colleague can already see, the colleague making a decision the customer was never told about, a promise made at the front that the back office cannot keep, and a hand-off with no acknowledgement, so the customer does not know whether to wait or do something.

The three shapes of breakdown are worth naming because they have different fixes. Handoff ambiguity: the transfer of responsibility is not marked, so both parties believe the other has it. The fix is structural — a named owner per state, and a visible acknowledgement to the customer that it is now in someone else's hands. Context loss: the receiving actor has to re-establish what the customer wants, which converts a five-minute interaction into a fifteen-minute one and produces a visible stumble on the channel the customer can see. Promise gap: what the front says will happen and the back does differently — a delivery window, a refund amount, a response time — and this is the one that produces complaints and churn, because the customer's first experience is of being told something and the second is of it not happening.

Researching a service instead of a screen

Screen research has a method and it does not transfer. Nobody will sit through twenty usability sessions on a service, and if they agree to it the data is useless — the first two minutes of a service journey are spent establishing context, and a person who does that twenty times has opinions rather than findings. So the methods have to be different and they are cheaper. Shadowing: follow a customer through one real episode, in person, and watch where they hesitate, leave the system, or do something you did not predict. One episode produces more about a service than twenty sessions, because the interaction is not the artefact being tested. Frontstage–backstage pairing: sit with the person doing each back-office step for an hour and count the times they leave the system. The complaint as a data source: read a hundred of them and code them by which step of the blueprint they occurred at — complaints are unusually well-located because the person was frustrated enough to write. Front-office shadowing of the colleague: sit in a contact centre and listen to fifty calls, because the language the customer uses and the language the screen uses diverge within the first two minutes, and the divergence is usually invisible to anybody who designs from requirements.

What these produce that a usability session cannot is a list of friction that nobody designed — the waits, the repetitions, the moments where the customer changes channel because the process does not support what they are doing. And that list is the more valuable output, because designed friction can be argued about and undDesigned friction usually cannot: nobody will defend a three-day delay on a refund, but somebody will defend a form field, and the list tells you which is which.

Making the case for service work

Service work is harder to fund than screen work for a reason that is worth naming rather than working around: its value is distributed across departments and its cost is on one balance sheet. A screen improvement has a traceable line from a number to a change. A service improvement moves three numbers owned by three teams and shows up in none of their quarterly reviews. So the argument has to be built differently — as a total cost across departments, or as a removal rather than an addition, or as a fix to a number that is already visible and already somebody's target.

The most effective of those is the removal argument. "We will stop asking customers for this four times" is a cost reduction somebody owns, because it removes work rather than adding it, and the departments that benefit are the ones who were doing the re-asking. The second is the total-cost argument: an abandonment at step four is a support contact, a retraining, a refund, a churned customer, and a marketing cost of acquiring the next one — all in different places, all attributable to the same step of the blueprint. Put them in one line and the number is usually an order of magnitude larger than the screen-level view of the same journey. And the third is to attach the work to a number somebody already owns, which is slower but has a much higher hit rate, because a metric with an owner has a budget and a metric without one has a discussion.

/* Screen research does not transfer, and the reason is structural. */
const WHY_SCREEN_METHODS_FAIL = {
  nobodyWillDo20Sessions: true,
  andIfTheyDo: 'the first two minutes of a service journey are spent establishing context',
  result: 'after twenty, the participant has opinions rather than findings',
};

/* Four methods that do work, all cheaper. */
const SERVICE_RESEARCH = [
  { method: 'shadowing', how: 'follow a customer through one real episode, in person',
    watchFor: ['hesitation', 'leaving the system', 'doing something you did not predict'],
    yield: 'one episode produces more about a service than twenty sessions, because the interaction is not the artefact being tested' },
  { method: 'frontstage-backstage pairing', how: 'sit with the person doing each back-office step for an hour',
    count: 'how many times they leave the system' },
  { method: 'complaints as data', how: 'read a hundred and code them by which step of the blueprint they occurred at',
    whyItWorks: 'complaints are unusually well-located because the person was frustrated enough to write' },
  { method: 'call listening', how: 'sit in a contact centre and listen to fifty',
    finds: 'the language the customer uses and the language the screen uses diverge within two minutes',
    invisibleTo: 'anybody who designs from requirements' },
];

const WHAT_THESE_PRODUCE = {
  item: 'friction that nobody designed',
  examples: ['the waits', 'the repetitions', 'changing channel because the process does not support what they are doing'],
  whyMoreValuable: 'designed friction can be argued about; undesigned friction usually cannot',
  exampleOfTheAsymmetry: 'nobody will defend a three-day refund delay, but somebody will defend a form field',
};

/* Why service work is harder to fund, and three arguments that work. */
const FUNDING = {
  reason: 'its value is distributed across departments and its cost sits on one balance sheet',
  contrast: 'a screen improvement has a traceable line from a number to a change; a service improvement moves three numbers owned by three teams',
  arguments: [
    { argument: 'the removal', say: 'we will stop asking customers for this four times',
      whyItWorks: 'it removes work rather than adding it, and the departments that benefit are the ones doing the re-asking',
      hitRate: 'highest' },
    { argument: 'the total cost', build: 'abandonment at step four = a support contact + a retraining + a refund + a churned customer + the marketing cost of the next one',
      effect: 'in one line, the number is usually an order of magnitude larger than the screen-level view of the same journey' },
    { argument: 'attach to an owned metric', hitRate: 'lower per attempt, higher when it lands',
      why: 'a metric with an owner has a budget and a metric without one has a discussion' },
  ],
};

Then the four moments the table above implies and screen-level work systematically omits. Arrival: how does somebody discover that this service exists, and how do they find out what to do first? This is where most services lose people, and it is usually owned by marketing and by a page nobody from the product team has read. Onboarding into the service, as distinct from onboarding into the account — the first successful outcome, which is the moment the customer decides whether the thing works. Handoff between channels and between people, covered in the next section. And the ending: how the service ends, whether that is cancellation, completion, or a decision to go elsewhere. The ending is where trust is decided and it is almost never designed; every organisation has a defined entry and an undefined exit.

/* Why screen-level UX cannot see the seams. */
const WHY_SEAMS_HIDE = {
  structuralReason: 'a seam is between two actors; each actors screen is designed by a different person with a different success definition',
  neitherSideOwnsIt: 'the customer has finished, the colleague has begun, nobody owns the interval',
  therefore: 'the classic failures are not interface defects',
  failures: [
    'the customer repeating information the colleague can already see',
    'the colleague making a decision the customer was never told about',
    'a promise made at the front that the back office cannot keep',
    'a handoff with no acknowledgement, so the customer does not know whether to wait or do something',
  ],
};

/* Three shapes of breakdown, three different fixes. */
const BREAKDOWN = [
  { shape: 'handoff ambiguity', meaning: 'the transfer of responsibility is not marked, so both sides believe the other has it',
    fix: 'a named owner per state, and a visible acknowledgement to the customer that it is now in someones hands' },
  { shape: 'context loss', meaning: 'the receiving actor must re-establish what the customer wants',
    effect: 'converts a five-minute interaction into a fifteen-minute one and produces a visible stumble',
    on: 'the channel the customer can see, which is why it reads as a service failure rather than a staffing one' },
  { shape: 'promise gap', meaning: 'what the front says will happen and the back does differently - a window, a refund, a response time',
    severity: 'the one that produces complaints and churn',
    why: 'the customers first experience is of being told something and the second is of it not happening' },
];

/* The four moments screen-level work omits. */
const MOMENTS = [
  { moment: 'arrival', means: 'how somebody discovers the service exists and finds out what to do first',
    wherePeopleAreLost: 'most services lose people here',
    ownership: 'marketing and a page nobody from the product team has read' },
  { moment: 'onboarding into the service, not the account', means: 'the first successful outcome',
    why: 'the customer decides here whether the thing works at all' },
  { moment: 'handoff between channels and between people', see: 'omnichannel, next section' },
  { moment: 'the ending', means: 'cancellation, completion, or a decision to go elsewhere',
    whereTrustIsDecided: true, usuallyDesigned: false,
    pattern: 'every organisation has a defined entry and an undefined exit' },
];

24.2 Reading & building a service blueprint

A service blueprint is a journey map with the operations layered underneath it, showing what the user sees and what invisibly supports it. Layers include the user journey, frontstage employee actions, backstage actions, and support processes, each annotated with evidence, pain, and failure points. Build one by walking a real journey with whoever owns it and mapping cost and system dependencies at each step. The invisible backstage layers are where cost, bugs, and broken promises breed.

Blueprint = a journey map with the OPERATIONS underneath it.
      customer actions:   requests return  →  gets label  →  drops off
      ── FRONT OF STAGE ────────────────────────────────
      touchpoints:        app form        →  email        →  courier
      ── BACK OF STAGE ────────────────────────────────
      staff actions:      approves return →  books pickup →  checks-in
      processes:          RMA queue       →  label engine →  hub routing
      ── SUPPORT ────────────────────────────────────────
      tools:              order DB       →  print job    →  courier API
// Lines between layers = where experience and operations meet.
// The "line of internal interaction" (tools) is where costs breed bugs
// invisible to users — until the promise they break shows up in reviews.

Building one that is worth the wall space

The blueprint is a diagnostic instrument rather than a presentation, and the difference shows up in what you do to build it. The method is a walkthrough with three to five people: one who has recently used the service, one who performs each step in the back office, and one who owns the process. You go left to right along a real journey, one step at a time, and at each step you fill every layer. The discipline that makes it work is that you do not describe anything — you ask what happens. "What do you do next?" produces the backstage action; "what would tell you that was wrong?" produces the failure point; "how long does that take?" produces the cost, which is the number that makes the later business case possible.

Three annotations carry most of the value. The failure point at each step, with what the customer sees when it fails and what the colleague sees — the asymmetry between those two is where the cost is hidden. The wait: queue time, elapsed time, and number of handoffs, because a journey with no failure can still be unbearable purely through waiting and it is invisible on any screen. The evidence: a ticket reference, a policy name, a system, a person, so each claim on the blueprint can be checked — a blueprint without evidence becomes a debate about memory, and everybody remembers the step they personally own.

Then the two lines that matter most, and the second is the one that changes budgets. The line of interaction is where the customer meets the organisation directly: frontstage employee actions and the touchpoints the customer sees. The line of internal interaction is where the organisation meets itself — the backstage actions, the processes and the tools one department's output is another's input. Every cost, every delay and every bug in a service lives on or below that second line, and it is invisible to the customer until a promise it broke surfaces in a review or a complaint. Design review that looks only above the line will miss the majority of what makes a service expensive.

/* The build. A walkthrough, not a description. */
const BUILD = {
  participants: ['one person who used the service recently',
                 'one person who performs each step in the back office',
                 'one person who owns the process'],
  method: 'left to right along a real journey, one step at a time, filling every layer',
  rule: 'do not describe anything - ask',
  questions: [
    { ask: 'what do you do next?', reveals: 'the backstage action' },
    { ask: 'what would tell you that was wrong?', reveals: 'the failure point' },
    { ask: 'how long does that take?', reveals: 'the cost, which is what makes the business case possible later' },
  ],
  annotationsThatCarryTheValue: [
    { what: 'the failure point', reveal: 'the asymmetry between what the customer sees and what the colleague sees - that asymmetry is where the cost is hidden' },
    { what: 'the wait', detail: ['queue time', 'elapsed time', 'number of handoffs'],
      why: 'a journey with no failure can still be unbearable purely through waiting, and it is invisible on any screen' },
    { what: 'the evidence', detail: ['a ticket reference', 'a policy name', 'a system', 'a person'],
      why: 'without it a blueprint becomes a debate about memory, and everybody remembers the step they personally own' },
  ],
};

/* The two lines. The second one is where the money is. */
const LINES = {
  lineOfInteraction: { what: 'where the customer meets the organisation directly',
                       contains: ['frontstage employee actions', 'the touchpoints the customer sees'] },
  lineOfInternalInteraction: { what: 'where the organisation meets itself',
                                contains: ['backstage actions', 'processes', 'tools'],
                                relationship: 'one departments output is anothers input' },
  conclusion: 'every cost, delay and bug lives on or below the second line, and it is invisible to the customer until a promise it broke surfaces in a review or a complaint',
  consequence: 'design review that looks only above the line misses most of what makes a service expensive',
};

An ASCII service blueprint layering customer actions, touchpoints, staff work, and support tools. Notice the dividing lines where experience meets operations and unreliability gets born.

24.3 Omnichannel: one memory across channels

Omnichannel means one consistent customer memory across every channel, so web, app, phone, and store tell the same story. The goal is seamless handoffs: no user should repeat themselves, re-verify what they just proved, or start over on the next device. In practice this is shared data, preserved context, and consistent service logic rather than another login. Context should travel with the user.

  • State carries across channels: a draft started on web finishes on mobile; support knowing what the app just showed.
  • Channel handoff should never require repetition ("read me your order number again"). That’s a UX failure of the back office, not the app.

    • Designing a handoff, specifically

    A handoff is a protocol with three parties and it needs three things: what state exists, who is now responsible, and what the customer is told. Teams usually specify the first two and forget the third, which is why handoffs feel like being dropped even when the work is proceeding correctly. The specification is short enough to write in a card. Before: the state, the data, and whether anything is in progress. During: the named owner from the moment of transfer, and the mechanism — an explicit assignment, not an implicit one. After: the acknowledgement to the customer, with a time and a channel, plus the internal note that carries the context the colleague will need so they do not ask for it again.

    The failure reply is the part that is missing almost everywhere. Every handoff needs a defined behaviour for the three states that will actually happen: the colleague cannot find the record, the policy does not cover the case, and the customer has disappeared. Without a defined reply each of these becomes improvisation by whoever is nearest, which is the mechanism by which a well-run operation produces inconsistent outcomes. With one, the improvisation is a bounded set of decisions the organisation has already made — and the blueprint's "failure reply" column is where those three replies get written down, which is a much better place to discover that nobody agreed on them than a customer complaint.

    The four repetitions that define omnichannel quality

    "Seamless" is not a quality; these four are. Re-verification: proving an identity again on a second channel because the systems do not share it. The cost is disproportionate to the inconvenience — a person who has to re-verify will describe the service as exhausting regardless of how fast everything else is. Re-statement: describing a situation again because the context did not travel, and the common instance is being asked for an order number by a colleague who can see it. Re-entry: filling in a form again, typically on a different device, because nothing was saved; the failure of this is the one that most reliably produces abandonment, because the person has already invested and now sees the cost stated twice. Re-explanation: explaining the same policy or fee to a second actor, which is where the front and the back disagree with each other in front of the customer.

    Designing for the discontinuity

    The interesting failures in omnichannel are not in the continuous cases, where a person moves from phone to app mid-session and everything is synchronised. They are in the discontinuous ones: an overnight gap, a device that is not the same device, an entry through a channel with no account, a return after weeks. In those cases the state has aged and something has to decide what a draft from nine days ago means. Three policies, and each has to be chosen deliberately because the default is that whatever the code happens to do is the policy. Expire and tell the person: old drafts are discarded and the person is told, rather than restored into a session that no longer makes sense. Restore with a summary: the state comes back but is presented as "here is what you had" with the staleness visible, so the person can decide. Keep indefinitely: correct only where the state is cheap and stable, and it is almost never about a form in progress.

    The second discontinuity is identity. A person who entered through a channel that does not require an account has a session, not an identity, and the moment they enter through a channel that does require one there is a merging question: do you match them silently on an email address, do you ask, or do you leave them as two records? All three are defensible and they have very different consequences — silent matching on an email address that a household shares will merge two people and then produce a data-protection incident; asking costs a moment; leaving two records creates a support problem later. The design answer is to ask, at the moment it matters, and to say what merging does and does not do, because a surprising silent merge is worse than an extra step.

    Then the fallback question, which almost nobody answers in advance. Any omnichannel service has channels that fail — an outage, a version of an app that is three releases behind, a third-party provider being down — and the fallback decision belongs to design because it is a customer-facing behaviour. What does the person see? Is the error specific? Is there a route to another channel and does it carry the state? Is the system honest about whether the thing was recorded? The specific failure worth designing for is the partial failure, where the action appears to have succeeded and has not, because that is the one that produces duplicate work and duplicate payments — and the check that catches it is asking whether every channel's success message means the same thing, which is a semantic question that no test on one channel will reveal.

    /* The interesting failures are discontinuities, not continuous sessions. */
const DISCONTINUITIES = {
  cases: ['an overnight gap', 'a device that is not the same device', 'entry through a channel with no account', 'a return after weeks'],
  theRealQuestion: 'the state has aged - what does a draft from nine days ago mean?',
  problem: 'the default is that whatever the code happens to do is the policy',
  policies: [
    { policy: 'expire and tell the person', behaviour: 'old drafts are discarded and the person is told',
      notThis: 'restoring into a session that no longer makes sense' },
    { policy: 'restore with a summary', behaviour: 'the state comes back as "here is what you had", with the staleness visible, so the person can decide' },
    { policy: 'keep indefinitely', correctOnlyWhen: 'the state is cheap and stable',
      almostNever: 'a form in progress' },
  ],
};

/* Identity across channels. */
const IDENTITY_MERGE = {
  situation: 'a person enters through a channel with no account and then through one that requires it',
  options: [
    { option: 'silent match on an email address', risk: 'a household-shared address merges two people and then produces a data-protection incident' },
    { option: 'ask', cost: 'a moment' },
    { option: 'leave two records', consequence: 'a support problem later' },
  ],
  answer: 'ask, at the moment it matters, and say what merging does and does not do',
  why: 'a surprising silent merge is worse than an extra step',
};

/* Fallbacks, decided in advance by design because it is customer-facing. */
const FALLBACKS = {
  trigger: ['an outage', 'an app three releases behind', 'a third-party provider down'],
  owner: 'design, because the fallback is a customer-facing behaviour',
  questions: ['what does the person see?', 'is the error specific?',
              'is there a route to another channel and does it carry the state?',
              'is the system honest about whether the thing was recorded?'],
  designSpecifically: { partialFailure: 'the action appears to have succeeded and has not',
    consequence: 'duplicate work and duplicate payments',
    check: 'ask whether every channels success message means the same thing',
    whyNotACaughtByTesting: 'it is a semantic question, and no test on one channel reveals it' },
};

    Two design consequences. First, state needs an explicit owner and an explicit lifetime: a draft is not a draft forever, and the question of what happens when a channel is closed mid-flow has to be answered deliberately rather than discovered. Second, consistent service logic is a separate requirement from shared data — the channels can hold the same record and still give different answers, and the customer experiences that as the company contradicting itself rather than as two systems disagreeing. So the test for omnichannel quality is not "can the agent see the customer's history" but "does the customer have to say anything twice" — and the second question is the one you can actually run a test on.

    /* A handoff is a protocol with three parties. Teams specify the first two
   states and forget the third, which is why handoffs feel like being dropped. */
const HANDOFF_PROTOCOL = {
  before:  { state: 'what state exists', data: 'what data travels', inProgress: 'is anything in progress' },
  during:  { owner: 'named, from the moment of transfer', mechanism: 'an explicit assignment, never an implicit one' },
  after:   { toCustomer: 'an acknowledgement with a time and a channel',
             toColleague: 'the internal note carrying the context they would otherwise have to ask for' },
  whatTeamsForget: 'the acknowledgement to the customer, which is why a handoff that is proceeding correctly still feels like being dropped',
};

/* The failure reply - missing almost everywhere, and improvisation is the
   mechanism by which a well-run operation produces inconsistent outcomes. */
const FAILURE_REPLY = {
  statesThatWillActuallyHappen: ['the colleague cannot find the record',
                                 'the policy does not cover the case',
                                 'the customer has disappeared'],
  withoutADefinedReply: 'each becomes improvisation by whoever is nearest',
  with: 'improvisation is a bounded set of decisions the organisation already made',
  whereToDiscoverNobodyAgreed: 'the blueprint failure-reply column - much better than a customer complaint',
};

/* "Seamless" is not a quality. These four are. */
const REPETITIONS = [
  { kind: 're-verification', means: 'proving identity again on a second channel because systems do not share it',
    cost: 'disproportionate to the inconvenience - a person who re-verifies describes the service as exhausting regardless of how fast everything else is' },
  { kind: 're-statement', means: 'describing the situation again because context did not travel',
    commonInstance: 'being asked for an order number by a colleague who can see it' },
  { kind: 're-entry', means: 'filling in a form again, typically on another device, because nothing was saved',
    whyWorst: 'it most reliably produces abandonment, because the person has already invested and now sees the cost stated twice' },
  { kind: 're-explanation', means: 'explaining the same policy or fee to a second actor',
    why: 'that is where the front and the back disagree in front of the customer' },
];

const OMNI_TESTS = [
  { requirement: 'state needs an explicit owner and an explicit lifetime',
    unansweredQuestion: 'what happens when a channel is closed mid-flow - decide it, do not discover it' },
  { requirement: 'consistent service logic is separate from shared data',
    why: 'two channels can hold the same record and still give different answers, and the customer experiences that as the company contradicting itself' },
  { requirement: 'the runnable test', question: 'does the customer have to say anything twice?',
    why: 'not "can the agent see the history" - that one is a systems question and this one is a design question' },
];
  • Map every handoff in the blueprint with an owner + SLA + failure reply. If the italicized step has no owner, that’s your redesign target.

24.4 Back-stage UX: your employees are users too

Back-stage UX treats the staff operating an internal system as users worth designing for, because tired or frustrated employees become customer pain. Internal tools deserve the same research, usability testing, and error prevention as front-stage software, including efficient workflows, bulk actions, and clear status. When a backend is confusing, mistakes leak to customers as wrong orders, slow answers, or mixed messages. Designing the backstage keeps front-stage promises true.

Designing for the person operating the thing

Internal tools are used for hours at a time under time pressure, often by people who were not hired for the role they are performing and were trained in a week. That combination changes every design decision, and the changes are systematic rather than cosmetic. Density beats whitespace, because the operator's constraint is time and each row of scrolling is a cost paid on every item. Keyboard over mouse, because the hands are busy and a mouse is slower than a shortcut. Batch over single, because operators process queues rather than individuals. Persistence over confirmations, because a confirmation dialog on an action they take a hundred times a day is a decision they will learn to dismiss without reading — which is the failure mode of every safety mechanism, and the reason the safety mechanism stops working precisely where it was needed.

The error-prevention argument is the strongest one and it is a business argument, so it is the one to make. Undo beats confirm, every time, because a confirm dialog produces the two habits that make it useless: reflexive dismissal and alert fatigue, and a person who has dismissed nine hundred dialogs does not read the thousandth. Where an action genuinely cannot be undone — sending, deleting, charging — the confirmation must be specific rather than generic, so the words are the name of the thing and the consequence, and the destructive action must not be the default focus. And where an action is high-volume, put the safety in the system rather than in the interface: a validation rule that catches the mistake before the record is created, a limit on the amount, a required second factor for the one action that is genuinely irreversible.

How to research the back office properly

Frontstage research methods are almost all wrong for backstage work, and the reasons are specific. You cannot watch someone use a tool for an hour and conclude anything useful about a task they have done ten thousand times, because the competence has moved from conscious procedure into habit and what you observe is the residue. Nor can you ask an operator to think aloud about something they do while answering a queue. What works instead is three techniques, and all three are more work than a usability test. Diary studies: the operator logs what they did and what interrupted them for two weeks, which is the only reliable way to find out what they actually spend their time on rather than what the process says they should. Work sampling at the boundary: count, for a week, every time the operator opens something that is not the tool, and record what it was for. That list is the tool's real design brief. Shadow the queue at peak: peak is when the design matters, because the graceful degradation of a tool is what shows up under load, and the behaviour under peak is nothing like the behaviour in a quiet afternoon.

Then the two artefacts that change backstage design more than any feature. The exception catalogue: every case that does not follow the expected path, with a frequency, so the team can see which are frequent enough to be in the main flow and which belong in a queue somebody handles. This is normally a surprise, because the frequency distribution is almost always bimodal — a long tail of one-offs and a handful of cases that account for most of the time — and the handful is usually not in the design at all. And the latency budget: what the operator can do while waiting, and what they currently do while waiting, which is usually nothing visible to the customer but is where half their working day goes.

And the measurement, because internal tools are measured worse than any other software and the standard is poor. Count: tasks per hour against a baseline, which is the only number that matters to an operator and the one nobody collects because it is noisy. Quality: the exception rate — what share of items required intervention, since an operator who fixes a hundred records a day and an operator who fixes one in ten are equally invisible to the business until something goes wrong. And learning: time to competence for a new hire, which is the strongest argument for good backstage design that exists, because the cost of that time is a known quantity and it is paid by every single person who joins.

/* Frontstage methods are wrong here, and each fails for a reason. */
const WHY_METHODS_FAIL = [
  { method: 'watch an hour of use', failsBecause: 'on a task done ten thousand times, competence has moved from conscious procedure into habit, so what you observe is the residue' },
  { method: 'think aloud', failsBecause: 'they cannot think aloud while answering a queue' },
];

/* What works instead. All three cost more than a usability test. */
const BACKSTAGE_RESEARCH = [
  { method: 'diary studies', how: 'the operator logs what they did and what interrupted them, for two weeks',
    onlyReliableWayTo: 'find out what they actually spend their time on rather than what the process says they should' },
  { method: 'work sampling at the boundary', how: 'for a week, count every time the operator opens something that is not the tool, and record what for',
    yield: 'that list is the tools real design brief' },
  { method: 'shadow the queue at peak', why: 'graceful degradation is what shows up under load, and peak behaviour is nothing like quiet-afternoon behaviour' },
];

/* Two artefacts that change backstage design more than any feature. */
const BACKSTAGE_ARTEFACTS = [
  { artefact: 'the exception catalogue', what: 'every case that does not follow the expected path, with a frequency',
    why: 'the distribution is almost always bimodal - a long tail of one-offs and a handful of cases that account for most of the time',
    surprise: 'the handful is usually not in the design at all' },
  { artefact: 'the latency budget', what: 'what the operator can do while waiting, and what they currently do while waiting',
    whereItGoes: 'often nowhere the customer can see, and it is where half the working day goes' },
];

const BACKSTAGE_METRICS = [
  { metric: 'count', what: 'tasks per hour against a baseline',
    note: 'the only number that matters to an operator, and nobody collects it because it is noisy' },
  { metric: 'quality', what: 'the exception rate - the share of items requiring intervention',
    why: 'an operator who fixes one in ten and one who fixes none are equally invisible until something goes wrong' },
  { metric: 'learning', what: 'time to competence for a new hire',
    whyItIsTheStrongestArgument: 'the cost of that time is a known quantity, paid by every person who joins' },
];

Then the three contexts that get missed. The exception, which is what an operator actually handles all day: the record that does not match, the customer who changed their mind, the payment that reversed. Every tool is designed for the happy path and every operator's day is composed of exceptions, so the exception path deserves the same design effort as the main one and there is a specific technique for it: sit with an operator for an hour and count how many times they leave the system to do something else, because that number is the real measure of internal tool quality. The handover, at shift change, where the context lives in one person's head and the next person starts from nothing. The escalation, where an operator needs authority they do not have, and the design question is whether the authority is available in the flow or requires a message to somebody else.

/* What makes internal tools different. Systematic, not cosmetic. */
const BACKSTAGE = {
  facts: ['used for hours at a time under time pressure',
          'often by people not hired for the role they are performing',
          'trained in a week'],
  consequences: [
    { prefer: 'density', over: 'whitespace', why: 'the constraint is time and every row of scrolling is a cost paid on every item' },
    { prefer: 'keyboard', over: 'mouse', why: 'the hands are busy and a shortcut is faster' },
    { prefer: 'batch', over: 'single', why: 'operators process queues, not individuals' },
    { prefer: 'persistence', over: 'confirmations', why: 'a dialog on an action taken a hundred times a day is a decision they learn to dismiss without reading',
      consequence: 'which is the failure mode of every safety mechanism: it stops working exactly where it was needed' },
  ],
};

/* Error prevention, argued as a business case rather than a safety case. */
const ERROR_PREVENTION = {
  undoBeatsConfirm: { because: 'a confirm dialog produces reflexive dismissal and alert fatigue',
                      consequence: 'a person who has dismissed nine hundred dialogs does not read the thousandth' },
  whereIrreversible: ['the words must be the name of the thing and the consequence',
                      'the destructive action must not be the default focus'],
  whereHighVolume: 'put the safety in the system, not the interface',
  systemLevel: ['a validation rule that catches it before the record is created',
                'a limit on the amount',
                'a required second factor for the one genuinely irreversible action'],
};

/* The three contexts that get missed. */
const MISSED_CONTEXTS = [
  { context: 'the exception', is: 'what an operator actually handles all day',
    examples: ['a record that does not match', 'a customer who changed their mind', 'a payment that reversed'],
    rule: 'every tool is designed for the happy path and every operators day is exceptions',
    technique: 'sit with an operator for an hour and count how many times they leave the system to do something else',
    thatNumber: 'the real measure of internal tool quality' },
  { context: 'the handover', at: 'shift change',
    problem: 'the context lives in one persons head and the next person starts from nothing' },
  { context: 'the escalation', need: 'authority the operator does not have',
    designQuestion: 'is the authority available in the flow, or does it require a message to somebody else' },
];

Customers feel every strike you save. If warehouse staff use a hostile internal tool, returns get slower and sloppier — and customers blame "your app". Design for the staff: kiosk density, scan-first flows, training what to do at exceptions. Internal UX is service design’s highest-leverage shop floor.

24.5 Prototyping services (before you build the whole thing)

Prototyping a service tests the experience before building the whole machine, using cheap methods that reveal the same failures a full build would. Walkthroughs act out the journey step by step, wizard-of-oz hides a human behind a plausible system, and small pilots run the real service with a handful of users. Place prototypes where risk and uncertainty are highest. Adjust and repeat until the journey feels stable.

  • Scene walkthroughs: act out the journey in a room — customers, staff, props (paper tokens as "the app").
  • Wizard-of-Oz: a human secretly simulates the "AI"/back office behind the scenes; you test the experience, not the technology.

    • Choosing the prototype for the uncertainty you have

    Service prototypes differ from screen prototypes in that what you are testing is a claim about how people will behave when several people and systems have to cooperate, and no amount of clicking through a front-end will surface that. So the method has to match the uncertainty, and the uncertainties are four. Does the journey hold together? Test with a scene walkthrough: a room, three to five people, paper tokens standing in for screens, and one person reading a script aloud as though they were a system. It takes ninety minutes and it reliably finds the steps where the customer does not know what is supposed to happen next, because a paper token cannot be forgiving about a missing state. Would the backstage work? Cannot be tested with a customer at all — it is tested by watching the staff, which is a different activity and is the one most often skipped. Would the automation be accepted? Wizard-of-oz: a human behind the curtain producing what would be the automated output. The point is to find out whether people accept the machine's behaviour and correct it when it is wrong, and to count the corrections, because a wizard who is correcting more than about one in five decisions is telling you the decision logic is not ready to automate.

    The rule on placement is simple and worth stating because it is the whole discipline: put the prototype where the risk is, not where the question is easiest to answer. Teams reliably prototype the visible part, because it is what can be shown, and then discover the visible part was fine and the risk was in the part nobody drew. So before choosing a method, write down which assumption would be most expensive to be wrong about, and prototype that one — usually an operational assumption rather than a design one.

    Pilots, and what they teach that a walkthrough cannot

    A pilot runs the real service for a small set of customers with a manual back office, and it is the only method that produces real operational data. What it finds that nothing else can: the true distribution of cases rather than the imagined one, the actual time each step takes, the exceptions that occur roughly weekly rather than annually, and the places where the customer and the colleague disagree about what is happening. Those four are why a manual pilot is worth its cost even when the automation is obviously going to be built anyway — because the automation will encode whatever process the pilot revealed, and encoding the imagined process is the expensive mistake.

    Running a scene walkthrough without ruining it

    A scene walkthrough fails in predictable ways and all of them are about who is in the room. The customer is not a real customer. A colleague standing in for one will follow the script politely, will not be confused, and will ask the questions the team expects — so the session produces no friction, and a friction-free session is a sign the session was badly run rather than a sign the service is fine. Use someone who has actually used the service if there is any chance of it. Staff who are too good. An experienced operator will unconsciously paper over gaps they have learned to work around, and the walkthrough will therefore miss exactly the workarounds that make the process slow in reality. Ask them to do the walkthrough as a new person would, or use a new joiner. The paper is too good. If the token standing in for the app can show a state the real app cannot, the walkthrough validates an impossible experience.

    Then the mechanics that make it productive. One room, one journey, no interruptions for at least forty minutes. Two artefacts only: tokens representing what the customer holds, and sheets representing what the customer sees. Every step gets three questions in order — what do you do next, what would tell you that was wrong, and how long does that take — and the "how long" is the one that gets skipped and the one that makes the blueprint usable later. Walk the whole thing once without stopping to fix anything, because a walkthrough that gets fixed as it goes stops being a diagnostic and becomes a rehearsal, and the problems are found in the second pass, not the first.

    Then what to do with the findings, because the failure mode is a workshop that produces a list nobody acts on. Every friction found gets written onto the blueprint at the step where it occurred, with the layer it lives on, and the ones that are not fixed get given a reason. Then the count becomes the argument: a ninety-minute walkthrough producing forty frictions, of which nineteen are the same two minutes of one step, is a finding worth a quarter of somebody's time, and it is much more persuasive in a business case than any observation-based argument at all — because it is a count, and it is reproducible.

    /* Three ways a walkthrough is ruined, each about who is in the room. */
const WALKTHROUGH_FAILURES = [
  { failure: 'the customer is not a real customer',
    behaviour: 'a colleague follows the script politely, is not confused, and asks the questions the team expects',
    result: 'a friction-free session, which is a sign the session was badly run rather than a sign the service is fine',
    fix: 'use someone who has actually used the service, if there is any chance of it' },
  { failure: 'the staff member is too good',
    behaviour: 'an experienced operator unconsciously papers over gaps they learned to work around',
    result: 'the walkthrough misses exactly the workarounds that make the process slow in reality',
    fix: 'ask them to do it as a new person would, or use a new joiner' },
  { failure: 'the paper is too good',
    behaviour: 'a token standing in for the app can show a state the real app cannot',
    result: 'the walkthrough validates an impossible experience' },
];

/* Mechanics. */
const WALKTHROUGH_MECHANICS = {
  room: 'one room, one journey, no interruptions for at least forty minutes',
  artefacts: ['tokens for what the customer holds', 'sheets for what the customer sees'],
  perStep: ['what do you do next?', 'what would tell you that was wrong?', 'how long does that take?'],
  theSkippedQuestion: 'how long - it is the one that makes the blueprint usable later',
  doNotFixAsYouGo: 'a walkthrough fixed as it goes is a rehearsal, not a diagnostic',
  whyTwoPasses: 'the problems are found in the second pass, not the first',
};

/* From findings to something that gets acted on. */
const FROM_FINDINGS = {
  procedure: ['write every friction onto the blueprint at the step where it occurred',
              'record the layer it lives on',
              'give the unfixed ones a reason'],
  theArgumentTheCountMakes: 'a ninety-minute walkthrough producing forty frictions, nineteen of which are the same two minutes of one step, is worth a quarter of someones time',
  whyPersuasive: 'it is a count, and it is reproducible - which no observation-based argument is',
};

    The design decisions a pilot forces, in order of how often people get them wrong. Where does the human-in-the-loop stay? Every manual step is a candidate for removal and each is also a candidate for a real exception — the judgement is which steps exist because of a genuine exception and which exist because nobody imagined a different process. What is the fallback? A pilot run manually has no failure mode to reveal, so decide in advance what happens when the automation is wrong, and who notices within how long. What do the operators need that customers do not? A backstage tool designed as the mirror of the frontstage one is always wrong; operators need queue order, bulk action, exception flags and a way to leave a note. Who absorbs the manual cost, and for how long? A pilot that succeeds and then extends is the common failure, because the manual version keeps working and nobody is ever scheduled to replace it.

    /* Four uncertainties, four methods. A front-end prototype surfaces none of them. */
const UNCERTAINTY = {
  doesTheJourneyHoldTogether: { method: 'a scene walkthrough',
    setup: 'a room, three to five people, paper tokens as screens, one person reading a script aloud as a system',
    cost: 'ninety minutes',
    reliablyFinds: 'the steps where the customer does not know what is supposed to happen next - a paper token cannot be forgiving about a missing state' },
  wouldTheBackstageWork: { testedWithACustomer: false, mustBe: 'watching the staff',
    note: 'a different activity, and the one most often skipped' },
  wouldTheAutomationBeAccepted: { method: 'wizard of oz',
    what: 'a human behind the curtain producing what the automation would produce',
    measures: ['whether people accept the machine behaviour', 'whether they correct it when it is wrong', 'how often they correct it'],
    threshold: 'a wizard correcting more than about one in five decisions is telling you the decision logic is not ready to automate' },
};

/* Placement rule. */
const PLACEMENT = {
  rule: 'put the prototype where the risk is, not where the question is easiest to answer',
  commonFailure: 'teams prototype the visible part because it is what can be shown, then find the visible part was fine',
  theRiskWasIn: 'the part nobody drew',
  howToDoItRight: ['write down which assumption would be most expensive to be wrong about',
                   'prototype that one'],
  usuallyIs: 'an operational assumption rather than a design one',
};

/* What only a pilot can find. */
const PILOT_FINDS = [
  'the true distribution of cases rather than the imagined one',
  'the actual time each step takes',
  'the exceptions that occur roughly weekly rather than annually',
  'the places where the customer and the colleague disagree about what is happening',
];
const WHY_WORTH_IT = 'the automation will encode whatever process the pilot revealed, and encoding the imagined process is the expensive mistake';

/* Decisions a pilot forces. */
const PILOT_DECISIONS = [
  { decision: 'where does the human-in-the-loop stay?',
    judgement: 'which manual steps exist because of a genuine exception, and which because nobody imagined a different process' },
  { decision: 'what is the fallback?',
    gap: 'a manual pilot has no failure mode to reveal',
    decideInAdvance: ['what happens when the automation is wrong', 'who notices', 'within how long'] },
  { decision: 'what do operators need that customers do not?',
    alwaysWrong: 'a backstage tool designed as the mirror of the frontstage one',
    actuallyNeeded: ['queue order', 'bulk action', 'exception flags', 'a way to leave a note'] },
  { decision: 'who absorbs the manual cost, and for how long?',
    commonFailure: 'a pilot that succeeds and then extends, because the manual version keeps working and nobody is scheduled to replace it' },

  • Service pilots: run the real service for a small customer set with manual back-office before automating. The manual version teaches you the flows automation should serve.

24.6 Measuring a service (not just its app)

Measuring a service tracks the whole journey, not just its app, so you can see where value actually breaks down. Watch handoff pain, resolution time, effort across touchpoints, and failure to complete, since the cost hides across departments. Define cross-channel moment metrics with the departments that own each step, then build a shared backlog from what surfaces. A service metric is a promise about an end-to-end experience.

Add service-level metrics to the screen-level ones: handoff pain (repetition count), resolution time end-to-end, FCR (first-contact resolution), effort score across the whole journey, and CSAT per touchpoint. The blueprint’s pain points become a ranked backlog — same severity logic as Ch.14.4, but across departments.

Defining a service metric that two departments both own

The hard part of a service metric is not the number, it is that the number crosses departmental boundaries and each department will measure it in its own way. "Resolution time end to end" is the classic case: sales, operations and support each hold one segment of it, each has a target for their own segment, and each can improve their segment while the total gets worse — by queueing work at the boundary they are measured on. So the definition has to say explicitly where the clock starts and stops, and that has to be agreed before the number is reported rather than after it has been published once. If the start is "when the customer contacts us" then a contact that arrives by phone and one that arrives by email have different clocks, and the metric is really two metrics wearing one name.

Four definitions worth writing carefully. End-to-end resolution time: from the customer's first contact to the outcome they asked for, with the start event defined and the completion event defined as an outcome rather than as a status change. Repetition count: how many times the customer was asked for information they had already given, counted per journey and reported as a distribution — a mean hides the fact that a small group of customers has a catastrophic experience. Handoff completeness: the proportion of transfers where the receiving actor could act without asking the customer a question, which is the single most diagnostic service number available because it is directly attributable to design. Effort across touchpoints: the number of distinct places the customer had to go to the same organisation about the same thing, which is the one that exposes a service that is technically omnichannel and experientially not.

Then how to build the shared backlog from the numbers, because a set of service metrics nobody acts on is the same as no metrics. The mechanism is a cross-department review with the blueprint as the agenda: bring the metric movement, bring the blueprint, and walk the journey until the movement is explained. Each explanation that lands on a specific step becomes an item, and the rule that makes this work is that each item is owned by one department with a date — because a finding owned by everybody is owned by nobody, and a service finding owned by one department is usually resisted for the same reason: it will make that department's number worse before it makes the total better. That resistance is the normal condition and should be anticipated rather than treated as opposition, which is usually what turns it into opposition.

The journey-level measures that do not decompose

Two classes of measure are needed and only one of them is usually present. Per-step measures decompose — they tell you which step improved — and they are what dashboards are built from. Journey measures do not decompose and are the only ones that catch a specific failure: the journey getting longer while every step gets faster. The four worth having, in the order they catch things. Total time in journey, including waiting, counted from the customer's first attempt to their outcome, and reported as a distribution rather than a mean because the tail is the whole story — a journey whose median is four hours and whose ninety-fifth percentile is nine days is a service that people have learned to distrust, and no step-level number will show it. Effort: touches and channels, how many distinct contacts and distinct systems the customer had to go through. Cohort retention by journey, not by product: of the people who entered this journey, what fraction reached the outcome, and how does that change over time for each entry point. And promise accuracy: the gap between what the service told the customer and what it did, measured directly by comparing a recorded promise against the outcome.

Promise accuracy is the one nobody measures and the one with the highest correlation to churn, because it is the only journey measure that is about the customer's model of the service rather than about the service itself. A customer whose delivery estimate was right and who waited four days is satisfied. A customer who was told three days and waited nine is not, regardless of whether nine days was operationally unavoidable — and if unavoidable, the fix is not to make it faster but to make the estimate honest, which is a design decision and costs nothing.

And the decomposition trap, which is worth being explicit about because dashboards create it. Per-step improvement can add up to a worse journey: each department removes a step from its own segment and the total number of handovers rises, so the customer does the integration work that used to be internal. This is measurable — count the handovers, not just the duration — and it is invisible in every per-step dashboard because every individual segment is improving while the service degrades. So the journey measures should be on the same page as the step measures and should be reviewed with the same seriousness, and the handover count belongs next to the duration measures rather than in a service-design appendix nobody opens.

/* Two classes. Only one is usually present. */
const MEASURE_CLASSES = {
  perStep: { decomposes: true, whatItTellsYou: 'which step improved', whyCommon: 'dashboards are built from it' },
  journey: { decomposes: false,
    whatOnlyItCatches: 'the journey getting longer while every step gets faster' },
};

const JOURNEY_MEASURES = [
  { name: 'total time in journey', from: 'the customers first attempt', to: 'their outcome',
    includes: 'waiting',
    reportAs: 'a distribution, not a mean',
    why: 'the tail is the whole story - a journey with a four-hour median and a nine-day ninety-fifth percentile is one people have learned to distrust, and no step number shows it' },
  { name: 'effort: touches and channels', what: 'how many distinct contacts and distinct systems the customer had to go through' },
  { name: 'cohort retention by journey, not by product', what: 'of the people who entered this journey, what fraction reached the outcome',
    cut: 'by entry point', overTime: true },
  { name: 'promise accuracy', what: 'the gap between what the service told the customer and what it did',
    how: 'compare a recorded promise against the outcome' },
];

const PROMISE_ACCURACY = {
  nobodyMeasuresIt: true,
  highestCorrelationToChurn: true,
  why: 'it is the only journey measure about the customers model of the service rather than about the service',
  worked: 'a customer told three days and who waited four is satisfied; told three days and waited nine is not, regardless of whether nine days was operationally unavoidable',
  theFixIfUnavoidable: 'make the estimate honest rather than making the service faster',
  whyItIsADesignDecision: 'and it costs nothing',
};

/* The decomposition trap, made by dashboards. */
const DECOMPOSITION_TRAP = {
  mechanism: 'each department removes a step from its own segment and the total number of handovers rises',
  consequence: 'the customer does the integration work that used to be internal',
  measurable: true,
  invisibleInDashboards: 'every individual segment is improving while the service degrades',
  fix: ['journey measures on the same page as step measures',
        'reviewed with the same seriousness',
        'the handover count next to the duration measures, not in an appendix nobody opens'],
};

And the honest limitation, worth stating in the review itself. Service metrics move slowly, and they move for reasons mostly outside design's control — staffing, seasonality, the arrival rate of demand. This means service metrics are excellent for knowing whether the experience is broken and poor at attributing a change to a specific design decision. So use two clocks deliberately: service metrics for the health of the journey, reviewed quarterly with the departments that own each step, and screen-level metrics for the effect of a specific change, reviewed weekly. Conflating the two produces either slow reaction to a broken journey or false confidence about a change, and both are common.

/* The hard part is not the number; it is that two departments hold one number. */
const SEGMENT_GAMING = {
  problem: 'each department holds one segment of the metric and has a target for its own segment',
  consequence: 'each can improve its segment while the total gets worse, by queueing work at the boundary they are measured on',
  fix: 'define where the clock starts and stops, agreed BEFORE the number is reported',
  trap: 'if the start is "when the customer contacts us", a phone contact and an email contact have different clocks - that is two metrics wearing one name',
};

const DEFINITIONS = [
  { metric: 'end-to-end resolution time',
    start: 'the customers first contact', stop: 'the outcome they asked for',
    notThis: 'a status change' },
  { metric: 'repetition count', what: 'how many times the customer was asked for information they had already given',
    reportAs: 'a distribution per journey, not a mean',
    why: 'a mean hides that a small group of customers has a catastrophic experience' },
  { metric: 'handoff completeness', what: 'the proportion of transfers where the receiving actor could act without asking the customer a question',
    whyItMatters: 'the single most diagnostic service number, because it is directly attributable to design' },
  { metric: 'effort across touchpoints', what: 'the number of distinct places the customer had to go to the same organisation about the same thing',
    exposes: 'a service that is technically omnichannel and experientially not' },
];

/* From metrics to a backlog with one owner each. */
const SHARED_BACKLOG = {
  mechanism: 'a cross-department review with the blueprint as the agenda',
  procedure: ['bring the metric movement', 'bring the blueprint', 'walk the journey until the movement is explained'],
  everyExplanationBecomes: 'an item owned by one department with a date',
  whyOneOwner: 'a finding owned by everybody is owned by nobody',
  expectResistance: { because: 'it will make that departments number worse before it makes the total better',

/* Two clocks, deliberately. */
const TWO_CLOCKS = {
  serviceMetrics: { for: 'the health of the journey', cadence: 'quarterly, with the departments that own each step',
    goodAt: 'knowing whether the experience is broken' },
