25 · Specialized Domains: From E-commerce to Enterprise

Specialized domains are environments with different trust, fear, and expectation profiles, so conventions matter more than taste. E-commerce competes on clarity and checkout fluency, fintech and health trade on trust, error prevention, and compliance, education needs scaffolding, and enterprise demands density and control. Each domain shifts what users fear, what they forgive, and what they demand. Research the domain first, because its hygiene factors are non-negotiable.

25.1 E-commerce & checkout25.2 Fintech & payments25.3 Healthcare & clinical tools25.4 Education & learning products25.5 Enterprise / B2B SaaS25.6 Localization, RTL & global products

Domains come with different physics: trust, regulation, density, stakes. This chapter maps the five environments you’re most likely to design in — and the conventions that change the rules.

25.1 E-commerce & checkout

E-commerce and checkout are where revenue lives or dies, so every choice is aimed at conversion. Surface price, stock, and shipping costs early, strip friction from the form, offer guest checkout, and present several trusted payment options. Build trust with clear policies, transparent totals, and returns designed as a feature rather than a penalty. Test the checkout funnel relentlessly, because abandonment often hides real demand lost in the last click.

// The e-commerce rules of gravity:
//  - price, stock, shipping, returns visible EARLY (surprise = cart-drop)
//  - checkout: fewer fields, guest-first, total before payment,
//    strip the "create account" toll booth (dark pattern, Ch.20)
//  - trust signals live where the decision happens: reviews near the
//    buy button, not on a separate "about us"
//  - recovery: abandoned carts by step, emails with the SAME items,
//    never a fake countdown unless real
//  - returns are a feature: show the policy next to the product; the
//    brands that make returns easy convert better, measurably.

Where carts actually die, and how to find out which one it is

The single most useful piece of checkout work is to stop treating abandonment as one number, because the average is a mixture of four entirely different failures and fixing the wrong one wastes a quarter. The first is price surprise: a shipping cost, a duty, a "you must be logged in to check out" barrier, or a discount that expires, appearing after the person has committed. That is the largest single cause on most sites and it is a pricing-page and cart problem, not a checkout problem. The second is form cost: too many fields, and specifically fields the seller already knows. The third is doubt: the person cannot find a review, a delivery estimate, or a returns statement at the moment of the decision, so they open a new tab and do not come back — which looks identical to abandonment in analytics and is the reason session replay exists. The fourth is payment failure: declined cards, wallets that are unavailable in the country, a form that rejects a valid address, or an OTP that never arrives.

So the diagnostic is not "where do people leave the funnel", it is "which of the four is this", and each has a different instrumentation. Price surprise shows up as a specific step in the funnel with a specific previous action — the person who reached the shipping step and did not complete. Form cost shows up as time-in-field and abandonment by field, and it is the only one that a session replay diagnoses well, because you can watch the person hunt for a field that is not there. Doubt shows up as new-tab opens and as a return to the product page from search, which is nearly invisible unless you join sessions. Payment failure shows up as a post-submit error, and the number nobody measures — the count of payments that failed for a technical reason rather than a financial one — is usually several times the count that failed for insufficient funds, and almost all of it is fixable.

/* Four causes. The average is a mixture of all of them, so fixing the
   wrong one wastes a quarter. */
const CART_DEATH = [
  { cause: 'price surprise', examples: ['a shipping cost appearing after commitment', 'a duty', 'a login barrier', 'a discount that expired'],
    where: 'the pricing page and the cart, NOT the checkout',
    size: 'the largest single cause on most sites' },
  { cause: 'form cost', detail: 'too many fields, and specifically fields the seller already knows',
    diagnosedBy: 'time-in-field and abandonment by field; also the best replay diagnosis, because you can watch the person hunt for a field that is not there' },
  { cause: 'doubt', detail: 'cannot find a review, a delivery estimate or a returns statement at the moment of the decision',
    behaviour: 'opens a new tab and does not come back',
    whyInvisible: 'this looks identical to abandonment in analytics, and it is the reason session replay exists' },
  { cause: 'payment failure', detail: ['declined cards', 'wallets unavailable in the country', 'a form that rejects a valid address', 'an OTP that never arrives'] },
];
const UNMEASURED = {
  metric: 'payments that failed for a technical reason rather than a financial one',
  relation: 'usually several times the count that failed for insufficient funds',
  fixable: 'almost all of it',
};

/* The form fields worth keeping. Anything the seller knows is friction. */
const FORM_FIELDS = {
  keep: ['email', 'delivery address', 'delivery method', 'payment'],
  askOnlyWhenNeeded: ['phone - only for delivery that genuinely requires it'],
  neverAsk: ['a second address when there is one', 'company name for a consumer purchase',
             'a registration number for a consumer purchase',
             'a postcode to calculate a shipping cost that could be shown before the address'],
  autofillFirst: 'address autocomplete and card scanning are worth more than any other single field improvement',
  theRealNumber: 'fields removed, not fields styled',
};

/* Doubt, and where the trust signal has to physically be. */
const TRUST_PLACEMENT = {
  rule: 'the signal has to be on the screen where the decision happens',
  atTheDecision: ['reviews near the buy control, not on a separate page', 'the delivery estimate in the cart, not in the policy page',
                  'the returns window beside the price, not in the footer',
                  'the security and payment methods beside the pay button, not in the footer'],
  theFailure: 'the person opens a new tab to look, and does not come back',
  consequence: 'analytics records it as abandonment and the team optimises the wrong thing',
};

/* The recovery sequence, and the one rule about it. */
const ABANDONMENT_RECOVERY = {
  sequence: 'the same items, in the same cart, in the same state, with the same delivery estimate',
  timing: { first: 'within an hour, while the decision is still live',
            last: 'at twenty-four hours' },
  theRule: 'never a fake countdown unless it is real',
  doNot: ['change the price between the abandon and the email', 'empty the cart', 'offer a discount that is worse than the next public sale'],
  whyPriceChangesFail: 'a person who returns to a changed price learns that the first price was not real, and stops buying from you entirely',
};

Comment-only cheat sheet: surface price, stock, and shipping early, strip checkout friction, and treat easy returns as a feature, because surprise is what drops carts.

25.2 Fintech & payments

In fintech and payment products, trust is the product, and users arrive nervous about their money. Use plain language for balances, transfers, and fees, show honest security messaging rather than scareware, and design edge cases such as overdrafts and disputes with grace. Errors must be hard to cause, clearly explained, and reversible where possible. Reassurance, not complexity, turns nervous users into loyal ones.

  • Trust is the product: plain-language money states ("authorized", "processing", "cleared"), receipts that read like the user’s story, and never-jokey money errors (Ch.12.4 tone).
  • Security without hostage-taking: MFA at the right moments, biometrics when available, transparent "why we ask".
  • Compliance bends flows: Know-Your-Customer steps, limits, hold periods — make each hurdle explain its own why ("we verify to protect transfers over $1,000").

    • The states nobody designs, which are most of the trust

    A money interface is trusted or not on its edge states rather than its happy path, and the reason is that the edge states are the ones a person is anxious about. So the specific work is enumerating them, and the enumeration is short enough to do in an afternoon and almost nobody does. Money in flight: pending, authorized but not captured, partially captured, and reversed — a person who sees a balance drop and a bank statement that does not yet agree is told the account is broken, and the fix is a line of copy that names the state and the expected time. Money out: scheduled versus sent versus delivered, which are three different words and people use them interchangeably. Money failed: declined by the issuer, declined by us, insufficient funds, expired card — and each needs different words and a different next action, because "declined" with no detail is the single most common cause of a support contact in payments.

    The two states that most products get wrong and that cost the most trust. Reversal: a payment is taken and then returned days later, and the customer sees a negative balance with no explanation; the design must predict it, explain it when it happens, and say what it will do about it. Partial failure: the transfer succeeded and the record did not, or the record exists and the money did not move. This is the state that produces the anxiety no error message can fix, because the person cannot tell which it is. The design answer is to make the outcome knowable from inside the product — a status the customer can see, a reference they can quote, and a stated time by which the state will be definite — rather than asking them to trust.

    Compliance as interface, not as a gate

    Regulatory requirements are usually implemented as a hurdle between the customer and the thing they want, and the result is abandonment that the business reads as loss of interest. The design task is to make each hurdle explain its own purpose at the moment it appears, and this is almost free: "we verify identity for transfers over £1,000 to protect your account" is one sentence, and the person who reads it complies rather than resents. Where the requirement genuinely cannot be softened — a hold period, a jurisdictional limit, a licence check — then the requirement is to show the constraint in advance so the person can plan around it, because a limit discovered at the payment step reads as a rejection and a limit shown during account setup reads as a product rule.

    The interface patterns that carry financial trust

    Four patterns do most of the work, and all four are about making the system legible to a person who does not trust it yet. Show the number before the action. A transfer screen that reveals the fee, the exchange rate and the arrival estimate only after the person presses send has created a rejection they will remember; the same information shown above the button is a decision they make. Make the pending state a real screen. A spinner communicates nothing; a screen with a reference, a state name and a stated resolution time communicates that a person exists on the other side of it. Reconcile visibly. Every account a person holds should show a running balance with a dated transaction list, because the absence of reconciliation is what makes a person check their bank statement, and a mismatch found there is fatal. Idempotency, expressed in the interface. Retrying a failed payment must not be able to charge twice, and the person should be able to press the button twice safely — which is not only a technical property but a promise the interface makes whether or not the engineering supports it.

    Then the two failure modes with the highest reputational cost in this domain. Silent defaulting: a foreign-currency payment settles at a rate the customer did not see, or a subscription renews at a price that changed without notice; both are technically compliant and both are the reason people describe a fintech as dishonest. Recovery theatre: an error page that says "something went wrong" with a reference number and no route forward. The person is now holding a problem with no action, and the only thing left is to contact support — which means the interface has converted an error into a cost centre ticket. The fix is small and specific: name the cause where known, give the next action where one exists, and where nothing can be done, say that too, because "nothing has happened and nothing will" is a genuinely reassuring sentence and it is almost never written.

    /* Four patterns that carry financial trust. */
const TRUST_PATTERNS = [
  { pattern: 'show the number before the action',
    detail: ['the fee', 'the exchange rate', 'the arrival estimate'],
    aboveThisControl: 'the send button',
    ifBelow: 'a rejection they will remember' },
  { pattern: 'make pending a real screen',
    contains: ['a reference', 'a state name', 'a stated resolution time'],
    communicates: 'that a person exists on the other side of it',
    insteadOf: 'a spinner, which communicates nothing' },
  { pattern: 'reconcile visibly',
    contains: 'a running balance with a dated transaction list',
    why: 'the absence of reconciliation makes a person check their bank statement, and a mismatch found there is fatal' },
  { pattern: 'idempotency expressed in the interface',
    promise: 'pressing the button twice is safe',
    isAlso: 'a technical property, and the interface promises it whether or not engineering supports it' },
];

/* The two failure modes with the highest reputational cost. */
const COSTLIEST_FAILURES = [
  { failure: 'silent defaulting',
    instances: ['a foreign-currency payment settling at a rate the customer did not see',
                'a subscription renewing at a price that changed without notice'],
    paradox: 'technically compliant, and the reason people describe a fintech as dishonest' },
  { failure: 'recovery theatre',
    what: 'an error page that says something went wrong, with a reference number and no route forward',
    consequence: 'the person now holds a problem with no action, and the only thing left is to contact support - the interface has converted an error into a cost centre ticket',
    fix: ['name the cause where known', 'give the next action where one exists',
          'where nothing can be done, say that too'],
    theSentenceNobodyWrites: 'nothing has happened and nothing will - genuinely reassuring, and almost never written' },
];

    Then tone, which in this domain is a correctness issue rather than a preference. Money errors are read at the worst possible moment and jokes are the wrong register entirely; the register that works is plain, specific, and unembarrassed about the customer's position. Two habits help: name the cause and the fix in the same sentence, and never make the customer feel stupid for asking — the most common support conversation in payments is somebody trying to pay twice because the first attempt did not tell them what happened, and the second attempt is a duplicate. Finally, the security messaging has a specific failure mode: scareware to build trust. It works for a week and it teaches people that the product's warnings are marketing, which removes the one channel you have for a genuinely important warning later.

    /* Enumerate the states. An afternoon of work, almost never done. */
const MONEY_STATES = {
  inFlight: ['pending', 'authorized but not captured', 'partially captured', 'reversed'],
  whyItMatters: 'a person who sees a balance drop and a bank statement that does not yet agree is told the account is broken',
  fix: 'a line of copy that names the state and the expected time',
  out: ['scheduled', 'sent', 'delivered'],
  whyTheseThree: 'they are three different words and people use them interchangeably',
  failed: [
    { kind: 'declined by the issuer', action: 'try another card or the issuer' },
    { kind: 'declined by us', action: 'why, and what to change' },
    { kind: 'insufficient funds', action: 'the amount available' },
    { kind: 'expired card', action: 'replace it' },
  ],
  theWorstOfThem: 'declined with no detail is the single most common cause of a support contact in payments',
};

/* The two that cost the most trust. */
const COSTLIEST = [
  { state: 'reversal', what: 'money is taken and returned days later', whatTheCustomerSees: 'a negative balance with no explanation',
    designMust: ['predict it', 'explain it when it happens', 'say what will be done about it'] },
  { state: 'partial failure', what: 'the transfer succeeded and the record did not, or the reverse',
    whyWorst: 'the person cannot tell which it is, and no error message fixes anxiety they cannot locate',
    designAnswer: ['a status the customer can see', 'a reference they can quote', 'a stated time by which the state will be definite'] },

/* Compliance as interface. */
const HURDLES = {
  principle: 'make each hurdle explain its own purpose at the moment it appears',
  example: { requirement: 'identity verification over a threshold',
             sentence: 'we verify identity for transfers over 1,000 to protect your account',
             effect: 'the person who reads it complies rather than resents' },
  whereItCannotBeSoftened: ['a hold period', 'a jurisdictional limit', 'a licence check'],

25.3 Healthcare & clinical tools

Healthcare and clinical tools carry high stakes, tired users, and sensitive data, so safety beats delight. Keep one task per screen to protect concentration, write plain wording for patients who are anxious or have lower literacy, and build in wrong-patient and wrong-dose prevention such as visible identity headers and forced confirmation. Compliance matters, but so does usability, because errors in a rushed workflow cost outcomes. Design for the ten-hour-shift worker.

RealityDesign response
High stakes, low patienceone task per screen, progressive disclosure, giant targets in the field
Jargon is a language barrierplain words for patients; exact codes the clinicians need, tabbed
Sensitive dataprivacy-first flows, consent visible, audit logs visible to patients where required
Users switch modes (nurse + admin + patient)role-based views (Ch.17 anti-personas), fast switching
Errors carry bodiesconfirmation on anything irreversible; wrong-patient prevention is a design requirement, not a nice-to-have

Designing for the worst day of somebody's life

The defining constraint in healthcare is not stakes or regulation — it is that the person is frequently having the worst day they have had in a long time, and the interface is competing with pain, fear, medication, a queue and somebody else's problems for a single person's attention. That produces a small number of design rules that are absolute rather than adjustable. Nothing above the task. No navigation, no marketing, no promo. One decision per screen, because the failure mode of a multi-task screen under distress is a wrong answer confidently entered. Never infer anything the person did not state: no pre-filled clinical fields, no defaults derived from a previous visit, no checkbox that is pre-ticked on a consent screen — and the exception is only where the inference is verifiable by the person in one glance. Every input is confirmable, because a mistyped number in a clinical tool is a dose, and confirmation is cheaper than the consequence.

The wrong-patient problem deserves its own treatment because it is the domain's characteristic failure and it is entirely a design problem. The mechanisms that work are all visual rather than procedural: a persistent patient identity band on every screen showing name, date of birth and an identifier in a fixed position with a fixed colour, present on the login screen and never on a screen where it can be mistaken for content; a colour and shape coding of arms on wristbands and charts so that identity is pre-attentive rather than read; and a forced scan-to-confirm before anything irreversible, where scanning the patient's own wristband is the act that commits — so the identity check is a physical action performed by the person holding the patient rather than a mental one. And a timeout with a deliberate reset, because a session that expires silently mid-task and then silently signs in as the previous user is how the wrong-patient class of error happens with no one having done anything wrong.

Safety, consent, and the two kinds of interruption

Three safety mechanisms are worth designing deliberately rather than inheriting. Timeouts with a deliberate reset: a session that ends must end loudly — an explicit sign-out, a cleared state, a visible message — because the silent version is the mechanism behind an entire class of wrong-patient and wrong-record events, and it is a bug that produces no error report. Interruptibility: any task must be saveable and resumable, and the save must be automatic, because the clinical reality is that the interruption is not a failure of the task, it is the environment. The correct test is whether a clinician can be called away at the worst possible moment and return ten minutes later to a screen that tells them exactly where they were and what has not been saved. Escalation without leaving the record: a clinical escalation almost always needs somebody with more authority, and if obtaining it requires a phone call the record is left in a state where two people believe they own it. So the escalation path has to live in the system, with the request, the reason and the response all recorded on the record itself.

Consent is the part with the most design failure, and the failures come from treating it as a gate rather than as a conversation over time. Three requirements, in order of how often they are missed. It must be specific: consent to "share my record with the cardiology team" is not consent to "share my record", and the interface that offers a single broad consent is the reason records get shared with a department the patient never mentioned. It must be revocable, in the same place it was given, in the same number of steps, with the consequence stated — which is often not deletion but "your referring clinician will no longer see this", and a person who is not told that will not revoke at all. It must be re-obtained when the purpose changes, which is the case nobody designs for: a record collected for treatment and then used for research, or for a service the patient was not told about, and a single broad consent at admission cannot cover a change of purpose years later.

Measuring a clinical tool without creating a second hazard

The obvious metrics are wrong here in a way that is specific and worth stating, because the incentive they create is actively dangerous. Time-on-task is the standard measure for every efficiency-oriented product and for a clinical tool it rewards a layout that lets a clinician enter a dose with the fewest clicks and no verification — which is a medication error. Completion rate rewards a tool that makes it easy to complete a task that should have prompted a question. Click count, the metric everybody reaches for first, is the most dangerous of the three for the same reason. So the measure has to include what the design is for: reconciliation of the interrupted-work queue, time from result-available to result-reviewed, the rate at which a result with an abnormal value is acknowledged, and — the one that is hard to measure and matters most — the rate of corrected entries, tracked as a learning signal rather than a performance one, because a tool whose correction rate is treated as a fault has its corrections suppressed.

/* Three safety mechanisms to design deliberately rather than inherit. */
const SAFETY = [
  { mechanism: 'timeouts with a deliberate reset',
    must: ['an explicit sign-out', 'a cleared state', 'a visible message'],
    theBugItPrevents: 'a session ending silently is the mechanism behind an entire class of wrong-patient and wrong-record events',
    whyItIsWorse: 'it produces no error report at all' },
  { mechanism: 'interruptibility',
    reality: 'the interruption is not a failure of the task, it is the environment',
    save: 'automatic',
    test: 'can a clinician be called away at the worst possible moment and return ten minutes later to a screen that says exactly where they were and what was not saved' },
  { mechanism: 'escalation without leaving the record',
    problem: 'if obtaining authority requires a phone call, the record is left in a state where two people believe they own it',
    requirement: ['the request', 'the reason', 'the response'],
    allRecorded: 'on the record itself' },
];

/* Consent, in the order it is most often missed. */
const CONSENT_REQUIREMENTS = [
  { requirement: 'specific', bad: 'consent to share my record', good: 'consent to share my record with the cardiology team',
    consequence: 'the single broad consent is why records reach a department the patient never mentioned' },
  { requirement: 'revocable',
    where: 'the same place it was given, in the same number of steps',
    mustState: 'the consequence, which is often not deletion',
    actualConsequence: 'your referring clinician will no longer see this',
    why: 'a person not told that will not revoke at all' },
  { requirement: 're-obtained when the purpose changes',
    examples: ['a record collected for treatment and then used for research', 'use for a service the patient was not told about'],
    whyNobodyDesignsForIt: 'a single broad consent at admission cannot cover a change of purpose years later' },
];

/* Metrics that are actively dangerous in a clinical tool. */
const DANGEROUS_METRICS = [
  { metric: 'time on task', rewards: 'a layout that lets a clinician enter a dose with the fewest clicks and no verification',
    consequence: 'a medication error' },
  { metric: 'completion rate', rewards: 'a tool that makes it easy to complete a task that should have prompted a question' },
  { metric: 'click count', note: 'the one everybody reaches for first, and the most dangerous of the three for the same reason' },
];
const CLINICAL_METRICS = [
  { metric: 'reconciliation of the interrupted-work queue' },
  { metric: 'time from result-available to result-reviewed' },
  { metric: 'rate at which a result with an abnormal value is acknowledged' },
  { metric: 'rate of corrected entries', hardestToMeasure: true, mattersMost: true,
    treatAs: 'a learning signal, not a performance one',
    why: 'a tool whose correction rate is treated as a fault has its corrections suppressed' },
];

Then the two audiences that break naive designs. Clinicians need exactness and speed under interruption: codes they can search, a scan-first pattern that puts the barcode in front of the keyboard, results that can be triaged, and critically a visible queue of interrupted work because the most common cause of a clinical error is a task that was not finished when the alarm went off and nobody returned to it. Patients need the opposite: plain words, one idea per screen, no abbreviations, a stated waiting time, and the ability to see what is happening to them — and the design mistake here is treating the patient interface as the clinician interface with the jargon removed, when the actual requirement is that it be built around the questions a worried person asks, which are almost never the ones the form asks.

/* Absolute rules, derived from the real constraint: the person is having
   the worst day they have had in a long time. */
const CLINICAL_RULES = {
  nothingAboveTheTask: ['no navigation', 'no marketing', 'no promo'],
  oneDecisionPerScreen: { why: 'the failure of a multi-task screen under distress is a wrong answer confidently entered' },
  neverInfer: { rule: 'nothing the person did not state',
    violations: ['pre-filled clinical fields', 'defaults derived from a previous visit', 'a pre-ticked consent checkbox'],
    exception: 'only where the inference is verifiable in one glance' },
  confirmEveryInput: { why: 'a mistyped number in a clinical tool is a dose; confirmation is cheaper than the consequence' },
};

/* Wrong-patient, entirely a design problem. All the mechanisms are visual. */
const WRONG_PATIENT = {
  mechanisms: [
    { name: 'persistent identity band',
      shows: ['name', 'date of birth', 'an identifier'],
      rules: ['fixed position', 'fixed colour', 'present on the login screen',
              'never on a screen where it can be mistaken for content'] },
    { name: 'colour and shape coding on wristbands and charts',
      why: 'identity becomes pre-attentive rather than read' },
    { name: 'forced scan-to-confirm before anything irreversible',
      why: 'scanning the patients own wristband is the act that commits, so the check is a physical action by the person holding the patient rather than a mental one' },
    { name: 'timeout with a deliberate reset',
      mechanismOfTheBug: 'a session expires silently mid-task and then silently signs in as the previous user',
      whyThatIsTheWrongPatientCase: 'it happens with nobody having done anything wrong at all' },
  ],
};

/* The two audiences, and the mistake of treating one as the other. */
const AUDIENCES = {
  clinicians: {
    need: ['exactness', 'speed under interruption', 'codes they can search',
           'scan-first so the barcode is in front of the keyboard', 'results they can triage'],
    criticalItem: 'a visible queue of interrupted work',
    why: 'the most common cause of a clinical error is a task not finished when the alarm went off, and nobody returned to it',
  },
  patients: {
    need: ['plain words, no abbreviations', 'one idea per screen', 'a stated waiting time',
           'the ability to see what is happening to them'],
    mistakeToAvoid: 'treating the patient interface as the clinician interface with the jargon removed',
    requirementInstead: 'build it around the questions a worried person asks, which are almost never the ones the form asks',

25.4 Education & learning products

Education and learning products succeed with scaffolding, a sequence that steadily builds competence rather than showering the learner with endless hints. Feedback and progress should teach and reassure, never shame or manufacture anxiety, and mistakes should be safe and recoverable. Structure learning objectives, spaced retrieval, and visible progress to sustain motivation. Design evaluation around growth over the course, not punishment for each error.

    Scaffolding, and how to know the scaffolding is working

    Scaffolding is a sequence, not a set of hints, and the sequence has a shape that is worth being precise about: full support, then partial support, then independent performance, then transfer to a different context. Products usually implement the first stage and then stall, because the second stage is harder to write and the third is harder to detect — the learner appears to be succeeding and is in fact being carried. The measure of scaffolding is therefore not engagement or completion but error rate under removal of support: does the performance hold when the hint is gone? A course that scores well while every screen is doing the thinking has produced a product the learner cannot use, and the only way to find out is to remove the support and watch. That experiment is uncomfortable and it is the whole point.

    Feedback is the second lever and it has three properties that separate teaching feedback from applause. It is immediate, because feedback that arrives after the learner has built a wrong model is teaching the wrong thing. It is specific to the action, naming what was done and what would have been different rather than marking the item right or wrong. And it does not shame, which is a design constraint rather than a tone constraint: a wrong answer is information about the model the learner holds, so the copy should say what the answer implies, which is the one thing that lets the learner repair the model. The wrong construction is "incorrect" with no further content, which gives the learner nothing to work with and a feeling about themselves.

    Then the retention mechanisms, where the research is unusually clear and the product implementation is usually weak. Spaced retrieval beats re-exposure for retention, and re-exposure is what every product does by default, because repeating a lesson is easy and scheduling a review is not. Interleaving — mixing problem types rather than blocking them — produces better discrimination at test time and a worse feeling during practice, so it needs a deliberate explanation or the product will feel broken and be abandoned. Desirable difficulty is the same idea from the other side: a session that is too easy is judged as low quality by the learner, which is a legitimate perception and not something to design away.

    The ethics, which are not optional

    Three specific prohibitions, all of which are dark patterns from chapter 20 wearing a friendly face. Streak loss: a learner who missed a day loses a visible count, and the mechanism works because the loss is public and the recovery is designed to be purchasable. That last detail is what makes it a pattern rather than a mistake — the emotional punishment creates the demand and then the demand is monetised. Anxiety as a retention lever: the countdown before an assessment, the "you are behind your class", the notification that a friend's result is better than yours. Each produces a short-term engagement spike and each teaches a person that the product is a source of stress, and the population most affected is the one that can least afford it. Progress theatre: a badge for logging in, a level that advances with time spent, a percentage complete that measures completion of the product rather than competence in the subject.

    Designing the assessment, which is the actual product

    In any learning product the assessment is the product and the content delivery is scaffolding, which is a reversal most teams never make explicitly and which explains a lot of bad design. Three consequences follow. The item, not the screen, is the design object: a question is a piece of interface with a stem, options, feedback and a decision about which distractors to include, and the distracters are the interesting part — a plausible distractor teaches by being rejected, and a silly one wastes the opportunity. Feedback is a designed artefact with a delay budget, and the budget is not a number of milliseconds but a number of intervening tasks: feedback that arrives after the learner has attempted two more items is teaching about the second item. The result screen is not a score: it is the moment where the product either tells the learner what to do next or tells them they are finished, and a screen that says "you scored 80%" without saying what to do next has converted a learning moment into a judgment.

    Then adaptivity, which is genuinely hard and where the honest advice is to be conservative. Three workable mechanisms. Prerequisite gating: do not let a learner into a topic whose prerequisite they have failed, and let them override it explicitly — the override is important, because a person who knows they can do it and is told otherwise will leave the product. Number and type variation: change the number of items and their type rather than building a content graph, which gives most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost. Hint escalation: first a nudge, then a worked example, then the answer — and record which level was needed, because that record is the most useful thing in the system and it is what tells an instructor where to intervene. What does not work reliably is a full adaptive engine, because it requires a knowledge graph nobody has built, and a product that has one usually has it because somebody hand-authored it and it silently rots.

    Accessibility, because it is where education products fail hardest

    Three requirements that are non-negotiable and routinely missed. Keyboard operation throughout, including the answer controls: a learner using a switch device or a screen reader cannot answer a multiple-choice question rendered as a set of divs, and the standard radio group is the correct element rather than a set of clickable boxes. Do not rely on colour alone for correctness feedback — a red border and a green tick is invisible to the ten percent of male learners with a colour vision deficiency, so the state must also be carried by an icon, a text label, or both, and this applies to the answer options and the progress indicators, not just the results. Captions and transcripts on every piece of video, not as a setting but as the default, because a learner who is not watching video rather than not hearing it is a real category and the interface should never require a choice to exclude them. And one more that is education-specific: timed assessments need a stated accommodation, because a tool that enforces a countdown with no extension mechanism excludes the learners who need it, and the exclusion is invisible in the completion statistics.

    /* The assessment is the product; content delivery is scaffolding. */
const ASSESSMENT_IS_THE_PRODUCT = {
  consequence1: { item: 'the item, not the screen, is the design object',
    parts: ['the stem', 'the options', 'the feedback', 'a decision about which distractors to include'],
    theInterestingPart: 'the distractors - a plausible one teaches by being rejected, a silly one wastes the opportunity' },
  consequence2: { feedback: 'a designed artefact with a delay budget',
    theBudgetIsNot: 'a number of milliseconds',
    theBudgetIs: 'a number of intervening tasks',
    why: 'feedback arriving after two more attempts is teaching about the second attempt' },
  consequence3: { resultScreenIsNot: 'a score',
    is: 'the moment the product either says what to do next or says they are finished',
    failure: 'you scored 80 percent with no next action converts a learning moment into a judgment' },
};

/* Adaptivity: three mechanisms that work, one that does not. */
const ADAPTIVITY = [
  { mechanism: 'prerequisite gating', how: 'do not let a learner into a topic whose prerequisite they failed',
    mustInclude: 'an explicit override',
    why: 'a person who knows they can do it and is told otherwise leaves the product' },
  { mechanism: 'number and type variation', how: 'change the count and the type rather than building a content graph',
    gives: 'most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost' },
  { mechanism: 'hint escalation', levels: ['a nudge', 'a worked example', 'the answer'],
    record: 'which level was needed',
    why: 'that record is the most useful thing in the system and it is what tells an instructor where to intervene' },
  { mechanism: 'a full adaptive engine', doesNotWorkReliably: true,
    because: 'it requires a knowledge graph nobody has built',
    whenPresent: 'somebody hand-authored it, and it silently rots' },
];

/* Accessibility, where education products fail hardest. */
const ACCESSIBILITY = [
  { requirement: 'keyboard operation throughout, including the answer controls',
    because: 'a learner using a switch device or a screen reader cannot answer a question rendered as a set of divs',
    correctElement: 'a standard radio group, not a set of clickable boxes' },
  { requirement: 'do not rely on colour alone for correctness feedback',
    affected: 'about ten percent of male learners with a colour vision deficiency',
    alsoAppliesTo: ['the answer options', 'the progress indicators'],
    mustAlsoBeCarriedBy: ['an icon', 'a text label', 'both'] },
  { requirement: 'captions and transcripts as the default, not a setting',
    because: 'a learner who is not watching video rather than not hearing it is a real category',
    rule: 'the interface should never require a choice to exclude them' },
  { requirement: 'a stated accommodation on timed assessments',
    consequence: 'a countdown with no extension mechanism excludes the learners who need it',
    howItHides: 'the exclusion is invisible in the completion statistics' },
];

    What to do instead is not softer, it is more effective at the horizon that matters. Mastery-based progress, where the visible state is what the learner can do, so the progress indicator means something. Honest difficulty signalling, so a person who is struggling learns it early and can change approach, rather than discovering at the end. Progress that survives absence: no visible decay of accumulated knowledge, because what the learner is building should not be a resource that can be depleted by taking a week off. And the reminder that does not guilt: "you were at chapter four" rather than "you are losing your streak", which conveys the same information and takes nothing away.

    /* The four stages, and the stage products usually stall at. */
const SCAFFOLD = {
  stages: ['full support', 'partial support', 'independent performance', 'transfer to a different context'],
  stallingPoint: 'the second stage - it is harder to write, and the third is harder to detect',
  theTrap: 'the learner appears to be succeeding while being carried',
  theMeasure: { notThese: ['engagement', 'completion'],
    actual: 'error rate under removal of support',
    experiment: 'remove the support and watch',
    uncomfortable: true, whyItIsThePoint: true },
};

/* Three properties that separate teaching feedback from applause. */
const FEEDBACK = {
  immediate: 'because feedback arriving after a wrong model has been built teaches the wrong thing',
  specificToTheAction: 'naming what was done and what would have been different, not right or wrong',
  doesNotShame: { why: 'a design constraint, not a tone constraint',
    mechanism: 'a wrong answer is information about the model the learner holds, so the copy should say what the answer implies',
    thatIs: 'the one thing that lets the learner repair the model',
    wrongConstruction: '"incorrect" with no further content - nothing to work with and a feeling about themselves' },
};

/* Retention mechanisms, where the research is clear and the implementation is weak. */
const RETENTION = [
  { mechanism: 'spaced retrieval', effect: 'beats re-exposure for retention',
    whatProductsDoInstead: 're-exposure, by default, because repeating a lesson is easy and scheduling a review is not' },
  { mechanism: 'interleaving', effect: 'better discrimination at test time and a worse feeling during practice',
    needs: 'a deliberate explanation, or the product feels broken and is abandoned' },
  { mechanism: 'desirable difficulties', effect: 'a session that is too easy is judged as low quality by the learner',
    note: 'a legitimate perception, not something to design away' },
];

/* Three prohibitions. All are dark patterns wearing a friendly face. */
const PROHIBITIONS = [
  { pattern: 'streak loss', mechanism: 'the loss is public and the recovery is designed to be purchasable',
    whatMakesItAPattern: 'the emotional punishment creates the demand and then the demand is monetised' },
  { pattern: 'anxiety as a retention lever',
    instances: ['a countdown before an assessment', 'you are behind your class', 'a notification that a friends result is better'],
    effect: 'a short-term engagement spike, and a person who learns the product is a source of stress',
    whoItHitsHardest: 'the population that can least afford it' },
  { pattern: 'progress theatre',
    instances: ['a badge for logging in', 'a level that advances with time spent', 'percentage complete measuring completion of the product rather than competence in the subject'] },
];

const INSTEAD = [
  { replace: 'mastery-based progress', means: 'the visible state is what the learner can do, so the indicator means something' },
  { replace: 'honest difficulty signalling', means: 'a person who is struggling learns it early and can change approach rather than discovering at the end' },
  { replace: 'progress that survives absence', why: 'what the learner is building should not be a resource depleted by taking a week off' },
  { replace: 'the reminder that does not guilt', bad: 'you are losing your streak', good: 'you were at chapter four',
    note: 'same information, nothing taken away' },
];
  • Design for scaffolding: reduce complexity step by step, then remove the crutch — the product’s job is learning transfer, not endless hints.
  • Feedback loops with instructive errors and spaced review; gamification only when it serves progress (badges that measure effort, not noise).
  • Ethics: don’t turn children’s anxiety into a retention metric. Honest progress, no guilt-dark-pattern reminders.

25.5 Enterprise / B2B SaaS

Enterprise B2B products serve expert power users who want density, speed, and control rather than spa-like whitespace. Support keyboard shortcuts, bulk actions, deep filters, configurable views, and honest performance at scale. Permissions, admin, and configuration decide whether enterprise tools sink or swim, and training and integration costs matter as much as the interface. Design for the long haul and the person operating ten tabs.

// Density is a feature: power users want MORE information per screen,
// keyboard-first workflows, bulk actions, and saved views — not spa-y
// whitespace. Respect that "beautiful" differs from consumer beauty.
// The three B2B systems that live or die:
//   1 permissions/roles/member mgmt (who can do what) — audit early
//   2 admin pages (tenants, billing, logs) — design them like products
//   3 configuration & migration legacy — your flows must survive weird data
// Selling point inside companies: reduce ramp time & support tickets.
// Measurable, and it's how enterprise UX wins budgets (Ch.23.5).

The three systems, in the order they should be built

Most enterprise products lose deals and lose renewals on three surfaces that receive almost no design attention, because they are not where the users are — the users are in the workspace, and the workspace is usually well designed. Permissions and membership come first because they are used rarely, by an administrator whose mental model is different from everybody else's, and because a mistake is not visible immediately: somebody is denied something six weeks later and by then the product is blamed. Design it as a set of questions a non-technical administrator can answer — not as roles and permissions, but as "what should this person be able to do" — with the inheritance and the exceptions made visible. The specific failure to avoid is a role whose name means nothing to the person assigning it, which produces a configuration nobody will revisit. Admin pages — tenants, billing, logs, integration keys — are a product for a different user with different goals, and they are usually built as CRUD screens; logs in particular deserve real design, because they are used by somebody having a bad day with no training. Configuration and migration come last in the build order and first in the risk: the flows must survive data that a sane person would not have entered, and the place this is discovered is a customer upgrade three years later.

Then the thing enterprise users actually want, which is the opposite of what a consumer product wants: they want control, and control means the ability to see everything, change everything, and get out. So the design priorities invert. Density over whitespace, and not as a maxim but because the operator's constraint is volume. Configurable columns, filters and sort, with the configuration saved per user rather than global, because a saved view that changes for everybody is a bug report. Bulk operations, with a preview and a count, because an operator processing eight hundred records will not click eight hundred times and will find a way around you instead. Export, because the enterprise user's real fear is being locked in, and an export that works is the single most effective retention feature available. And undo for anything reversible, which in a bulk context means a single undo for the whole batch.

Keyboard-first is not a preference here, it is the difference between a tool that works and a tool that is fought. Expert users build speed through muscle memory, and a mouse-driven interface caps that speed at a level that makes people leave the product for a spreadsheet — and they will, because a spreadsheet allows what the product forbids: bulk paste, arbitrary columns, and their own formulas. The design response is not to make the spreadsheet unnecessary by being slow; it is to be faster than the spreadsheet for the things it is good at, which means a shortcut for every frequent action, a command palette, and paste support in the places where paste is the obvious approach.

/* Three surfaces that lose deals, because the users are not in them. */
const THREE_SYSTEMS = [
  { system: 'permissions and membership', buildFirst: true,
    who: 'an administrator whose mental model is different from everybodys',
    whySoRisky: 'used rarely, and a mistake is not visible immediately - somebody is denied something six weeks later and by then the product is blamed',
    designAs: ['questions a non-technical administrator can answer', 'not roles and permissions',
               'inheritance and exceptions made visible'],
    failureToAvoid: 'a role whose name means nothing to the person assigning it produces a configuration nobody will revisit' },
  { system: 'admin pages', what: ['tenants', 'billing', 'logs', 'integration keys'],
    reality: 'a product for a different user with different goals, usually built as CRUD screens',
    priority: 'logs deserve real design - they are used by somebody having a bad day with no training' },
  { system: 'configuration and migration', lastToBuild: true, firstInRisk: true,
    rule: 'the flows must survive data a sane person would not have entered',
    whereDiscovered: 'a customer upgrade three years later' },
];

/* What enterprise users want is the opposite of a consumer product. */
const CONTROL = {
  means: 'see everything, change everything, get out',
  priorities: [
    { want: 'density', why: 'not a maxim - the operators constraint is volume' },
    { want: 'configurable columns, filters, sort, saved PER USER',
      why: 'a saved view that changes for everybody is a bug report' },
    { want: 'bulk operations with a preview and a count',
      why: 'an operator processing eight hundred records will not click eight hundred times and will find a way around you' },
    { want: 'export',
      why: 'the real fear is being locked in, and a working export is the most effective retention feature available' },
    { want: 'single undo for a whole batch', why: 'anything reversible' },
  ],
};

/* Keyboard-first, and the spreadsheet. */
const KEYBOARD = {
  notPreference: 'it is the difference between a tool that works and a tool that is fought',
  reason: 'experts build speed through muscle memory, and a mouse-driven interface caps it at the level that makes people leave for a spreadsheet',
  whatTheyDoThere: 'bulk paste, arbitrary columns, their own formulas',
  therefore: 'be faster than the spreadsheet for the things it is good at',
  how: ['a shortcut for every frequent action', 'a command palette',
        'paste support where paste is the obvious approach'],
};

Comment-only guide to enterprise UX: density beats whitespace, and the three systems that make or break a B2B product are permissions, admin, and configuration.

25.6 Localization, RTL & global products

Global products are designed from the start for translation, not translated at the end. Plan for text growth of roughly thirty percent in many languages, maintain mirrored layouts for right-to-left scripts, and support locale-specific numbers, dates, and currencies without breaking layout. Culture also shapes conventions such as color, iconography, and formality. Test with real users in each market rather than assuming the same UX travels.

  • Design for text growth: labels that reflow (never "13px, fixed"), tables that tolerate +40% length, buttons that survive long German words.
  • RTL: languages like Arabic/Hebrew mirror the whole layout (not just text). From the start, mirror-aware: icons flip direction-sensitively, alignment flips, numbers stay LTR.
  • Culture is UI: color meanings, date/address/phone formats, currency local precision, and what "polite" errors look like differ by market.

    • What breaks when you localise, and why it is structural

    Most localisation failures are not translation failures; they are layouts that were written in a language with unusually forgiving geometry and a code that encoded that geometry. The structural reasons are four. Text growth is not uniform — German and Finnish commonly run thirty to fifty percent longer than English, and a button that fits "Continue" needs to fit "Weiter" plus a German compound noun somewhere in the button. Text height changes — line counts vary, so anything sized to a fixed number of lines clips. Script direction is structural, not cosmetic: right-to-left means the entire layout mirrors, including the reading order of a form, the direction of a progress indicator, the side a scrollbar appears, and the position of an icon that implies direction. Locale formatting — dates, times, numbers, currencies and addresses are all different, and a hard-coded format is a bug in every market except the one it was written in.

    The pipeline that makes localisation cheap

    The reason localisation is expensive is almost always process rather than translation, and the process fix is a specific sequence. Externalise every string on the day it is written, into a resource file, with a key that describes the meaning rather than the position — cart.checkout.submit, not button_label_3, because the second cannot be translated at all once the layout changes. Assume plural and gender forms from the start: a language with six plural cases cannot be served by a string with one, and the common workaround of "just adding an s" is a bug in every market it ships to. Reserve space, do not let it be computed: a button whose width is derived from its English label will clip in German, and the fix is a minimum width and a test at the longest plausible translation rather than an exception for one language. Treat dates, numbers and currencies as data, formatted by a library with the locale attached, never assembled from strings. And keep the source language in the repository, not only in the translation platform, so a developer can see what the sentence originally meant — which is the single most common blocker when a translator asks a question about context.

    Then the two things that are usually discovered too late. Right-to-left is a second implementation, not a setting. Test it from the first component rather than at localisation, because a codebase that assumes left-to-right has the assumption in its layout code and not only in its text. Sorting, searching and filtering behave differently: collated ordering differs between locales, search ignores diacritics in some and not others, and a filter labelled with a month name has to select months in the reader's locale. Each is a small thing and each is discovered by a user in one market at a time unless it is on the checklist.

    /* Why localisation is expensive: process, not translation. This is the sequence. */
const PIPELINE_STEPS = [
  { step: 'externalise every string on the day it is written',
    key: 'describe the meaning, not the position',
    good: 'cart.checkout.submit', bad: 'button_label_3',
    why: 'the second cannot be translated at all once the layout changes' },
  { step: 'assume plural and gender forms from the start',
    reality: 'a language with six plural cases cannot be served by a string with one',
    theCommonWorkaroundIsABug: 'just adding an s is a bug in every market it ships to' },
  { step: 'reserve space rather than computing it',
    problem: 'a button whose width is derived from its English label clips in German',
    fix: ['a minimum width', 'a test at the longest plausible translation'],
    notThis: 'an exception for one language' },
  { step: 'treat dates, numbers and currencies as data, formatted with the locale attached',
    never: 'assembled from strings' },
  { step: 'keep the source language in the repository, not only in the translation platform',
    reason: 'a developer can then see what the sentence originally meant',
    whyItMatters: 'that is the most common blocker when a translator asks about context' },
];

/* Two things discovered too late. */
const DISCOVERED_LATE = [
  { thing: 'right-to-left',
    isNot: 'a setting - it is a second implementation',
    testFrom: 'the first component, not at localisation',
    why: 'a codebase that assumes left-to-right has the assumption in its layout code, not only in its text' },
  { thing: 'sorting, searching and filtering',
    differsBy: ['collated ordering between locales',
                'whether search ignores diacritics',
                'a month-name filter selecting months in the readers locale'],
    discoveryPattern: 'each is small, and each is found by one user in one market unless it is on the checklist' },
];

    And then the ones that are about content rather than layout. Pseudolocalisation is the technique that finds all of them: generate a fake locale with accented characters, padded strings, and reversed or mirrored text, and run the whole product under it. It reliably finds the hard-coded widths, the truncated labels, the single-character assumptions, the input masks that reject valid local formats, and the icon whose direction is baked in. It is thirty minutes to set up and it converts a class of bugs that would otherwise be found by users in each market, one report at a time, forever. String externalisation is the discipline that makes it possible: every user-visible string in a resource file, no concatenation, no plurals built by appending an "s", and — the one that is nearly always broken — no text embedded in images.

    /* Four structural reasons localisation fails. None of them are translation. */
const STRUCTURAL = [
  { problem: 'text growth is not uniform', detail: 'German and Finnish commonly run 30-50% longer than English',
    example: 'a button that fits "Continue" must fit "Weiter" plus a compound noun' },
  { problem: 'text height changes', consequence: 'anything sized to a fixed number of lines clips' },
  { problem: 'script direction is structural',
    mirrors: ['the whole layout', 'the reading order of a form', 'the direction of a progress indicator',
              'the side a scrollbar appears', 'the position of an icon that implies direction'],
    notThis: 'translating the text' },
  { problem: 'locale formatting', detail: ['dates', 'times', 'numbers', 'currencies', 'addresses'],
    consequence: 'a hard-coded format is a bug in every market except the one it was written in' },
];

/* Pseudolocalisation. Thirty minutes, and it finds a whole class. */
const PSEUDO = {
  generate: ['accented characters', 'padded strings', 'mirrored or reversed text'],
  finds: ['hard-coded widths', 'truncated labels', 'single-character assumptions',
          'input masks that reject valid local formats', 'icons whose direction is baked in'],
  why: 'otherwise these are found by users in each market, one report at a time, forever',
};

/* The discipline that makes it possible. */
const EXTERNALISATION = [
  'every user-visible string in a resource file',
  'no concatenation',
  'no plurals built by appending an s',
  'no text embedded in images - nearly always broken',
];

/* Mirroring: what flips and what does not. */
const MIRRORING = {
  flips: ['alignment', 'reading order', 'progress indicators', 'breadcrumbs', 'scrollbars',
          'directional icons: arrows, media transport, a "return" glyph'],
  doesNotFlip: ['numbers inside a run of text stay left to right', 'brand marks and logos',
                'media that shows an actor facing a known direction', 'a chart whose axis direction carries meaning, unless deliberately mirrored'],
  partialMirror: 'an icon whose meaning is "forward" flips; an icon whose meaning is "this side of the app" also flips; an icon that is purely decorative does not',
  theTest: 'ask what the glyph means - if removing the direction would make it meaningless, it flips',
};

/* Culture, and the parts nobody localises. */
const CULTURE_NOT_LOCALISED = [
  'colour meaning - a colour that signals success or danger is not universal',
  'iconography - a hand gesture or a pictogram can be offensive or meaningless',
  'formality - the same message needs a different register in different markets',
  'what an error message is allowed to say - some cultures will not accept an apology from a system at all',
  'the shape of an address, a name, and a phone number, all of which break naive validation',
  'units and measurement, including the currency precision and where the symbol goes',
  'the calendar: week start, week numbering, and which day is the first day of the year',
  'the name field - it may be one field, two fields, or none, and the ordering matters',
];

/* The testing discipline. */
const LOCALISATION_TESTING = {
  minimum: ['run the product under a pseudo locale before every release', 'have the string length budget in code review'],
  perMarket: 'a native speaker reviewing the real screens, not a translation reviewing the copy',
  whatToAskThem: ['what is wrong with this', 'what would you never say', 'what is confusing but not wrong'],
  whyNotJustCorrectness: 'a translation can be perfect and the screen still fail, because the screen was designed around the assumptions of the source language',
};
  • Translate content, not just copy: measurement (imperial vs metric), examples, empty states, and the tone of your product’s voice.

Exercises 25

  1. Analyze a checkout you know and list 3 trust signals + 3 that could be hidden-copy drops.
  2. Sketch one "edge money" state (declined-but-pending) for a fintech you use.
  3. Take one screen of yours and redesign the layout for Arabic (mirror test).

26 · Designing for AI & Data Products

Designing for AI turns commands into delegation, where users state intent and the system proposes the journey, while data products demand honesty with numbers. AI adds new patterns but no new ethics: states, feedback, and trust still apply. The design questions are about control, explainability, and how failures are handled. Together, AI and analytics interfaces are the fastest-moving design conversation right now, so principles matter more than tooling.

26.1 The shift: from commands to delegation26.2 Core patterns: chat, streaming, grounding & tools26.3 Trust: help users route around confabulation26.4 Dashboards & honest data visualization26.5 Explainability & control

AI changes the user relationship from commands to conversation and delegation. And dashboards teach the numbers-of-truth discipline. Together they’re the fastest-growing design conversation in the industry right now.

26.1 The shift: from commands to delegation

Delegation shifts the interaction from clicking every step to stating an intent and letting the model propose the journey. The designer’s job is making delegation auditable: visible control points, an approved plan, undo and branching, and honest evidence at each stage. Users should understand what the AI is about to do and be able to redirect it mid-task. Delegation works only while the user stays in charge.

Old UIAI-era UI
user does every stepuser states intent, AI proposes a journey
binary outcomesstreaming, partial, "best effort" outcomes
errors are rare & unusualconfabulations are expected — design for them
one right answermultiple plausible answers with sources
user controls alluser delegates with visible control points

What delegation actually changes about the interface

The shift in the table above is not that screens became chatty. It is that the unit of work changed from a step to a plan, and every interface consequence follows from that. In the old model the user held the state and the system held nothing; clicking a button was the record of what had happened. In the delegated model the system holds the state and the user's job is to supervise it, which means the interface has to acquire a component that did not previously exist: a plan the user can read before it runs. Not a spinner, not a progress bar — a plan, in the user's terms, with the steps enumerated, the tools named, and the point at which something irreversible will happen marked. A person who has not seen the plan cannot supervise it, and a person who cannot supervise it has been told that they are still in charge while not being in charge.

So the design work is three things, in this order. A pre-flight view. Before anything acts, show what is about to happen, in the domain's language: "I will read these 6 files, then draft a summary, then post it to the channel you picked. Nothing is sent until you approve." That sentence is the whole component. Control points that are actually placed. Not one approval at the end — approval at each point where a decision becomes costly to reverse, and the definition of costly is the designer's judgement, so it has to be made explicitly for each product rather than inherited. Branch and undo. Undo after a delegated run is hard because the run may have touched a hundred things, which means undo has to be built as a compensating action rather than a literal one: state that can be restored, not actions that can be reversed.

The interface states of a delegated run

A run has a lifecycle, and each phase needs something specific from the interface rather than a generic loading treatment. Six phases, and the thing each one must communicate. Planning: what the system believes the task is — because a plan the user has not read is a plan the user cannot correct, and a misunderstanding discovered at step four is a wasted run while the same misunderstanding corrected at step zero is free. Executing: which step, what tool, and what it read — as a live count, not a spinner. Waiting on something external: which tool and for how long, because a long wait against an external system and a long wait against a slow model feel identical and are diagnosed differently. Blocked: a decision only the user can make, surfaced as a question with options rather than as an error, because the most common cause of a stalled delegated run is that the system needs something the user has and was not asked for. Partially complete: which parts succeeded, which did not, and what state the failures left behind. And finished: a summary the user can verify, listing what was done, what was changed, and what it recommends next — not a "done" state with a link.

Then the interruptibility design, which is where most delegated interfaces fail and where the failure is invisible until an incident. The requirements are four and they are not negotiable, because each corresponds to a real loss. Cancel is immediate and total: the click stops the rendering, not just the request, and no further tool calls are issued — a cancel that leaves a request in flight has cancelled nothing. Partial work is preserved and visible: what was already done, what it did, and whether it can be reversed, because a user who cancels without knowing what was already committed will either lose work or lose the ability to reason about the state. Cancel offers a choice about what happens next: keep what is done and stop, revert everything and stop, or save the partial draft and stop — one dialog, three outcomes, and the default should be the reversible one. And cancel is not buried: it must be reachable during execution without a confirmation that requires reading, because the person who most needs to stop is the person least able to read a dialog.

Auditing a delegation after the fact

The audit trail is the third piece of auditable delegation and it is the one that has to be built as a product rather than as a log, because nobody reads a log. Three views, serving three different questions. The one-pager: what the system did, in plain language, with each action attributed to a reason and a source — and this is what a person pastes into a ticket, so it must be copyable and must not be truncated at the interesting part. The trace: the full record, per step, with the inputs, the outputs, the tool versions, the timestamps and the model version — this is the artefact an engineer needs when something was wrong and it is the reason model versions have to be recorded at all. The cost and the effect: tokens, tools invoked, objects changed, and what the change did to whatever it touched — because a delegated run that quietly modified four hundred records is a fact the user needs before the next one, and the only way they can know is if the interface told them.

One last thing, because it decides whether any of this is usable: the design must assume the user will not read the plan. Not because people are careless, but because the plan is only interesting when the user already suspects a problem, and a person who suspects a problem is usually in a hurry. So the plan has to be legible at a glance — three lines, not thirty — with the details available rather than displayed, and with the single most consequential step at the top rather than buried in the sequence. Anything that requires reading in order is a control that does not exist under time pressure, and under time pressure is the condition in which a wrong delegation does damage.

/* Six phases, and what each must communicate. */
const PHASES = [
  { phase: 'planning', mustShow: 'what the system believes the task is',
    why: 'a plan the user has not read cannot be corrected, and a misunderstanding found at step four is a wasted run while the same one found at step zero is free' },
  { phase: 'executing', mustShow: ['which step', 'what tool', 'what it read'],
    as: 'a live count, not a spinner' },
  { phase: 'waiting on something external', mustShow: ['which tool', 'for how long'],
    why: 'a wait against an external system and a wait against a slow model feel identical and are diagnosed differently' },
  { phase: 'blocked', mustShow: 'a decision only the user can make, as a question with options rather than an error',
    why: 'the most common cause of a stalled run is that the system needs something the user has and was not asked for' },
  { phase: 'partially complete', mustShow: ['which parts succeeded', 'which did not', 'what state the failures left behind'] },
  { phase: 'finished', mustShow: ['what was done', 'what was changed', 'what it recommends next'],
    notThis: 'a done state with a link' },
];

/* Interruptibility. Each requirement corresponds to a real loss. */
const INTERRUPT = [
  { requirement: 'cancel is immediate and total',
    means: 'the click stops the rendering, not just the request, and no further tool calls are issued',
    theBug: 'a cancel that leaves a request in flight has cancelled nothing' },
  { requirement: 'partial work is preserved and visible',
    shows: ['what was already done', 'what it did', 'whether it can be reversed'],
    why: 'a user who cancels without knowing what was already committed will either lose work or lose the ability to reason about the state' },
  { requirement: 'cancel offers a choice about what happens next',
    options: ['keep what is done and stop', 'revert everything and stop', 'save the partial draft and stop'],
    default: 'the reversible one' },
  { requirement: 'cancel is not buried',
    why: 'the person who most needs to stop is least able to read a confirmation dialog',
    notThis: 'a confirmation that requires reading' },
];

/* Three audit views for three questions, and nobody reads a log. */
const AUDIT_VIEWS = [
  { view: 'the one-pager', question: 'what did it do, in plain language, with each action attributed to a reason and a source',
    mustBe: 'copyable, and not truncated at the interesting part',
    usedFor: 'pasting into a ticket' },
  { view: 'the trace', question: 'what happened at each step',
    contains: ['inputs', 'outputs', 'tool versions', 'timestamps', 'the model version'],
    whyTheModelVersionMatters: 'it is the reason model versions have to be recorded at all' },
  { view: 'the cost and the effect', question: 'what did it change, and what did that do',
    contains: ['tokens', 'tools invoked', 'objects changed', 'the effect on whatever was touched'],
    why: 'a run that quietly modified four hundred records is a fact the user needs before the next one' },
];

/* The assumption that decides whether any of it is usable. */
const ASSUME_NOT_READ = {
  assumption: 'the user will not read the plan',
  whyNotCareless: 'the plan is only interesting when the user already suspects a problem, and a person who suspects a problem is usually in a hurry',
  consequence: ['three lines, not thirty', 'details available rather than displayed',
                 'the single most consequential step at the top rather than buried in the sequence'],
  rule: 'anything requiring reading in order is a control that does not exist under time pressure, and under time pressure is when a wrong delegation does damage',
};

The failure modes are worth naming because they look like success until the complaint arrives. The over-confident plan: a plan so plausible that it does not occur to the user to check it, so a wrong plan is accepted by inertia — and the interface's job is to make checking cheap by putting the evidence next to the assertion. The unbounded loop: an agent that keeps working after the useful part is done, because nothing told it to stop, and the user's only defence is a cancel button they may not notice. The silent scope expansion: it read 6 files, then 200. The plan said six. Nobody sees this happen unless the interface is counting out loud. And the confident partial: an outcome that is genuinely "best effort" presented in the visual language of a completed action — the single most damaging error in this family, because a partial result styled as a final one is indistinguishable from a bug to the person who has to defend it downstream.

/* The unit of work changed from a step to a plan. */
const DELEGATION = {
  before: { whoHoldsState: 'the user', whatSystemHeld: 'nothing',
            record: 'clicking a button was the record of what had happened' },
  after:  { whoHoldsState: 'the system', usersJob: 'supervise' },
  theNewComponent: 'a plan the user can read before it runs - not a spinner, not a progress bar',
  reasonItIsRequired: 'a person who has not seen the plan cannot supervise it, and a person who cannot supervise it has been told they are still in charge while not being in charge',
};

/* The three things to build, in this order. */
const THREE_JOBS = [
  { job: 'the pre-flight view',
    content: 'in the domains own language: which files, what it will draft, what it will post, and where nothing happens until approval',
    example: 'I will read these 6 files, draft a summary, and post it to the channel you picked. Nothing is sent until you approve.',
    thatSentenceIs: 'the whole component' },
  { job: 'control points that are actually placed',
    notThis: 'one approval at the end',
    but: 'approval at each point where a decision becomes costly to reverse',
    designDecision: 'costly is the designers judgement, so it is made explicitly per product rather than inherited' },
  { job: 'branch and undo',
    problem: 'a delegated run may have touched a hundred things, so literal undo is impossible',
    answer: 'undo built as a compensating action - state that can be restored, not actions that can be reversed' },
];

/* Failure modes that look like success until the complaint arrives. */
const FAILURE_MODES = [
  { mode: 'the over-confident plan',
    mechanism: 'a plan so plausible that checking it does not occur to the user, so a wrong plan is accepted by inertia',
    designJob: 'make checking cheap by putting the evidence next to the assertion' },
  { mode: 'the unbounded loop', mechanism: 'it keeps working after the useful part is done because nothing told it to stop',
    userDefence: 'a cancel button they may not notice' },
  { mode: 'silent scope expansion', instance: 'the plan said six files; it read two hundred',
    visibility: 'only if the interface is counting out loud' },
  { mode: 'the confident partial', what: 'a genuine best-effort outcome presented in the visual language of a completed action',
    mostDamaging: true,
    why: 'indistinguishable from a bug to the person who has to defend it downstream' },
];

The UX job: make delegation auditable — show what the AI did, why, on what evidence, and how to undo it.

26.2 Core patterns: chat, streaming, grounding & tools

Chat compresses the interface, streaming returns results progressively as they generate, grounding ties answers to real sources, and agent tools let the model act beyond plain text. Each is now a core UI pattern with design jobs attached: show progress during streaming, make grounded citations visible, and confirm tool actions on consequential steps. Real-time feedback and cancel options keep delegation honest and alive. Users need to know what is happening now and why.

// Chat UI is a UI now (not a novelty):
//  - real streaming tokens; stop/edit on user message click
//  - grounding: cite sources visibly (RAG) — ungrounded answers are
//    fishing trips; "sources" + "confidence" make them honest
//  - long-running "agents": show step cards (planning → searching →
//    reading → writing) with cancel; a 2-min silent agent = dead UX
//  - tools/buttons inside the convo: "edit in draft", "apply",
//    "retry with more context" — the conversation must not dead-end
// Guardrails UI: temperature/reasoning selectors belong to power users;
// defaults should be default-safe for newcomers.

Streaming, and the states it creates

Streaming is not a performance feature; it changes the state machine, and the states it introduces have to be designed rather than inherited from whatever the framework renders. There are five. Composing: text is arriving and there is nothing to act on yet. The requirement is a stop control that is genuinely immediate, and a rule about what happens to partial text when the user stops — most products discard it, some keep it as a draft, and the choice has to be deliberate because "I stopped it halfway and my words are gone" reads as data loss. Interrupted: the user sent a follow-up while the first was still composing. The requirement is that the first is cancelled rather than queued, because a queued response arriving after the correction is a worse outcome than no response. Failed mid-stream: the connection dropped after 400 tokens. The requirement is that the 400 tokens survive and there is a retry that continues rather than restarting. Complete: the normal end state, which needs a visible boundary — a streamed answer that simply stops is indistinguishable from one that was cut off, so the interface marks where generation ended. And Superseded: a newer answer replaced an older one, which needs a way to see the old one, because people compare.

Then the three things that make a streamed answer usable rather than merely watchable. A stop control that is immediate, meaning the interface stops rendering on click rather than after the request is cancelled, because the perceived latency of cancellation is the thing people complain about.
