A visible boundary, so the last token is identifiable. And actions that do not require waiting: copy, retry, and the follow-up composer must all be live while streaming, because a person who has read enough to know what they want next is the normal case and making them wait for the paragraph to finish is the most common unnecessary friction in this pattern.

Tools, and where a human has to be in the loop

A tool call is the point at which a language model stops being a text generator and becomes a program, and it is where the design responsibility is sharpest. Three distinctions to hold on to. Reading is different from writing. A tool that fetches, searches, or queries changes nothing in the world, and the person can be told afterwards. A tool that sends, deletes, charges, publishes, or notifies changes the world, and the design requirement is a preview plus an approval — with the preview showing the actual payload, not a description of it, because "send an email to 200 recipients" and "send an email to 213 including the list you edited 40 seconds ago" are different actions with the same name. Reversibility decides approval. A tool that can be undone should not stop for approval; a tool that cannot should stop every time, including when it is the same tool and the same arguments as last time. The rule to avoid is a confirmation that appears once and is then suppressed, because a person who approved it once will approve it a hundred times by reflex and the mechanism has become decoration. Scope is a first-class thing to show. "Reading 6 files" is the useful number; the interface should keep counting and the user should be able to see when it exceeds the plan.

Then grounding, where the design question is narrower than it looks. The requirement is not that citations exist — it is that a citation is verifiable in place, which means the specific passage, not the whole document, and a preview the person can read without leaving what they were doing. The most common failure is a citation that opens a large PDF at page one when the claim is on page forty, because the citation is technically present and practically unusable; the fix is a fragment-level link with the passage quoted inline, so the check takes seconds rather than a minute. And the honest default for an ungrounded answer is to say so: "I could not find this in your sources, so this is from general knowledge and may be wrong" is a better product than a fluent answer with a citation that does not support it, because the second teaches people not to check citations at all.

/* Five states streaming creates. Inherited ones are not designed ones. */
const STREAM_STATES = [
  { state: 'composing', actionable: 'nothing yet', requires: 'a stop control that is genuinely immediate, and a rule for partial text when the user stops',
    options: ['discard the partial text', 'keep it as a draft'],
    whyItMatters: 'I stopped it halfway and my words are gone reads as data loss' },
  { state: 'interrupted', instance: 'the user sent a follow-up while the first was still composing',
    mustDo: 'cancel the first rather than queue it',
    why: 'a queued response arriving after the correction is worse than no response' },
  { state: 'failed mid-stream', instance: 'the connection dropped after 400 tokens',
    mustDo: ['the 400 tokens survive', 'retry continues rather than restarting'] },
  { state: 'complete', requires: 'a visible boundary',
    why: 'a streamed answer that simply stops is indistinguishable from one that was cut off' },
  { state: 'superseded', instance: 'a newer answer replaced an older one',
    requires: 'a way to see the old one',
    why: 'people compare' },
];

const STREAM_MAKE_USEFUL = [
  { thing: 'a stop control that is immediate', means: 'stops rendering on click rather than after the request is cancelled',
    why: 'the perceived latency of cancellation is what people complain about' },
  { thing: 'a visible boundary', so: 'the last token is identifiable' },
  { thing: 'actions live during streaming', which: ['copy', 'retry', 'the follow-up composer'],
    why: 'a person who has read enough to know what they want next is the normal case' },
];

/* Tools. Three distinctions to hold. */
const TOOLS = {
  readingVsWriting: {
    reading: 'a tool that fetches, searches or queries changes nothing; the person can be told afterwards',
    writing: 'sends, deletes, charges, publishes, notifies - requires preview plus approval',
    previewMustBe: 'the actual payload, not a description of it',
    example: 'send an email to 200 recipients and send an email to 213 including the list you edited 40 seconds ago are different actions with the same name',
  },
  reversibilityDecidesApproval: {
    undoable: 'do not stop for approval',
    notUndoable: 'stop every time, including the same tool with the same arguments as last time',
    avoid: 'a confirmation that appears once and is then suppressed - the person approves it a hundred times by reflex and the mechanism has become decoration',
  },
  scope: 'reading 6 files is the useful number; keep counting, and let the user see when it exceeds the plan',
};

/* Grounding: the citation has to be verifiable in place. */
const GROUNDING = {
  notEnough: 'that citations exist',
  requirement: 'a citation is verifiable in place - the specific passage, not the whole document',
  with: 'a preview the person can read without leaving what they were doing',
  commonFailure: 'a citation that opens a large PDF at page one when the claim is on page forty',
  why: 'technically present, practically unusable',
  fix: 'a fragment-level link with the passage quoted inline, so the check takes seconds rather than a minute',
  honestUngroundedDefault: 'I could not find this in your sources, so this is from general knowledge and may be wrong',
  beats: 'a fluent answer with a citation that does not support it',
  whyItBeatsIt: 'the second teaches people not to check citations at all',
};

Comment-only playbook for AI chat: stream tokens live, ground answers with visible sources, show step cards for agents, and never let the conversation dead-end.

26.3 Trust: help users route around confabulation

Since language models sometimes invent plausible facts, the design must help users route around confabulation. Ground answers in linked sources the user can open and verify, keep the tone appropriately modest rather than falsely confident, and gate consequential actions behind human approval. Show uncertainty honestly without pretending false precision. Design the failure modes so that doubt surfaces clearly rather than being hidden.

  • Assume the model will invent a citation sometimes. Surface "verify before high-stakes use", link sources, and log what evidence backed each answer.
  • Don’t present the model as omniscient authority: "based on your docs + internet, here’s my best take" is honest and lands better.
  • Human-in-the-loop for consequential actions (payments, medical advice, legal drafts): AI proposes, human approves, tool logs who approved what.

Making a plausible falsehood checkable

The instruction to ground answers is correct and incomplete, because a citation proves that a document exists rather than that it says what the answer claims. Both halves have to be designed, and the second half is the one that fails: an answer that says "per your policy, refunds are available within 30 days", citing a document that exists and says something else about refunds, is worse than an answer with no citation at all, because it has consumed the user's checking behaviour. So the grounding work is three layers. The claim, in quotation or close paraphrase, so the person can read what is being asserted without reading the answer. The passage, inline, with the specific lines. And the mismatch flag: where the retrieved material supports only part of the claim, the interface says which part, because a partially-supported answer presented as fully supported is the specific failure mode that destroys trust fastest.

Then the tone question, which is more delicate than it looks because false modesty is also a failure. The problem with a hedging register — "it seems", "possibly", "you might consider" — is that it is undifferentiated: it hedges the arithmetic as readily as the contested claim, so the user learns that the hedging carries no information and is right to ignore it. What works is calibrated modesty: confidence is expressed by specificity rather than by adverb. "This is not in your sources" is precise and low-confidence. "There may be some uncertainty" is imprecise and carries nothing. Concretely: name the source of the claim, state what you could not determine, and reserve explicit uncertainty language for the parts that are actually uncertain. A system that says "I am not sure" once in a paragraph is worth reading; a system that says it in every sentence is not.

Designing so doubt surfaces rather than disappears

The instinct is to make the confident answer the easy path and the checking path a deliberate extra step, and that instinct is wrong in a way that is measurable. A person who is given a fluent answer and a person who is given a fluent answer with a verification hint behave differently only if the hint costs nothing; the moment checking is expensive, they skip it, and the resulting behaviour is indistinguishable from never having designed for doubt. So the design work is to make checking nearly free at the moments it matters: the specific passage quoted inline next to the claim, a one-click way to see the surrounding context, a keyboard shortcut for "show me the sources for this paragraph", and a visible marker wherever the answer used something the system retrieved versus something it inferred. That last one is the highest-value signal available and almost nobody builds it — a person who knows a paragraph is inferred treats it differently from one that is quoted, and the interface can tell them at zero cost.

Then the parts of the product that must not be model-generated, which is a design decision with a specific list. Anything with a legal or contractual effect. Anything that constitutes advice in a regulated domain. Anything irreversible and hard to reverse for the user. And anything about the user's own data that would be a disclosure — a summary of what is stored about them, for instance, is a statement about the world that must come from the world, and a model paraphrasing a user's own record is a place where a confabulation becomes an accusation. The design response for each is a stated boundary the user can see: "this is generated, verify before sending", and for the genuinely generated documents, a template with generated fields rather than generated prose, because a template with a wrong field is corrected by the reader in one pass and a paragraph with a wrong clause is trusted until it is too late.

And the recovery path, which is the thing that decides whether a bad answer becomes an incident. When something is wrong — and in a system of this kind it will be — the person needs three things and the order matters. To find out how far it spread: if a wrong answer was sent to forty people, the person who received it has to know before anybody responds to it, and that means the system's own record has to answer "what did we send, to whom, when" faster than the person can ask a colleague. To correct it in the same place it was wrong, because a correction that lives in a different channel is not a correction for most people. And to know whether it can recur, which is a question about the process rather than about the model, and the honest answer is usually that the process allowed it, so the fix is a boundary or a gate rather than a better prompt.

/* Make checking nearly free, at the moments it matters. */
const DOUBT_SURFACES = [
  'the specific passage quoted inline next to the claim',
  'one click to see the surrounding context',
  'a keyboard shortcut for showing the sources for this paragraph',
  'a visible marker wherever the answer used retrieved material rather than inference',
];
const RETRIEVED_VS_INFERRED = {
  almostNobodyBuildsIt: true,
  whyItIsHighestValue: 'a person who knows a paragraph is inferred treats it differently from one that is quoted, at zero cost to the system',
};
const BEHAVIOURAL_ARGUMENT = {
  assumption: 'give a fluent answer plus an expensive check, and checking is skipped',
  consequence: 'indistinguishable from never having designed for doubt',
  requirement: 'checking costs nearly nothing at the moments it matters',
};

/* What must not be model-generated. */
const NOT_GENERATED = [
  { what: 'anything with a legal or contractual effect' },
  { what: 'anything constituting advice in a regulated domain' },
  { what: 'anything irreversible and hard for the user to reverse' },
  { what: 'anything that is a statement about the users own data',
    why: 'a summary of what is stored about them must come from the world; a model paraphrasing a record turns a confabulation into an accusation',
    designResponse: 'templates with generated fields, not generated prose - a wrong field is corrected in one pass, a wrong clause is trusted until too late' },
];

/* Recovery, in the order it has to happen. */
const RECOVERY = [
  { step: 1, need: 'find out how far it spread',
    requirement: 'the systems own record answers what did we send, to whom, when, faster than the person can ask a colleague' },
  { step: 2, need: 'correct it in the same place it was wrong', why: 'a correction in a different channel is not a correction for most people' },
  { step: 3, need: 'know whether it can recur',
    note: 'this is a question about the process, not the model',
    usualAnswer: 'the process allowed it, so the fix is a boundary or a gate rather than a better prompt' },
];

And the escalation ladder, which is the part that decides whether the human-in-the-loop is real or decorative. Four tiers by consequence. No gate: reading, drafting, summarising, anything reversible and internal. Show the action, execute automatically: sending a message into a channel the person controls, since it is reversible by posting a correction and the cost of a gate is a habit of approving without reading. Show the action, require approval: anything leaving the organisation, anything that spends money, anything a person would not expect to be shared. Require approval with a named human: irreversible and consequential — payments over a threshold, deletions of bulk data, anything with a legal or regulatory dimension, and in the medical and legal domains, anything that a person might act on clinically. The ladder is worth writing down explicitly, because the default in most products is a single undifferentiated confirm, and the undifferentiated confirm is used exactly as often as it is dismissed.

/* A citation proves a document exists, not that it says what you claim. */
const GROUNDING_LAYERS = [
  { layer: 'the claim', as: 'quotation or close paraphrase, so the assertion is readable without the answer' },
  { layer: 'the passage', as: 'the specific lines, inline' },
  { layer: 'the mismatch flag', as: 'where the material supports only part of the claim, say which part' },
];
const WORST_FAILURE = {
  what: 'an answer citing a document that exists and says something else about the claim',
  worseThanNoCitation: true,
  why: 'it has consumed the users checking behaviour',
  consequenceOverTime: 'a partially-supported answer presented as fully supported destroys trust fastest',
};

/* Calibrated modesty, not false modesty. */
const TONE = {
  problemWithHedging: 'it is undifferentiated - it hedges the arithmetic as readily as the contested claim',
  resultingLearning: 'the hedging carries no information, so the user is right to ignore it',
  rule: 'express confidence by specificity, not by adverb',
  preciseLowConfidence: 'this is not in your sources',
  impreciseCarryingNothing: 'there may be some uncertainty',
  practice: ['name the source of the claim', 'state what you could not determine',
             'reserve explicit uncertainty language for the parts that are actually uncertain'],
  frequencyMatter: 'a system that says I am not sure once in a paragraph is worth reading; one that says it in every sentence is not',
};

/* The escalation ladder. Written down, because the default is one
   undifferentiated confirm, used exactly as often as it is dismissed. */
const LADDER = [
  { tier: 0, gate: 'none', actions: ['reading', 'drafting', 'summarising'],
    qualifier: 'reversible and internal' },
  { tier: 1, gate: 'show the action, execute automatically', example: 'posting into a channel the person controls',
    why: 'reversible by posting a correction, and a gate here creates a habit of approving without reading' },
  { tier: 2, gate: 'show the action, require approval',
    actions: ['anything leaving the organisation', 'anything that spends money', 'anything the person would not expect to be shared'] },
  { tier: 3, gate: 'approval with a named human',
    actions: ['irreversible and consequential', 'payments over a threshold', 'bulk deletion',
              'anything with a legal or regulatory dimension',
              'in medicine and law, anything a person might act on clinically'],
    why: 'the user is not the only audience for the decision' },
];

26.4 Dashboards & honest data visualization

Dashboards and honest data visualization treat numbers with the rigor they deserve, because axes and context decide what any chart says. Start axes at honest scales rather than exaggerated ones, annotate every dip or spike with its cause, and surface the one metric an operator must act on first. Support comparison against history and keep chart choices simple. The goal is a truthful picture, not an impressive one.

// Chart honesty rules (missing dates are worse than noisy ones):
//  - axis always starts at a defensible zero unless the scale's a lie
//  - donut/single-value charts hide the story; show the reference
//  - annotate the WHY next to every dip (a chart with no context is
//    a screenshot; a chart with context is a decision)
//  - order and hierarchy: the ONE number the operator needs first
// Planning dashboards: state narrative ("signups up, conversion down —
// checking funnel") — the metric set is a conversation, not wallpaper.

The chart decisions that quietly change the story

Axis truncation is the famous one and it is the least dangerous, because it is easy to spot and has a well-understood fix. The three that actually change decisions are subtler. Stacked areas hide the series you care about. Everything except the bottom band is unreadable, which means the bottom band has to be the one you chose first — and if the metric of interest is the thin band on top, a stacked area is the wrong chart regardless of how attractive it looks. Dual axes manufacture correlation. Two series on two scales with different units will always appear to move together, and readers will conclude a relationship that is an artefact of the scaling; the honest alternatives are two panels, or indexing both to a common base. Aggregation hides the event that matters: a monthly line that is steady can contain a single day that accounts for a third of the quarter's total, and the fix is to allow the reader to drill to the granularity at which the decision is actually made, which is often a day or an hour and never the aggregation the dashboard happens to have precomputed.

Then the four that are less about technique and more about honesty of framing. A truncated axis is acceptable when the scale is genuinely arbitrary — a temperature change of 0.4 degrees, a latency in the tens of milliseconds — and the rule is that it must be visible, not that it must be zero-based. A percentage without a denominator is not a number, and "conversion up 15%" is meaningless without the traffic it applies to; a percentage change on a base of forty people and on a base of forty thousand are different facts wearing the same glyph. Colour on a chart carries meaning only if it means something, so a red line for the metric you are worried about and grey for the rest is legitimate, while a rainbow palette with no encoding is decoration that reads as information. And a comparison needs a baseline and a window: "up" relative to what, over what period, and is the seasonal pattern accounted for — a week-over-week comparison on a business metric is usually a comparison against a weekend.

/* Axis truncation is the famous one and the least dangerous: it is easy to
   spot. These three change decisions. */
const CHART_LIES = [
  { chart: 'stacked areas', problem: 'everything except the bottom band is unreadable',
    requirement: 'the bottom band must be the metric you chose first',
    wrongChartEntirely: 'when the metric of interest is the thin band on top' },
  { chart: 'dual axes', problem: 'two series on two scales will always appear to move together, and readers conclude a relationship that is an artefact of the scaling',
    alternatives: ['two panels', 'indexing both to a common base'] },
  { chart: 'pre-aggregated lines', problem: 'a steady monthly line can contain one day that is a third of the quarter',
    fix: 'let the reader drill to the granularity the decision is made at - often a day, never the aggregation the dashboard happened to precompute' },
];

/* Framing honesty, which is less about technique. */
const FRAMING = [
  { rule: 'a truncated axis is acceptable when the scale is genuinely arbitrary',
    examples: ['a temperature change of 0.4 degrees', 'latency in the tens of milliseconds'],
    requirement: 'it must be visible, not that it must be zero-based' },
  { rule: 'a percentage without a denominator is not a number',
    example: 'conversion up 15 percent is meaningless without the traffic it applies to',
    why: 'a change on a base of forty and on a base of forty thousand are different facts wearing the same glyph' },
  { rule: 'colour carries meaning only if it means something',
    legitimate: 'red for the metric you are worried about, grey for the rest',
    decoration: 'a rainbow palette with no encoding, which reads as information' },
  { rule: 'a comparison needs a baseline and a window',
    mustAnswer: ['up relative to what', 'over what period', 'is seasonality accounted for'],
    gotcha: 'week-over-week on a business metric is usually a comparison against a weekend' },
];

Comment-only rules for honest charts: defensible axes, annotated whys, and one hero number — context turns a screenshot into a decision.

26.5 Explainability & control

Explainability and control are the answers to the question of who is in charge in an AI product. Every suggestion needs a why stated at the user’s level of expertise, plus an override such as accept and edit rather than accept or reject. Preferences that persist act as steering wheels so the model aligns to the user over time. If users cannot explain or redirect the output, the design has failed.

  • Explain the what and why at the level the user needs: "recommended because it also has AH left" beats "recommended by model v4".
  • Give overrides: accept/edit/reject on every proposed action; persisted preferences ("never suggest this vendor") are user steering wheels.
  • Feedback without harm: "wrong" on an AI answer should tune behavior safely, not count toward a shame score.

Writing an explanation a person can act on

An explanation is only useful if it changes a decision, and the test for that is whether it distinguishes between the options the user was considering. "Recommended by model v4" does not; "recommended because it also has 3 hours left in AH, and your other two have none" does, because it tells the user which attribute the recommendation traded away and therefore whether to override. So an explanation has three parts and missing any one of them makes it decorative: the driver, named as the attribute that decided it; the trade-off, the thing that would have made a different recommendation; and the confidence, expressed as what would change the answer. "This is a close call" is not that — "this changes if the delivery date is not required" is, because it is falsifiable and it tells the user what to do next.

The level question in the bullet above deserves more precision, because "at the user's level" is not one level but two decisions. Vocabulary: the user's nouns, not the model's. An explanation using a feature name the user has never heard of communicates that a person with internal knowledge made this, not that the product is helping. And granularity: one driver at a time, not a paragraph — a list of five reasons is not an explanation, it is a scoring function dumped into the interface, and the person cannot tell which one mattered. When there really are several drivers, show the top one and make the rest available, because the useful question is always "why this one and not that one".

Persisted preferences as a steering mechanism

The bullet about preferences is the most important item in this section and it is the one most often implemented as a settings page, which defeats it. A preference only steers if it is expressed in the system's language and if the user can tell it took effect. "Never suggest this vendor" is steering; a toggle labelled "Include vendor suggestions" buried in a preferences screen is not, because the user cannot connect the setting to any particular suggestion they will later see or not see. So the design requirements are four: preferences are stated in the domain's vocabulary rather than as product switches, the ones that matter are reachable from the point where the behaviour is visible, the system confirms that it understood by acting differently immediately, and the preference has an owner and a scope — global, this project, this kind of task — because a preference whose scope is unstated produces an explanation nobody can give.

Then the honest account of what steering does and does not achieve, which is worth stating because it is routinely oversold. Persisted preferences reliably handle corrections: after two or three rejections of a particular kind, the behaviour changes and the user can verify that it changed. They handle constraints well: a stated limit is a hard filter and it will be honoured. They handle style and format reasonably: length, tone, and structure are learnable from a small number of examples. They do not handle judgement — there is no preference that makes a system know what a good decision looks like in an unfamiliar situation, and any product claiming otherwise is describing a capability it does not have. The design consequence is that a preference should never be presented as a way to fix a bad output; it should be presented as a way to constrain a category of output, and the interface that implies otherwise sets an expectation it will break.

The audit and the exit, which are the same work

Both are the same requirement seen from two directions, and both are systematically omitted. An AI feature that can be used should be able to be inspected and switched off, and the inspection has to answer four questions in one place: what has it done on my behalf, as a human-readable list with times; what did it learn about me, which for a personalised system is the only honest account of the data; what would it do differently, in the form of the preferences above, presented as a review rather than as a form; and stop, which must be immediate and must not require a support ticket. The reason these are omitted is that they are not part of the happy path and no metric rewards them — which is exactly why they have to be specified rather than left to be discovered, because the person who has to discover them is a user who has decided they no longer trust the feature.

And one thing to design deliberately rather than inherit: the state a person is in when they look at any of this. Somebody reading a list of automated actions is either verifying something they suspect, cleaning up after something that went wrong, or deciding whether to subscribe in the first place — and those three people need different things from the same screen. A verifying user wants the last action first and the reasoning attached. A cleaning-up user wants a bulk undo. A prospective user wants a plain-language summary of what would happen on their own data, which is the hardest thing on the screen and the one that most improves the decision, because most people will not read a policy and will read a description of what happens to their Thursday evening.

/* A preference only steers if it is expressed in the systems language and
   the user can tell it took effect. */
const PREFERENCES = {
  steering: 'never suggest this vendor',
  notSteering: 'a toggle labelled include vendor suggestions, buried in a preferences screen',
  why: 'the user cannot connect the setting to any particular suggestion they will later see or not see',
  requirements: [
    'stated in the domains vocabulary, not as product switches',
    'the ones that matter are reachable from the point where the behaviour is visible',
    'the system confirms it understood by acting differently immediately',
    'an owner and a scope - global, this project, this kind of task',
  ],
  whyScope: 'a preference whose scope is unstated produces an explanation nobody can give',
};

/* What steering does and does not achieve. */
const STEERING_LIMITS = [
  { handles: 'corrections', detail: 'after two or three rejections of a particular kind the behaviour changes and the user can verify it' },
  { handles: 'constraints', detail: 'a stated limit is a hard filter and it will be honoured' },
  { handles: 'style and format', detail: 'length, tone and structure are learnable from a small number of examples' },
  { doesNotHandle: 'judgement',
    detail: 'there is no preference that makes a system know what a good decision looks like in an unfamiliar situation',
    consequence: 'any product claiming otherwise is describing a capability it does not have',
    designRule: 'never present a preference as a way to fix a bad output - present it as a way to constrain a category of output' },
];

/* Inspection and exit, which are the same requirement. */
const INSPECTION = {
  questions: [
    { q: 'what has it done on my behalf', as: 'a human-readable list with times' },
    { q: 'what did it learn about me', note: 'for a personalised system, the only honest account of the data' },
    { q: 'what would it do differently', as: 'the preferences presented as a review rather than a form' },
    { q: 'stop', must: ['be immediate', 'not require a support ticket'] },
  ],
  whyOmitted: ['not part of the happy path', 'no metric rewards them'],
  whySpecifyAnyway: 'the person who has to discover them is a user who has already decided they do not trust the feature',
};

/* Three people, one screen. */
const AUDIENCES_AT_REVIEW = [
  { person: 'verifying', believes: 'something is wrong', wantsFirst: 'the last action, with the reasoning attached' },
  { person: 'cleaning up', believes: 'something went wrong', wantsFirst: 'a bulk undo' },
  { person: 'prospective', believes: 'deciding whether to start', wantsFirst: 'a plain-language description of what would happen on their own data',
    why: 'the hardest thing on the screen and the one that most improves the decision',
    evidence: 'most people will not read a policy and will read a description of what happens to their Thursday evening' },
];

Then the feedback mechanism, where the harm the third bullet warns about comes from a specific design choice. A thumbs-up and thumbs-down pair on a model answer is unsafe, because the negative is used as a training signal for the whole system and a person who is annoyed taps it without thinking — so a large fraction of negative votes are about tone, length or irritation rather than accuracy, and the system learns to be less useful for reasons nobody intended. The safer designs are: ask a specific question rather than a general one ("did this contain anything that was not in your documents?"), which converts a mood into a signal; separate this answer was wrong from I would not use this again, which are different signals; and make the negative path require a reason, which drops the volume by an order of magnitude and makes the remaining data usable. The volume drop is a feature — a feedback channel that everybody uses is not a measurement.

/* An explanation is only useful if it changes a decision. */
const EXPLANATION_PARTS = [
  { part: 'the driver', as: 'the attribute that decided it, named in the users vocabulary',
    example: 'it also has 3 hours left in AH' },
  { part: 'the trade-off', as: 'the thing that would have made a different recommendation',
    example: 'your other two have none' },
  { part: 'the confidence', as: 'what would change the answer',
    notThis: 'this is a close call', thisInstead: 'this changes if the delivery date is not required',
    why: 'the second is falsifiable and it tells the user what to do next' },
];
const DECORATIVE = 'recommended by model v4 - it does not distinguish between the options the user was considering';

/* Two decisions inside "at the users level". */
const LEVEL = {
  vocabulary: 'the users nouns, not the models',
    symptomOfFailure: 'a feature name the user has never heard of communicates that a person with internal knowledge made this, not that the product is helping',
  granularity: 'one driver at a time, not a paragraph',
    whyNotFive: 'a list of five reasons is a scoring function dumped into the interface, and the person cannot tell which one mattered',
    whenThereAreSeveral: ['show the top one', 'make the rest available'],
    theUsefulQuestion: 'why this one and not that one' },
};

/* Feedback, and where the harm comes from. */
const FEEDBACK = {
  unsafe: 'a thumbs-up and thumbs-down pair on a model answer',
  why: 'the negative is a training signal for the whole system',
  whatActuallyArrives: 'a large fraction of negative votes about tone, length or irritation rather than accuracy',
  consequence: 'the system learns to be less useful for reasons nobody intended',
  safer: [
    { design: 'ask a specific question instead of a general one',
      example: 'did this contain anything that was not in your documents?',
      effect: 'converts a mood into a signal' },
    { design: 'separate this answer was wrong from I would not use this again',
      note: 'they are different signals' },
    { design: 'make the negative path require a reason',
      effect: 'drops the volume by an order of magnitude and makes the remaining data usable' },
  ],
  theVolumeDropIsAFeature: 'a feedback channel that everybody uses is not a measurement',
};

27 · Frontend for Designers: The Browser as Canvas

Frontend for designers teaches HTML, CSS, and JavaScript as the actual medium your product is built in, turning the browser into the canvas. A designer who can read code ships faster, argues better with engineers, and prototypes in the real medium. Learn how layout, variables, and interactivity map to your design decisions, and you move from handing off images to building live product. The browser is not a less accurate Figma; it is the accurate one.

27.1 The box model & flow — the physics of layout27.2 Implementing your tokens in CSS27.3 Responsive with flex/grid, not just breakpoints27.4 Browser prototyping: interactive states without a tool27.5 The developer viewport: what devs see that design tools hide27.6 The design-engineering bridge role

Designers who read code ship faster, argue better, and prototype things tools can’t. This chapter is the designer’s path into HTML/CSS/JS — not to become a developer, but to become fluent in the medium the product is actually built in.

27.1 The box model & flow — the physics of layout

The box model is the physics of layout: every element is a box with content, padding, border, and margin whose sizes compose in predictable ways. Normal flow stacks blocks vertically and runs inline content, while flex handles alignment and distribution along one axis and grid handles two. Once spacing becomes grammar rather than magic, you can predict why a layout behaves a certain way. Master this model and the browser stops surprising you.

/* Every element is a box: margin | border | padding | content */
.card{ margin:16px;        /* space OUTSIDE (between boxes) */
       border:1px solid;   /* edge */
       padding:12px;       /* space INSIDE (between edge and content) */ }
/* Flow: block boxes stack (vertical now), inline flows (horizontal) */
/* Then layout engines take over: flex (one axis) & grid (two axes) */
.flex-row{ display:flex; gap:12px; justify-content:space-between; align-items:center; } /* one axis */
.grid{ display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(12,1fr); gap:16px; } /* two axes */
/* Reading this is design grammar: spacing = margin/padding, not magic */

The four boxes, and which one a designer is usually thinking of

The four-box model is the thing a designer has to internalise in order to predict a layout without trying it, and the reason it stays confusing is that the number everyone remembers is the wrong one. Every element is content, then padding around it, then a border, then margin around that. Padding is inside the element and is coloured with it; margin is outside it and is always transparent. The consequence that catches people out is that a margin does not push apart two elements inside a parent that has a background — it pushes the elements apart inside a gap that shows the parent's background through, so "a card's background stops short of where the card visually begins" is a padding mistake and "two cards have a gap the colour of the page instead of the colour between cards" is a margin decision that was made without looking.

Then the collapsing rules, which are the reason margins are unpredictable to anyone reasoning about them the way they reason about padding. Adjacent vertical margins collapse: two siblings with 24 px bottom and 24 px top end up 24 px apart, not 48. Parent and first-child margins can collapse, so a heading's top margin can move the whole parent down, which is why a card with a heading inside it sometimes has a mysterious gap above it that no margin value accounts for. An empty block's own margins collapse through it, so a spacer div with no content and a margin is not a reliable spacer at all. And margins never collapse horizontally, which is why left and right margins are additive and behave the way people expect while top and bottom do not. Padding has none of this behaviour, which is the single most useful reason to prefer padding for internal spacing and margin only for external separation.

Flex and grid, and knowing which one you have

Flex is one-dimensional: it distributes space along a single axis and aligns along the cross axis. Grid is two-dimensional: it places items into rows and columns that are defined independently of the items. The design consequence is not that one is better — it is that a designer who reaches for the wrong one produces layouts that fight back. Everything that is a row of related things, a vertical stack that needs independent spacing, or a bar whose items should size to content, is flex. Everything that is a page structure, a card grid where the cards should align across rows as well as down them, or a form where the label and field columns must line up over many rows, is grid. The symptom of the wrong choice is specific: flex cards of differing height in a wrapping row produce a ragged bottom edge with no way to fix it, because flex does not know about the row below — and that ragged edge is a grid problem, solved by letting the grid own the row height.

Then the properties worth memorising, because they are the ones a designer needs in order to predict rather than experiment. gap replaces margin-based spacing and does not collapse, so it should be preferred even where margins would work. minmax and auto-fit make a grid that reflows without a single media query. flex: 1 means "take the remaining space" and flex-basis says how much space to start from — which matters for the case where a long word would otherwise push the layout. aspect-ratio sets a proportion without padding hacks. And place-items, place-content and place-self are shorthands for the four align and justify pairs, and using them is what turns a stylesheet into something a designer can read.

/* The box model, as a designer needs it: which box do you mean? */
const BOXES = [
  { box: 'content', contains: 'the text and images', designerCares: 'the size they specified' },
  { box: 'padding', inside: true, paintedWith: 'the elements own background',
    use: 'internal spacing', behaviour: 'never collapses' },
  { box: 'border', paintedWith: 'its own colour', use: 'a visible edge' },
  { box: 'margin', inside: false, paintedWith: 'nothing - always transparent',
    use: 'external separation', behaviour: 'collapses vertically' },
];

/* The four collapse rules. Padding has none of them, which is the
   strongest reason to use padding for internal spacing. */
const COLLAPSE = [
  { rule: 'adjacent vertical margins collapse',
    instance: '24px bottom and 24px top end up 24px apart, not 48',
    survivesHorizontally: 'no - left and right margins are additive' },
  { rule: 'parent and first-child margins can collapse',
    symptom: 'a card with a heading inside has a mysterious gap above it that no margin value accounts for' },
  { rule: 'an empty blocks own margins collapse through it',
    consequence: 'a spacer div with no content and a margin is not a reliable spacer' },
  { rule: 'margins never collapse horizontally',
    consequence: 'left and right behave the way people expect while top and bottom do not' },
];

/* Flex or grid: this is the decision, not the preference. */
const WHICH_TOOL = [
  { use: 'flex', oneDimensional: true, for: [
    'a row of related things',
    'a vertical stack that needs independent spacing',
    'a bar whose items should size to content' ] },
  { use: 'grid', twoDimensional: true, for: [
    'page structure',
    'card grids that must align across rows as well as down them',
    'a form where label and field columns line up over many rows' ] },
  { symptomOfTheWrongChoice: 'flex cards of differing height in a wrapping row give a ragged bottom edge with no fix, because flex does not know about the row below',
    itIs: 'a grid problem, solved by letting the grid own the row height' },
];

/* The properties that make a layout predictable rather than experimental. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'gap', why: 'replaces margin-based spacing and does not collapse' },
  { p: 'flex: 1', meaning: 'take the remaining space' },
  { p: 'flex-basis', why: 'says how much space to start from - this is what stops a long word pushing the layout' },
  { p: 'minmax + auto-fit', why: 'a grid that reflows without a single media query' },
  { p: 'aspect-ratio', why: 'a proportion with no padding hack' },
  { p: 'place-items / place-content / place-self', why: 'shorthands for the four align and justify pairs, and using them is what makes a stylesheet readable' },
];

CSS rhythm: every element is a margin-border-padding-content box; flex handles one axis and grid two, so spacing becomes readable grammar instead of magic numbers.

27.2 Implementing your tokens in CSS

Implementing design tokens in CSS means turning colors, spacing, type, and radii into named custom properties, then referencing those names everywhere instead of hardcoding values. Centralize the definitions so one change re-themes the product, moving dark mode or brand swaps from an edit marathon to a value swap. Keep token names semantic rather than literal. A designer who wires tokens into CSS keeps the system true.

:root{
  /* your design tokens become CSS custom properties */
  --space-1:4px; --space-2:8px; --space-4:16px;  /* 4-8-16 scale */
  --color-text-primary:#1c2128;
  --color-bg-canvas:#f6f7f9;
  --font-body: 'Inter', system-ui, sans-serif;
}
.card{ padding:var(--space-4); color:var(--color-text-primary);  /* tokens by name */
       background:var(--color-bg-canvas); }
/* Theme switch = swap the VALUES of the same names (Ch.9.3). */
/* If you see #1c2128 anywhere but a variable, a token got bypassed. */

One name, one decision, and why a token is not a variable

A design token and a CSS custom property are the same mechanism and different intents, and the distinction decides whether the system survives contact with a second theme. A variable is a name for a value so the value can be changed in one place. A token is a named decision about the design — "body text is this colour", "space between sections is this much" — with the value as an implementation detail that can change without changing the decision. So --surface-1 is a token and --grey-900 is a variable, and the difference shows up the moment a theme wants a different palette: with the first, one mapping changes; with the second, every usage has to be found. That is the whole argument, and it is why the naming convention matters more than the tooling — a token named after its value is a variable, and it will be treated like one the first time the value changes for a reason.

Then the three tiers, which is how a real token system is shaped and which most hand-rolled ones skip. Primitives are the raw palette and scale: --blue-600, --space-4, --radius-2. They carry no meaning and are never referenced by a component. Semantic tokens carry the meaning: --text-primary, --surface-raised, --border-subtle, --danger-text. These are what components reference. Component tokens exist where a component genuinely needs its own lever: --button-padding-inline, which is the right thing to expose and which is also how a token system starts to rot. The rule that keeps it healthy: a component token must be set from a semantic token, never from a primitive, or the component becomes a fourth place where the design decisions live.

Then the mechanics a designer needs to know, because they explain what is possible and what is not. Custom properties inherit, so setting --text-primary on a container recolours everything inside it — which is how dark mode and a themed embed both work, without a single selector targeting them. They work in media queries and in calc(), so a token can be a step in an arithmetic expression rather than a fixed value. A fallback is written as a second argument, var(--x, 4px), which matters when a token might be undefined — and the important consequence is that a typo in a token name does not fail loudly; it silently renders as nothing or falls back, so the check that a token exists is worth automating. And they are not typed: a token intended for a length can be given a colour and the browser will discard the declaration rather than warn.

/* A token is a named decision; a variable is a name for a value. */
const TOKEN_VS_VARIABLE = {
  token: { example: '--surface-1', is: 'a named decision about the design',
    value: 'an implementation detail that may change without changing the decision' },
  variable: { example: '--grey-900', is: 'a name for a value so the value can be changed in one place' },
  whyItMatters: 'when a theme wants a different palette, with a token one mapping changes; with a variable every usage has to be found',
  namingIsTheArgument: 'a token named after its value is a variable, and will be treated like one the first time the value changes for a reason',
};

/* Three tiers. Components reference tier two, never tier one. */
const TIERS = [
  { tier: 'primitive', examples: ['--blue-600', '--space-4', '--radius-2'],
    carriesMeaning: false, referencedByComponents: false },
  { tier: 'semantic', examples: ['--text-primary', '--surface-raised', '--border-subtle', '--danger-text'],
    carriesMeaning: true, referencedByComponents: true },
  { tier: 'component', examples: ['--button-padding-inline'],
    existsWhen: 'a component genuinely needs its own lever',
    rule: 'must be set from a semantic token, never from a primitive',
    why: 'otherwise the component becomes a fourth place where the design decisions live' },
];

/* Mechanics: what is possible, and what fails silently. */
const MECHANICS = [
  { feature: 'custom properties inherit',
    enables: ['setting --text-primary on a container recolours everything inside it',
              'dark mode with no selector targeting it',
              'a themed embed'] },
  { feature: 'they work inside media queries and calc()',
    enables: 'a token can be a step in an arithmetic expression rather than a fixed value' },
  { feature: 'a fallback is the second argument: var(--x, 4px)',
    mattersWhen: 'a token might be undefined' },
  { feature: 'a typo in a token name does not fail loudly',
    consequence: 'it silently renders as nothing, or falls back',
    therefore: 'checking that a token exists is worth automating' },
  { feature: 'they are not typed',
    consequence: 'a token intended for a length given a colour is silently discarded by the browser',
  },
];

/* The rule the whole library in this repo runs on. */
const NEVER_HARD_CODE = 'if you see a raw hex, a px value or a colour in a component, a token got bypassed';

Design tokens become CSS custom properties on :root, and the card references them by name, so consistency and theming come from swapping those values once.

27.3 Responsive with flex/grid, not just breakpoints

Responsive layout built on flex and grid lets containers collapse naturally instead of relying on breakpoint whack-a-mole. Use patterns such as auto-fit tracks and minmax sizing so content reflows by available space at every width, not just at preset points. Flex handles one axis with wrapping and alignment while grid reflows rows and columns. Breakpoints then fine-tune rather than rebuild the layout.

/* Let the layout WANT to collapse: */
.cards{ display:grid; gap:16px;  /* fluid, not fixed */
        grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(240px,1fr)); }
/* auto-fit + minmax = natural reflow at ANY width, no magic numbers */
/* Flex for small row/column decisions; grid for the page scaffold.
   Breakpoints then fine-tune, they don't do the whole job (Ch.11.2). */

Content decides the breakpoint, and you can find it

The best breakpoint is the width at which the design breaks, and the useful discovery is that this is measurable rather than guessed: put the content in a narrow container and widen it slowly until something wraps badly, an element's text becomes unreadable, or a target falls below 44 px. That number is the breakpoint. Everything else — the device widths in a stats panel, the tablet size, the one somebody mentioned — is a coincidence of the current content, and encoding it means the next content change silently invalidates the layout and nobody finds out until a device nobody tested on shows it. The corollary is that a breakpoint list should be treated as derived data: change the content and the list should be re-derived, not defended.

Then the difference between breakpoints and intrinsic responsiveness, because the second removes most breakpoints entirely. Intrinsic means the layout responds to its container rather than to the viewport, using auto-fit and minmax(), clamp() for fluid type, and flex-wrap. The consequence is that the same component works in a sidebar, in a modal and in a full page without a variant for each — and, more importantly, that it works at widths nobody anticipated, including the widths produced by a third-party embed, a browser with a scrollbar, or a future redesign of a page the component has nothing to do with. Container queries do the same job explicitly: a card can style itself according to the width of the card rather than the width of the page, which is the only version of responsive that is correct for a component designed to be reused.

Then the four things that break responsive layouts, which are worth naming because they are all avoidable and all look like a CSS bug. Fixed-width containers — a width: 400px on anything that holds text is a horizontal scrollbar on a phone, and the fix is max-width: 100% as a habit. Images without intrinsic sizing: without width and height attributes the browser cannot reserve space before the image arrives, so the layout jumps; that is a performance problem expressed as a design problem. Long unbreakable strings — a URL, an email, a token — which need overflow-wrap: anywhere and are the single most common cause of a page being unusable on a narrow screen. And touch targets that shrink with the layout, because a button that was comfortably large on a desktop becomes 28 px on a phone and the design looks fine in any screenshot.

/* The best breakpoint is measurable, not guessed. */
const FINDING_THE_BREAKPOINT = {
  method: ['put the content in a narrow container', 'widen it slowly',
           'stop when something wraps badly, text becomes unreadable, or a target falls below 44px'],
  theNumberYouFind: 'the breakpoint',
  everythingElse: 'device widths from a stats panel, tablet sizes, what somebody mentioned',
  whyNotThose: 'they are coincidences of the current content, so the next content change silently invalidates the layout and nobody finds out until a device nobody tested on shows it',
  therefore: 'treat the breakpoint list as derived data - change the content, re-derive the list, do not defend it',
};

/* Intrinsic versus breakpoint-driven. */
const INTRINSIC = [
  { technique: 'auto-fit + minmax()', enables: 'a grid whose column count follows available width with no media query' },
  { technique: 'flex-wrap', enables: 'a row that wraps instead of overflowing' },
  { technique: 'clamp() for fluid type', enables: 'a size that scales between a minimum and a maximum' },
  { technique: 'container queries', enables: 'a card styled by the width of the card rather than the width of the page',
    whyOnlyCorrectForReusable: 'a component in a sidebar, a modal and a full page all need it' },
  { consequence: 'layouts work at widths nobody anticipated - including a third-party embed, a scrollbar, or a future page redesign' },
];

/* Four things that break responsive layouts, all avoidable. */
const BREAKS = [
  { cause: 'fixed-width containers', instance: 'width: 400px on anything holding text',
    effect: 'a horizontal scrollbar on a phone', fix: 'max-width: 100% as a habit' },
  { cause: 'images without intrinsic sizing',
    mechanism: 'with no width and height attributes the browser cannot reserve space before the image arrives',
    effect: 'the layout jumps', reframedAs: 'a performance problem expressed as a design problem' },
  { cause: 'long unbreakable strings', instances: ['a URL', 'an email address', 'a token'],
    fix: 'overflow-wrap: anywhere',
    why: 'the single most common cause of a page being unusable on a narrow screen' },
  { cause: 'touch targets that shrink with the layout',
    instance: 'a comfortable desktop button at 28px on a phone',
    whyNobodyNotices: 'the design looks fine in any screenshot' },
];

auto-fit with minmax makes card grids reflow naturally at any width, so breakpoints fine-tune instead of doing the whole responsive job.

27.4 Browser prototyping: interactive states without a tool

Browser prototyping shows real interactive states without a prototyping tool, using plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. A clickable, stateful prototype can live in about twenty lines of code, covering native focus, hover, validation, and storage. Native browser behaviors come for free, giving stakeholders a live artifact instead of a simulation. It is a lightweight way to test real behavior before committing to the full build.

<!-- A clickable, stateful prototype in 20 lines: -->
<button onclick="count.value++; this.disabled = ok.checked">Add item</button> <!-- increments, locks when checked -->
<output id="count">0</output> <!-- live result -->
<label><input type="checkbox" id="ok"> Allow bulk add</label>
<!-- Then add: transitions for motion, localStorage / URL hash to
     remember state, and the browser's native focus & validation
     (Ch.4.4 already used these). This IS a real prototype toolkit. -->

What a prototype in the browser can do that a static mock cannot

The reason to prototype in the browser is not fidelity — it is that a browser removes the categories of questions that static mockups cannot answer. Four of them, and each is a question somebody will ask anyway. State. A mockup shows one state; a prototype shows what happens after the click, and the second state is where most of the disagreement about a design actually lives. Sequence. A prototype shows the order, including the transitions and the back behaviour, so "what does the user see while this is happening" gets answered on the spot. Real content. A prototype can be fed a name with 34 characters and a date in the wrong format, which is the only reliable way to find out that a layout has no idea what to do with real content — a name of 8 characters proves nothing. And edge behaviour. Empty, loading, error and too-much-data are states a mockup never shows and every reviewer asks about, and building them in the prototype makes the cost of forgetting them visible rather than shipping them.

Then the technique, which is to build the behaviour and not the design. No styling beyond enough to be legible; a border and some padding are enough. The point is that a prototype should cost about twenty minutes, and anything that takes longer has become a production page and stopped being a prototype. What makes it fast is that the behaviour is tiny: a click handler that swaps a state variable, a submit handler that writes output into a region marked as live, and one condition that changes the outcome. Everything else is unnecessary, and the discipline to leave it out is what keeps the artefact alive long enough to be tested on somebody.

Prototyping the states that get shipped wrong

There is a short list of states that are consistently absent from prototypes and consistently present in production, and building them is the highest-value use of an hour. The empty state. Not "no data" — the three empty states that matter are: never used, cleared by the user, and filtered to nothing, and each needs different copy and a different call to action. The loading state. Skeleton versus spinner versus optimistic, chosen deliberately per component, because a spinner on a two-second action and a skeleton on a page load are both defensible and the same choice in both places is not. The error state. What failed, what did not, whether retrying is safe, and what the user should do — the same four questions as anywhere else, and a prototype that shows an error forces the answer. And the partial state: some data loaded, some did not, which is the state that most often reaches production because nobody built it in the prototype.

One caution, because this is where prototype quality turns into production quality by accident. A prototype built as one HTML file with inline handlers is excellent for testing and is not a component — it has no props, no state contract and no separation between what it is and what it does. So the value a prototype creates has to be captured somewhere that survives the rewrite, and the cheapest thing that works is the state list: the states demonstrated, the transitions between them, and the copy chosen, kept as a short specification next to the artefact. Without it, what transfers is an impression.

/* Why prototype in the browser: it answers questions a mockup cannot. */
const QUESTIONS_ONLY_A_PROTOTYPE_ANSWERS = [
  { question: 'state', why: 'a mockup shows one state; the second state is where most of the disagreement about a design lives' },
  { question: 'sequence', why: 'a prototype shows the order, including transitions and back behaviour, so what does the user see while this happens is answered on the spot' },
  { question: 'real content', whyTest: 'a name with 34 characters and a date in the wrong format',
    why: 'it is the only reliable way to find out a layout has no idea what to do with real content - a name of 8 characters proves nothing' },
  { question: 'edge behaviour', why: 'empty, loading, error and too-much-data are states a mockup never shows and every reviewer asks about' },
];

/* Build the behaviour, not the design. */
const TECHNIQUE = {
  styling: 'enough to be legible - a border and some padding',
  budget: 'about twenty minutes',
  beyondBudget: 'it has become a production page and stopped being a prototype',
  theBehaviourIsTiny: ['a click handler that swaps a state variable',
                       'a submit handler that writes output into a region marked as live',
                       'one condition that changes the outcome'],
  everythingElse: 'unnecessary, and leaving it out is what keeps the artefact alive long enough to be tested on somebody',
};

/* The states consistently absent from prototypes and present in production. */
const MISSING_STATES = [
  { state: 'empty', notJust: 'no data', actually: ['never used', 'cleared by the user', 'filtered to nothing'],
    needs: 'different copy and a different call to action for each' },
  { state: 'loading', choose: ['skeleton', 'spinner', 'optimistic'],
    rule: 'per component, not globally - a spinner on a two-second action and a skeleton on a page load are both defensible' },
  { state: 'error', mustSay: ['what failed', 'what did not', 'whether retrying is safe', 'what the user should do'],
    why: 'a prototype that shows an error forces the answer' },
  { state: 'partial', instance: 'some data loaded, some did not',
    whyItSlipsThrough: 'nobody built it in the prototype' },
];

/* What transfers to production. */
const HANDOVER = {
  notThis: 'a single HTML file with inline handlers is not a component - no props, no state contract, no separation between what it is and what it does',
  capture: ['the states demonstrated', 'the transitions between them', 'the copy chosen'],
  where: 'a short specification next to the artefact',
  withoutIt: 'what transfers is an impression',
};

Twenty lines of plain HTML deliver a clickable, stateful prototype — button, live output, and checkbox gate — using the browser’s native capabilities.

27.5 The developer viewport: what devs see that design tools hide

The developer viewport shows the costs design tools hide: font byte weight, image bytes, reflow, scroll performance, and state machines. Inspect the real runtime with browser dev tools, measure network weight, and watch how a change in layout cascades through the page. Handoff improves when you deliver real states, structural accessibility, and performance-conscious assets. Deliver what developers actually consume rather than vibes.

Dev realityWhat changes in handoff
Font loading costs bytesself-host woff2 subsets; avoid 9 heavy weights
Images kill performancelazy-load, share sizes, use AVIF/WebP, no giant CLS shifts
Reflow is expensivedesign for baseline reflow before animation polish
States are code, not omensdeliver the full state machine (Ch.5.2), not "hover feel" vibes
Accessibility is structuralhand semantic HTML + focus + ARIA with the visual spec (Ch.7)

Which devtools panel answers which design question

The design questions that reach a developer are more specific than "make it look nice", and each has an owner in the browser. Computed styles answer "what colour and size is this actually" — including the values inherited from a token, which is how a designer verifies that a colour really came from a token rather than from somewhere else. The box model overlay answers "where is that space coming from", and it is the fastest way to see the padding-versus-margin confusion. Grid and flex overlays answer "why is that there", because they draw the tracks and the gaps that the design never mentions. The colour picker answers "what exactly is this colour", and it is also the fastest way to discover that two colours that looked identical on one screen are four percent apart. Rendering / paint flashing answers "why is this repainting", which is the performance question that a designer can ask meaningfully. Media and emulation answer "how does it look on a device I do not have", and the local device list is not enough — the CPU throttling setting is what reproduces the performance problem on a mid-range phone.

Then the measurements a designer should be able to read off a page without a tool, because a designer who cannot read them cannot specify. Line height and font size, and the resulting measure — the number of characters per line, which should be roughly 45 to 75 for body text, and which is the real reason a "wider text box" request is sometimes wrong. Contrast ratio, which the colour picker gives directly and which is the only way to know whether the grey-on-white pair is 4.5:1 or 3.1:1. Tap target sizes, which are visible in the box model overlay. And the rhythm: whether spacing is actually on a scale or is a pile of values that happen to be similar.

Reading a layout the way a designer reads a grid

There are four questions that resolve most "it looks off" reports without a meeting, and they are all answerable in the box model overlay or computed styles. Is the space on the scale? A 13 px gap next to a 12 px one is invisible to nobody and wrong to everybody, and it is the single most common reason a design reads as unpolished. Is the alignment real? Optical alignment is not geometric alignment — an icon beside a text label needs to be shifted by a pixel or two because the shapes have different visual weights, and the overlay tells you whether the boxes line up geometrically while the eye tells you they do not. Is the type scale consistent? Every size in the interface should be a step on one scale, and a size that exists only in one component is the beginning of an inconsistent system. And is the density right for the context? The same component legitimately needs different densities in a table, a card and a settings screen, and density is the first thing to check when a review says the design feels crowded or empty — the answer is usually that a table is carrying card spacing.

Accessibility and performance, which are design decisions before they are fixes

Both are routinely discovered as bugs and both are actually design decisions that were skipped earlier. On accessibility, four checks a designer can perform before a screen reaches a developer, all of them in the same panel. Tab order. Tab through the screen and press it again with the mouse — the sequence should match the visual order, and the first stop should be the first thing in the reading order, not the skip link buried at the top-left which is correct but annoying and which everybody nevertheless leaves there because it is correct. Focus visibility. Every interactive element must show focus. The most common failure in a polished design is a outline: none added to remove the default ring, and the removal is invisible to the person making it because focus is not visible when you are using a mouse. Names. Every control has an accessible name, and the check is simply the accessibility tree in devtools, where a control with no name shows up as an empty entry. And contrast of the states, not just the resting state: a disabled control at 2.8:1 is a design decision that will be reversed by an accessibility report.

On performance, four numbers a designer should know and what each means as a design decision rather than an engineering detail. Largest Contentful Paint is a design question — it is usually the hero image, and a designer chose its dimensions, its format and whether it is above the fold. Cumulative Layout Shift is almost always a design question too — an image without dimensions, a banner inserted above content, a font swapping, or a consent bar that pushes the page down after it renders. Interaction to Next Paint is where a design decision hides: a click handler that does real work, a dropdown with two thousand options, an animation that runs on the main thread. And Total Blocking Time measures how long the page is unresponsive, which is invisible until somebody taps during it and nothing happens. The useful framing is that all four are caused by decisions somebody made earlier — the asset, the placeholder, the component — so they are cheap to fix at design time and expensive afterwards.

/* Four accessibility checks a designer can do before it reaches a developer. */
const A11Y_PRECHECK = [
  { check: 'tab order',
    method: 'tab through, then press again with the mouse',
    expects: 'the sequence matches the visual order, and the first stop is the first thing in reading order',
    tension: 'the skip link is correct and annoying, and is left in place only because it is correct' },
  { check: 'focus visibility',
    expects: 'every interactive element shows focus',
    commonFailure: 'outline: none added to remove the default ring',
    whyInvisible: 'focus is not visible when you are using a mouse' },
  { check: 'names', how: 'the accessibility tree in devtools',
    symptom: 'a control with no name shows up as an empty entry' },
  { check: 'contrast of the states', not: 'the resting state',
    example: 'a disabled control at 2.8:1',
    outcome: 'a design decision reversed later by an accessibility report' },
];

/* Four performance numbers, each a design decision that was skipped. */
const PERF_AS_DESIGN = [
  { metric: 'Largest Contentful Paint', usually: 'the hero image',
    decidedByDesign: ['its dimensions', 'its format', 'whether it is above the fold'] },
  { metric: 'Cumulative Layout Shift', usually: ['an image without dimensions',
                                                 'a banner inserted above content',
                                                 'a font swapping',
                                                 'a consent bar that pushes the page down after it renders'] },
  { metric: 'Interaction to Next Paint', hides: ['a click handler that does real work',
                                                  'a dropdown with two thousand options',
                                                  'an animation running on the main thread'] },
  { metric: 'Total Blocking Time', measures: 'how long the page is unresponsive',
    whyItSlipsThrough: 'invisible until somebody taps during it and nothing happens' },
];
const FRAMING = 'all four are caused by decisions somebody made earlier - the asset, the placeholder, the component - so they are cheap at design time and expensive afterwards';

And one thing worth stating because it is the boundary of the whole role: a developer can tell you what the browser is doing and why, and can tell you which of two specified behaviours is cheaper, and can tell you that a spec will cost a week. They cannot tell you which behaviour is right. The questions that reach them should therefore arrive with the constraint attached — "this needs to work at 320 px and stay readable at 75 characters, and the brand forbids the alternative colour" — because a constraint is answerable and a preference is a negotiation.

/* Devtools panels mapped to the design questions that reach a developer. */
const PANELS = [
  { panel: 'computed styles', question: 'what colour and size is this actually',
    designValue: 'shows the inherited value, so you can verify a colour really came from a token' },
  { panel: 'box model overlay', question: 'where is that space coming from',
    designValue: 'the fastest way to see the padding-versus-margin confusion' },
  { panel: 'grid / flex overlays', question: 'why is that there',
    designValue: 'draws the tracks and gaps the design never mentions' },
  { panel: 'colour picker', question: 'what exactly is this colour',
    designValue: 'also the fastest way to discover two colours that looked identical are four percent apart' },
  { panel: 'rendering / paint flashing', question: 'why is this repainting',
    designValue: 'the performance question a designer can ask meaningfully' },
  { panel: 'device emulation', question: 'how does it look on a device I do not have',
    designValue: 'CPU throttling is what reproduces the mid-range phone problem, not the device list' },
];

/* Readable without a tool. */
const MEASURABLE = [
  { what: 'line height, font size, and the resulting measure',
    target: 'roughly 45 to 75 characters per line for body text',
    why: 'this is the real reason a wider text box request is sometimes wrong' },
  { what: 'contrast ratio', how: 'the colour picker gives it directly',
    why: 'the only way to know whether the grey-on-white pair is 4.5:1 or 3.1:1' },
  { what: 'tap target sizes', how: 'the box model overlay' },
  { what: 'the rhythm', question: 'is spacing actually on a scale, or a pile of similar values' },
];

/* Four questions that resolve most it-looks-off reports. */
const DIAGNOSIS = [
  { question: 'is the space on the scale',
    commonFailure: 'a 13px gap beside a 12px one',
    why: 'the single most common reason a design reads as unpolished' },
  { question: 'is the alignment real',
    note: 'optical is not geometric - an icon beside a text label needs shifting a pixel or two because the shapes have different visual weights',
    whatTheOverlayTellsYou: 'whether the boxes line up geometrically' },
  { question: 'is the type scale consistent',
    rule: 'a size that exists in only one component is the beginning of an inconsistent system' },
  { question: 'is the density right for the context',
    rule: 'a table, a card and a settings screen legitimately need different densities',
    usualAnswerToCrowded: 'a table is carrying card spacing' },
