/* The boundary of the role. */
const BOUNDARY = {
  developerCan: ['say what the browser is doing and why',
                 'say which of two specified behaviours is cheaper',
                 'say that a spec will cost a week'],
  developerCannot: 'say which behaviour is right',
  therefore: ['ask arrives with the constraint attached: it must work at 320px, stay readable at 75 characters, and the brand forbids the alternative colour',
               'a constraint is answerable; a preference is a negotiation'],
};

27.6 The design-engineering bridge role

The design-engineering bridge role, often called design engineer, ships code: prototypes in the real codebase, tokens wired to live styles, and motion in real keyframes. Even reading a component file or wiring a token to CSS buys back the arguments that normally get stuck in handoff. The role exists to close the gap between concept and production. It moves faster with less quality loss between design and delivery.

  • Design engineer = designer who ships code — prototypes in the product codebase, tokens wired to real styles, motion in real keyframes. The role closes the "design vs build" gap.
  • Even without that title: learn to read a component file, review a PR’s a11y story, and prototype in the browser weekly. Every hour of code fluency buys back handoff arguments.

Exercises 27

  1. Build one token-based card + button in plain HTML/CSS (no framework).
  2. Make a 2-state interactive prototype (add/remove item) using the browser’s native features.
  3. Redo your Ch.11 mobile layout with auto-fit/minmax and delete 2 breakpoints.

The role, and the three failures it exists to prevent

A design-engineering bridge role — a designer who can write production code, an engineer who owns design quality, or a dedicated role on a team large enough to have one — exists to prevent three specific failures, and it is worth being precise about them because each has a different remedy and only one of them is about skill. The specification is ambiguous and both sides guess. The designer means one thing by "roomy" and the engineer builds a different thing, and the mismatch is discovered late because nobody could tell what was intended. The design is internally inconsistent and nobody notices. Three components each use a sensible spacing value and no two match; the inconsistency is invisible in any single screen and obvious when the screens are side by side. Nobody owns the seams. The states, the empty screen, the error, the loading, the print view, the focus ring: these are nobody's feature, so they are nobody's work, and they ship as whatever the default happened to be.

The remedy for the first is shared vocabulary, not shared opinions, and the practical version is a component with documented states and measured values rather than a document describing them. The remedy for the second is a token layer, which is what makes inconsistency structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged — because a component that can only reference a semantic token cannot disagree with another component about what "gap between sections" means. The remedy for the third is a list, and it has to be written once: every state and every environment a component can be in, which is a short list and is almost never written down, and a component delivered without its states is a component that will be completed by whoever touches it next, under deadline, with nobody to ask.

How the role actually works week to week

The useful description is not a job title but a set of habits, and three of them do most of the work. Build the real thing early. A clickable prototype proves a concept; a component in the product proves the concept, the states and the constraints simultaneously, and it costs about twice as long, which is why it needs to happen while the design is still cheap to change. Make the design executable where it is ambiguous. If a spacing question or a state answer exists only in a conversation, it is lost; if it is a line of CSS or a component prop, it is reviewable by both sides and it cannot be re-litigated. And treat the component library as the design system's actual output. Screens are made once and are forgotten; components are made once and are used a hundred times, so the quality of the library is the quality of everything built on it, which means library review deserves more time than screen review even though it is less visible and less fun.

Arguments that are worth learning before they are needed

The bridge role spends a lot of its time mediating between two legitimate positions, and the useful skill is recognising the four that recur and knowing the resolution for each. "That specification is ambiguous." Both sides are right and it is not a complaint: a specification written in prose is genuinely ambiguous, and the resolution is to make it executable — a value in a token, a state in a component — because an executable specification cannot be misread. "Accessibility will slow this down." Usually true about effort and almost never true about the result, because accessible work done early is cheaper than accessible work done late; the exception worth conceding honestly is a custom component with no native equivalent, where the cost is real and the mitigation is to build it once, properly, as a library component rather than eleven times. "That design is not feasible." Sometimes true, and the right response is to ask which part — the cost, the capability, or the deadline — because the three have different answers and only the deadline is negotiable. And "we can do it later." This is the one to resist hardest, because the specific items deferred are the states, the empty screen, the error state and the responsive behaviour, and those four are the entire difference between a screen that works and a screen that works except in the situations people will actually be in.

Then how the role is measured, because a role with no measure gets redefined by whoever benefits from it. The honest measures are unglamorous: how many screens use the library rather than assembling their own; how many components have all their states built before first release rather than after a bug report; how many designs ship at every supported width without a per-device fix; and how many accessibility defects were caught before a release rather than in it. None of these is a design award and none should be — the role's output is that other people do not have to redo the work, which is invisible by construction and needs a number attached to it or it will be judged on the visible things instead.

What this looks like when it goes well

The end state is a codebase where a new screen is assembled rather than authored: a designer picks components and sets tokens, and the state list for each component already exists because it was built when the component was first made; an engineer reviews the composition rather than redrawing it; and the accessibility, the responsiveness and the states are properties of the library rather than of any screen. The design system's quality becomes the ceiling on what any screen can be, which is the argument for investing in the library before there is pressure to — under pressure, the library is always the thing that gets deferred, and it is also the thing whose absence costs the most per screen thereafter. And the second-order benefit is the one that makes the role worth having: when the design decisions live in tokens and components rather than in screenshots, they survive the people who made them, which is the only durability test that matters for anything a team builds.

/* Four recurring arguments, and the resolution for each. */
const ARGUMENTS = [
  { claim: 'that specification is ambiguous', bothSidesRight: true, isAComplaint: false,
    because: 'a specification written in prose is genuinely ambiguous',
    resolution: 'make it executable - a value in a token, a state in a component - so it cannot be misread' },
  { claim: 'accessibility will slow this down', usually: 'true about effort, almost never about the result',
    why: 'accessible work done early is cheaper than accessible work done late',
    exceptionWorthConceding: 'a custom component with no native equivalent, where the cost is real',
    mitigation: 'build it once, properly, as a library component rather than eleven times' },
  { claim: 'that design is not feasible', response: 'ask which part - the cost, the capability, or the deadline',
    note: 'only the deadline is negotiable' },
  { claim: 'we can do it later', resistHardest: true,
    whatGetsDeferred: ['the states', 'the empty screen', 'the error state', 'the responsive behaviour'],
    why: 'those four are the entire difference between a screen that works and a screen that works except in the situations people will actually be in' },
];

/* How the role is measured. Unglamorous, and necessary. */
const MEASURES = [
  'how many screens use the library rather than assembling their own',
  'how many components have all their states built before first release rather than after a bug report',
  'how many designs ship at every supported width without a per-device fix',
  'how many accessibility defects were caught before a release rather than in it',
];
const MEASURES_NOTE = 'none of these is a design award, and none should be - the output is that other people do not have to redo the work, which is invisible by construction and needs a number or it will be judged on the visible things instead';

/* What it looks like when it works. */
const GOOD_STATE = {
  newScreen: 'assembled rather than authored',
  how: 'a designer picks components and sets tokens, and the state list for each component already exists',
  engineersRole: 'review the composition rather than redraw it',
  accessibilityResponsivenessStates: 'properties of the library rather than of any screen',
  consequence: 'the design systems quality becomes the ceiling on what any screen can be',
  investmentRule: 'invest in the library before there is pressure to - under pressure the library is always deferred, and its absence costs the most per screen thereafter',
  secondOrderBenefit: 'when decisions live in tokens and components rather than in screenshots, they survive the people who made them - the only durability test that matters',
};

Then what the role needs from each side, because it fails when this is asymmetric. From design: components built from the same primitives rather than assembled fresh per screen, states designed rather than filled in later, content written with real lengths, and accessibility decided rather than tested. From engineering: the design system treated as production code with review, deprecations actually done, and a component's contract — its props, its states, its behaviour — treated as an API, because a component whose contract changes without notice is the same defect as a function signature that changes between releases. And from both: a shared vocabulary short enough to be learned, which means tokens and component names rather than a glossary, because a glossary that is not enforced becomes a document nobody reads.

/* The role exists to prevent three specific failures. */
const FAILURES_AND_REMEDIES = [
  { failure: 'the specification is ambiguous and both sides guess',
    instance: 'the designer means one thing by roomy and the engineer builds another',
    discoveredLate: 'because nobody could tell what was intended',
    remedy: 'shared vocabulary, not shared opinions: a component with documented states and measured values',
    notThis: 'a document describing them' },
  { failure: 'the design is internally inconsistent and nobody notices',
    instance: 'three components each use a sensible spacing value and no two match',
    whyInvisible: 'no single screen shows it; it is obvious only when screens sit side by side',
    remedy: 'a token layer, which makes inconsistency structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged' },
  { failure: 'nobody owns the seams',
    things: ['the states', 'the empty screen', 'the error', 'the loading', 'the print view', 'the focus ring'],
    consequence: 'they ship as whatever the default happened to be',
    remedy: 'a list, written once - every state and environment a component can be in',
    note: 'it is a short list, it is almost never written down, and a component delivered without its states is completed by whoever touches it next, under deadline, with nobody to ask' },
];

/* Habits, not a title. Three do most of the work. */
const HABITS = [
  { habit: 'build the real thing early',
    proves: ['the concept', 'the states', 'the constraints'],
    cost: 'about twice a clickable prototype',
    whyEarly: 'while the design is still cheap to change' },
  { habit: 'make the design executable where it is ambiguous',
    why: 'a spacing question existing only in a conversation is lost; a line of CSS or a component prop is reviewable by both sides and cannot be re-litigated' },
  { habit: 'treat the component library as the systems actual output',
    argument: 'screens are made once and forgotten; components are made once and used a hundred times',
    consequence: 'library review deserves more time than screen review, though it is less visible and less fun' },
];

/* What the role needs from each side. It fails when asymmetric. */
const NEEDS = [
  { from: 'design', items: ['components built from the same primitives rather than assembled fresh per screen',
                           'states designed rather than filled in later',
                           'content written with real lengths',
                           'accessibility decided rather than tested'] },
  { from: 'engineering', items: ['the design system treated as production code, with review',
                                 'deprecations actually done',
                                 'a components contract - props, states, behaviour - treated as an API',
