28 · Motion, Voice & New Interfaces

Motion, voice, and spatial interfaces express the same UX principles through different media. Motion explains state and tells a story, voice carries on a conversation, and spatial designs live in depth, occlusion, and scale. All the states, feedback, and trust you already know apply here; only the delivery changes. Learn each medium’s physics and constraints and the principles carry over.

28.1 Motion principles beyond "add animation"28.2 The motion toolkit: Smart Animate, Lottie, CSS keyframes28.3 Voice & conversational interfaces28.4 Spatial / AR-VR / XR UX28.5 Wearables, automotive & ambient computing28.6 Accessibility in the new interfaces

The final frontier: interfaces that move, speak, and live in space. These disciplines reuse everything you know — states, feedback, trust — through different media, and they’re exactly what "senior" portfolios branch into.

28.1 Motion principles beyond "add animation"

Motion done well explains first and feels good second: it communicates state, hierarchy, and spatial relationships rather than decorating them. Shared elements move between screens to preserve context, elements settle into place with spring-based easing tuned to the weight of what moves, and the easing sets the tone of the whole product. Respect the reduced-motion preference as a non-negotiable accessibility requirement. The goal of motion is meaning, not spectacle.

// Motion must explain, then feel good:
//  - spatial continuity: an element that navigates should MOVE from
//    where it was (shared elements), not fade from nowhere
//  - anticipation & overshoot: brief lead-in before the move; a
//    spring settle (overshoot) communicates "done" naturally
//  - timing & easing = your tone (Ch.5.3): a calm product eases slow,
//    a play-product snaps and bounces
//  - reduce-motion is a requirement, not an option (WCAG 2.3.3)
// Prototype motion in order: state logic → timing → easing → flourish.
// A flourish before the states work is a GIF, not a prototype.

What motion is for, and the three jobs

Motion earns its place when it does one of three jobs, and every other use of it is decoration that costs performance, distracts from content and becomes a motion preference within a year. Continuity — showing that one thing became another thing: a card expanding into a detail view, a row becoming a page, a value moving to a summary. The user learns the relationship once and reuses the expectation, which is why a shared-element transition teaches the product's model faster than a label does. Feedback — confirming that an input registered and that the system has responded, which is the difference between an interface that feels alive and one that feels like a form. And Attention — moving the eye to something that changed or became available, in a way that is not a flash. The distinction that separates the three from decoration is direction: motion that explains has a purpose and an end, motion that decorates has neither.

Then timing, which is the part that is usually guessed. The principle is that movement should feel like the physical world the user lives in, and the two standard durations follow from it. Small elements, small movements — a checkbox, a toggle, a tooltip — complete in roughly 100 to 200 ms, because a longer duration on something small feels sluggish rather than smooth. Large elements, large movements — a full-screen transition, a drawer, a page change — take 300 to 500 ms, because the distance is longer and a short duration makes the movement look like a jump. The most common error is using one duration everywhere, which produces an interface where the small things feel sluggish and the large things feel like teleports. Easing matters as much as duration and is more often neglected: motion should ease in when accelerating and ease out when arriving, and an animation that arrives and then bounces reads as playful only if that is intended — a spring with overshoot is a statement about tone, not a default.

Reduced motion, and why it is not a smaller motion problem

prefers-reduced-motion is not a request for less animation; it is a request that animation not be the carrier of meaning. A vestibular disorder is triggered by large-area movement, parallax, zoom and spinning, and the correct response is to replace those with something else rather than to shorten them. So: transitions between views become an instant change or a cross-fade, auto-playing video and carousels do not move at all, parallax and scroll-linked transforms are disabled, and anything where the motion is the explanation is replaced with a static equivalent that carries the same relationship. The distinction is important enough to state twice — a reduced-motion implementation that halves every duration leaves a cross-fade where the content jumps and a zoom where the content spins, and satisfies the letter of the requirement while producing the very symptom it exists to prevent.

/* Three jobs. Anything else is decoration. */
const MOTION_JOBS = [
  { job: 'continuity', shows: 'one thing became another thing',
    examples: ['a card expanding into a detail view', 'a row becoming a page',
               'a value moving to a summary'],
    why: 'the user learns the relationship once and reuses the expectation, so a transition teaches the product model faster than a label' },
  { job: 'feedback', shows: 'an input registered and the system responded',
    why: 'the difference between an interface that feels alive and one that feels like a form' },
  { job: 'attention', shows: 'the eye should go to something that changed or became available',
    not: 'a flash' },
];
const TEST_FOR_DECORATION = 'motion that explains has a purpose and an end; motion that decorates has neither';

/* Timing: one duration everywhere is the most common error. */
const TIMING = [
  { size: 'small', instances: ['a checkbox', 'a toggle', 'a tooltip'], ms: '100 to 200',
    tooLongFeels: 'sluggish rather than smooth' },
  { size: 'large', instances: ['a full-screen transition', 'a drawer', 'a page change'], ms: '300 to 500',
    tooShortFeels: 'like a teleport' },
  { mistake: 'one duration everywhere',
    result: 'small things feel sluggish and large things feel like teleports' },
];
const EASING = {
  rule: 'ease in when accelerating, ease out when arriving',
  springWithOvershoot: 'a statement about tone, not a default',
  note: 'easing is more often neglected than duration',
};

/* Reduced motion: replace, do not shorten. */
const REDUCED_MOTION = {
  isNot: 'a request for less animation',
  is: 'a request that animation not be the carrier of meaning',
  triggeredBy: ['large-area movement', 'parallax', 'zoom', 'spinning'],
  replace: [
    { what: 'transitions between views', with: 'an instant change or a cross-fade' },
    { what: 'auto-playing video and carousels', with: 'no movement at all' },
    { what: 'parallax and scroll-linked transforms', with: 'disabled' },
    { what: 'any motion that IS the explanation', with: 'a static equivalent carrying the same relationship' },
  ],
  stateTwice: 'a reduced-motion implementation that halves every duration leaves a cross-fade where the content jumps and a zoom where the content spins, satisfying the letter while producing the symptom it exists to prevent',
};

Motion should explain first: shared-element continuity, spring overshoot for completion, and timing that matches tone, with reduced-motion support required by WCAG.

28.2 The motion toolkit: Smart Animate, Lottie, CSS keyframes

The motion toolkit is about matching the tool to the job. Figma Smart Animate previews transitions quickly without code, Lottie ships rich vector animation into production across platforms, CSS keyframes handle product UI motion directly in the browser, and high-fidelity video sells the vision. Each tool trades off fidelity, control, and file weight differently. Choose the smallest tool that delivers the effect.

ToolBest forHonest limit
Figma Smart Animatedesign-doc transitions quicklyprototype-only; can’t ship
Lottie (JSON animation)shipping rich icon/illustration motionneeds a Motion engineer to author right
CSS/Web Animations APIUI motion in product (100x cheaper than GIFs)complex illustrations aren’t its job
Video (After Effects → previews)communicating a visionnot interactive; easy to over-promise

Choosing a tool by what it cannot do

Tool choice in this field is usually made by feature list, which is the wrong axis, because the features overlap heavily and the differences that matter are limitations. Four questions separate the categories, and they are worth asking before anything is opened. Is it interactive? A high-fidelity static tool produces something a stakeholder will mistake for a decision, which is worse than a rough prototype because the conversation shifts from whether the idea is right to whether the pixels are right. Does it model state? Most visual tools model screens; the ones that model transitions and states are the ones worth learning, because the states are where the disagreement lives. Does it survive real content? A tool with fake text will not show that a label needs 34 characters, and the single most common late surprise in any product is a layout that was only ever tested with eight-character names. Is the output inspectable? Anything a tool produces that cannot be handed to engineering as a specification has cost the team a rebuild, and the cost is not the rebuild — it is that the rebuild happens from scratch rather than from the decisions.

Then the honest cost of each category, because the table above sells them and the cost is what decides. Static visual tools are the fastest to learn and the most likely to be mistaken for a deliverable; their discipline is to always present them as questions rather than answers. Prototyping tools pay for themselves when a design has real state and cost real time when it has not — the tool cannot create the states, it can only make existing ones easy to express, so a prototype built in an hour with no state is a static mockup with extra steps. Code in the browser has the highest ceiling and the highest cost, and it is worth it precisely when the design is a component rather than a screen, because the second time that component is used it is already built. Real-time 3D is the only category that answers spatial questions no other category can, and it is worth its cost only for a physical product, a space, or a vehicle interface.

Handing work over, and the three things that get lost

Whatever tool produced the work, three things are lost in the handover and each has a cheap mechanism to prevent it. The reasoning. The tool holds the decision, not the reason: why this control and not that one, why this spacing, why this empty state copy. A screenshot cannot carry it and an export cannot either; the mechanism is a short written rationale attached to the spec, and the test of whether it is sufficient is whether an engineer could make a different decision and be defended against it. The states. A tool demo shows the happy path because that is what is easiest to present, so the handover artefact is a state list rather than the set of screens that exist in the file. The content. Real names, real lengths, the longest plausible value, the empty field, the zero, the enormous number — because a design that has only ever been seen with four-word lorem values has not been designed, it has been sketched, and the difference appears on the first day of development.

And the thing that is worth writing down for the team: which part of the work a tool is allowed to be authoritative about. The honest arrangement is that a tool is authoritative about appearance and about nothing else — it is a good way to agree on how something looks and a bad way to decide what it should do, what happens when it fails, or how it responds to a person on a bad day. Everything in the previous two paragraphs belongs in text for exactly that reason, and a team that has written that down stops having the conversation.

/* Three things lost in handover, and the mechanism for each. */
const LOST = [
  { thing: 'the reasoning', heldInTheTool: 'why this control and not that one, why this spacing, why this empty copy',
    cannotBeCarriedBy: ['a screenshot', 'an export'],
    mechanism: 'a short written rationale attached to the spec',
    sufficiencyTest: 'could an engineer make a different decision and be defended against it' },
  { thing: 'the states', heldInTheTool: 'the happy path, because that is easiest to present',
    mechanism: 'a state list rather than the set of screens in the file' },
  { thing: 'the content',
    values: ['real names', 'real lengths', 'the longest plausible value', 'the empty field', 'zero', 'an enormous number'],
    consequenceOfOnlyLetingFourWords: 'the design has been sketched, not designed, and the difference appears on day one of development' },
];

/* What a tool may be authoritative about. */
const AUTHORITY = {
  authoritativeAbout: 'appearance',
  notAuthoritativeAbout: ['what it should do', 'what happens when it fails', 'how it responds to a person on a bad day'],
  whyText: 'every one of those belongs in writing, and a team that has written it down stops having the conversation',
};

Then what a designer should be able to produce themselves, which is a short list and the answer to "will I be replaced by a tool". Not the tool: the specification of the states, the content rules, the accessibility behaviour and the responsive behaviour, in a form engineering can build from. The tools compress the production of pixels and none of them compress the decisions — the state list still has to be enumerated, the copy still has to be chosen for the empty case, the contrast still has to be checked. A tool that generates a screen from a description has not removed the work, it has moved it earlier and made it less visible, which is why the designer who can define states and behaviours is more valuable than ever rather than less.

/* Feature lists overlap; the differences that matter are limitations. */
const CHOOSING = [
  { question: 'is it interactive',
    consequenceIfNo: 'a stakeholder mistakes it for a decision, and the conversation shifts from whether the idea is right to whether the pixels are right' },
  { question: 'does it model state', why: 'most visual tools model screens; states are where the disagreement lives' },
  { question: 'does it survive real content',
    evidence: 'it will not show that a label needs 34 characters',
    note: 'the most common late surprise in any product is a layout only ever tested with eight-character names' },
  { question: 'is the output inspectable',
    consequenceIfNo: 'the team pays a rebuild, and the real cost is that the rebuild happens from scratch rather than from the decisions' },
];

/* The honest cost of each category. */
const COSTS = [
  { tool: 'static visual', learns: 'fastest', risk: 'mistaken for a deliverable',
    discipline: 'always present it as a question rather than an answer' },
  { tool: 'prototyping', paysForItself: 'when a design has real state',
    costsRealTime: 'when it has not',
    why: 'the tool cannot create the states, only make existing ones easy to express',
    therefore: 'an hour-long prototype with no state is a static mockup with extra steps' },
  { tool: 'code in the browser', ceiling: 'highest', cost: 'highest',
    worthItWhen: 'the design is a component rather than a screen, because the second use is already built' },
  { tool: 'real-time 3D', uniquelyAnswers: 'spatial questions no other category can',
    worthItOnlyFor: ['a physical product', 'a space', 'a vehicle interface'] },
];

/* What a designer still produces. */
const NOT_REPLACED = {
  notReplaced: ['the enumeration of states', 'the copy chosen for the empty case',
                'the contrast check', 'the content rules'],
  toolEffect: 'a tool that generates a screen from a description has not removed the work - it has moved it earlier and made it less visible',
  conclusion: 'the designer who can define states and behaviours is more valuable than ever, not less',
};

28.3 Voice & conversational interfaces

Voice interfaces are scriptwriting combined with state machines: you write what is said and specify how the conversation moves between states. Confirm critical actions out loud, repair failures gracefully with helpful fallback prompts, and always offer a visible on-screen fallback so no one is stranded in a dead-end exchange. Manage conversation load and provide multimodal feedback. Design for failure states, because speech recognition will fail.

// Conversation design = scriptwriting + state machines:
//  - turns: greet → ask → repair → resolve → exit (with fallback
//    when comprehension fails: "did you mean the burner or oven?")
//  - VUI has no visual state: confirm out loud ("Adding 2 dinners"),
//    time-out gracefully, and ALWAYS offer visible fallback on-screen
//  - typos/apologies: never dead-end "I didn't quite catch that"
//    (3x; then transfer politely)
//  - multi-modal: voice + screen together outperform either alone
// Test VUIs with wizard-of-oz (Ch.24.5) before building any engine.

The state machine, because voice has no undo

Voice interfaces fail in a way screens do not, and the reason is that there is no visible state and no obvious way back. A screen shows its entire state at once; a voice interface exposes one question at a time and the user cannot see the shape of what they are inside. So the design work is the state machine, and seven states cover nearly everything. Greet and set expectations — what this can do, and what happens when it does not understand. Ask, one question at a time, phrased so a wrong answer is still useful. Repair, which is the state everybody underdesigns: the first failed recognition is not an error, it is the beginning of a conversation, and the correct response is to re-ask differently rather than to repeat the same question. Resolve, meaning perform the action and report it in the domain's words. Confirm aloud for anything consequential — and the confirmation must include what is about to happen, not "are you sure". Exit, so every flow has a way out that is not "cancel the whole session". And fallback, the answer to "I did not catch that" that is not silence and not an error code.

Then the design constraints that follow from the medium and are worth knowing before designing anything. Turns are expensive. Every exchange costs the user a decision to speak, and a flow that takes twelve turns will be abandoned where the same task takes three clicks in a form. Recognition is probabilistic. Any name, number, address or free-text field is a recognition risk that scales with how unusual the value is, so the design must assume a percentage of inputs will be wrong and provide a way to hear what was heard. Nobody can see the screen. A voice interface used on a drive, while cooking, or with a screen out of reach must work entirely by ear, which means no "as shown on screen", no "the third option", no "below". And the display is for the other person. A voice interface in a call centre or a booking is usually used by an operator while a customer waits, so the visual half is designed for the person who is not speaking — a transcript for them to check, with the confirm button on screen for the agent.

Testing without an engine

Wizard-of-oz testing — a person plays the system, another plays the user — is the method that makes voice design possible before any machine learning exists, and it is more informative than it looks because it isolates the two things that are usually confused: whether the conversation works and whether the recognition works. Running it with a human in the machine deliberately leaves recognition perfect, so every failure the tester hits is a failure of the script, the wording, the state machine or the error handling — that is, a failure a designer can fix. Swapping in real recognition afterwards tests a different thing entirely, and it is the wrong order: it mixes the model in with the design and the result is a conclusion about the model. The practical procedure is short: write the flow as a script with the states named, run ten turns with one person and no other context, and count the points where the tester paused, rephrased, or said "what?" — each of those is a defect in the design, and the count is a number rather than an impression.

/* Seven states cover nearly every voice flow. */
const VOICE_STATES = [
  { state: 'greet', must: ['what this can do', 'what happens when it does not understand'] },
  { state: 'ask', rule: 'one question at a time, phrased so a wrong answer is still useful' },
  { state: 'repair', underdesigned: true,
    note: 'the first failed recognition is not an error, it is the beginning of a conversation',
    correctResponse: 're-ask differently, rather than repeat the same question' },
  { state: 'resolve', must: 'perform the action and report it in the domains words' },
  { state: 'confirm aloud', when: 'anything consequential',
    mustInclude: 'what is about to happen',
    notThis: 'are you sure' },
  { state: 'exit', requirement: 'a way out that is not cancelling the whole session' },
  { state: 'fallback', answers: 'I did not catch that',
    notThis: ['silence', 'an error code'] },
];

/* Constraints that follow from the medium. */
const MEDIUM_CONSTRAINTS = [
  { constraint: 'turns are expensive',
    why: 'every exchange costs a decision to speak',
    consequence: 'a twelve-turn flow is abandoned where the same task takes three clicks in a form' },
  { constraint: 'recognition is probabilistic',
    worst: ['names', 'numbers', 'addresses', 'free text'],
    rule: 'assume a percentage of inputs will be wrong, and provide a way to hear what was heard' },
  { constraint: 'nobody can see the screen',
    contexts: ['on a drive', 'while cooking', 'with the screen out of reach'],
    therefore: ['no as shown on screen', 'no the third option', 'no below'] },
  { constraint: 'the display is for the other person',
    where: ['a call centre', 'a booking'],
    visualHalf: 'a transcript for them to check, with the confirm button on screen for the agent' },
];

/* Wizard of oz, and why the order matters. */
const WIZARD_OF_OZ = {
  setup: 'a person plays the system, another plays the user',
  enables: 'testing before any machine learning exists',
  isolates: ['whether the conversation works', 'whether the recognition works'],
  deliberatelyPerfect: 'recognition, so every failure is a failure of the script, the wording, the state machine or the error handling - that is, a failure a designer can fix',
  wrongOrder: 'swapping in real recognition first mixes the model in with the design, and the conclusion is about the model',
  procedure: ['write the flow as a script with the states named',
               'run ten turns with one person and no other context',
               'count the points where the tester paused, rephrased, or said what'],
  meaning: 'each is a defect in the design, and the count is a number rather than an impression',
};

Voice flows read like a script plus a state machine: greet, ask, repair, resolve, exit, confirm aloud, and always keep a visible on-screen fallback.

28.4 Spatial / AR-VR / XR UX

Spatial AR, VR, and XR interfaces use depth, occlusion, scale, and proximity to communicate hierarchy in ways a flat screen cannot. Comfort rules the medium: keep camera control with the user, avoid forced movement that induces sickness, and make every selection deliberate and undoable. Even gaze-only selection needs a deliberate confirmation step. Respect human comfort and intent rather than spectacle.

  • Depth is a language: occlusion (objects behind things), parallax, and scale communicate hierarchy — but motion sickness is real; keep camera control with the user, avoid forced locomotion.
  • Comfort rules: keep text at readable distance/angles, stable world anchoring, no sudden bright flashes (epilepsy-spot absolute minimum, Ch.7).
  • Hand/eye input: gaze = cursor, hand = pointer; Fitts applies in 3D (bigger + closer targets) and "select" needs a deliberate, undoable action.

The three constraints that change the design process

Spatial computing is not a screen with two more axes; it is a different set of physics, and three constraints account for almost every design decision that differs from a flat interface. Comfort. Near content causes discomfort because conflicting depth cues make the visual system work to reconcile them; far content is comfortable but requires more effort to reach and more visual attention to hold. The working rule is a comfortable distance band for reading, with anything dense placed to the side rather than in front, and the honest answer that most teams reach late is that a two-dimensional panel is better than a badly placed three-dimensional object. Fatigue. Depth has no natural resting position, so an interface in space imposes a continuous postural cost on the user, and the design consequence is that interaction must be reachable without the user holding their arms up, because an interface that requires a raised hand is an interface with a session length limit. Input precision. Gaze is coarse, hands are imprecise, and controllers are precise but present; so the rule is that coarse inputs select and precise inputs commit — a gaze-to-ray highlight, then a pinch to confirm — and that select should always be a deliberate, undoable action rather than a look.

Then the design questions that only exist in this medium, which are worth listing because they have no equivalent and are easy to assume away. Where is the user's attention anchored, and what happens when they look away from it — does the content follow, persist, or vanish, and what is the correct behaviour differs per content and is never "the default". What is the persistence model: spatial content exists in a room, so it must have a lifecycle — placed, saved, re-found, and eventually removed — and "removed" is the one everybody forgets, which leaves rooms full of yesterday's objects. How are two people in the same space given a shared reference, since "over there" is not a coordinate and the second person has a different view of it. What does occlusion mean when a real object is behind a virtual one and the user moves: real furniture should occlude, and a design that ignores this produces a headset full of objects that appear to float through a table.

Automotive, which has the opposite constraint

Automotive specifics worth designing for

Beyond the glance budget, an automotive interface has four properties that are not present in any other category and each one has a design consequence. It is used while moving. Every interaction that requires sustained attention is unavailable by definition, so the interface is designed for a ceiling of two glances and the honest conclusion is that any flow longer than that belongs on a device that is not being operated from a driver's seat. It has a physical environment that changes. Daylight, night, tunnel, tunnel-exit, and the moment where the driver's eyes adapt and the screen brightness is wrong — which means brightness and contrast have to be automatic and legible in both, and a fixed theme chosen for the office is a defect. It is a safety system with a user interface. Anything that can be operated at speed is a control that can be mis-operated at speed, so the interface has to make the destructive actions hard to reach and hard to confirm without a confirmation that itself takes a glance to read. And it has a long life. A vehicle is fifteen years old and the interface is expected to still work, which means the design cannot assume the hardware of the day, and it means a voice assistant's capability will improve underneath an interface designed for the assistant that existed when it shipped.

Then the design questions unique to this context, which are worth enumerating because they get answered by circumstance rather than by choice. What is the handover between a driving task and a parked task — the mechanism by which a task started moving becomes a task completed stationary, and if there is no explicit handover the person arrives at a parking lot with a half-configured destination. What is the attentional contract — what does the vehicle say, unprompted, and what has it learned not to say because it interrupted once and was ignored. What is the legible state of something the driver cannot see: a route in progress, a phone connected, a message waiting, an automation running. And what happens when two systems want attention — the vehicle and the phone, both with notifications, competing for the same pair of eyes, which is the exact situation multi-modal design has made more common and not less.

/* Four properties unique to automotive, each with a design consequence. */
const AUTOMOTIVE_PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'it is used while moving',
    means: 'every interaction requiring sustained attention is unavailable by definition',
    ceiling: 'two glances',
    conclusion: 'a flow longer than that belongs on a device not operated from a drivers seat' },
  { p: 'it has a physical environment that changes',
    states: ['daylight', 'night', 'tunnel', 'tunnel exit'],
    trap: 'the moment the eyes adapt and the screen brightness is wrong',
    therefore: 'brightness and contrast are automatic and legible in both; a fixed theme chosen for the office is a defect' },
  { p: 'it is a safety system with a user interface',
    means: 'anything operable at speed is a control that can be mis-operated at speed',
    therefore: ['destructive actions are hard to reach',
                 'destructive actions are hard to confirm without a confirmation that itself takes a glance to read'] },
  { p: 'it has a long life',
    reality: 'a vehicle is fifteen years old and its interface is expected to still work',
    constraints: ['cannot assume the hardware of the day',
                  'a voice assistants capability improves underneath an interface designed for the assistant that existed at ship time'] },
];

/* Answered by circumstance unless they are asked. */
const AUTOMOTIVE_QUESTIONS = [
  { q: 'the handover between a driving task and a parked task',
    means: 'a task started moving becomes a task completed stationary',
    ifMissing: 'the person arrives at a parking lot with a half-configured destination' },
  { q: 'the attentional contract',
    means: 'what does the vehicle say unprompted',
    learned: 'what it has stopped saying because it interrupted once and was ignored' },
  { q: 'legible state of something the driver cannot see',
    items: ['a route in progress', 'a phone connected', 'a message waiting', 'an automation running'] },
  { q: 'two systems want attention',
    instance: 'the vehicle and the phone, both notifying, competing for the same pair of eyes',
    note: 'the exact situation multi-modal design has made more common and not less' },
];

A vehicle interface is the one place where the interface must be understood in glances measured in fractions of a second, by a person whose attention is elsewhere and who may be the least qualified person ever to use it. Three requirements, all structural. Task completion must be short enough to interrupt: any task that cannot be completed in a glance pair belongs on the phone or nowhere, and the honest conclusion most automotive designers reach is that the car should handle the routine and the phone should handle the rest. The hierarchy must be legible in one glance: the number of simultaneously visible controls is a hard budget, and it is set by glance time, not by how much the screen can fit — which is why a single large control beats three small ones in every measured case. Distraction management outranks functionality: a design that competes with the road is worse than a design that does less, and this means the interface has to know when it may be visible at all, which is a system behaviour rather than a screen behaviour.

/* Three constraints account for almost every difference from a flat interface. */
const SPATIAL_CONSTRAINTS = [
  { constraint: 'comfort',
    cause: 'conflicting depth cues make the visual system reconcile near content',
    workingRule: ['a comfortable distance band for reading', 'anything dense placed to the side rather than in front'],
    honestAnswerMostTeamsReachLate: 'a two-dimensional panel beats a badly placed three-dimensional object' },
  { constraint: 'fatigue', cause: 'depth has no natural resting position, so there is a continuous postural cost',
    designConsequence: 'interaction must be reachable without holding arms up',
    because: 'an interface requiring a raised hand has a session length limit' },
  { constraint: 'input precision', reality: 'gaze is coarse, hands are imprecise, controllers are precise but present',
    rule: 'coarse inputs select, precise inputs commit - a gaze-to-ray highlight, then a pinch',
    select: 'always a deliberate, undoable action, never a look' },
];

/* Questions with no flat-interface equivalent. */
const SPATIAL_ONLY_QUESTIONS = [
  { q: 'where is the attention anchored, and what happens when they look away',
    note: 'does content follow, persist, or vanish - and the right answer differs per content and is never the default' },
  { q: 'what is the persistence model',
    detail: 'spatial content exists in a room, so it has a lifecycle: placed, saved, re-found, removed',
    forgottenStep: 'removed, which leaves rooms full of yesterdays objects' },
  { q: 'how do two people in one space share a reference',
    why: 'over there is not a coordinate, and the second person has a different view of it' },
  { q: 'what does occlusion mean', test: 'move while a real object is behind a virtual one',
    rule: 'real furniture should occlude',
    failure: 'a design that ignores this produces a headset full of objects appearing to float through a table' },
];

/* Automotive: the opposite constraint. */
const AUTOMOTIVE = {
  situation: 'understood in glances measured in fractions of a second, by somebody whose attention is elsewhere and who may be the least qualified person ever to use it',
  requirements: [
    { r: 'task completion must be short enough to interrupt',
      consequence: 'a task that cannot be completed in a glance pair belongs on the phone or nowhere',
      conclusion: 'the car handles the routine; the phone handles the rest' },
    { r: 'the hierarchy must be legible in one glance',
      detail: 'the number of simultaneously visible controls is a budget set by glance time, not by what the screen can fit',
      evidence: 'a single large control beats three small ones in every measured case' },
    { r: 'distraction management outranks functionality',
      reasoning: 'a design that competes with the road is worse than a design that does less',
      therefore: 'the interface must know when it may be visible at all - a system behaviour, not a screen behaviour' },
  ],
};

28.5 Wearables, automotive & ambient computing

Every medium reshapes UX around its own constraints: watches need glanceable, one-handed reading, car interfaces demand eyes-off-road interaction, ambient devices work without screens or reading, and public kiosks serve strangers with no training. Constraints become the design language rather than enemies. Design for the context, the user’s attention, and the public space the device lives in. Clarity under constraint beats feature richness.

MediumConstraint that reshapes UX
Wearable (watch/ring)glance-able: 3–8 s interactions, worst case for tiny text
Automotive dashboardseyes-off-road: glance minimums, voice/touch priority, no color-only alert (red/green rule, Ch.1.3)
Ambient / IoTno screen at all: feedback happens in the room (lights, sound, haptics)
Kiosks & POSpublic, no accounts, recover after timeouts, chair-bound accessibility

The four contexts that break ordinary assumptions

Kiosks, point of sale, embedded displays and public information screens all look like small versions of a website and none of them behave like one. There is no account and no session. A kiosk is handed to a stranger, so the interface has to be usable by somebody who knows nothing, has read nothing, and leaves after ninety seconds — which means the task has to be completable in very few steps and the interface has to assume the previous user left it in a state. There is a queue behind you. This changes everything about feedback: anything that takes a second has to be explained, because a person who does not know whether it worked will press it again, and pressing it again is the mechanism behind most of the double-payment complaints in this category. Every slow operation needs a visible acknowledgement immediately and a progress state afterwards. Somebody else uses it after you. Public hardware requires a reset that is real — a timeout that clears state, clears the keyboard focus, and clears anything personal — and the implementation detail that matters is that the timeout must be tested with the screen still lit, because a device that goes dark usually stops responding to touch and looks broken to the next person.

Then the accessibility requirements for public hardware, which are stricter than for a personal device in one specific way. Height and reach. A kiosk's usable area may start above a seated user's head, so the whole flow has to fit within the reach of somebody in a wheelchair — which is a design constraint that has to be measured against the real mounting, not against a drawing. Audio is often the only channel. A public display is often silent by policy, so nothing can depend on sound, and anything that would normally be announced has to have a visual equivalent designed for reading from two metres away. Target size and contrast have to survive conditions — bright sunlight, a scratched screen, a user wearing gloves — so the values used on a personal device are not sufficient and the reason is the environment rather than the person. And there is no keyboard in many of these contexts, so the whole interface has to be operable by touch alone, which removes every hover-dependent affordance and every shortcut-only action.

What a public device has that a personal one does not

The properties of shared hardware are worth naming because each one has a design consequence that is easy to miss. The audience is unknown and cannot be trained. The design has to be self-explanatory on first contact, which rules out almost every convention that depends on a learned model. The device is not yours. Anything the user did has to be cleaned up by somebody else's action or a timeout, and "sign out" has to be real because the next user is a stranger. The failure is public. An error screen on a kiosk is shown to the person behind you, so error handling has a social dimension that personal products do not have — a screen that says something is very wrong in front of a queue is a design failure beyond the technical one. And the device is a liability. A public screen that shows content from a previous session is a privacy incident, and the rule is that state does not persist across a session, including cached content, including anything typed into a form, including anything visible in a picture-in-picture the browser never cleared.

The ten-minute test for a public device

Before a public device goes live, five checks that take ten minutes and that almost nobody runs, each of which corresponds to a class of report that arrives afterwards. Walk away mid-task and come back. A stranger who starts a transaction and abandons it must not leave the device in a state the next person can complete — the browser's session and the form's contents both have to be gone, not merely hidden. Stand further away than feels right. The intended viewing distance is usually assumed rather than measured, and the content that matters is often unreadable at the distance the device actually is at, which is a mounting decision as much as a type-size decision. Use it with one hand and no precision. Everything that needs a specific touch becomes unusable, and on a device in a queue that is not an edge case. Interrupt it. Take the power, lose the network mid-transaction, and let the screen go dark and time out mid-flow — the recovery has to be a design, and the most likely recovery state is a screen that says something vague while the queue waits. And check what a passer-by can read. A public device is read by people who are not going to use it, so anything sensitive on the screen — a previous session's data, a staff member's note, a debug overlay — is a disclosure the design has to prevent by never putting it there.

Then the two constraints that get a deployed device wrong and are decided before deployment: the timeout value, which is not a technical default but a decision about how long a stranger will wait, and it interacts with the queue in front of it — a timeout longer than the queue's patience produces abandoned mid-payments, and a shorter one produces a person who has to start again while people watch. And what happens when the device is offline, which is the second most common public-device incident after power loss and the one most often left showing a stale screen, because the offline case is usually designed as an error state in the application and the device has no way to reach the application at all.

/* Five checks, ten minutes, before a public device goes live. */
const FIVE_CHECKS = [
  { check: 'walk away mid-task and come back',
    must: 'a stranger who starts and abandons a transaction cannot leave the device completable by the next person',
    includes: ['the browsers session', 'the forms contents'],
    note: 'gone, not merely hidden' },
  { check: 'stand further away than feels right',
    why: 'the intended viewing distance is assumed rather than measured',
    decisionType: 'as much a mounting decision as a type-size decision' },
  { check: 'use it with one hand and no precision',
    consequence: 'everything needing a specific touch becomes unusable',
    whyNotEdgeCase: 'a device in a queue' },
  { check: 'interrupt it', do: ['take the power', 'lose the network mid-transaction',
                                 'let it go dark and time out mid-flow'],
    must: 'the recovery is a design',
    likelyStateWithout: 'a vague message while the queue waits' },
  { check: 'check what a passer-by can read',
    why: 'a public device is read by people who are not going to use it',
    rule: 'never put sensitive content on the screen - previous session data, a staff note, a debug overlay' },
];

/* Decided before deployment, wrong after. */
const DEPLOYMENT_DECISIONS = [
  { d: 'the timeout value', notA: 'technical default', isA: 'a decision about how long a stranger will wait',
    interactsWith: 'the queue in front of it',
    tooLong: 'abandoned mid-payments', tooShort: 'a person starting again while people watch' },
  { d: 'the offline case',
    ranking: 'the second most common public-device incident after power loss',
    usualCause: 'the offline case was designed as an error state in the application, and the device has no way to reach the application at all',
    symptom: 'a stale screen' },
];

And the maintenance reality, which is a design input and not an engineering one. A device in a public place is touched by strangers, cleaned by staff, left on for months, and looked at by nobody who built it. So the design has to be recoverable without a technician: a way back from a bad state that is not a reboot, because reboots are what technicians do and technicians are not there. And it has to be legible to somebody who is not the designer — an operator who has to change one line of copy at midnight needs an interface for that which is obviously safe, or they will not change it at all and the wrong text will stay up for six months. Both of these are design decisions, both are almost never made, and both determine whether a deployed device is still correct after ninety days.

/* Public hardware: not small versions of a website. */
const CONTEXT_BREAKS = [
  { context: 'kiosk and POS', assumptionBroken: 'there is an account and a session',
    reality: 'handed to a stranger who knows nothing, has read nothing, and leaves after ninety seconds',
    requires: ['completable in very few steps', 'an assumption that the previous user left it in a state'] },
  { context: 'a queue behind you', changes: 'everything about feedback',
    why: 'a person who does not know whether it worked will press it again, and pressing it again is the mechanism behind most double-payment complaints',
    therefore: 'every slow operation needs a visible acknowledgement immediately and a progress state afterwards' },
  { context: 'somebody else uses it after you',
    requires: ['a real reset', 'a timeout that clears state, clears keyboard focus, and clears anything personal'],
    implementationTrap: 'test the timeout with the screen still lit, because a dark device usually stops responding to touch and looks broken to the next person' },
];

/* Stricter than personal in one specific way. */
const PUBLIC_A11Y = [
  { requirement: 'height and reach', why: 'the usable area may start above a seated users head',
    measure: 'against the real mounting, not a drawing' },
  { requirement: 'audio is often the only channel available to the operator',
    but: 'the display is often silent by policy',
    therefore: 'nothing may depend on sound, and anything normally announced needs a visual equivalent readable from two metres away' },
  { requirement: 'target size and contrast must survive conditions',
    conditions: ['bright sunlight', 'a scratched screen', 'a user wearing gloves'],
    note: 'values used on a personal device are not sufficient, because the reason is the environment rather than the person' },
  { requirement: 'there is no keyboard',
    consequence: 'the whole interface must be operable by touch alone',
    removes: ['hover-dependent affordances', 'shortcut-only actions'] },
];

/* Properties shared hardware has. */
const SHARED_PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'the audience is unknown and cannot be trained',
    design: 'self-explanatory on first contact', rulesOut: 'almost every convention depending on a learned model' },
  { p: 'the device is not yours',
    requires: 'state cleaned by somebody elses action or a timeout, with a real sign-out because the next user is a stranger' },
  { p: 'the failure is public',
    extraDimension: 'an error screen is shown to the person behind you',
    why: 'a screen saying something is very wrong in front of a queue is a design failure beyond the technical one' },
  { p: 'the device is a liability',
    rule: 'state does not persist across a session',
    includes: ['cached content', 'anything typed into a form', 'anything in a picture-in-picture the browser never cleared'] },
];

/* Maintenance is a design input. */
const MAINTENANCE = {
  reality: 'touched by strangers, cleaned by staff, left on for months, looked at by nobody who built it',
  decisions: [
    { d: 'recoverable without a technician',
      requires: 'a way back from a bad state that is not a reboot',
      why: 'reboots are what technicians do, and technicians are not there' },
    { d: 'legible to somebody who is not the designer',
      instance: 'an operator changing one line of copy at midnight',
      requires: 'an interface for it that is obviously safe',
      ifMissing: 'they will not change it at all, and the wrong text will stay up for six months' },
  ],
  consequence: 'both determine whether a deployed device is still correct after ninety days',
};

28.6 Accessibility in the new interfaces

Accessibility in new interfaces re-asks the same four principles, perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust, for each new medium. Never depend on a single modality such as screen, voice, or gesture, because any modality can fail or be unavailable to some users. Offer a non-temporal path as a fallback for anything time-based. Build accessibility into the medium itself rather than bolting it on later.

  • Voice UIs need visible text alternatives; spatial UIs need alternative input (hand shake, gaze dwell, controller).
  • Never depend on a single modality (voice-only, motion-only): every prompt must have a non-temporal path.
  • The questions stay the same: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust — just re-asked in a new medium.

What accessibility practice must change for a spatial interface

Most of the existing practice transfers unchanged, and it is worth saying which parts, because the instinct is to treat a new medium as requiring new accessibility work and that produces work that adds nothing. Semantic structure, focus order, name and role, and contrast all apply, because they are properties of the application rather than of the medium. What changes is a specific set of things, and they are the ones that existing practice has nothing to say about. Where focus is shown. A reticle or highlight is the focus indicator, it is visible against unpredictable real-world backgrounds, and it must be legible against whatever is actually behind it — which is why focus styling in this medium needs a contrast strategy rather than a single colour. Whether gaze can substitute for a pointing device. It can, for selection, and it should not, for anything requiring accuracy, and the design has to know which is which. Held gestures as an accessibility hazard. A pinch held for two seconds excludes anybody with limited hand mobility and anybody with tremor, so every held gesture needs an alternative and the alternative has to be as easy, not as an option at the bottom of a list. And motion sensitivity is not a preference in this medium: content that moves through the user's field of view when they move their head is a direct trigger, and it must be disabled by default rather than by setting.

Then the accessibility requirements specific to automotive and voice, because they are different in kind rather than in detail. For automotive, a screen a driver should not be reading is an accessibility failure for the person with impaired vision, and the design has to make the "do not read this while driving" state a real interface with a real alternative rather than a modal. Voice interfaces must be operable entirely by ear, which rules out every visual-only affordance including error identification — a voice flow that identifies an error visually is broken for exactly the people who most need the repair path. And speech input has to be usable by people who cannot speak clearly, which means every spoken prompt needs a touch or switch equivalent, because a dysarthric user and a user in a noisy room are the same design problem.

The audit, and what it cannot see

Designing the accessible states from the start

The general principle carries across media and it is worth stating once in its own terms: the accessible version of a component is a set of states, and a component delivered without them has an accessibility defect that is invisible until somebody meets it. The set, in this order of how often it is missed. Focus, visible, keyboard-reachable, and in a logical order that follows the reading order rather than the DOM order. Disabled, which must be announced as disabled rather than merely being grey, must still be discoverable, and must not become a control the keyboard skips entirely without warning. Error, tied to its field programmatically, described in text, and stated before submission rather than appearing on a lost focus — and the copy has to say what to do, not what went wrong. Loading, announced to assistive technology and not only drawn, because a visual spinner is invisible to somebody listening. Empty, which is a state a screen reader user encounters as silence unless it is labelled. And expanded and collapsed, on anything that reveals, so the control's current state is available rather than inferred from an icon.

Then the two accessibility mistakes that survive a professional audit and are worth naming because they are about content rather than markup. A label that describes the control instead of its purpose. "Search" on a button that submits is fine; "Go" is not, because "go" tells a screen reader user nothing about where they will end up, and the disambiguation has to happen in the accessible name rather than in nearby text that may not be read in sequence. And an error message that is technically associated but practically unusable — announced, but written for somebody who can see the field it belongs to. "Invalid entry" next to a date field is announced as "invalid entry" and understood by nobody; "Enter a date as day, month, year" is understood by the person using the screen reader and is the only version of the message that works for both audiences, which is why writing it for the audible reader is usually the better writing.

/* The accessible version of a component is a set of states. */
const ACCESSIBLE_STATES = [
  { s: 'focus', must: ['visible', 'keyboard reachable', 'in logical order following reading order, not DOM order'] },
  { s: 'disabled', must: ['announced as disabled, not merely grey',
                          'still discoverable',
                          'not skipped by the keyboard without warning'] },
  { s: 'error', must: ['tied to its field programmatically',
                        'described in text',
                        'stated before submission rather than on a lost focus'],
    copyRule: 'say what to do, not what went wrong' },
  { s: 'loading', must: 'be announced to assistive technology as well as drawn',
    why: 'a visual spinner is invisible to somebody listening' },
  { s: 'empty', must: 'be labelled',
    why: 'otherwise a screen reader user encounters silence' },
  { s: 'expanded / collapsed', appliesTo: 'anything that reveals',
    must: 'the controls current state is available, not inferred from an icon' },
];

/* Two mistakes that survive a professional audit. */
const SURVIVING_MISTAKES = [
  { mistake: 'a label that describes the control instead of its purpose',
    fine: 'search on a button that submits', notFine: 'go',
    why: 'go tells a screen reader user nothing about where they will end up',
    fix: 'disambiguation belongs in the accessible name, not in nearby text that may not be read in sequence' },
  { mistake: 'an error message that is technically associated but practically unusable',
    instance: 'invalid entry next to a date field',
    asHeard: 'invalid entry', understoodBy: 'nobody',
    better: 'enter a date as day, month, year',
    rule: 'writing it for the audible reader is usually the better writing, because it has to serve both audiences' },
];

An automated accessibility audit checks a fraction of the problems and the fraction it checks is dominated by things that are easy to automate — contrast values, missing names, missing alt attributes, heading order. Everything that actually makes an interface unusable is judgement: whether the error message says what to do, whether the focus order matches the visual order, whether a person can complete the task without a mouse, whether the timeout is long enough for a screen reader user who has to hear the field label again. So the audit is a floor, and the useful process pairs it with three things it cannot replace: a keyboard-only pass, a screen reader pass on the core flows, and a session with somebody who uses the product differently every day. The third is the one teams skip and the one that finds the most, because the first two check conformance and only the third checks whether the product is actually usable.

/* What transfers unchanged. */
const TRANSFERS = ['semantic structure', 'focus order', 'name and role', 'contrast',
  'because they are properties of the application rather than of the medium'];

/* What changes, and what existing practice says nothing about. */
const CHANGES = [
  { what: 'where focus is shown',
    now: 'a reticle or highlight', must: 'be legible against whatever is actually behind it, because real backgrounds are unpredictable',
    therefore: 'focus styling needs a contrast strategy rather than a single colour' },
  { what: 'whether gaze substitutes for a pointing device',
    can: 'selection', shouldNot: 'anything requiring accuracy',
    requiresTheDesignToKnow: 'which is which' },
  { what: 'held gestures',
    hazard: 'a pinch held for two seconds excludes anybody with limited hand mobility and anybody with tremor',
    requirement: ['an alternative for every held gesture', 'the alternative is as easy, not an option at the bottom of a list'] },
  { what: 'motion sensitivity',
    note: 'not a preference in this medium - content moving through the field of view when the head moves is a direct trigger',
    requirement: 'disabled by default rather than by setting' },
];

/* Different in kind, not in detail. */
const OTHER_MEDIA_A11Y = [
  { medium: 'automotive', failure: 'a screen a driver should not be reading',
    whoItFails: 'a person with impaired vision',
    requirement: 'a real interface with a real alternative rather than a modal' },
  { medium: 'voice', rule: 'operable entirely by ear',
    broken: 'any visual-only affordance, including error identification',
    why: 'a flow that identifies an error visually is broken for exactly the people who most need the repair path' },
  { medium: 'speech input', must: 'be usable by people who cannot speak clearly',
    requirement: 'every spoken prompt needs a touch or switch equivalent',
    sameProblem: 'a dysarthric user and a user in a noisy room' },
];

/* The audit is a floor. */
const AUTOMATED_COVERS = ['contrast values', 'missing names', 'missing alt attributes', 'heading order'],
  AUTOMATED_MISSES = ['whether the error message says what to do',
                      'whether focus order matches the visual order',
                      'whether a person can complete the task without a mouse',
                      'whether a timeout is long enough for a screen reader user who must hear the field label again'];
const PAIRS_WITH = ['a keyboard-only pass', 'a screen reader pass on the core flows',
                    'a session with somebody who uses the product differently every day'],
  WHY_THIRD: 'the first two check conformance; only the third checks whether the product is usable, and it is the one teams skip';

Exercises 28

  1. Prototype one spatial-continuity transition (a selected item "moving" into a detail view) and argue its timing.
  2. Script a 10-turn voice flow with repair and fallback; run it wizard-of-oz on one person.
  3. Pick XR-comfort or automotive: list the 3 constraints that most change your design process.

Appendix · Glossaries, Cheat Sheets & Roadmap

The appendix is the quick reference that holds the whole course within reach: a survival glossary of the vocabulary you will actually use, a one-sheet cheat sheet of what to reach for at each moment, pointers to every exercise, and a phase-by-phase roadmap of your career arc. It turns the course from something you read into something you consult. Skim it whenever a term slips.

A.1 Survival glossaryA.2 The one-sheet cheat sheetA.3 Answers & pointers to every exerciseA.4 UI/UX roadmap by phase (your career arc)

A.1 Survival glossary

The survival glossary gives quick one-line definitions of the vocabulary actually used in day-to-day design work: affordances, fidelity, design tokens, journey maps, mental models, and more. It is meant to be skimmed whenever a term slips, so you can rejoin a conversation without a full refresher. Definitions are kept plain and oriented to how each term is used in practice. Consider it a decoder ring for design meetings.

TermMeaning in one line
Affordance / signifierwhat you can do vs the clue that shows it (a clickable-looking button)
Fidelityhow finished a prototype looks (low→high)
Heuristic evaluationexpert review against usability heuristics
Information architecturehow content is organized and labeled so it’s findable
Mental modelthe user’s expectation of how things work from past experience
Design tokena named design value (color, spacing) reused everywhere
Card sorting / tree testingusers group / users find within an unbuilt structure
Journey mappersona’s steps + emotions over time for a scenario
Dark patterninterface engineered to trick the user
PERCLOS-free clause… just kidding. You made it this far — you know the vocabulary.

A.2 The one-sheet cheat sheet

The one-sheet cheat sheet compresses the course into a single reference you can print, pin, and consult while working. It lists what to reach for at each moment, from starting a problem through making a claim, such as which methods, tests, and heuristics apply first. Its job is recall under pressure and consistency across projects. When stuck, run the sequence: frame, research, test, measure, explain.

MomentReach for
Starting any problemDouble diamond + "how might we" + research before pixels
Reviewing my screenNielsen’s 10 → squint test → accessibility scan → state table
Feels off but why?Hierarchy (size/contrast/space), consistency, whitespace test
Writing copyaction-first buttons, what/why/next errors, plain language
Deciding optionshypothesis → prototype → test → evidence; choices, not presentations
Making a claim"here’s the user, here’s the video, here’s the metric"

A.3 Answers & pointers to every exercise

The answers and pointers to every exercise are deliberately light on packaged answers, because each exercise passes if you followed its chapter process. When you get stuck, it points you back to the section the exercise names rather than giving the output away. This preserves the learning and keeps grading simple: process beats output. Use it to self-check progress without spoiling the practice.

No packaged answers — that would rob the re-applying skill. Instead the invariant: every exercise is passable if you followed the chapter’s process. If you got stuck, re-read the section named in the exercise — the skill lives there, not in the answer key.

A.4 UI/UX roadmap by phase (your career arc)

The UI/UX roadmap maps your career arc phase by phase, from foundations to senior, telling you what to study, which chapters to read, and the milestone that proves you are ready for the next step. Each phase builds on evidence, shipped work, and demonstrated judgment rather than raw years. It gives you a way to plan forward and to verify you are ready before moving on.

PhaseChaptersMilestone you should reach
1 · Foundations (weeks 1-3)0–2, 6, 9can critique a screen with reasoning, and interview one user
2 · Craft (weeks 3-6)1, 4, 8, 10, 11ship a token-based prototype, responsive, in Figma/HTML
3 · Process (weeks 6-9)3, 13, 14, 15run a full double-diamond small project end-to-end
4 · Specialization (weeks 9-12)5, 7, 12, 16, 17deep deliverable: states, a11y, mobile, tested forms
5 · Senior (ongoing)18–21measure an A/B, run critique, defend ethically, present to stakeholders
6 · Advanced electives (ongoing)22–28DesignOps, UX strategy, service design, domain specialists, AI/data, frontend fluency, motion/voice/XR — pick one and go deep

How to read the phases, and why the week ranges are fiction

Read the table as a dependency order, not a schedule. The week ranges assume full-time study with a job or school running in the background, and they assume a person who already reads documentation comfortably and has seen some code; both assumptions are optimistic and the second one is usually wrong for somebody arriving here from a non-technical field. The honest reading is that each phase takes as long as it takes to produce the evidence, and the evidence is the only thing that advances you. A person who can critique a screen with reasoning in two weeks has skipped something that will cost them later; a person who takes six weeks has done the work. The failure mode this table is designed to prevent is the opposite one — treating the week ranges as targets, hitting them, and moving on without having built anything, which produces somebody with twelve phases of knowledge and no work to show for it.

Three things distinguish a phase that has actually been completed from one that has been read. There is an artefact. Not a document describing what you would build: a file, a repository, a running URL, a recording of somebody using it. Somebody else has used it and you watched. This is the part that is skipped and it is the part that makes the difference, because the gap between what you intended and what happened is only observable in front of a person. And you were surprised by something. A phase in which nothing surprised you was probably done with existing intuition rather than by testing, and intuition that was never tested is the thing the phase exists to replace.

Phase by phase, with the evidence that closes it

Each phase below lists what to study, what to build, and the specific check that says you are ready — plus the mistake that phase is most often failed on, which is generally not the one people expect.

Phase 1 · Foundations. Study visual hierarchy, colour, typography, spacing, and the anatomy of an interface; read chapters 0 to 2, 6 and 9. Build a critique of six real screens, written to the point where a designer could disagree with you — a critique that says "the hierarchy is weak" is not a critique, because it cannot be wrong. Interview one person about a task they do regularly and watch them do it. The readiness check: you can name three specific things you would change about a screen and justify each against an observed problem rather than a preference. The mistake here is criticising from taste. Before the foundation work, a critique is mostly a statement about what the critic finds attractive, and it is nearly impossible to tell the difference from inside.

Phase 2 · Craft. Study spacing scales, type scales, colour systems, states, and responsive behaviour; read chapters 1, 4, 8, 10 and 11. Build a token-based prototype: a design system slice with real tokens, a component with all its states, and it must work at 320 px and at 1440 px. The readiness check: somebody else can change a value in one place and the whole interface updates, and every state of every control exists. The mistake here is shipping the happy path — the missing empty state is discovered by the first person who filters a list to nothing, which is usually a customer, not a colleague.

Phase 3 · Process. Study discovery, framing, requirements, research and validation; read chapters 3, 13, 14 and 15. Run one small project end to end: talk to people, define the problem, design, test, ship, measure. The readiness check: you can show the reasoning chain from an observed problem to a shipped decision, including the decisions you reversed. The mistake is designing first — the entire discipline is that the design is downstream of evidence, and a person who has never reversed a decision has not yet been tested by one.

Phase 4 · Specialization. Pick a direction — complex states, accessibility, mobile, forms and data entry — and go deep; read chapters 5, 7, 12, 16 and 17. Build one deliverable to a professional standard in that direction, reviewed by somebody who works in it. The readiness check: the deliverable survives review by a practitioner, which means it has the unglamorous parts — the error copy, the focus states, the data limits. The mistake is staying general. Generalists are fine up to phase 3; after that the market pays for depth in one thing, and a person who is a competent generalist with no specialism competes against specialists on the one axis where they are weakest.

Phase 5 · Senior. Study measurement, experimentation, critique leadership, and ethics; read chapters 18 to 21. Run an A/B test end to end, including reading its results and acting on them whether or not they are significant. Facilitate a critique. Present a design decision to a stakeholder who does not want it, and hold the position with evidence rather than conviction. The readiness check: you can defend a decision you believe is wrong, using the person's stated objective rather than yours. The mistake is doing measurement as reporting — a dashboard nobody acts on is a way of looking rigorous without being useful, and it is the single most common failure at this level.

Phase 6 · Advanced electives. Pick exactly one of chapters 22 to 28 and go deep: service design, domain UX, enterprise, AI and data, frontend fluency, or motion/voice/XR. The readiness check: you can teach the thing to somebody else, which is the only reliable test of depth. The mistake is completing all seven shallowly, because a lead who has read all seven and can do none of them has replaced a specialist with a generalist who is now nobody's first call.

/* A phase is completed when three things are true, not when the weeks run out. */
const PHASE_COMPLETE = {
  artefact: 'a file, a repository, a running URL, a recording of somebody using it - not a document describing what you would build',
  observed: 'somebody else used it and you watched',
  surprised: 'you were surprised by something',
  whySurprisedMatters: 'a phase where nothing surprised you was done with existing intuition rather than by testing',
};

/* The table is a dependency order, not a schedule. */
const READING_THE_TABLE = {
  is: 'a dependency order',
  isNot: 'a schedule',
  assumes: ['full-time study with a job or school running', 'a reader comfortable with documentation and some code'],
  reality: 'the second assumption is usually wrong for somebody arriving from a non-technical field',
  honestReading: 'each phase takes as long as it takes to produce the evidence, and the evidence is the only thing that advances you',
  failureMode: 'treating the week ranges as targets, hitting them, and moving on without having built anything',
  consequence: 'twelve phases of knowledge and no work to show for it',
};

/* What each phase is failed on. */
const PHASE_MISTAKE = [
  { phase: 1, mistake: 'criticising from taste',
    before: 'a critique is mostly a statement about what the critic finds attractive',
    tells: 'it is nearly impossible to tell the difference from inside' },
  { phase: 2, mistake: 'shipping the happy path',
    discovery: 'the missing empty state is found by the first person who filters a list to nothing',
    who: 'usually a customer, not a colleague' },
  { phase: 3, mistake: 'designing first',
    why: 'the whole discipline is that design is downstream of evidence',
    evidence: 'a person who has never reversed a decision has not been tested by one' },
  { phase: 4, mistake: 'staying general',
    note: 'generalists are fine to phase 3; after that the market pays for depth',
    consequence: 'a competent generalist with no specialism competes on the axis where they are weakest' },
  { phase: 5, mistake: 'doing measurement as reporting',
    instance: 'a dashboard nobody acts on',
    why: 'it is a way of looking rigorous without being useful - the most common failure at this level' },
  { phase: 6, mistake: 'completing all seven electives shallowly',
    instance: 'a lead who has read all seven and can do none',
    consequence: 'a specialist has been replaced by a generalist who is now nobody first call' },

What to do when the plan does not fit

Three situations are common and each needs a different response. You have no time. Then do one phase at a time with a month each rather than five phases in five weeks; the phases are dependencies, so a partial phase is usually wasted except the reading, and the reading is the cheap part anyway. You already have experience in one area. Then skip to the first phase whose milestone you genuinely cannot evidence, and check yourself honestly — most people over-estimate their own phase 1 and under-estimate their phase 5, and the mistake in both directions is the same: moving on without the evidence. You are stuck at a phase. Then the useful question is which of the three completion conditions you cannot satisfy: no artefact means scope, no observation means you have not tested, no surprise means you have not tested. Two of the three point at the same remedy, which is to put something in front of somebody and watch, and that is nearly always the answer.

The portfolio evidence each phase produces

The artefact from each phase is worth little on its own, and what makes it worth something is what the portfolio shows about the reasoning. So for each phase, the thing to capture is not the file but the case study around it, and the six questions below are the ones a reviewer asks and the six things to have ready. Written in this order — problem, evidence, options considered, what was rejected and why, the result, what you would do differently — a case study is short to produce and hard to fake, which is the point. A portfolio of screens proves that somebody made screens; a portfolio of case studies with rejected options proves that somebody made decisions, and the second is the thing being hired for.

Then the evidence standard for the claim on each row, because "I did a test" is not evidence of anything. A usability test is evidenced by a plan (tasks, what was measured, what would have counted as a failure), a recording, the counts, and at least one change that resulted — a study with no resulting change is a study that either found nothing or found something and was not acted on, and both need to be stated. An experiment is evidenced by a hypothesis written before it ran, the effect size with an interval, and a decision made in light of it including the decision to ship when it did not win. An accessibility pass is evidenced by the checklist, the defects found, and the fixes. A business case is evidenced by the metric it moved and over what period. Anything presented without its measure reads as opinion regardless of how good the pixels are, and the measure is often one sentence.

/* A case study, in the order that is short to produce and hard to fake. */
const CASE_STUDY_ORDER = [
  'problem - the observed problem, not the requested feature',
  'evidence - what you watched, read or measured, and how many',
  'options considered - including the ones you did not build',
  'what was rejected and why',
  'the result',
  'what you would do differently',
];
const WHY_THIS_ORDER = 'a portfolio of screens proves somebody made screens; a portfolio of case studies with rejected options proves somebody made decisions, and the second is what is hired for';

/* What counts as evidence for each claim. */
const EVIDENCE_STANDARD = [
  { claim: 'I did a usability test', not: 'a plan, a recording, the counts, and at least one resulting change',
    ifNoneChanged: 'either nothing was found, or something was found and not acted on - say which' },
  { claim: 'I ran an experiment', not: 'a hypothesis written before it ran, the effect size with an interval, and a decision made in light of it',
    include: 'the decision to ship when it did not win' },
  { claim: 'I did an accessibility pass', not: 'the checklist, the defects found, and the fixes' },
  { claim: 'I made the business case', not: 'the metric it moved, and over what period' },
];
const EVIDENCE_WARNING = 'presented without its measure, a case study reads as opinion regardless of how good the pixels are, and the measure is often one sentence';

/* Phase -> artefact, for the portfolio index. */
const PORTFOLIO_INDEX = [
  { phase: 1, artefact: 'six written screen critiques, each disagreeable enough to be argued with',
    plus: 'one recorded observation of somebody doing a task' },
  { phase: 2, artefact: 'a token-based prototype with every state built, working 320px to 1440px',
    proves: 'one value changed in one place updates the interface' },
  { phase: 3, artefact: 'one end-to-end small project, from observed problem to shipped decision',
    proves: 'a reasoning chain, including a decision that was reversed' },
  { phase: 4, artefact: 'one depth deliverable reviewed by a practitioner in that specialism',
    shows: 'the unglamorous parts - error copy, focus states, data limits' },
  { phase: 5, artefact: 'one experiment read and acted on regardless of outcome, one facilitated critique, one decision defended to a resistant stakeholder',
    proves: 'you can defend a decision you believe is wrong using their objective rather than yours' },
  { phase: 6, artefact: 'one elective taught to somebody else',
    test: 'the only reliable test of depth' },
];

Finish-line philosophy. The course gives you 20% of what a designer will ever use — the craft, the tests, and the honesty. The rest is built by doing the exercises again on different products and shipping. Close this file and go watch someone use the thing you made. That’s the real graduation.
